Examination of the fluid dynamics in each of the respective areas shows how filtration can be minimized through specific designs of the core bit and the inner tube pilot shoe. The low invasion coring system combines application of this new equipment with proper coring parameters and a low spurt loss coring fluid. The system was field tested very successfully in the Stevens sandstone in the Elk Hills field (California). Filtrate tracer and fluid saturation results show no significant filtrate invasion or fluid flushing beyond 0.5 inch into the 4-inch diameter core, and indicate the invasion depth is not related to formation rock permeability. The system is a valuable tool for providing quality core samples suitable for accurate laboratory analyses.

title: Core Preservation - an Alternative Approach
caption: FIGURE 2 SEM PHOTOMICROGRAPHS - CLAY FABRIC PRESERVATION
figure_reason: SEM images contrasting intact smectite fabric in CPC-preserved core with collapsed fabric in unpreserved air-dried sample.
tldr: Describes a glass Core Preservation Container that stores whole core immersed in compatible liquid under nitrogen, with field trials and screening showing preserved clay fabric and Swi stability.
summary: Conventional wrap-and-seal core preservation allows oxygen ingress, fluid loss and wettability or clay-fabric alteration. The author developed the Core Preservation Container (CPC), a sealed glass vessel holding whole core (up to 11 in x 5.25 in) immersed in deoxygenated brine or oil under a 15-20 psig nitrogen blanket, and gives guidelines for immersion liquid choice. Field trials led to design changes (foam-lined crate, improved cradle, safe-glass sleeve) to prevent glass fracture in transit. SEM showed smectite honeycomb fabric intact after 60 days in a CPC but collapsed in an unpreserved chip. Amott indices on two sandstone sets gave limited, inconclusive wettability differences, while Statoil data showed Swi changes of +1 to +2% for CPC plugs and -1 to -3% for laminate versus -37 to +19% for unprotected or strippable-plastic plugs after cleaning.
abstract: The preservation of consolidated core samples for petrophysical and petrological analysis in an effective and efficient manner is of particular importance for the production of accurate and representative reservoir data. To provide an alternative to the more conventional method of "wrap and seal", the Core Preservation Container (CPC) has been developed. The new method rapidly isolates selected whole core samples in an environment which minimizes physical and chemical alteration of the mineral grains and pore fluids, by the prevention of oxidation, evaporation and drying. The design of the CPC draws upon the recommendations made in the literature as to the effectiveness of preserving core under anaerobic conditions. This is achieved by immersing the core sample in a compatible liquid, contained within a sealable glass vessel. Initial screening in the laboratory suggests the technique will preserve key core parameters such as the insitu clay fabric and wettability during transportation and storage. Field trials have been used to establish a suitable methodology and to test whether the technique is practical and safe at the wellsite. Modifications have been made to address the problems encountered, for example fracturing of the glass body while in transit from the wellsite to the laboratory.

title: Laboratory Induced Damage - a Review of the Problem
caption: FIGURE 4 Rate versus pressure differential
figure_reason: Rate versus pressure differential plot distinguishing Darcy flow, turbulence and fines movement damage.
tldr: Reviews how core handling, cleaning, drying and high-rate flow tests induce laboratory damage, and recommends mineralogical screening, compatible brines and critical velocity tests to avoid it.
summary: The paper reviews laboratory practices that alter core samples and yield data unrepresentative of the reservoir. It covers plug drilling fluids, Soxhlet cleaning with toluene/methanol, and hot-oven drying at 105 C, which can collapse illite and make clays brittle. For flow tests it discusses incompatible brines, clay swelling, mica alteration and fines migration, and the traditional 6 cm3/min end-point rate, which far exceeds field velocities (about 166 ft/day in a 1.5" 15% porosity plug). High rates can cause non-Darcy flow, fines movement and excessive downstream net confining stress. The authors recommend XRD, infrared spectroscopy and SEM screening, synthetic brines matched to formation brine, and critical velocity tests to set maximum flow rates.
abstract: Laboratory data indicating possible formation damage can too often be a result of laboratory practices and be misinterpreted as a reservoir problem. All core handling, cleaning, drying, preparation and analysis procedures can, if incorrectly performed, be a source of laboratory induced damage, especially on core from formations with delicate mineralogy. Fluid flow tests, in particular, are potentially damaging. For many years the industry standard for liquid permeability and unsteady-state relative permeability testing has required an end-point flow rate of $6 \text{ cm}^3 \cdot \text{min}^{-1}$ . When this is scaled to field conditions it greatly exceeds flow velocities usually encountered, typically $166 \text{ ft.day}^{-1}$ through a 1.5" sample with 15% porosity. These excessive laboratory flow rates can cause movement of fines, or non-Darcy flow which provides data of limited value. Flow pressures required to achieve a flow rate of $6 \text{ cm}^3 \cdot \text{min}^{-1}$ can be very high, requiring, in turn, even higher confining pressures which may cause stress damage to the core sample. Analysis of flow pressure variation during a constant flow rate test can indicate if permeability damage has occurred. Laboratory techniques exist to avoid problems. Detailed sample screening prior to any other analysis is invaluable, to identify the sample mineralogy and mineral morphology. Flow parameters are established by determining critical velocity, the velocity above which fines become mobile, or Darcy flow is exceeded. With critical velocity information all subsequent flow tests can be designed to yield data which is representative of reservoir behaviour.

title: Special Core Analysis Loading Conditions for a Friable, Stress-Sensitive Sandstone
caption: FIGURE 1 Air permeability and helium porosity as a function of overburden pressure.
figure_reason: Shows progressive stress-induced changes in air permeability and porosity under isotropic overburden loading, motivating the study.
tldr: Anisotropic loading of vertical plugs from friable Gryphon sandstone gives stable grain packing versus isotropic loading, and lab sonic data suggest near-wellbore formation damage affecting logs.
summary: Isotropic overburden testing of horizontal plugs from friable, high-porosity (35%+) Gryphon sandstone caused progressive non-recoverable deformation and hysteresis, with horizontal stresses exceeding in situ values. A modified Hoek cell was used on vertical plugs from Wells B, C and D, loaded isotropically or anisotropically (axial 2600 psig; jacket 1800 or 1400 psig) over two cycles, with pore volume, axial strain, kerosene permeability and sonic times monitored. The anisotropic set with 1400 psig jacket pressure gave the most stable deformation, and hysteresis acceptance criteria were defined. Stable tests showed about 5-6% pore volume reduction, up to 1% axial strain, and porosity correction factors of about 0.94-0.95 (range 0.898-0.985), while oil permeability was only marginally sensitive to loading type. Lab sonic velocities were faster than log values, implying a damaged zone of roughly 5-18 inches around the wellbore. Dry triaxial tests gave apparent internal friction angles of 54-63° at higher initial stresses.
abstract: It has b been found that the conventional "overburden condition" methods of isotropically loading poorly consolidated homogeneous sandstone core material from the Gryphon Field can cause progressive sample deformation and failure during the Special Core Analysis Laboratory (SCAL) testing. Such deformations have resulted in test condition grain packings and hence porosities that are only poorly controlled and of questionable relevance to the insitu condition of the formation sampled. Anisotropic loading, with independent control of axial and confining loads on vertical plug samples has been found to result in appreciably more stable grain packing conditions. It is not possible to prove the stable grain packings obtained are representative of reservoir conditions, however, the stability of the grain packings suggests that they may be and also makes the loading procedure attractive for use in the SCA laboratory. In addition to the investigation of loading methods, sample mechanical behaviour and sonic transit time data has been gathered that calls into question the mechanical integrity of the formation at and beyond the borehole wall and hence the degree to which the responses of some borehole logging devices may be indicative of undisturbed formation characteristics in the Gryphon reservoir.

title: SCA1990-07EURO
caption: FIGURE 7 Application of theoretical methods - Triassic
figure_reason: Applies theoretical correction methods to Triassic porosity-stress data, showing resulting compaction factors.
tldr: Hydrostatic, slow-loading and biaxial tests on Central North Sea sandstones show compaction corrections below 0.95, with loading rate mattering more than stress state; uniaxial correction is questioned.
summary: Core compaction correction in the North Sea is commonly taken as 0.95, derived from hydrostatic tests plus a uniaxial correction factor of 0.62 based on linear elasticity (Teeuw). The authors tested 24 Jurassic and Triassic sandstone plugs using three-cycle hydrostatic loading to 10,000 psi (8 hours), single-cycle loading at 750 psi/day (10 days), and biaxial loading with radial/axial ratios of 0.65-0.85 derived from fracture gradients. At 6000 psi effective stress, porosity reduction factors were about 0.89 (Jurassic) and 0.93 (Triassic) for three-cycle tests, and 0.87 and 0.90 for 10-day tests, so slow loading (creep) gave larger reduction. Biaxial results were similar to or within 1% of three-cycle results, indicating rate of loading matters more than stress regime. They argue the uniaxial correction is invalid because porosity-stress curves are nonlinear, and recommend measuring porosity at an in-situ-equivalent hydrostatic stress (about 0.856 of effective overburden) applied slowly.
abstract: Core compaction correction in the North Sea is frequently assumed to be in the region of 0.95. The core compaction correction is that factor by which ambient core porosities are multiplied to correct to reservoir condition porosities. The core compaction correction is often arrived at by measuring porosity reduction under hydrostatic "effective overburden" conditions. An empirical uniaxial correction is then applied to simulate the reservoir stress conditions. A study has been made on core samples from the Jurassic and Triassic sandstones of the Central North Sea area, so as to better evaluate the core compaction correction. Three laboratory techniques for the measurement of porosity at stress were used, and pore volume compressibility and core compaction correction were calculated. Firstly, the samples were subjected to 'net hydrostatic' overburden pressure conditions at 1000 psi increments up to 10 000 psi, in three cycles, and pore volume reduction measured at each increment. Secondly, the same apparatus was used in a single pressure cycle, building from ambient to simulated reservoir stress in 750 psi/day increments. The samples were then left for a minimum of three days at these reservoir stress conditions to monitor 'creep'. Finally, samples were subjected to conditions where axial and radial stresses were varied independently on vertically cut core plugs. Simulated overburden loads were applied axially, and loads equivalent to 0.65 to 0.85 of overburden applied radially. These 'horizontal' loads are derived from in-situ stress data from hydraulic fracturing work. Our results indicate that core compaction corrections are very sensitive to the application of simulated reservoir stress. Core compaction correction values somewhat less than 0.95 were observed, which suggests that this value may be overly optimistic in this, and perhaps other North Sea areas. Previous calculations of core compaction correction may be in error due to the use of low values of in-situ stress, to compaction tests run too quickly or to stress cycling, and/or the incorrect application of the uniaxial correction.

title: Development of Coring and Electronic Data Logging Systems Enhance Data Quality and Quantity Facilitating Improved Oriented Core Analysis
caption: FIGURE 2 Quantity of usable data per foot of core recovered. Conventional oriented coring and Corienting/EM system.
figure_reason: Shows the key result: usable data per foot of core for conventional versus Corienting/EM systems.
tldr: A new Corienting core barrel with an electronic multishot survey tool and computer-aided goniometers raises oriented core data success above 90% and cuts overall orientation error to under ±8 degrees.
summary: Conventional oriented coring used photo-mechanical multishot tools with failure rates above 50%. They required stopping coring and circulation every 5-6 ft, risking stuck pipe, core damage and lost rig time. The authors describe the Corienting barrel, which isolates the survey tool in a non-magnetic inner-barrel section and reduces scribe-line spiralling, combined with a solid-state electronic multishot tool holding 2000 records and sampling about 6 shots per foot while drilling. Reported results include over 90% success in obtaining full orientation data, with about 95% of runs having tandem verification. Usable analysed data rose from 28% for conventional coring to 60-70%, and about 1 hour of rig time was saved per 60 ft cored at 20 ft/hr. Error budgets give ±6.5 to ±12 degrees for Corienting/EM versus ±11.5 to ±17.5 degrees for conventional systems. Computer-aided goniometers reduce reorientation error to ±1-2 degrees, giving overall error under ±8 degrees.
abstract: Historically, the unreliability and inaccuracy of results has inhibited the frequency of oriented coring. The advent of a new core orientation system has increased mechanical reliability and enhanced the quality of data. The system affords positive placement of the survey tool which is in turn protected from mechanical and hydraulic disturbances. Core spiralling is also reduced, enhancing the quantity and quality of data. Introduction of programmable Electronic Survey Logging Tools has had very significant impact on the quality and quantity of directional data during oriented coring operations. Ruggedness, associated with solid state technology, has increased reliability to acceptable levels (>90%), whilst the ability to record directional data during coring minimises drilling risks and reduces damage to cores. Repeatability and accuracy of data is verifiable when tandem instruments are used and, by reducing instrument alignment errors to around +/- 1 degree, high quality data for analyses of formation directional trends is provided. Scrutiny of the raw data output from the probe can reveal much about conditions during coring and vibrations, torque and penetration rates can be inferred. Large memory and programmable sample rates can track even the most severely spiralling scribe line leading to successful analysis where previous technology has failed. The accuracy and density of data provided by these systems allows detailed geological analysis (paleocurrent trends, fracture determination) of cored material to be carried out with minimal error margins. The introduction of computer aided goniometers has further reduced error margins in the reorientation of planar features in cores to < +/-2 degrees. This has resulted in overall error margins, from downhole survey to reorientation of planar features, to be reduced to < +/-8 degrees.

title: A Computerised Electromagnetic Goniometer and Its Applications in the Study of Reservoir Anisotropy
caption: Figure 4. Dip Log Of A Fluvial Sequence Using The Electromagnetic Goniometer
figure_reason: Dip log (tadpole plot) of a fluvial sequence showing the goniometer's main output format.
tldr: Describes a computerised electromagnetic goniometer for measuring bedding and fracture orientation on core, and shows how its data plots help interpret reservoir anisotropy.
summary: Bedding structures and fractures control reservoir anisotropy, so accurate orientation data from core are needed for geological models. The paper describes an electromagnetic goniometer with a 3D digitizing stylus, roller core holder and menu-driven software that records bedding and fracture orientation, corrected for well deviation. Accuracy is ±2 degrees, checked with a plastic calibration core. Core orientation methods (downhole survey, dipmeter/structural map, palaeomagnetism) are reviewed. Examples show fracture dip logs, stereonets and rose diagrams, a fluvial channel sequence where unit-by-unit cross-bed plots reveal channel trend, and an aeolian sequence where foreset azimuths separate seif from barchan/transverse dunes.
abstract: Accurate measurement of bedding features and fractures on whole core and slabbed core can be made using an electromagnetic goniometer. Data manipulation and plotting of data in coloured dip logs and stereonet, rose diagram and histogram plots allows the orientation of the features of interest to be identified. This has applications in determining the orientation of features affecting reservoir anisotropy such as fracture patterns and sand body geometry.

title: The Use of Core Derived Quantitative Mineralogical Data to Improve Formation Evaluation
caption: FIGURE 4 Calculated vs core porosity (Mineralog grain density).
figure_reason: Shows improved match between log porosity using Mineralog grain density and core porosity.
tldr: FTIR-based quantitative mineralogy (Mineralog) on Brent Group core improves deterministic and statistical (Optima) log evaluation of porosity and clay, and aids sand correlation.
summary: Log evaluation usually ignores geological information, so mineral effects on density, neutron and gamma ray responses cause errors. The paper applies FTIR spectroscopy (Mineralog, accurate to within ±5 wt%) to a North Sea Jurassic Brent Group well and compares log-derived results with core porosity, grain density and clay. Using a constant 2.65 g/cc grain density gives clear porosity errors in siderite-rich intervals (siderite up to ~50% in the Broom sand, grain density up to ~3.3 g/cc); each 1% siderite lowers porosity by ~0.8 porosity percent. Mineralog grain density improves the match, and a mica correction improves it further (maximum grain density discrepancy 0.04 g/cc at 16% muscovite). Mineralog total clay calibrates gamma-ray Vcl, which is distorted by K-feldspar, mica and non-radioactive kaolinite. Feeding mineral volumes into the Optima statistical program gives excellent agreement with core porosity, and distinct mineral assemblages can fingerprint the four Lower Ness sands for correlation.
abstract: For a selected, representative North Sea well the sequence of formations comprising the Jurassic Brent Group has been evaluated using advanced core and log analysis techniques. The mineralogy of these formations has been quantified using Fourier Transform Infra-red Spectroscopy and used, along with conventional core measured petrophysical parameters (porosity, permeability and grain density), to control, optimise and substantiate the log evaluation results. Mineral analysis results were generated in a format which enables direct incorporation into an advanced statistical log evaluation procedure. A minimum logging suite comprising acoustic, density, photo-electric, compensated neutron, gamma ray and resistivity was used as input to the evaluation procedure. The results of this log analysis approach have proven to be more representative of core measured values than those derived through conventional deterministic log evaluation procedures. In addition, minerals which characterise the individual formations can be recognised and used for improved in-field geological correlation and subsequent reservoir development.

title: A Simple Check for the Presence of Solid Salt in the Pore Space of Gas Reservoirs by Comparing Porosity and Grain Density Changes Resulting from Salt Extraction
caption: FIGURE 1 Core-graph. Alteration of petrophysical data due to salt extraction.
figure_reason: Core-graph showing porosity, permeability and grain density shifts caused by salt extraction, illustrating the key evidence for solid salt.
tldr: Compares porosity and grain density before and after salt extraction to compute the density of removed material, distinguishing natural solid salt from drying or mud-filtrate artifacts in North German gas reservoirs.
summary: North German gas reservoir cores often give porosities and grain densities that are too low when measured on uncleaned, oven-dried plugs, because of salt in the pore space. Porosity and grain density were measured by the Archimedes (isopropanol buoyancy) method before and after salt extraction, with repeatability of ±0.1 p.u. and reproducibility of ±0.2 p.u. The average density of the extracted material and an excess porosity term (accounting for 15% evaporation residue of saturated brine) classify samples into three types: no solid salt, natural solid salt (density 2.16 ± 0.2 g/cm3), or salt plugging pore throats. In a middle Bunter core, most of the 26 samples showed porosity rising from about 5% to 25% after extraction and extracted-material densities near 2.2 g/cm3, confirming halite. The error analysis shows interpretation becomes unreliable below a porosity change of 2 p.u. A routine screen of 200 wells flagged 15 as probably containing solid salt, found only in the middle Bunter and Zechstein. Only five of these had been noted in the original core reports. Plugs should be drilled with mineral oil if solid salt is indicated, since fresh water drilling raised permeability from 40 to 400 mD.
abstract: The measurement of petrophysical properties on uncleaned, oven-dried plugs followed by a second measurement after salt extraction is a common practice in the evaluation of North German gas reservoirs. The calculated density of the extracted material allows a check for solid salt if porosity and grain density are accurately determined. The presence of naturally occurring solid salt in the reservoir is indicated by a porosity change greater than 15 % by volume and an average density of the extracted material close to $2.16 \text{ g/cm}^3$ . The evidence of plugged pore throats due to the precipitation of salt during the drying process is also indicated. A core-graph computer program allows on a routine basis a check for solid salt and gives an indication whether it occurs naturally or originates either from drilling mud filtrate or formation water.

title: The Role of Bound Water and Capillary Water in the Evaluation of Porosity in Reservoir Rocks
caption: FIGURE 7 Pore size distribution.
figure_reason: Mercury pore size distributions show how clay type controls microporosity, explaining the water distribution differences.
tldr: Thermogravimetry/evolved water analysis on North Sea sandstones and Berea shows capillary water far exceeds bound water, up to 10 times in chlorite-rich rock.
summary: The paper examines how bound and capillary water affect porosity evaluation in reservoir sandstones. Core from three North Sea reservoirs (A kaolinite, B illite, C chlorite; porosity 20-27%) and Berea sandstone were equilibrated at 0.55 RVP (bound water) and 0.9735 RVP (capillary water, pores up to 0.08 µm, 3.63 MPa equivalent). Evolved water was quantified by TG/EWA heating to 200°C, and combined with XRD, SEM, krypton surface area and mercury porosimetry. Bound water was only 1.1-2.4% of pore volume, while water at 0.9735 RVP was 6.0% (Berea), 7.1% (A), 18.5% (B) and 22.6% (C). The capillary/bound ratio rose from 4.7-5.5 for kaolinite to 7.7 for illite and 9.8 for chlorite, versus 2.5 for non-microporous material, reflecting clay morphology and microporosity.
abstract: Knowledge of the quantity and distribution of the different types of water contained within the interconnected pore volume of a reservoir rock is fundamental to formation evaluation. Three main water types have been identified as bound, capillary and free waters. Bound water includes both water held to the net-negatively charged mineral surfaces, and the water of hydration associated with the mineral charge balancing counter-ions. Capillary water is immobile water held by capillary forces in regions of microporosity, for example dead end pores and pendular rings. Free water is water that is able to flow under a given pressure gradient. A new laboratory technique, thermogravimetry/evolved water analysis TG/EWA, has been used to quantify these different water types. Bound/capillary water relationships are presented for core taken from three different North Sea reservoirs that exhibit very different clay mineralogy. Berea sandstone was included in the study. The data have been integrated with measurements of porosity, surface area, mercury porosimetry, SEM and XRD to explain the influence that rock structure and mineralogy have on the quantity and distribution of water types. All the rocks studied contain much more capillary held water than bound water. The amounts held are strongly dependent on the type of clay mineral that predominates, along with its morphology and location within the pore system. This study has shown that reservoir rocks that contain chlorite as the major clay mineral can hold up to 10 times more capillary water than bound water.

title: Poroperm Evaluation on in Relation to Applied Stress States for a Gas Reservoir
caption: FIGURE 12 Klinkenberg Permeability Change at 1000 v 4000 psi
figure_reason: Shows Klinkenberg permeability change between 1000 and 4000 psi, the main result on rock-type and stress influence.
tldr: Porosity and Klinkenberg permeability of North Sea Rotliegendes sandstones were measured under hydrostatic, biaxial, triaxial and uniaxial stress; stress-corrected permeability averages matched DST values better than conventional data.
summary: Conventional core analysis is run at non-standard confining stresses, so the effect of stress state and rock type on porosity and permeability was tested. Plugs from Permian Rotliegendes lithic and sublithic arenites (aeolian, fluvial and lake margin facies) were loaded from 500 to 4000 psi in a purpose-built core holder, with helium porosity and Klinkenberg permeability measured at each step. Porosity fell by up to 18.5% (4000 vs 1000 psi), more under hydrostatic than biaxial loading and independent of facies. Permeability fell by roughly 15 to 70%, depending mainly on facies and less on stress state, and most of the reduction occurred in the first 1500 psi, possibly from sleeve compliance and stress-relief cracks. Facies-based conversion factors gave pseudo-stress permeability averages closer to DST permeabilities than conventional core data in most intervals.
abstract: The results of a study conducted on sandstone samples from a North Sea gas reservoir, indicate that the response of a core plug subjected to a laboratory stress, can be influenced not only by the stress state imposed on the sample but also by its rock type. Changes in equivalent liquid permeability with increasing stress can be seen to be influenced by rock type and to a limited extent by the stress state. Changes in Helium porosity due to a stress increase is observed to be strongly influenced by the stress state imposed and is quite independent of the rock type. The majority of the permeability and porosity reduction is shown to occur during the initial 1500 psi of stress application. The permeability data from several producing wells were used to calculate psuedo-stress permeability averages, and these are in better agreement with calculated drill stem test permeabilities than those derived from conventional core analysis data. The study suggests that caution should be employed when core analysis data generated under different stress conditions, particularly at low values of stress, are compared. Consideration of the permeability/stress response of the rock types encountered in a reservoir should be used in the compilation of core analysis studies.

title: A Fresh Look at Predictive Equations for Compressional Wave Velocity - Porosity
caption: FIGURE 12 Modified acoustic impedance equation predictions.
figure_reason: Shows the proposed modified acoustic impedance equation closely matching measured velocity-porosity data for sediments and basalts.
tldr: Using ODP Leg 123 sediment and basalt data, the authors compare porosity-velocity models and propose a semi-empirical acoustic impedance transform that fits better than Wyllie, Wood or Wyllie-Wood.
summary: Established porosity-velocity equations (Wyllie time average, Wood, Wyllie-Wood, Nafe-Drake, Raymer, Raiga-Clemenceau) are tested against shipboard index property and 500 kHz velocity measurements on sediments and basalts from ODP Leg 123 (Sites 765 and 766), covering porosity from near 0 to 100%. The time average equation fails over the full range, and fitting it requires unrealistically low matrix and pore water velocities (5800-6200 and 1050 m/s). The Wood equation predicts well above about 62% porosity, and a Wyllie-Wood form with porosity-weighted rigidity terms improves the fit. A new semi-empirical acoustic impedance equation, with q equal to 0.22 (Poisson's ratio 0.42), fits better over both high and low porosity. Regressing predicted on measured velocities gives slope 0.90 and R2 of 96 for the impedance equation, against slope 0.70 and R2 of 95 for the modified Wyllie-Wood.
abstract: The Wyllie time average equation has, for many years, been universally applied to predict porosities from compressional wave velocities, or visa-versa. However, it has long been recognized that the Wyllie equation does not adequately describe the actual relationship between these two parameters, and there have been many attempts to improve upon it. These have included the use of a simplified Wood equation, the concept of acoustic formation factor, and a wide range of empirical relationships. In many cases these models have been derived by testing them against a set of data representing a relatively narrow range of porosity values and, similarly, the use of the Wyllie equation has often been justified by virtue of a pseudo-linear relationship over a narrow range of porosity values. Some of the limitations of the time average equation were also recognised by Wyllie and his co-workers who amended the Wood emulsion equation to partially take account of the rigidity of the materials. Further modifications to this Wyllie-Wood equation have been shown here to not only describe the relationship between porosity and velocity more closely than the time average equation, but also more closely than some of the alternative proposals suggested by contemporaries of Wyllie and since. A semi-empirical acoustic impedance relationship has been developed which is shown to provide a more accurate porosity-velocity transform, using realistic material parameters, than has hitherto been possible.

title: NMR Imaging of Fluid Saturation Distributions in Core Samples Using a High Magnetic Field
caption: Figure 6 50 $\mu$ m-thick slice showing the distribution of oil inside the porous medium containing oil and water
figure_reason: Chemical-shift image showing oil distribution in a core containing oil and water, the key result.
tldr: Using a 9.4 Tesla MRI spectrometer, the authors image 50 µm slices of limestone and sandstone cores and separate oil from water by chemical shift without doping.
summary: The paper explores high-field (9.4 T) NMR micro-imaging to visualize fluid distributions in porous media. Experiments used 3 cm by 1 cm cores of Fontainebleau sandstone (15% porosity, 2 D) and bioclastic limestone (30% porosity, 300 mD), saturated with water, with Soltrol 130 oil, or with both. Spin-warp sequences gave 512x512 images of 50 µm-thick slices, about 30 times thinner than the 1.5 mm CT slices. A chemical-shift selective sequence separated oil and water images without doping agents. The FLASH fast sequence gave no image on water-saturated limestone, possibly because of local magnetic susceptibility heterogeneity at high field.
abstract: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) now used in medical research should result in progress in the understanding of flows in porous media. This paper describes several applications of the Magnetic Resonance Imaging technique to study fluid distributions in porous media using a high magnetic field of 9.4 Tesla. The different applications studied are: - - determination of local porosity through the intensity of the NMR signal of a fluid in a porous medium, - - visualization of oil and water distribution by chemical-shift selective excitations. Improvements obtained by using a high magnetic field for studies related to fluid distribution in porous media are shown. In addition the limitations of using such a magnetic field will be discussed.

title: Appliciations of Magnetic Resonance Imaging in Special Core Analysis Studies
caption: FIGURE 4 Halved core of Portland Limestone, one half saturated in n-decane, the other in water (a) total fluid profile; (b) oil profile; (c) water profile; (d) total fluid map; (e) oil map; (f) water map.
figure_reason: Shows oil and water profiles and 2-D maps in a halved Portland limestone core, validating species discrimination.
tldr: Chemical shift MRI at 0.4 T images oil and water distributions in limestone, sandstone and bead-pack cores, including static, centrifuge and low-rate waterflood experiments.
summary: The paper evaluates magnetic resonance imaging, especially chemical shift imaging (CSI), as a tool for mapping fluid saturations in special core analysis. Experiments used a 0.4 T system with voxels of about 0.94 x 0.94 x 4.5 mm on 25.4 mm Portland limestone (12%, 30 md), Lochaline sandstone (20%, 3000 md) and glass bead packs. Oil (n-decane) and water are separable by a roughly 3.7 ppm chemical shift. Line broadening by the rock is strong in some sandstones (linewidths up to 18.6 ppm). 1-D profiles take about 4.5 min and 2-D 64x64 images about 4.5 h. A low-rate waterflood (10 cm/day) in Portland limestone showed strong water channelling that persisted on repeat flooding and through to residual oil, and a Xanthan polymer bank could be imaged. Irreducible water after centrifuging (0.35 PV) was imaged, but short T2 signals were underestimated at a 40 ms echo time.
abstract: Computerised tomography (CT) scanning has been extensively used in the petroleum industry for measurement and imaging of saturation distributions in core floods. So far, the majority of applications have used X-Ray CT scanning, which essentially "sees" the character of the heterogeneous rock and the position of "doped" (added contrast) fluids. A number of processes other than X-Ray scanning lend themselves to tomographic imaging and one of the most promising is nuclear magnetic resonance imaging (NMRI or MRI for short). The MRI technique, which "sees" the fluids in the pore spaces rather than the rock, is shown to have a number of important complementary advantages over other imaging methods. The results of experimental studies have shown factors that help to discriminate between different fluid species, and to quantify saturation distributions in static and dynamic conditions in cores. The technique has a particular advantage in enhanced oil recovery (EOR) core studies in that it can be made molecular species specific and can be used to image simultaneously the distributions of oil and water and the distribution of EOR additives. From preliminary experiments it appears that there is a potential for high resolution MRI, down to micro scale, which could lead to fundamental and detailed study of entrapment and mobilisation of residual fluids in porous systems.

title: Quality Control of Waterfloods on Heterogeneous Core Samples Using Computer Tomography
caption: FIGURE 2 Miscible displacement of chloride water by iodide water, at 60 ml/h for 21 hours. The scale is increasing concentration of iodide water; 0.0 (black) to 1.0 (white).
figure_reason: CT images of miscible displacement reveal the layered permeability structure that explains channeling in all later floods.
tldr: X-ray CT visualization of water- and oilfloods on a layered North Sea sandstone shows channeling that makes Swi, Sor and JBN relative permeability unreliable; firing changes wettability and clay structure.
summary: Displacement tests on heterogeneous North Sea reservoir sandstone gave high Swi, high Sor and unusual relative permeability curves, so a layered 1.5-inch sample was studied with X-ray CT during miscible, oil- and waterfloods. The miscible displacement revealed a high-permeability middle zone (~2700 mD) and outer zones (~900 mD). Swi depended on the method: about 0.13 by centrifuge, 0.40 with viscous oil flood and about 0.50 with low-viscosity oil flood at 400 ml/h. Sor was about 0.30, nearly independent of Swi and only slightly dependent on rate, because oil was produced mainly from the permeable layer. Firing at 600 °C made the sample strongly water-wet (Amott water index 0.9, oil index 0.0), lowered and evened out Sor, and altered clay morphology (kaolinite, illite) and porosity. The authors conclude that JBN-type relative permeability calculation should be avoided on strongly layered samples and that CT should be used to select homogeneous samples.
abstract: This paper presents X-ray Computer Tomographic (CT) visualizations of water- and oilfloods performed on a heterogeneous reservoir sandstone sample. The CT-images show more or less pronounced capillary end-effects, and a layered structure in the sample is clearly shown by a miscible displacement. The porosity distribution and permeability to water for each layer are quantified. The value of initial water saturation, $S_{wi}$ , is strongly dependent on the method used to establish $S_{wi}$ . The oil is produced mainly from the more permeable zone of the sample, and the residual oil saturation, $S_{or}$ , is independent on the $S_{wr}$ -value. The effect of rate on $S_{or}$ is also studied. Additional characterization of the sample was obtained by oil/water capillary pressure curve, mercury injection data, thin section and SEM analyses. Wettability tests on parallel samples indicate a near neutral wetting characteristics. The sample became water wet after firing.

title: Electrical Resistivity Imaging of Core Samples
caption: FIGURE 7 A Formation Factor Image of Figure 5 showing very great variability.
figure_reason: Formation factor image of the sandstone shows large small-scale petrophysical variability revealed by the imaging.
tldr: Describes a four-electrode, multi-current-source imaging system (CORE-RES) producing high-resolution quantitative resistivity images of core, tested on schist and sandstone to calibrate FMS borehole images.
summary: FMS borehole resistance images are high resolution but only relative, so they cannot be converted to quantitative resistivity or porosity. The authors built a computer-controlled core imaging system using a pad of 64 gold-plated point potential electrodes (4 by 16 grid, 0.2 inch spacing) and multiple feedback-controlled point current sources that generate a uniform current field. On a low-porosity metamorphosed Precambrian core compared with FMS data, resistivity ranged from 20 to 120 ohm-m (12 ohm-m saturant), showing more local variability than expected, though saturation was uncertain. In a 25% porosity Sherwood Sandstone, a carbonate-cemented altered band showed higher resistivity, and repeat scans reproduced major features with small differences attributed to pad positioning. Converting the images to formation factor showed large property variation within one core, and the system can also probe anisotropy by directing current axially or perpendicular to the core.
abstract: High resolution imaging of the electrical resistivity of whole and half core is described. The technique aims to provide a calibration of downhole information on the resistance images that up to now provide only qualitative information on the formation resistivity structure. The resistivity imaging of core is shown to be sensitive to the same fabric and structural detail as available electrical image data and to provide a means of converting electrical resistance images into physical properties. Examples are presented for various lithologies from the BGS core archive, and also synthetic laboratory models. The measurement system is novel and it outlined along with the geophysical array required to produce the high resolution resistivity measurements. The measurement technique is able to provide an assessment of resistivity anisotropy in terms of constraining the electrical current flow either horizontally or vertically in the core sample. The core images are shown to be diagnostic of grain fabrics, and allow resistivity and resistance images to be understood in terms of sedimentary fabric. It should also prove of use in studies of climatic cycles, definition of mineral-filled fractures, and will provide better constraints on models of current conduction within formations in situ.

title: Sensitivity Analysis of Errors in Reserve Evaluations Due to Core and Log Measurement Inaccuracies
caption: FIG. 1a SOUTHERN NORTH SEA EXAMPLE (ROTLIEGENDE GAS FIELD)
figure_reason: Shows reserve change versus ±10% errors in each Archie parameter for the Rotliegende gas example.
tldr: A simple one-at-a-time ±10% sensitivity analysis of Archie parameters shows which core and log measurements most affect volumetric reserves, illustrated for Rotliegende gas and Brent oil examples.
summary: Reserve estimates depend on water saturation, which is computed from Archie parameters (porosity, m, n, Rw, Rt). The authors propose a quick sensitivity analysis that perturbs each parameter individually by ±10% (with m=n=2) around representative values and recomputes reserves using a volumetric constant. Applied to a typical Southern North Sea Rotliegende gas field (1 Tcf assumed) and a Northern North Sea Brent oil field (100 MMbbl assumed), the results show reserves are most sensitive to porosity, then m and n, and least sensitive to Rw and Rt. In the Rotliegende case a 10% change in m changed GIIP by +14%/-17%, and n by about ±6-7%, while Rw gave about ±4%. Brent sensitivities were generally smaller, and responses to m and Rt are non-linear at larger errors. The method assumes independent parameters, clean formations or shale-corrected values, and consistent porosity definitions, and it helps prioritise coring, core analysis and logging effort.
abstract: Reserve evaluations, using the volumetric reserves equation, are very dependent on the accuracy of measurements used to calculate initial water saturation. Water saturation is calculated from petrophysical parameters including porosity, cementation and saturation exponents, formation water resistivity and true formation resistivity. The effect of inaccuracies in these parameters upon reserves is often intuitively, rather than quantitatively, understood by geologists, engineers and management. Sensitivity analysis of the petrophysical parameters address this problem by using a set range of errors for each individual parameter. The benefit of sensitivity analysis is that it can rapidly establish the most significant core and log measurements in terms of the greatest quantitative effect on calculated reserves. They are simple to use and can be performed in a minimal amount of time at negligible cost. Establishing the most significant reserve sensitivities leads to the objective identification of priorities regarding which petrophysical parameters require greatest precision. Thus, a systematic approach can be applied to planning of coring and logging programmes. The result is improved confidence in the planning and cost effectiveness of coring, core analysis (special and conventional), SEM and petrological studies and wireline logging programmes when evaluating reserves. Examples representative of a Rotliegende Group gas reservoir and a Brent Group oil reservoir and of the Southern and Northern North Sea respectively illustrate why analyses should be conducted using values representative of the actual reservoir. The results also demonstrate that precision in some petrophysical parameters is a greater requirement than for others. In these examples, reserve evaluation is far more sensitive to porosity, cementation and saturation exponent inaccuracies in the Rotliegende than in the Brent example. This is significant since porosity, cementation exponent and saturation exponent are measured by core analysis and not with such confidence from wireline logs. Reserves in both examples are relatively insensitive to formation water resistivity and log-derived true resistivity.

title: Alternative Methods for Determining Water Saturations in Core Plugs
caption: FIGURE 4 Karl Fischer-method used on fresh reservoir sandstone samples
figure_reason: Compares Karl Fischer saturations with chloride titration on 17 fresh reservoir plugs, showing agreement and the ±0.02 accuracy.
tldr: Presents Karl Fischer, chloride titration, tracer, density, CT and GOR methods to verify core plug water saturation, finding Karl Fischer, chloride titration and CT accurate to ±0.02-0.03 Sw.
summary: Material balance errors can corrupt all saturation values in a waterflood series on a core plug, so independent checks of Sw are needed. The authors describe six alternatives: Karl Fischer titration of solvent, chloride titration after miscible displacement by nitrate brine, oil volume by nonane tracer or by density difference, CT scanning, and a gas-oil-ratio method at reservoir conditions. Tests used Bentheim and Berea sandstone, sintered Al2O3 and reservoir sandstones (porosity 20-35%, permeability 30-8000 mD, near-neutral to strongly water-wet) and compared the methods with material balance, weighing and CT. Karl Fischer accuracy was about ±0.02 Sw and chloride titration about ±0.03 Sw. Material balance was often inaccurate because of hold-up volumes and emulsions, and CT deviated on heterogeneous plugs. Karl Fischer, chloride titration and CT are recommended, while the tracer and density methods need further work.
abstract: This paper presents some alternative methods for determining water saturation in plugs during and after water/oil floods. Detailed procedures, comparison tests with other methods and a discussion on complications and possible systematic errors are presented. Tests have been performed on plugs during oil and water floods and on plugs to which were added a known volume of water.

title: SCA1990-21EURO
caption: FIGURE 5 Resistivity index vs. water saturation.
figure_reason: Resistivity index versus water saturation, the basis for the saturation exponents at ambient and reservoir conditions.
tldr: Porous-plate capillary pressure and resistivity tests on water-wet North Sea sandstones show lower saturation exponents at reservoir than ambient conditions, with n rising slightly with confining stress.
summary: The study asks whether capillary pressure and the Archie saturation exponent measured at ambient conditions represent reservoir conditions for water-wet North Sea sandstone. Five well-consolidated plugs were drained by the porous plate method with nitrogen at ambient conditions, then with refined oil (Isopar-M) at reservoir conditions (98°C, 414 bar pore pressure, 180 bar net stress), then with refined oil at ambient conditions. Amott tests gave water-wet indices of 0.93–1.00 before testing, and sample 3 was still 0.87 afterwards. Mean saturation exponents were 2.26 at reservoir conditions, 2.45 for ambient oil/water and 2.23 for ambient gas/water, the last possibly biased by electrode wetness. Capillary pressure ratios (ambient to reservoir) averaged 1.70 for oil/water and 2.66 for gas/water. Increasing net stress from 180 to 344 bar raised n by about 5%, with no change in endpoint saturation.
abstract: Saturation exponents have been determined at ambient conditions and at reservoir conditions on sandstone core plugs from a North Sea reservoir. The samples were drained for water using the porous plate method. Five samples were first measured at ambient conditions with nitrogen displacing water, then at reservoir conditions with refined oil displacing water. After the test at reservoir conditions the samples were measured at ambient conditions with refined oil displacing water. At the end of the reservoir conditions measurements, the effect of reductions in the reservoir pore-pressure on the water saturation and the resistivity index were investigated. The wettability preference of the samples was tested, showing that the plugs remained water-wet throughout the measurements. The results from the electrical measurements both for the tests at ambient conditions and for the tests at reservoir conditions confirm the relationship between the resistivity index and water saturation described by Archie. The results from the electrical resistivity measurements show that the saturation exponents obtained at reservoir conditions are lower than the saturation exponent obtained at ambient conditions with refined oil displacing water. The formation resistivity index and thus the saturation exponent slightly increased when the net confining pressure was increased. For this water-wet reservoir it is found that the capillary pressure obtained at ambient conditions is directly proportional to the capillary pressure obtained at reservoir conditions.

title: Hysteresis of the Resistivity Iy Index in Berea Sandstone
caption: FIGURE 4a Hysteresis effect in oil-wet core.
figure_reason: Oil-wet core resistivity index over drainage and imbibition cycles, showing strong hysteresis.
tldr: Steady-state resistivity tests on water-wet and oil-wet Berea cores show no saturation hysteresis in water-wet cores (n≈2) but strong hysteresis in oil-wet cores, with n rising during imbibition.
summary: The study examines how saturation history affects the resistivity index–brine saturation relationship in Berea sandstone. Ten plugs, water-wet or made oil-wet with Quilon-S and checked by Amott index, were put through primary drainage, imbibition and sometimes secondary drainage. Steady-state kerosene/brine flooding was used with four-electrode resistivity measurement and continuous weighing. Water-wet cores showed no hysteresis and a saturation exponent of about 2 (1.74–1.95 for cores initially oil-saturated). Oil-wet cores had n of about 2–3 in primary drainage, which rose strongly during imbibition and stayed high in secondary drainage, because brine trapped as isolated drops is not remobilized. The authors attribute drainage behavior mainly to brine fingering and imbibition behavior mainly to trapping, and conclude that lab saturation procedures should mimic the reservoir history.
abstract: The paper reports an investigation of the influence of saturation history on resistivity of oil-wet and water-wet Berea sandstone. Four-electrode resistivity measurements were conducted on the sandstone plugs with varying brine saturation. The resistivity was measured continuously during the saturation cycles: primary drainage, imbibition, and repeated drainage. The data from 10 plugs indicated that the saturation history did not influence the brine saturation/resistivity index relationship of water-wet cores, while on oil-wet cores, the saturation history strongly influenced the relationship. In the oil-wet cases, the saturation exponent, $n$ , was about three and had a slightly increasing trend during the primary drainage cycle. During imbibition it increased strongly to about six and then fell back to a value of about three to four during the secondary drainage.

title: Transition from Laminar to Non-Darcy Flow of Gases in Porous Media
caption: Fig. 7 Critical flow velocity against a characteristic length of the media ( $k/\phi$ ).
figure_reason: Shows critical flow velocity correlating with √(k/φ), the paper's best correlation for onset of non-Darcy flow.
tldr: Gas flow tests on 23 North Sea plugs show slippage-corrected plots give the onset of non-Darcy flow, which correlates with permeability and √(k/φ) rather than a Reynolds number.
summary: The paper investigates the gas velocity at which flow in porous media departs from Darcy's law, which matters for core analysis and high-rate gas wells. Porosity (helium expansion), Klinkenberg permeability and Forchheimer inertial coefficients were measured on 23 North Sea core plugs using air at varied flow rates. Plotting pressure drop squared against flow rate, with and without a Klinkenberg slippage correction, gave the onset of deviation. Including slippage raised the critical velocity, by up to about 20 times in low-permeability plugs and only about 5% near 100 md. Critical Reynolds numbers based on the β·k length were about 1 for 10–100 md, about 0.1 for 1–10 md and about 0.05 for 0.1–1 md, and the length scale decreased with increasing permeability, which contradicts expectation. Critical velocity correlated with permeability and better with √(k/φ), so the authors recommend measuring it directly from slippage-corrected plots.
abstract: Experimental investigation has been carried out to examine critical velocities at which transition from laminar to non-Darcy flow of gases take place. The critical velocities were evaluated from back-pressure plots of pressure gradient against flow rates. Incorporating the gas slippage effects into these plots resulted in significantly higher critical velocities. The critical velocities were found to be related petrophysically to the permeability, porosity and pore structure of the sample.

title: Jack Haugen
caption: Figure 5 Stability Number, $N_s$ , versus recovery at breakthrough.
figure_reason: Shows recovery at breakthrough versus stability number, identifying onset of unstable displacement and C = 150.
tldr: Multi-rate unsteady-state waterfloods on intermediate-wet North Sea sandstone show lower scaling coefficients suffice for stabilized flow, while high rates cause viscous fingering per Peters' stability number.
summary: Unsteady-state relative permeability tests on intermediate-wettability cores are problematic because scaling criteria from strongly wetted rock demand unrealistically high rates. Waterfloods were run at several rates on the same North Sea sandstone plugs (107 to 870 mD) with brine and refined oil at ambient conditions. Amott tests showed mixed wettability (WI -0.01 to 0.07), and reproducibility checks showed stable base permeability and wettability. Oil relative permeability was rate-independent early but showed a systematic rate effect at the end of displacement. A scaling coefficient Lμv > 0.10 was enough to stabilize the front at breakthrough, far below the 1-5 for strongly wet rock. Peters' stability number with wettability parameter C = 150 identified viscous fingering at high rates, and a pressure drop of 2.7-6.8 kPa was a useful guideline.
abstract: Measurement of relative permeability by the unsteady-state technique poses problems when dealing with rocks of intermediate wettability. Scaling criteria established for cores with strongly wetted rock require flooding rates much higher than a realistic reservoir rate and may cause an unstable displacement or a non-representative flow regime. This paper presents results from waterfloods on reservoir sandstone cores of intermediate wettability. The tests presented were conducted at ambient conditions using synthetic brine and laboratory oil. The flooding rate was varied in steps from low to high, and the absolute permeability varied from 107 mD to 870 mD. The results show that the type of scaling criteria applied to strongly water-wet cores probably also holds for intermediate wettability systems but with different critical values. This means that correctly scaled experiments can be performed on intermediate wettability systems at lower rates than for strongly wetted systems. The high rate tests were, according to the stability criteria used, influenced by viscous fingering, and should therefore not be used for calculation of relative permeability.

title: Using Explicit and Implicit Methods to Calculate Relative Permeabilities from in Situ Measurements
caption: FIGURE 9. Comparison of the relative permeabilities calculated with the explicit and the implicit methods.
figure_reason: Compares relative permeability curves from the explicit and implicit methods, the paper's main result.
tldr: Oil-water relative permeabilities are derived from a long-core drainage test with tracer saturation and pressure data, using explicit Darcy analysis and implicit simulator history matching.
summary: Relative permeability determination is limited by poor pressure gradient estimates. A drainage experiment on a 77.8 cm Clashack sandstone core (permeability 0.952 D, porosity 0.183) used a 22Na tracer in the water phase and a germanium detector to measure water saturation at two points 10.1 cm apart, along with differential pressures at those points and the inlet. In the explicit method, the pressure gradient is obtained from the pressures at equal saturation at the two points and a constant saturation front velocity (0.0067 cm/s), and Darcy's law then gives kr. In the implicit method, a simulator with spline-interpolated kr curves is fitted to the data by chi-square minimization. Saturation profiles are sensitive mainly to endpoint kr, whereas pressure gradients are sensitive to the intermediate low-total-mobility region. Delayed pressure transducer response was a problem and required a time-scale correction.
abstract: In a drainage experiment the water saturation is measured with a nuclear tracer method as a continuous function of time in two points on the core. The differential water pressure with respect to the outlet is measured at the same two points. It is shown how the pressure gradient can be derived with great accuracy, and how this result can be used to find the relative permeabilities as functions of the saturations by an explicit use of Darcy's equation. The relative permeabilities are also derived by an implicit method where a simulator is used to find relative permeabilities which give optimal fit to the experimental data.

title: Principles, Practice and Applications of Laboratory Minipermeametry
caption: FIGURE 4. Average minipermeameter flowrates plotted against Hassler-sleeve permeability (Ka). The best-fit line is derived from equation (1), $K = 1.92 \times q$ .
figure_reason: Shows minipermeameter flowrate versus Hassler-sleeve permeability on homogeneous plugs, validating the analytical calibration for the large probe.
tldr: Describes Statoil's automated laboratory minipermeameter, its calibration against Hassler-sleeve plugs and an analytical solution, core handling changes, and applications showing dense grid data reveal heterogeneity missed by plugs and logs.
summary: The paper argues that laboratory minipermeametry should become a standard core analysis method and documents Statoil's automated x,y-table minipermeameter (nitrogen, constant pressure 10-900 mbar, 1 mD to 15 D, <3% uncertainty, <1% repeatability). Calibration was done on homogeneous plugs and by the Goggin et al. analytical solution; for the large probe, calculated/measured permeability ratios were 0.89-1.01, while the small probe gave values about 20% too low. Fresh versus dried core showed drying matters for 2-20 mD material but not above 100 mD. Edge effects were under 5% even with half the tip over the edge, and revised core handling (minipermeametry before slabbing and 1" plugging) is proposed. Dense grids revealed more heterogeneity than CT images, up to 41% differences between orthogonal faces, and in a laminated reservoir gave a net-to-gross of 0.66 at a 20 mD cutoff versus 1.00 from plugs and logs; N0 tests suggested optimal spacing of 7-10 cm for plugs.
abstract: Laboratory minipermeametry provides a rapid, non-destructive measurement of permeability which is at least as accurate as conventional Hassler-sleeve measurements and several orders of magnitude cheaper. A high level of experimental precision is attained by automation of all measurement functions including positioning of the minipermeameter probe. Automation gives rapid return on investment in terms of time saved. Conversion of minipermeameter flowrates to mD values is recommended in two ways, by minipermeametry and Hassler-sleeve measurement on standard homogeneous core plugs, and by use of an analytical solution. Core handling procedures can be improved to optimalise conditions for minipermeametry, which at the same time enhance geological description and cause less core damage. Minipermeametry has the potential to supercede 1" core plugs as the routine method for characterizing permeability in cores. Measurements made on dense sampling grids resolve fine scale heterogeneities not visible on CT-scan images. The low cost and rapidity of minipermeametry permits collection of large numbers of measurements which form statistically significant data sets, and give an accurate impression of reservoir heterogeneity. We believe that improved characterization of core permeability contributes directly to improved reservoir management.

title: Principles, Practice and Applications of Laboratory Minipermeametry
caption: FIGURE 4. Average minipermeameter flowrates plotted against Hassler-sleeve permeability (Ka). The best-fit line is derived from equation (1), $K = 1.92 \times q$ .
figure_reason: Shows minipermeameter flowrate versus Hassler-sleeve permeability for homogeneous plugs, with the analytical-solution fit validating calibration.
tldr: Describes Statoil's automated laboratory minipermeameter, its calibration against Hassler-sleeve plugs and an analytical solution, core handling changes, and applications showing dense minipermeameter data better capture heterogeneity.
summary: The paper argues that laboratory minipermeametry should become a routine core analysis method because it is non-destructive, cheap and fast. Statoil's automatic minipermeameter uses an x,y-table with 0.01 mm positioning, constant-pressure nitrogen flow (10-900 mbar), a ~25 N probe force, and measures about 1 mD to 15 D with better than 3% uncertainty and 1% repeatability. Calibration with homogeneous plugs and the Goggin et al. analytical solution agreed well for the large probe (Kmp/Ka about 0.97-1.01) but underestimated permeability by about 20% for the small probe. Edge effects were found to be small (<5% even with half the seal over an edge), and revised core handling procedures are proposed to preserve core for measurement and geological description. Dense-grid data revealed heterogeneity beyond CT-scan images, up to 41% permeability differences between adjacent faces, net sand definition in laminated reservoirs, and N0 tests showing plug sampling at 25 cm intervals is statistically inadequate.
abstract: Laboratory minipermeametry provides a rapid, non-destructive measurement of permeability which is at least as accurate as conventional Hassler-sleeve measurements and several orders of magnitude cheaper. A high level of experimental precision is attained by automation of all measurement functions including positioning of the minipermeameter probe. Automation gives rapid return on investment in terms of time saved. Conversion of minipermeameter flowrates to mD values is recommended in two ways, by minipermeametry and Hassler-sleeve measurement on standard homogeneous core plugs, and by use of an analytical solution. Core handling procedures can be improved to optimalise conditions for minipermeametry, which at the same time enhance geological description and cause less core damage. Minipermeametry has the potential to supercede 1" core plugs as the routine method for characterizing permeability in cores. Measurements made on dense sampling grids resolve fine scale heterogeneities not visible on CT-scan images. The low cost and rapidity of minipermeametry permits collection of large numbers of measurements which form statistically significant data sets, and give an accurate impression of reservoir heterogeneity. We believe that improved characterization of core permeability contributes directly to improved reservoir management.

title: 1990 Sca Conference Paper Number 90001
caption: Figure 9.--Relationship between pore types and throat sizes. (Modified from McCreesh et al., 1990.)
figure_reason: Shows the derived relationship between pore types and throat sizes from regression with mercury injection data, the main result.
tldr: Petrographic image analysis of thin sections yields 3-10 pore types per reservoir; regression against mercury injection links each type to a characteristic throat size, supporting permeability modelling.
summary: The paper presents petrographic image analysis (PIA), which measures pore size and shape from thin-section porosity patches (porels) using erosion-dilation differencing to build smooth/rough spectra. An unmixing algorithm (SAWVECB) applied to a set of related samples, ten or more, derives 3-10 discrete pore types and their proportions in each sample. Multiple regression of mercury injection saturation increments on pore type proportions gives the throat-size distribution of each type, shown for the Benoist Sandstone with R2 of 0.78-0.95. Most reservoirs show a pore type/throat size association, strongest in unbioturbated, clay-poor rocks and persisting in recrystallized dolomites. The association is attributed to depositional domains of like pores, which also raises a sample support problem for small plugs. NMR T1 modes and imbibition/drainage curves are cited as independent support.
abstract: consequence of the same reason, or is controlled by thermodynamic factors affecting the pore surface area of a recrystallized rock. To a first approximation, the coordination of all macropores is likely the same. If so, then the number of pore throats per unit volume will be proportional to the number of pores per unit volume. In this case, holding both porosity and capillary properties constant, the rock with the smaller sized pores will be the more permeable. This arises because the greater abundance of smaller pores results in greater numbers of pore throats.

title: 1990 Sca Conference Paper Number 90002
caption: Figure 7.- Regression surfaces with pore size and connectivity as independent variables, and permeability as dependent variable. Solid circles are the data projected on the surfaces (predictions) and vertical lines indicate the distances between data points and their projections (residuals).
figure_reason: Regression surfaces show permeability predicted from pore size and connectivity, the main result.
tldr: Erosion-dilation image analysis of thin sections gives pore size and a rough-area connectivity indicator that correlate with permeability in unconsolidated heavy oil sands from Alberta.
summary: The paper uses petrographic image analysis to estimate permeability from small samples. An erosion-dilation algorithm gives a generalized pore size distribution without identifying individual pores, and the ratio of rough to total pore area serves as a 2-D connectivity indicator. The method was applied to 22 horizontal plugs from the Provost Upper Mannville B Pool, with permeability measured on 19. Vertical and horizontal thin sections (16 images each) were analyzed, and permeabilities from about 2 to 12 darcy were regressed on mean pore size and connectivity. Both regressions were significant at the 5% level, with vertical sections giving the better relationship because they sample horizontal laminae. Unmixing identified four pore end members tied to lithofacies, from large connected pores in blocky channel sands to small pores in channel margin sands.
abstract: Petrographic image analysis has the potential to estimate flow properties of a reservoir rock by analyzing its pore geometry and pore structure. This analysis can be performed on samples which are too small for conventional flow experiments. Special image analysis algorithms have been used to measure pore size distributions and pore connectivities from two-dimensional pore images and the results have been related to measured permeability data.

title: Direct Measurement of the Constituent Porosities in a Dual Porosity Matrix
caption: Figure 1 - Comparison of mean porosities measured on various samples using helium porosimetry and the dual scan CT method. Samples include Berea sandstone, various carbonates, and EP Porous Structures Grade 15. Ideally all data points would fall on the dotted line.
figure_reason: Validates CT porosity against helium porosimetry across several rock types.
tldr: A two-scan X-ray CT method with xenon contrast gas measures matrix and fracture porosities directly in dual porosity cores without mineralogy or fracture-width assumptions, agreeing with helium porosity.
summary: Fractured, dual porosity cores are hard to characterize because single-scan CT porosity needs mineralogy assumptions and thresholding misses narrow fractures. The authors subtract CT images of the evacuated core from images of the xenon-saturated core in an aluminum pressure vessel, using a fourth-generation scanner at 120 kVp with 2 mm slices. Mean CT porosities agree with helium porosimetry for Berea, carbonates and a porous ceramic. Beam hardening gives a minimum porosity distribution width of about 4.5% of the mean. Time-sequenced scans of Monterey shale showed a high-permeability bed filling to 26.5% porosity and a bimodal porosity histogram. Bakken shale showed thin high-porosity beds along the core axis, and a coal sample had 10% fracture porosity at 30 s and stored 2.9 times the surrounding gas density after 4.3 days. Longer scans (8 s, 75 mA) and a minimized annulus gave the best images.
abstract: A direct measurement of core porosity by x-ray computed tomography (CT) has been used to determine the storage capacities (porosities) of several dual porosity systems. A contrast agent, time sequenced scanning, and image subtraction techniques are used to measure the porosities of both components of a dual porosity system. The method requires no knowledge of core mineralogy or assumptions about fracture width. To perform the measurement, a clean, dry, evacuated core contained in an aluminum pressure vessel is scanned. Then a single location in the sample is scanned repeatedly after introducing a radiopaque fluid. After the system comes to equilibrium, the saturated core is re-scanned. Subtraction of the evacuated images from the invaded images, after scaling, provides quantitative porosity images. The porosity of narrow fractures, which may be invisible to a thresholding technique, can be quantified. This sequential scanning procedure can determine fracture/matrix permeability ratios if the fracture permeability is an order of magnitude different than the matrix permeability. The porosity images provide statistically accurate porosity distributions. The width of the porosity distribution is a good indicator of porosity heterogeneity. The mean of the distribution agrees very well with helium porosity measurements. Data from samples of Monterey shale, Bakken shale, and coal are used to illustrate the method. Fracture porosity and permeability are of great interest because of their effects on hydrocarbon capacity and producibility of highly fractured reservoirs. Previously published techniques for detecting fractures in whole core samples include methods such as epoxy impregnation of the core and CT measurements in which a contrast agent is injected into the sample prior to scanning (Bergosh and Lord, 1987). The first method is destructive. The second requires an assumption of the fracture width, and the contribution to the porosity of very small fractures is missed because of the thresholding method used. We present here a method of measuring the constituent porosities of dual porosity systems which uses an X-ray contrast agent along with multiple X-ray computed tomography (CT) scans of a core to obtain direct measurements of the porosity. Unlike estimates made using single scans, this technique requires no assumptions of either fracture width or core mineralogy. In the following, the methods used to measure porosity and to detect dual porosity using CT are described. The effects of several experimental variables on the statistics and errors of the measurement are examined. Finally, data from three fractured samples are provided as examples of the technique.

title: Advances in APEX Technology
caption: Figure 7. Comparison of Permeability Values.
figure_reason: Compares APEX upper and lower bound permeability estimates with measured air and brine permeabilities.
tldr: Bivariate pore-body and pore-throat distributions from constant-rate mercury porosimetry (APEX) feed parameter-free models of Archie's m and permeability, matching limited measurements on sandstones and carbonates.
summary: Slow constant-rate mercury injection (APEX) resolves pore space into pore bodies (subisons) and throats (risons), each with entry pressure and volume. From these, subison and rison bivariate distribution functions are built, shown for Berea sandstone and San Andres dolomite. The subison distribution gives residual non-wetting saturation and the residual-initial relationship. The rison distribution, used in a parallel capillary tube formalism, gives Archie's lithologic exponent (m = 1 + log(S/2)/log φ) and permeability (k = 477φ/S Σ A_r/Pe²), with upper and lower bounds depending on how unfilled pore space is treated. Comparison with measurements on 1/2 inch and 1 inch samples (Berea, Bentheim, San Andres, Red River, chert) shows good agreement: sandstone m values lie near the lower bounds, carbonates near the upper bounds, and air permeabilities generally fall between bounds. The author notes the comparison set is limited and that more data and tests with one-ended mercury entry are needed.
abstract: The study of porous media using data obtained from slow constant-rate mercury intrusion experiments is continued. The apparatus is referred to as APEX (Apparatus for Pore Examination). APEX resolves the pore space into pore bodies (subisons) and pore throats (risons) each of which are characterized by entry pressure and volume. Bivariate distribution functions of subisons and risons are developed which represent the pore space fraction found at a given entry pressure and volume. These distribution functions are used in expressions for macroscopic rock properties which demonstrate that it is possible to represent macroscopic properties of porous media in terms of pore-scale properties. The subison bivariate distribution function is used in expressions for residual non-wetting phase saturation and residual-initial relationship while the rison bivariate distribution function is used in expressions for Archie's lithologic exponent and absolute permeability. Two of the parameters are flow properties and their expressions are derived from simple pore models which contain average pore throat properties that are explicitly determined from APEX rison data. APEX models have no free parameters. The formation resistivity factor (from which Archie's lithologic exponent is obtained), porosity and residual non-wetting phase saturation are simply related. The permeability model presented here relates permeability to residual non-wetting phase saturation, porosity and the rison-averaged square pore diameter. Excellent agreement is found between APEX models and experimental measurements on a limited set of one inch samples for which Archie's lithologic exponent, absolute permeability and additional APEX data have been measured. However, more extensive comparisons between theory and experiment are needed to confirm the relationships derived in this paper. The current work lays the foundation for future APEX study of more complicated rock properties.

title: Pore Volume Compressibilities under Different Stress Conditions
caption: Figure 5: Pore volume compressibility (under simulated production) as a function of pore pressure
figure_reason: Shows pore volume compressibility under simulated production versus pore pressure, the key result including rising compressibility in some samples.
tldr: Pore volume compressibility of sandstones measured under hydrostatic compression and simulated uniaxial-strain drawdown differs by up to a factor of two, so hydrostatic values misrepresent production conditions.
summary: Routine pore volume compressibility is measured under hydrostatic compression at constant (atmospheric) pore pressure, which does not reflect reservoir drawdown with constant overburden and zero lateral strain. Seven relatively unconsolidated sandstones were tested: three twin pairs (Group A) under both hydrostatic compression and simulated production, and four samples (Group B) under simulated production only. Drawdown ran from 4800 to 2000 psi with confining pressure servo-controlled to hold lateral strain constant. At equivalent effective mean stress, simulated-production compressibility was up to about twice the hydrostatic value (e.g., A-3 at 4200-2000 psi: 30.4 vs 22 ×10^-6 psi^-1; A-2: 28.9 vs 6). Samples A-1, A-2 and B-4 showed rising compressibility with drawdown, attributed to microfracturing and pore collapse driven by deviatoric stress. The authors conclude hydrostatic values should not be used directly for reservoir characterization and that compressibility depends on absolute pore pressure, not effective stress alone.
abstract: Pore Volume Compressibilities were determined for reservoir rocks at different in-situ conditions representative of reservoir drawdown. Such conditions are simulated in the laboratory by subjecting a reservoir rock sample to virgin in-situ conditions as described by the overburden stress, average lateral stress, pore pressure and temperature, followed by pore pressure drawdown. During pore pressure drawdown, zero lateral deformation (representing horizontal restraint) and constant axial stress (representing constant overburden) are maintained. Pore volume compressibilities for sandstone were measured under simulated in-situ conditions and hydrostatic compression (conventional). The results show the pore volume compressibilities measured under the two conditions can differ by as much as a factor of two. This can have significant impact on designing reservoir management strategies. Based on the assumption that the rock bulk and the pore system deform elastically, the relationships between pore volume compressibilities measured at simulated drawdown conditions with other conventional methods, as well as the relationship to different compressibilities are presented in the paper. In addition the experimental methods used will be described. Modification of the reservoir effectivive stress by virtue of production impacts the volumetric changes in pore spaces in a reservoir. The engineering parameters quantifying these volumetric variations are compressibilities.
