The application of reliable compressibility includes reservoir pressure maintenance and subsidence evaluations (Ruddy et al., 1989; Johnson et al., 1989; Geertsma, 1973). Production forecasting is intimately related to a total system compressibility combining the saturation weighted compressibilities of liquid and gaseous phases in the pore space and the pore volume compressibility, often referred to as formation compressibility. Correlations are often used (Hall, 1953). These, although readily applicable, may be in error by an order of magnitude (Earlougher, 1977). Correlations such as this as well as certain laboratory determinations are applied with risk largely because of poor appreciation of the mechanics of compressibilities and the stress paths during laboratory testing. For formations that will be subject to nonlinear elastic or inelastic pore deformation with changes in reservoir pressure, there is need to determine its pore compressibility along pressure/strain history paths encountered during production and water injection (flooding). Three types of compressibilities are often cited in characterization of a porous medium. There is Bulk Compressibility, $C_b$ , representing the relative changes in bulk volume of the medium; Solid (Grain) Compressibility, $C_s$ , describing the relative changes in the solid portion of the medium; and, Pore Volume Compressibility, $C_p$ , describing relative changes in pore volume. The most often used definitions of compressibility are as follows: $$C_{bc} = \frac{-1}{V_b} \left( \frac{\partial V_b}{\partial P_c} \right)_{P_p} \quad \text{and} \quad C_{bp} = \frac{1}{V_b} \left( \frac{\partial V_b}{\partial P_p} \right)_{P_c} \quad (1)$$ $$C_{pc} = \frac{-1}{V_p} \left( \frac{\partial V_p}{\partial P_c} \right)_{P_p} \quad \text{and} \quad C_{pp} = \frac{1}{V_p} \left( \frac{\partial V_p}{\partial P_p} \right)_{P_c} \quad (2)$$ $$C_{sc} = C_{sp} = \frac{-1}{V_b} \left( \frac{\partial V_b}{\partial P_c} \right)_{P_p} = \frac{1}{V_p} \left( \frac{\partial V_p}{\partial P_p} \right)_{P_c}, \quad (d(P_c - P_p) = 0) \quad (3)$$ where: - • subscript $b$ denotes bulk volume, - • subscript $p$ represents pore pressure or pore volume, - • subscript $c$ indicates confining pressure is applied, - • subscript $s$ denotes solid volume (grain portion of the rock), - • $P_c$ and $P_p$ denote confining and pore pressure, respectively, and, - • Subscript outside of parenthesis indicates the pressure to be maintained constant. In the foregoing equations, the first subscript indicates the volume component of interest, while the second indicates the pressure/stress causing the relative volume change. The interrelationship between all of the above compressibilities can theoretically be derived based on stress conditions and constraints, Zimmerman (1986), for example, derived such relationships: $$C_{bp} = C_{bc} - C_{sc} \quad (4)$$ $$C_{pc} = (C_{bc} - C_{sc})/\phi \quad (5)$$ $$C_{pp} = [C_{bc} - (1 + \phi)C_{sc}]/\phi \quad (6)$$ where $\phi$ is the sample porosity. The two bulk compressibilities, ( $C_{bc}$ and $C_{bp}$ ), and grain compressibility ( $C_{sc} = C_{sp}$ ) are measured directly from specimen volumetric deformation. Pore compressibility ( $C_p$ ), the fundamental compressibility from a production perspective, can only be determined indirectly through measurement of volume changes of the pore fluid. Therefore, the measurement of $C_p$ is complicated by a number of factors. These include the compressibility of the pore fluids, the degree of saturation, the pore space connectivity, the morphology, distribution and aspect ratio of the pore structure and the compressibility of the test system. To minimize the effect of these factors and to simplify testing procedures, most routine industrial pore volume compressibility measurements are performed by subjecting a sample to hydrostatic compression with constant pore pressure, usually atmospheric pressure (so that no pore fluid compressibility problem is involved). This is a special case of $C_{pc}$ : $$C_{pc} = \frac{\partial V_p}{V_p \partial P_c}, \quad (P_p = 0, \text{ or constant}) \quad (7)$$ or even more simplified, $$C_{pc} = \frac{\partial V_b}{V_b \partial P_c}, \quad (P_p = 0, \text{ or constant}) \quad (8)$$

title: Investigation of Cycle Dependent Centrifuge Capillary Pressure and Wettability Index Behavior for Water-Wet High Permeability Sandstones
caption: Figure 4. - Capillary pressure results for plug A from high RPM, long-term centrifuge tests.![](_page_19_Figure_5.jpeg)
figure_reason: Capillary pressure curves for plug A across cycles show hysteresis and shifting imbibition curves, the central result.
tldr: Multi-cycle centrifuge drainage/imbibition tests on fired Bentheimer and Berea sandstones show wettability index falling with successive cycles, non-uniform CT saturations, and Teflon jackets failing to stop edge imbibition.
summary: The study examines cycle-dependent hysteresis in centrifuge capillary pressure and USBM wettability index for water-wet, high-permeability fired sandstones: Bentheimer (3500 md) and two Bereas (1330 and 832 md). 3.8 cm Teflon-wrapped plugs were cycled through drainage and imbibition with brine and Soltrol 100 at up to about 200 kPa, using 1 h or 48 h equilibration, with mercury porosimetry, Amott cells and CT scanning as support. Hysteresis appeared in every multi-cycle test; imbibition curves shifted to lower water saturation, and wettability index decreased with cycling, likely due to increased oil trapping. Hassler-Brunner and Rajan solutions were similar, with Rajan more consistent, and equilibration time (1 vs 48 h) had little effect. CT showed piston-like, non-uniform saturation distributions until about 800 RPM, differing between rocks, and brine imbibed around plug margins despite the Teflon jacket. A report form for documenting centrifuge test parameters is proposed.

title: 1990 Sca Conference Paper Number 9007
caption: Fig. 6: Oil Recovery at Breakthrough vs Average Wettability Index
figure_reason: Shows oil recovery at breakthrough correlating with average wettability index, a key result.
tldr: Radial waterfloods on 22 Berea cores, with Amott wettability and mercury porosimetry on plugs, link surface area and pore-throat size to wettability, oil recovery and residual oil.
summary: The study examines how surface area and pore-size distribution affect oil recovery at breakthrough and floodout, residual oil saturation and wettability in Berea sandstone. Waterfloods were run on 22 radial Berea cores (12.7 cm diameter, 5.08 cm long) with 10 cp oil at 35°C. Twenty-four plugs from each core were then used for Amott wettability tests and mercury porosimetry. Wettability indices ranged from +0.45 to +1.00, indicating heterogeneous, hydrophilic-dominated wetting. Regression showed wettability rising with irreducible water saturation and falling with residual oil saturation, and both recoveries rose with wettability and surface area. Median pore-throat size was about 15 µm, and tortuosity (retention time) was inversely related to median pore-throat size. Mercury hysteresis and entrapment were attributed to ink-bottle pores and related to differences in Sor.
abstract: 24 core plugs were extracted from each of the 22 waterflooded Berea sandstone cores and were used in the wettability and porosimetry studies. Amott's method was used to determine the average wettability indices. Results indicated that the wettability of Berea Sandstone rocks is heterogeneous with hydrophilic dominance. Furthermore, regression analysis indicated that the average wettability index was directly proportional to the average irreducible water saturation and inversely proportional to the average residual oil saturation, and wettability was directly proportional to oil recovery at breakthrough and oil recovery at floodout.

title: Relative Permeability Technology and Applications
tldr: A review of relative permeability: controlling factors, formation damage, gas-condensate, three-phase and EOR processes, reservoir-condition testing, saturation measurement technology and use of models in simulation.
summary: This review covers the factors controlling relative permeability, including saturation, rock properties, wettability, hysteresis, initial saturation and flow rate. It discusses how relative permeability tests reveal formation damage, and how heterogeneity, bedding, vugs and fractures complicate measurements. It stresses testing at reservoir conditions with live fluids and net confining stress, and covers gas-condensate, three-phase (ternary isoperms, hysteresis, CO2 versus nitrogen) and chemical, thermal and gas EOR behavior. It also summarizes steady-state, unsteady-state and centrifuge methods and in situ saturation techniques (CT, NMR imaging, X-ray, microwave, with accuracy around ±2%). Empirical and statistical models, agreement with well tests, and pseudo relative permeabilities for simulation are addressed; no new experimental data are presented.

title: Obtaining Relative Permeability Data Using a Combination of Steady-State and Unsteady-State Corefloods
caption: Figure 2. Steady-state and USS waterflood results for carbonate core.
figure_reason: Carbonate case showing steady-state and JBN unsteady-state curves, with kro shape defined near residual oil.
tldr: Combining steady-state and unsteady-state waterfloods in one coreflood extends the saturation range of oil-water relative permeability data and checks unsteady-state validity, shown on three core examples.
summary: Unsteady-state waterfloods give no relative permeability data before breakthrough and can be corrupted by viscous fingering or heterogeneity, while steady-state tests struggle near residual oil saturation. The authors run steady-state oil-water flow at one or more fractional flows and then an unsteady-state waterflood without returning the core to low water saturation, using JBN analysis. They argue theoretically that the JBN results are insensitive to initial water saturation. Three cases are presented: a 95 md carbonate composite where the waterflood after 3% oil fractional flow defined the kro shape near residual oil, a 0.12 md shaly siltstone where steady-state points at 80% and 20% oil fractional flow covered the transition-zone saturations, and a 4560 md sandstone composite with viscosity ratio 131 where a 2% oil steady-state point confirmed the unsteady-state data with no apparent fingering. In all cases the steady-state and unsteady-state data were consistent and complementary.
abstract: Oil-water relative permeability curves are commonly measured on core samples in the laboratory by either steady-state or unsteady-state fluid displacement techniques. Experimentally, the unsteady-state waterflood is the simpler technique; however, the valid interpretation of ut of unsteady-state data depends on the flood being unaffected by viscous fingering and core heterogeneity. If such non-ideal effects are significant in an unsteady-state waterflood, the calculated relative permeability curves can have serious errors. A second drawback of the unsteady-state method is that it fails to provide data near irreducible water saturation. By combining the steady-state and unsteady-state techniques in a single experiment, we have been able to obtain relative permeability data that would not be available from either technique separately. In the combined experiment, steady-state measurements are made by pumping oil and water through the core simultaneously. The steady-state measurements are followed by an unsteady-state waterflood, without returning the core to low water saturation. Three examples of applying these techniques are presented, each illustrating a different advantage of combining steady-state and unsteady-state measurements.

title: Pore Structure Characteristics of Low Permeability Shales from Deep Formations
caption: Figure 3: Typical pore size distribution (from Katsube et al., in preparation).
figure_reason: Shows typical unimodal pore size distributions, with Type-A and Type-B shales concentrated at nanometre scale.
tldr: Porosity, mercury porosimetry, formation factor, resistivity and texture data on ten deep Venture field shales suggest clay-lined surface networks distinct from macropore networks control ionic transport.
summary: Ten shale samples from 4693-5557 m in the Venture Gas Field, offshore Nova Scotia, were studied to understand pore structure and diagenetic controls on very low permeability. Effective porosity (0.8-9.3%), formation factor (240-1600, with 17600 for one sample), bulk and surface resistivity, mercury porosimetry and XRD/SEM/thin-section texture analysis were combined. Pore size distributions are unimodal in the 2.5-25 nm range with geometric means of 8.7-16.2 nm, and are classed as Type A, B or AB. Pore sizes derived from permeability and formation factor (9-11 nm) match the mercury means, indicating that pores larger than 25 nm are not part of the main flow paths. Comparison of porosity and resistivity parameters indicates a network of clay-lined surfaces that need not coincide with the macropore network, so diffusion may persist even where cementation blocks pores to flow.
abstract:
A petrophysical study consisting of porosity, permeability, formation factor and electrical resistivity measurements have been carried out on a set of shale samples taken at depths between 4500m and 5600m in the Venture Gas field offshore Nova Scotia. In addition, shale texture analysis, which includes scanning electron microscope analysis were performed on some of the samples. The purpose of the study is to obtain information on the mechanisms related to the porosity and permeability changes with progressive depths during sedimentary basin development. This information is necessary for quantitative sedimentary basin modelling, and to understand the reasons for the very low permeabilities exhibited by many tight shales.

A previous study indicated that the permeabilities of these shales are of the order of 10^-22 - 10^-20 m^2 and that this is because the main flow paths are very tortuous with pore sizes in the order of 8 to 16nm, and with porosity concentrated in the extremely small pores.

Results of this study suggests the existence of a network of clay-lined surfaces that do not necessarily coincide with the network of pores. This implies that even when cementation occurs and completely blocks the pores to fluid flow, it does not necessarily prevent the transport of chemical species by diffusion, the network of clay-lined surfaces most likely being the pathway. Lack of clay-lined surfaces in well cemented rocks could not only isolate the pores, but could cause resistance to later development of pores by dissolution. Well-cemented shales with little or no clay-lined surfaces may play an important role in preserving porosity during basement development, and preserving high pressure fluids.

title: Advances in Centrifuge Methodology for Core Analysis
caption: Fig.6a—Exponential Fit to Long Time Production Data
figure_reason: Shows stretched exponential fit extrapolating one-day data to ten-day production for Berea, key to equilibrium extrapolation.
tldr: Reviews centrifuge capillary pressure analyses, presents an automated ultracentrifuge and stretched-exponential extrapolation, and shows history matching with fixed Pc gives less biased oil relative permeability than simultaneous Pc estimation.
summary: The paper reviews centrifuge methods for capillary pressure and relative permeability, recasting Hassler-Brunner and later finite-core-length corrections (Hoffman, van Domselaar, Rajan) in a common form alongside an exact solution. An automated Beckman ultracentrifuge with a line camera records oil and water production at 4 µl resolution for six cores. Multi-stage gravity drainage on ~200 mD Berea and reservoir samples showed equilibrium was not reached after 24 hours, and a stretched exponential with β = 0.77 extrapolated one-day data to ten days. History matching with an automatic simulator (rotational discrimination) compared fixed Pc (Procedure I) with simultaneous Pc and kr estimation (Procedure II). Procedure II misrepresented the sharp Pc elbow, and the kr curves differed by up to an order of magnitude below 30% saturation, so fixing Pc from Hassler-Brunner points is recommended.
abstract: The centrifuge provides a powerful tool for the determination of relative permeability, capillary pressure, and residual saturation. Experiments may be performed rapidly, and over a wide range of accelerations, to effectively displace fluid from core samples. Advances in instrumentation have provided information on fluid production, with high volumetric and temporal accuracy. Advances in analysis utilize semi-analytic and numerical techniques to obtain detailed information on displacement mechanisms. Experimental results are presented for Berea sandstone, and for reservoir rock samples, emphasizing the transient production of oil in a gravity drainage process. A critical review is provided of the usual methods of centrifuge methodology for core analysis. Lack of mechanical equilibrium, and the stripping of non-wetting phase residual (Critical Bond number effects) may compromise the determination of capillary pressure. Finite core length effects will be described as well. The usual analysis of transient production for relative permeability neglects the effects of capillary retention of fluid. This will bias the resulting relative permeability, leading to artificially high values of residual saturation. History matching can provide the correction of capillary pressure for lack of equilibrium, and the correction of relative permeability as capillary retention becomes important. However, the results may be dependent upon the models of relative permeability and capillary pressure which are introduced. It is shown how a combined analytical / numerical approach can provide unbiased estimates of these curves. Recommended core analysis methodologies, both experimental and analytic, are provided.

title: "Correlations of Liquid and Air Permeabilities for Use in Reservoir Engineering Studies"
caption: Figure 6
figure_reason: Effective oil versus air permeability correlation for the clayey reservoir, used to predict oil permeability and cut costs.
tldr: Correlates air permeability with oil and brine permeability for 1868 samples, showing air permeability approximates liquid permeability and can predict effective oil permeability in a clayey reservoir, cutting costs.
summary: Amoco analyzed 40 years of specific permeability data from 875 wells to test whether routine air permeabilities can represent liquid permeabilities. Air-versus-oil data for 1868 samples (1117 sandstones, 422 dolomites, 329 limestones; 0.1 to 10,000 md) correlate closely, with oil slightly lower, attributed to the Klinkenberg effect. Brine permeability is lower, with a brine-to-air ratio of about 0.5 across the range, and rock types show similar deviations. For a clayey reservoir (16% smectite, 4% chlorite, 3% kaolinite), effective oil permeability measured on 71 of 282 samples was correlated with air permeability. The oil-to-air ratio is about 1.0 at 10,000 md, 0.53 at 1000 md and 0.12 at 1 md. The correlation estimated oil permeability for the other 211 samples, so oil permeability was measured on only about 25% of samples, reducing costs.
abstract: Specific (single phase) permeabilities to air, brine and oil are routinely measured in conjunction with relative permeability tests conducted in our laboratories. These data, including the standard air permeabilities, are used to evaluate reservoir quality, to aid in development of a reservoir description, and to approximate reservoir flow characteristics. Specific permeabilities were analyzed for data that have accumulated on numerous reservoirs over the past 40 years. Included are comparisons of specific air permeabilities to both oil and brine permeabilities for 1868 samples from sandstone and carbonate reservoirs, covering a permeability range from 0.1 to 10,000 md. The results show a strong correlation between specific permeabilities and that air permeabilities are valuable in the characterization of reservoir quality. A correlation of effective oil permeability to air permeability covering a wide range in permeability was developed for a clayey reservoir. This illustrates a second application for the use of air permeabilities in reservoir descriptions. The correlation was successfully used for predicting effective oil permeabilities from standard air permeabilities measured on cores throughout the field. The method reduced overall core analysis costs by limiting the number of oil permeability measurements required to get a good estimate of reservoir permeability.

title: The Measurement of Gas Relative Permeability for Low Permeability Cores Using a Pressure Transient Method Sca Paper 9013 by
caption: Fig. 11 Relative Permeability Curves for Sam Hughes No. 1 Cores
figure_reason: Gas relative permeability versus water saturation curves for Sam Hughes cores, showing the method's main output.
tldr: A modified pressure-transient apparatus measures gas relative permeability and water saturation together on tight Travis Peak cores without removing them, in days rather than weeks.
summary: Steady-state gas relative permeability measurements on tight cores take weeks because flow rates are very small. The authors rebuilt a Texas A&M pressure-pulse apparatus (CPD cart) with a flow-through, minimal-volume downstream system. Water can then be produced stepwise from the core while it stays in the holder, and gas porosity and permeability are history-matched from each pulse test. Eight Travis Peak sandstone cores (absolute permeability 4 µd to 0.63 md) were tested at about 2,000 psi net stress and 1,000 psi pore pressure with 50 psi pulses. Helium, pressure-transient and weight porosities agreed within about 5%. A full drainage curve took 1 to 7 days, and the one-phase interpretation was accurate below 50% Sw and acceptable to 70%. Room-temperature fluctuation scattered the data on the lowest-permeability cores. The workable absolute permeability range is about 1 µd to 1 md.

title: The Determination of Fracture Toughness of Rocks by Chevron-Notched Brazilian Disk Specimens
caption: Figure 7. Chevron-notched Brazilian disk (CDISK) specimen
figure_reason: Shows the CDISK specimen geometry and parameters central to the proposed method and its equations.
tldr: Proposes the chevron-notched Brazilian disk for rock fracture toughness in lateral crack directions; tests on sandstone and limestone show higher toughness for the smallest disks.
summary: Existing ISRM methods (Short Rod, CENRBB) give only Mode I toughness and restrict crack direction, so lateral propagation relevant to hydraulic fracturing cannot be tested. The authors adapt the chevron-notched Brazilian disk (CDISK), deriving a dimensionless stress intensity coefficient Y* from the Munz simplified method and straight-crack solutions, and tabulating minimum values for disk and saw sizes. Thirty-six disks (2.125, 3.125 and 4.125 in. diameter) of Vosges sandstone and Indiana limestone were dried and loaded in an MTS frame at 0.04 in/min with load cycling. Mean K_Ic was 0.76, 0.48 and 0.58 MPa√m for sandstone and 1.55, 1.36 and 1.25 MPa√m for limestone at 2.125, 3.125 and 4.125 in. respectively. The smallest disks gave the highest toughness (37% above 3.125 in. for sandstone), indicating a size effect. The compressive stress near the crack tip is argued to limit the process zone, so toughness can be taken directly from peak load.
abstract: During the past decade, many laboratory techniques have been developed in an attempt to measure the fracture toughness of rocks. This has led, unfortunately, to a lack of consistency in the already scarce data bank. Differences as large as one order of magnitude have been reported for the same rock formation. In order to standardize the testing procedure, the International Society for Rock Mechanics recently published two Suggested Methods; one based on the Short Rod geometry (SR), and one on the bending of circular cores, the Chevron Edge Notch Round Bar in Bending test (CENRBB). However, these methods have some limitations; they will only provide Mode I fracturing parameters and are limited in scope as far as the propagation direction is concerned. Indeed, the SR can only accommodate crack propagation down the core length; while the CENRBB test imposes a fracture to propagate in a direction perpendicular to its axis. Hence, when considering for example the case of a man-induced hydraulic fracture, one of the pertinent horizontal growth directions cannot be studied by either test. The Chevron-notched Brazilian Disk (CDISK) geometry, described in this paper, addresses this particular situation: it provides a complementary procedure allowing the investigation of lateral fracture propagation. Hence, the inherent toughness anisotropy can also be studied in great detail. The advantages of this particular geometry can be summarized as follows: i) the specimen is core-based; ii) the measured fracture toughness is determined in the most pertinent direction, particularly when contemplating hydraulic fracturing stimulation treatments; iii) the specimen is easy to prepare; and, iv) the testing is trivial. In addition to Mode I fracture tests, this approach may also be used to investigate mixed-mode fracturing situations. Two types of rock were used in this preliminary study: a fine grained Vosges Sandstone and an Indiana Limestone. Different sizes of disks were also considered in order to investigate any potential size effect.

title: Wettability Evaluation During Restored State Core Analysis
caption: Fig. 3 – Imbibition and secondary drainage capillary pressure curves with crude oil in the “AS RECEIVED” cores.
figure_reason: Capillary pressure curves for as-received cores with crude oil show oil-wet/mixed-wet behavior, USBM -1.12, and mixed-wet model.
tldr: Sequential solvent cleaning, unlike Dean-Stark, makes North Sea sandstone cores water-wet; aging restores mixed wettability, and much remaining oil in mixed-wet cores is a capillary end effect.
summary: The study evaluates wettability changes through restored state core analysis of North Sea sandstone cores (200–500 md, porosity about 0.25) to estimate remaining oil saturation after waterflooding. An automated centrifuge gave USBM and Amott indices; as-received cores were oil-wet (USBM about -1.12), and Dean-Stark toluene plus chloroform-methanol cleaning left them intermediate-wet. A multi-solvent sequence (alphamethylnaphthalene, toluene, chloroform, chloroform-methanol, methanol) raised USBM to about 1.0 and remaining oil saturation from 9% (crude, as received) to 28% (refined oil), still below the 37.5% water-wet value. Aging 28 days in crude made cores mixed-wet and lowered residual oil by about 0.13; Dean-Stark cores stayed more oil-wet, differing by about 0.04 in residual oil. Brownell-Katz analysis and CT scans showed that remaining oil in mixed-wet cores is mainly held by capillary end effects with film-drainage production, so reservoir remaining oil must be computed from relative permeability and buoyancy.
abstract: Wettability changes during stages of restored state core analysis were evaluated for a North Sea reservoir. The goal was to determine the proper technique for estimating the remaining oil saturation after waterflooding from core analysis. The traditional methods for quantifying wettability, i.e., USBM and Amott indices and the Brownell-Katz correlation, were evaluated. It was found that the USBM and Amott procedures, when modified slightly, could be interpreted to give a good indication of wettability. The traditional method of cleaning cores by Dean-Stark extraction with toluene followed by chloroform/methanol was found to be ineffective in making a core water-wet. To overcome this difficulty, we evaluated core cleaning procedures that employ a sequence of solvents. The remaining oil saturation increased from 9% with crude oil in the "as received" state to 28% with refined oil after the third cleaning. Once the cores were made water-wet, aging the cores in a North Sea crude oil returned them to a mixed-wet state. However, the restored state cores were not as oil-wet as the "as received" state cores. Even after aging, there was a significant difference between the cores cleaned by Dean-Stark extraction and by a sequence of solvents. The mixed-wet condition with the North Sea crude oil is, therefore, expected to apply to the field: the crude oil base number, isoelectric point, effluent pH during core floods, and bottle wettability tests support this contention. --- Copyright 1990, SPE SPE 20506, 1990 SPE Ann. Tech. Conf. (Sept. 23-26, 1990), New Orleans Examination on of the Brownell-Katz number correlation and the capillary pressure curves showed that much of the remaining oil saturation in a mixed-wet core during core analysis could be due to retention by a capillary end effect. This was supported by a CT scan of the core. In this mixed-wet reservoir, the remaining oil saturation is not equal to the residual oil saturation, but must be calculated using the appropriate relative permeability curve and the effect of buoyancy.

title: Horizontal Core Acquisition And Orientation For Formation Evaluation
authors: Monte M. Mann Diamant Boart Stratabit
caption: Figure 13 - Comparison Of EMI And Observed Principal Scribe Line Rotation
figure_reason: Shows EMI-derived scribe line rotation versus observed laboratory groove rotation, demonstrating orientation accuracy including scribe skip cases.
tldr: Describes coring assembly, stabilization, electronic multishot survey and laser alignment improvements that give near-complete recovery and accurate orientation of horizontal core from fractured carbonates.
summary: Horizontal drilling in fractured carbonates needs core to define facies and fractures, but recovery and orientation were unreliable. Oryx and service companies developed a medium-radius coring assembly with fiberglass inner barrels, multiple core catchers, a modified core head and dual-stabilizer outer barrel. The dual-stabilizer design (1/8 in and 1/2 in undergauge) held inclination drop to about 0.1°/30 ft versus 0.3° for a slick assembly and 0.7° for two-point stabilization, giving near-100% recovery on four projects. Orientation used an Electronic Multishot Instrument with non-magnetic collars, shock absorber, blade centralizers and a patent-pending Laser Alignment System accurate to ±1°, versus errors up to 26° with optical telescope alignment. Laboratory comparison of EMI toolface with observed groove rotation agreed closely, and 'scribe skip' of up to 86° was identified as unique to horizontal coring; fractures were measured by goniometer and classified as natural or induced.
abstract: The increase in horizontal drilling activity has produced a need for improved coring technology. The development of a reliable horizontal (medium radius) coring and orientation system has greatly improved the acquisition of information necessary for formation evaluation and reservoir engineering. A concerted effort between Oryx Energy Company and service companies has resulted in newly developed hardare and methods for obtaining horizontal core sections. Horizontal coring presents for the first time an opportunity to directly examine the lateral evolution of rock facies, reservoir heterogeneity, vertical fracture spacing, and fluid distribution. These data are essential to understanding horizontal well behavior and are particularly useful in reservoir modeling. Reservoir description is the foundation for designing, operating and evaluating the performance of a horizontal wellbore.

title: Paper - SCA # 9018 Imbibition Flooding with CO2-Enriched Water
caption: Fig. 4 - Cumulative Oil Displaced - Limestone, 29 md
figure_reason: Shows carbonated water versus brine imbibition recovery in a 29 md limestone, including the CO2 evolution effect on production.
tldr: Spontaneous imbibition of 1% carbonated water in 1-in. sandstone and limestone cores gives faster, higher oil recovery than brine, by 6-16% OOIP over 72 hours.
summary: Fractured, low-permeability matrix reservoirs leave much oil behind because injected fluids bypass the matrix, so the authors tested carbonated water to improve imbibition rate and recovery. Visual imbibition cells held 1-in. sandstone and limestone cores saturated with 35 API diesel. Cores were soaked 72 hours at 70°F and atmospheric pressure in 20,000 ppm NaCl brine or 1% CO2 water (pH 5). Carbonated water recovered an extra 6% OOIP in a 420 md sandstone, 8% in a 76 md sandstone, 14% in a 29 md limestone and 16% in a 7 md limestone. Limestone dissolved 0.4-0.5% by weight, and oil permeability rose by about 13 md in sandstone and 6 md in limestone. CO2 also reduced capillary retention of oil droplets on the rock face and the contact angle, and depressurization gave solution-gas drive. The Graham and Richardson sqrt(k/φ) correlation held for sandstone but not limestone.
abstract: The objectives of the laboratory research were to evaluate the improvement in the imbibition rate and recovery efficiency at room temperature and atmospheric conditions in core samples by using CO2-enriched water in place of regular formation brine. Tests were run using 1 in. diameter cores in visual imbibition cells. The results of laboratory experiments show the inclusion of CO2 into the imbibed water improves both the imbibition rate and the recovery efficiency. A 1% carbonated water solution recovered an additional 8% of oil in place in a 76 md sandstone, and an additional 16% of oil in place from a 7 md limestone during a standard soak time of 72 hours. The study of the new displacement method with the 1in. cores indicated a substantial portion of mobile oil remains attached to the rock face as oil droplets because of capillary retention during brine imbibition. The inclusion of CO2 in the flood water greatly reduced both the effect of capillary retention and the contact angle. The release of the oil held by capillary retention along the walls of a fracture system in a reservoir stimulated both oil recovery and imbibition rate. The major factors affecting the increased recovery appear to be the increase in oil mobility, the introduction of a gas phase that acts as solution-gas drive when a drawdown is induced, and the reduction of interfacial tension. Another significant factor is the matrix dissolution of carbonate rocks and clay mineral clean up.

title: Improved Method for Extraction and Quantification of Hydrocarbon Content of Sponge Core Liners
caption: Fig. 6 - Belridge sponge core oil recovery.
figure_reason: Shows measured versus injected oil volume for Belridge crude, demonstrating accuracy of the extraction and quantification method.
tldr: Freon-11 Soxhlet extraction of sponge core liners, partial distillation and GC residual-solvent correction accurately recover oil volumes for crudes of 15-40 API gravity.
summary: Sponge core oil quantification was unreliable in a 1985 blind test of service company methods, showing random and systematic errors. The authors selected Freon-11 as extraction solvent because it does not swell polyurethane, dissolves crude well with little asphaltene precipitation, and boils at 23.8°C. They designed Soxhlet extractors for one-foot sponge sections in aluminum liners, with sintered stainless steel solvent dispersers and a chilled 5-bulb Allihn condenser, refluxing about one pore volume per hour for 48 hours. Extracts were partially distilled to 65°C vapor temperature, removing about 85% of the Freon, and residual Freon was measured by GC and subtracted, with centrifugation and KOH used to remove sponge material. Tests on synthetic samples with four oils showed good agreement between injected and measured volumes, and over 3000 feet of sponge core have been analyzed, with good agreement with log saturations.
abstract: We report a technique to extract and accurately quantify the amount of oil in a sponge core liner. We have successfully tested this technique for crudes having a wide range (15 to 40) of API gravities. The main advantages of sponge coring are that it is a comparatively inexpensive alternative to pressure core and operationally simpler. As the core is cut, it enters a half-inch thick polyurethane sponge liner inside the inner core barrel. As the core is brought to the surface, expanding gases displace otherwise immobile oil which is then captured by the sponge liner. By adding the amount of oil captured in the sponge to the amount left in the core, one obtains more accurate values of oil saturation. ![](_page_1_Picture_0.jpeg) However, a major disadvantage of sponge coring had been the absence of a reliable technique to quantify the amount of oil retained by the sponge. Various techniques had been tried by various service companies, including solvent extraction, hydraulic press, and retorting. We observed problems with each of these techniques. These included incomplete extraction of oil, mistaking extracted sponge components for oil, and the inability to either completely separate or account for the amount of solvent remaining in the crude extracts. We have found that Freon-11 (trichlorofluoromethane) is a good solvent for the extraction of crude oil from the sponge liner. Freon-11 is gentle on the polyurethane sponge, has good solvating power for all crude components, and its low boiling point allows easy removal of most of the solvent from the extracted crude oil. In this paper we describe the apparatus and procedures for extracting crude oil from sponge core.

title: Petrophysical Applications of Automated Proton High Resolution NMR Spectroscopy
caption: FIGURE 1 - 1H NMR SPECTRA OF (A) FREON-EXTRACTED BLANK SPONGE, (B) 0.84% VOL. AND (C) 15.87% VOL. OIL IN FREON-EXTRACTED BLANK SPONGE. RESONANCES IN (A) ARE CONSISTENT WITH POLYURETHANE BASED ON THE CURING OF AN AROMATIC DIISOCYANATE WITH A POLYESTER/POLYETHYLENE GLYCOL COPOLYMER. MAJOR OIL RESONANCES APPEAR AT 0.8 AND 1.3 PPM. CORRESPONDING TO METHYL AND REPEAT UNIT METHYLENE PROTONS.
figure_reason: Spectra of blank sponge and oil-spiked sponge extracts show the oil and polyurethane resonances underlying the quantification method.
tldr: Automated high-resolution 1H NMR quantifies oil and water in freon, chloroform/methanol and xylene core extracts accurately, and estimates crude viscosity from T1 relaxation.
summary: Routine core extraction solvents are normally discarded, though they contain oil and water that can be measured. Shell used automated high-resolution 1H NMR spectrometers with 120-tube sample changers and microVAX processing to analyze freon-11 extracts of polyurethane sponge liners, chloroform/methanol miscible flood extracts, and xylene Dean-Stark extracts. Spiked tests gave standard errors of about 0.04 cc (2%) for sponge extracts, 0.05 cc for oil and water in chloroform/methanol, and 0.03 cc (1.5%) in xylene. Distillation/GC over-read oil by 1-2 cc below 3 cc because residual urethane was counted as oil. T1 of the oil in dilute extracts correlates with undiluted crude viscosity. NMR of eleven chloroform/methanol flushes showed pure methanol still removed 0.6 cc brine (33% of initial water) after oil was fully extracted. The method takes about 10 minutes per sample and is in routine use.
abstract: INTRODUCTIONAlmost all of the procedures used in routine and special core analysis involve extracting fluids from cores with various solvents. In most cases, the core petrophysical quantities are determined by weight and volume measurements, and the extracts are normally discarded. However, automated high resolution proton NMR spectroscopy on these extracts can be used independently to obtain high accuracy measurements of oil and water content as well as estimates of oil properties such as viscosity. With the addition of $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR, further details of oil molecular structure such as aliphatic/aromatic ratio, C/H ratio, and branching can be obtained.

title: Rapid, Room-Temperature Quantitative Analysis of Oil in Sponge Core
caption: FIGURE 4. SPONGE CORE ANALYTICAL DATA
figure_reason: Validation data comparing known and measured oil volumes, showing accuracy of the method.
tldr: A room-temperature method shreds sponge core in methylene chloride and quantifies extracted oil by visible absorbance, recovering known oil volumes with 5.6% average error.
summary: Sponge coring corrects oil saturation for oil lost during core recovery, but this correction depends on complete oil extraction and accurate volume measurement. The paper presents a patent-pending method that soaks the sponge liner in methylene chloride, separates it from the aluminum liner, and shreds it with a high-speed rotary cutter in a sealed vessel for 20 minutes at room temperature. Oil in the filtered solvent is quantified by visible absorbance at 440 nm against calibration mixtures made with representative stock tank oil. Validation used 17 water-saturated sponge samples (6 in long, 4 in diameter) injected with known oil volumes. Blank correction for sponge dissolution was under 0.2 ml, detection was possible down to 0.04 ml, and average error was 5.6%, with the largest relative errors at trace oil volumes.
abstract: A new procedure (U.S. Patent Pending) for the rapid and quantitative extraction of oil from sponge core has been developed. Oil volumes are determined following extraction by optical spectrometry. Previously described methods for extraction of oil from sponge core rely on Soxhlet extraction or high pressure solvent washing techniques. Our method involves high speed disaggregation of the sponge in a pressure tight disposable container. Typically, oil is quantitatively extracted from a sponge sample at room temperature within 20 minutes. Water removal prior to oil extraction is unnecessary.

title: Laboratory Measurements of Capillary and Electrical Properties of Rock Samples at Reservoir Conditions : Effect of Some Parameters
caption: Fig. 12 - Comparison of IR vs. Sw for sandstone B. Illustration of the effect of wettability on n. n increases as the core becomes more oil-wet
figure_reason: Shows IR vs Sw for sandstone B with refined and crude oil, n rising from 2.05 to 2.90 as core becomes oil-wet.
tldr: Porous-plate resistivity and capillary pressure tests at reservoir conditions on sandstones and carbonates show n rises with stress history and oil-wetness, reaching 2.9 with crude oil.
summary: Archie parameters m and n are usually measured at ambient conditions with simulated fluids, which can bias saturation estimates. The author adapted a porous-plate cell with four-electrode resistivity measurement to reservoir temperature, effective stress, crude oil and formation brine, and tested reproducibility (n = 2.45 in two runs). Raising effective stress from 3 to 20 MPa increased formation factor by about 15% in sandstone versus 12% in carbonate, with little effect on n (sandstone 2.08 to 2.11, carbonate 1.65 to 1.63). Drainage and imbibition resistivity indices differed by up to about 5% PV in saturation for strongly water-wet samples. Comparing refined oil with restored-state crude oil on nine samples, n increased in 7 of 9 as wettability shifted toward oil-wet, with a maximum of 2.05 to 2.90 in one sandstone, and a vuggy carbonate showed two-slope IR/Sw behaviour. The author recommends using crude oil and representative restored samples for determining n.
abstract: The evaluation of saturations and thus oil reserves from resistivity logs requires laboratory determination of both the cementation factor ( $m$ ) and the saturation exponent ( $n$ ) under conditions as representative as possible of reservoir ones. A special laboratory equipment using actual fluids (crude oil and formation brine) at reservoir temperature and under effective overburden pressure has been developed. Saturation was varied by the porous-plate technique adapted for reservoir conditions. Drainage (water saturation decreasing) and imbibition (water saturation increasing) were investigated to evaluate the hysteresis effect. Prior to the test, the effect of overburden pressure on porosity and on the formation factor can be studied. To evaluate the effect of wetting properties, the resistivity index and the oil-brine capillary pressure were measured, for each rock sample, first with refined oil and then with crude oil. In addition, wettability indices were determined using Amott-IFP test. Data were collected with cores from sandstone and carbonate reservoirs. These measurements indicate that the restoration of the effective overburden pressure gave an increase for the cementation factor ( $m$ ) depending on the nature of the rock sample. The value of the saturation exponent ( $n$ ) obtained when using crude oil was generally higher than the one obtained with refined oil. This increase of $n$ was attributed to the change in the wetting properties. Saturation exponent increases up to 2.9 as the core becomes more oil-wet. Finally, this paper emphasizes the need to determine electrical and capillary properties under conditions close to the ones prevailing in the reservoir.

title: Pore Level Fluid Imaging Using High Resolution Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Imaging and Thin Slab Micromodels
caption: Figure 5, (a-f) MRI images of two-phase fluid distribution in sandstones and bead packs. The oil phase is shown in yellow and the aqueous phase is shown in cyan. The pixel resolution for the sandstone plugs is 64x64 and that for the bead pack is 128x128. (a) X/Y-section of Shannon sandstone plug 6 mm dia. and 7 mm long. (b) X/Z-section of Shannon plug. (c) X/Y-section of Berea sandstone plug 5 mm
figure_reason: MRI sections showing oil and aqueous phase distribution in Shannon, Berea plugs and bead pack, the main imaging result.
tldr: A modified NMR spectrometer provides 3-D projection-reconstruction MRI of oil and water in small sandstone plugs and bead packs, complemented by optical rock-slab micromodels.
summary: Pore-scale fluid imaging in rock is limited by clinical MRI resolution and by the simplified geometry of conventional micromodels. The authors modified a 270 MHz NMR spectrometer with a gradient coil system (350 mT/m) and 3-D projection reconstruction, imaging deuterium-oxide brine and Soltrol oil in layered Berea and Shannon sandstone plugs (120 micron pixels) and polymer bead packs (50 micron). Rock line widths (700 Hz deuterium, 2,000 Hz proton), broadened by paramagnetic clays, limited useful rock resolution to about 200-250 microns. Rock-slab micromodels (2-3 mm slabs) allowed optical observation up to 1200X of trapped oil blobs, oil ganglia from viscous bypassing, three-phase gas displacement, and fingering in Berea but not in layered Shannon. Laminations strongly affected fluid distribution and trapping, and MRI (static, 3-D, single phase selective) and optical micromodels (dynamic, high resolution) proved complementary.

title: Time-Domain Curve Fitting for Automated Oil Core NMR Spectral Analysis
caption: Figure 5. Proton NMR for water and Soltrol-130 in Bentheim sandstone as described in Table 1, second pass. a) Real and imaginary parts of the time-domain FID (solid lines) with theoretical fit (dashed lines). b) Experimental (solid line) and theoretical (dashed line) spectra. Note that the first several points of the FID were left out of the fit. The kink at the beginning of the data corresponds t
figure_reason: Shows time-domain FID with fitted curve and resulting spectra for oil/water in Bentheim, demonstrating the fitting approach.
tldr: Fitting a few Lorentzian, Gaussian or powder-pattern functions to the NMR free induction decay in the time domain automates oil/water quantification in cores despite missing initial data points.
summary: Fourier transforms of NMR free induction decays with missing initial points (RF breakthrough, ring-down) give distorted baselines that need manual correction. The authors fit sums of Lorentzian, Gaussian and 13C carbonate powder-pattern functions to the time-domain data by minimizing chi-square with the IMSL global minimizer ZXMWD. For 1H oil/water in Indiana limestone, Bentheim sandstone and Bakers dolomite plugs, time-domain oil fractions were similar to Fourier-domain and mass-balance values, with fits averaging 78 s. For 13C of Wasson crude in whole cores, about 150 µs of initial data was discarded; Berea oil weight was estimated at 17.6 g (aliphatic) or 16.7 g (aliphatic+aromatic), versus 20.8 g by mass balance and 13.8 g by hand-processed Fourier spectra. Carbonate powder-pattern fits took about 5 minutes. Time-domain fitting extrapolates to time zero, but some short-T2 oil may still be missed.
abstract: Automated analysis of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra is critical for accurate quantification of oil and water in cores: ultimately, one can expect to process hundreds of samples per day. In the NMR experiment, several data points at the beginning of the NMR signal are missing because of radiofrequency (RF) pulse breakthrough or electrical ring-down of the receiving coil. A Fourier transform of the incomplete data produces a distorted spectrum. Also, quantification depends on knowledge of the signal amplitude at time zero, and the rapid decay of the NMR signal in some rocks can lead to inaccuracies. For water and oil in rocks, the number of spectral components is small. Therefore we have taken the approach of fitting a small number of functions to the time-domain data to find the global minimum of the chi-square difference between theory and data. The minimization (using a commercial mathematical routine) generally takes a few minutes and results in values for the amplitudes and decay constants of the time-domain signals corresponding to the various spectral components. Time-domain fitting allows back projection to time zero of signals that are attenuated by decay (e.g. water and oil in shaly sandstones).

title: Net Pay Application for Nuclear Magnetic Resonance, Nugget Sandstone, Wyoming Thrust Belt
caption: Figure 8 - The Bessie Bottom well deliverabilities could be predicted using the NMR pay method. Maximum deliverability was at the top of the column and water production was obtained at the bottom.
figure_reason: Shows application of the NMR pay method to Bessie Bottom well, predicting deliverability and water production zones.
tldr: An NMR-based net pay method combining relative permeability and capillary pressure partitions Nugget sandstone porosity to predict water cut and deliverability on log strip charts.
summary: Poor and inconsistent production from low-porosity (<8%) eolian Nugget sandstone reservoirs in three Wyoming thrust belt fields could not be explained by facies or core permeability. Deliverability differences were attributed to natural open fractures (Anschutz wells with effective permeability of 8 md/ft versus 0.05 md/ft at Bessie Bottom) and connate water saturation effects. A net pay method was developed that links NMR bound/free fluid porosity to water saturations chosen from relative permeability, fractional flow and mercury capillary pressure data. Linear regressions on core samples gave free fluid = 0.67*porosity − 1.1 at 40% Sw (first water cut) and 0.41*porosity − 1 at 70% Sw (80% fractional flow). Overlaying porosity*Sw against the bound-fluid curves on a log strip chart separates water-free, increasing water cut and water-productive zones, and would have predicted Bessie Bottom performance.
abstract: Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (N.M.R.) test results from the Jurassic Nugget sandstone in the Wyoming thrust belt were combined with other core tests to develop net pay criteria that would reflect water cut and deliverability in addition to hydrocarbon pore volume. The producing characteristics of the Nugget sandstone had previously been correlated to eolian dune facies in the first several years of thrust belt exploration. Inconsistencies in facies-to-pay correlations from new discoveries and longer production histories required a new method to evaluate net pay that would evaluate the impact of connate water saturation on reservoir behavior. This N.M.R. pay method approach integrates relative permeability, capillary pressure and N.M.R. test evaluations and resultant estimates of reservoir behavior affected by connate water saturation. These tests quantify fractional flow, pore throat size, and relative permeability for any selected water saturation value. The N.M.R. test results partition total porosity by calculating what percentage of the pore space will flow water as determined by the other core tests for selected values of water saturation. Since N.M.R. relates porosity to other core tests, wireline log porosity values can be correlated to reservoir behavior. Regression analysis on a suite of samples will calculate a linear equation for the percentage of porosity that partitions predicted reservoir behavior as a function of total porosity. The intercept accounts for the difference in connate water binding behavior in a range of porosities for a given rock type. Final net pay is calculated on a log strip chart that overlays total porosity, the partitioned pore space and water saturation curves. The deliverability and water cut characteristics (reservoir behavior) are predicted when the connate water saturation values fall within the partitioned porosity boundaries. Net pay is selected by eliminating zones with predicted poor reservoir behavior. This net pay method successfully established the relationship between porosity, water saturation and deliverability.

title: Accuracy and Reliability of Electronic Instrument Core Orientation Surveys
caption: Figure 10 - E.S.I. reference groove compass orientation reported by company A for the first oriented core taken from the SFBU No. 4-62 well. In the 1st report accelerometer data obtained during coring was used to determine the vertical reference for each shot point. The 2nd report used data recorded while the tool was stationary in the hole prior to the start of coring.
figure_reason: Shows two reports for core #1 versus observed groove orientation, illustrating the effect of vertical reference choice and clockwise drift.
tldr: Case studies from two Texas wells show electronic core orientation surveys suffer from vibration, torque, time-depth and setup errors; quality control procedures and paleomagnetic checks are recommended.
summary: Electronic survey instrument (E.S.I.) core orientation replaces multishot photography but is prone to errors from tool setup, vibration, torque, data editing and core handling. In a west Texas Ellenburger well (SFBU 4-62), eight oriented cores were taken under foam drilling with severe vibration. Multiple reports for the same core differed by up to 170°, subjective editing hid scatter of up to 173° in raw shots, and one core was misoriented by about 144° because of incorrect time-depth correlation. Paleomagnetic orientation exposed these errors, and corrected E.S.I. reports then agreed within about ±15° (±5° for the time-corrected core). A south Texas well showed alignment errors of about 20° from a loose telescope, bent barrel and miscalibrated cross-hair, fixed with a rifle sight and level calibration verified to ±1°. The paper gives a checklist of quality control procedures including stationary readings, stopwatch timing, a Master Orientation Line on core, and routine paleomagnetic checks.
abstract: Comparison of electronic instrument core orientation survey results with direct core measurements and paleomagnetic core orientation data for a west Texas well shows that the accuracy of electronic surveys can be seriously reduced by operator error, drilling induced vibration and tool torque. An example from a south Texas well demonstrates the need for careful tool setup and alignment at the well site. Guidelines for proper tool setup, core handling and data analysis to minimize these problems include the following: (1) Use a multiplexer in the survey tool that scans rapidly, at least 30 cycles per second, and be sure all electrical connections are tight. (2) Center the tool with properly sized rubber finger or straight, rotating spring stabilizers and scratch a mark across each threaded connection to show if any of the joints loosen or tighten during coring. (3) Before coring, record a measurement with the tool stationary in the hole to obtain a reliable vertical reference for subsequent magnetometer measurements during coring. (4) Accurately correlate time with depth during coring by recording, at about two minute intervals, the time, measured with a stop-watch, and the corresponding geolograph depth. (5) After coring, assemble the core into physically continuous intervals, record interval depths and mark each interval with a straight reference line. Measure the angle between this line and the survey reference groove and compare this value with the angle predicted by the survey. (6) Compare the original, complete tool data with the final, edited report. Paleomagnetics can be used to check the electronic survey and may be required to obtain accurate orientation data if much vibration is encountered during coring.

title: Core Analysis to Calibrate Geological Interpretation
tldr: A keynote review arguing that core data, integrated with logs, test data and petrophysics, are essential for calibrating geological reservoir descriptions during appraisal.
summary: The paper gives a personal view of how core and core analysis support geological interpretation and reservoir description in appraisal projects, and argues for production geology as a discipline within petroleum engineering. It reviews core-based tools: orientation and fracture logging, FMS/dipmeter calibration, minipermeametry, X-ray CT, NMR, XRD/XRF, SEM, petrography, image analysis, mercury porosimetry and surface spectroscopy for wettability. It stresses porofacies and rock-type groupings that are petrophysically meaningful, beyond simple porosity-permeability transforms. It cautions about sampling bias, scale effects, and artifacts from coring, plugging and cleaning, and notes that 2D and limited 3D images cannot resolve pore connectivity. It concludes with a checklist of questions on uncertainty and sample suitability, and no numerical results are presented.
abstract: This keynote paper constitutes a personal view of the role and place of core data in geological interpretations for reservoir description in appraisal projects. No apologies are made for placing the geologist in an engineering setting for this purpose and this approach is strongly argued. Core is of pivotal importance in achieving the integrated interpretations which are required for the consideration of development options. This paper reviews many of the applications of new and older technologies in reservoir description for appraisal projects, with the emphasis on maximising their impact by data integration.

title: Core Analysis to Calibrate Geophysical Interpretation
caption: FIGURE 7 Calibration of (a) compressional-wave sonic log and (b) sonic-predicted porosities with core data.
figure_reason: Shows core-based calibration of sonic log and sonic-predicted porosity versus time-average, the main application result.
tldr: Reviews how porosity, pore geometry, saturation, fluid type and clay affect core acoustic velocities, and shows how core data calibrate seismic and sonic interpretation.
summary: The paper reviews how rock and fluid properties control acoustic velocity and how core measurements can calibrate geophysical interpretation. Core data show that velocity depends on porosity but also on pore geometry (vuggy dolomites have higher velocity at a given porosity), clay content (Han et al. regressions for Vp and Vs), stress, saturation and fluid type. Compressional velocity in tar sand can fall as much as 30% with heating versus 3-5% in water-saturated sand, supporting seismic monitoring of thermal EOR fronts. Applications include gas bright-spot discrimination using P and S waves, conversion of tomograms to porosity maps, and sonic log calibration, where upscaled core velocities agree with the sonic log within 3% in rapidly varying intervals. Core-derived velocity-porosity relations predicted reservoir porosity better than the time-average equation, which underestimated it. The authors caution that frequency dispersion and scale differences limit direct transfer of laboratory results to seismic and sonic scales.
abstract: This paper comprises a brief review of some aspects of rock and fluid properties and their effects on acoustic measurements. We illustrate the effect of pore geometry, saturation, fluid type and shaliness on velocity measurements on cores and we present some field applications of these laboratory measurements including qualitative and quantitative interpretation of seismic, repetitive seismic and sonic data.

title: Core Analysis to Calibrate Well Log Interpretation
caption: Figure 3 Porosity and saturation from log and core
figure_reason: Compares log-derived and core porosity and saturation in North Sea chalk, showing core verification of log results.
tldr: Reviews how core data calibrate and verify log interpretation of lithology, porosity, saturation, permeability, net/gross and compaction, with North Sea examples and scale and uncertainty issues.
summary: The paper reviews how core analysis is used to calibrate well-log interpretation for static and dynamic reservoir description. It covers lithology and clay mineralogy, porosity response equations, Archie saturation and shaly-sand corrections, J-function capillary pressure, net/gross, permeability, fluid contacts, recovery and rock mechanics. A North Sea chalk example shows density-log porosity and Archie Sw agreeing with core porosity (approaching 50%) and Dean-Stark saturations on average over the cored interval, despite thin laminations not resolved by the log. Brent 'mica' sands illustrate how radioactive minerals cause shaly log response and underestimated porosity unless calibrated with core. The saturation exponent can only be derived from core and depends on wettability. Scale differences between measurements and core and log representativeness are discussed, and improved standards are called for.
abstract: Coring and logging (electrical coring) has contributed greatly to the understanding of the petrophysical properties of reservoir rocks and the dynamic behaviour of reservoirs for the last 70 years. Today it is seldom seen that wells are drilled without being logged, and quite a high percentage are being cored. This paper deals with the integration of core and log data to determine lithology, estimate porosity, net/gross ratio, fluid saturations, permeability and other petrophysical parameters. The analysis relates both to the static and dynamic description of reservoirs. Attention is also given to the merits of core and log analysis with respect to the dynamic behaviour of reservoirs.

title: Increasing the Value of Core Analysis
tldr: Describes Enterprise Oil's contractual work schedules and report structures that make core contractors record wellsite, laboratory and experimental observations, with examples showing practical benefits.
summary: Historical core analysis reports are often bare data tables with a covering letter, which limits later reuse and can mislead inexperienced users. Enterprise Oil formalised work schedules, backed by contract penalty clauses, covering coring, wellsite core catching, laboratory core fitting, plugging, routine analysis, photography, preservation and reporting. Routine analysis includes separate horizontal and vertical plugs, Hassler permeability at 200 and 400 psi, Klinkenberg and overburden tests. Reports follow a 20-section routine structure and a special core analysis structure that includes plug history sheets, a reference volume of worksheets and calibrations, and data on magnetic media. Examples show benefits: a wellsite technician's report explained poor core recovery, core break continuity coding eased depth matching, and a saw-blade wear observation led to a toothed core head with savings of about $6 x 15k per well.
abstract: Too much of the core analysis historical record can loosely be described as a single page letter saying "thank you for the work...hope we get some more" and a series of tables of data. Nothing more, nothing less. No real information. As a result, trying to incorporate and compare twenty year old data with recent data becomes something of a dubious art. This paper describes some of the steps taken by Enterprise Oil to try to ensure that as much information as possible is collated and reported. The aim has been to encourage the core contractors to participate actively in the work and the reporting. Contractors handle a large volume of core and thereby have a large wealth of experience. Furthermore, when working with core the individuals will be mentally comparing and judging, forming views about the core in front of them. Yet, seldom does any of this get reported. This is wasted opportunity, added value that will not be realised. This paper will present some of the steps taken by Enterprise to improve core reports and examples where the capture of additional information has resulted in real benefits.

title: Pressure Coring: Better Cores for Better Analyses
caption: FIGURE 2. Percentage comparison of pore space saturation alterations.
figure_reason: Shows how depletion and flushing alter core pore-space saturations relative to in-situ values, the key rationale for pressure coring.
tldr: Describes the pressure core barrel, its operation, low-invasion coring and analysis, and a coal seam case showing pressure cores give more accurate gas content than other sampling methods.
summary: The paper reviews pressure coring, which retrieves core at near bottomhole pressure to avoid fluid expulsion and gas loss during retrieval. It describes the double-tube barrel (6.0 and 8.0 in OD, 10,000 and 5,000 psi ratings, about 80% average pressure retention), the pressure regulator, ball valve seals, optional non-invading gel, and surface flushing and freezing procedures. Low-invasion PDC bit technology and low fluid loss mud are presented as ways to limit filtrate flushing, which pressure coring alone does not prevent. A 1983 field record showed 165 cores, 83.6% core recovery and 69% average pressure recovery. In a Fruitland coal case (San Juan Basin), a temperature-compensated pressure core gave 601.4 SCF/ton, while sidewall cores were 5.6% off, conventional cores 7-13% low and drill cuttings 24-28% low.
abstract: In critical applications where reservoir engineers and geologists need to analyze samples in near in-situ conditions, pressure coring may be the only method of obtaining complete core analysis. The procedure can be used for any project in which success is dependent upon accurate calculation of reserves in place, or the reaction of reservoir rock to alternative recovery techniques. The self-contained pressure coring system provides a means of capturing and maintaining the core at or near bottomhole pressure, preventing gas expansion and fluid loss. A flushing gel is used to displace drilling mud from the core barrel while keeping in-situ pressure constant. Still contained in the inner tube barrel, the cores are frozen for transport to the laboratory, where controlled thawing allows accurate fluid saturation measurements. A case history is presented to illustrate operation and results of the pressure coring system, which is able to provide types of information unobtainable with conventional means. In addition to fluid saturation data, pressure coring provides wettability and relative permeability measurements, mechanical property data such as compressibility and shear strength, and measurements of methane content and deliverability. Thus, use of this system results in greater accuracy in core analysis, and affords greater precision in evaluation of hydrocarbon reserves.

title: Quantitative Analysis of Oil Based Mud Filtrate Invasion
caption: Figure 12Depth vs C16 Isoprenoid : nC15 Ratio for Central Core Region
figure_reason: Calibration curve of isoprenoid:nC15 ratio versus filtrate content, the basis of the quantification and its scatter.
tldr: A tracer-free gas chromatography fingerprint method quantifies oil-based mud filtrate invasion in core trims, accurate to about ±2 wt%, demonstrated on a North Sea sandstone.
summary: Oil-based mud filtrate can alter core wettability, so invasion must be minimised and quantified. The method extracts hydrocarbons from small core trims (1.5 in diameter, 0.25 in thick) with boiling toluene, concentrates the extract and analyses it by GC. The C16 isoprenoid:nC15 peak-area ratio separates crude (R=0.38) from mud base oil (R=0.76), and a calibration curve built from known mixtures converts the ratio to filtrate weight fraction, with error of about ±2 wt% below 20 wt%. In a case study on a permeable sandstone cored at 90 ft/hr and plugged on site with vacuum assistance, 6 of 8 samples showed negligible invasion beyond 1 in. Adjacent plugs showed the same invasion profile. The method needs no on-site tracer and can be applied retrospectively.
abstract: Mud filtrate invasion into core material taken from oil reservoirs may cause problems for future core analysis studies due to the potentially damaging effect of the mud filtrate upon the rock's wettability. It is therefore desirable in these situations to minimise the degree of invasion and accurately measure the success of this minimisation. There is much discussion in the literature of tracer techniques but all of these require well site activity as well as tracer purchase and handling. A quantitative technique is presented which requires no tracer to be used and is quick and easy to perform. The process involves Gas Chromatography finger print analysis of both reservoir crude and mud filtrate. High contrast characteristics are identified and quantified for known ratios of mud and crude thus generating a calibration curve. Hydrocarbons are then solvent extracted from the core trims which may be as small as 1.50" diameter and 0.25" thick. The effluent is then boiled down (taking care to minimise carry over) to concentrate the hydrocarbons extracted. The residue is then analysed using GC and related to the calibration curve generated previously. Experimentation to date has suggested that the technique is accurate to within approximately +/- 2 wt%. The resolution also depends to some extent on the hydrocarbons present.

title: Core Surface Analysis for Wettability Assessment
caption: FIGURE 5 Amott wetting indices Vs. organic carbon levels determined on reservoir 1 core samples.
figure_reason: Plots Amott wetting index against surface organic carbon for reservoir 1 cores, the central correlation result.
tldr: XPS surface organic carbon is compared with core flooding and Amott wettability on Berea, sandstone and carbonate cores; carbon tracks oil wetness, but cleaning and masking limit quantification.
summary: The study tests whether surface chemical composition measured by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), mainly organic carbon, can indicate core wettability. Berea plugs aged with crude oil (80°C, three weeks) shifted from an Amott index of +0.85 to 0, and organic carbon rose from 19.4 to 28.7 at% after standard cleaning, showing that cleaning only partly restores the original surface. For reservoir 2 sandstone, oil-wet cores consistently had the highest carbon contents. For reservoir 1 carbonate, Amott indices were all near 0.1 despite carbon of 25–49 at%, so intermediate wettability corresponded to roughly 30–45 at% carbon. Air-borne carbon (10–20 at%) and masking of the mineral signal limit quantitative use, and milder cleaning is recommended.
abstract: Rock wettability is determinant for the behaviour of a reservoir subjected to any oil recovery process. As the surface chemical composition of the mineral is indeed mostly responsible for its wetting behaviour we investigated the relation between wettability and surface chemical composition. The examination of the surface was achieved mainly through X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) whereas wettability determination was established through detailed interpretation of core flooding experiments and wettability index measurements. In the first part of this paper, the procedure to restore the original wettability of a core in a laboratory is examined. The wetting state of a reservoir is often difficult to assess because it is carried out on reservoir cores which have generally been contaminated by the various chemicals during drilling. Berea cores have been used to assess the validity of the restoration procedure of polluted cores, by measuring the organic carbon content of the mineral surface layer. Starting from a virgin clean core, wettability was changed by aging with crude oil. The surface was studied before and after cleaning. The results show that the surface organic carbon content is well correlated with the wetting behaviour of the material defined by petrophysical measurements. In the second part of the paper, we present the use of the surface analysis for the characterization of the intrinsic wettability of a given core. The aim was to establish the correlation between surface composition and the wetting characteristics of the mineral. A variety of cores has been investigated, which include Berea samples as well as reservoir cores. For very different cases, ranging from totally water to intermediate wet, a relation between surface chemical composition (mainly organic carbon concentration) and wettability has been investigated. Results concerning sandstone and carbonate originating from oil producing reservoirs are presented. We discuss the validity of the correlation for predicting core wettability.

title: Petrophysical Significance of Oriented Sidewall Cores for Improved Reservoir Characterization
caption: FIGURE 2. Rotary-drilled sidewall core. The borehole end (BH), formation end (FM), groove cut by the diamond drill bit (G) and line marking the top of the core are shown.
figure_reason: Shows the rotary-drilled sidewall core with borehole end, formation end, bit groove and top marking central to the orientation method.
tldr: Shows how rotary-drilled sidewall cores can be oriented from tool marks and televiewer images, enabling AMS, oriented thin sections, directional permeability and skin damage studies.
summary: Whole core is often unavailable, so the authors examine whether rotary-drilled sidewall cores can be oriented and used for directional petrophysical and sedimentologic work. Top and formation/borehole ends are identified from diamond bit tool marks and marked with ink, and magnetic orientation is obtained by locating core holes on borehole televiewer (CAST) images. In 30 cores from two wells in Cretaceous sandstone, AMS foliation dips (4.2° and 5.8°) were compared with dipmeter dips (5-15°), agreeing in one well but differing by 90° in the other. Berea tests indicated vertical permeability above 0.1 mD can be measured on drilled sidewall cores. In a nine-well Devonian sandstone study of 195 cores, 86% showed increased permeability after trimming to the formation end, though trimming and ultrasonic cleaning may contribute. The authors describe these as preliminary studies needing further validation.
abstract: The advent of drilled sidewall cores has made it possible to obtain much more information than was previously available from percussion sidewall cores. Directional equipment on the coring tool enables the azimuth and deviation of the bit to be recorded for each core. Inspection of the core in the laboratory, in most cases, provides information to determine the top of the core as well as the formation versus borehole ends. These parameters make it possible to completely orient the drilled sidewall core with respect to the horizon and geographic north. Directional rock fabric studies (which require well oriented samples), such as AMS (anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility) in conjunction with dense core sampling, dipmeter data and CAST images have been successfully completed. Marked core tops enable the petrographer to obtain valuable information from sparsely sampled intervals or formations. When sampling is adequate, sedimentologic studies in formations are possible from oriented, drilled, sidewall cores. The orientation of laminations and features such as graded bedding have been established and compared to detailed dipmeter data. Directional permeability, migration of fines and skin damage studies have been made on samples drilled from the borehole wall and depth correlated to well logs with a gamma ray.

title: Automated Mineral Identification of Sandstone Samples Using SEM/Image Analysis Techniques
caption: FIGURE 5a Mineralogically classified image derived from Figure 2a, the colours are indicative of the mineral found on the basis of X-ray analysis (See Colour Plate VI at the back of this publication.)
figure_reason: Mineralogically classified colour image showing the main output of the automated procedure.
tldr: An automated SEM/EDX/image-analysis method quantifies mineralogy, grain texture and pore structure in epoxy-impregnated sandstone, cutting unclassified objects from 8% to under 1% and guiding acid selection.
summary: Conventional thin-section point counting is subjective and semi-quantitative, so the authors built a fully automated SEM/EDX/image-analysis system for sandstone petrography. Epoxy-impregnated, automatically polished samples are imaged in BSE (512x512 pixels, 1.8x1.8 mm field), grains are segmented by morphological operations, and each grain is scanned for X-rays in nine elemental windows. Classification uses pseudo elemental ratios (0/1/2) against reference minerals, cutting analysis time per grain from 10 s to 3 s, with a second vector-comparison algorithm for clays and lithics. Unclassified objects fell from about 8% to under 1%, at the cost of about one hour per field of view containing 500-800 objects. Examples include arkosic and shaly sandstones and an acidisation study where regular mud acid dissolved most calcite cement and risked matrix collapse, while half-strength mud acid dissolved it only partly and raised porosity and permeability.
abstract: A combination of scanning electron microscopy, X-ray analysis and image analysis (SEM/EDX/IA) has been used to perform automatic petrographic analysis of sandstone samples. The methods developed involve the use of backscattered electron (BSE) imaging and X-ray analysis together with image analysis procedures to determine and to quantify the mineralogical composition and grain texture information. The samples to be investigated can be core plugs, sidewall samples or cuttings. Prior to analysis the samples are impregnated with epoxy resin and subjected to high-quality automatic polishing. The analysis procedure starts with the collection of a BSE image from the SEM, this image is stored in the memory of the image analysis system. Thereafter the locations of the grains and mineral structures in the image are determined and converted to coordinates on the sample surface. The individual grains and mineral structures are then scanned with the electron beam of the SEM. During the scanning of the individual objects, X-rays are generated, and these are detected and analysed in terms of their elemental information.
