NaCl brines and brine-saturated Indiana limestone showed linear NMR intensity versus salinity, with the limestone linear from 500 to 200,000 ppm. NMR sodium mass in carbonates and sandstones agreed with weighed values to 3.1% on average, with underestimation increasing with shaliness. Solid sodium minerals have linewidths at least ten times broader than mobile sodium, so a narrowband probe rejects them. 1-D diffusion in Berea gave an effective D of 0.58e-5 cm2/s, a diffusional formation factor of 10.0 versus an electrical value of 13.7. Imaging of salt effusion and infusion in Berea and Bentheim cores showed nonuniform transport that 1H images largely failed to reveal.
abstract: Sodium ( $^{23}\text{Na}$ ) is an NMR-active nucleus with considerable petrophysical importance because sodium is the predominant cation in reservoir brines. This paper presents the first NMR images of $^{23}\text{Na}$ inside cores. Several core applications are demonstrated, including measuring core salinity, 1-D profiling, and 3-D imaging of brine ingress into cores.

title: Use of a High Magnetic Field to Visualize Fluids in Porous Media by MRI
caption: Figure 5 : Comparison between experimental MRI profiles and simulated profiles.
figure_reason: Compares experimental MRI saturation profiles with simulation, demonstrating validity of the MRI profiles.
tldr: 9.4 T MRI images oil and water in small cores during drainage, validates saturation profiles against a 1-D simulator, and reconstructs 3-D gas-oil displacement showing preferential gas paths.
summary: The paper applies high-field (9.4 T) MRI to visualize fluids in small cores (1 cm diameter, 2.5 cm long) of Fontainebleau sandstone and bioclastic limestone. Chemical shift sequences separated oil and water images in the limestone, with slices 50 µm thick and about 100 µm in-plane resolution. For the sandstone, D2O replaced water because signals could not be separated, and oil saturation profiles were obtained during constant-pressure drainage (0.045 bar). Profiles compared with a 1-D two-phase Darcy simulator matched well, especially near residual water saturation (0.3), with deviations attributed to core heterogeneity; relative permeability and capillary pressure curves were estimated from the profiles. A 13-slice multislice experiment reconstructed in 3-D showed gas flowing along a preferential path that a 1-D model cannot represent.
abstract: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is very useful in core analysis because it gives information about petrophysical parameters: porosity and fluid saturations. This paper deals with several applications of MRI to the study of fluid distribution in porous media, with a strong 9.4 tesla magnetic field. The use of a strong magnetic field coupled with high gradients produces images with good resolution and enables very thin slices to be obtained. Oil and water were visualized in small core samples (1 cm in diameter and 2.5 cm in length). The MRI profiles were compared to those from a numerical simulator based on generalized Darcy's law. Good agreement was observed between experiment and simulation showing the validity of MRI profiles. A 3-D reconstruction of oil distribution was presented for oil and gas. The 3-D visualization showed a preferential path for gas.

title: Fluid Velocities in Oil Cores During Water Injection
caption: Figure 23 - San Andres Dolomite Slice 7 Positive Flow Image
figure_reason: Positive flow image in heterogeneous dolomite showing flow channeling into a few high-porosity regions and unswept areas.
tldr: A 3DFT MRI flow pulse sequence maps axial water velocities in Casper sandstone and San Andres dolomite cores, showing flow channeling into high-porosity regions and detecting channels.
summary: Conventional coreflood experiments give only core-averaged properties, and CT-based flow imaging needs a displacement front. This work uses a modified 3DFT MRI flow-encoding sequence on a 2-tesla imager with a bird-cage coil to measure steady-state axial velocities during water injection. Two cores were studied: Casper sandstone (T2 5.4 ms, 77-88 md, 16.1% porosity) and heterogeneous San Andres dolomite (T2 35 ms, 10-60 md, ~16% porosity). Echo time was 15 ms, with 16 slices and 32 averages. In Casper sandstone, flow near the inlet was piston-like, then became channeled into high-porosity layers further along, with some apparent backflow regions. In the dolomite, flow channeled into a few high-porosity regions and along a channel where the epoxy sleeve separated, leaving the second half of the core largely unswept. Low signal-to-noise remained a limitation near the core ends.

title: Proton MR Two - Component Chemical Shift Imaging of Fluids in Porous Media
caption: Figure 4. Chemical-shift 1-D profile images of the sand pack sample containing water and machine oil. (a) and (b) are the water and oil images, respectively, obtained using magnitude-of-sum and difference techniques (Dixon's technique). (c) water image, and (d) oil images obtained using method described in the text.
figure_reason: Compares Dixon method with the proposed method in the sand pack, showing clear water/oil separation.
tldr: A modified Dixon-type spin-warp chemical shift imaging method with phase correction separates water and oil images quantitatively in sand packs and cores, even with overlapping resonance lines.
summary: Relaxation-based and spectrally selective MRI methods struggle to separate water and oil in porous media when resonance lines overlap and signals decay quickly. The authors improve Horsfield's phase-shift technique by acquiring in-phase and opposed-phase images to map field inhomogeneity and susceptibility phase errors, then acquiring ±90° phase-shifted images that give separated components by vector sum and difference. Tests used a water/machine-oil Ottawa sand pack (3.5 ppm shift, 2.4 ppm linewidth), Bentheim sandstone cores (23% porosity) saturated with brine, Soltrol 130 or both, and a carbonate core during oil flooding at 0.1 ml/min. In Bentheim cores, cross-contamination in the single-fluid cores was under 4%, and the combined water and oil signal in the mixed core agreed with the ordinary image. The carbonate flood gave time-lapse water and oil saturation maps with well-behaved displacement fronts. A limitation is a noisy phase map where water and oil signals are about equal.
abstract: An NMR chemical shift imaging modality is presented for quantitative determination of the spatial distribution of water and oil saturation in porous samples. It is applicable to those samples for which the two resonance lines overlap severely, and for which significant signal decay occurs during the chemical shift evolution period. We have used this method to demonstrate the separation of water and oil images in sand packs and core samples.

title: Salinity Dependence of Shaly Sand Parameters from Membrane Potential Measurements
caption: Figure 2. Salinity Dependence of the Shaly Sand Formation Resistivity Factor.
figure_reason: Shows normalized F* versus clay-to-brine conductivity ratio, the key result of salinity-dependent F* for Group 2 and Bigfoot samples.
tldr: Membrane potential measurements on Waxman-Smits Group 2 and new Bigfoot shaly sands show clay conductivity, F*, m* and λ vary with salinity, especially in montmorillonite-bearing samples.
summary: Waxman-Smits assumes constant F* and relies on Qv, which ignores clay geometry. The paper uses the Yuan-Diederix equation to derive clay conductivity directly from membrane potential, then F*, m* and quadrature conductance versus salinity. Data are the 27 Waxman-Smits Group 2 samples plus four new montmorillonitic Bigfoot samples measured for conductivity, membrane potential and phase angle (14–234 mmho/cm NaCl). For kaolinite-illite samples clay conductivity falls with salinity and F* stays constant while clay conductivity is below brine conductivity. For montmorillonite samples clay conductivity is much larger than brine conductivity, and F* rises (at least 50% for the shalier samples) with decreasing salinity, with m* following. Bigfoot λ values agree with Vinegar-Waxman data, and phase angle is shown to relate directly to clay conductivity.
abstract: The Yuan-Diederix equation relates the conductivity of a brine saturated rock sample to the brine conductivity and membrane and Nernst potentials for the sample for a given salinity contrast. It can be used for determining the salinity dependence of shaly sand parameters because the equation can be determined from parameters measured at essentially one salinity. This paper applies membrane potential measurements and the Yuan-Diederix equation to describe the salinity dependence of the clay conductivity, $C$ , the shaly sand formation resistivity factor, $F^*$ , the shaly sand lithology exponent, $m^*$ , and the equivalent quadrature conductance, $\lambda$ . Data from the Waxman-Smits Group 2 samples for which conductivity and membrane potential data have been simultaneously measured allow the determination of $C$ , $F^*$ and $m^*$ as a function of salinity. The clay conductivity generally decreases with decreasing salinity. Accordingly, any shaly sand model should incorporate a salinity dependent clay conductivity as the Waxman-Smits model does. When the clay conductivity is smaller than the brine conductivity, $F^*$ is found to be constant, verifying that the Waxman-Smits assumption of constant $F^*$ is valid. When the clay conductivity is larger than the brine conductivity, $F^*$ generally increases with decreasing salinity implying that the Waxman-Smits assumption of constant $F^*$ is not always valid. A consequence of salinity-dependent $F^*$ is that membrane potential measurements may be necessary for cases where the clay conductivity exceeds the brine conductivity. In this salinity range, $m^*$ also increases. The salinity effects are much greater for samples containing montmorillonite. New simultaneous conductivity, membrane potential and induced polarization data are reported here for a set of very shaly sandstones which confirm the salinity dependence of $C$ , $F^*$ and $m^*$ . The new data are used also to determine the salinity dependence of the equivalent quadrature conductance, $\lambda$ . The results agree very well with Vinegar-Waxman induced polarization data on shaly sands. It is found that induced polarization measurements also directly yield the clay conductivity. $$C_o = (C_w + C_e)/F^* \quad (1)$$ where $C_o$ is the conductivity of the brine saturated shaly sand, $C_o^o$ is the brine conductivity, $C_w^w$ is the clay conductivity and $F^*$ is the shaly sand formation resistivity factor. In the WS interpretation of equation (1) the salinity dependence of $C_o$ is determined by assuming $F^*$ to be constant and equal to the reciprocal slope of the straight line (high salinity) portion of $C_o - C_e$ plot. Shaly sand $C_o - C_e$ plots show non-linearity at low salinities. Once $F^*$ is obtained, $C_e$ is determined from $C_o^o$ and $C_w^w$ . The clay conductivity, $C_c$ , is expressed by WS as the product of the equivalent counterion conductance, $B$ , and the cation exchange capacity, $Q_v$ . The factor, $B$ , is dependent upon salinity, temperature and cation type and in general is independent of the particular sample of interest while $Q_v$ is a measure of the sample shaliness. The salinity dependence of $B$ is determined from a set of $C_o - C_e$ measurements to determine $C_o$ and then additional $Q_v$ measurements yield corresponding $B^w$ values. However, it has been found recently that $B$ also depends on clay geometry2,3 and therefore can depend on the sample of interest. This is because the factor, $Q_v$ , is determined by disaggregating the sample and performing conductometric titration on the crushed sample. Effects of clay geometry on clay conductivity appear in the $B$ factor because effects of clay geometry on $Q_v$ have been strongly diminished. Membrane potential measurements also yield the clay conductivity and because membrane potential measurements are performed on the sample with the clay geometry intact, the clay conductivity correctly incorporates clay geometric effects. Cation exchange capacity from membrane potential is denoted as $Q_v^e$ for effective cation exchange capacity. The effect of clay geometry is properly incorporated in $Q_v^e$ and thus the $B$ factor becomes independent of clay geometry when $Q_v^e$ is used to determine $B$ . Moreover, the determination of clay conductivity is independent of $F^*$ . By using membrane potential and conductivity measurements performed at essentially a single salinity, the need for high salinity data to determine $F^*$ is eliminated. The main objective of this paper is to describe the salinity dependence of shaly sand parameters based on membrane potential measurements. Another objective of the paper is to introduce a second data set where conductivity, membrane potential and induced polarization measurements were simultaneously made. The paper focusses on the analysis of experimental data although limited discussion of shaly sand models is given. However, reference is made to the WS model because it is on their Group 2 data that this paper is largely based. Discussion is also devoted to the Vinegar-Waxman model of quadrature conductivity of shaly sands because of the phase angle measurements presented here. Many shaly sand models exist and have been reviewed by Worthington4. More recent publications on membrane potentials and conductivity of shaly sands have also appeared. Steward and Burck focussed on improving $Q_v$ determination from membrane potential measurements5. Silva and Bassiouni published a theory of membrane potential of shaly sands6 based on the dual water

title: Observations of Rock Fabric Controls on the Electrical Properties of Sandstones
caption: Figure 15 In aeolian sands, low values of $n^*$ tend to be associated with high values of minimum brine saturation.
figure_reason: Shows n* in laminated aeolian sands rising as minimum brine saturation decreases, the key correlation.
tldr: Chevron's 15-year dataset on 323 clean sandstones shows m* is narrowly distributed (~1.87) while n* varies widely (0.6-2.6), controlled by laminations, hairline pores and cementation.
summary: The paper compiles electrical property measurements on 323 clean, consolidated sandstones from 11 fields and one quarry, measured at net reservoir pressure and room temperature and clay-corrected with Waxman-Smits. The cementation exponent m* averages 1.87 (SD 0.10), with 95% of values between 1.7 and 2.1, and increases with cementation, as seen in Fontainebleau samples (a*=0.13, m*=2.8). The saturation exponent n* ranges from 0.6 to 2.6; finely laminated aeolian sandstones show n* of 0.6-1.4 because saturation varies lamina to lamina, giving curved RI*-Sw log-log plots. Homogeneous low-porosity samples with hairline pores along grain contacts also show low n* (1.0-1.6). n* correlates fairly with porosity, which gives bounds but not a predictive formula. Appendix errors from centrifuge desaturation, wettability and evaporation are estimated to bias n* by about 0.2 or less.
abstract: We report electrical properties measurements on 323 sandstone samples with minimal amounts of predominantly authigenic clays. All measurements were made at Chevron during the past 15 years using net effective reservoir pressure and room temperature. Almost all of the samples are fairly well consolidated. The most common clay is kaolinite with lesser amounts of illite, chlorite, glauconite, and traces of smectite. Our objectives in this paper are to document the ranges of the cementation ( $m$ ) and saturation ( $n$ ) exponents in our data and to relate the values of $m$ and $n$ to rock fabric. We "clay corrected" the measured values of resistivity index ( $RI$ ) and formation factor ( $F$ ) using the Waxman-Smits equations (1968) and the $B$ value from Juhasz (1981) to obtain $F^*$ , $RI^*$ , $m^*$ and $n^*$ , the clay corrected cementation and saturation exponents. These clay corrections are typically less than 0.05 to $m$ and 0.1 to $n$ . Henceforth, we shall refer only to the "clay corrected" or geometric parameters: $F^*$ , $RI^*$ , $m^*$ and $n^*$ . For the distribution of $m^*$ , 95% of the values are between 1.7 and 2.1 with a sharp peak between 1.8-1.9. Consistent with prior observations (e.g. Wyllie and Gregory, 1953), the relatively small variation in $m^*$ appears to be controlled by grain shape and cementation. The values of $n^*$ are broadly distributed between 0.6 and 2.6. The large variation in $n^*$ appears to be related to cementation, pressure solution, and depositional environment (e.g. laminations). Samples without visible laminations, as identified from thin-section photographs, have $n^*$ values ranging from 1.0 to 2.6. Such samples with low values of $n^*$ tend to have an appreciable fraction of their pore volumes consisting of well-connected, hairline pores. Because of their high capillarity, these pores remain brine saturated high in the hydrocarbon column and act to preserve conductivity as brine is drained from the rock. Finely-laminated, aeolian sandstones tend to have low saturation exponents, i.e., $0.6 \leq n^* \leq 1.4$ . Their $n^*$ values are strongly correlated to the inverse of the minimum brine saturation attained during desaturation. Such low values of $n^*$ are consistent with a simple model which accounts for systematic variations in capillary pressure and brine saturation in laminated samples. The value of $n^*$ in our dataset is fairly well correlated with porosity. This correlation is useful for establishing bounds on $n^*$ .

title: Fifth Annual Technical Conference San Antonio, Texas - August 1991 Laboratory Measurements of Cementation Factor and Saturation Exponent Under Reservoir Conditions on Asab Reservoir Rock Samples
caption: Fig. 7 : Effect of $m$ and $n$ on calculated $Sw$ values
figure_reason: Shows the combined effect of new m and n values on calculated Sw across facies, the paper's practical result.
tldr: Archie m and n were measured on Asab carbonate plugs at ambient and reservoir conditions; n rose 9-34% under reservoir conditions as cores became more oil-wet.
summary: Resistivity-log saturations in the mixed-wet Asab Thamama Zone B carbonate depended on m and n values measured under non-representative conditions. Twenty-five plugs from five facies were measured for formation factor and resistivity index at room conditions, then formation factor under stress at 121°C, and resistivity index by porous plate with crude oil on one sample per facies. At 2610 psi effective stress m rose by up to about 6% (to 1.79-1.87), roughly 10-15% below the values previously used for logs. Under reservoir conditions n was always higher than at ambient (9-34%, up to 2.5), tied to wettability index falling from cleaned to restored cores. Averaged n values per facies group (2.22, 1.94, 1.98) combined with the new m values change calculated Sw, giving oil saturation corrections of up to about five saturation units.
abstract: The evaluation of saturations and thus of oil reserves from resistivity logs requires determination of both the cementation factor ( $m$ ) and the saturation exponent ( $n$ ) used in Archie's equation. Special laboratory apparatus using actual fluids (formation brine and crude oil) at reservoir temperature and under effective overburden pressure has been developed. Saturation was varied by the Porous Plate technique adapted for reservoir conditions. Prior to the test the effect of net overburden pressure on porosity and the formation factor was evaluated. For each rock sample, the formation factor and the resistivity index were measured first under room conditions and then under reservoir conditions. In addition, wettability indices were determined using Amott's test. Data were collected on cores from the five main facies of the Asab Thamama Zone B reservoir. The restoration of the effective overburden pressure gave a relative increase for $m$ of about 6 % depending on the facies. Under reservoir conditions, the value of $n$ was always higher than under room conditions. This increase of $n$ was attributed to the change in the wetting properties. $n$ increases up to 2.5 as the core becomes more oil-wet. The consequence of the new $m$ and $n$ values on the calculated Sw is also discussed. Finally this paper emphasizes the need to determine electrical and capillary properties under reservoir conditions.

title: A Saturation Interpretation Model for the Dielectric Constant of Shaly Sands
caption: Fig.4 Regression of the dielectric constant on Qbv
figure_reason: Regression of dielectric dispersion on Qbv, the key result showing porosity-independent clay response.
tldr: Develops an empirical dielectric model (1 MHz–1 GHz) for shaly sands with clay and Maxwell-Wagner terms, showing clay dispersion scales with Qbv and is saturation independent.
summary: The paper addresses estimating oil saturation and shaliness in fresh water shaly sands from dielectric measurements. The dielectric constant is modeled as a high-frequency limit (Hanai-Bruggeman, matrix 4.4, depolarization factor L=1/3) plus a clay double-layer polarization term and a Maxwell-Wagner geometric term. Fits on 27 clastic samples at 0.01 molal show clay dispersion scales with CEC per bulk volume (Qbv) independent of porosity, whereas Qv gives porosity-dependent slopes. The geometric term is linear in porosity and scales with frequency/brine conductivity. A 49-sample set at 0.01–0.60 molal shows the clay term decreasing with salinity and varying roughly as 1/√ω. Saturation tests with fluorinert show the clay term is saturation independent, while the geometric term decreases linearly with Sw, equivalent to a porosity or salinity change.

title: Measurement of "Rock Properties" in Coal for Coalbed Methane Production
caption: Fig. 10. Comparison of Gas-Water Relative Permeability for Core B Measured by the Unsteady-State and the Steady-State with Sodium Iodide Methods
figure_reason: Directly compares unsteady-state and steady-state sodium iodide relative permeability on Core B, showing the methods agree.
tldr: Modified core-analysis methods on undried coal cores give cleat porosity near 2% or less, declining water permeability, and consistent gas-water relative permeability from unsteady- and steady-state tests.
summary: Standard porosity, permeability and relative permeability methods need modification for coal, where flow occurs in cleats and drying alters structure. Four undried cores (three San Juan Basin, one Warrior Basin) were tested using a lithium chloride miscible displacement tracer, water permeability measurements and helium-water unsteady-state relative permeability with JBN analysis. Cleat porosities were 1.6% ± 0.3 or less and matched mobile water porosity within error, implying little irreducible water. Water permeability fell by up to an order of magnitude (to 0.04 md) with continued flow, attributed to fines migration, possibly face plugging, but did not significantly affect relative permeability. Dead volume uncertainty strongly affects unsteady-state results, while sodium iodide adsorption biases steady-state saturations; the two methods nonetheless agreed within error on Core B.
abstract: Standard laboratory techniques for measurement of rock properties (porosity, permeability and gas-water relative permeability) must be modified when applied to coal for use in coalbed methane reservoir engineering studies. Coal is unlike most conventional reservoir rock in that fluid flow occurs in a network of naturally occurring microfractures or cleats. Drying coal alters the cleat structure. Therefore, a miscible displacement technique, in which coal cores are not dried, was used to determine an upper limit for cleat porosities of around 2% for cores from coalbed methane wells. There is no significant difference between the cleat porosity measured with the miscible displacement technique and the mobile water porosity for a coal core, indicating there is little or no irreducible water saturation in the cleat network. (The mobile water porosity is the volume of water which is driven out of a water-saturated core by helium injection divided by the bulk volume of the core.) Absolute permeability to water in coal cores can decrease with continued flow by an order of magnitude, probably due to fines migration. Unsteady-state gas-water relative permeability techniques can be modified to handle both the small volumes of water produced from cores with less than 2% porosity and the decreasing absolute permeability. Representative unsteady-state gas-water relative permeability curves for San Juan and Warrior Basin cores which have been used in coalbed methane reservoir engineering studies are presented. In steady-state gas-water relative permeability measurements using sodium iodide as a tracer, sodium iodide adsorption on the coal surfaces will result in systematic error in saturation values. However, within the experimental error with which saturations in the cleat networks can be determined, unsteady-state and steady-state with sodium iodide gas-water relative permeability measurements yield the same results.

title: Static and Dynamic Testing of Coal Specimens
caption: Figure 9. S-wave velocity as a function of effective stress.
figure_reason: Shows S-wave velocity decreasing with saturation, the key unusual finding for coal.
tldr: Ultrasonic velocities were measured on stepwise-ground coal during triaxial and hydrostatic loading; dynamic moduli exceeded static ones, and saturation raised P-wave but lowered S-wave velocity.
summary: Static and dynamic elastic properties of coal are poorly documented, and friability complicates specimen preparation. Stepwise grinding into a 60-sided polygon caused the least cleat disturbance compared with coring or water-saturated freezing. Two Pennsylvania-type coals (apparent porosity 4.2% and 7.1%) were tested dry and oil-saturated, with 1 MHz P and S velocities measured concurrently with strain during hydrostatic and triaxial loading. Dynamic Young's and bulk moduli exceeded static values and were most stress-sensitive at low effective stress, while Poisson's ratio showed no static-dynamic relationship. P-wave velocity rose with saturation, but S-wave velocity fell, which the authors attribute to fluid in cleats reducing solid contact and damping shear transmission, raising dynamic Poisson's ratio. Cyclic tests at 2000 psi confinement showed modulus falling from 470 to 310 ksi as cleat pressure rose from 500 to 1500 psi.
abstract: Substantial public domain information exists, documenting discrepancies in measured values of elastic properties determined from static and dynamic measurements made on conventional reservoir rocks. There is relatively limited public domain information available for coal, especially the relationship between static and dynamic properties as stress conditions are changed. In studying coal mechanical behavior, one difficulty arrises because of the extremely friable nature of coal. In searching for "optimal" sample preparation procedures, several techniques have been used. These techniques have included coring samples using nitrogen, stepwise grinding to the desired dimensions, and, water-saturated freezing and subsequent coring to avoid disintegration of the coal. The most effective procedure attempted to date is the stepwise grinding. To understand static-dynamic mechanical behavior characteristics in coal, ultrasonic wave velocities were measured on relatively "undisturbed" coal samples concurrently with triaxial and hydrostatic compression. Effects of saturation on coal static-dynamic behavior were also examined. Dynamic bulk and Young's moduli and Poisson's ratio were calculated from the wave velocities. The dynamic moduli of the tested samples were greater than the static moduli and increased with increasing effective confining stress. This increase was greatest during initial increments of effective confining stress. P-wave velocity increased with an increase in pore pressure. However, S-wave velocity decreased with an increase in pore pressure. Such a decrease in S-wave velocity resulted in an increase in dynamic Poisson's ratio as calculated from elastic relationships.

title: Characterization of Devonian Shales with X-Ray Computed Tomography
caption: Figure 2. Storage Images In Dynamic Experiment - Slice No. 3.
figure_reason: Time series of xenon storage images in slice 3 showing nodule and fractures filling over time.
tldr: Dual-scan xenon X-ray CT quantifies gas storage in a Cleveland Shale plug, detecting sub-resolution fractures and finding storage far above porosity.
summary: Devonian shales are heterogeneous, with very low matrix permeability and fractures, so conventional core tests give averaged values of limited use. The authors applied a dual-scan X-ray CT method with xenon at 50 psia and room temperature to a 1.5 inch Cleveland Shale plug. Voxel-by-voxel differencing of evacuated and xenon-saturated scans gave a storage ratio (xenon attenuation in rock over bulk gas attenuation) that equals porosity unless adsorption, solution or densification occurs. Measured porosity of an adjoining sample was 6.3%, while the average storage of slice 3 was 0.15 and about a quarter of the slice reached 25%. Thin sections showed that the high-storage streaks were unmineralized fractures, probably induced by coring, and that a pyrite nodule stored much xenon. Fractures of tens of microns, below scanner resolution, were detected, and results are consistent with very low matrix permeability and strong adsorption.

title: Determination of Fluid Flow Mechanisms in Berea Using Mercury Porosimetry and A Stochastic Model to Relate These Mechanisms to Oil Recovery SCA Number 9123 by
caption: Fig. 3: $R_p^2$ vs Number of Parameters Plot
figure_reason: Shows R2p versus number of parameters, justifying reduction to six variables.
tldr: Builds a regression model predicting waterflood oil recovery in Berea sandstone from surface area, pore-entry diameter, tortuosity, wettability and saturations, outperforming literature models.
summary: The study relates rock skeletal properties from mercury porosimetry, Amott-Harvey wettability and tortuosity to waterflood oil recovery in strongly water-wet Berea cores flooded at 1 ft/day, where capillary forces dominate (viscous/capillary ratio 1.3e-7). A first-order regression of ultimate oil recovery on nine variables gave R2 = 94.4% and s = 0.0096. All-possible-regressions screening using R2p, Cp and MSE identified a six-variable subset (surface area, pore-entry diameter, tortuosity, wettability index, Sor, Soi) with R2 = 92.8%, s = 0.0754 and Cp near p. Reducing it further to five variables raised bias (Cp = 22.2) and lowered R2 to 83%. Literature models from Donaldson et al. and Arnold and Crawford fit these data less well (R2 of 72.8% and 77.1%), so adding surface area, pore-entry diameter and tortuosity improved prediction.
abstract: This work is part of on-going research aimed at correlating rock skeletal properties to oil recovery from sandstone, limestone and dolomite cores and incorporating these properties into a stochastic model for predicting oil recovery. As such, this report is divided into the analyses and interpretation of experimental data collected from core floods and correlated against measurements of wettability, tortuosity, pore entry diameter, surface area and pore length and the presentation of a stochastic model based on data obtained from these laboratory experiments which relates rock skeletal properties to oil recovery.

title: Measurement of Pore Compressibility Characteristics in Rock Exhibiting "Pore Collapse" and Volumetric Creep
caption: FIG. 3 Variable Loading Rate Hydrostatic Compaction Test on Diatomite
figure_reason: Shows diatomite void ratio versus log stress at three loading rates, demonstrating the loading-rate shift of the yield point.
tldr: Hydrostatic compaction and creep tests on diatomite and carbonate show fast lab loading overestimates pore-collapse stress; a log-rate extrapolation corrects compaction predictions to field depletion rates.
summary: Standard lab pore compressibility tests load rocks at hundreds of psi/hr, versus about 0.01 psi/hr in the field, so rocks that creep show an apparent preconsolidation and an overestimated pore-collapse stress. Hydrostatic tests with tetradecane as pore fluid were run on a diatomite and a moldic carbonate, varying loading rate from 1000 to 10 psi/hr and including a 10-day constant-stress creep hold at 1500 psi. Creep was linear in void ratio versus log time, about 0.05 per log cycle for diatomite, matching the separation between loading-rate curves. Extrapolating five log cycles lowers the diatomite yield estimate by about 250 psi and the carbonate by about 1300 psi, and in a hypothetical 200 ft diatomite example raises predicted compaction from 4 ft to 20 ft. Incomplete pore pressure dissipation, seen as an overshoot after yield, can mimic rate effects; diatomite matrix permeability (0.003 md) was far below flow-through permeability (0.05 md), requiring about two hours between load steps.
abstract: This paper presents data showing the importance of creep measurements when determining the compressibility characteristics of reservoir rocks that undergo volumetric yield (often referred to as "pore collapse"). Rocks exhibiting pore collapse under hydrostatic loading are characterized by volumetric strains that are predominantly elastic prior to yield and plastic afterwards. Limestones, chalks, and diatomite reservoir rocks have been shown to exhibit pore collapse and high degrees of volumetric creep. Reservoir calculations involving pore compressibility, especially reservoir compaction and subsidence calculations, are often very sensitive to the stress level at which pore collapse is assumed to initiate. This is because there is usually an order of magnitude difference in the compressibility between the elastic (pre-yield) and inelastic (post-yield) regions. It has been shown by others that materials that exhibit volumetric creep under constant stress can be characterized by a family of compaction curves (porosity or void ratio vs. confining stress) corresponding to different loading rates, from laboratory test rates to reservoir depletion rates. Standard loading rates used in laboratory pore compressibility tests (typically 500 psi/hr) do not allow time for creep to occur and can predict pore collapse stresses that are up to several thousand psi too high, depending on the creep rate of the material and the rate at which the reservoir is depleted. If this overestimated collapse stress is a significant portion of the estimated total pressure drop in the reservoir, pore volume change calculations will result in substantial underpredictions of reservoir compaction. Test results are presented for two reservoir materials exhibiting pore collapse and substantial volumetric creep behavior. A method for measuring creep is discussed, and it is shown that the creep is generally linear on a $\log(t)$ plot. A method is proposed for estimating the correct or "field" compaction curve based on extrapolation of the laboratory data to reservoir depletion rates. Examples are given that illustrate the degree to which reservoir compaction is underestimated using standard, non-creep-corrected laboratory compressibility data.

title: Extracting Information from Digital Images of Core
caption: Figure 8 - SFL vs PAD1 of the FMS cross plot with paylog on the Z axis.
figure_reason: Cross plot of SFL versus FMS pad 1 with paylog coloring, showing sand/shale separation from core image processing.
tldr: Describes ImageLog, a color-discrimination system using ellipsoid models in RGB space to quantify sand, shale and fluorescing oil sands in core images for log calibration and thin-bed analysis.
summary: The paper presents ImageLog, a system for quantitative analysis of digital core images captured in white, UV and infrared light. Users pick a few training pixels, and an ellipsoid fitted to the color cloud by principal component analysis (covariance eigenvectors) classifies similar colors, avoiding the inappropriate colors included by rectangular RGB boxes. Outputs include dip-oriented net/gross ("paylog"), sand flag, bed thickness and global net/gross every 1/120 ft. Applications shown include calibrating FMS and CBIL borehole images, orienting core fractures, depth shifting, and image enhancement. In a thin-bed example, FMS pad 1 versus SFL cross plots with beds under 1 ft removed gave a 4 ohm-m sand/shale cutoff, whose predictions compared favorably with core-image sand/shale ratios in a second cored well.
abstract: Quantitative image analysis is becoming routine as digital images gain popularity. The trend seems to be accelerating each year, as the cost to create, store, and process digital images declines. Digital images of core were captured in white, ultraviolet, and infrared light using a video camera or scanner. The ultraviolet and infrared images can be used to detect hydrocarbons, discriminate mineralogy, and to observe features of a rock through black crude oil covering its surface. Digital images can be easily manipulated for presentation alongside conventional wireline logs and borehole images. Such presentations enhance the usefulness of both the wireline and core data. They can help the user orient the core, compensate for missing or lost sections, and rapidly calibrate logs. Our image processing system can perform color discrimination of features in core images. It can be used to quantify the amounts of sand and shale. With our system, the user simply clicks one at a time on a handful of pixels in the image whose colors represent the range of colors exhibited by the feature of interest (e.g. tan-fluorescing oil sands). This trains the computer to recognize these selected colors and all similar colors. This training process is implicit rather than explicit. Unlike other systems, the user doesn't have to worry about setting acceptance windows for red, green, and blue intensities. The user simply picks out the representative colors visually and lets the computer handle the mathematical details. In this way, one can quantify various features such as percent fluorescing oil sands, number of sand or shale laminae, thicknesses of these laminae, and bedding angles to improve reservoir description and correlation to logs. Computer processing of images also relieves geologists of the tedious and often inaccurate task of trying to manually quantify these features.

title: Extended Range Particle Size Distribution Using Laser Diffraction Technology: A New Perspective
caption: FIGURE 9
figure_reason: Compares laser-diffraction clay content with XRD for three Gulf Coast sample sets.
tldr: Laser diffraction gives rapid, reproducible particle size distributions of unconsolidated sands including silt and clay, agreeing with sieve, settling and XRD data and supporting Vshale and permeability estimation.
summary: Traditional sieve, settling and thin-section grain size methods are slow and cannot classify silt and clay fractions. The paper adapts a Leeds & Northrup laser diffraction analyzer (5 mW, 750 nm laser, recirculating flow loop, about 30 s per measurement) to friable and unconsolidated Gulf Coast sands after disaggregation and sonication. Repeat and split-sample runs show good reproducibility. Results agree with dry sieving between 0.044 and 0.35 mm, with laser sizes exceeding sieve sizes above 0.35 mm because of elongate grains, and with a 20-minute settling test. Laser clay fractions compare favorably with XRD clay content for three Gulf Coast sample sets. The full distribution allows Folk and moment sorting parameters and Vshale to be computed, and a texture coefficient correlates with plug permeability (log k = 0.059·TC − 1.03, r = 0.955) for sidewall core permeability estimation.
abstract: Grain size distribution has been traditionally characterized in the oil and gas industry using sieve analysis, settling tube analysis and thin section petrography. These techniques are relatively time consuming and more importantly, do not permit detailed classification of the silt and clay size fractions. Existing laser optics technology developed initially for the powder industry is mature, reliable and can be readily adapted to size distribution analysis of friable and unconsolidated sediments. The measurement range is sufficiently broad, the size determination is rapid and the data are reproducible. The laser optics data compare favorably with sieve analysis and settling tube analysis over traditional measurement ranges and the clay size fraction typically compares favorably with clay content determined by x-ray diffraction. The extended range data can offer improved insight into well completion strategies, sedimentology, log evaluation and core analysis. From a well completion perspective, both sand and potentially mobile fines can be quantified. The application of the data in sedimentology to determine sediment uniformity can be enhanced since the entire distribution is typically measured. This permits accurate computation of Folk and moment sorting parameters. Also, the measurement range is such that classification of "soft" shales is practical. In addition to these typical applications of particle size distribution, the data have utility in log evaluation. The extended measurements range provides for rapid determination of Vshale on cores. Permeability values on percussion-style sidewall cores, typically determined by visual estimation, can be significantly improved with laser optics data.

title: Benefits of High Resolution Computed Tomography in Core Analysis
caption: Figure 2. Tomogram at approximately the same plane in the core sample shown in Figure 1 prepared using an ICT scanner.
figure_reason: ICT tomogram of the same silicified core as the medical scan, showing improved resolution of pores and pyrite.
tldr: Industrial CT scanning (420 keV, down to 0.05 mm resolution) of varied cores shows better imaging of fine pores, fractures and coring artifacts than medical CT, at longer scan times.
summary: Medical CT scanners have roughly 1 mm resolution, which limits their use in core analysis. The paper tests an industrial CT system (420 keV source, detector apertures of 0.05 to 1 mm, scan times of 1.5 to 18 minutes per tomogram) on consolidated and unconsolidated sandstones and carbonates as plugs and 4-inch segments, combining digital radiography with selected tomograms. Compared with a medical scanner on a silicified conglomerate, ICT resolved pores down to 0.1 mm and pyrite more clearly, though with lower contrast sensitivity. It imaged Berea bedding and dissolution porosity, halite distribution, filled fractures in algal limestone, fracture/porosity relationships in a fractured carbonate, gaps in foil-sleeved unconsolidated plugs, and pulverization of a percussion sidewall core (less than 10% undamaged). Drawbacks are longer inspection times and higher equipment cost.
abstract: Medical computed tomography systems, or CAT scanners, are being used with increased frequency to nondestructively evaluate core samples. Most medical CAT scanners, however, have spatial resolutions on the order of one millimeter, which restricts the applications that computed tomography can address in core analysis. A new generation of computed tomography technology has been developed specifically for inspecting non-medical objects and industrial products. Some of these new industrial computed tomography (ICT) systems can provide greatly improved spatial resolution, approaching 0.05mm. These ICT systems can also provide high resolution images with relatively high source radiation energies of 420 KeV to allow nondestructive evaluation of large and dense core samples. Examples of new core analysis capabilities provided by high resolution ICT systems include screening of core plugs and whole core for relatively fine inhomogeneities, microfractures/induced fractures, and characterization of preserved and sleeved plugs.

title: Computerized Neutron Tomography for Core Analysis
caption: Figure 6. Cross-sectional slices using neutrons (left) and 100 keV x-rays (right).
figure_reason: Direct comparison of neutron and x-ray CT slices showing greater internal detail in the neutron image.
tldr: Describes a thermal-neutron CT system at the MIT reactor that images water in a San Andres dolomite core, showing more internal detail than x-ray CT.
summary: X-ray CT is relatively insensitive to hydrocarbons and water in dense rock, and steel barrels degrade it further. The authors built a thermal-neutron tomography system using a 5 cm beam (2.4e8 n/cm2/s) from the MIT reactor, a 6LiF-ZnS scintillator, a mirror and lens, and a cooled CCD camera. A 2.54 cm water-saturated San Andres dolomite core was imaged at 45 angles in about three minutes, with an optical resolution of about 0.2 mm. Neutron slices showed more internal detail than 120 kVp x-ray CT. A counting-statistics analysis gives porosity errors of roughly 0.6-44% depending on core diameter, porosity, and barrel and mud layers, for 1 mm voxels and 1e9 neutron fluence. Practical use needs compact accelerator or plasma-focus neutron sources, as D-T generators would need about three hours per scan.
abstract: The imaging of core samples using both x-ray computerized tomography (CT) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) have shown the usefulness of imaging techniques as ways of measuring the porosity of saturated cores by producing images of the hydrogen content. In this paper, we describe a method for tomographic imaging using thermal neutrons which has the advantage of imaging directly the hydrogen content of samples with high sensitivity. We have made three dimensional images of a brine-saturated sample of San Andres dolomite using thermal neutrons from the MIT research reactor. The interaction of thermal neutrons varies greatly from element to element but the interaction probability is particularly large for hydrogen. As an example, the absorption length for $\text{SiO}_2$ is approximately $0.3 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ while water is approximately $3.4 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ . This is in marked contrast to x-ray CT where materials of high atomic number dominate the absorption. The mineral matrix is essentially transparent to the neutrons and thus neutron CT images provide a direct way to image the water or hydrocarbon content of cores and hence to obtain porosity information. The neutron absorption of typical steel core holders is also relatively small, and it is possible to image cores while they are inside steel core barrels.

title: The Precision of Grain Volume Porosimeters
caption: FIGURE 4 PRECISION OF THE TYPICAL HELIUM POROSIMETER
figure_reason: Experimental helium porosimeter precision versus grain volume compared with stochastic curves, showing real precision beats transducer-spec prediction.
tldr: Stochastic modelling and repeat measurements on aluminium billets show gas expansion porosimeters are far more precise than transducer specs imply, and helium is preferred over nitrogen.
summary: The paper examines the precision of grain volume measurement in a gas expansion (Boyle's law) porosimeter. A stochastic model, with Gaussian pressure errors propagated through the calibration regression, was compared with repeat experiments using ball bearings and aluminium billets whose true volumes were established by chemical-composition density, Archimedes and small-chamber porosimetry. Quoted transducer precision (0.0025 of full scale) is really an accuracy; actual repeatability is about 0.0001–0.001, well within the 0.004 fractional error needed for grain density within ±10 kg/m³. Precision degrades when grain volume falls below 50% of chamber volume, and the optimum reference-to-sample chamber ratio is 0.25–0.5; initial pressure has little effect if the gauge range matches it. Caliper-derived volumes were inadequate as calibration standards, and nitrogen gave slightly lower grain volumes than helium on sandstones (up to 0.3%), suggesting adsorption, so helium is recommended.
abstract: The precision of grain volumes determined by a gas expansion porosimeter is examined by both a theoretical method (stochastic modelling) and an experimental method (repeat experimentation). The results show that the porosimeter is more accurate than would be expected based on published “precisions” for the pressure transducer that it uses. This is because this “precision” is actually an accuracy. Because systematic errors are calibrated out during operation of the instrument, the true precision of the device is much better than the quoted precision of the transducer. The results indicate that a reference chamber to sample chamber volume of 0.25 to 0.50 is optimal, and that grain volume to sample chamber volume should be greater than 0.5. Experimental evidence is given to show that grain volumes found using helium are consistently larger than those found using nitrogen. This is likely due to adsorption effects.

title: Liquified-Gas Extraction and Near-Infrared Analysis of Core
caption: Figure 6 NIR Regression for Asphaltenes. A good correlation ( $R=.996$ ) was found between the percentage of asphaltenes of this training set of crudes and the corresponding near-infrared spectra. In a perfect correlation, all the points would lie exactly on the $45^\circ$ equal value line. The regression equation was based on the absorbances at three wavelengths, 1604, 1744, and 2262 nm.
figure_reason: NIR regression for asphaltenes shows the strong correlation (R=.996) on the equal-value line.
tldr: Describes cold liquified-gas (cyclopropane) Soxhlet extraction of core to recover pure crude and water, plus near-infrared regression to predict crude properties from tiny extract samples.
summary: Dean-Stark extraction heats core, risks damaging gypsum or clay, and discards the extracted crude. The paper proposes liquified-gas extraction in a pressurized Soxhlet using cyclopropane, vinyl chloride or Freon-152a at room temperature, with a 3A molecular sieve desiccant to trap water and leave nearly pure crude in the flask. A Berea plug saturated with 33.3° API crude gave an extract of 32.7° API, and a following toluene extraction showed no colour. Cyclopropane is judged the best overall choice, vinyl chloride the best solvent but carcinogenic, and Freon-152a a poor solvent. NIR regressions on crude spectra (1100-2500 nm) gave R=0.996 for asphaltenes, 0.972 for API gravity and density, and 0.997 for API over 13.9-60.2°. They work on samples as small as 12 microliters, and training with deliberately topped samples can predict produced-crude API gravity before light-end loss.
abstract: This paper describes two new techniques, liquified-gas extraction and near-infrared analysis, which can be used separately or in tandem to analyze core and the crude oil in core. Liquified-gas extraction of core utilizes solvents such as cyclopropane or vinyl chloride (which boil far below room temperature) to clean core in a pressurized Soxhlet. Because the extraction is conducted at or below room temperature, it can be performed on heat-sensitive core such as those containing gypsum. After the liquified gas is vented, essentially pure crude oil remains in the boiling flask and recovered water is collected in a desiccant trap. The weights of extracted crude oil and water are obtained from the weight changes of the boiling flask and desiccant, respectively. When sufficient crude is extracted, one can directly measure physical properties such as API gravity (requires $\geq 0.1$ ml) or viscosity (requires $\geq 1.0$ ml) as well. Near-infrared analysis is a powerful technique for estimating properties of crude oils or other materials from their near-infrared spectra. One can perform near-infrared analysis on the liquified-gas extracted crude oil to predict percentage of asphaltenes, gas-oil ratio, API gravity, and viscosity, not only of the extract, but of the corresponding produced crude (before the loss of light ends). Near-infrared analysis can be done using as little as 0.012 ml of sample.

title: Quantitative Porosity Mapping of Reservoir Rock Cores by Physically Slice Selected NMR
caption: FIGURE 9. Comparison of porosity profiles for the composite core sample. Uncertainty of each NMR experimental point is approximately $\pm 0.6\%$ porosity.
figure_reason: Composite core NMR porosity profile versus gravimetric profile and convolution prediction shows heterogeneity mapping and slice resolution.
tldr: A physically slice-selected NMR probe maps axial porosity profiles in long brine-saturated cores, agreeing with gravimetric porosity within about 0.5 porosity units for homogeneous cores.
summary: The paper develops quantitative physical slice selection NMR for porosity profiling of long cores, which exceed the size of a typical NMR probe. A 100 mm diameter short-strut probe with 30 mm slice thickness (and an RF-screened variant) was built, and its slice profiles and B1 maps were characterized at 0.66 T. A pulse-acquire protocol with stretched-exponential extrapolation over the receiver deadtime was calibrated against a MnCl2 water reference. Berea sandstone gave 13.0±0.3% NMR porosity versus 13.4±0.1% gravimetric, and Bedford limestone 13.8±0.3% versus 13.3±0.1%. A five-core composite gave 19.8±0.6% versus 20.8±0.1%, and the smoothed profile was reproduced by convolving the slice profile with the gravimetric porosity profile.
abstract: A unique feature of NMR saturation measurements is the facility to study the saturation state in a defined region of a long ( $\geq 1$ foot) core sample and thus measure the porosity profile. This paper addresses the three steps necessary to implement quantitative physical slice selection: (i) construction of a NMR probe of dimensions commensurate with the slice thickness required, (ii) demonstration that the characteristics of the probe are appropriate for quantitative porosity measurements and (iii) establishing and testing a NMR measurement protocol. The results reported were obtained with a Bruker MSL300 console in conjunction with a Bruker 2 kW class C amplifier and an Oxford Instruments 31 cm horizontal bore superconducting magnet operating at 0.66 T (28.3 MHz for $^1\text{H}$ NMR). The dimensions of the physical slice are primarily controlled by the size of the NMR probe and the position of radiofrequency screening. Two options can be considered to define a physical slice; first, the slice thickness can be determined solely by the length of the NMR probe, and second, radiofrequency screening can be implemented to modify the slice profile from a longer length probe. Both approaches have been evaluated, the first in detail. This method has been developed into a practical system and used to measure the axial porosity profiles of three brine saturated long core samples: Berea sandstone, Bedford limestone and a composite core sample. For the Berea core a mean NMR porosity of $13.0 \pm 0.3\%$ was obtained; the gravimetric porosity was $13.4 \pm 0.1\%$ . The corresponding values for the Bedford core are $13.8 \pm 0.3$ and $13.3 \pm 0.1\%$ porosity, respectively. Both of these samples exhibit homogeneous porosity distributions. To investigate heterogeneous porosity distributions a composite of five short cores, including both sandstones and carbonates, was studied. The NMR porosity profile obtained clearly maps the porosity variation, based on the individual core porosities, and integration of the profile gave a mean porosity of $19.8 \pm 0.6\%$ ; the gravimetric porosity was calculated similarly giving $20.8 \pm 0.1\%$ .

title: Quantification of Permeability Variations Across Thin Laminae in Cross Bedded Sandstone
caption: FIGURE 10 Smoothed graph of probe permeameter measurements with linear fit and Kh values from 7 m tabular crossbedded sandstone unit.
figure_reason: Smoothed probe permeability profile over the 7 m crossbedded unit showing crossbed-scale permeability structure and Kh comparison.
tldr: Probe permeameter measurements on plugs, cubes and whole core quantify lamina-scale permeability in crossbedded Statfjord sandstone and give a unit permeability estimate consistent with well test.
summary: The study uses an automated probe permeameter to characterize permeability of thin laminae in tabular crossbedded fluvial sandstone from the Statfjord Formation (Gullfaks Sør). Fine-grid probe scans, 1-inch plugs (23 Kh, 27 Kv) and 23-24 mm cubes with confined three-direction permeability were compared. Arithmetic probe averages best matched Kh (R² 0.91) and harmonic averages best matched Kv (R² 0.89, 0.93 after removing five plugs with thin laminae). The unconfined probe overestimates permeability of laminae thinner than the tip-seal, with laminae of about 1-5 mD read as 13-15 mD on cube surfaces. Cubes of visually homogeneous or micaceous material showed Kv/Kh of 0.54-0.78 not explained by probe data, indicating sub-probe-scale anisotropy. For a 7 m unit, crossbed-level averaging with a residual-saturation correction of 1.7 gave about 806 mD versus a thickness-corrected well test permeability of 816 mD.
abstract: An automated precision probe permeameter has been used to investigate the influence on the flow properties of thin laminae in cross bedded sandstone. The material analysed is characterized by lamination, some easily visible and shown to have high permeability contrasts between laminae, but also more subtle lamination in material appearing virtually massive. Because of the unconfined flowgeometry of the probe permeameter, the permeability of low-permeable laminae thinner than the diameter of the probe tip-seal will be overestimated. This is shown by having cubes cut parallel to the laminae. The permeability in three orthogonal directions have been measured conventionally in a core-holder and compared to probe permeameter measurements on the sides of the cubes. This method has also demonstrated and quantified permeability anisotropy on a scale smaller than the dimensions of the probe. Probe measurements on plugs show that horizontal (Kh) and vertical (Kv) conventional plug permeabilities may give reliable information about the higher contrast lamination. With lower contrast lamination, local variations in permeability shown by the probe permeameter to exist even in visually very homogeneous material, make conclusions drawn from Kv and Kh more uncertain. The results from the small-scale measurements have been combined with probe measurements on a 7 m interval of tabular crossbedded sandstone to estimate a probable permeability interval for the unit. Comparison of the permeability estimated from the core data with well test permeability shows reasonable agreement.

title: Acoustic Properties and Their Dependence on Porosity, Mineralogy, and Saturation: Applications to Field-Scale Measurements
caption: Figure 4: P and S velocity vs. partial saturation at sonic (30 kHz) and ultrasonic (500 kHz) frequencies. The difference between measurements and the Gassmann prediction is attributed to saturation heterogeneities at the pore scale and local flow frequency dispersion.
figure_reason: Shows P and S velocity versus partial saturation at sonic and ultrasonic frequencies against Gassmann prediction, the key finding.
tldr: Lab P and S velocities on shaly sandstones show porosity and clay control and Gassmann failure at partial saturation; calibrated relations are applied to sonic log interpretation.
summary: The study addresses how porosity, clay content, saturation and frequency affect P and S velocities in a North Sea shaly sandstone reservoir. Thirteen core samples (porosity 0.9-14%, clay 0-50%) were measured by pulse transmission at sonic and ultrasonic frequencies, up to 37 MPa confining pressure, with mineral moduli from drained unjacketed tests. Linear regressions of velocity on porosity and clay content were derived, showing clay affects shear velocity most and saturation mainly affects Vp. Gassmann underestimates the dry-to-brine velocity increase; a local-flow unrelaxed-frame model explains much of the dispersion, and a mixed relaxed/unrelaxed bulk modulus relation describes partial saturation. Core relations matched well-log data and were used to estimate porosity from shear sonic and to identify gas zones from Vp/Vs, confirmed by neutron-density crossover.
abstract: A laboratory study was conducted to investigate the influence of porosity, mineralogy (shaliness), partial saturation and frequency on P and S velocities. Acoustic measurements were conducted at sonic (20-50 kHz) and ultrasonic (300-700 kHz) frequencies on shaly sandstones covering a range of porosities from 1 to 14% and clay content from 0 to 50%. To quantify the influence of mineralogy on acoustic properties, elastic moduli of the mineral phase were measured directly from drained, unjacketed mechanical tests. Results of this study show that most of the scatter in the velocity-porosity relations is attributed to mineralogy and may be accounted for from the knowledge of shaliness. This is especially true for shear velocity which is strongly affected by clay content. For partial saturation we find that the velocity versus saturation relation is not modeled adequately using the Gassmann theory (1951). This is due to heterogeneities in the saturation at the microscopic scale and velocity dispersion due to intrinsic attenuation. We propose a relationship that takes into account saturation heterogeneities and local flow dispersion mechanism to describe the velocity dependence on partial saturation. Results of this laboratory study were applied to the interpretation of sonic measurements in terms of porosity and saturation.

title: A New Technique to Obtain the Real Capillary Pressure-Saturation Curve Directly from Centrifuge Experiments
caption: FIGURE 6 Air-brine capillary presssure curves comparison of the most permeable samples.
figure_reason: Compares end-piece capillary pressure curve with Rajan, Forbes and inlet-piece curves for the most permeable air-brine samples.
tldr: A porous end-piece in capillary contact at the outlet of centrifuged sandstone plugs gives capillary pressure curves directly, matching Rajan and Forbes solutions and inlet-piece data without mathematical correction.
summary: Centrifuge capillary pressure data normally require mathematical correction because only average saturation is measured and the outlet end effect biases it. The authors attach a 1 cm porous end-piece of the same lithology to the outlet of 5 cm sandstone plugs, using brine-wetted paper for capillary contact, and weigh only the core sample at each speed. Air-brine and oil-brine drainage was run on Berea and reservoir sandstones (31.7-757 mD) up to 3500 rpm. Results were compared with Rajan and Forbes interpretations and with the inlet-piece curve from samples cut into five 1 cm pieces. The end-piece method matched these curves within experimental error (<3%), and the end effect was confined to the last centimeter.
abstract: Determination of the true capillary pressure vs. saturation curve by the centrifuge method has been and still is object of several studies. This problem was first solved with mathematical algorithms whose solutions are derived using some assumptions and approximations which are not always correct. The new approach, described in this paper, enables the analyst to obtain hard saturation data directly from centrifuge experiments. The advantage of this technique is that saturation data have not to be corrected by complex mathematical equations. The new idea is to avoid having an average saturation, which is affected by the end effect in the sample. The far end of the centrifuged sample is equipped with a porous end-piece whose capillary contact with the rock sample is ensured by a layer of cellulose fibre. The whole assembly is then treated as a unique sample undergoing the very same activities as standard samples. The validation of this technique is demonstrated by the comparison of the capillary pressure curve of samples in capillary contact with the end-piece with that obtained through the application of the most recent mathematical formulae. This technique is supported also by comparison with the experimental capillary pressure curve of the inlet piece obtained subdividing the samples in several pieces. drainage on Sandstone samples having different permeabilities are presented together with an analytical discussion of the results.

title: Improvement of Diaphragm Method for Drainage Capillary Pressure Measurement with Micro Pore Membrane
caption: FIGURE 3: Capillary pressure curves with porous plate and membrane for cores G-1 and G-2.
figure_reason: Shows drainage capillary pressure curves from membrane and porous plate for two cores, demonstrating agreement between methods.
tldr: A thin micropore membrane replaces the ceramic plate in oil-brine drainage capillary pressure measurements on Berea sandstone, giving comparable curves with roughly ten times shorter equilibration time.
summary: Ceramic porous plate capillary pressure measurements take weeks because the thick disk controls equilibration. The authors replaced the plate with thin water-wet membranes, testing Nuclepore polycarbonate and Millipore cellulose types, and selected a 0.08 µm Nuclepore membrane with 4 bar entry pressure. They built a coreholder and an endpiece with a support screen, glue and protective Millipore membrane to prevent twisting, rupture and leakage. Oil-brine drainage curves were measured on Berea cores (about 100-500 md) at ambient conditions, and two cores were compared against commercial porous plate data with fairly good agreement. Fitting 32 recovery curves with a Langmuir-type function gave an average characteristic time of 25.8 h for the plate versus 3.1 h for the membrane, about a factor 8-10 faster. Premature oil breakthrough still occurred occasionally, and the authors propose uncertainty-based rules for ending each pressure step.
abstract: A procedure is presented for measuring the drainage liquid-liquid capillary pressure curves by the diaphragm method. The customary ceramic porous plate is replaced by a thin micropore membrane that significantly reduces measurement time. A coreholder with a rubber sleeve allows for confining pressure on the core and is used with a refined oil-brine system at ambient conditions. Eight drainage capillary pressure curves have been measured by the membrane method on Berea sandstone cores with different permeability's. For two of the core samples, the curves were also recorded by the traditional ceramic plate method. There is good agreement between the results of the micropore membrane and the ceramic plate methods. The main advantage of the new method is the reduction in equilibration time. Plots of produced volumes following a step increase in differential pressure exhibit a considerable decrease in equilibration time when the micropore filter is used. The time ratio between the two methods is typically a factor of 10. A drainage capillary pressure curve measured by the micropore membrane method with e.g. seven data points may take approximately ten days, compared with about 3 months for the ceramic disk method.

title: The Use of Footbaths in Centrifuge Capillary Pressure Curve Measurements
caption: FIGURE 4 Effect of footbath on capillary rise
figure_reason: Capillary bundle schematic explains why the Pc=0 condition fails without a footbath, the paper's central interpretation.
tldr: Air/brine centrifuge capillary pressure curves on six sandstones measured with and without footbaths show about 4% Vp lower Sw with footbaths, indicating Pc=0 fails without them.
summary: The Hassler and Brunner centrifuge data processing assumes zero capillary pressure at the sample bottom face, which a footbath physically imposes. Six low-permeability North Sea sandstone samples (preserved and unpreserved sets) were run in a Beckman ultracentrifuge with a PIR-20 rotor, with and without footbaths, in air/brine drainage up to 15,000 rev/min. At Pc = 55 bar, Sw was on average 3.9% Vp lower with a footbath (standard deviation 1.9% Vp), with individual differences from -2.8 to 9.8% Vp. A capillary bundle model explains this: without a footbath the lower meniscus helps hold brine so Pc≠0 at the bottom. The author concludes footbaths give more representative curves and should be standard procedure.
abstract: Fluid production data measured in a centrifuge experiment need to be converted according to some model in order to extract a capillary-pressure curve. A widely applied procedure is the method developed by Hassler and Brunner in the 1940's. Various alternative procedures have been proposed since. All conversion procedures require the assumption introduced by Hassler and Brunner that at the bottom face of the sample the capillary pressure is zero. This paper reports on ultracentrifuge experiments performed with and without a footbath on the same six sandstone core samples. The effect of a footbath is physically to impose the Hassler and Brunner boundary condition. Before each run the samples were fully saturated with brine, while air was used as the displacing phase. Data were processed using the Hassler and Brunner procedure, which was modified in order to account for the effect of the non-uniform gravitational field in the sample both in direction and in magnitude. In our experiments, the wetting phase saturations corresponding to a given capillary pressure were on average about 4% $V_p$ lower when a footbath was used. The observed effect of a footbath is explained by considering the capillary bundle model, leading to the conclusion that the Hassler and Brunner boundary condition does not hold in the case that no footbath is used (as is the conventional procedure). Consequently, centrifuge capillary-pressure curves measured with a footbath are more representative of the true capillary behaviour.

title: An Empirical Method for Evaluation of Capillary Pressure Data
caption: FIGURE 9 Pc measurements compared to Pc vs. Sw evaluated by the different methods.
figure_reason: Compares measured Pc–Sw curves with those predicted by each method, showing the new method's fit at high capillary pressure.
tldr: Proposes an empirical equation linking water saturation, permeability and capillary pressure; on 120 North Sea samples it beats the Leverett J-function and matches Johnson's method.
summary: The paper addresses correlating capillary pressure data with permeability to predict water saturation. A new empirical method, extending Wright and Wooddy (1955), fits Sw = A'·ln(K) + B' with both slope and intercept as power laws of Pc. It was compared with the Leverett J-function, the Caplog multilinear regression and Johnson's method using 120 porous-plate drainage curves from 11 wells in 6 North Sea reservoirs (five sandstone, one chalk; permeability 0.05–25000 md). Average R² was 0.84 for the J-function, 0.89 for Caplog, and 0.93 for both Johnson and the new method. The new method and Johnson's were less sensitive to porosity and best at high capillary pressure, while none predicted Sw well below 0.2 bar. The author recommends applying both the new and Johnson methods and choosing the better fit.
abstract: An empirical method for the evaluation of capillary pressure data is presented. This method, an extension from Wright and Wooddy (1955), relate water saturation, permeability and capillary pressure in one equation. The method is well suited for computer processing. Water saturations, as functions of permeability and capillary pressure, are compared with the corresponding predictions from a similar method by Johnson (1987), from the Leverett J-function and from the Caplog method (multilinear regression) used by Alger et al. (1989) Capillary pressure data from 120 core samples from 6 different reservoirs were used in the comparison. Based on each methods capability to predict the observed relationship between input parameters and the raw capillary pressure data it was found that the new method was superior to the Leverett J-function in all cases, in general superior to the Caplog method and equal to the Johnson method.

title: Predicting the Interfacial Tension of Brine/Gas (or Condensates) Systems
caption: Fig 13 - Correlation $z1(0.5)$ - All data![](_page_18_Figure_10.jpeg)
figure_reason: Shows all IFT data on the improved z1(0.5) correlation, the paper's main result.
tldr: Reviews literature data to predict brine surface tension and gas/brine interfacial tension, improves the Firoozabadi-Ramey correlation with a parachor/molar mass correction, and tests it on a gas/brine case.
summary: Capillary pressure conversion from ambient to reservoir conditions requires estimates of brine surface tension and gas or condensate/brine interfacial tension (IFT). The paper compiles literature data and derives salt-specific coefficients for the increase in brine surface tension (e.g. 1.63 mN/m per molal for NaCl, about 3 for MgCl2 and CaCl2). Alkane/brine IFT increments are 0.84 to 0.95 of the surface-tension values, and may scale with Kelvin temperature. The Firoozabadi & Ramey correlation is re-examined against pure hydrocarbon, gas and C1-C10 mixture data. It is improved with a parachor/molar mass correction, which gives separate gas (δρ>0.7 g/cm3) and liquid hydrocarbon (δρ<0.5) domains, but it still fails for gas-liquid mixtures. In a real methane-rich gas/brine case at 120-130°C and 353-453 bar, predicted IFTs agreed with measured values of 42-45 mN/m within about ±0.5 to 2 mN/m, though the temperature trend was wrong.
abstract: This paper reviews the available literature data that can be used for estimating : (1) the surface tension of brines at ambient conditions, (2) the interfacial tension between a brine and a gas (or condensate) at reservoir conditions. When dealing with the first problem (surface tension of brines), the increase in surface tension due to the salts is often neglected, although there are enough available data to account for it. For the second problem, the paper reviews the literature data on the interfacial tension between water and hydrocarbons (gas, non polar liquids, or mixtures of both), and tries to improve an earlier correlation introduced by Firoozabadi et al. (1988). Still, the improved correlation does not handle properly mixtures of gas and neutral oils, and the need for more laboratory measurements is outlined. Salinity corrections similar to those for surface tensions are presented. The practical use of the predictive correlations is illustrated and compared with laboratory measurements at reservoir conditions on a real gas/brine case.

title: Effect of the Flow Rate on an Imbibition Capillary Pressure Curve: Theory Versus Experiment
caption: FIGURE 4A Dynamic capillary pressure curves (L13)
figure_reason: Measured dynamic capillary pressure curves for limestone L13 at three flow rates, showing the main flow-rate dependence.
tldr: Waterfloods at 1, 5 and 15 cc/hr show imbibition capillary pressure and relative permeabilities increase with flow rate; an averaging-based dynamic capillary pressure term is proposed.
summary: The standard two-phase flow framework assumes capillary pressure and relative permeability depend only on saturation. Waterfloods were run at 1, 5 and 15 cc/hr on a limestone (L13) and a sandstone (M5500), with local pressures in both phases and ultrasonic saturation measured in situ to obtain dynamic capillary pressure curves. Higher flow rates gave higher capillary pressure and a lower dPc/dS. Relative permeabilities history-matched with the measured dynamic Pc increased with flow rate: in L13, end-point water kr rose 30% and oil kr 40% from 1 to 15 cc/hr, and curvature vanished. Using quasi-static Pc instead overestimated the water end point (0.12 vs 0.09 at 5 cc/hr). A theoretical dynamic term, Pc,dyn = Pc,stat + λ ∂(φS)/∂t, was derived by averaging and irreversible thermodynamics, and λ was found to decrease roughly inversely with flow rate.
abstract: Dynamic capillary pressure measurements have been performed during waterfloods, at various flow rates. The capillary pressure is shown to be flow rate dependent: it increases with the flow rate and its derivative with respect to saturation mostly decreases when the flow rate is increased. These dynamic capillary pressure measurements have been used to interpret the flow experiments and calculate the relative permeabilities. Relative permeabilities were found to increase with the flow rate. These results cannot be interpreted in the standard framework of modelling two-phase flow in porous media. A new model, based on an averaging technique is presented.

title: SCA1992-10EURO
caption: Figure 3
figure_reason: Shows progression of a stable flood front through the core by slice, key to the in-situ saturation monitoring results.
tldr: Core waterfloods with in-situ X-ray saturation monitoring gave Sor of 0.23-0.29, reconciled with a lower log Sor (0.20) by using a reduced saturation exponent for hysteresis.
summary: Log analysis of a water-swept zone in a Central North Sea Palaeocene sandstone gave residual oil saturation of 0.20, while relative permeability core data implied a higher value. Four plugs were mildly cleaned, desaturated to Swi on a porous plate, and waterflooded with in-situ saturation monitoring by X-ray attenuation (2 mm slices) followed by a bump flood. Core Sor ranged 0.23-0.29 (average 0.26), with low endpoint water relative permeability (0.11-0.15), little post-breakthrough and bump production, indicating water-wet behaviour. Stable flood fronts and even profiles confirmed homogeneous samples. Reducing the log saturation exponent from 2.0 to about 1.6-1.7 to reflect imbibition hysteresis raised log Sor from 0.204 to 0.235-0.249, largely reconciling log and core values.
abstract: The residual oil saturation (Sor) of a North Sea sandstone reservoir has been measured by two different techniques. Log analysis of a zone swept by vertical water flow from the aquifer yielded a range of values. Carefully performed core analysis using in-situ saturation monitoring has provided an independent check on residual oil saturation. By examining petrophysical parameters, taking saturation hysteresis into account, reconciliation of log and core Sor has been achieved. Application of the results using a Land-type1,2 approach to describe dependence of Sor on initial oil saturation (Soi) furnishes high quality input data for reserves calculations and numerical reservoir simulation. In-situ monitoring of oil and water saturation within core samples was achieved through measuring the attenuation of X-rays. Water saturation (Sw) measurements accurate to 1-2 saturation units were obtained in 2mm contiguous slices down the length of the core over a 30 second scanning period. This detailed, real time saturation profile measurement can identify uneven and therefore unrepresentative initial water saturation (Swi) and Sor profiles. The technique can also identify instability in the flood front due to rock heterogeneities or viscous fingering. Since Sw measurement is made in-situ, it is inherently less prone to the errors suffered by traditional volumetric techniques. The accuracy of this residual oil saturation measurement therefore gives confidence in the values obtained and shows consistency with log-derived Sor.

title: Laboratory Measurement of Oil/Water Saturations by an Ultrasonic Technique
caption: FIGURE 5 Calibration curve for a Vosges sandstone. Relative velocity vs. scanner saturations.
