figure_reason: Shows porosity-Young's modulus relationship failing at low confining pressure and developing with stress, the key result.
tldr: Stress sensitivity of permeability and Young's modulus in Rotliegendes sandstones depends on facies; the porosity-modulus trend fails at low stress, indicating core-recovery microcracks.
summary: The study examines stress sensitivity of porosity, permeability, electrical conductivity and Young's modulus in low permeability Rotliegendes sandstones from three depositional facies (aeolian, fluvial, lake margin sabkha). Plugs were tested up to 34.5 MPa mean stress, with properties fitted by a dual exponential function, and elastic properties measured in a Hoek triaxial cell with strain gauges. Permeability dropped by 13% to over 90%, and Young's modulus rose by a factor of about 2 to 3.5 between 6.9 and 34.5 MPa. Stress sensitivity clustered by facies, with aeolian samples least and sabkha most sensitive in Young's modulus. The expected porosity-Young's modulus relationship developed only at high confining pressure. Anisotropy of Young's modulus, Klinkenberg slip-factor exponent (-0.37 at 6.9 MPa), and SEM/thin-section grain-boundary cracks support stress-relaxation microcracks, so low-stress routine core data may not represent in situ structure. Facies-based correction is proposed.
abstract: This paper presents the results of an investigation into the stress sensitivity of the petrophysical and mechanical properties of low permeability gas bearing sandstones from the UK Southern North Sea. The stress sensitivity of both Young's modulus and permeability is found to be influenced by the deformation characteristics of different depositional facies. It is demonstrated that an appreciation of the mechanical property stress sensitivity can aid the interpretation and application of permeability stress sensitivity behaviour. From the literature it is known that a linear relationship between porosity and Young's modulus exists at reservoir stress levels which is thought to reflect their dependence on the in situ mineral framework. The work reported here confirms this observation but also shows that for the low confining pressure levels encountered in routine core analysis the relationship fails to develop. It is proposed that structural alteration associated with the formation of stress relaxation microcracks, during core recovery, is the most likely explanation for this behaviour. Evidence from SEM and thin sections supports this suggestion. Microstructural alteration related to strain relaxation effects could lead to inaccuracies in the interpretations attached to core data and its applications, particularly in low permeability/low porosity formations which are often very stress sensitive. However, the study indicates that the association of depositional facies with the petrophysical and mechanical stress sensitivity character of sandstones may be a key to reconciling the problem.

title: A Novel Method for the Determination of Water/Oil Capillary Pressures of Mixed Wettability Samples
caption: Fig. 6 Capillary pressure cycle for mixed-wettability sand: 1) primary drainage 2) and 3) secondary imbibition 4) secondary drainage $P_c < 0$
figure_reason: Capillary pressure cycle for mixed-wet sand (f=0.5), showing symmetric positive and negative parts central to the paper.
tldr: A semi-dynamic steady-flow method with outlet washing and ultrasonic saturation measurement gives full positive and negative capillary pressure cycles for sands and Berea of varying wettability without membranes.
summary: Standard porous plate and centrifuge methods struggle to give imbibition and negative capillary pressure curves for mixed-wettability rocks. The authors propose a semi-dynamic method: one fluid is injected at stepped rates (5–500 cc/h) while the in-situ fluid washes the outlet face at 20 cc/h, so Pc is obtained from a pressure tap and local ultrasonic saturation measurements. Tests used sand packs (about 4.6 D) with silane-treated oil-wet fractions f=0, 0.5, 1, and a 130 mD Berea sample. Water-wet and oil-wet sands gave mirror-image cycles with plateaus near 40 mbar, while f=0.5 gave more symmetrical curves with smaller plateaus, interpreted with two interpenetrating wettability networks. The Berea positive Pc agreed with porous plate data, though the maximum rate did not reach irreducible water saturation. Results are considered qualitative owing to low pressures and dead volumes.
abstract: Capillary pressure curves are generally obtained by the porous plate or the centrifuge methods. Both methods have their drawbacks, especially for imbibition curves and mixed wettability samples. We developed a method which easily provides the whole cycle of capillary pressure (drainage and imbibition for both positive and negative $P_c$ ) and for any type of wettability. The principle of our method is to realise a steady flow in the sample and to deduce the capillary pressure $P_c$ from the local balance between viscous and capillary forces. The set-up is a standard displacement cell with a pressure tap. The outlet face is washed by a continuous flow of the in-situ fluid to realise the condition of known uniform pressure and permit the invasion of this fluid. Ultrasonic transducers along the sample give the local saturation after calibration by using the effluent balance. For the first time, whole pressure cycles are obtained for sandstone and sands of different wettabilities. The positive $P_c$ qualitatively agree with results obtained by standard methods. The effect of wettability on the shape of the cycles can be interpreted by assuming the existence of an oil-wet and a water-wet network in the sample. Compared to the centrifuge, the main advantage of this method is to give the positive imbibition curve (and negative drainage). Compared to the porous plate, there is no need for semi-permeable membranes. This technique can be used at high pressure and high temperature in a modified Hassler cell. In addition, it can be easily automated.

title: Wetting and Waterflood Oil Recovery of a Moderately Viscous Crude Oil
caption: Fig. 7. Ultimate waterflood oil recovery and residual oil saturation for cores aged in crude oil at different temperatures.
figure_reason: Shows ultimate waterflood recovery and residual oil saturation versus aging temperature, the paper's central result.
tldr: Aging Berea cores in 46 cp Schuricht crude at higher temperature lowers water-wetness (Amott index) and improves waterflood recovery; micromodels and history matching support this.
summary: The study tests whether wettability alteration trends seen for lighter crudes also hold for a 46 cp Schuricht crude oil. Berea sandstone cores (about 550-735 md, 21% porosity) were aged at initial water saturation for 3-30 days at 26-80°C. Amott indices fell to about 0.4 after 12 days of aging at 53°C. The Amott index to water was 0.61 at 26°C aging and about 0.5 at 53°C, while imbibition rate and recovery decreased with aging temperature (32% to 27% from 26°C to 80°C). Waterflood recovery improved as cores became less water-wet, but it decreased slightly with injection rate (7.5-30 ml/hr). Micromodel floods showed that short aging gave water-wet displacement with ganglia trapping, whereas 80°C aging gave intermediate wetting and more efficient displacement. History matching with a 1D simulator gave Pc and kr curves, and Amott indices from the simulated Pc were reasonably consistent with measured values. The expected leftward shift of the kr crossover with decreasing water-wetness was not observed.
abstract: A laboratory waterflood study of a moderately viscous crude oil is reported. Schuricht crude oil, with room temperature viscosity of 46 cp, is shown to alter wetting and waterflood oil recovery. The extent of wetting alteration is a function of both the duration and temperature at which a Berea core containing connate water is aged in the oil, as has been shown for less viscous crudes. Core tests include rate and extent of imbibition, waterflood recovery as a function of wetting and flood rate, and history matching with a coreflood simulator to estimate capillary pressure and relative permeabilities. Micromodel visualization tests provide further evidence for the alteration of wetting by Schuricht crude oil.

title: Water-Oil Relative Permeabilities in the Case of a Mixed-Wet Carbonate Reservoir: Influence of Experimental Conditions
caption: Fig. 10 Comparison of kr curves. Room versus reservoir conditions.
figure_reason: Final comparison of relative permeability curves at room versus reservoir conditions, the main result.
tldr: Waterflood relative permeabilities for mixed-wet Asab carbonate cores at room versus reservoir conditions, with history matching including imbibition Pc; reservoir conditions give 10% lower Sorw and better curves.
summary: Water-oil relative permeabilities were determined for the mixed-wet M2 facies of the Asab carbonate field. Unsteady-state floods were run on five cleaned plugs at room conditions and on a restored five-plug composite core at 121°C and 2900 psi, at high (150 cm3/hr) and low (3 cm3/hr) rates. Amott indices showed restored-state wettability (WI -0.26) matched the preserved state (-0.21). Residual oil saturation was 28% at reservoir conditions versus 38% at room conditions. History matching with a 1D simulator showed capillary forces matter even at high rate; including the porous-plate imbibition Pc required a significantly modified kro, and a single kr/Pc set matched both high and low rate tests. Ignoring Pc makes JBN-derived relative permeabilities too pessimistic.
abstract: This paper describes a comparison of water-oil relative permeability curves obtained by the "Unsteady-State" technique with core samples from a mixed-wet carbonate oil reservoir located in the Middle East. Coreflood tests were conducted firstly at standard (room) conditions, with synthetic fluids, using five cleaned core samples and, secondly, at reservoir conditions with a restored composite-core, built with the cores previously studied at room conditions. In addition, history matching of the coreflood tests was performed using a one-dimensional two-phase numerical model. Capillary forces were taken into account through an imbibition capillary pressure curve obtained separately by the "Porous Plate" technique adapted to reservoir conditions. It has been demonstrated that the history matching of the coreflood test at a rate equivalent to the field rate is very sensitive to the spontaneous imbibition capillary pressure curve. The effect of the restoration of the reservoir conditions on the shape and the level of relative permeability curves has also been quantified. The residual oil saturation, $S_{Orw}$ , is 10% lower, and the relative permeability curves are more favorable at reservoir conditions than at room conditions. Finally, this paper emphasizes the need to restore reservoir conditions and to numerically interpret coreflood tests when determining relative permeability curves for a mixed-wet carbonate reservoir.

title: A Novel Approach to Testing Core Samples at Reservoir Conditions
caption: Figure 3. Time-dependent changes in the composition of the fluid (a and b) and permeability (c) during brine injection in Test #7. Note the steep decline in permeability during the early hours of flooding, which is due to particle migration and deposition. The minipermeanter traverse (d) shows some natural variation in permeability along the core.
figure_reason: Shows fluid chemistry and permeability decline during brine flooding plus minipermeameter traverse for Test #7.
tldr: A re-circulating, inert core flood rig with on-line HPLC shows Clashach sandstone permeability falls with brine injection but rises with distilled water, depending on fluid chemistry and sample preparation.
summary: Seawater injection in North Sea reservoirs may trigger poorly understood diagenetic reactions, so the authors built a re-circulating plug-flow core flood rig with on-line HPLC sampling of 10-20 µl volumes at reaction temperature and pressure. The rig uses PEEK and titanium wetted parts, confines cores to 68.9 MPa and 34.5 MPa pore pressure, and heats to 100°C. A chloride pulse tracer test checked flow behaviour. Clashach sandstone cores (200 mD to 1 D) were flooded at 80°C, 13.8 MPa effective stress and 0.3 cm3/min for 2-5 weeks. Artificial brine reduced permeability to about 70% (Test #7) and 45% (Test #8) of initial values, while distilled water doubled permeability in a pre-flushed core but dropped it to 12% initially in an unflushed core, recovering to about 63%. The authors conclude that waterflooding is chemically active and that sample preparation strongly affects permeability results.
abstract: Diagenetic reactions associated with the injection of sea water for pressure maintenance and secondary oil recovery in North Sea reservoirs are poorly understood at present. This study describes the development and application of a unique core flood apparatus capable of reproducing in situ North Sea reservoir conditions in standard rock cores while flooding with fluids of different compositions. The basic design is a plug flow reactor which incorporates on-line high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), allowing chemical analysis on small volumes of solution at the temperature and pressure of reaction. Results are presented which show how the permeability of core samples varies with the composition of the injected fluid. These show that the injection of sea water into reservoirs cannot be considered a chemically "passive" process, and in most cases, leads to a reduction in permeability.

title: Effects of Using Live Versus Dead Crude Oils on Unsteady-State Water/Oil Relative Permeabilities
caption: Figure 2. Results of Live Vs Dead Waterfloods on Composites from North Sea Reservoir "A".
figure_reason: Compares live and dead oil water-oil relative permeability curves for North Sea A composites, the paper's main result.
tldr: Unsteady-state waterfloods with live and dead crude oils on preserved cores and Berea showed no consistent relative permeability difference where saturation ranges overlapped; Berea results were irreproducible.
summary: The study asks whether relative permeabilities measured with dead (de-gassed) crude oil differ from those with live oil, since live-oil testing is costly. Unsteady-state waterfloods were run on composite cores for three crude oil systems: North Sea A (preserved core, 34° API), a French reservoir (preserved core, 37° API), and North Sea B (aged Berea, 23° API). Each composite was flooded with live oil and then dead oil, or in reverse order, at reservoir temperature and pressure. Saturations were checked by brine elution and vacuum distillation, and relative permeabilities were computed with the JBN method. Dead oil gave earlier breakthrough and a broader saturation range because of its higher viscosity. Where the curves overlapped, no consistent live-versus-dead difference appeared in the preserved cores; differences tracked initial water saturation (3-4% HCV spread after normalization). The Berea/North Sea B tests were not reproducible, probably because of unstable wettability and viscous fingering, so no conclusion was possible for that case.

title: Wettability Changes Due to the Deposition and Presence of Asphaltenes in Crude Oil
caption: FIG. 3 EVALUATION OF THE EFFECT OF AGING IN CRUDE OIL AMOTT INDEX (12 DAYS, 14.7 PSI)
figure_reason: Compares Amott indices before and after 12-day aging for different oils and rocks, showing the shift toward oil-wet.
tldr: Amott tests on Venezuelan reservoir cores and Berea show asphaltene-rich crude and pentane-induced precipitation shift wettability toward oil-wet; a flow-through cleaning method restores water-wetness.
summary: The study examines how asphaltene content and precipitation change core wettability, using Venezuelan reservoir cores and Berea plugs with four crudes (asphaltenes 1.1 to 17 wt%) and a desasphalted oil. Wettability was measured with a modified Amott test on 42 samples (103 tests), reproducible within ±0.05. Soxhlet cleaning with toluene-methanol or dichloroethane-methanol failed to make reservoir cores water-wet, while a flow-through sequence of dichloroethane, methanol and formation brine at 65°C gave strongly water-wet cores with no spontaneous oil imbibition. Aging in crude for 6 to 38 days and pentane-induced deposition both shifted cores toward oil-wet; Berea indices fell from about +0.95 to as low as -0.75 with high-asphaltene oils, but only to intermediate-wet with the low-asphaltene oil M or desasphalted oil. The degree of alteration depended on cleaning, rock type, asphaltene amount and asphaltene properties, and adsorption alone could alter wettability without visible precipitate.
abstract: Wettability is one the most important properties affecting oil recovery efficiency of a reservoir. There is abundant evidence that rock wettability could change due to rock interactions with injected fluids and to the adsorption of the petroleum heavy ends (asphaltene and resin fractions) on the pore walls. In addition to formation damage considerations, the issue of wettability modification is a crucial one for core sampling and core studies. In order to optimize production through core analysis reliability, it is necessary to have a good understanding of the mechanisms controlling these changes. In this work, the effect of oil asphaltene content and eventual precipitation on wettability were investigated. Fluids and cores of Venezuelan reservoirs with different asphaltene contents and as well as Berea core plugs were used to carry out the study. Wettability was measured using a modified version of the Amott imbibition test. Before performing the tests to determine wettability changes due to the asphaltenes, the wettability of cores "as received" and after cleaning were evaluated. Cleaning procedures reported in the literature were tested on reservoir cores, resulting ineffective, the wettability index was less than the expected value for strongly water-wet conditions, even after a third cleaning. To resolve this, a flow-through core cleaning procedure was developed. Once the reservoir and Berea cores were made partially or strongly water-wet, some of them were saturated with brine, flushed with crude oil and aged at several temperatures for a period ranging from 6 to 38 days and their Amott indices were measured. Others were flushed with pentane, to induce asphaltene precipitation, and then wettability was determined. Cores aged in high asphaltene content crude oil (for 12 a 38 days) and those where asphaltene precipitation was induced, showed similar wettability changes toward the oil-wet conditions. Cores aged in desasphalted oil or low-asphaltene content oil, showed an intermediate-wet state. It was found that core cleaning before aging and the nature of the rock affected the degree of wettability alterations of samples evaluated.

title: Computed Microtomography of Reservoir Core Samples
caption: Figure 3: GT scans and microtomograms of sandstone samples. GT samples were 2.54 cm and CMT samples were 2 mm in diameter. Note greatly increased resolution and measurement sensitivity in CMT.
figure_reason: Compares medical CT scans and CMT images of three sandstones with histograms, showing pore-scale detail and mineral contrast.
tldr: Synchrotron X-ray computed microtomography at about 5 µm resolution images sandstone pore structure, minerals and connectivity, with porosity compared against helium porosimetry and SEM.
summary: Medical CT scanners are too coarse (about 0.25 x 0.25 x 1.5 mm) for pore-level imaging, so the authors applied synchrotron X-ray computed microtomography (CMT) at the NSLS X26C beamline. Three sandstones were epoxy-impregnated and 2-3 mm microcores were scanned at 5 µm voxel resolution, with imaging times of 8-90 minutes per slice. Comparison with medical CT showed core-scale and pore-scale heterogeneity can differ. Minerals such as quartz, feldspar and siderite or pyrite were identified from attenuation coefficients (810, 1320 and 2690 m-1 in sandstone #2). CMT porosity agreed with helium porosity for sandstones #1 and #2 (24.5% vs 27.3%, 22.1% vs 21.6%), but sandstone #3 gave 12.7% vs 21.3%, attributed to sub-resolution pores. Stacking 95 slices gave a 3D volume and pore-connectivity maps usable as input for pore-level flow simulation.
abstract: X-ray computed tomography (CT) is often utilized to evaluate and characterize structural characteristics within reservoir core material systems. Generally, medical CT scanners have been employed because of their availability and ease of use. Of interest lately has been the acquisition of three-dimensional, high resolution descriptions of rock and pore structures for characterization of the porous media and for modeling of single and multiphase transport processes. The spatial resolution of current medical CT scanners is too coarse for pore level imaging of most core samples. Recently developed high resolution computed microtomography (CMT) using synchrotron X-ray sources is analogous to conventional medical CT scanning and provides the ability to obtain three-dimensional images of specimens with a spatial resolution on the order of micrometers. Application of this technique to the study of core samples provides two- and three-dimensional high resolution description of pore structure and mineral distributions. Pore space and interconnectivity is accurately characterized and visualized. Computed microtomography data can serve as input into pore-level simulation techniques. A generalized explanation of the technique is provided, with comparison to conventional CT scanning techniques and results. Computed microtomographic results of several sandstone samples are presented and discussed. Bulk porosity values and mineralogical identification were obtained from the microtomograms and compared with gas porosity and scanning electron microscope results on tandem samples.

title: Characterization of Fractures and Multiphase Flow in Fractured Permeable Rocks Using NMR Imaging Techniques
caption: Fig. 5. Comparison of images using regular spin-echo sequence [(a) and (c)] and using IRSE sequence with a selected TIofr,t,, so that fluid distribution in the porous matrix is highlighted [(b) and (d)]. The sample is
figure_reason: Compares conventional spin-echo with fracture-suppressed IRSE images, showing improved matrix bedding contrast.
tldr: Inversion-recovery spin-echo NMR imaging selectively suppresses fracture or matrix signal to identify fractures, image matrix faster, and monitor two-phase displacement in fractured cores.
summary: Fractures in permeable rock are hard to detect with conventional spin-echo NMR images because of poor contrast and signal-to-noise between fracture and matrix. The authors use an inversion-recovery spin-echo sequence with the inversion time chosen to null either the fracture or the matrix signal, exploiting their different T1 relaxation. Tests used Berea, Arkansas Gold and Calico samples and Indiana limestone with natural or artificial fractures (beads up to 250 µm) in a 2-T imager. Fractures under about 100 µm and low-porosity fractures in laminated Berea were identified unambiguously, and suppressing fracture signal revealed matrix bedding in Calico limestone. Shorter TR/TI pairs cut imaging time to 40% with better S/N. Apparent fracture widths were larger than bead sizes because of linebroadening. A D2O-oil displacement in a fractured Arkansas Gold sandstone showed water bypassing through the fracture in the central region.
abstract: A new noninvasive method is presented for laboratory characterization of fractures in permeable media using relaxation-weighted NMR imaging techniques. The method is based on the fact that relaxation rates in fractures and those in surrounding porous matrix are substantially different. Thus, by selectively suppressing imaging signals from either fractures or porous matrix, one can highlight fluid distributions in either of these regions so that fractures can be unambiguously identified and surrounding porous structures can be characterized. The advantages over conventional NMR spin-echo imaging are demonstrated. We also demonstrate that the technique can be used to speed acquisitions of images of fluid distributions in porous matrix. In addition, a two-phase displacement experiment was conducted to investigate transport features related to fractured systems. Introduction distributions. Many petroleum producing reservoirs and water supplying aquifers around the world are fractured sedimentary rocks. The presence of fractures greatly complicates the dynamics of flow within porous media, particularly in situations for which multiple fluid phases are present. Most models for multiphase flow (see, e.g., Refs. 1&2) are based on simplified or idealized conceptual representations which generally have not yet been sufficiently validated with experimental data. A key reason for this has been the lack of availability of tools to probe the detziled fracture and fluid flow CT x-ray scanning and nuclear magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provide unprecedented opportunity to characterize fractures and flow distributions within porous media. CT scanning is used routinely for sample screening3. It has also been used for detailed fracture characterization and analysis of gas flow within porous media4. Petrophysical applications of MRI, which have generally been less well developed, offers a number of advantages compared to CT scanning. One interesting characteristic is that there is a wider range of operations available so that experiments can be designed to enhance various physical features. Here, we develop relaxation-weighted MRI .techniques for characterizing fractures and flow in fractured media. Through selection of the imaging protocol, the signal from either the fractures or matrix can be highlighted, while the other signal can be virtually eliminated. A similar approach5f6 has been used previously in medical areas for improving contrasts between lipid and organs or between tumor and fatlmuscle; its petrophysical application has not been explored. The considerable improvement of these techniques compared to conventional spin-echo imaging for investigating fractured media is demonstrated. The method for rapid imaging acquisition using this approach is presented. The use of MRI techniques to monitor multiphase displacement in fractured media is also demonstrated.

title: The Use of Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy to Probe Microscopic Structures and Fluid Distributions in Porous Media
caption: Figure 4. Fluid distributions for three rock samples at different saturations, shown with both linear and log scales for pore volume-to-surface area ratio V/S.
figure_reason: Shows fluid phase distributions evolving with decreasing saturation for sandstones and limestone, the paper's main application result.
tldr: A B-spline, Tikhonov-regularized inversion of NMR T1 data, with surface relaxivity calibrated by NMR diffusion V/S, gives pore-size and fluid distributions in sandstones and limestone.
summary: Conventional pore-structure methods (mercury porosimetry, nitrogen adsorption, thin sections) are destructive and poorly suited to multiphase systems, so the authors develop an NMR spin-lattice relaxation approach. The T1 distribution is recovered from inversion-recovery data by representing it with B-splines and solving a nonnegativity-constrained, second-derivative Tikhonov problem, with the regularization parameter set to the largest value that does not degrade the fit. Surface relaxivity is obtained by comparing average relaxation time with pore volume-to-surface area ratios (V/S) from short-time restricted diffusion measurements, which agreed with values calculated for glass bead packs. For Bentheimer, Berea and Texas Cream limestone, surface relaxivities were 9.3, 9.8 and 7.1 µm/s and V/S were 11.6, 6.9 and 3.5 µm. Pore-size distributions were consistent with thin-section observations, and the maximum V/S of about 30 µm satisfied the fast-exchange condition. Distributions at partial saturation showed water leaving the large pores first during drainage.
abstract: Nuc1ea.r magnetic resonance (NMR) spin-lattice relaxation mea,sureme~lts are used to investigate pore structures a,nd fluid phase distributions in porous media. A new method for estimating relaxation time distribution functions from measured relaxation da.ta is presented. A B-spline basis is used for representing the distribution function, and Tikhonov regularization is employed to stabilize the estimation problem. A new approach to determine the surface relaxivity, which is required to convert rela,xation time distributions to pore-size distributions or fluid pha.se distributions at partial saturations, is presented. It is based on pore volume-to-surfa.ce area ratios estimated by NMR diffusion measurements. This approa.cl1 wa.s validated by analyzing certain model porous media with known pore volume-to-surface area ratios. The use of the methodology is demonstrated by determining pore-size and fluid phase distributions of sandstone and carbonate samples.

title: Core Analysis by Low Field NMR
caption: Figure 1: Comparison of NMR porosity mea- Figure 2: The relative error in 85 MHz NMR sured at three field strengths to buoyancy porosity crossplotted with CEC and paramporosity. o is 85 MHz data, + is 2 MHz data, agnetic impurities. The open circles indicate is1 MHz data. CEC values and the solid circles are weight percent Fe plus Mn.
figure_reason: Shows 85 MHz NMR porosity underestimated versus 1 and 2 MHz agreeing with buoyancy porosity, the key low-field advantage.
tldr: Low field (about 2 MHz) NMR T2 measurements on cores give accurate porosity, pore-size distributions, free fluid, clay bound water, permeability, and oil saturation and viscosity.
summary: Core NMR is traditionally done at high field, where internal gradients from paramagnetic minerals degrade T2 signals; this paper evaluates low field (1–2 MHz) T2 measurements to support NMR logging tools. At 85 MHz porosity was underestimated in shaly sands, correlating with Fe+Mn and CEC, while 1 and 2 MHz matched gravimetric porosity. 2 MHz porosity agreed with buoyancy porosity for 210 sandstones/diatomites (slope 0.98, SD 0.8 p.u.) and 71 carbonates (slope 0.97). T2 distributions resemble mercury injection pore-size distributions. T2 cutoffs of 33 ms (sandstone) and 92 ms (carbonate) predict free fluid from 100 psi centrifuge, and a 3 ms cutoff estimates clay bound water. Permeability k = 4.6 T2ML^2 φ^4 fits 110 sandstones, truncating vugs at 750 ms improves Clearfork dolomite estimates (error factor 4.8 to 2.6), and T2ML correlates inversely with oil viscosity (0.7–1000 cp). D2O soaking of native-state Belridge diatomite isolates oil, gives gas and oil saturation matching Dean-Stark, and allows in situ viscosity.
abstract: NMR core measurements have been made customarily in.high magnetic fields, emphasizing TI for pore-size evaluation or using chemical shift spectroscopy for quantitative differentiation of oil and water. However, new NMR logging tools use T2 measurements made at low field strengths and these measurements should be supported by core analysis. This paper illustrates that low field NMR T2 measurements made on water-saturated rock cores can be used to measure total porosity and extract T2-distributions. The T2-distributions are shown to be closely related to pore size distributions. Our experiments demonstrate that low field measurements are quantitative, even for cases where high field measurements fail. T2-distributions from water-saturated plugs are used to estimate producible fluids for sandstones and carbonates and to estimate clay bound water and matrix permeability. Although chemical shift spectroscopy is not feasible at low fields, a method is demonstrated on native state diatomites that permits the measurement of oil, water and gas saturation. In the case presented, it is also possible to determine the oil viscosity, in situ.

title: In-Situ Saturation Distributions: The Key to Understanding Core Analysis
caption: FIG 3: SPATIAL/TEMPORAL RESOLUTION FOR THREE PHASE ATTENUATION
figure_reason: Shows spatial/temporal resolution trade-offs for three-phase attenuation, comparing gamma and X-ray scanning performance.
tldr: Reviews gamma attenuation, X-ray attenuation and gamma emission methods for in-situ saturation measurement in core floods, with accuracy analysis and wettability and gravity drainage examples.
summary: The paper reviews ionising-radiation techniques for measuring in-situ saturation distributions of up to three phases during core floods: gamma attenuation, X-ray attenuation and gamma emission. It gives the saturation equations and a statistical error analysis relating photon intensity accuracy to saturation accuracy. For 1% PV saturation accuracy, intensity accuracy of 0.004% is needed for decane/brine/air and 0.04% for decane/brine, relaxed to 0.089% and 0.47% with 10% NaI dopant. X-ray scanning improves temporal resolution by about an order of magnitude over gamma attenuation, while gamma emission is the practical option for steel pressure vessels. Examples show waterflood ROS of 0.42 in a water-wet core versus 0.21 after ageing, and gravity drainage profiles revealing end effects that would cause mass balance to overestimate residual oil to gas.
abstract: In order to ensure accurate interpretation of core flood experiments, in-situ saturation measurements are considered to be essential. This paper provides a review of in-situ saturation measurement methods based on ionising radiation and incorporates gamma attenuation, X-ray attenuation and gamma emission. These techniques are routinely employed during reservoir and ambient condition core floods to determine the in-situ saturation distributions of up to three mobile phases. The measurement techniques are described, together with their relative strengths, weaknesses and accuracies thus enabling selection of the optimum technique for a particular application. Examples of in-situ saturation measurements from studies of wettability and gravity drainage are presented to illustrate the value of this capability. Without this knowledge, core scale artefacts can lead to significant errors when interpreting experimental data. The ability to determine in-situ saturation measurements during gravity drainage enables oil and brine permeabilities to be derived. This capability is attractive since it enables key data to be generated in a flow regime which is representative of the reservoir.

title: Heterogeneous Systems: An Integrated Approach Based on Different Imaging Techniques
caption: FIGURE 5 Photograph of a thin section of the core (a) compared to corresponding NMR images acquired after saturation with oil (b) and flooding with D,O (c).
figure_reason: Compares thin-section photo with NMR images before and after D2O flooding, showing fluid displacement from vuggy regions.
tldr: MRI and X-ray CT, combined with SEM and petrography, characterize fluid distribution and porosity in a vuggy, fractured dolomite core before and after deuterated water flooding.
summary: Standard core analysis performs poorly on vuggy, fractured carbonates, so the authors combined MRI, X-ray CT, SEM and thin-section petrography on a dolomite breccia core (10 cm x 11.7 cm) and a 1" x 2" plug. The core was oil-saturated and flooded with 3 PV of D2O, which is invisible to MRI, with images taken at each step. NMR indicated 11% porosity versus 7.15% from conventional tests, and water retained after drying was 40%, falling to 30% after D2O flooding. MRI showed oil in large vugs and microvuggy zones being swept, while strongly trapped water sat in fine microporosity of a few microns. CT detected a thin cemented fracture that MRI missed, showing the techniques are complementary, and T1 distributions were compared with SEM pore sizes (100-250 µm pores in a fine microporous matrix).
abstract: The study is based on the application of two different techniques: MRI and CT X-Ray. MRI is sensitive to hydrogen nuclei and reveals fluids distribution and therefore porosity, while X-Ray CT may give important details on rock matrix heterogeneity because of its sensitivity to the density of the medium. This type of analysis could be applied efficiently in a preliminary estimation of the cores, providing data to integrate successive localised microscopic examinations (SEM), which constitute an input for petrography. Both techniques provided complementary information on a submillimetrical scale of a Dolomite reservoir sample. The sample, saturated with water and oil, was analysed and successively flooded with deuterated water, which is MRI invisible. Images were taken after the waterflooding step and data analysed to evaluate macroscopic porosity connections. Significant changes in fluid distributions after the displacement, were observed. In a successive step, the petrographic analysis of thin sections of the sample allowed establishment of relations between the distribution of fluids and the peculiar porosity of this kind of rock.

title: EFFECTS OF CORING ON PETROPHYSICAL MEASUREMENTS. Rune M. Holt, IKU Petroleum Research and NTH Norwegian Institute of Technology, Trondheim, Norway release effects can be studied in a systematic way
caption: Figure 2: Volumem~c strain vs. experiment time during an unloading - reloading cycle for three dflerent unloadingpuths.
figure_reason: Shows volumetric strain through unloading-reloading for different paths, revealing permanent porosity loss after anisotropic unloading.
tldr: Synthetic sandstones formed under in situ stress and then unloaded and reloaded show that simulated coring permanently reduces porosity, sound velocities and compaction stiffness in weak sandstone.
summary: Core damage from stress release, pore pressure release, temperature change and non-native fluids can permanently alter core properties, so core data may not represent the in situ rock. Weak synthetic sandstones (about 30% porosity, unconfined strength below 5 MPa) were cemented with sodium silicate and CO2 under 15 MPa axial and 7.5 MPa radial stress in a triaxial cell. They then went through unloading-reloading cycles simulating coring, with anisotropic or isotropic unloading, fast or slow. Anisotropic unloading left permanent porosity reductions of 0.5-1% units, which implies a 10-15% permeability reduction by a Kozeny-Carman estimate. P- and S-wave velocities fell 30-50% during unloading and stayed 5-15% lower after reloading. The reloaded rock was 50-100% softer than virgin rock at low stress, so core data would overestimate reservoir compaction.
abstract: When a core sample is taken fiom great depth to the surface, it may be permanently altered by several mechanisms. This Paper focusses on possible effects of stress release on petrophysical measurables, such as porosity, permeability, acoustic velocities and compaction behaviour. title: Alteration of Wettability by Drilling Mud Filtrates
caption: Figure 2. Changes in wettability after exposure to water-based drilling mud filtrates.
figure_reason: Shows post- versus pre-filtrate wettability index for the seven mud filtrates, the main result identifying the least-altering mud.
tldr: Amott indexes on Berea cores show water-based mud filtrates alter wettability far less than individual additives, with a KCl/FCLS/Drispac mud causing minimal change across initial wettabilities.
summary: Drilling fluids can alter core wettability, compromising measurements on fresh cores. Seven common water-based mud additives were flushed individually through strongly water-wet Berea sandstone (about 600 md), and filtrates of seven practical water-based muds were flushed through cores prepared with initial wettability from strongly water-wet to strongly oil-wet. Wettability was assessed by Amott and Amott-Harvey indexes before and after exposure. All additives reduced water-wetness and increased oil-wetness, with polymers showing strong concentration dependence, and Drispac and XC caused plugging. Filtrates caused much less alteration than individual additives, attributed to adsorption of surface-active components on clay removed in the mud cake. The KCl/FCLS/CMC/Drispac filtrate (DF-4) changed the index by less than 0.20 overall and less than 0.1 for moderately oil-wet to moderately water-wet cores, while the XC-polymer muds (DF-3, DF-7) caused the largest changes.
abstract: Reservoir core samples are usually exposed to some kind of drilling fluid filtrate during coring, recovery, shipping, and storage. Choice of drilling fluid is generally dominated by operating conditions, rather than by wettability preservation concerns. If useful laboratory measurements of oil displacement behavior are to be made on core samples in their recovered state (so-called fresh cores), knowledge of possible alterations in wettability due to the drilling fluid is required. Individual components of drilling muds and filtrates prepared from whole muds were investigated. Solutions of individual components were flushed through strongly water-wet (untreated) Berea sandstone cores. Changes in wettability were assessed by measurement of Amott indexes for brine and refined oil. In the study of mud filtrates, suites of treated Berea sandstone cores were prepared with a wide range of initial wetting conditions. Amott indexes were compared before and after cores were flushed with the filtrates. In general, the effect of the drilling fluid components on the wettability of strongly water-wet (untreated) cores is overestimated by examining them individually. It appears that surface-active components adsorb on clays and are removed from the filtrate by formation of the mud cake. Results of this study point to practical drilling mud formulations that cause only minor changes in wetting over a wide range of initial wetting conditions.

title: Investigation of Discrepancies in Laboratory Measurements of Liquid Permeability
caption: Figure 6. Permeability measurements comparing non-degassed to degassed fluids.
figure_reason: Shows permeability changes between degassed and non-degassed fluids, the key quantitative result on gas evolution effects.
tldr: Glass micro-model, phase-diagram and Berea core flow tests show that incomplete miscible cleaning, gas evolution and gravity effects cause erroneous liquid permeability; degassing and gravity-stable flushing are recommended.
summary: Discrepancies in laboratory liquid permeability are investigated, focusing on experimental technique and fluid properties during miscible flow-through cleaning and saturation. Ternary phase diagrams (3% KCl brine, toluene, methanol) show that 2% hydrocarbon contamination greatly enlarges the two-phase region. GC effluent analysis on a Berea core and glass bead-pack micro-models show that toluene and methanol flushes leave residual contamination that appears as phase separation when brine is injected, even with clean fluids. Permeability tests on Berea in a Hassler cell show that non-degassed or resaturated fluids cause dramatic permeability changes because gas evolves when brine displaces methanol. Gravity-stable vertical flushing improved cleaning in micro-models, but bottom injection of methanol produced fingering and poor cleaning; the authors recommend in-line degassing, backpressure and gravity-stable flush capability.
abstract: We have observed increasing reports of discrepancies in laboratory measurements of liquid permeabilities. Possible explanations include rock-fluid interactions, viscous coupling, poor experimentation, and inadequate test procedures. Our initial work focuses on the influences of experimental techniques and fluid properties on permeability measurements. We found that single liquid phase conditions are often not present within the core samples during flow-through cleaning by miscible solvents. Trace amounts of hydrocarbon contamination in the solvents increases the two phase region of the phase diagram and two phase flow leads to inadequate cleaning. Understanding the gas saturation and solubility behavior of the fluids used in miscible cleaning and liquid saturating processes is critical in developing laboratory liquid permeability systems. For example, our data on glass micro-models clearly showed the development of a gas saturation when brine displaces methanol. This gas saturation is due to the difference in gas solubility between methanol and brine. Reliance on visual methods and/or specific flush volume criteria for determining solvent cleaning effectiveness are not adequate. Clear, single phase effluent does not signify pure component flow. Sweep efficiency and gravity effects can cause a miscible solvent mixture to be produced for extended periods.

title: Evaluation of Fracture Aperture and Wettability, Capillary Properties of Oil-Bearing Fractured Granite
caption: Fig. 5 : Comparison between fracture aperture calculated from resistivity 002) and permeability data (bl)
figure_reason: Compares fracture apertures from resistivity and permeability, the key result showing systematic offset but linear relationship.
tldr: Lab study of fractured granite from offshore Vietnam: fracture aperture from simultaneous permeability and resistivity, plus wettability and imbibition showing water-wet matrix and intermediate-wet fractures.
summary: Fractured granite basement reservoirs (Bach Ho field, offshore Vietnam) have macrofractures, microfractured matrix and tight matrix. Air-water capillary pressure curves on ten full-size cores (226-19250 mD, porosity 3-10%) gave a fracture/vug partition coefficient of 0.22-0.46, so microfractured matrix holds most pore volume; matrix cementation exponent m was 1.36. Simultaneous permeability and resistivity measurements on six reassembled fractured models in a Hassler cell (15-400 bar overburden) showed a good resistivity-permeability relationship, strong hysteresis, and resistivity-derived apertures systematically larger than permeability-derived ones, attributed to fracture roughness. Amott-IFP (130-140°C, 50 bar) and contact-angle tests showed water-wet matrix (WI>0.8, 41-62°) and mostly intermediate-wet fracture surfaces (75-112°). Spontaneous imbibition gave high recoveries, higher than in carbonate matrix of similar porosity, and was lower in samples without residual water.
abstract: Oil-bearing fractured rocks of a crystalline granite basement has been discovered offshore Viet Nam. For this type of rock, fracture is the main factor controlling the rocks permeability. Based on a large number of core analysis data, pore space of the rock was divided into the following main elements: macrofracture, matrix with microfractures and tight non-permeable matrix. Cores of full sizes were used to determine the rock porosity, permeability and petrophysical properties. Contribution of each pore element was evaluated by air-water capillary pressure curve. From this analysis, the main contribution of pore volume is matrix with microfractures. Physical models of fractured granite of a single or double macrofracture and matrix with microfractures had been created. Electrical resistivity and water permeability of this media were measured simultaneously in Hassler cell at two saturation states: full and partial brine saturations (nonconductive matrix). By controlling effective overburden pressure, fracture aperture and sample's permeability were varied and a good relationship between resistivity and permeability were obtained in both cases of saturation. Hysteresis behavior of resistivity and permeability versus overburden pressure was investigated and large hysteresis was found. Comparison of these results shows that the apertures calculated from resistivity data are systematically more than those from permeability data, but in good relationship. In this paper, laboratory data of rock wettability, capillary properties are reported. For such a type of collector, these characteristics are the main factors in controlling the oil recovery process. Integral wettability was determined by modified Amott-method: Separate determination of wettability of the fracture surface and matrix was carried out by contact-angle method. Results of these studies show that rock matrix is typically water wet (hydrophilic) and wettability of fracture surface changes in wide range from hydrophilic to hydrophobic, but in most cases is intermediate wet. Intensity of the oil-water capillary exchange process was studied under restored reservoir conditions and the numbers of curves of oil displacement coefficient versus time were obtained.

title: Deciphering Core and Log Porosity Differences and Evaluating the Scale Dependence of Core Analyses in a Complex Lithology
caption: Figs 8 and 9. Full-diameter permeability compared to data measured on a plug cut from full-diameter for siliciclastic (Fig 8) and carbonate (Fig 9) lithofacics.
figure_reason: Plug versus full-diameter permeability crossplots show plugs underestimate carbonate permeability below about 80 mD, unlike siliciclastics.
tldr: Core porosity (~20%) versus log porosity (~30%) in a bioturbated West African reservoir is explained by borehole rugosity from washed-out burrows; plugs underestimate permeability below 80 mD.
summary: Core porosities averaged about 20% while density and neutron-density log porosities averaged about 30% in a mixed siliciclastic/carbonate reservoir offshore West Africa, creating reserves uncertainty. Three new wells were cored and measured at full-diameter, 1-inch plug and minipermeameter scales, with redundant Archimedes, caliper and Boyle's Law measurements for quality control. Vugs made up under 4% of the section, so they did not explain the gap. Mottled siltstones with porous burrow fills in tight silty dolomite were heterogeneous: plug ends differed by up to three orders of magnitude, and plugs underestimated permeability below about 80 mD, so a power-law scale-up was applied. Full-diameter porosity exceeded plug porosity in carbonates by 1.6 p.u. on average. The log porosity excess coincided with burrow mottling, where washed-out burrows created small-scale borehole rugosity that the density pad read as extra porosity.
abstract: Core porosities from a mixed siliciclastic/carbonate reservoir in offshore West Africa average close to 20%, whereas log porosities average 30% over the same interval. This discrepancy resulted in large uncertainties in estimations of reserves and remaining oil in place. It was assumed that the reservoir was vuggy and that core analysis techniques were underestimating porosity. As a prerequisite to a waterflood feasibility study of the field, it was essential to resolve the core/log porosity differences. Three new wells were cored and great care was taken in developing the core analysis program. Measurements were made at full-diameter, plug, and minipermeameter scales, and quality control steps were incorporated into the program.

title: Effects of Core Sample Dimensions and Orientation on Two-Phase Flow Properties Determination
caption: Fig. 1 : kr from the full size
figure_reason: Relative permeability curves from the full-size sample, the reference case for comparison.
tldr: Waterfloods on a full-size North Sea core and vertical and horizontal plugs from it show that plugs, especially horizontal ones in laminated rock, give unrepresentative relative permeabilities.
summary: The study asks how sample size and orientation affect relative permeability from unsteady-state waterfloods in a laminated North Sea reservoir. A full-size core (10 cm diameter, 20.4 cm long) was flooded, then one horizontal and one vertical big plug (5 cm x 8.5 cm) were drilled from it and flooded under the same frontal velocity with gamma-ray saturation monitoring. Each experiment was history matched independently with a 1D simulator. Remaining oil saturation varied from 36.6% to 20.8% in the full size versus 23.3% to 21.4% in the vertical plug, and end effects covered about 30% of plug length. The horizontal plug showed early breakthrough (0.02 PV) from layers at about 30° to the axis not detected by CT, so 1D matching was invalid. Simulating the full-size flood with horizontal-plug curves gave 46.5% recovery versus 51.9% with the correct curves. Full-size samples with heterogeneities perpendicular to flow are recommended.
abstract: Two-phase flow properties determination for water/oil systems is one of the most important tasks of Core Analysts. This work is based firstly on an experimental approach (corefloods) and secondly on an appropriate numerical interpretation (history matching using a one-dimensional model based on generalized Darcy's law). Consequently, the quality of the relative permeability and capillary pressure curves depends strongly on the quality of the core sample selection as well as on its representativity. This is particularly true in the case of heterogeneous reservoirs for which the selected core sample should be free of important heterogeneities at its scale in order to obtain appropriate results. The aim of this study was to investigate as completely as possible the influence of core sample dimensions (full size or whole rock versus plugs) and orientations (vertical versus horizontal) on the two-phase flow properties and deduce some recommendations for laboratory experiments. In this study, a "vertical" sample is a core sample drilled perpendicular to the reservoir laminations, and an "horizontal" sample is a core sample drilled parallel to the reservoir laminations. Of course, many other parameters such as core sample preparation, wettability restoration, experimental conditions, type of experiments (steady state or unsteady state), etc... may influence the final results. They were not the purpose of this study, and therefore have been kept constant during this work.

title: Two Dimensional Imaging of Viscous and Capillary Effects in a Dipping Stratified Heterogeneous Media
caption: Figure 5 : Evolution of the water saturation during the imbibition process (the saturation fields are represented from top to bottom every 3 hours).
figure_reason: Shows time evolution of 2D water saturation during waterflood, revealing uneven sweep in the central block.
tldr: Gamma-ray 2D saturation imaging of drainage and waterflood in a 45-degree dipping three-block Aerolith/sandstone medium reveals capillary redistribution and viscous-capillary competition controlling recovery.
summary: The study addresses two-phase flow in layered heterogeneous media where average flow direction differs from the layering. A composite 5 cm block medium was built from two Vosges sandstone blocks (about 550 mD, 26% porosity) and a central high-permeability Aerolith-10 block, joined at 45 degrees with filter paper for capillary contact. Primary drainage at 5 ml/min, a 65-hour no-flow period, a 6 ml/h waterflood and a 2 ml/h second drainage were imaged with gamma-ray attenuation using NaI brine. During the no-flow period water saturation fell in the Aerolith block and rose slightly in the sandstone through capillary equilibrium. In the waterflood, water broke through at 0.38 PV and recovery was better in the low-capillary block, but the upper part of the Aerolith block was poorly swept, attributed to gravity versus capillary competition, possible loss of contact, and short injection time. Capillary end effects and dip angle strongly influenced recovery, and 2D saturation maps improved interpretation.
abstract: This paper presents experimental results on flow of two immiscible fluids in a heterogeneous medium consisting of three blocks of porous rocks connected at a layer angle of 45 degrees. The central block was made of Aerolith-10, an artificial sintered porous medium of high porosity and permeability, while the two other blocks were made up of Vosges sandstone in order to have a high permeability contrast and therefore a high capillary contrast between the strata. The physical properties (porosities, permeabilities, capillary pressures, end-point saturations) of the blocks composing the heterogeneous media were measured independently on isolated samples. Both media were found water-wet. Drainage and waterflood experiments were performed in the heterogeneous medium. Two-dimensional saturation fields were obtained by the use of a gamma-ray attenuation apparatus. The system was first driven to immobile water saturation by a high rate oilflood. During the following non-flow period of 65 hours, the fluids reached capillary equilibrium and a significant redistribution under capillary forces of the fluids was recorded, we observed a decrease of water saturation in the high permeability layer. The two-dimensional saturation fields recorded during the low-rate waterflood showed a significant difference in behaviour in the different layers due to the contrast of physical properties (permeability and capillary pressure). The flow is the result of the competition between the viscous and capillary forces. For this low flow-rate, the viscous effect in the high permeability layer is comparable to the capillary effect in the low permeability media. It is concluded that two-dimensional local saturation information in larger scale three dimensional slabs of porous rocks significantly improves the interpretation of the recovery mechanisms in heterogeneous porous media.

title: Distribution of Clays in Sandstones by Image Analysis: Quantification, Representativity and Effects on Petrophysical Properties
caption: Figure 11. Variograms calculated for pores, clays, quartz and feldspars on two perpendicular sections of a reservoir sample (ordinate: variograms in arbitrary units)
figure_reason: Variograms of pores, clays, quartz and feldspars show where plateaus are reached, establishing the representative number of images.
tldr: SEM backscattered image analysis quantifies clay distribution in sandstones, with variograms checking representativity; permeability formulas fit model sandstones but fail for North Sea reservoir sandstones.
summary: The study quantifies clay distribution in Fontainebleau, model clayey and North Sea reservoir sandstones using backscattered SEM images and image analysis. Variograms of mineral amounts across adjacent images determine how many images are needed for representative means, from a few images in homogeneous samples to about twenty, or more than the sample allowed, in reservoir samples. Granulometric parameters (perimeter, maximal projection) and geostatistical covariance parameters (volumic surface area, range) were derived, and image-based mineral contents agreed fairly well with elemental analysis and plug porosity. Poiseuille, Kozeny-Carman and Jacquin relationships generally overpredicted permeability. They could be adjusted for model sandstones, but failed for reservoir sandstones, where diagenetic clays change pore geometry in ways the parameters do not capture. Image processing such as erosion and dilation strongly changed the measured porosity and surface area, so it was avoided.
abstract: Distribution of clays in sandstones was quantified using Scanning Electron Microscopy image analysis. Prior to estimation of mean values, representativity was checked using variograms, which gave the size of sample to be studied. Several parameters were calculated, either from granulometric or from geostatistical procedures. Attempt was made to correlate these parameters to permeability: straightforward use of well-known formalisms was likely to give acceptable values for model sandstones, but failed in the case of reservoir sandstones, where the spatial relationship between framework grains and clays is more complex.

title: Resistivity and Permeability Mapping at the Lamina Scale
caption: Figure 7. Permeability - Formation resistivity factor relationship (lamina-scale) for the sample.
figure_reason: Log-log crossplot of formation factor versus permeability showing the strong lamina-scale correlation (R²=0.90).
tldr: A new resistivity probe with permeameter-matched geometry maps a laminated sandstone, showing a strong lamina-scale formation factor–permeability correlation (R²=0.90).
summary: Published resistivity–permeability correlations are usually weak, which the authors attribute to unaccounted heterogeneity within the sampled rock volumes. They built a resistivity probe whose tip geometry matches a pressure-decay probe permeameter and mapped a laminated aeolian Locharbriggs sandstone slab on a 2 mm grid. Permeability ranged from 56 to 3900 mD, and resistivity was measured in brine-saturated (100,000 mg/l NaCl) conditions on part of the slab. Resistivity and permeability maps looked alike and showed the same low-permeability lamination. A log-log fit of formation factor against permeability gave R²=0.90, k_est = 1.29×10^9 F^-5.8 (the printed Eq. 5 omits the negative sign), predicting permeability to within about ±40%. The relationship is expected to be facies-specific, and brine degradation limited the scanned area.
abstract: The physics of transport through porous media indicates that there should be an underlying functional relationship between permeability and resistivity. Despite this, previously published experiments have usually failed to demonstrate a convincing relationship. We think this is because the volumes of rock investigated included unaccounted for geological heterogeneities. We explored the relationship between resistivity and permeability in sedimentary rocks at the sub-lamina scale, using a probe permeameter and a new resistivity probe for the measurements. The resistivity probe has a functional geometry comparable to existing probe permeameter instruments. Measurements were made on a highly laminated aeolian sandstone sample. When compared, maps of both resistivity and permeability showed a similar character. We noted a strong correlation between conductivity and permeability. The resistivity data could be used to predict the probe permeability to, at worst, within $\pm 40\%$ (one standard deviation). These results provide evidence that permeability within individual laminae may be accurately predicted from resistivity data, when acquired at similar scales. Development of a method for obtaining reliable resistivity - permeability relationships would improve assessment of the rock flow characteristics using wireline micro-resistivity data.

title: Electrical Resistivity Anisotropy Due to Pore Scale Structure
caption: Figure 1- Plan structure of a layer. A- square. B-rhombic.
figure_reason: Shows square and rhombic layer geometry that defines the sphere packs whose anisotropy is studied.
tldr: Resistivity of brine-saturated systematic sphere packs measured in orthogonal directions and matched by equivalent pore-network calculations shows that pore topology alone produces electrical anisotropy.
summary: Archie-based saturation interpretation ignores electrical anisotropy, which matters for deviated and horizontal wells. The authors built four systematic packs of 2 cm plastic spheres (orthorhombic, rhombohedral, tetragonal, hexagonal; porosities 25.95-39.54%), saturated them with 5-10 wt% NaCl brine, and measured resistance with a four-electrode method at 2000 Hz in two perpendicular directions. Each pack's void space was reduced to an equivalent pore-throat network and solved with Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws to calculate formation factor. Calculated and measured formation factors agreed well (e.g., pack 1: 3.62 vs 3.44 perpendicular, 2.82 vs 2.92 parallel). Anisotropy coefficients were 1.13, 1.25 and 0.97 experimentally, and packs 2 and 4 with identical porosity had very different F, showing that pore topology controls anisotropy. The authors recommend measuring the resistivity tensor (at least six directions) in cores.
abstract: Electrical resistivity measurements are used to estimate the water saturation in hydrocarbon reservoirs. For clean rocks the interpretation methods are based on Archie's equations, but these equations do not consider directly any heterogeneity or anisotropy of the porous media. Electrical anisotropy is the variation of electrical resistivity with the direction of measurement; i.e., the resistivity varies in different directions (tensor). This paper studies both experimentally and theoretically the electrical anisotropy in clean, fully saturated porous media due to the pore level structure characteristics. Systematic packs of spheres of known structure and morphology have been built, their pore space saturated with brine and the resistivity measured in orthogonal directions. The pore space structure of these packs were determined and mathematically reduced to an equivalent network and the electrical formation resistivity factor calculated using these pore space dimensions. The calculated resistivity in perpendicular directions gave good agreement with the experimental results. These studies show that anisotropy within a bed plane can exist due to the tensor characteristics of the electrical resistivity. This resistivity characteristic has importance in log interpretation, not only for vertical wells, but also and especially for deviated and horizontal wells.

title: Amplitude-Versus-Offset Interpretation, Scaling Factors, and Other Challenges Associated With Acoustic Data Integration
caption: Figure 7. Water saturation effects on P-wave, S-wave, and Poisson's Ratio.
figure_reason: Shows P-wave velocity and Poisson's ratio changes with brine saturation, the key laboratory result.
tldr: Ultrasonic P- and S-wave measurements on sandstone plugs at varying brine saturation and pressure constrain Poisson's ratio and Zoeppritz AVO modeling, supporting integration of core, log and seismic data.
summary: AVO inversion for hydrocarbons is non-unique and often lacks petrophysical control, so the authors use core measurements to constrain it. Ultrasonic (50-200 kHz) P- and S-wave velocities were measured on vertically oriented fluvial sandstone plugs at 0, 33, 70 and 100% brine saturation and four confining pressures at room temperature. Poisson's ratio rose from about 0.2 (dry) to nearly 0.3 (brine-saturated), and P-wave velocity differences between dry and saturated states ranged 2 to 35%, while S-wave velocity changed little. Velocities rose with pressure up to about 5000 psi, indicating microcrack closure. Zoeppritz modeling with lab sand values and wireline shale values gave a gas-sand/shale reflection coefficient rising from +0.008 at normal incidence to under +0.06 at 30°, while the wet sand became less negative, consistent with seismic CMP data. The paper also discusses reconciling data across seismic, log and lab scales.
abstract: The need to obtain better shear wave data is becoming increasingly more important in petroleum exploration and production. Recent advancements in wireline multipole sonic logging and seismic amplitude processing provides an opportunity for improved formation evaluation and reservoir delineation. An important concern in sonic log and seismic interpretation is the non-uniqueness of the inversion process, i.e., extracting rock properties from acoustic waveforms. Ambiguity in acoustic inversion was overcome by constraining oversimplified models with laboratory data. The classical interpretation relating amplitude-versus-offset (AVO) to Poisson's ratio and other petrophysical properties is based on the idealistic assumptions of elasticity and isotropy. Correlation of AVO with rock properties is critical in determining whether or not variations of amplitude with incident angle are indicative of hydrocarbons. Acoustic energy sources are poorly understood and the physics underlying compressionaland shear-wave data acquisition show marked differences. Elastic parameters when measured in the laboratory at ultrasonic frequencies were consistently higher than dynamic data measured by sonic logs. Results from the acoustic laboratory evaluation indicate that sample selection, orientation, partial fluid saturation, viscoelasticity, experimental conditions, and intrinsic rock properties cause large variations in acoustic response. This complicates fbrther the challenge of acoustic data integration. The effects of scale can be significant, but manageable if fbndamental rock and fluid properties are understood. To address issues, associated with acoustic data integration, a program using reflection seismic, wireline log, and laboratory data was initiated to study the effects of scale (rock volumes) in sandstones.

title: Estimation of Relative Permeability and Capillary Pressure Functions Using Transient and Equilibrium Data from Steady-State Experiments
caption: Figure 2: Experimental case. a) Measured and predicted production (left) and pressure drop (right); b) Estimated relative permeability (left) and capillary pressure (right) functions with 95% confidence intervals. Independent measurements of the capillary pressure is shown.
figure_reason: Experimental chalk case: fit to production and pressure drop, estimated curves with confidence intervals, and Pc compared with independent measurements.
tldr: Relative permeability and capillary pressure are estimated simultaneously by inverse regression with B-splines on transient and equilibrium steady-state data, validated on simulated and chalk core data.
summary: Conventional steady-state relative permeability tests assume uniform saturation and discard transient data, while capillary pressure usually needs a separate experiment. The authors fit B-spline representations of kr and Pc to production and pressure-drop data recorded throughout each rate fraction, using a regression approach with the CENDRA core flood simulator and Levenberg-Marquardt optimization. Spline knots are added guided by residuals across the sequence of rate fractions, and linearized covariance analysis gives 95% confidence intervals. A simulated water-wet drainage case recovered the true curves within the confidence intervals over most of the saturation range. In a primary drainage test on Beer Stone outcrop chalk with a rate step-up scheme, the data were matched well and the estimated Pc agreed with micro-membrane and mercury injection curves scaled by the Leverett J-function, except at high saturations. Confidence intervals were large below Sw of about 0.15, where saturations were not reached.
abstract: A method for simultaneous determination of relative permeability and capillary pressure from transient and equilibrium data gathered during steady state experiments is developed and tested. The method uses B-spline representation of the unknown properties and determines the parameters within that representation through a regression-based approach. A linearized covariance analysis is utilized to calculate the confidence intervals for the estimated functions. Two sets of production and pressure drop data are successfully analyzed; one simulated and one experimental case. The results show that it is possible to determine the functions quite accurately over a relatively large saturation range.

title: SCA1994-19
caption: Figure 4 Gas Displacing Oil Relative Permeability for 800mD Sandstone with 11 psi Differential Pressure
figure_reason: Same 800 mD sandstone at 11 psi gives well-behaved curves, contrasting with the low-pressure run and supporting the criterion.
tldr: An automated gas-liquid permeameter allows higher flow rates for high-permeability cores, and a minimum differential pressure of about 10 times capillary pressure is proposed for reliable unsteady-state relative permeability.
summary: Unsteady-state gas-displacing-oil relative permeability tests on high-permeability samples often run at too low a differential pressure, so capillary forces dominate and the data are unreliable. Manual data collection (about 3 s per point) limits flow rate; for a 1 darcy, 2 in. by 3 in. sample this gives only about 0.5 psi. The authors built an automated permeameter with a balance for liquid volumes, mass flow meters for gas, and a ballast tank downstream of the flow meters to suppress back-pressure regulator hysteresis (a ballast 100 times the upstream volume gives 1% error). Using the Jones-Parra and Calhoun stabilized-front length, they argue front length scales with the ratio of capillary pressure to differential pressure. Saturation profiles and tests at different pressures (an 800 mD sandstone at 2.5 psi versus 11 psi) support minimum differential pressures of about 4 psi for gas-oil and 6 psi for gas-water, or roughly 10 times a capillary pressure of 0.4 psi.
abstract: High permeability samples create problems in getting reliable unsteady-state gas displacing oil relative permeability because of the difficulty in getting the differential pressure high enough to prevent the capillary forces from dominating the flow. When running the test manually, the reliable rate of data colIection limits the maximum flow rate and therefore the differential pressure that can be used. An automated unsteady-state gas displacing liquid permeameter was designed and built to improve the reliability of gas displacing oil data by allowing higher flows without problems with data recording. The minimum differentid pressure for unsteady-state relative permeability tests is discussed in terms of the capillary pressure. By using arguments derived from fractional flow equations and saturation profile measurements, the minimum differential pressure should be 10 times the capillary pressure for the saturations expected during the test.

title: Pseudo Steady State Technique for Relative Permeability Measurement by
caption: Figure 8 - Relative permeability curves from steady- and pseudo-steady-state experiments.
figure_reason: Compares experimental relative permeability curves from steady-state and three pseudo-steady-state tests on Berea, showing the main experimental result.
tldr: A pseudo-steady-state relative permeability method with continuously ramped flow rates is tested by simulation and Berea experiments, giving valid results faster than steady-state, best when combined with one steady-state point.
summary: Conventional steady-state relative permeability tests need long times to reach equilibrium at each fractional flow. The authors ramp the oil and water injection rates slowly and continuously, and derive a non-linear optimal ramping path from an accuracy parameter γ, the difference between inlet and outlet fractional flow. Simulations with CENDRA, using Corey curves and a 497.7 mD core, show that with zero capillary pressure the ramping error in total mobility is below 1% at γ=0.01. Capillary pressure causes larger errors than ramping, and steady-state curves are equally affected. On a Berea core, one steady-state test and three pseudo-steady-state tests were run; the best results came from one steady-state point (Sw about 42%) followed by pseudo-steady-state ramping at γ=0.01. A ramp with γ=0.02 was too fast, and one starting from low water saturation was dominated by errors at low Sw.
abstract: In steady-state relative permeability measurements, two phases (typically oil and water) are injected into a core sample simultaneously at a series of discrete ratios. Data for relative permeability calculations are taken at equilibrium conditions, when the flow rates of oil and water exiting the core are at the same as those entering the core, and when the pressure drop across the core is constant. In the pseudo-steady-state method, flow rates of oil and water entering the core are changed slowly and continuously. Data for relative permeability calculations are taken under near equilibrium conditions, i.e. flow rates at the core outlet differ slightly from those at the inlet, and the pressure drop is changing slowly.

title: Three-Phase Relative Permeabilities and Trapped Gas Measurements Related to Wag Processes
caption: Figure 13. Trapped gas from water displacement after gas injection or WAG experiments
figure_reason: Shows trapped gas saturation versus initial gas saturation with Land-type fit, a key result.
tldr: Unsteady-state gas and water injections on Berea and North Sea sandstones give three-phase relative permeabilities, trapped gas relations and a new gas hysteresis model for WAG.
summary: The paper addresses microscopic displacement efficiency and three-phase relative permeability in WAG processes. Unsteady-state gas and water injection sequences were run on 40-100 cm composite cores of Berea, silanized Berea and four North Sea reservoir sandstones (30-2000 mD) at ambient or reservoir conditions (about 300 bar), with wettability characterized by Amott index. Residual oil saturation in three-phase flow was significantly lower than in two-phase waterflood or gas injection. Wetting-phase kr depended mainly on its own saturation, whereas gas kr showed strong hysteresis, lower for decreasing gas saturation, regardless of wettability. Trapped gas depended strongly on maximum gas saturation (0.17-0.21 in WAG tests) and fitted a Land-type equation; a new hysteresis model implemented in ECLIPSE reasonably predicted WAG effluent and pressure data.
abstract: Three-phase relative permeability has been calculated from unsteady state experiments. Gas or water were the injected phase in these displacements. The core material include both outcrop and reservoir sandstones with different wettability. The results show that the residual oil saturation can be significant lower by three-phase flow compared to two-phase waterflood or gas injection. The paper summarize the results of threephase relative permeability at different wettability for water-wet, intermediate and more oilwet cores. Relations for trapped gas from three-phase flow were investigated, and a new approach to model relative permeability hysteresis for WAG processes have been proposed.

title: Effect of Procedure on Wettability Index to Water
caption: Figure 4. Wettability index to water as a function of Swi.
figure_reason: Shows Iw versus Swi for all samples and treatments, the key result that Iw decreases with increasing Swi.
tldr: Iw measured on limestone samples from water, transition and oil zones varies with how Swi is established; Iw falls as Swi rises, though samples remain distinguishable.
summary: The paper examines how test procedure affects the Cuiec/Amott-type wettability index to water (Iw) in a limestone reservoir. Nine preserved plugs from water, transition and oil zones were tested, along with cleaned twin samples, with Swi set by flushing, centrifugation or porous plate, using dead crude and refined oil. Preserved samples showed Iw above 0.9 near the water-oil contact, decreasing upward, but Iw shifted to lower values for centrifuged and porous-plate samples. Wettability alteration was ruled out, since refined-oil samples behaved the same; instead Iw decreases as Swi increases (e.g. type I water-zone Iw from 0.98 at Swi 14% to 0.62 at 50%), because Sor and spontaneously imbibed water both decline. Absolute Iw is therefore not significant alone, but remains a good comparative index when Swi values are similar, and low Swi best reveals water-wetness.
abstract: The wettability index to water (Iw) is the ratio of the quantity of water spontaneously imbibed to the total quantity of mobile water. This index is largely used to characterize the wettability of rock reservoirs which is an important factor for the understanding and design of the recovery processes. This paper presents the results of measurements of Iw on different samples taken at different levels in a limestone reservoir : water zone, transition zone and oil zone.
