Iw was determined on preserved and cleaned samples at different initial water saturation (Swi). No restoration was conducted. Swi was established by different ways : flooding, centrifbgation and porous plate. When considering a series of determination conducted under identical experimental conditions, Iw's show a consistent variation of wettability from more water-wet to less water-wet when moving up in the reservoir. But Iw is different from one series to another. This is explained by a decrease of both residual oil saturation (Sor) and quantity of water spontaneously imbibed when Swi increases. These decreases are dependent on wettability and rock structure.

title: Some Observations on the Capillary Pressure Hysteresis Using the Ultracentrifuge
caption: Figure 6: Irreducible water saturation for seconcl drainage plotted against the irreducible water saturation for the first drainage.
figure_reason: Compares first and second drainage irreducible water saturation across all sample types, showing the shift pattern.
tldr: Ultracentrifuge tests on about 60 plugs show irreducible water saturation shifts between first and second drainage, depending on fluids, wettability and rock type, and correlating with sample depth.
summary: Centrifuge capillary pressure hysteresis differs from porous plate hysteresis, with irreducible water saturation shifting between first and second drainage. About 60 plugs were tested: Berea sandstone, Baker dolomite and native and restored carbonate pinnacle reef cores from Western Canada, using crude and refined oils at room and reservoir temperature. Refined oil gave negligible shifts, while crude oil gave the widest hysteresis. Berea and Baker cores showed lower irreducible water saturation in the second drainage, whereas restored reef cores consistently showed higher values; native cores were split. The saturation difference trended with wettability (USBM index, RDI, Amott water index) but not with porosity or permeability, and the best correlation was with sample depth relative to the gas/oil and water/oil contacts, suggesting reservoir saturation history matters.
abstract: The use of centrifuge technology for the determination of capillay pressure chasacteristics of resel-voir rocks has received increasing attention in the recent decades. In recent experiments it has become evident that the hysteresis obsei-ved 111 the centsifuge experiments is different than the hysteresis obsei-ved in the traditional ?orous plate measurements. More specifically, the value of the "in-educible" wetting phase saturation seems to shift between the fisst drainage cycle and the second drainage cycle. This phenomenon was studied in some detail in our laboratoiy. Approximately sixty (60) core plugs were tested under a vaiety of conditions which included crude and refined oils at room and reseivoir temperatures. The cores used were Berea sandstone, Baker dolomite and plugs from vasious casbonate pinnacle reefs of Westein Canada. The tests were conducted using reseivoir core that was in both native and restored state. It was found that the widest hysteresis occui~ed when crude oil was used. The hysteresis was more significant in casbonates than in sandstones. This can be only pa-tially attsibuted to the fact that the casbonates have significantly smaller pore volumes (i.e. a higher expected expeiimental relative error). However, the trends on clean carbonates (Baker dolomite) are opposite to the ones of reseivoir rock. Also, there seems to be 110 significance on the effect of saturation history (i.e. whether or not the displacement was single or multi step).

title: Comparative Study of Drainage Capillary Pressure Measurements Using Different Techniques and for Different Fluid Systems
caption: Fig13 : Fluid system comparison on sample 3
figure_reason: Compares the three fluid systems on one sample, showing the oil-brine versus gas-liquid difference.
tldr: Drainage capillary pressure on six water-wet samples compared across porous plate, centrifuge and mercury injection and three fluid pairs; gas-liquid data do not transfer to oil-brine.
summary: The paper compares drainage capillary pressure curves from porous plate, centrifuge and mercury injection on six samples (sandstones, dolomite, oolitic limestone) cleaned to be water-wet. Centrifuge runs used air-brine, air-oil and oil-brine on big plugs, while porous plate and mercury injection used small companion plugs. Air-brine curves from all three techniques agree well, with mercury data scaled by the interfacial tension ratio (6.85) and zero contact angle; no size effect was seen, and centrifuge differences at high saturation were attributed to insufficient equilibration time in low-permeability samples. Air-oil curves lie 3 to 8 saturation points from air-brine, while oil-brine curves end about 5 to 10 saturation points higher in saturation, so gas-liquid data are not transposable to oil-brine. Mercury injection diverges from air-brine centrifuge data when clay exceeds about 7%, by over 20 saturation points at 20% kaolinite/dickite.
abstract: The determination of representative capillary pressures (PC) is needed for the forecast of the fluids distribution in the reservoir. The initial water saturation and the accumulation depend directly on this parameter. However variations between measurements obtained by various standard techniques (mercury injection, porous plate, centrifugation) or for different fluid systems have been often observed and reported in the literature. This study tries to establish relationships between drainage PC curves obtained from various techniques. With this goal, a series of drainage experiments was systematically achieved on samples from various lithological facies and with different core properties, with the samples having been made as water-wet as possible. - The comparison of these measurements leads to the following observations: for the air-brine system, both of the techniques (porous plate, centrifugation) fit accurately on the majority of the samples in spite of different cleaning procedures and sample sizes, with moreover a good agreement of the mercury injection PC curve using a suitable scaling factor, - the Pclo curves for the three pairs of fluids have the same relative position for each sample (where o is the interfacial tension of the fluid system), - the maximum gas saturation for an air-oil drainage is close, although always superior, to'the one for the air-brine system. On the contrary, a systematic 5 to 10 saturation unit difference is observed between the asymptotic limit of gas-liquid and oil-brine PC curves. With regard to a gas-liquid system and for fairly clay free samples, the three techniques appear to be valuable to describe the capillary balance. Oil reservoirs must be subject to particular measurements in order to estimate the oil-brine system behaviour. Drainage centrifuge experiments using pseudo reservoir fluids are then qualified to provide reliable data.

title: Centrifuge Capillary Pressure Data Interpretation: Gravity Degradation Aspect Consideration
caption: Figure 3. Bentsen's Log Model Figure 4. Chen et al.'s Reversal Curvature Model
figure_reason: Compares capillary pressure curves recovered by 3D and 2D theories for synthetic data, showing the high-saturation discrepancy.
tldr: A 3D centrifuge theory including gravity at low rampup speeds is used to interpret capillary pressure, showing 2D models misestimate the high-saturation zone for high-permeability sandstones.
summary: At low initial speeds (<500 rpm) in horizontal-rotor Beckman centrifuges, gravity distorts the centrifugal field in high permeability and porosity sandstones, which biases capillary pressure interpretation near threshold pressure. The authors extend a three-dimensional centrifuge theory with equipotential surfaces and use implicit parameter estimation with simple capillary pressure functions (Bentsen log, Chen reversal-curvature) on synthetic data (k>700 md, φ>20%, 50–1000 rpm) and two SCA survey samples (EF3, FA4). Curves recovered with the 3D theory lie above those from Christiansen's 2D model at high saturation, with differences of 1 to 5 saturation percent. Simple functions with few parameters can shift or force-bend the recovered curve beyond the low-speed range. Pivoted rotor heads are suggested to minimize the effect, and experimental verification remains to be done.
abstract: The gravity degradation phenomenon at low speeds (less than 500 rpm when initiating centrifuge capillary pressure experiments) has been identified as one of the problems for high permeability and porosity sandstone core samples. For these samples, the gravitational acceleration distorts the horizontal centrifugal force field distribution inside the core plug, thereby leading to inaccurate interpretation of capillary pressure information in the high saturation zone (near the threshold pressure). On the basis of a thre? dimentional centrifuge theory characterizing such an effect, this paper investigates the numerical technique which allows the gravity acceleration at low speed to be included for traditional Beckman centrifuges. Several capillary pressure versus saturation relationships are used to conduct parameter estimation.9. Tested examples show that the implicit parameter estimation algorithm based on the three-dimensional model of centrifuge experiments can provide more accurate information in the high saturation zone.

title: Water-Oil Capillary Pressure and Wettability Measurements Using Micropore Membrane Technique
caption: Fig 6: $P_c$ loop (test No.2), Vosges sandstone, aged in crude oil, $I_{HL} = 0.65$ .
figure_reason: Full capillary pressure loop for aged sandstone showing intermediate wettability and its HL index.
tldr: A micropore membrane coreholder measures full four-curve water-oil capillary pressure cycles in days, and a new area-based HL wettability index is proposed and tested on sandstone and carbonate.
summary: Full capillary pressure cycles (spontaneous and forced imbibition and drainage) by the porous plate method take months. The authors built a coreholder with thin water-wet and oil-wet micropore membranes and short, large-diameter cores (5 cm diameter, 2 cm thick) to speed this up. Tests used Vosges sandstone and Estaillade carbonate, both native water-wet and aged in Lagrave crude oil. Drainage curves agreed well with mercury injection and porous plate data, and full cycles took 20-30 days, about 30 times faster than standard porous plate. They propose the Hammervold-Longeron index, an Amott-like index weighting the four saturation intervals by the areas under the capillary pressure curves. HL values were 0.85 (water-wet sandstone), 0.97 (water-wet carbonate) and -0.01 (aged carbonate), compared with Amott and USBM indices.
abstract: This paper describes a new technique to simultaneously measure the capillary pressure curves and wettability indices for an oil - brine - rock system. By improving the porous plate method, the full cycle of four capillary pressure curves, i.e. spontaneous and forced drainage and imbibition, is measured in days instead of months. This is achieved by the use of thin oil- and water-wet micropore membranes and short samples with large diameter. Measurements have been done on sandstone and carbonate outcrop cores with wettabilities ranging from strongly water-wet to oil-wet. A reduction in experimental time by a factor of 10 or more is gained by the new method for a full cycle of the four capillary pressure curves. In addition, a new measure of wettability is suggested as an improvement of the USBM test, incorporating all four areas between the capillary pressure curves and the saturation axis. The new wettability index may be conceived as an extension of the Amott test, with the four saturation intervals weighted by the corresponding areas under the capillary pressure curve and may better discriminate between mixed-wet and spotted-wet samples.

title: New Procedure and Apparatus for Combined Reservoir Condition Gas-Brine Relative Permeability, Capillary Pressure, and Electrical Property Measurements
caption: FIGURE 7. Imbibition cycle nitrogen gas FIGURE 8. Calculated water content
figure_reason: Steady-state imbibition gas and brine relative permeability curves demonstrating the combined test output.
tldr: A patented outlet endpiece with a porous ceramic disk enables desaturation and steady-state gas-brine relative permeability and resistivity tests at 150°C and 55 MPa, with humidification control identified via X-ray and resistivity.
summary: Special core analysis of deep Norphlet sandstone required 55 MPa net confining pressure, 150°C, and brine above 200,000 ppm, with initial brine saturation near 20%. Gas flow alone could not reach irreducible brine saturation, so a patented outlet endpiece combining a porous ceramic disk and a Berea flow insert was built. It allows capillary desaturation and then steady-state imbibition and drainage relative permeability and resistivity measurements without disturbing the sample. Saturations were tracked by X-ray scanning (NaI-doped brine) and resistivity. Gas humidification was the main difficulty: under- or over-humidified gas dehydrated or wetted plugs, detected by off-trend resistivity versus X-ray saturation and by ΔP/Qg changes. The humidifier had to run cooler than the coreholder to match brine vapor pressure, and Berea data demonstrated the method.
abstract: In designing special core analysis programs for the deep Norphlet sandstone found in the U.S. Gulf of Mexico offshore Alabama, we found that several experimental conditions warranted a new approach. Simulating reservoir conditions required net confining pressures of 55 MPa, temperatures of 150°C, and a brine salinity exceeding 200,000 ppm. Program objectives included achieving brine saturations in the range found in situ before conducting imbibition and drainage steady-state relative permeability and resistivity measurements. The test sequence required driving a fully brine-saturated sample to a connate brine saturation condition as a starting point for the imbibition portion of the relative permeability experiment. Desaturation with gas flow did not adequately drive plugs to irreducible brine saturation; therefore, capillary pressure desaturation was necessary to complete this process. A method was devised to desaturate a core plug through a porous plate, then alternatively bypass that flow path and conduct normal steady-state two-phase flow experiments. A new endpiece device for the outflow end of the test apparatus was designed and patented to allow this procedure. The endpiece provides capabilities to desaturate to a desired saturation range and to continue with flow, resistivity, or capillary pressure versus saturation measurements without having to disturb the sample or cycle between ambient and test temperature and pressure conditions. Plug permeabilities and saturations were significantly affected by the moisture content of the gas. Humidifying the gas so that it neither added nor subtracted water from brine within core plugs proved to be challenging. Plug saturations were determined from X-ray scans and resistivity measurements. The effects of under- and oversaturating gas with water vapor were identified from significant changes in resistivity versus X-ray-determined saturation trends at low brine saturations. Once identified, these effects were eliminated by fine-tuning the humidifier. The new procedures and designs developed for this project yielded data sets which were adequate for accomplishing the goals of the core analysis program.

title: Interpretation of centrifuge data using local saturation
caption: Fig. 4: Saturation profiles at equilibrium during drainage of sample S2. A quasi-spontaneous drainage is observed at low speed. The saturation at the faces ( $R_{min}$ and $R_{max}$ ) are not measured.
figure_reason: Equilibrium saturation profiles show quasi-spontaneous drainage at low speed in the intermediate-wet sample.
tldr: Ultrasonic local saturation measured during multi-speed centrifuge runs matches computed Pc curves on water-wet to oil-wet samples but does not improve relative permeability determination.
summary: Centrifuge Pc and Kr are normally derived from production data, so the authors measured local saturation during spinning using ultrasonic transit times at up to 5 locations on 7 cm plugs. Three samples were tested (water-wet, intermediate-wet, oil-wet) in drainage and forced imbibition with a 15 cP oil. Rotation effects on transit time required empirical corrections, up to 100% at the largest radii, and the saturation error is about 4% PV. Direct local Pc curves agreed with those computed from production and confirmed zero Pc at the outflow face, and local data revealed quasi-spontaneous drainage and fluid redistribution after the centrifuge stopped. Kr curves from production, single channels and all channels differed, because the inversion is very sensitive to Pc and to small heterogeneities, so local saturation gave no practical improvement.
abstract: We report multi-speed centrifuge experiments in which local saturation were measured while spinning. The local saturation are deduced from the transit time of ultrasonic waves travelling through the sample. The precision of the measurements depends on empirical corrections applied on the data to take into account pressure and stress effects on the sample. Local measurements permitted the observation of different processes, for instance a quasi-spontaneous drainage at low speed of rotation and fluid redistribution at the end of drainage before forced imbibition. The measured saturation profiles are consistent with the assumptions of zero capillary pressure at the outflow face. We did not observe any contradiction between the direct determination of the Pc curves and the computed ones. However, the direct determinations are not perfectly superimposed, due to errors of measurements and small heterogeneities. Local saturation measurements in multi-speed centrifuge experiments do not improve in practice the determination of relative permeability curves due to the high sensitivity of the computation to the values of capillary pressure.

title: Design of Three-Phase Relative Permeability Experiments
caption: Figure 3: a) Trajectories for all the experiments; b) Sections for study of water relative permeability; c) Sections for study of oil relative permeability; d) Sections for study of gas relative permeability.
figure_reason: Shows saturation trajectories of all experiments and the sections used to interpret confidence intervals, explaining which regions the data cover.
tldr: Linearized covariance analysis gives confidence intervals on three-phase relative permeability surfaces, comparing six steady- and unsteady-state flooding designs; steady-state data and added water-gas data improve accuracy.
summary: Accurate estimation of three-phase relative permeability functions depends on how floods are designed and what data are collected. The authors extend a linearized covariance analysis to three phases, using a black-oil coreflood simulator (CENDRA) and bivariate B-spline representations of kr surfaces (51 effective parameters) to compute pointwise confidence intervals. Six DDI-type designs, built from steady-state and unsteady-state experiments with water-oil, gas and water-gas injections, were compared with simulated production and pressure-drop data (errors of 0.005 PV and 20 kPa). Relative permeabilities are well determined only in saturation regions covered by the data, roughly Sw 0.3-1 and Sg 0-0.6. Steady-state data gave tighter intervals than unsteady-state data, often by an order of magnitude, and adding water-gas injection greatly improved the water and gas relative permeabilities in otherwise poorly constrained regions.
abstract: This paper presents, for the first time, a systematic approach to the selection of experimental designs leading to accurate determination of the three-phase relative permeability functions. The approach is based on a linearized covariance analysis which is utilized to determine the confidence intervals on estimated relative permeabilities. These confidence intervals define the accuracy with which the relative permeabilities can be determined for the given data, their accuracy, and the chosen flooding scenario. In this paper, the confidence intervals are utilized to quantitatively assess the utility of different designs towards accurate three-phase relative permeability determination. For the cases considered here, we demonstrate that accurate estimates may be obtained in the parts of the saturation region which are reflected in the experimental data.

title: Steady-State Relative Permeability Measurements and Interpretation with Account for Capillary Effects
caption: Figure 9. Capillary pressure recovered from tubing measurements at various rates and core lengths.
figure_reason: Shows capillary pressure recovered from tubing measurements versus input at varied rates and core lengths, key result.
tldr: A multirate steady-state method corrects capillary effects in relative permeability, and 2D simulations show a membrane inlet end piece makes individual phase pressures measurable.
summary: Conventional steady-state relative permeability interpretation neglects capillary pressure, causing errors especially near residual saturations. The paper presents a multirate method in which total rate is varied at fixed inlet fractional flow, giving inlet saturation, relative permeabilities and capillary pressure from average saturation and phase pressure drops. Tests on synthetic 1D data recover the input curves, while Darcy-based interpretation remains in error even at 2 cc/min. Individual phase pressures require a modified inlet end piece with semi-permeable membranes, which was studied in 2D simulations (60x4 grids, 18.8 cm core, rates 2.0 and 0.2 cc/min). Without a membrane, oil counterflow into the water tubing creates a water-pressure discontinuity (Type 1 end effect). The membrane removes it, but separate fluid injection leaves non-uniform inlet saturation (Type 2), reduced by low rates, longer cores and sandwiched injection geometry.
abstract: A multirate steady-state technique to measure relative permeabilities is presented. The technique eliminates interpretation errors related to the capillary end effect. To determine relative permeabilities of the two phases, individual phase pressure drops across the core have to be measured or calculated. In order to make the individual phase pressure drops measurable. a modified construction of the inlet end piece is suggested. Capillary end effects taking place during core flooding experiments at steady-state conditions both at inlet and outlet ends are theoretically andysed and studied by simulations in 2D.

title: Residual Oil Saturation and Multiphase Relative Permeability Measurements on a Water-Wet Sandstone Reservoir and a Limestone Reservoir of Mixed Wettability
caption: Figure 2. Water-wet Sandstone Reservoir. Saturation Paths of Centrifuge and Steady-State Experiments. Arrows : Direction of Saturation change
figure_reason: Ternary diagram showing saturation paths covered by centrifuge and steady-state tests, basis for the isoperm construction.
tldr: Combining gamma-ray steady-state and automated centrifuge tests, the paper measures three-phase relative permeability and residual oil in a water-wet sandstone and a mixed-wet limestone, finding gas recovery lower in tertiary mode for the limestone.
summary: Tertiary gas injection design requires reliable residual oil saturation and three-phase relative permeability data. The authors combined steady-state tests with dual-energy gamma-ray in situ saturation monitoring (high oil saturations) and automated video-monitored centrifuge tests (high gas saturations) at ambient conditions on plugs from a water-wet sandstone and a mixed-wet limestone. In the sandstone, water relative permeability was the same function of Sw in two-phase and three-phase drainage, so both datasets could be merged to build oil isoperms, and a Fayers or modified Stone 1 model fitted them. Residual oil was very low in both secondary and tertiary gas floods. In the limestone, Sorw depended mainly on permeability rather than wettability, and gas beat water in secondary recovery except at very low column heights and low permeability. Tertiary Sorwg values lay between Sorg and Sorw, so gravity drainage was less efficient in tertiary than in secondary conditions.
abstract: This paper presents three phase data regarding a water-wet sandstone reservoir and a limestone reservoir of mixed wettability. These data originate from a laboratory method set up for a direct and comprehensive determination of tertiary recovery by gas injection, using both centrifuge and steady-state techniques. The three-phase relative permeability determination experiments are performed using in situ saturation measurements by dual energy gamma-ray. The steady-state technique was used to derive water, oil and gas oil relative permeability isoperms at high oil saturations. Automated centrifuge tests were carried out to determine residual oil saturations resulting from both secondary and tertiary gas floods and oil and water three-phase relative permeabilities at high gas saturations. The experiments show that residual oil saturations reach a very low value both in secondary and tertiary gas floods for the studied water-wet reservoir sandstone. It is also possible from reliable experimental three-phase oil relative permeability data to ascertain the choice of an analytical three-phase model for numerical modelization. In the case of the carbonate reservoir of mixed wettability, the residual oil saturations are not always as low as expected from secondary gas flood. Results indicate that permeability may be more important than wettability to influence the total recovery in the studied limestone reservoir. The residual oil saturations and three-phase relative permeability data for a variety of wettability and permeability values reported in this paper are expected to provide the basis for added insight into tertiary gas injection phenomenology.

title: Analysis of Viscous Fingering Reproducibllity in Consolidated Natural Porous Media
caption: Figure 5 : Saturation maps of slices 1 through 7 Figure 6 : Saturation maps of slices 7 through
figure_reason: Saturation maps from repeated waterfloods show reproducible finger locations and change when the core is inverted.
tldr: CT-imaged unstable waterfloods in two Vosges sandstone cores show viscous fingering is reproducible, gravity- and heterogeneity-controlled, self-similar, with rate-dependent oil relative permeability and fractional flow.
summary: The study uses X-ray CT to visualize viscous fingering during waterfloods (0.823 cP KI brine displacing 244 cP mineral oil) in two homogeneous, water-wet Vosges sandstone cores (417 and 497 mD, porosity about 0.23). Porosity and saturation were computed voxel by voxel from CT scans, with beam hardening correction bringing CT porosity (0.227, 0.232) in line with conventional values. Eight unstable floods at 0.3 or 0.5 cm3/min, including runs with the core inverted, showed repeated finger locations that changed when the core was turned, indicating deterministic fingering controlled by gravity and minor heterogeneity. Saturation data collapsed onto single response curves versus xD/tD. Oil relative permeability and fractional flow depended on injection rate, while water relative permeability did not, and a slope break indicated fingering and stable zones. Solvent-cleaned sample #1 showed more scatter than sample #2, suggesting solvent alteration of the rock.
abstract: The purpose of this work is to apply computerized X-Ray tomography techniques to visualize the development of viscous fingering during the displacement of an oil phase through an homogeneous, natural and consolidated porous media.Viscous fingering during two-phase flow is obtained by appropriate selection of both injection rate and mobility ratio. The porosity and saturation profiles have been computed by means of image analysis through the use of a graphical interpretation software. The image analysis of the cross sections shows that, under conditions of hydrodynamic stability, the displacement of water by oil occurs as predicted by the pistonlike model, with small gravitational effects. On the other hand, when the oil phase is displaced by a water phase under unstable hydrodynamic conditions, the injected water flows through well defined regions of the porous media. Gravity segregation is also observed in this case. Provided the injection parameters and the connate water saturation are kept constant, the water saturation profiles as a hnction of self-similar dimensionless variable (xD 1 t~ ) merge to a single curve. For the same injection conditions, it was observed that the curves of oil permeability versus water saturation overlap themselves. Such overlapping also happens with the water relative permeability versus water saturation curves. It was evident that the oil relative permeabilities are strongly influenced by the injection rate of a higher mobility fluid. The shape of the water relative permeability curves indicates the existence of two Qfferent displacement mechanisms taking place along the core. Moreover, the water fractional flow curve is characteristic of unstable displacement.

title: A New Method to Measure Water, Oil and Gas Saturation Profiles in Three-Phase Gas Injection
caption: Figure 6: Comparison between the saturation profiles obtained with the present method and those measured with CT-scanner
figure_reason: Validates the method by comparing final saturation profiles with CT-scanner measurements.
tldr: Combining electrical resistivity and gamma-ray attenuation gives three-phase saturation profiles in gravity-assisted gas injection; positive spreading coefficient gives far higher oil recovery (54% vs 13%).
summary: The paper presents a method to measure water, oil and gas saturation profiles simultaneously during tertiary gas injection, using resistivity from eight electrodes for water saturation and Americium gamma-ray attenuation for oil and gas. It was applied to gravity-assisted gas injection in water-wet sandpacks (about 120 µm grains, porosity 0.35-0.36) with spreading (S=+13 mN/m) and non-spreading (S=-2 mN/m) fluid systems. Profiles agreed with double-energy CT-scanner profiles and with bulk saturations from weighing recovered fluids, with errors under 3% for water and 4.5% for gas saturation. Spreading conditions recovered 54% OOIP with local residual oil down to 2%, versus about 13% recovery and Sorg near 11% for non-spreading. Oil relative permeabilities derived from profile evolution were very low and, used in a simulator, gave a good history match of recovery curves.
abstract: In the present paper an original method is presented to acquire simultaneously water, oil and gas saturation profiles as a function of time in tertiary gravity assisted gas injection. The method consists in combining local electrical resistivity and $\gamma$ -ray attenuation measurements. Resistivity measurements give the local water saturation whereas the oil and gas saturations are calculated based on the $\gamma$ -ray attenuation profiles. The method has been applied to measure three-phase local saturations during gravity assisted gas injection experiments in water-wet sandpacks; in these experiments the ability of oil to form films on water in presence of gas, that is characterised by the spreading coefficient, was investigated. The results are in very good agreement with local saturation CT-scanner measurements and with bulk saturations obtained by continuous weighing of the recovered fluids. As a validation of the method the oil relative permeability is calculated, based on the evolution of the saturation profiles and it is used to simulate the experiments. A good numerical description of the experimental behavior is obtained. Throughout the same experiments it is proved that the spreading coefficient plays a major role on the fluid distribution and recovery efficiency in tertiary gravity assisted gas injection e.g. when water is mobile.

title: Comparing Hysteresis Models for Relative Permeability in Wag Studies
caption: Figure 4 Oil recovery 1D core-floods
figure_reason: Compares oil recovery from Carlson, Killough and SL models in 1D core-floods against experiment.
tldr: Simulations of immiscible WAG compare Carlson, Killough and a modified SL hysteresis model, showing standard two-phase models cannot capture reduced gas and water mobility seen experimentally.
summary: Standard two-phase relative permeability hysteresis models cannot reproduce the drop in gas and water mobility between primary and tertiary processes observed in intermediate-wet systems during WAG. The authors simulated 1D core-floods and a 2D reservoir cross-section (Eclipse 94) using the Carlson, Killough and a modified SL model with input taken from measured curves and a modified Stone I oil model. A tolerance limit added to the SL model's jump between high- and low-mobility envelopes stabilized the runs and halved CPU time for the 3000-day cross-section. In 1D core-floods, Carlson and Killough gave about 13.2% final oil saturation and SL 11.6%, versus 5% experimentally, from 66% initially. In 2D, SL gave delayed gas breakthrough (900 vs 400 days) and larger gas-swept area. Water mobility representation (primary, secondary or pseudo-hysteresis) strongly changed recovery and water segregation, and the Killough wetting-phase scheme was judged of little use for WAG.
abstract: Immiscible WAG have been simulated by use of dfferent relative permeability hysteresis models. The oil relative penneabilities were generated by a modified Stone I model. Experimental results especially from intermdate wetting systems have shown a significant drop in gas relative permeability between primary processes (gas saturation increasing first time) and tertiary processes ( gas saturation increasing after an increasing-decreasing sequence). Numerical simulation of both ID core-floods and 2D reservoir cross-sections were used in order to investigate WAG. The input to each model is selected from experimental measured data. The results show that standard hysteresis models for non- wetting phase relative permeability is lacking flexibility to describe experimental data important for the performance of the WAG process.

title: Gas Relative Permeability and Flow Behaviour in a Retrograde Gas/Condensate Reservoir Under Depletion
caption: Figure 1: Flow diagram for gas condensate studies
tldr: Gas relative permeability, critical condensate and trapped gas saturations were measured on a vertical composite sandstone core under depletion, with simulation showing gravity-to-capillary control explains unusual curve shapes.
summary: The study addresses how retrograde condensate dropout below the dew point alters gas relative permeability in a North Sea gas/condensate field. A custom vertical high-pressure rig (69 MPa, 180°C) held a 50 cm composite core of seven sandstone plugs (70-340 mD), tested first with a synthetic condensate (temperature reduction at 16 MPa) and then with recombined live reservoir fluid depleted from 50 MPa at 130°C. The synthetic fluid gave a smooth curve with a critical condensate saturation of 29% PV and krg of 0.30. The real fluid gave a non-monotonic krg, with a local maximum at about 16-20% condensate saturation, a maximum condensate saturation of 19.7% PV, and a trapped gas saturation of 24.9% PV after condensate flooding. FRAGOR compositional simulation with IFT-dependent relative permeability showed gravity-dominated distribution near the dew point shifting to capillary- and viscous-controlled redistribution in the heterogeneous core, explaining the curve shape and its rate dependence.
abstract: The dropout of retrograde liquid when depleting a gas/condensate reservoir below the dew point may lead to alterations of the gas flow behaviour. Near the wellbore, both gas and liquid condensate are expected to flow, resulting in a trapped gas saturation, whilst further out in the reservoir, the hydrocarbon liquid may be immobile until a critical condensate saturation is reached. Because of its importance in field development, gas relative permeabilities at various hydrocarbon liquid saturations, together with critical condensate and trapped gas saturations, were determined for a North Sea gas/condensate field. Specially designed equipment was constructed for this purpose, and measurements were conducted under constant composition expansion on a long vertical composite core. Synthetic fluids and then real reservoir fluids at the appropriate conditions of pressure and temperature were used. To aid in the interpretation of the experiments, compositional simulations were also carried out. For the case of the system with real reservoir fluids, the balance between gravitational and capillary forces was found to be of the greatest importance determining the distribution of the liquid condensate in the composite core. The experiments, combined with numerical simulation, showed that, when the pressure has dropped sufficiently below the dew point, capillarity replaces gravity as the dominant force governing the distribution of liquid in the composite core. This explains the somewhat unusual shape of the measured gas relative permeability curve vs. liquid saturation. The force dependence on the flow behaviour is enhanced by the vertical flow in the heterogeneous core. The study also yielded realistic values of critical condensate and trapped gas saturations.

title: Performance and Numerical Interpretation of Gas Drainage Core Tests Under Secondary and Tertiary Conditions
caption: Figure 5 - Production curves Three-Phase Displacement (Exp and Sim.)
figure_reason: Shows experimental versus simulated production curves for a three-phase gas displacement, demonstrating the history-match quality.
tldr: Three-phase relative permeabilities are derived by history-matching gas-injection production curves with tabulated Krw, Kro, Krg versus Sw and Sg, starting from a pseudo steady-state estimate.
summary: Steady-state three-phase relative permeabilities poorly represent displacements, especially with non-spreading oil. Gas drainage tests were run on Fontainebleau and Vosges sandstones (about 3000 md, 40-70 cm long) with brine, Soltrol 170 and nitrogen, from two-phase and three-phase initial saturations. A quick pseudo steady-state calculation and isoperm curvature arguments gave preliminary Kr tables, which were then adjusted over several simulation cycles until simulated oil, water and gas production matched experiments. Gas drainage gave lower residual oil than waterflood (Sorg 0.15 vs Sow 0.29). Krw depended on Sw alone, Krg on Sg alone in two Sw domains (above and below 0.35), and Kro on both Sw and Sg with strongly curved isoperms.
abstract: This paper introduces a new method to determine the relative permeabilities of three-phase system -gas-oil-water-flowing in a porous medium. Gas injections in porous media are performed in multiple conditions of initial saturations. The recovered quantities of fluid are recorded versus time A model is applied to simulate a gas injection process and to describe oil, water and gas production in the case of each experiment. Required input to the model are the values of the relative permeabilities for the three phases, written in the form of tables as functions of water and gas saturation. The relative permeability tables are modified until a good fit is found between the experimental and the calculated productions. These relative permeability values are then considered as the relative permeabilities that actually correspond to the displacements. Using these tables allows to well describe the multiple phenomena encountered during a gas injection, even the behavior of an immobile phase obtained in two-phase conditions and displaced subsequently by gas.

title: Calculation of Three-Phase Relative Permeabilities from Displacement Experiments with Measurements of in-Situ Saturation
caption: Figure 8. Trapped gas saturation compared Figure 9. Relationship between trapped gas
figure_reason: Shows trapped gas versus initial gas saturation compared with Land equation, a key result.
tldr: Three-phase relative permeabilities in water-wet Clashach sandstone were derived from unsteady-state floods with tracer-imaged in-situ saturations; water kr depends on Sw alone, oil kr shows scatter and hysteresis.
summary: The paper examines how saturation history affects two- and three-phase relative permeability in a water-wet Clashach sandstone core (234 md). Sequences of water, oil and gas injections were run with nuclear tracer imaging to measure in-situ saturations, and three-phase kr was calculated analytically (Virnovsky method). Two-phase displacements were also history-matched with a Levenberg-Marquardt optimization of kr and capillary pressure, which showed limits when only production and pressure data were used and when viscous fingering was not modeled. Trapped gas increased with initial gas saturation and did not fit a Land equation with C=1.9 (C≈3.0 fit better), and trapped gas lowered residual oil. Water kr depended on water saturation alone, gas kr appeared to depend on gas saturation at high saturations, and oil kr showed considerable scatter and hysteresis, suggesting dependence on other phases' saturations.
abstract: Unsteady state coreflood experiments in a water wet Clashach core have been used to calculate three-phase oil, water and gas relative permeabilities. From the experimental results the following observations were made; relative permeabilities to the oil and gas phase depend on more than one phase saturation, hysteresis from increasing and decreasing saturations was most pronounced for the oil phase. By using an optimization algorithm relative permeabilities and capillary pressure have been simultaneously estimated from data gathered during two-phase displacements. The importance of in-situ saturation information in relative permeability determination is demonstrated in this paper.

title: Dual Energy Gamma-Ray Absorption Technique Applied to Oil Relative Permeability Determination During a Tertiary Gas Gravity Drainage Experiment
caption: Fig. 8 : Oil saturation distribution during gasflooding
figure_reason: Oil saturation profiles during gas injection show tertiary oil drainage and capillary retention zones from gamma-ray monitoring.
tldr: Dual-energy gamma-ray absorption monitored three-phase saturations in a tertiary gas gravity drainage coreflood; history matching with a compositional simulator validated the Stone 1 oil relative permeability model.
summary: Predicting tertiary oil recovery from waterflooded reservoirs depends strongly on the three-phase relative permeability model, which is rarely validated experimentally. A 58 cm composite water-wet sandstone core was waterflooded and then subjected to tertiary gas gravity drainage at 230 bar and 71°C with low-IFT equilibrium fluids, while a dual-source (Am-241/Cs-137) gamma-ray rig monitored oil, gas and water saturations in situ. Waterflood recovered 70% IOIP, but residual oil profiles were non-uniform (35% at top, 10% at bottom) owing to capillary end effects. Gas drainage produced tertiary oil, reaching 57% TOIP and 8.5% average oil saturation before core plugging at 1.3 PV gas, with near-zero oil saturation in the upper core. The Foulser method gave Kro falling from 1e-3 to 1e-5 as So dropped from 25% to 10%, and compositional simulation matched production and saturation profiles using the Stone 1 model.
abstract: For several years a dual energy gamma-ray absorption measurement apparatus has been routinely performing in situ three phase saturation monitoring during coreflood experiments in reservoir conditions. This paper presents this sophisticated equipment and the application of the technique to determine the three phase oil relative permeability at low oil saturations during a tertiary gas gravity drainage experiment. The test was carried out on a 58 cm long composite of a water wet reservoir sandstone. The oil relative permeability was a crucial point to validate the economic feasibility of this tertiary oil recovery process for a waterflooded reservoir in South-East Asia. Using the gamma-ray absorption technique it was possible to visualize the fluid saturation distribution in the core as a function of the volume of gas injected. The production of tertiary oil by gravity drainage was put into evidence at the top of the core. The three phase oil relative permeability curve was deduced from the oil saturation profiles using an analytical calculation. The experiment was finally correctly reproduced with a generalized compositional simulator, emphasis being put on the match of saturation profiles. A triphasic relative permeability model was then validated and will be used for field-scale simulation.

title: Method for Correlating NMR Relaxometry and Mercury Injection Data
caption: Figure 9: Cross plot of core permeability vs. NMR analog of Swanson's parameter, rna~(BVNw.T2)~~~, showing distinct trends for different rock types.
figure_reason: Shows NMR Swanson analog versus permeability with distinct rock-type trends ordered by relaxivity.
tldr: NMR T2 distributions are matched to MICP data to get effective relaxivity, a fractional-flow immobile-water cutoff, and a relaxivity-scaled Swanson-type permeability predictor.
summary: The paper correlates NMR T2 distributions with mercury injection capillary pressure data on 17 plugs (3 clean sandstones, 5 shaly sandstones, 7 limestones, 2 dolostones) covering 6.4–27 p.u. porosity and 0.078–4450 md permeability. Matching the distributions by cross-correlation gives effective relaxivities: limestones 1.0–3.2 µm/s, dolomites 4.6–5.4, sandstones 6.4–25, with no clear clean versus shaly sand difference. A new immobile-fluid definition uses fractional flow (Fw = 0.01) computed from the T2 distribution via Standing's relative permeability equations. It gives cutoffs from a few ms to several hundred ms, independent of relaxivity, and generally higher immobile saturation than a fixed 33 ms or 50 psi cutoff. An NMR analog of the Swanson parameter, max(BVNW·T2), shows three rock-type trends against permeability; multiplying by effective relaxivity collapses them to one trend as good as the MICP Swanson parameter, while porosity does not correlate with permeability.
abstract: We describe a methodology for correlating mercury injection capillary pressure (MICP) data with NMR transverse relaxation time (T,) distributions to obtain estimates of immobile water saturation and permeability. Surface relaxivities determined from correlations computed for a suite of rock cores having diverse origins and properties are consistent with prior studies which show that carbonates generally have lower relaxivities than sandstones. A new, trial definition of immobile fluid volume based on fractional flow concepts is introduced and compared to existing interpretation models that use a fixed T, cutoff to distinguish mobile vs. immobile fluid. An NMR-based analog of the Swanson parameter is shown to be an excellent predictor of permeability whereas porosity is essentially uncorrelated with permeability.

title: Technique for Observing Oil-Wetting of Carbonate Surfaces Using FT-IR
caption: Figure 3 Stock Tank Oil Spectra (a) KBr pellets, (b) Contacted $t = 0$ , (c) Subtracted $t_{S_2} - t_0$
figure_reason: Compares KBr, initial contacted and subtracted spectra for crude oil, showing adsorption peaks and valleys that define the technique.
tldr: ATR FT-IR on ZnSe crystals sputter-coated with calcite tracks crude oil component adsorption over time, showing polar O, S and N species adsorb and equilibrate near 130 hours.
summary: Bulk wettability measurements give little information on molecular-level oil-carbonate interactions. The authors sputter-coated zinc selenide ATR crystals with an 8.5 nm calcium carbonate layer (verified by XPS and IR) and contacted them with a 27° API Middle East stock tank oil, its cyclohexane maltenes, and weak acid and aromatic fractions. Subtracting the initial spectrum from later spectra over 96 to 672 hours revealed adsorption at about 1100-1150, 1610 and 3350-3400 cm-1, with loss of C-H bands at 2850-2930 cm-1, indicating adsorption of polar oxygen, sulfur and possibly nitrogen compounds while less polar hydrocarbons are displaced. Asphaltenes (0.42 wt%) significantly altered the adsorption and hydrogen bonding behavior, and aromatics adsorbed similarly to whole crude. Adsorption leveled off at roughly 130 hours, and residual absorbance after cleaning suggested strongly bonded material.
abstract: Standard methods for describing wettability and wettability changes rely on measurements of bulk properties such as contact angle or wettability indices. Information on molecular level interactions that affect reservoir wettability is scarce. A new technique for observing adsorption of oil components on carbonate surfaces is described. Zinc selenide attenuated total reflectance (ATR) crystals were sputter coated with an 8.5 nm. layer of calcium carbonate. Coating thickness and composition were determined using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). Crude oil was brought into contact with the carbonate surface and Fourier Transform Infrared (FI'-IR) spectra were observed over a period of time. By subtracting the initial spectrum from subsequent spectra, it was possible to observe the interactions associated with certain functional groups and a carbonate surface. Equilibration time for the adsorption process was observed to level out at approximately 130 hours in the absence of water.

title: The Use of Attenuation Standards for CT Scanning
caption: Figure 7. Two Phase Saturations Along Core Length. Average of slices shows closer agreement with volumetric when calibration is used.
figure_reason: Shows saturation profiles along core with and without calibration, demonstrating improved agreement with volumetric results.
tldr: Describes CT number drift in core scanning and three laboratories' attenuation-standard calibration methods, showing standards improve saturation accuracy to about 1%, with recommendations to minimize drift.
summary: CT numbers measured on core drift over time because of tube and detector aging, beam filtration, temperature, beam hardening and noise. A drift of only 10-20 CT units can cause significant saturation errors. Three calibration methods are presented. Schlumberger-Doll scans plastic and magnesium rods with each Berea core to normalize every slice to true density. Mobil scans fused quartz and aluminum standards before each core, and water saturations then agree with volumetric values within about 1% rather than about 4% without standards (average error 0.98% vs 3.54% in two-phase tests). Calgary checks a reference material of known density and adjusts tube gain or reruns the scanner standardization. The paper ends with eight recommendations, including using reference materials of similar effective atomic number, documenting the calibration, and warming up the tube.
abstract: Use of CT scanning and related technologies to view and characterize reservoir core in conjunction with routine or special core analysis is widespread and increasing. Currently, CT scanning of core materials is accomplished at many different laboratories, utilizing a wide variety of instruments. Drift in the measured attenuation response has been identified and been shown to shift CT values. This reduces the accuracy and reliability of CT results and hinders comparison of data. During the 1994 SCA workshop on CT scanning, routine calibration against attenuation standards was recommended to increase integrity, validity and comparability of results. This paper discusses the need for standards and presents methods used by three different laboratories. Overall recommendations for minimization of errors induced by drift are provided.

title: A Hydraulic (Flow) Unit Based Model for the Determination of Petrophysical Properties from NMR Relaxation Measurements
caption: Figure 16: Permeability from FZI based Model
figure_reason: Shows measured permeability versus FZI/NMR-model permeability, the paper's main predictive result.
tldr: Links hydraulic flow units to NMR T1 relaxation to derive surface relaxivity, T1 cutoff, pore throat size and permeability, validated on 17 core plugs.
summary: The paper links the hydraulic unit (flow zone indicator) concept to NMR relaxation so that wireline NMR can be calibrated to core data. Equations relating FZI, specific surface area, tortuosity, surface relaxivity and T1 are derived, along with a permeability model based on FZI and NMR bound-water saturation. Seventeen brine-saturated 1-inch plugs were measured by T1 inversion recovery at 1 MHz and compared with CMS-300 porosity/permeability, mercury injection, centrifuge capillary pressure and thin sections. NMR porosity matched core porosity closely, and NMR-based zonation reproduced the four hydraulic units from core data for all samples but one. Surface relaxivity varied from 0.005 to 0.054 µm/ms between the worst and best units, and a T1 cutoff of about 10 ms matched 400 psi centrifuge irreducible water, while 20 ms matched 50 psi. The regression-based permeability model matched measured permeability within the calibration database.
abstract: This paper presents preliminary results of a Hydraulic Units (HU) based research program aimed at establishing guidelines for the use of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) tools for petrophysical evaluation. We show obvious but crucial relationships between the HU concept and NMR relaxation data which form the basis for linking NMR wireline log data to laboratory NMR measurements. Mathematical relationships between Flow Zone (hydraulic unit zonation) Indicators (FZI), specific surface area (S,), tortuosity (r), surface relaxivity (p) and NMR longitudinal relaxation time TI are developed. A permeability model based on FZI and NMR porosity is developed. Laboratory T, measurements at 1 MHz with CORESPEC-1000, together with core analysis data of permeability, porosity, centrifuge capillary pressure and thin section petrography have been used to validate the model. We also developed and validated HU-based predictive algorithms for estimating p and longitudinal relaxation time cut-off (T,,) from pore throat size distributions (mercury injection data), and centrifbge capillary pressure data. We show that the observed variability in p is due to the existence of different hydraulic units in the reservoir rock. We also show that T1, used for determining producible fluid from NMR relaxation time distributions may vary as a function of rock types.

title: Characterization and Saturation Determination of Geothermal Rock by CT and NMR
caption: Fig. 5 - CT investigation of drilling fluid transport by vapor convection.
figure_reason: CT slices of xenon injection show vapor transport through the core and a fracture, supporting the invasion mechanism.
tldr: Pressure coring of Geysers geothermal graywacke with tritium tracer, NMR saturation and CT flooding shows coring-fluid invasion grows with downhole delay and occurs by vapor transport.
summary: Water saturation in Geysers geothermal graywacke (1-5% porosity, ~400 F) is hard to measure by Dean-Stark, so a wireline pressure-coring method with frozen core recovery and tritium-tagged coring fluid was developed. NMR was used for saturation, with a feasibility accuracy of about ±20% PV (±0.04 ml). Core Run #69, held downhole ~24 h, showed 30-50% central invasion (50-70% in outer donuts), while rapidly recovered Run #88 appeared uninvaded with Sw of about 3-13%. Whole-core CT could not separate invasion from edge x-ray attenuation artifacts. Liquid injection advanced only ~1 cm in 8 h at 500 psi (k ≈ 0.0005 md), Fick diffusion was two orders too low, and Darcy vapor-flow calculations plus xenon CT flow tests supported vapor convection as the invasion mechanism.
abstract: This paper presents the results of special core studies to determine rock characteristics and brine saturations for the Geysers geothermal field, California. A coring procedure was developed to combine wireline retrieval with pressurized core recovery. Tritium in the coring fluid provided a means for detecting invasion. Nuclear magnetic resonance was applied as a new approach for saturation determination. Although reported water contents for some cases were below confidence levels, the NMR analyses offered relative comparisons and an alternative to uncertain Dean-S tark determinations. The tracer studies indicated that invasion increases with time when the core is detained downhole. The first core, detained for about 24 hours, had invasion levels (central core) in the range of 30% to 50%. The second core, recovered rapidly, appeared uninvaded with formation water saturations estimated to be low (3 % to 13 %). CT core flooding and modeling studies indicated vaporization and convection as the primary mechanism for coring-fluid invasion.

title: Variations in the Electrical Behavior of the Ekofisk Field in the North Sea
caption: Figure 16: Comparison of the saturation exponents calculated from well logs with those determined in the laboratory.
figure_reason: Shows laboratory saturation exponents after imbibition agree with well-log derived values in a waterflooded Tor zone, the key validation.
tldr: Resistivity measurements on 200+ Ekofisk chalk plugs show formation factor varies with quartz content and saturation exponent rises after imbibition, matching well-log results.
summary: Laboratory electrical properties of Ekofisk chalk were measured on over 200 extracted plugs from 14 wells to improve well-log saturation interpretation. Plugs were saturated with 1.2 M NaCl brine and desaturated with n-decane by centrifuge (validated by MRI and porous disc), then measured at 10 kHz under 1580 psig hydrostatic stress, at Swi and after spontaneous imbibition. Formation factor depended on quartz content: a=0.72, m=2.14 for low-quartz Tor and lower Ekofisk, while a=1, m=2 fit the upper Ekofisk and tight zone. Saturation exponents at Swi were consistent with Archie behavior and matched deep-resistivity logs. After imbibition the saturation exponent was significantly higher, varied with final water saturation and depth, and its histogram matched an independent log-derived value in a waterflooded Tor zone.
abstract: Laboratory measurements on a limited number of core plugs often present an incomplete and possibly inaccurate description of the electrical properties used for the interpretation of open-hole well logs. This paper presents the methods and results of an extensive field-wide study for the highly fractured Ekofisk field to better understand the variation in the resistivity properties throughout the chalk reservoirs. Core plug preparation and accurate determination of the resistivity and fluid saturation utilized conventional laboratory methods. The use of extracted core plugs, refined oil, and synthetic brine to simplify the testing was supported by the direct comparison of resistivities from laboratory measurements with conventional well log resistivities. The laboratory results also showed that the formation factor varied with the mineralogical content of the chalk. Non-Archie electrical behavior was observed in the chalk after imbibition. The water saturation exponent after an imbibition waterflood diverged significantly from that at initial water. A comparison of the histogram of after imbibition laboratory measurements with an independent well log determination of the water saturation exponent for a water flooded zone supported the laboratory measurements. This study developed a data base of measurements on 200 plus core plugs from which correlations and techniques can be further developed to improve conventional well-log interpretation for the field.

title: Constructing Core Petrophysical Groups: A Key Step to Reconcile Petrophysical and Geological Core Data in Reservoir Modelling
caption: FIGURE 2 - PETROPHYSICAL GROUPS AND SEDIMENTARY BODIES
figure_reason: Shows vertical organization of Petrophysical Groups within sedimentary bodies and well correlation, the key reconciliation result.
tldr: Clustering plug porosity, permeability and grain density into six Petrophysical Groups, then distributing them within geostatistically modelled sedimentary bodies, reduces property dispersion versus 17 lithofacies in a mixed carbonate-siliciclastic reservoir.
summary: In a mixed carbonate-siliciclastic Albian reservoir, properties vary widely within sedimentary facies because of diagenesis, so facies are poor predictors of rock properties. Over 1000 plug measurements of porosity, gas permeability and grain density from two wells were clustered into six Petrophysical Groups (Group 0 for k<0.1 mD). Capillary pressure and relative permeability were assigned per group, and thin sections and XRD linked groups to dolomitization and dissolution. Five sedimentary bodies were generated by 3-D object modelling, Groups were simulated within them by sequential indicator simulation, and porosity and permeability were simulated per group. Within groups porosity dispersion stayed below 3.9 p.u. and permeability below 0.48 decades, versus 4.5-7 p.u. and 0.7-1 decade within the original 17 lithofacies.
abstract: This paper outlines a method for improved mapping of reservoir properties using Petrophysical Groups derived fiom core analysis. The method is illustrated through a case study of a mixed lithology oil reservoir. This reservoir is characterized by a large vertical variability of reservoir properties within each sedimentary facies as a result of combined sedunentological and diagenetic effects. Hence, in order to determine rock properties, for reservoir simulation purposes, reliance could not be placed on sedimentary facies. It was therefore decided to develop a new modelling method which gives a more accurate representation of the actual petrophysical heterogeneities. A three stage modelling process was tested on a 201n-thick interval. The first stage consisted in subdividing the whole reservoir into Petrophysical Groups. A petrophysical Group is a set of reservoir zones having similar porosity, permeability, grain density and capillary pressure curves. Six Petrophysical Groups were constructed fiom the whole set of core measurements using clustering techniques. Within each Group, variability of petrophysical parameters was relatively narrow and relationships between properties such as water saturation as a function of permeability and capillary pressure were established. Relative permeability functions were assigned to each Group using two phase flow measurements. These measurements were conducted on hll size samples representative of the Petrophysical Groups. The second stage consisted in the recognition of five sedimentary bodles based on core description and sedimentological interpretation of the facies associations. Sedimentary bodles were then generated in three dimensions using a geostatistical conceptual model. The third stage consisted in hstributing Petrophysical Groups in each sedimentary body. Study of thin sections within each petrophysical Group proved that diagenetic effects could be related to petrophysical properties. The areal and vertical extensions of the Petrophysical Groups with each sedimentary body were therefore determined through magenetic trends. Petrophysical attributes were then generated using the narrow dstributions and the relationships established during the first stage for each of the six Groups. In this complex reservoir, the method proved to enhance the representation of petrophysical heterogeneities compared to the conventional deterministic modelling methods.

title: Stress Dependence of the Cementation Exponent
caption: Fig.5 Relative change in the cementation exponent between 50 an 700 bar, p/o#ed versus the porosity at aim ospheric conditions lor sandstones (black squares) and syntheiic synthetic samples (grey dots)
figure_reason: Shows change in cementation exponent versus porosity, contrasting sandstones and glass beads; the key result.
tldr: Formation resistivity factor and porosity of outcrop sandstones and glass-bead packs were measured up to 700 bar; the cementation exponent's stress response depends on porosity, with large increases in low-porosity rocks.
summary: The cementation exponent in Archie's equation is usually treated as constant, but resistivity and porosity both change with stress. Formation factor and porosity were measured on Castlegate, Bentheim, Darley Dale and Fontainebleau outcrop sandstones and sintered glass-bead samples under isostatic stress up to 700 bar. Between 50 and 700 bar porosity fell by 4-8% in all samples, but the formation factor rose by 5-20% in the high-porosity sandstones and by 100-300% in Fontainebleau, versus only 1.5-4% in glass beads. The cementation exponent increased with stress below about 15% porosity and decreased slightly above about 20%, while glass beads showed a porosity-independent decrease. Reservoir core data confirmed the trends, and errors of more than 10% in hydrocarbon saturation can arise in low-porosity rocks if stress is not simulated. Tangential grain contacts closing under stress are proposed as the explanation for the sandstone behaviour.
abstract: The effects of simulated reservoir stress conditions on the cementation exponent of various outcrop sandstone samples and synthetic glass-beads samples were investigated. It was foluld that the ce~nentation exponent can increase or decrease with increasing stress, dependent on sample porosity. The stress dependence of the cementation exponent of glass-beads samples tunled out not to depend on porosity. The different behaviour of sandstone and synthetic samples is qualitatively explained by different types of grain to grain contacts. To assess the i~npact of these findings on core analysis, core data were co~npnred with those obtained on the outcrop sandstones. The trends found with outcrop sandstones could be confirmed with the reservoir sandstones. The impact of these findings on hydrocasbon assessment is especially important for low porosity rocks (\$ < 12%). The results show that laboratory measuretnents at in-situ stress conditions are important to reduce uncertainties in hydrocasbon estimation. It is demonstrated that outcrop sandstone is well suited for experiments intended to help to better understand core resistivity. Results obtained on synthetic samples on the other hand have to be interpreted with great care as with such samples the behnviour of reservoir rock can often not be properly mimicked.

title: Measurement of Gas Permeabilities Under Different Compaction Modes on Tight Reservoir Samples
caption: Figure 2 : Loading scheme for gas permeability testing
figure_reason: Shows the stepwise loading scheme used between gas permeability measurements, key to the test procedure.
tldr: Gas permeability and porosity of tight sandstones and carbonates were measured under hydrostatic and uniaxial compaction; uniaxial loading gave smaller permeability and porosity reductions.
summary: Permeability is usually measured under hydrostatic load, which does not reproduce reservoir stress paths during depletion. The authors built an unsteady-state gas permeameter (pulse decay for low permeability, draw-down for higher) with Klinkenberg correction. Three tight sandstones and two dolomite samples (about 0.01 to 0.9 mD) were loaded hydrostatically and uniaxially up to 1200 bar (sandstone) or 700 bar (carbonate). Hydrostatic permeability reductions were 57-65% in sandstones versus 32-45% uniaxial, while carbonates showed only 5-8% uniaxial reduction. Lower-permeability rocks lost proportionally more permeability, and higher-permeability sandstones (6.5 and 12.6 mD) lost under 21% (uniaxial) and 29% (hydrostatic). Hydrostatic tests alone overestimate property loss, and no general correction factor can be derived.
abstract: Reliable core measurements of permeability are very important for reservoir engineers predicting, well productivity, and its change versus time. In most laboratories, permeabilities are usually measured under hydrostatic loads that do not reproduce reservoir in-situ conditions (deviatoric stresses, oedometric deformations among others) while failing to simulate the reservoir stress path during production. For the purposes of comparison, both hydrostatic and uniaxial compactions were applied to low permeability samples [from less than 1 mD to $10^{-2}$ mD] cored in a carbonate reservoir and in an overpressured sandstone reservoir. As steady state methods are delicate and time consuming for tight rocks, an original and user-friendly unsteady-state gas permeameter was developed. These tests aimed at determining the gradual evolution of permeability and porosity when effective stresses increase over the major depletions contemplated. Results show that permeabilities strongly vary with stress paths. Permeability reductions under uniaxial compactions are 25% to 60% lower when compared to isotropic conditions. Furthermore, the lower the intrinsic permeability, the higher the permeability reduction. Permeability decreases are noticed to be consistent with deformations. This study demonstrates that choosing hydrostatic or uniaxial compactions (the latter being more closely related to actual reservoir conditions) is of the highest importance with respect to low permeability formations evaluation. The difference may become critical for rocks with permeabilities close to the cutoff level.

title: Shaly Sand Analysis with Thermal Membrane Potentials
caption: Fig. 3 The transport number ft as measured with TMP compared to the CMP derived Qv for the samples with Qv < 0.3 meqlml
figure_reason: Main result: TMP-derived transport number correlates excellently with CMP-derived Qv across the samples.
tldr: Thermally induced membrane potentials are introduced to measure clay conductivity (Qv) on brine-saturated cores, showing excellent agreement with concentration membrane potentials and potential use at reservoir conditions.
summary: Excess clay conductivity (Qv) in shaly sands is traditionally measured by chemical titration, Co-Cw curves or concentration membrane potentials (CMP), each with limitations such as crushing, long durations, or the need for flushing. The authors present a static thermal membrane potential (TMP) method, extending thin-membrane irreversible thermodynamics to core samples, and built a two-vessel set-up with a pressurised core holder. Eleven brine-saturated cores (Qv 0.03-1.5 meq/ml, porosity 12-33%, permeability 1-1700 mD) were tested at 8.4-50 g/l NaCl, cycling temperature at 4 °C/h. The potential was linear with temperature difference, and the cation transport number correlated excellently with CMP-derived Qv with similar uncertainties. The constant B was the same for all samples (0.204 ± 0.002 mV/°C), suggesting single-salinity measurements may suffice. Oil-saturated samples gave too much scatter due to oil seepage, and the lowest-Qv sample gave t+ of 0.57 versus the expected 0.38.
abstract: A new method is described to investigate the contribution of clay conductivity, as characterised by the parameter Qv, to the conductivity of rock. This method, which makes use of Thermally induced Membrane Potentials (TMP), allows the measurement of Qv at reservoir conditions. A new experimental set-up, devised and constructed at KSEPL, has been shown to accurately measure Qv of a core sample saturated with brine at laboratory conditions. First measurements confirm that TMP can also be measured on oil-saturated samples, although a new core-holder and better experimental procedures are necessary for quantitative evaluation. It is speculated, that the liquid permeability of a sample can be measured as a by-product.

title: Pore Geometry and Rock Properties
caption: Fig 3. lmage Porosity Vs Permeability
figure_reason: Shows strong linear relationship between image porosity and permeability, the paper's key result.
tldr: Backscattered electron image porosity from 82 North Sea sandstone samples predicts permeability far better than core porosity and gives a reciprocal estimator for formation factor.
summary: The study compares special core analysis data with pore parameters from backscattered electron image analysis on 82 Tertiary submarine-fan sandstone samples from nine North Sea wells. Image porosity, which captures mainly pores larger than about 3 µm, underestimates gas-expansion porosity by 10-15 porosity units and does not correlate with it. However, image porosity predicts permeability with R² = 0.855 and σ = 0.284 log10 units, versus σ = 0.637 for core porosity. Adding a pore length-squared term improves this to σ = 0.266 (R² = 0.875). Formation factor is approximated by 4.3 + 1/image porosity for about 80% of the data (Trend A), while well E is an outlier and was excluded from the regressions. The authors conclude that image porosity approximates effective, flowing porosity rather than total porosity.
abstract: This article summarises the early results of a research project carried out over the past 4 years. The principle objective of the project, was to compare special core analysis measurements with parameters derived from the processing of back scattered electron images. The data base consists of 82 samples from 9 wells. Each sample has 0, FRF and pore measurements acquired from 1066 image fields, (1 3lsample).

title: Coupling of Wall-Slip and High-Velocity Flow for Determination of Gas Permeability
caption: Figure 4: Model A (a) and Model B (b) with kr, ,8, and b, fitted to experimental data.
figure_reason: Shows Model A and Model B fits to high-velocity data with all parameters fitted, the main result.
tldr: Gas flow experiments on a tight sandstone show wall-slip and high-velocity inertial flow are coupled; the coupled Model B fits better than uncoupled Model A.
summary: Gas permeability determination at high velocity normally applies Klinkenberg and Forchheimer corrections separately. The authors compare an uncoupled model (Model A, Jones) with a coupled model (Model B, Skjetne and Gudmundsson) using nitrogen flow through a short, tight Obernkirchner sandstone plug (9.55 mm long, porosity 0.2015). Low-velocity Klinkenberg tests gave kl = 6.914e-15 m2 and b = 3.35e4 Pa, taken as true values. In a 64-point high-velocity series, Model A with fixed kl and b fit poorly, while Model B fit well. When all parameters were fitted, Model A underestimated kl by 21% and overestimated the rock-dependent Klinkenberg term by 935%, versus 6.7% and 50% for Model B. The simple approximation of Model B (Eq. 9) is recommended.
abstract: Wall-slip in the high velocity flow regime has traditionally been accounted for by correcting the permeability and not the inertial resistance. A recent theory for gas flow includes a coupling between wall-slip velocity and high-velocity pressure loss. Flow experiments were done on a short sample of low permeability. Models for uncoupled and coupled wall-slip and high-velocity flow were compared to experimental results. It was found that there is a significant coupling effect which is described by the new theory.

title: Estimation of Hydraulic Conductivity from Complex Electrical Measurements
caption: Figure 5 Permeability coefficient estimated from field data (Spectral IP-Measurements) vs. permeability coefficient from grain size parameters.
figure_reason: Field spectral IP permeability estimates compared with grain-size-derived values, showing the prediction's accuracy at aquifer scale.
tldr: Permeability of unconsolidated sands is estimated to within about one order of magnitude from formation factor and surface area derived from a single low-frequency complex conductivity measurement.
summary: The paper relates hydraulic permeability to complex electrical conductivity using a constant phase angle model below 1 kHz. Formation factor and the surface-area-to-porosity ratio, obtained from the real and imaginary conductivity components, enter a modified Kozeny-Carman equation with fractal pore-surface assumptions. Forty unconsolidated Pleistocene sand samples saturated with NaCl brine were measured. Regression of K*F against the imaginary conductivity gave exponents of about 2.8 (K from grain size) and 3.9 (K from water permeation). Field spectral IP data on aquifers agreed with grain-size-derived hydraulic conductivity. A relative permeability extension, tested on Vinegar and Waxman shaly sandstone data, showed only self-consistency since no relative permeability measurements were made.
abstract: Electrical and hydraulic properties are closely related in porous rock. Complex electrical behaviour is caused by polarization accompanied by charged grain surface and constrictions along the capillaries. Since both electrical phenomena and hydraulic flow are governed by the shape of pore channels, complex electrical conductivity may be used to improve indirect measurement of hydraulic permeability. Determination of the formation factor and surface area is based on a constant phase angle model of conductivity. A modified Kozeny-Carman-equation and the assumption that the internal surface area has a fractal behaviour are both used to estimate permeability. Both experimental and published data are used to study the relationship. Analysis suggests that, in the case of water saturated rock, the estimation of permeability with an accuracy of one order seems to be possible. The model should be applicable for the investigation of relative permeability. It is the purpose of this paper to contribute to the quantification of the effects of permeability on lab measured as well as in-situ complex rock conductivity. These relationships will allow the petrophysicist to better estimate permeability from lab and log as well as surface measurements

title: The Influence of Intergranular Microcracks on the Petrophysical Properties of Sandstone - Experiments to Quantify Effects of Core Damage
caption: Fig.4. Volumetric compressibility of non-heated and heated Bentheim sandstone as a function of isostatic stress up to 200 bar; from 200 up to 700 bar the data points for non-heated and heated samples overlap
figure_reason: Shows heated samples have higher volumetric compressibility below 60 bar, converging with non-heated at higher stress.
tldr: Heating Bentheim sandstone to 650°C to mimic coring damage widened grain boundaries, lowering Vp by 25%, raising low-stress compressibility 30% and lowering resistivity; reservoir sandstone showed similar widths.
summary: Coring-induced intergranular cracking may make core data unrepresentative of in-situ rock. Core damage was simulated by heating Bentheim outcrop sandstone to 650°C for 24 hours, and grain boundary widths were measured on SEM photomicrographs. Grain boundary widths rose from 0.1-0.3 µm to 0.1-0.9 µm and porosity from about 23.7% to 24.3%. Compressional velocity dropped about 25% (water-saturated MD3 from 3.06 to 2.21 km/s), volumetric compressibility rose about 30% below 60 bar, and formation resistivity factor fell about 10%. Differences vanished above 60 bar, but heated samples had more inelastic compaction (inelastic/elastic ratio about 0.55 versus 0.14). A gas reservoir sandstone showed grain boundary widths of 0.2-2.8 µm, similar to or wider than the heated samples, suggesting the boundaries opened during or after coring.
