caption: Figure 2. The effect of noise on inversion $T_{2k} = 2^{k+1}, k = 1, 2, \dots, 9$ (a-c) and $T_{2k} = 2^k$ , $k = 0, 1, 2, \dots, 10$ (d-e). (“ $\Sigma$ ”: model and “ $\Upsilon$ ”: fit). The underlying model data in Plots a and d contains 12 p.u. CBW and 12 p.u. BVI, the model in Plots b and e contains 12 p.u. BVI, and that in Plots c and f contains 12 p.u. CBW only. Comparing the top row and bot
figure_reason: Shows CBW leaking into effective porosity bins under noise, comparing 9- and 11-bin fits.
tldr: Synthetic CPMG data show clay-bound water leaks into NMR effective porosity depending on noise and TE; a time-domain subtraction using 0.6 ms echoes corrects it.
summary: NMR effective porosity from CPMG data can be overestimated in clay-rich rocks because clay-bound water (CBW) signal leaks into effective porosity bins. Using synthetic echo trains with Gaussian noise (1 p.u.) and SVD inversion, the authors examine the effects of T2 bin range, noise and echo spacing TE (0.6, 0.9, 1.2 ms). With 12 p.u. CBW and 12 p.u. effective porosity, a 9-bin fit gave PHIE of 16.27 p.u., and 11 bins reduced but did not eliminate the leakage. Without noise, components down to about TE/7 can be resolved if the bin range is broad enough, but noise degrades short T2 components, so effective porosity depends on TE. A correction subtracts the CBW decay, reconstructed from a high-SNR 0.6 ms echo train, from the first 12 echoes of the 1.2 ms train before inversion. In simulations (500 sets, SNR=60), CBW was estimated within ±10% at 80% confidence.
abstract: Deriving accurate T2 relaxation spectra from nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) CPMG measurements is critical to the determination of total and effective porosities, irreducible water saturations, and permeability from NMR logs and core measurements. Accurate spectra are also essential to estimate coefficients for the film model or Spectral Bulk Volume Irreducible (SBVI) model. This paper analyzes the effects of noise, inadequate sampling rate, and CBW on the estimation of T2 distribution and effective porosity. Synthetic data were used so that it is easy to compare the results with underlying model inputs. A new method is described which utilizes the partial porosity distributions obtained from two echo trains acquired with different TEs. High signal-to-noise ratio echo data with sampling time TE of 0.6 ms are used to obtain the CBW T2 distribution. These data are then used to reconstruct CBW contributions to the time domain early echoes of the conventional effective porosity echo data (TE = 1.2ms). This residual signal is then subtracted from the original echoes. The effective porosity distribution is estimated from the reconstructed echo train.

title: Combination of NMR and Ultracentrifuge Techniques for Effective Carbonate Reservoir Characterization
tldr: NMR T2 spectra combined with centrifuge drainage and waterflood on carbonate cores indicate adsorption of heavy crude components in the largest pores, implying wettability alteration.
summary: The paper addresses detecting adsorption of heavy crude oil fractions and associated wettability alteration in carbonate reservoir rock. Six aged reservoir carbonate plugs, three clean carbonates, and Berea and Baker dolomite references were brine saturated, centrifuged to Swi (6000 RPM), oil saturated (16 mPa.s oil), aged at 82 °C, and waterflooded in the centrifuge, with NMR T2 measured at each step. Bulk oil mean T2 correlated with viscosity on a log-log line, and NMR porosity and Swi matched mass balance (e.g., sample R2 Swi 0.087 vs 0.083). Oil-saturated carbonates showed shorter T2 components than 100% water saturation, and waterflooded cores showed longer T2, with the shift inversely related to Swi. Produced oil spectra shifted to higher T2 and showed new long-T2 components, interpreted as heavy-component retention and possible in-situ upgrading; Baker dolomite and Berea showed much smaller effects.
abstract: The combination of NMR and Ultracentrifuge techniques provides an easy and fast way of estimating the physical properties of rock/fluid systems such as wettability and irreducible saturation, capillary pressure and pore size distribution, fluid distribution in porous media and relative permeability curves. In this work, an extensive experimental program was conducted for the characterization of pores from some carbonate reservoirs and outcrops. During the experimental procedure, the difference between the mechanisms of rock/fluid and fluid/fluid interactions in restored state and natural state core was evaluated. As a result of our investigation it is established that the performance procedures provide the qualitative indication of adsorption of the heavy components of oil on the pore surface. Adsorption of the heavy fractions on a pore surface can take place not only in reservoirs containing heavy oil but also in light oil reservoirs with low concentrations of heavy fractions as indicated by the analysis of the recovered oil. Adsorption of the heavy components seems to take place predominantly in the largest pores which contain thinner films of irreducible water. This conclusion is made in view of similar work on cores with variable petrophysical properties. Modern laboratory systems and procedures, including NMR and Ultracentrifuge, provide the opportunity to estimate the changes of the thermodynamic conditions in a reservoir, at which additional adsorption of heavy hydrocarbon will not take place. Moreover, the procedures used in this work can be directed to increasing the hydrocarbon recovery efficiency.

title: MR Laboratory Measurements: Requirements to Assure Successful Measurements That Will Enhance MRI Log Interpretation
caption: Figure 3: Initial Acauisition results showing an apparent uni-modal result. For fig. 3 - 7 bold solid = incremental T2, bold dashed = cumulative T2, light solid = previous incremental T2 and light dash = previous cumulative T2.
figure_reason: Initial acquisition with all parameters wrong gives misleading unimodal T2 result, illustrating the paper's central warning.
tldr: Provides guidelines for planning low-field NMR core measurements, from sample selection and desaturation to acquisition settings, and shows how lab T2 data calibrate BVI and permeability models for logs.
summary: The paper gives practical guidance for designing low-field MR laboratory projects that support MR log interpretation. It covers sample selection and preparation, brine saturation, a test sequence with brine-saturated and air-brine desaturated states at several interecho spacings, and choosing a desaturation pressure to represent BVI. A worked example shows how wait time, interecho spacing, pulsing time and signal-to-noise, if set wrongly, distort T2 distributions, for example turning a bimodal distribution into an apparent unimodal one. Examples interpret micropore/clay-bound water, internal gradients from Fe-bearing minerals, multiphase effects and wettability change. Lab data are used to calibrate cutoff T2 BVI models and permeability models (Straley average-T2, Coates FFI/BVI with slope 6.2 in the example), with strengths and weaknesses compared in a table.
abstract: Low field Magnetic Resonance (MR) laboratory measurements are performed to enhance the interpretation of MR logs. This is best accomplished when the laboratory project starts with a well designed set of objectives based on the desired down-hole tool applications. These objectives are achieved when procedures are listed step-by-step addressing key elements of the laboratory measurements that affect the outcome. The quality of the results is controlled by several factors from the type of sample, it's size, how it was selected and how it was prepared to the instrument settings, such as wait time (T,), the number of echoes, the interecho spacing (T,) and the signal-tonoise ratio. Without these preliminary steps required for proper data acquisition, enhancement andlor development of interpretive models becomes elusive. This paper addresses these issues providing guidance and methods to achieve quality measurements. Examples are presented that show how improper instrument settings can mislead interpretations, as well as, how laboratory measurements can be interpreted and used to enhance the interpretation of subsequent MR logs.

title: Capillary Pressure Scanning Curves by Direct Measurement of Saturation by
caption: Figure 10. Imbibition Pc for Berea plug.
figure_reason: Berea imbibition Pc data showing positive and negative portions crossing Pc=0 at Sw 62%.
tldr: Centrifuge-established saturation profiles, frozen in place with octadecane and mapped by MRI, give direct capillary pressure drainage and imbibition scanning curves for Berea sandstone and chalk.
summary: Conventional capillary pressure methods infer saturation indirectly or take weeks to months, so complete drainage-imbibition scanning curves are rarely reported. The authors centrifuged plugs with a free water level inside the plug, froze the octadecane phase, and imaged the remaining water by MRI, getting 105 to 133 saturation points per profile, calibrated against air-water weight saturations. Placing the free water level along the plug gave positive and negative Pc simultaneously. Berea imbibition crossed Pc=0 at Sw 62% and secondary drainage at 69%, suggesting slightly less water-wet behavior, and closure of the bounding curves was not achieved. Chalk imbibition and secondary drainage both crossed at 72% and overlaid with no hysteresis. Each equilibrium step took about 2 days for Berea and up to 12 days for chalk, giving total test times of about 16 days and 1.5 months.
abstract: There is relatively little literature reporting of water/oil capillary pressure data that include development of complete primary drainage, imbibition and secondary drainage curves. Major reasons for the lack of such data are the difficulty, expense and time to obtain them. Direct measurement of saturation profiles in plugs can significantly reduce these negatives. Saturation profiles for water/oil capillary pressures were established with the centrifuge and then locked in place by freezing the oil phase while still in the centrifuge. Magnetic resonance imaging was used to map the saturation profiles, obtaining over a hundred measurements per profile. Both positive and negative portions of the capillary pressure curve were obtained simultaneously by positioning the free water level along the length of the plug. Drainage or imbibition was achieved by centrifuging the plug under hydrocarbon or water by starting with the appropriate saturation state. The capillary pressure range was controlled by the speed of the centrifuge, the height above the free water level and the sample length. Comparisons of repeated measurements assured that an equilibrium saturation state was achieved. Measurements of bounding drainage and imbibition curves were made for two diverse rock types, Berea sandstone and reservoir chalk.

title: Calculation of Constituent Porosity in a Dual-Porosity Matrix: MRI and Image Analysis Integration
caption: Figure 3. Slice 3: intensity map in false colors (fig. 3a), and the effects of different threshold levels: threshold=0.16M0 max gives = 4.22 (figure 3b), threshold=0.21M0 max gives = 2.74 (fig. 3c)
figure_reason: Shows how threshold choice changes computed partial porosity (4.22% vs 2.74%), motivating the automatic method.
tldr: A software tool segments 2D MRI images of dolomite cores to separate vug and fracture porosity from matrix, with results agreeing with SEM at ~1 mm resolution.
summary: Conventional porosity measurements cannot separate vug and fracture porosity from matrix porosity, and thin-section SEM loses 3D information. The authors built an image analysis tool that statistically classifies pixels of MRI (multi-slice multi-echo CPMG, TE 4.8 ms) images into classes, from which a petrophysicist selects fracture and vug classes and shapes to compute constituent porosity. Nine water-saturated plugs (2 in x 3 in) from a fractured dolomite reservoir were imaged in eight 5 mm slices, with porosity calibrated against a reference sample. Manual thresholding was shown to be subjective: thresholds of 16% and 21% of maximum intensity changed partial porosity from 4.22% to 2.74%. MRI total and constituent porosities agreed reasonably with lab and SEM values for features of about 1 mm or larger, and T2 maps clearly showed the longest T2 in fractures; background noise could add up to 9% of the signal.
abstract: Fracture and vug porosity and permeability measurement still remain an open problem for core analysis labs. These data are of primary importance, mainly in carbonate reservoirs, for a correct simulation of the field performance in terms of stored hydrocarbon volume, fluid dynamics and matrix/fracture exchange. Conventional image analysis on core by scanning electron microscope (SEM) on thin sections does not retain the complete 3D information. Use of non-destructive imaging techniques such as CT X-ray and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) seems to be the more interesting approach to the problem. In this paper we present a proprietary software tool which allows the interactive processing and interpretation of 2D and 3D MRI of core. Currently MRI data are used in laboratory analysis, mainly for semi-quantitative description of core samples. We will highlight that MRI core data can be better and more cost effectively exploited if numerical processing and analysis are applied to gather quantitative information about petrophysical properties, namely porosity and permeability. We will present how numerical core analysis can be performed on 2D MRI data, by means of a software tool which is based on computerized image analysis and processing techniques. In particular, this tool can significantly contribute to the quantitative analysis of MRI data for calculating constituent porosity in a dual porosity matrix. Moreover, innovative modeling techniques are incorporated in the tool, in order to automatically segment core images, to separate different porosity contributions (vugs, fractures, microporosity or other). We will then show how these techniques can be directly applied to 3D MRI core data and discuss a case study.

title: Accuracy of Gas - Oil Relative Permeability from Two-Phase Flow Experiments
caption: Figure 2. Oil and gas relative permeability, from long core gas injection.
figure_reason: Shows oil and gas relative permeability from long-core gas injection at different rates, the key rate-dependence result.
tldr: Gas-oil relative permeability from long-core gas injection, constant pressure gradient and centrifuge drainage varies with Bond and capillary number, a dependence not explained by capillary end-effects alone.
summary: Gas-oil drainage relative permeability is often calculated neglecting capillary forces, and the resulting errors are rarely discussed. Berea and Bentheimer sandstone cores (about 100 to over 2,000 mD) were tested with three methods. These were long-core gravity-oriented gas injection at 0.85, 1.43 and 8 times the critical rate with X-ray saturation scanning, constant pressure gradient gas injection, and centrifuge drainage at 500-2500 rpm. Higher gas rate gave earlier breakthrough, a more dispersed front and higher gas relative permeability, while oil relative permeability changed less. In centrifuge tests oil kr rose with rpm (Bond number 1e-7 to 1e-3), with a critical Bond number of about 6e-5 to 1e-4 depending on permeability. Simulations including capillary pressure still gave different kro curves at 500 and 2500 rpm, so the variation is not only an end-effect. Covariance analysis showed kr is well defined except near the endpoint saturations.
abstract: Gas - oil relative permeability of sandstone cores has been derived from constant rate and constant pressure gradient displacements, and also from drainage experiments by centrifuge. The paper discusses results from these types of measurements and the accuracy of estimated relative permeabilities. The relative permeabilities have been calculated from analytical methods neglecting capillary forces and by simulations of the experiments including capillary effects. The relative permeability is found to vary with viscous - capillary force balance, and the changes in relative permeability cannot fully be explained by capillary end-effects.

title: Gas Injection and Heterogeneous Wettability: What Is the Relevant Information That Petrophysics Can Provide
caption: Figure 1: Oil recovery curves for three different core wettabilities.
figure_reason: Shows oil recovery curves for water-wet, oil-wet and heterogeneous packs, the key evidence of reduced sweep efficiency.
tldr: Gravity-assisted gas injection in water-wet, oil-wet and layered-wettability sandpacks shows an oil-wet stratum cuts recovery; simulations using homogeneous-core Kr and Pc reproduce the heterogeneous case.
summary: The paper examines how a decimetric wettability heterogeneity affects gas injection. Gravity-assisted secondary gas injection was run in ~50 cm long unconsolidated sandpacks (porosity ~0.35, permeability ~10 D): uniformly water-wet, uniformly oil-wet (silylated), and two water-wet sections separated by a 2 cm oil-wet layer, with 3-phase saturation profiles from dual-energy CT. Oil recovery was 86.8% OOIP (Sorg 11%) in water-wet, 74.8% (21%) in oil-wet and only 67.6% (24%) in the heterogeneous pack, because the oil-wet layer behaves like a fracture that isolates and traps oil in the upper water-wet part. History matching of homogeneous cases gave three-phase relative permeabilities, which together with centrifuge capillary pressures reproduced the heterogeneous recovery and gas profiles well. Omitting capillary pressure in the heterogeneous simulation gave a flat gas profile and poor recovery prediction.
abstract: The objective of the present paper is to look at the effect of small wettability heterogeneities (decimetric) on the phase distributions, recovery kinetics and sweep efficiency during a gas injection process. Secondary gas injection experiments have been performed in unconsolidated porous media of well controlled wettability: uniformly water-wet, uniformly oil-wet, and an heterogeneous sandpack consisting of two long water-wet parts separated by a 2 cm thick oil-wet stratum. 3-D saturation profiles of water, oil and gas were obtained with a dual energy CT scanner. The experiments were simulated using a reservoir simulator. In the uniform wettability cases, three-phase relative permeabilities as a function of the three fluids saturations were obtained by history matching of the recovery curves and the experimental saturation profiles. These relative permeabilities along with the corresponding capillary pressures were introduced into a simulator representing the heterogeneous structure. Both, experiments and simulations, demonstrated that wettability heterogeneities play a major role on the global efficiency of a gas injection by drastically affecting phase distributions and displacement mechanisms. It is also shown that relative permeabilities and capillary pressures for the homogeneous structures properly incorporated into a reservoir model, taking into account the geometric characteristics of the heterogeneity, describe very satisfactorily oil recovery and fluid distribution in the heterogeneous porous medium.

title: The Uniqueness and Accuracy of Porous Media Multiphase Properties Estimated from Displacement Experiments
caption: Figure 4: Number of runs vs. objective function value. a) Step 1-4 of spline expansion and the Corey representation. b) Step 5-8 of the spline expansion and the Chicrici representation.
figure_reason: Shows J versus runs for each estimation step against expected-value ellipses, illustrating the criteria being met by step 8.
tldr: Proposes chi-square and runs-test criteria to validate relative permeability estimates from displacement data; shows Corey and Chierici fits fail while adaptive B-splines pass.
summary: The paper addresses the ill-conditioned inverse problem of estimating relative permeability and capillary pressure from displacement experiments. It proposes two statistical criteria for accepting an estimate: the weighted least-squares objective J must be consistent with a chi-square distribution, and the number of runs in the residuals must lie within a confidence interval of m/2. In a simulated multirate unsteady-state drainage example (800 data points), Corey and Chierici fits gave J of about 20,000 and 1,500 against an expected value of about 800, and run counts of 132 and 316 against an expected 400, so both fail. A regression-based quadratic B-spline method, adding parameters stepwise, met the criteria at step 8, and linearized covariance analysis gave confidence bands containing the true curves. A second example shows that constant-rate production-only data with negligible capillary pressure determine only the ratio kro/krw, so the individual curves cannot be found.
abstract: Criteria are presented for validating estimates of relative permeability and capillary pressure functions from laboratory data. Examples are provided to show that methods used to calculate relative permeability from displacement data may provide inaccurate estimates when these criteria are not met.

title: Forty Comparisons of Mercury Injection Data with Oil/Water Capillary Pressure Measurements by the Porous Plate Technique
caption: Figure 2g
figure_reason: Shows DS correlating with clay content in shaly sandstones, a key finding.
tldr: Forty paired tests on adjacent samples show scaled mercury injection systematically underestimates irreducible water saturation versus reservoir-condition porous plate oil/brine drainage, with differences tied to heterogeneity, clay structure and carbonate mineralogy.
summary: The paper asks whether mercury injection can substitute for reservoir-condition oil/brine porous plate drainage capillary pressure. Forty tests on adjacent samples (25 sandstones, 15 carbonates; Gulf of Guinea and North Sea) compared water saturation at 4 bar oil/brine Pc (DS) and displacement pressure. Mercury injection always gave lower Swi, with DS from 0 to 30 %PV in sandstones and up to 0.28 in limestones. Equilibrium time, sample dispersion and compaction explained little of the difference. In sandstones DS rose with clay content, shale lamination/bioturbation, pore-access heterogeneity (SI) and cementation exponent, probably through brine trapping in 1D oil placement. Clean well-sorted sandstones matched, while in carbonates DS was larger for limestones and calcite-rich samples, suggesting a wettability effect.
abstract: Mercury injection is a relatively quick and low cost technique to obtain capillary pressure data. In this paper we address the following question : Can mercury injection data be used to properly estimate oil/water drainage capillary pressure curves representative of the reservoir ? This question has been discussed in several previous papers, but there is a relative scarcity of relevant experimental data. This paper presents results from forty comparative tests which have been conducted over several years on consolidated core samples originating from the Gulf of Guinea and the North Sea. Each test consisted in measuring capillary pressure by two different techniques on two adjacent samples. Mercury injection with capillary pressure values up to 1000 bars was used on one sample and a higher cost oil/brine porous plate technique was applied on the adjacent sample. This latter technique consisted in measuring capillary pressure with stock tank oil and brine under stress and temperature. The effective confining stress, the concentration of the brine and the temperature were chosen in order to be representative of reservoir conditions. Such measurements are assumed to be more representative of the actual reservoir oil/water drainage capillary pressure. Various lithologies were tested : 25 sandstones (either clean, laminated or bioturbated), 10 dolomites (non vuggy and vuggy), 5 limestones. The tested samples had a wide range of permeability and porosity values. Mercury injection data were scaled to oil/brine conditions with IFT values measured in the laboratory. Comparisons of these scaled data with the porous plate data were then conducted. Results show that mercury injection systematically underestimates water saturation when compared to oil/brine results in the high Pc region. The differences of water saturation between the two techniques were then analyzed per type of facies. This complete set of tests reveals some relationships between mercury injection data and oil/water capillary pressure measurements for oil reservoirs. Local heterogeneities (bioturbations, non-uniform pore access radius distribution, tortuosity) were found to be the main responsible factors to explain these differences in sandstone reservoirs. Oil wettability seems to play an important role in carbonates (especially for limestones). Some general trends, provided in the paper, can help the core analyst to correct its mercury injection data into more representative ones. However, more tests should be carried out to confirm and precise these relations and to point out new ones. Only such relations can justify the use of the low-cost mercury injection technique for Pc studies in oil reservoirs.

title: Analysis of Centrifuge Relative Permeability Data
caption: Figure 4 Absolute Differences Caused by Varying Parameters (Base Case)
figure_reason: Shows which experiment regions are sensitive to each fitting parameter in the base case, central to the findings.
tldr: Simulation of multi-speed centrifuge drainage shows wetting-phase exponents are well determined, non-wetting exponents poorly so, and capillary pressure should be fitted separately; ignoring speed ramp-up biases results.
summary: The paper simulates multi-speed centrifuge relative permeability experiments using Corey relative permeability and Bentsen capillary pressure curves with a finite-difference model including finite capillary pressure, non-uniform acceleration and finite non-wetting mobility. Grid-block number (N=40) and saturation-change time step (0.001) were chosen from convergence studies. Sensitivity tests with an assumed production error of 0.06 cm3 show the wetting exponent is determined accurately in all cases, while the non-wetting exponent is poorly determined unless non-wetting viscosity is high (error bar ±0.29 base case, ±2.59 at 0.01 cp). Capillary pressure parameters influence the whole experiment, and the wetting and non-wetting exponents influence different time regions after speed changes. History matching of random-error-corrupted data recovered exponents near 2.0, whereas ignoring a 1000 rpm/min ramp-up shifted the wetting exponent to 2.195. Recommendations are to compute capillary pressure separately, choose speeds near threshold pressure, weight early data after speed changes, and account for ramp-up.
abstract: AbstractThis paper presents a simulation study of the displacement process that occurs during a multi-speed, centrifuge relative permeability experiment. Using Corey-type relative permeability and Bentsen-type capillary pressure curves, with parameters typical of water-wet rocks, synthetic production data sets are generated for a simulated drainage experiment. The sensitivities of the production data to small changes in the parameters of the curves are then tested. By examining the deviation between the resultant production data and the original data, different regions of the experiment are identified with sensitivities to different parameters. The production data is then “corrupted” by adding random errors. The resulting data sets are history-matched to determine the best curve parameters, that is, the parameters that result in the least-square-error between the “corrupted” data and a new simulation. As a final test, a production data set which includes the effect of ramp-up is generated, then history-matched assuming that speeds change in an instantaneous manner.

title: Crude Oil/Brine Contact Angles on Quartz Glass
caption: Fig. 4 Contating angles for decane/PB brine/treated plates aged at high temperature.
figure_reason: Shows large advancing angle increases (to 150-170°) for quartz aged at high temperature, the key wetting-alteration result.
tldr: Wilhelmy plate contact angles on crude-oil-aged quartz glass vary with pH, aging time and temperature, oil composition and brine; porous media prove more water-wet than angles suggest.
summary: The study quantifies wetting alteration of quartz glass by adsorption from crude oils using dynamic Wilhelmy plate contact angles against decane under brine. Variables were brine pH (4-10) and NaCl molarity, aging time (1-500 h), aging temperature (room vs 88°C), oil composition (A'93, A'95, CS crudes and A'93 maltenes), measurement temperature, and synthetic reservoir brines with 10- and 100-fold dilutions. Aging at room temperature left plates water-wet (angles up to about 60°), whereas aging at 88°C in A'93 crude gave advancing angles of 150-170° beyond 96 h. The asphaltic crude altered wettability much more than its maltenes or the low-asphaltene CS oil. Advancing angles were lower at reservoir temperature and rose with brine dilution. Compared with imbibition and waterflood results in Berea and Aerolith cores, trends agreed qualitatively, but porous media appeared more water-wet than flat-quartz angles indicated.
abstract: The initial wettability of a reservoir is the result of complex interactions between the crude oil, the connate water, and the rock surfaces. Adsorption of heavy polar organic material, commonly identified with the asphaltenes in crude oil, is responsible for alteration of wetting properties of the rock. Measurements of contact angles provide a convenient and conceptually simple approach to quantification of the wettability given by oleic/aqueous liquid pairs at a smooth mineral surface. Flat quartz surfaces are often used as a representative surface for sandstones. This study reports changes in wetting induced by adsorption from crude oil on quartz glass by brine/crude oil pairs. Wilhelmy plate wettability measurements were made with either crude oil or a refined oil as the oleic phase. Wettability changes induced by an asphaltic crude oil were much greater than those given by its maltenes or by a crude oil with very low asphaltene content. Brine compositions included solutions of sodium chloride, three synthetic reservoir brines, and ten- and hundred-fold dilutions of the reservoir brines. Contact angles decreased with increase in brine concentration and with increasing temperature of measurement. Contact angle results are compared with changes of wettability in Berea sandstone and in synthetic cores exposed to brine and crude oils.

title: A Quality Control Program in Core Analysis
caption: Figure 1. Permeability measurements on selected samples at various labs.
figure_reason: Shows lab-to-lab permeability scatter on check plugs, especially at high permeability, the key consistency result.
tldr: Mobil's lab pre-qualification and data consistency program shows labs can reproduce check-plug porosity to ±0.3%, permeability to ±15% and grain density to ±0.01 g/cc.
summary: Mobil describes a core analysis QC program used since 1992 that has evaluated 30 labs on five continents. Labs measure porosity, permeability and grain density on circulated 3.8 cm check plugs (sandstones, limestones, ceramics, metal-encased composites) and undergo on-site inspection. Overburden pore volume porosity agreed within ±0.3%, grain density within ±0.01 g/cc, and permeability within ±10% below 1000 mD (±15% for labs good at high permeability). One lab was judged unqualified. Many labs could not measure permeability reliably above 2000 mD and only one recognized its limit. Repeat measurements at a second lab on about 5% of plugs exposed a permeability problem from screens clogged with fines in the loading pistons and a porosity error from incomplete pressure equilibration. Comparison with a database caught anomalous formation factors likely caused by incomplete saturation.
abstract: Mobil's core analysis quality control program has two major parts. The first is a lab evaluation that we use to pre-qualify labs in various areas of core analysis. The second is a consistency check of routine and special core analysis data. Routine property measurements are repeated on a sub-set of samples at a second lab. Special core analysis data are compared against a database of measurements on similar samples tested under similar conditions. Provided that consistent procedures are used, it is possible for most core analysis laboratories to reproduce measurements on high quality check plugs to +I- 0.3% in porosity, +I- 15% in permeability, and +I- O.Olg/cc in grain density. Some of the scatter remaining in the data appears to be systematic, and would probably be larger for plugs that are more irregular, smaller, or have lower porosity.

title: Centrifuge Data Analysis Techniques : An Sca Survey on the Calculation of Drainage Capillary Pressure Curves from Centrifuge Measurements
caption: Figure 12 : Additionnal error bar on saturation due to the interpretation process for the different solutions and different centrifuge / core geometries (B, N values).
figure_reason: Gives additional saturation error bars for each solution across centrifuge geometries, the survey's main practical result.
tldr: An SCA survey tests about 19 centrifuge capillary pressure interpretation solutions on ten synthetic datasets, finding geometry-dependent errors up to 10 saturation units and only a few reliable methods.
summary: The 1993 SCA centrifuge survey showed large scatter between laboratories, and it was unclear whether measurement or interpretation caused it. This survey gave 14 contributors ten synthetic centrifuge datasets, built from known Pc curves and varied core/centrifuge geometries (B, N parameters) with added experimental error. Contributors used 19 solutions (HB, DOM, Sα, Sαβ, RW, HER, spline, parameter estimation etc.), with and without radial correction, giving about 50 interpretations per case. Interpretation error depended mainly on geometry: for 1"x1" cores at 21.5 cm many solutions stayed within ±3 saturation units, but elsewhere errors of ±10 units were common. Most methods bias saturation negatively, so averaging methods does not help, and more rotation steps or lower measurement error did not help. Only SPL and Sαβ with radial correction and consistency constraints and proper numerical implementation kept errors near ±3 saturation units across geometries.
abstract: Fourteen contributions were received. Nineteen different solutions of the centrifuge problem were used, most of them with and without the radial correction. Data sets were interpreted close to 50 times, enough to produce a reliable statistical analysis of the error related to each solution in use (that is the error in addition to experimental error).

title: Resistivity measurements while centrifuging
caption: Figure 8 : Simulation of resistivity index vs local saturation at entry, local saturation at the electrodes level, and for mean saturation in thick slices centered at the electrodes level.(triangles : 36 mm, squares : 106 mm, diamonds : 240 mm thickness)
figure_reason: Simulated RI versus local and slice-mean saturation explains the curved experimental trend and the effective measured volume.
tldr: A centrifuge device with rotary contacts and radial four-electrode geometry measures resistivity index during capillary pressure drainage; simulation links curved RI-Sw trends to non-uniform saturation.
summary: The paper presents a light-weight centrifuge coreholder that records rock resistance during drainage using rotary electrical contacts and six radial electrodes pressed on the plug by a compression kit or heat-shrink casing. Tests used 23 mm diameter Fontainebleau and Vosges sandstones, then two North Sea reservoir samples, with Soltrol 130 oil and brine. The radial-to-longitudinal resistance ratio was 0.5, showing the measurement is less local than expected and integrates about half the sample volume. Resistivity index versus mean saturation was curved because of the saturation gradient; local saturations from Forbes' algorithm and a 40x20x20 grid simulation with Archie's law reproduced this shape, with n = 2 fitting Vosges sandstone end points. Reservoir samples gave higher n values, consistent with oil-wet or mixed-wet behavior.
abstract: Resistivity indices can be obtained during capillary pressure measurements using the porous plate or the membrane method. This paper describes an alternative method based on the centrifuge technique. The main idea is to use "rotary contacts" in order to record intensity and potential while centrifuging. In addition, a radial "four electrodes" setting is used. In such a way, resistivity is measured through a thick rock slice at the middle of the sample. Both techniques, rotary contact and radial electrode geometry, have already been used and tested for other purposes. Nevertheless, specific problems remained. Some were experimental: how to keep a good contact between the electrodes and the sample while minimizing the weight and volume of the device. This has been solved by an original (and patented) method that ensures both electrode pressure and sealing of the lateral face of the sample. The second kind of problem met was the non-uniformity of the saturation due to the centrifugation process. A simulation of the resistivity index values depending on local or mean saturations is proposed. In the calculation, the local saturation is derived from the local capillary pressure curve (Forbes'method). The conclusion of this study is that reliable resistivity indices and Pc curves can be simultaneously obtained by centrifuge measurements. Application to reservoir rocks is begun.

title: Full Imbibition Capillary Pressure Measurements on Preserved Samples Using the Micropore Membrane Technique
caption: Figure 5: Full imbibition curves for 3 plugs extracted from the same preserved core. The plug 1 curve (square) was obtained under non-equilibrium conditions. For this plug, various tests were performed to test the reliability of the measurements. Curve for plug 2: triangle. Curve for plug 3 (circle) is rescaled to crude oil/brine IFT value.
figure_reason: Shows full imbibition curves for the three plugs, including the non-equilibrium plug 1, the main result.
tldr: Full imbibition capillary pressure curves were measured on preserved North Sea sandstone plugs with micropore membranes; exponential production fitting gives an equilibrium criterion, and premature steps bias Sor by about 6 saturation units.
summary: Full imbibition capillary pressure curves are needed to assess waterflooding in non-strongly water-wet reservoirs. The authors measured them with the CAPWET micropore membrane apparatus on three thin plugs (about 39.5 mm diameter, 24 mm long) from a preserved Rannoch sandstone core, using only oil and water flooding to resaturate and no cleaning or ageing. A capacitance level detector resolves about 0.01 cc of produced brine. The curves had nearly vertical positive parts and most saturation change in one negative step (about -10 to -80 mBar), indicating intermediate wettability. An inadequate equilibrium criterion on plug 1 gave a 1-Sor about 6 units lower than companion plug 2 (70 vs 76%). Fitting each pressure step with P = Pex(1 - exp(-t/tc)) and stepping at t = 4tc gives a non-empirical equilibrium criterion. Waxy crude may have plugged the membrane, so refined oil is recommended when temperatures above 40°C cannot be used.
abstract: The determination of the full imbibition capillary pressure curve is essential to evaluate the potential of water flooding of reservoirs that are not strongly water wet. We show how the positive and negative parts of the imbibition capillary pressure curve can be measured using preserved samples without an ageing procedure. The micropore membrane technique (CAPWET) is used on thin samples extracted from a full size reservoir core. A simple procedure is performed to resaturate the sample after drilling in the laboratory. Drainage and imbibition capillary pressure experiments were performed on three samples from the same core using both refined and crude oil. The experiments were conducted by imposing successive pressure steps across the sample and the two water-wet and oil-wet membranes. Cumulative volume of water expelled or entering the sample is measured using a capacitive based detector. Due to the oil-wetting nature of the porous medium, capillary equilibrium is achieved only over very long periods of time. Equilibrium criterion based on a maximum flowrate are inadequate because the volume resolution ( $<0.01\text{ cc}$ ) required is very small. Observations from this work suggest that true equilibrium at each pressure step is required to reach a representative residual oil saturation (Sor). It is shown that production data can be fitted with exponential functions leading to a characteristic time and the asymptotic production for each pressure step. This leads to a simple criterion to find the experimental time required to insure capillary equilibrium. A lack of equilibrium can lead to an overestimation of the residual oil saturation by as much as 6 saturation units.

title: An Integrated Petrophysical Tool Measurements and Data Interpretation
caption: Fig. 6- Primary drainage Pc curves for sample #1 and #2: Average and local saturation and comparison with centrifuge data
figure_reason: Primary drainage Pc curves with average and local saturation, compared against centrifuge data for both samples.
tldr: An integrated tool based on semi-dynamic steady-state injection measures the full Pc cycle, resistivity index and partial Kr on one sandstone sample, matching standard methods for one sample.
summary: The paper presents the Integrated Petrophysical Tool (IPT), an extension of the semi-dynamic capillary pressure method, to measure the complete Pc cycle, resistivity index and parts of the Kr curves in a single experiment. A modified Hassler cell with six pressure taps and electrodes is used, with local saturations calculated from effluent production by an analytical (Ramakrishnan) and numerical 1D approach. Two water-wet reservoir sandstones (porosity 0.22, permeability about 0.125 and 1.19 darcy) were tested at room conditions with Soltrol and brine, in about 30 steps over roughly four weeks. Kr agreed with standard steady-state results and Pc with centrifuge data for sample 1, but Pc was too low for the high-permeability sample 2, likely due to pressure sensor accuracy. Formation factors were 18.9 and 17 (m of 1.94 and 1.90), and resistivity index gave a saturation exponent near 2 using four-electrode local potentials. Main error sources were leaks, dead volumes and pore volume determination, which affect effluent measurement.
abstract: The Integrated Petrophysical Tool (IPT) is derived from the semi-dynamic method for capillary pressure measurement presented at the 1993 and 1995 Society of Core analysis meetings. The IPT simultaneously measures the following properties : complete oil/water capillary pressure cycle, resistivity index, end-points and parts of the relative permeability curves. The paper describes the methodology used to acquire and to interpret the data. Examples are given for two reservoir samples. The IPT is based on the steady-state injection of one fluid through the sample placed in a modified "Hassler" cell, equiped with pressure taps and electrodes. Local saturations are not measured but calculated from the effluent production using a combined analytical and numerical method. Measurements were performed at room condition with oil (Soltrol) and brine on sandstone reservoir cores. The whole cycle consisted in about 30 steps at various oil or water flow rates and took about four weeks for a 120 mD sample (1st drainage, positive and negative imbibition, 2nd drainage). Relative permeabilities agree with standard steady-state measurements and capillary pressures with centrifuge results for one sample. There is no comparison for resistivity index, but the results are in agreement with literature data. The main technical difficulty is the need for accurate determination of effluent production. For this purpose, several improvements are proposed. In conclusion, the Integrated Petrophysical Tool is as accurate as standard methods but has the advantage to provide the various parameters on the same sample and during a single experiment.

title: An Improved Model for Relative Permeability and Capillary Pressure Incorporating Wettability
caption: Figure 5. Water-oil relative permeability model-data comparison.
figure_reason: Compares model predictions with measured Berea relative permeability for imbibition and drainage, the only validation of the model.
tldr: A log-normal pore-size model links capillary pressure, relative permeability, USBM and Amott-Harvey wettability indices consistently, and is checked against Berea relative permeability data.
summary: Capillary pressure, relative permeability, residual saturations and wettability are usually measured separately and are often inconsistent. The authors build an integrated model that assumes a log-normal pore/throat size distribution for the free pore volume. It gives analytical capillary pressure curves for primary imbibition and secondary drainage, from which USBM and Amott-Harvey indices follow. Corey-Burdine integrals then give relative permeability for each segment. Sample calculations with USBM indices from 0.477 to -0.046 show that relative permeability hysteresis grows with capillary hysteresis, and that the kro-krw crossover moves left as the system becomes less water-wet. Predictions were compared with NIPER data on a 260-mD fired Berea (sigma=1.3, mean Pc=2.5 psi), with adjusted end points: the model matched the measured crossover points and the lower drainage krw. Capillary pressure curves could not be compared for lack of data.
abstract: Pore sizes, pore structures, relative permeability, capillary pressure, and wettability are measured as part of special core analysis. Inconsistency among measurements sometimes occurs because, for example, residual fluid saturations are different in different experiments, and preferential wettability changes during laboratory handling, experimentation, and core restoration. Furthermore, it is expensive to conduct different experiments that duplicate information on the same porous media. This memorandum presents a model that integrates relative permeabilities, capillary pressure, wettability indices, and pore size distribution in a consistent manner. The model has the potential to be used in reservoir simulations to populate unmeasured rock-fluid properties based on limited measurements. It can be used for relative permeability and capillary pressure scaling up. In near future, we will fine-tune the model with measurements and published data. We will then extend the model to incorporate lithological data and core-level parameters such as absolute permeability, porosity, residual saturations, and end-point permeabilities.

title: Computer simulation of Special Core Analysis (SCAL) flow experiments shared on the Internet
tldr: Describes SCORES, a web-accessible Shell simulator for unsteady-state, steady-state and centrifuge SCAL experiments, and how history matching resolves relative permeability and capillary pressure interference.
summary: Capillary end-effects and the interference between relative permeability and capillary pressure can bias SCAL results, with residual oil saturation overestimated by up to about 10 saturation units. Shell developed SCORES, a 1-D simplified version of its MoReS reservoir simulator, offered free through a WWW interface that returns results by e-mail as spreadsheets. The paper details the gridding, entrance/exit blocks, fluid inputs and outputs for USS, steady-state and centrifuge (including footbath, RPM table and gravity handling) experiments. It explains that raw JBN or Hassler-Brunner relative permeabilities reproduce production with zero capillary pressure (a 'trivial match') but not saturation profiles. The authors recommend history matching a (U)SS run, a single-speed centrifuge run and a multi-speed centrifuge run with one consistent relative permeability and capillary pressure data set.
abstract: Measurement artefacts due to the interference of relative permeability and capillary pressure (as will occur in any SCAL flow measurement) may lead to residual oil saturations that are 10 saturation units higher than the true residual oil saturation. Simulations of the experiments have proved to be an excellent tool to unravel that interference. Also, simulation of SCAL flow experiments has been very successful for a reconciliation of seemingly contradicting results that may come out of different flow experiments on the same core plug. Therefore, there is significant business value in interpretation by simulation. The simulation technology as applied on the scale of oil and gas reservoirs is well advanced, but the application of simulations on the scale of the core plug is still relatively immature. SIEP - RTS is investigating how Shell developed SCAL simulation technology could be shared with the industry, as a contribution to the advancement of SCAL measurement technology. This paper will discuss in detail the capabilities of a full-fledged SCAL flow simulator that, as a pilot test, has been made available through WWW pages on the Internet. The simulations are provided free of charge. The three major experimental techniques, i.e. the UnSteady State (or Welge) technique, the Steady-State and the Centrifuge technique, are handled with one common "look and feel". The WWW interface has been designed to require a minimum of user input and to provide a detailed report of the evolution in time of water and oil production, pressure drop and saturation profile. The results of the simulation are E-mailed back to the user in the form of a spreadsheet.

title: Petrographic Image Analysis for Prediction of Petrophysical Properties and Waterflood Displacement Efficiency: Some Missing Links
caption: Figure 1. Initial water saturation determined by several methods on suites of samples from the same reservoir but from two different producing intervals. Samples from both intervals had approximately the same porosity and, in the case of the mercury capillary pressure, centrifuge and air-brine capillary pressure, were tested to similar maximum capillary pressures.
figure_reason: Shows Swi from several test methods on samples from two intervals, illustrating core-test variability that motivates PIA.
tldr: Reviews petrographic image analysis of 2-d thin sections for predicting porosity, permeability, capillary pressure, Swi and Sor, showing pore size and shape govern these properties.
summary: The paper reviews Petrographic Image Analysis (PIA), which quantifies 2-d pore geometry in epoxy-impregnated thin sections using erosion-dilation and Q-mode factor analysis to define pore types, then regresses them against core-test properties. Although throats cannot be seen in 2-d, permeability and drainage capillary pressure can be predicted, attributed to the correlation between pore and throat sizes. An empirical permeability model using porosity and the largest inscribed circle diameters gave R² of 0.90. For two sandstone reservoirs (North American and North Sea), pore-type models explained 72% and 73% of Swi variation and 64% and 79% of Sor variation. Swi rises with the volume of small pores, while Sor increases with pore non-uniformity and decreasing connectivity. PIA requires a training set of tested samples and supplements rather than replaces core testing.
abstract: PIA is a method used to quantify the two dimensional aspects of pore geometry comprehensively and rapidly and, using statistical techniques, to identify those pore types or attributes which are the best predictors of petrophysical properties of interest. Pore types, once identified, are used to predict petrophysical properties where core test data are not available. PIA provides the most effective method available for understanding how specific rockpore attributes affect fluid flow and displacement processes. PIA also has applications in predicting petrophysical properties of interest in samples too small for conventional core testing, for example drill cuttings or core rubble. This presentation is restricted to a review of the applications of PIA to prediction of porosity, permeability, drainage capillary pressure, initial water saturation (Swi) and waterflood residual oil saturation (Sor). Throat sizes cannot be identified or measured on 2-d surfaces through porous rocks and, since permeability and drainage capillary pressure are primarily affected by throat size, it is surprising that these properties can be successfully estimated by PIA. Part of the explanation rests with the pervasive correlation between pore sizes and connecting throat sizes in porous rocks. The reasons for these relationships are not yet understood. PIA results indicate that specific size and shape characteristics of pore types have strong effects on permeability, drainage capillary pressure, Swi and Sor and that the necessary information to predict these properties is contained on 2-d sections of reservoir rock.

title: Determination of Saturation Functions of Tight Core Samples Based on Measured Saturation Profiles
caption: Fig. 5. Measured data. kro is approximated Fig. 6. Measured data. Calculated pc comby a polynomial of order three. pared to pc from Hg injection.
figure_reason: Shows measured drainage kro and capillary pressure for chalk M113, compared against mercury injection data.
tldr: Uses capillary end-effect saturation profiles measured by 1D NMR, with parameter estimation and Killough scanning, to derive drainage and imbibition relative permeability and capillary pressure in tight chalk.
summary: Strong capillary end effects in low-permeability cores are exploited rather than avoided to determine relative permeability and capillary pressure. Steady-state saturation profiles from 1D NMR (4.7 T, 0.4 mm resolution) and total pressure drop are fitted by non-linear least squares, with threshold pressure included in the objective function. Reversing the flow direction shifts the end effect and creates an intrinsic imbibition process, handled with Killough scanning curves and Land trapping. The method reproduced synthetic input functions from an ECLIPSE-simulated drainage case. On a water-wet Maastrichtian chalk plug (M113, 26.36% porosity, 0.70 mD) the drainage kro and Pc were obtained; the Pc plateau was at significantly different pressure from scaled mercury injection data. Simulations showed that the hump in the reversed-flood profile results from scanning behavior, while the imbibition parameter estimation remains to be demonstrated.
abstract: The end effect of displacement experiments on low permeable porous media is used for determination of relative permeability functions and capillary pressure functions. Saturation functions for a drainage process are determined from a primary drainage experiment. A reversal of the flooding direction creates an intrinsic imbibition process in the sample, which enables determination of imbibition saturation functions. The saturation functions are determined by a parameter estimation technique. Scanning effects are modelled by the method of Killough. Saturation profiles are determined by NMR.

title: 2D-Imaging of the Effects from Fractures on Oil Recovery in Larger Blocks of Chalk
caption: Fig. 4. Second waterflood on fractured Block CHP-4.
figure_reason: Saturation map sequence for waterflood of fractured block CHP-4 showing flow redirected by fractures and gravity segregation.
tldr: 2-D 22Na tracer imaging of waterfloods in whole and fractured water-wet chalk blocks shows fractures redirect flow but leave oil recovery essentially unchanged.
summary: The study examines how fractures affect waterflood flow paths and oil recovery in large (about 20 x 12 x 5 cm) strongly water-wet outcrop chalk blocks from Rørdal and Dania, Denmark. Brine saturation was mapped in 2-D by gamma emission from 22Na-labeled brine on a 2 cm grid, before and after sawing the blocks to create open and 'closed' vertical and horizontal fractures. Whole blocks at low initial water saturation showed a dispersed water front, whereas higher Swi gave uniform saturation increase. In fractured blocks, brine did not cross a fracture until the upstream matrix was near final water saturation, and gravity segregation occurred in the open fracture. Oil recovery was similar for whole and fractured blocks (e.g. 62 vs 60 %OIP for CHP-6), and results were unaffected by fracture roughness or by constant rate versus constant pressure flooding, with good repeatability.
abstract: The effect of fractures on the movement and recovery of hydrocarbons from large blocks of strongly water-wet chalk has been studied in the laboratory using 2-D nuclear tracer saturation imaging. The objectives of the experiments were to study the impact of fractures on fluid flow mechanisms, total oil recovery, distribution of residual oil and to evaluate the effect of capillary continuity across the fractures. Tracking the water flow paths in constant pressure and constant rate waterfloods on whole and then fractured chalk blocks showed that brine imbibition of the whole block occurred as a gradual uniform increase in brine saturation throughout the block with high initial water saturation, while frontal advancement of a water bank was observed with lower initial water saturation. The fractures in the blocks impeded and redirected the flow of water but total oil recovery was similar for fractured and unfractured blocks. In general, no fracture was crossed until the preceding matrix was nearly at final water saturation. Gravity segregation of fluids in open fractures was identified and had a significant impact on the flow pattern. Repeatability of the waterflood in the fractured blocks was very good.

title: Core Sample Permeability Estimation Using Statistical Image Analysis
caption: Figure 5. Permeability predictions from individual image data within the 95% confidence region: (a) Model IV; (b) Correlation of Berryman and Blair (1986).
figure_reason: Compares image-based permeability predictions of Model IV and Berryman-Blair against measured core permeability.
tldr: Permeability is predicted from 2-D BSE image porosity and autocorrelation integral scale via a power-law model; about 10-40 images per sample suffice.
summary: The paper develops a phenomenological permeability model, k = A<phi>^B<I>^C, using average image porosity and the integral scale of the autocorrelation function from 2-D back-scatter SEM images. It was calibrated on 14 core samples from four Western Canadian formations (about 60 images each, permeability spanning three orders of magnitude). Image porosity and ACF integral scale were found to be independent, supporting the two-parameter form. The model performed better than the Berryman-Blair Kozeny-Carman approach, which suffers from magnification-dependent specific surface area, and predicted permeabilities of Coskun and Wardlaw's sandstones well. Monte Carlo trials showed the effective permeability estimate is least sensitive to image count, with little gain beyond about 40 images.
abstract: The statistical description of pore space seen in a 2-D section has been successfully applied for the characterization of the pore structure of different types of porous media using 1) the optical porosity and 2) the spatial distribution of porosity, which can be described by the autocorrelation function(ACF) of pore space seen in 2-D space. Statistics obtained from images include the image porosity, specific surface area, and a length scale obtained from the integral of the image autocorrelation function. The number of images required to predict the permeability of a core sample accurately, using the porosity(\$,) and the integral scale of the autocorrelation function for an image (Ii), is adressed in this paper. The following phenon~enological permeability model was found to describe the behavior of many samples: $$k = A \langle \phi_i \rangle^B \langle I_i \rangle^C$$ where k is the predicted absolute permeability of the sample, <\$,> and < Ii> are the average porositv and average integral scale of ACF of all images respectively, while A, B, and C are parameter values determined by fitting experimentally determined permeabllities of tested core samples. The proposed correlation accounts not only for reservoir porosity, but also the pore structure characteristics of the medium as determined from statistics of 2-D images. The proposed form of permeability correlation is more robust than other similar methods. Furthermore, at least 10 randomly taken images from a section are required to make a reasonable estimate of the permeability of a core sample. The permeability distribution at the scale of 512 by 512 pixels with 1.5 microns resolution can be estimated using Monte Carlo trials if the number of images taken for any given sample is 40 or greater.

title: High Resolution Laboratory X-Ray Tomography on Rocks
caption: Figures 24 and 25: Grey level histograms of samples CAR1 and CAR4
figure_reason: Grey-level histograms of CAR1 and CAR4 with deconvoluted peaks underpin the quantitative porosity and mineral fraction results.
tldr: An electron microprobe is converted into an X-ray microtomograph with about 10 µm 3D resolution, used to image pore networks and minerals in sandstones, explaining permeability differences.
summary: The authors convert an electron microprobe into a laboratory X-ray microtomograph, using a focused electron beam on a niobium thin target as a point source, with a rotating specimen and CCD detector. Radiographic resolution reaches 2 µm, and 256³ reconstructions from 120 projections at 3° steps give better than 10 µm resolution. Tests on glass beads in a capillary, Fontainebleau sandstone and three Brent sandstone samples (CAR1, CAR3, CAR4) were compared with SEM images, showing reliable reconstruction of surface morphology. Grey-level histogram deconvolution gave total pore-plus-clay fractions in agreement with global measurements (e.g., 29 vs 28% for CAR1). CAR1 has large, poorly connected macropores, explaining its lower permeability, while CAR3 and CAR4 have well-connected macropores. Feldspars can be segmented, but kaolinite cannot be reliably separated because its absorption is close to quartz and its size is near the resolution limit.
abstract: Conversion of a standard electron microprobe for use as an X-ray microtomograph is described. Only minor modifications are required, indeed several of the utilities of the microprobe can be used to ensure high resolution radiography and tomography. The impact of the focalized electron beam on a thin film is used to form a " point " X-ray source. This system is capable of 2 micron resolution radiographic imaging. A specimen rotation mechanism allows multiple radiograph acquisition and tomographic reconstruction of the specimen texture. Tomographic resolution depends on the number of acquired radiographs, better than 10 micron resolution in three directions having been demonstrated for 256 x 256 x 256 tomographs reconstructed from 120 radiographs at 3° intervals on small objects. System performance was evaluated by analysis of model and real reservoir rock: glass spheres in a capillary tube, Fontainebleau sandstone and Alwyn sandstone containing quartz, feldpars, and a large amount of kaolinite. Comparison with scanning electron micrographs shows reliable reconstruction of external morphology and helps for identification of minerals. The internal pore structure of the sample and the 3D-distribution of a particular phase can be studied a posteriori using the tomography data. Both are useful for the understanding of the macroscopic behavior of the rock in terms of petrophysical properties and wettability.

title: A Novel Study of the Dielectric Dispersion in Porous Media in the Frequency Range 10 Hz to 10 MHz
caption: Figure 5: Dielectric constant versus frequency for simulated sand-packs with different clay content saturated with 20 000 ppm NaCl brine.
figure_reason: Shows dielectric constant versus frequency scaling with clay content, supporting the double-layer polarization conclusion.
tldr: Two- and four-electrode impedance measurements from 10 Hz to 10 MHz introduce a reactivity index exponent for saturation and show double-layer polarization controls clay-dependent dielectric dispersion.
summary: The paper measures complex impedance of partially saturated Berea sandstone, tight-gas sands and Ottawa sand-bentonite packs (n-decane/NaCl brine) from 10 Hz to 10 MHz using two- and four-electrode setups. The Archie saturation exponent n is about 2.1 below 100 kHz but decreases at higher frequencies. A reactivity index exponent n* (from reactance ratios) is defined, with values of 3.5 at 10 kHz and 3.1 at 0.5 MHz for Berea, and for frequencies below 0.1 MHz it follows n* = 2n − p. n* can estimate saturation above 0.1 MHz where n fails. A generalized Maxwell-Wagner double-layer model shows dielectric constant scales roughly linearly with clay fraction, confirmed by tight-gas-sand data, implying double-layer polarization dominates dispersion.
abstract: Two and four-electrode setups have been developed to measure the complex impedance of partially saturated Berea sandstone, tight-gas-sand rocks, and Ottawa sand-bentonite mixtures saturated with n-decane and NaCl brine solutions. The effects of water saturation, clay content, and frequency on both the real and imaginary parts of the rock impedance are investigated between 10 Hz and 10 MHz. A reactivity index exponent (analogous to the resistivity index exponent) is defined and shown to be related to the water saturation by an Archie-type relation. A linear relationship between the resistivity index exponent and the reactivity index exponent has been observed experimentally at frequencies below 0.1 MHz, and has been deduced algebraically as well. The reactivity index exponent can be used to estimate water saturations at frequencies above 0.1 MHz where the resistivity index exponent is found to be inadequate. A generalized Maxwell-Wagner model, that accounts for double layer dielectric dispersion, is used to explain the experimentally observed trends. As the clay fraction is increased by a factor of 2, the dielectric constant of a simulated sand pack is found to increase by approximately the same factor at almost all frequencies from 10 Hz to 10 MHz. This linear dependence between rock dielectric constant and clay percentage has also been observed with the two-electrode data for tight-gas-sand samples of similar porosities and permeabilities. These results show the dominant effect of double layer polarization as a mechanism of dielectric dispersion in porous media in the range of 10 Hz to 10 MHz.

title: Prediction of Electrical and Flow Properties of Reservoir Rocks of Varying Wettability Characteristics
caption: Fig.7 Effect of Coordination Number on Resistivity Index Curve
figure_reason: Shows resistivity index sensitivity to coordination number, the most influential model parameter.
tldr: A pore-network model with triangular throats, corner and film flow predicts resistivity index and relative permeability for water-, mixed- and oil-wet rocks, and is most sensitive to coordination number.
summary: The paper presents a network model of spherical pore bodies and triangular pore throats that includes corner and thin-film transport, to predict resistivity index and relative permeability as a function of wettability. Effective medium theory and Bethe-tree accessibility give network conductances, and pore size distributions come from mercury injection data. Film thickness follows a measured disjoining pressure isotherm. For sandstone sample S-28, parameters were optimized against measured porosity, permeability and formation factor (0.297, 5200 md, 9.17), giving predicted values of 0.298, 5080 md and 9.13. Sensitivity analysis shows the strongest influence from coordination number, then shape factor and the throat length parameters C and alpha. Water in corners and films strongly affects resistivity index but has little effect on relative permeability, and the relative permeability predictions need further improvement.
abstract: A model for predicting the resistivity and relative permeability behavior of reservoir rocks samples is presented, in which the porous media is represented as a network of pore bodies and pore throats. Pore throats are modeled as tubes of triangular cross-section such that the contribution of corners and thin films to the electrical and fluid transport is conveniently included, in addition to the primary network transport. Mathematical formulations for the electrical and fluid transport in individual tubes containing one and two fluid phases are incorporated in the model. Pore size distribution functions interpreted from mercury injection capillary pressure curves are used and the effect of intrinsic wettability of the sample on the electrical resistivity and relative permeability to wetting and non-wetting fluids is studied by varying the film thickness according to the measured disjoining pressure isotherm. Sensitivity analysis indicates that model predictions are very sensitive to the coordination number, the shape factor and the parameters relating pore length to its cross-section area. According to the model predictions, wettability plays a critical role in determining the electrical and fluid transport in reservoir rocks and the apparent wettability of sample may be different from the intrinsic wettability. Model predictions are in reasonable agreement with the measured resistivity index vs. saturation data.

title: Log Interpretation Parameters Determined from Chemistry, Mineralogy and Nuclear Forward Modeling
caption: Figure 2. Relationship between aluminum and total clay shows a very tight linear relationship.
figure_reason: Shows tight linear aluminum-total clay relationship (r=0.98), the paper's central result.
tldr: Core FT-IR mineralogy, geochemistry and nuclear forward modeling show clay, sigma matrix, neutron porosity and hydrogen index correlate better with aluminum than gamma ray in two wells.
summary: Log interpretation parameters such as clay volume are often scaled arbitrarily from gamma ray ranges. Core plugs from a European well and a Texas gas well were analyzed by dual-range FT-IR mineralogy (±2 wt%) and extensive elemental chemistry, then used with SNUPAR-based nuclear forward modeling to compute gamma ray, sigma matrix, neutron porosity and hydrogen index. In the European well, clay correlated with aluminum at r=0.98 (standard error 2.6 wt%), versus r=0.86 (8.7 wt%) for gamma ray and r=0.95 for neutron-density separation. Sigma matrix, matrix neutron response and hydrogen index also correlated better with Al than with gamma ray. In the Texas well, gamma ray scaled 0-60% clay gave ~20 wt% errors, and the Bhuyan-Passey approach missed sands at 3600-3700 and 4950 ft affected by volcanic ash, while Al-derived clay did not. Regression parameters are tabulated for both wells.
abstract: The determination of suitable parameters to properly interpret log data in terms of porosity, clay content and water saturation is often arduous. For example, classical estimates of clay volume frequently use the range of observed gamma ray values over a depth interval as a clay calibration. An improved procedure presented here integrates core mineralogy and chemistry as well as nuclear forward modeling. Accurate mineralogy ( $\pm 2$ wt %) from the Dual-Range Fourier Transform Infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy procedure is used. The chemical element analysis includes not only the major compositional elements but also all trace and minor elements that can significantly influence log responses. The chemical and mineralogical data are then used with nuclear forward modeling to provide the log response of logging sondes such as gamma ray, matrix density, hydrogen index, photoelectric absorption cross section, and thermal and epithermal neutron responses. It is then usually straightforward to see simple relationships between available logging variables and desired parameters. Data from two example wells show that total clay content is linearly correlated with aluminum (Al). This is particularly useful since simulated aluminum concentration logs can be obtained in both open- and cased-hole environments from induced gamma ray spectroscopy sondes. With classical gamma ray interpretation, several reservoir intervals would be overlooked due to moderately high gamma ray levels. These same intervals have low aluminum concentrations. Thermal neutron porosity is close to total porosity only in the cleanest intervals. A simple relationship is observed between aluminum and the modeled thermal neutron porosity response. The Al-corrected neutron porosity agrees well with core porosity. The thermal neutron capture cross section, sigma matrix, also correlates linearly with aluminum. Most important logging parameters are demonstrated to be simply related to clay content and thus to aluminum. This integration of chemistry, mineralogy and nuclear response data is an efficient way of providing necessary parameters for accurate log interpretation.

title: A Novel Laboratory Technique to Determine the Saturation Status of Shale
caption: Fig. 3 - Volume of Water Absorbed vs. Bulk Volume Expansion for North Sea Shale
figure_reason: Shows North Sea shale water absorbed vs bulk volume expansion, including drying data, demonstrating saturated behavior on the 1:1 line.
tldr: Compares water uptake with bulk volume change after humidity hydration to tell whether shale is saturated; finds restoring altered shale does not restore its swelling behavior.
summary: Shale cores that lose moisture during retrieval or storage develop capillary voids that alter their mechanical and physico-chemical properties, so their saturation state must be checked before testing. The authors propose comparing water absorbed with bulk volume expansion (Archimedes immersion in LVT-200 oil) after hydrating samples in controlled-humidity desiccators with saturated salt solutions for 7-10 days. Saturated shale plots on the 1:1 line, while unsaturated shale falls above it. The stored Alaska shale absorbed 0.13 cc of water but expanded only 0.10 cc at 84% RH (unsaturated). The freshly cored North Sea shale, preserved in non-aqueous base fluid, absorbed 0.25 cc and expanded 0.25 cc (saturated). Drying removed moisture without a matching volume loss, creating voids. Slightly altered samples (84% to 92% RH) nearly recovered their moisture content and volume when restored, but strongly altered ones did not. Even restored shales swelled more in KCl than native shale, indicating irreversible matrix changes.
abstract: Drilling for oil and gas is concentrated in sedimentary basins of which 60% of the formations are shales. Worldwide drilling records indicate that most borehole instability occurs while drilling shaley formations. Study of shale core behavior in the laboratory is the prime method for obtaining information for instability control. However, subsurface shale cores are usually highly altered and thus not suitable for laboratory studies. Results obtained using the saturation technique for one saturated and one unsaturated core are presented. The field handling technique recommended for acquiring and storing shale is also presented.

title: Dual-Range FT-IR Mineralogy and the Analysis of Sedimentary Formations
caption: Figure 6. Measured elemental concentrations compared with concentrations reconstructed from the FT-IR mineralogy and the end-member concentrations in Table 2. The solid line is a 1:1 line. The agreement shows the accuracy of the FT-IR mineralogy.
figure_reason: Measured versus FT-IR-reconstructed elemental concentrations on a 1:1 line validate the mineralogy accuracy.
tldr: Combining mid- and far-IR spectra with an expanded standards set improves quantitative FT-IR mineralogy of oilfield samples, validated by reconstructing measured elemental chemistry to about ±1 wt%.
summary: Quantitative FT-IR mineralogy was extended to handle natural variability in oilfield samples after more than 1000 analyses. The new procedure merges mid-IR and far-IR spectra (300-5200 cm-1), matches KBr blank scattering, optimizes spectral offset, applies wavelet-based weighting, and uses end-member feldspar standards. The standards set grew from 14 to 29 minerals (49 species). Re-analysis of the earlier artificial-mixture test set showed that adding far-IR and the expanded standards reduced errors for most minerals (e.g. illite 2.6 to 1.6 wt%, calcite 1.8 to 1.0 wt%), with accuracy about ±1 wt% for most. For 45 samples from a European well, elemental concentrations reconstructed from mineralogy matched measured Si, Ca, K and Mg well, while Ti, Th, Gd and U were underestimated owing to organic matter and heavy minerals. Observations included kaolinite order speciation (detrital versus authigenic), illite varieties, and muscovite averaging 19% of illite, which XRD would likely miss.
abstract: Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) has been successfully used as an alternative to X-ray diffraction in the analysis of sedimentary minerals. Many common minerals exhibit unique absorbance spectra in the mid-IR range, which extends from 400 cm-1 to 4000 cm-1. Several authors have shown that the mineral concentrations of an artificial mixture can be quantitatively derived from the mixture spectrum and the spectra of the mineral standards using the mid-IR. There are some limitations to the use of FT-IR that can result in errors in such an analysis, particularly for real sedimentary rock samples as opposed to laboratory mixtures. A new procedure was developed that combines mid-IR and far-IR into a single spectrum covering the range 300 cm-1 to 5200 cm-1. The inclusion of the far-IR enables a better analysis of carbonate minerals since the metal-oxygen bond energies are included. Other improvements include compensation for variable light scattering by potassium bromide pellets, wavelet-based weighting of spectra, and use of end-member feldspar standards. Analysis of over 1000 oilfield samples shows that for many minerals, available library mineral standards have appreciably different FT-IR spectra than are found in oilfield samples. As a result, the mineral standard set has been expanded and now includes 49 mineral species of 29 distinct sedimentary minerals including 5 calcites, 4 dolomites, 5 kaolinites and 4 illites. The sample's FT-IR spectrum is solved as a linear combination of the standard spectra, so the individual mineral species' concentrations are available. The accuracy of the analyses is confirmed by comparing chemical concentrations measured on a split of the samples with concentrations reconstructed from the mineral concentrations. The new level of quantitative analysis has already resulted in a quantitative lithology analysis for total clay, carbonate, anhydrite and sand that is implemented for open- and cased-hole geochemical log analysis.

title: Multiphase Flow in Fractures
