This allows the determination of petrophysical parameters and dynamical quantities. We then compare MRI saturation fronts with numerical simulations, initializing the dynamical model with the petrophysical data from MRI. In this way we validate the consistency of the experimental procedure with the data interpretation and, finally, with the numerical model.

title: Improved Characterisation of Fine Scale Structure: Integration of Downhole and Core Electrical Image Data
caption: Figure 4. Piece C3 Well C (from left to right): Core non-contact resistivity log, core photograph, core resistivity image.
figure_reason: Shows core non-contact resistivity log with core image for Piece C3, confirming core values over FMS.
tldr: Compares FMS borehole electrical images with laboratory core resistivity images from three North Sea wells, finding FMS resistivity values can differ substantially from core values at fine scale.
summary: Fine-scale heterogeneity such as laminae affects resistivity-based reserve estimates, and downhole electrical images are not established as quantitative petrophysical data. The authors compared Formation MicroScanner (FMS) images with laboratory resistivity images of slabbed half-round core, acquired with a 5 mm grid of over 500 electrodes using four-electrode technology. Core pieces of 100-300 mm length came from three North Sea sand-shale wells (A, B, C), and depth matching used core photographs, gamma ray, electrical logs and borehole images. Core images resolved lithological changes and fine dipping layers that appeared diffuse or absent in the FMS images. In Piece C3, FMS resistivity values on either side of a high-resistivity layer disagreed with the core image, and non-contact induction measurements supported the core values. The authors conclude that FMS data alone may give substantially erroneous resistivities for fine-scale structure.
abstract: Downhole images provide detailed information of the textural and structural variation at the borehole wall, enabling the construction of the geological framework in which core is located. While it is widely accepted that these images provide quantitative dip and textural information, their use for deriving quantitative petrophysical properties is not yet established. In contrast, electrical core images provide quantitative resistivity values at a similar resolution to the downhole images which can then be used to evaluate traditional

title: NMR Studies of an Iron-Rich Sandstone Oil Reservoir
caption: Figure 1. Chlorite content (XRD wt%) versus T1/T2 ratio
figure_reason: Shows the key correlation between chlorite content and T1/T2 ratio, supporting the magnetic-gradient interpretation.
tldr: Lab NMR on twelve plugs from a chlorite- and glauconite-rich North Sea sandstone shows chlorite, not glauconite, shortens T2, raises T1/T2 and biases CMR porosity and BVI cut-offs.
summary: CMR logs and core calibration were used in a North Sea sandstone with abundant glauconite (18-38 vol%) and chlorite (4-26 wt%), where porosity is 25-35 PU but permeability is poor. Twelve twin seal-peel plugs were measured with T1 and T2 NMR at 2.04 MHz when water saturated and at Swirr with decane, along with Karl Fischer titration, petrography and standard petrophysics. T1/T2 ratios for decane-saturated plugs at Swirr ranged from 2.0 to 10.9 and correlated with chlorite content, which the authors attribute to chlorite-induced internal magnetic gradients that shorten T2 but not T1. Porosity underestimation by CMR (2-15 PU) and the lab NMR-helium porosity difference (up to about 7.5 PU) increased with chlorite but not glauconite. A 33 ms T2 cut-off mismatched titrated Swirr in chlorite-rich plugs (effective cut-offs 3.3-10.5 ms), while a 150 ms T1 cut-off matched. Even so, 33 ms gave the best Timur/Coates permeability estimates.
abstract: A special NMR study is performed on a sandstone oil reservoir in the North Sea that is characterised by high contents of glauconite and abundant chlorite. Tar zones complicate the reservoir characterisation further. Standard logs indicate porosities of 25 to 35 PU throughout the reservoir column, but core analyses (and well tests) show a very poor relation between porosity and permeability, expected to be caused mainly by the chlorite content. A high proportion of intra-particle micro-porosity confined in the glauconite grains creates an additional uncertainty with respect to fluid saturation and distribution. In order to obtain more information about the productivity of the individual reservoir zones a specially designed programme was set up including NMR logging, special core analyses and laboratory NMR measurements. Several interesting aspects regarding the NMR log responses were revealed; (i) by applying the normally used 33 ms cut-off value for BVI, substantial deviations from the measured Swirr values were found; (ii) the T1/T2 ratios range from 2 to 10 for oil saturated core plugs (at irreducible water saturation); and (iii) the difference between NMR log derived porosity and total porosity is a function of the chlorite content rather than the glauconite content. The suggested interpretation of the latter observations is that the fine-grained chlorite is inducing magnetic gradients on the pore level causing the T2 relaxation times to be shortened dramatically. The sand-grain-sized glauconite, in contrast, affects a much smaller fluid interface and is therefore less detrimental to the T2 relaxation. This knowledge is essential to the understanding and interpretation of NMR logs and in particular for the parameter input to the permeability model.

title: Improving Estimation of NMR Log
caption: Figure 5 shows the T2cutoff values for 13 core samples analyzed with the new procedure. These samples were selected among several sets of NMR core plugs from clastic reservoirs in North and South America, and exhibit significant discrepancies in T2cutoff due to noise level differences. Five hundred echoes were used in the analysis. Our inversion method automatically adjusts regularization for SNR.
figure_reason: Shows T2cutoff for 13 core samples at original, SNR=10 and SNR=20, demonstrating the noise-induced shift.
tldr: Two methods calibrate NMR T2cutoff for logs, adding noise to core echoes or matching capillary-pressure BVI to log spectra, improving BVI and permeability estimates.
summary: Core-derived T2cutoff values are often inconsistent with NMR logs because logs have lower SNR, stronger regularization effects, and different TE and echo counts than core data. The authors show that noise and regularization broaden short-T2 spectra and bias BVI, using core plugs and synthetic log data. Method one adds Gaussian noise to the Sw=1 core echo trains (3-4 realizations) to match log SNR before computing T2cutoff. In 13 clastic core samples, original T2cutoff values below about 10 ms shifted noticeably upward at SNR=10, with the discrepancy greatly reduced at SNR=20. Method two finds T2cutoff by matching log cumulative porosity to depth-matched capillary-pressure BVI; in a North Sea clastic reservoir nine samples gave 80 ms, with a 1:1 BVI crossplot and good agreement of core and log permeability using Coates parameters (C=10.91, m=4, n=1.73).
abstract: Accurate determination of T2cutoff values is a vital step for the estimation of bulk volume irreducible water and permeability from NMR logs. The generalized T2cutoff values used for clastics (33 ms) and carbonates (90 ms) are frequently found to be unrealistic for log interpretation, due to mineralogy-dependent surface relaxivity effects which shift the T2 spectra. Thus, it is often desirable to calibrate T2cutoff values with core NMR measurements. We assessed the various differences between the NMR log and core data and their effects on the T2cutoff estimation. The signal-to-noise level and the regularization strength can affect T2 spectral resolvability and, consequently, the estimates of T2cutoff values. In addition, differences in the echo time and number of echoes, N, can not be ignored. Thus, it is necessary to first account for these effects before we can derive core NMR-based T2cutoff values applicable to NMR log data. This is particularly important for log data acquired in low-porosity and high-noise environment reservoirs. Two methods are developed to address this problem. The first method adds random noise to the core echo data to render the SNR comparable to that of the log data. Then, the T2cutoff is derived from these "noisy log-like" core data. The procedure is repeated with several noise realizations to reduce the "randomness" of the added noise. The second method involves using BVI values determined from capillary pressure measurements to calibrate NMR T2cutoff values. In this method, calculated from NMR log data, the T2cutoff value is chosen such that the cumulative porosity matches the core capillary-pressure-based BVI. This procedure is performed for NMR log data after careful core to log depth-matching. The advantage of the first approach is that there is no need to depth match core samples to log data. The advantage of the second approach is that the T2cutoff is calibrated from capillary pressure data, which conceptually is closely related to BVI and there is no need to match the SNR of the core and NMR log data. The application of either technique for calibrating the T2cutoff improves both BVI and permeability estimation.

title: Diffusion in Internal Field Gradients
caption: Fig. 3 Relaxation time distributions of T1, T2 (TE=0.2 ms), and T2 (TE=2 ms) of Soltrol with brine at Swir in North Burbank sandstone.
figure_reason: Shows strong echo-spacing dependent T2 shortening of Soltrol and brine peaks in North Burbank while T1 stays at bulk.
tldr: Chlorite-coated North Burbank sandstone and chlorite powderpacks show strong internal-gradient diffusion shortening of T2 with echo spacing, unlike Berea and kaolinite; a flake-microchannel model explains the gradients.
summary: Chlorite-coated sandstones may violate default NMR assumptions because iron-rich chlorite creates strong internal field gradients. T1 and T2 (TE 0.2 and 2 ms) were measured at 2 MHz on Berea and North Burbank sandstones with brine, Soltrol 130 and SMY crude, and on chlorite and kaolinite powderpacks saturated with brine, hexane, Soltrol and crude. North Burbank shows strong echo-spacing dependent T2 shortening, even of the oil peak, while T1 stays at bulk values, so it is not a wettability change; Berea shows negligible effect. Gradients from 1/T2 vs t² slopes are an order of magnitude larger for chlorite than kaolinite and far exceed logging-tool applied gradients. A model of chlorite flakes forming microchannels gives maximum gradients G = ΔχB0/R consistent with the measured orders of magnitude. Crude oil shows little diffusion effect because of low diffusivity and fast bulk relaxation.
abstract: The similarity of the values of NMR surface relaxivity of sandstones has led to the adoption of a default value of the $T_2$ irreducible water saturation cut-off for all sandstones. Chlorite coated sandstones should be treated as an exception since the $T_2$ distribution is strongly dependent on the echo spacing. Chlorite coated North Burbank sandstone shows a much stronger diffusion effect due to internal field gradients on NMR $T_2$ measurements compared to Berea sandstone. This can also result in a shortened relaxation time for the oil phase, which can be mistaken as a wettability change. North Burbank sandstone has a $T_1/T_2$ and $r_2/r_1$ that is larger than most values reported in the literature. A series of experiments on chlorite and kaolinite powderpacks with a variety of fluids were performed. There is clear evidence of strong internal magnetic field gradients in chlorite/fluid systems. This gradient is due to the high magnetic susceptibility contrast between chlorite and pore fluids. Kaolinite has a low magnetic susceptibility due to absence of iron and thus shows much less gradient effect. Not only the type of clay, but also how the clay is distributed in rocks, determines the extent of the gradient and diffusion effects on $T_2$ measurements. Chlorite is particularly important because this clay is often paramagnetic and lines the pore walls. The significance of the effect of diffusion due to internal field gradients depends on the magnitude of this effect compared to the relaxation rate due to bulk fluid relaxation and surface relaxation.

title: Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Versus Air/Brine Capillary Pressure Permeability Correlations : How Good Are Our Assumptions in the Empirical Determination of Permeability ?
tldr: Tests Timur, Coates, Swanson, Rapoport-Leas and a new critical-saturation permeability correlation on 160 air/brine capillary pressure curves; Swanson and Rapoport-Leas perform best, and NMR analogs struggle in shaly sands.
summary: NMR permeability correlations derive from capillary pressure work, so the authors tested them on 160 air/brine capillary pressure curves from sandpacks and twenty sandstone fields (0.02 to 22,900 md, 124 ambient and 36 stressed samples). Swanson's and Rapoport-Leas's equations predicted permeability with a standard error of about a factor of two without adjusting constants. Timur and Coates overestimated permeability, especially at low values, with standard errors of about 3.7 to 3.9. A new critical-saturation equation using Corey parameters and krw=0.01 (a=674, b=1.82) matched Swanson's accuracy. Ambient and stressed data were statistically indistinguishable for all models. In a very shaly sand case with six plugs, NMR analogs of Swanson, critical saturation and Seevers performed poorly, likely because surface relaxivity was high (median 48 µm/s) and variable. Adjusted Timur and Coates models with a 6 ms T2 cutoff worked best.
abstract: The estimation of permeability from nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) logs has largely been a result of correlations adopted from capillary pressure research. Equations developed by Timur, Coates et al., Swanson, and Rapoport and Leas all provide different solutions in the empirical determination of permeability. A number of questions arise when one attempts to apply these formulae in reservoir evaluation: - 1. Can these equations be validated using a capillary pressure database and how sensitive are the key input parameters? - 2. What level of accuracy and precision can be expected using indirect permeability estimates? - 3. Are the equations based on ambient data applicable at reservoir conditions? The above issues were addressed by testing permeability correlations on a diverse sandstone data set using 160 air/brine capillary pressure curves and basic core analysis data. Data from twenty fields around the world with a broad range of geological ages, depositional environments, shaliness, porosity and permeability are included. Leverett and Corey laboratory sandpack data as well as stressed and unstressed core data from 0.02 to 22,900 millidarcys are included in the database. Swanson's permeability correlation, derived from unstressed mercury injection data, predicted permeability from the air/brine apex point with little need for statistical adjustment--although the standard error was a factor of two. Capillary pressure and permeability data measured at reservoir stress also fit the original equation; however, Swanson's correlation provided the best permeability prediction from unstressed data. A permeability prediction equation dependant on surface to pore volume ratios published by Rapoport and Leas and modeled after the work of Carman-Kozeny was found to provide good agreement with much of the laboratory data set. Timur and Coates et al. equations performed similarly for unstressed data and both methods overestimated stressed permeability with standard errors of about a factor of three. A new equation based on the work of Swanson and Corey that uses relative permeability and capillary pressure performs as well as Swanson's equation but surpasses the Timur and Coates et al. equations in single phase permeability predictions. In addition the method defines critical water saturation and can be used to estimate the fractional flow of water during production. Given Corey's capillary pressure parameters, a preselected relative permeability to water, e.g. .01, is used to compute the critical water saturation and define this point on the capillary pressure curve. Permeability is then calculated from a ratio determined at this point analogous to that in Swanson's method. Applicability of the various permeability correlations for use with NMR logs was tested on a core dataset from a field with very shaly sands. Measurements included air/brine and mercury injection curves and T2 distributions.

title: A Viscous Coupling Model for Relative Permeabilities in a Fracture
caption: Fig. 2. Relative permeability versus saturation using the coupling model and the corresponding power law approximation for $m=1$ ; 0.5 ; 0.1
figure_reason: Shows model Kr curves versus saturation and their power-law approximations for several viscosity ratios.
tldr: A viscous coupling model for two-phase flow in a fracture gives analytical Kr relations that match air-water data well when plotted against the Lockhart-Martinelli parameter.
summary: Two-phase relative permeabilities in fractures lack a general predictive model, and measured Kr values often sum to less than 1. The authors model the fracture as two parallel planes with a planar interface, with the wetting fluid at the walls. Solving Stokes' equation with no slip at the interface gives analytical Kr expressions that depend on saturation and viscosity ratio. Corey-type power-law fits give a wetting exponent of 1.66 and a non-wetting exponent a_G = 3exp(-1.6m), which is 2.91 for air/water. Against air-water data from Fourar and Bories (glass plates with 1 mm aperture, and clay bricks), Kr versus saturation fits poorly. Kr versus the Lockhart-Martinelli parameter fits well, and the model can convert flow rates to saturation for simulators.
abstract: Two-phase flow properties are required for modeling fluid flows and pollutant transport through fractured media. Several laboratory experiments have been reported in the literature but so far there is no general model to predict the two-phase conductivity of a fracture for a given pair of flowing fluids. In this paper we propose a simple model based on viscous coupling between two fluids flowing simultaneously in a single fracture. This viscous coupling model leads to simple analytical relationships between the relative permeabilities (Kr) and either saturation or fluid velocities. This model also explains the dependence of the non-wetting fluid Kr on the viscosity ratio. Results obtained with this model were compared to several series of data available in the literature with air and water. The fit between predicted and measured Kr is good when the ratio of flow rates is used as variable (Lockhart-Martinelli parameter). For use in numerical simulations, the saturation can be derived from the flow rates using the same model. The proposed model can improve the relative permeability curves that are used in the numerical simulations.

title: Correlation of Rock Permeability and Anisotropic Stress Conditions for the Integration of Rock Mechanical and Hydraulic Flow Models
caption: Fig. 7: Correlation of Measured Compressional Test Data by the Use of the Formula 1 – Flechtinger Bausandstein.
figure_reason: Model fit to sandstone permeability versus stress ratio, showing the minimum and dilatancy branch.
tldr: Triaxial compression permeability tests on sandstone, gneiss, salt and coal show a permeability minimum at a critical stress ratio, fitted by an empirical correlation linked to Poisson ratio.
summary: Laboratory-to-in-situ permeability transfer usually assumes isotropic stress, but stresses near cavities and wells are anisotropic. The authors ran triaxial compression tests with nitrogen flow (pore pressure up to 1 MPa, 20 °C) on Rotliegendes sandstone, KTB gneiss, rock salt and subbituminous coal. Permeability decreased to a minimum at a characteristic axial/radial stress ratio and then rose through dilatancy and microfracturing. Cyclic tests on gneiss showed softening when loaded parallel to foliation (2.2 to 4.5 nD over three cycles) and hardening when perpendicular. An empirical power-law/exponential correlation fitted all four rocks with regression better than 94%, giving critical stress ratios of 1.92 to 5.28. The minimum converts to a critical Poisson ratio consistent with independent measurements.
abstract: The transfer rules of hydraulic rock parameters from laboratory to in-situ conditions are mainly basedon isotropic,elastic rock deformation principles. However the stress field in the neighborhood of underground cavities, like shafts, tunnels, wells etc is not isotropic. Biaxial stress conditions have been realized in experiments to investigate the relationship between rock permeability and axial and radial stress. From deep drilling projects, gneiss rock samples, a metamorphic sedimentary rock and Rotliegendes sandstone samples from an outcrop have been investigated in compression tests to correlate permeability change and deviatoric stress magnitude. For both rock type samples a characteristic ratio between axial and radial stress could be determined where permeability reaches a minimum value. A further increase of the deviatoric stress magnitude increases permeability by pore volume dilatancy, the formation or reopening of microfractures. A mathematical correlation has been developed to describe the characteristic permeability performance with varying radial and axial stresses. This correlation is capable to define the critical boundary of rock dislocation by shear-stress and to couple hydraulic and mechanical models.

title: Experimental Study of the Stress Paths Influence on Monophasic Permeability Evolution
caption: Figure 8 : Mechanical and petrophysical Figure 9 : Influence of the stress path thresholds for various loading paths. on the permeability reduction rate.
figure_reason: Shows permeability and damage thresholds in p'-q plane for all loading paths, and reduction rate versus stress path.
tldr: Triaxial tests on two Vosges sandstones show a p'-q permeability-change criterion; outside it, 20% porosity rock loses permeability while 17% porosity rock gains it at damage onset.
summary: Depletion-induced stress changes can raise or lower reservoir permeability, and the role of the stress deviator is unclear. Triaxial tests were run on Vosges sandstone samples of about 19.5% porosity (320-460 mD) and 17% porosity (<1 mD), using oil and steady-state flow, with vertical loading, proportional loading and constant mean stress paths at various confining and pore pressures. A criterion in the p'-q plane separates a domain of nil or small permeability change from one with significant change. In the 19.5% samples permeability falls by up to 60% beyond the threshold, at a constant rate for a given stress path, with the criterion lying below the damage threshold. In the 17% samples permeability increases beyond a threshold that coincides with mechanical damage, attributed to microcrack opening and propagation.
abstract: Permeability changes have been measured during triaxial tests performed on two sets of Vosges sandstone core samples characterized by their mean porosity : about 20% for one set, 17% for the other one. Several loading paths have been investigated, the samples being loaded up to rupture : constant confining pressure, constant mean stress, proportional loading. Attention was paid to the levels of confining pressure and pore pressure in order to emphasize the possible influence of the stress deviator q. The results are analyzed in order to evidence this influence and the influence of the effective mean stress p' (total mean stress minus pore pressure). It is shown that a criterion can be defined in the (p'-q) plot for the permeability evolution. Inside the domain defined by the criterion, the permeability change is nil or small whatever the loading path is. Outside this domain, the permeability change appears to depend on the initial porosity. Indeed the permeability of 20% porosity sandstones steadily decreases, and the permeability reduction rate can be determined for a given stress path and a given level of the stress deviator. At the contrary outside the domain of low permeability variation, the permeability of the 17% porosity sandstones increases and the threshold for permeability increase appears to coincide with the threshold of mechanical damage.

title: Stochastic Description of Experimental 3D Permeability Fields in Vuggy Reservoir Cores
caption: Figure 4 - Surface map of the sample A2 (permeability scale in mD).
figure_reason: Surface permeability map of sample A2 showing vug clusters and tight matrix strip, central to heterogeneity characterization.
tldr: Dense probe permeameter maps on seven vuggy cores feed geostatistical 3D permeability fields; upscaled permeability often matches measured values, and correlation lengths of 2-7 cm limit waterflood suitability.
summary: Anomalous waterflood relative permeabilities in vuggy cores are attributed to small-scale heterogeneity. Flow simulation of a unit cell with one vug (20% vug volume) gave K* = 1.48 Km, so vug size or porosity distributions poorly indicate permeability. Seven full-size cores (0.8-29 mD) were mapped with a probe permeameter at 5 mm spacing (>1000 points each), semivariograms were computed, and 3D fields were generated by sequential Gaussian and indicator simulation. Upscaled Kzz matched measured permeability for four samples (A5, A7, A2, A6), overestimated it for A1 (probe leaks at large vugs), and underestimated it for A3 and A4, where a tracer test on A3 showed parallel preferential paths missed by surface data. Vertical correlation lengths of 2-7 cm (10-44% of core length) and s_logk of 1.14-2.65 meant only sample A6 appeared suitable for relative permeability measurement.
abstract: Unsteady-state core waterfloods on vuggy samples often result in early water breakthrough. The interpretation of transient production data frequently leads to anomalous relative permeability curves. This might be attributable to small-scale heterogeneity. To confirm this assumption, 1) the effect on permeability of a single vug within a unit matrix cell was simulated, 2) the quantification of small-scale heterogeneity was carried out on seven long vuggy reservoir cores used for waterflood tests. Finally the comparison between the 3D fields of local permeabilities and global transport properties was performed. For each vuggy whole-core the following sequence of tasks was performed : 1) A dense probe permeameter data set was gathered, using a 5mm spacing along 24 lines of the core surface. More than 1000 permeability values were approximately obtained for a 20 cm long sample. 2) Experimental semivariograms of local permeability were obtained from the probe data set. 3) Multiple images of 3D permeability fields were generated according to the experimental semivariogram. More than 20000 grid cells were usually populated with permeability for each core sample. 4) Global sample permeability was calculated with a single-phase simulator for each realisation of the 3D core. 5) Experimental and calculated global sample permeability were compared. The following conclusions were drawn : 1) An isolated vug within a unit matrix cell results in a low increase of permeability. It also means that the distribution of vug diameters has a small effect on overall permeability. Quantification of small-scale heterogeneity should directly focus on permeability distribution rather than porosity. 2) Local permeability histograms are very different from one sample to another. 3) The permeability correlation length ranges from 2 to 7 cm. Using short horizontal plugs rather than long vertical samples might result in sample-spanning high permeability paths and erroneous waterflood results. 4) Comparison between experimental and calculated global sample permeability often shows a good agreement. It confirms that dense surface probe permeameter data is often, but not always, able to capture most of the permeability heterogeneity on vuggy cores.

title: Frim: A Fast Resistivity Index Measurement Method
caption: Figure 4: Same as Figure 3 but for a synthetic porous medium (2400 mD). The duration of the experiment is reduced to about 2 hours. A single pressure step of 450 mD was applied and the break in the production curve (upper panel) is due to a data acquisition problem with no effect on the Ir curve. The resistivity index curve is best fitted by $n=2.08$ .
figure_reason: Shows continuous Ir curve, production and local exponent n for the 2400 mD sample, fitted by n=2.08 in 2 hours.
tldr: A fast drainage resistivity index method using radial electrodes and a semi-permeable filter gives accurate Ir curves in hours to days without capillary equilibrium.
summary: Resistivity index measurements are usually tied to slow porous-plate capillary equilibrium, while centrifuge or flooding methods suffer from saturation-profile effects. The FRIM method imposes one to three oil pressure steps on a small plug (40 mm diameter, 25 mm long) with a water-wet membrane at the outlet, measuring average saturation and radial resistance simultaneously. Experiments on an 80 mD Vosges sandstone (about 42 hours) and a 2400 mD synthetic core (about 2 hours) gave continuous Ir curves well fitted by Archie exponents of 2.05 and 2.08. 1D displacement and 3D electrical simulations show the radial (parallel-mode) measurement is insensitive to non-uniform profiles for Sw below about 0.7-0.8, but not at high Sw where percolation dominates. Two pressure steps appear optimal, and thick ceramics with higher pressure steps give similar duration and accuracy.
abstract: Measurements of electrical conductivity of core samples as a function of saturation are usually combined with porous-plate type capillary pressure measurements. Other methods for changing the saturation of the sample (centrifuge, flooding) have proven difficult to interpret due to the extreme sensitivity of the electrical measurements to the saturation profile. We propose a method derived from porous-plate experiments for measuring the resistivity index curve of a sample (Ir) independently of the capillary pressure curve (Pc). In essence, this method has some similarity with the continuous injection technique but differ fundamentally in the way of measuring resistivity: (i) the radial resistivity measurement is much less sensitive to non uniform saturation profiles (ii) the entire sample is investigated during the electrical measurement. We show experimentally that the order of magnitude of the time required to measure a continuous Ir versus Sw curve, vary from a few hours to a few days depending on the permeability of the sample (from 2000 down to 100 mD respectively). The drainage experiments are performed on small samples (2.5 cm long and 4 cm in diameter), with a radial measurement of resistivity and one semi-permeable filter at the outlet face. The procedure is similar to a porous-plate type experiment in which different pressure steps are imposed and the average saturation and resistivity are measured simultaneously. However, capillary equilibrium is not needed and one to three pressure steps are successively imposed. The numerical simulations of the 'porous plate' displacement process and the resistivity measurements confirm that the method is not sensitive to saturation profile in intermediate to low water saturation. The behaviour at high water saturation is not well predicted because the displacement is dominated by a percolation process which cannot be represented by a model based on Darcy's laws. Influence of permeability and Pc curve of the sample, membrane thickness, saturation exponent n, imposed pressure step are also qualitatively studied by numerical simulations.

title: CORE ANALYSIS: IS IT REALY WORTH IT? Konstantin Mirotchnik3 Apostolos Kantzas2,3 1: Epic Consulting Services, Calgary, Alberta, Canada, 3: TIPM Laboratory, Calgary, Alberta, Canada
caption: Figure 13: After Tax Cashflow profiles
figure_reason: Shows after-tax cashflow profiles differing across models, the paper's key economic result.
tldr: Simulated waterflood of a hypothetical reservoir with lab versus estimated relative permeability shows large cashflow differences, supporting the economic value of special core analysis.
summary: The paper asks whether expensive special core analysis (oil-water relative permeability, up to C$15,000 per plug) is justified compared with correlations. A black-oil simulation of two inverted five-spot patterns (1 year primary, 9 years waterflood) was run with twelve saturation-function sets: synthetic Corey curves, laboratory unsteady-state curves from Eolian sandstone, and lab endpoints with estimated Corey exponents. Each set was applied either by three porosity-keyed rock types or by a single rock type. Output was fed into an economic package (NPV10, payout, ROR, PIR). Initial oil in place differed by over 10% between models (1.79 vs 1.61 million m3), and 10-year recovery was 33.3%, 38.6% and 37.7% for the three heterogeneous cases. NPV10 of fully synthetic (6397 $K) and lab-data (6357 $K) cases matched only by coincidence, as annual cashflow profiles differed strongly; single-rock-type models over- or under-predicted performance.
abstract: Discoveries of large petroleum fields in Western Canada and the United States are becoming increasingly rare in recent times. One might therefore question the value added by implementation of expensive laboratory testing, particularly since there are various correlations available to approximate some of the essential parameters that influence reservoir response and subsequent economic return. To address this question, a comparison has been made on the oil recovery and economic viability that can be projected from a hypothetical reservoir with and without the guidance of relative permeability data as derived from laboratory analysis and correlations. A synthetic model was constructed with input of several laboratory-derived relative permeability functions. This model was used as the "Base Field Data". Various simplifications of the reservoir model were then made by assigning in some cases only one set of rock tables, and in others, data that is based upon estimates for the data to be used in Corey type relative permeability correlation. The model output was run through an economic analysis, and comparisons of cashflow and profitability were made. It was found that significant gaps exist in the annual cashflow projections. As some corporations live and die on cashflow projections, the gathering of laboratory data that will enhance production forecasts should be viewed as a necessary step in field development and management.

title: To Study the Mechanism of Waterflooding in Sand Rocks
caption: Fig.8 Oil recovery of different sized pores in core plug No.1 at different water injection stages
figure_reason: Shows recovery versus injection stage for large, medium and small pores, the paper's key finding.
tldr: Low-field NMR T2 spectra, scaled to pore size with image analysis and mercury injection, track oil recovery by pore size during D2O waterflooding of sandstone plugs.
summary: The paper uses low-field NMR (5 MHz, CPMG) to follow oil displacement by D2O in four sandstone core plugs, so that only oil signal is detected. T2 distributions were converted to pore size distributions using a surface relaxivity of about 0.1, calibrated against petrographic image analysis and mercury injection data. NMR was measured at irreducible water saturation and after 0.1, 0.3, 1.5 and 3.0 PV of injection. Oil in pores below a cutoff size (2.58 for plug No.1) was not displaced, which allows moveable oil percentage to be computed. Large pores reach a fixed recovery quickly, medium pores recover steadily, and small pores recover slowly, leaving residual oil mainly in medium and small pores.
abstract: The use of low field nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) for characterizing water displacing oil in sandstone is investigated. A new pore size distribution technique which is based on NMR transverse relaxation time (T2) distribution is developed and demonstrated. Considerable advantages over conventional flooding experiment techniques for characterizing the oil distribution in different sized pores at each injection stage are demonstrated. The recoveries in various pores at different injection stages show that pore size has a profound effect on the incremental rate of recovery.

title: Geological Description and Flow Characterization of a North Sea Chalk Containing Stylolites and a Gouge-Filled Fracture
caption: Figure 5 – Comparison of residual fluid distributions throughout a gas displacement experiment.
figure_reason: MRI images of fluid distribution at each pressure show matrix desaturating while the gouge-filled fracture retains decane.
tldr: MRI-monitored gas displacement in a North Sea chalk core shows stylolites do not affect flow, while a gouge-filled fracture has higher displacement pressure from reduced pore size.
summary: Gouge-filled fractures and stylolites are common in Shetland Group chalks of the Ekofisk area, and their effect on flow was unknown. A 6.6 cm diameter, 14 cm long whole core containing both features was examined by SEM and thin section, then subjected to a porous-membrane nitrogen displacement of decane with D2O as water phase, imaged by MRI at each pressure step. SEM showed cataclasis in the fracture: broken coccoliths and platelets, smaller grains and pores, and lower porosity than the matrix. The bulk matrix began producing decane between 10 and 20 psi, whereas the gouge-filled fracture retained its decane up to 75 psi, indicating higher capillary entry pressure. Residual oil was about 39 to 35% of pore volume, stylolites showed no effect, and no fluid holdup or bypass was found; a second constant 75 psi test gave the same fracture retention.
abstract: A geological description and fluid displacement experiment have been conducted on a core sample containing both stylolites and a gouge-filled fracture to investigate their effect on fluid flow and their fluid retention characteristics. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) was utilized during the displacement experiment to monitor fluid movement within the core sample. Scanning electron microscope (SEM) and MRI analyses indicated that both the grain and pore size within the gouge-filled fracture had been reduced with respect to the adjacent chalk matrix. This reduction resulted from the mechanical breakdown of the coccolith fragments that made up the bulk of the chalk matrix into their constituent, submicron size platelets, as opposed to the crushing of individual calcite crystals. The reduction in pore size contributed to an increased degree of capillarity within the gouge-filled fracture, as was evidenced in MRI images during the displacement experiment. During the gas displacement experiment, the core sample, containing decane and residual water, was progressively desaturated by the injection of nitrogen. MRI analyses were performed at each level of desaturation. The gouge-filled fracture was observed to exhibit a displacement pressure that was greater than that of the adjacent bulk matrix. MRI analyses also indicated that the effect of the stylolite on fluid flow was negligible. The final distribution of the residual fluids upon desaturation indicated that the stylolites and the gouge-filled fracture did not act as an impediment to fluid movement.

title: A Capacitance Technique for Measuring Production While Centrifuging
caption: Figure 4 : Calibration of the production measurements in drainage mode for an end-piece designed for a 25 % porosity sample. Thin line: measurements, thick line: regression line. The linear region yields a volume range of 13 cc.
figure_reason: Shows linear calibration of the capacitance detector response versus volume, key to accuracy claims.
tldr: A capacitance level detector in rotating centrifuge core holders measures production at 200-4000 rpm with about 1.5% pore volume accuracy, for drainage and forced imbibition Pc curves.
summary: Optical production measurement in centrifuges struggles at low speed because of vibration, alignment and contrast. The authors developed a capacitance-based level detector (coated metallic rod) in core holders for a modified large-radius Jouan centrifuge, holding four 4 cm by 6 cm samples and transmitting signals through a slip ring. Calibration is linear over about 13 cc with resolution of 0.013 cc, and the signal is independent of brine salinity and only weakly temperature dependent. Tests on Vosges sandstone and plastic plugs showed stability better than 0.2 cc, and accuracy of 1-2% of pore volume. Air-brine drainage and oil-water forced imbibition examples were shown, with Pc ranges of 0.011-3.3 bar in drainage and -0.013 to -5 bar in imbibition, plus slow acceleration (1000 rpm/hr) for relative permeability.
abstract: The centrifuge technique is a very useful tool for measuring capillary pressure curves and for desaturating core samples. Saturation measurements while spinning are usually performed using optical devices. We present a capacitance based detector measuring a fluid level in the rotating core holder that avoids problems related to optical detection (contrast, low speed limitation). The system is simple and yields an accuracy of about 1.5% of the pore volume at any speed of rotation (from 200 up to 4000 rpm). This accuracy is needed for data interpretation. The capillary pressure range covered is 0.011 to 3.3 Bar in drainage and -0.013 to -5 Bar in forced imbibition for oil-water. We present different tests and experiments demonstrating the essential aspects of the device: stability and calibration of the detector, sensitivity to temperature, accuracy of production measurements. The same core holder is used for drainage and forced imbibition and four samples can be analyzed at the same time. For Pc curve measurements, the standard plug size is 4 cm in diameter and 6 cm in length. Long samples (9 to 10 cm) can also be centrifuged for further use in water-flooding experiments but production measurements while centrifuging are less precise. Special attention has been paid to the design of the core holders to allow an accurate measurement of effluent production after centrifugation at the end of both drainage and forced imbibition cycles. The centrifuge has also been modified to accelerate slowly (1000 rpm/hr), facilitating production measurements and relative permeability curves calculations.

title: The "Spinning Disk" Approach to Capillary Pressure Measurement with a Centrifuge Experiment
tldr: First experimental test of the spinning disk centrifuge geometry, where the Hassler-Brunner expression is exact, using sand and glass-bead packs with average-saturation and video methods.
summary: The spinning disk method spins a cylindrical sample about its own axis of symmetry, unlike the standard offset centrifuge geometry. The authors show analytically that for this geometry the truncated Hassler-Brunner expression gives local saturation exactly from average saturation data, and that large-diameter samples are preferred. Experiments used a plastic sample cell in a Beckman J6-B centrifuge with unconsolidated 20-40 mesh sand and 80-120 and 120-170 mesh glass-bead packs (permeability 8.5 to 154 darcies, initial saturation about 95%). Threshold pressures from the centrifuge (0.25 to 0.85 psi) agreed with independent measurements, and the capillary pressure curves matched those from standard geometry. Video-derived saturations agreed with the differentiated average saturation data above Sw of about 0.2, but differed at lower saturations. Unequal drainage among the four collection vessels was a complication.
abstract: The "spinning disk" approach to measurement of capillary pressure was first proposed almost 10 years ago, but the method has never been tested. In this paper, the theoretical foundation of the method will be described, and the first experimental observations will be presented. In the spinning disk approach, a cylindrical sample of porous material is spun on its axis of symmetry. That is, the axis of the rotor is the same as the axis of symmetry of the cylindrical specimen. This approach is markedly different from the standard centrifuge experiment in which the material is spun at some distance (usually about 10 cm) from the axis of the rotor. An advantage of the spinning disk method is that large samples of porous material can be easily tested. In fact, large diameter samples are preferred. In this paper, the capillary pressure relationship is obtained in two ways from the experimental observations. First, the relationship is calculated from a set of average saturations measured at different spin rates. The expression for processing the data is the truncated Hassler-Brunner expression. For the spinning disk geometry, the truncated expression is precisely correct. Secondly, the capillary pressure relationship is obtained with direct visual methods that were first demonstrated in our laboratory in 1997.

title: Electrical Resistivity Measurements on Unconsolidated Core
caption: Figure 5 (a) Archie 'm' value varies with grain shape for unconsolidated sands (b) Grain shape also affects the electrial and fluid flow observations
figure_reason: Shows Archie m varying with grain shape and resistivity-permeability relationships for sands.
tldr: Reviews oceanography-derived laboratory cells and imaging methods for measuring electrical resistivity of unconsolidated sediments, deriving Archie m, porosity, permeability relationships and heterogeneity.
summary: Resistivity measurement on unconsolidated core is difficult because sample packing changes with handling. The paper reviews cells for three sediment types: a modified oedometer cell for cohesive clays, porosity and permeability cells for redeposited cohesionless sands, and a cylindrical multi-electrode cell for intact friable sediments. In a clay loaded from about 85% to 65% porosity, the log-log formation factor-porosity line gave Archie m and showed a not equal to 1. For clean sands, m increased with decreasing grain sphericity, while grain size distribution changed resistivity and porosity but not m. High-resolution surface electrode imaging (2.5 mm grid) and saline tracer tests showed that porosity heterogeneity controls flow pathways.
abstract: Unconsolidated core is generally characterised by its lack of lithification or cementation. The gross material properties of the core are controlled, however, by the grain size; coarser sandsized material is often difficult to sample intact due to its cohesionless nature while finergrained material may be cohesive and retain its structure well. Consequently characterising unconsolidated samples in the laboratory varies with lithology. The accurate measurement of electrical resistivity in unconsolidated sediments can be problematical. Changes to the physical state of the core can lead to determinations of the resistivity which are not representative of the insitu state. This variability in packing can, however, be used to advantage in allowing for the determination of an Archie 'm' value for that individual sample. Thus loose sediments provide a means of studying consolidation behaviour that is not possible using cemented rock samples where subtle changes in texture can mask the underlying process of interest. The soft nature of the unconsolidated material can also reduce electrode problems often associated with more competent rock. Such measurements have been used in the oceanographic field for several decades; this contribution reviews relevant experimental techniques previously applied in the study of seafloor sediments which may be appropriate for use in the hydrocarbons industry. We demonstrate a range of different approaches for dealing with unconsolidated material in the laboratory. Using a variety of laboratory cells it is possible to investigate the relationships between electrical resistivity and both porosity and permeability, and to deduce Archie 'm' values. Furthermore it is possible to use the electrical resistivity to deduce the insitu porosity from insitu resistivity measurements. Using high spatial resolution resistivity measurements it is possible to produce laboratory images of unconsolidated sediments which relate to the degree of heterogeneity of the pore space (porosity). Introducing saline tracers provides a means for assessing the variability of fluid flow pathways and a dynamic heterogeneity can be evaluated.

title: Application of Core-Log Correlation and Artificial Neural Networks to Better Define Permeability, Porosity and Lithology
caption: Fig. 7 shows the relationship between neural network permeability logarithm and core porosity
figure_reason: Shows ANN permeability versus core data correlation (r=0.9381) compared with empirical transform, the main result.
tldr: A backpropagation neural network trained on core data predicts porosity, permeability and lithofacies from gamma ray, resistivity and density logs in Venezuelan Misoa sands, outperforming regression transforms.
summary: Permeability prediction from logs is hard because of non-linear dependence on porosity, shale content and other variables. The authors trained a feed-forward backpropagation neural network (five hidden nodes) on core data, using gamma ray, deep resistivity and density porosity logs as inputs. The case study is a laminated Misoa Formation reservoir (C2 and C3 units, Maracaibo Lake) with porosity of 11-18% and permeability of 20-500 mD. Core log-permeability versus porosity was linear for facies S3 and S31 but quadratic for S2 and S11, supporting a non-linear approach. The ANN permeability correlated with core at r = 0.9381, against 0.8155 for the empirical KCOREL2 transform, and ANN lithofacies agreed well with core descriptions.
abstract: Determining petrophysical parameters such as permeability, porosity and lithology from logs often requires the use of either empirical relationships or some form of multiple non-linear regression, because of the non-linear nature of the variables involved. A major problem of the non-linear method lies in the difficulty in choosing an appropriate mathematical model and matching the sensitivity of the model to the input variables. Recent application of Artificial Neural Network (ANN) techniques, which use detailed core-log integration, have allowed these difficulties to be overcome. In this paper the use of a Backpropagation ANN model to provide petrophysical solutions, validated by detailed core analysis, will be demonstrated in several case studies. Permeability determination presents a major problem because of the non-linear nature and interdependence of the reservoir variables, which constitute it. ANN's that are trained using core data are better suited to non-linear applications and yield better permeability results. For lithofacies identification ANN techniques are faster than multivariate log-based methods because they can handle large amounts of data more efficiently. Several case studies taken from Venezuelan reservoirs are considered. Neural network permeability and porosity transforms are developed and compared to transforms generated by conventional log-core correlation. Lithofacies are identified and are used to predict permeability corresponding to each facies. Each case study makes extensive use of core-log integration.

title: Use of Well Logs to Support and Validate Laboratory Results in Chalk by
caption: Figure 8: The comparison between different interpretation methods showed general agreement for the near well bore saturations of a waterflood zone.
figure_reason: Crossplot of Archie versus C/O log water saturation validates the laboratory-derived Archie interpretation in the waterflooded zone.
tldr: Laboratory water saturation versus porosity trends on chalk plugs are compared with well logs from waterflooded zones to validate core preparation, wettability and Archie parameters.
summary: Laboratory and well-log data are interdependent, so matching them can require iteration. Highly paraffinic stock tank crude with a cloud point near 70°F caused artifacts (pore plugging, permeability loss, variable wettability), so plugs were Soxhlet-extracted with toluene and methanol and tested with n-decane, which preserves a mobility ratio near 1.0. Spontaneous Imbibition Index, stress-corrected saturations (1580 psig) and Archie parameters, including a larger imbibition n, were measured on plugs. A carbon/oxygen log confirmed Archie saturations in a waterflooded zone, and near-wellbore saturation/porosity trends matched lab forced and highly water-wet imbibition data. Deep-resistivity trends away from the wellbore differed from the lab data, showing that multiple core preparation procedures may be needed to match field behavior.
abstract: Support or validation of laboratory measurements on field cores can be obtained by comparing measurements with that obtained from field well logs. Since the laboratory measurements are needed for interpretation of field electrical measurements, the process of matching field and laboratory data can become an iterative one. In many cases, measurements through this process can indicate the appropriate saturation and wettability state of the reservoir and the appropriate core plug preparation procedures. In our studies, laboratory data were compared to well log data from water-flooded zones of a chalk reservoir. Our primary core preparation method, the Soxhlet extraction of chalk core plugs with toluene and methanol, did not match field results, indicating that in some cases more than a single core preparation technique may be needed in the laboratory. N-decane for most laboratory tests was found to be more suitable than field stock tank crude oil. Saturation versus porosity trends were found capable of indicating wettability and

title: Measurement of Capillary Pressure by Direct Visualization of a Centrifuge Experiment
caption: Figure 8 : Measured Capillary Pressure Relationship, Sample 4
figure_reason: Capillary pressure curve from visualization compared with Hassler-Brunner for sand pack, main result.
tldr: Video imaging of sand packs and Berea slices during centrifuge drainage yields capillary pressure curves matching Hassler-Brunner and suggests the outlet boundary condition fails above Bond number 0.0012.
summary: The study tests a visualization method for centrifuge capillary pressure measurement, motivated by doubts about the zero-capillary-pressure outlet boundary condition. A custom circular rotor with transparent holders was used in a Beckman J6-B centrifuge, with four sand packs and four Berea slices (2x3x0.2 in) saturated with dyed water and imaged at each spin rate with a video camera. Local saturation was obtained from a gray-level correlation built from the centrifuge data itself, and Pc was computed from radius and spin rate. Capillary pressure curves agree qualitatively with Hassler-Brunner results, though with scatter. Saturations fell below 5% at Bond numbers above 0.00001, consistent with King et al., and the standard outlet condition may fail in sand packs above Bond number 0.0012 but was not clearly seen failing in Berea.
abstract: A visualization method for obtaining capillary pressure relationships during centrifuge experiments was tested. It consists of recording and processing the video images of a rock sample at every spin rate. From these images, the local saturation at any location on the sample is obtained using a correlation that relates gray level to saturation. The capillary pressure is calculated using the measured average distance from the center of spin to the location of the local saturation measurement. With the visualization method, gas-water capillary pressure curves for sand packs and for Berea rock were obtained that agree with those determined with the algorithm of Hassler and Brunner. The irreducible water saturations were observed to be quite low in experiments at high spin rates for Bond numbers greater than 0.00001. Using video images, it was possible to explore the failure of the standard outlet boundary condition for centrifuge experiments, which maintains that the saturation of the displaced wetting phase during a drainage experiment is 100% at the outlet face of the sample. Results suggest that the standard outlet boundary condition fails for Bond numbers in excess of 0.0012.

title: The Uses of Surface Area Data Obtained on Reservoir Core Samples
caption: Figure 5: Qv versus surface area, Cooper basin and Malay basin.
figure_reason: Shows linear Qv versus surface area for two basins, yielding surface charge density and supporting shaliness use.
tldr: Surface area measured on Australasian reservoir cores correlates with permeability, irreducible water, CEC/Qv and cementation exponent, supporting its routine measurement for petrophysical interpretation.
summary: Surface area is rarely measured in routine core analysis, although it influences permeability, irreducible water saturation and excess conductivity. Over a two-year project, polar molecule adsorption surface area was measured on cores from Australasian reservoirs (Cooper, Bonaparte, Malay basins) and compared with other petrophysical data. Surface area correlates with permeability and 50 psi irreducible water saturation within a reservoir, though no universal permeability correlation exists. A 15 nm water film assumption roughly predicted irreducible saturation. Surface area is linearly related to Qv, giving surface charge densities of 0.30 and 0.34 C/m2, and it can serve as a shaliness indicator and Archie/non-Archie criterion. A limited nine-sample dataset suggests m* increases with surface area. Links to NMR T1, flow units and Klinkenberg permeability are discussed.
abstract: Surface area measurements performed on reservoir core samples can provide important characterisation data. Surface area controls or partially controls permeability, irreducible water saturation and excess conductivity. At this time surface area is rarely measured during routine core analysis, which is perhaps unfortunate given the potential uses of the data. The main objective of this work is to describe and illustrate the potential uses of surface area data measured during the course of a 2 year project performed to develop a set of methods to extend the interpretive capability of core data. During this work a number of interesting and useful correlations have been found between surface area and other petrophysical parameters. Some of the correlations appear to be generally applicable, whilst others are more tenuous and require further investigation. Previous work is briefly reviewed and the correlations obtained are discussed from a theoretical basis, and illustrated using real data. Surface area is shown to correlate well with permeability and irreducible water saturation. Surface area data generated from cuttings may allow the geoscientist to obtain permeability/irreducible water saturation data from uncored wells based on formation specific correlations. The relationship between surface area and cation exchange capacity allows surface area data to be used as a core based shaliness parameter, particularly when measured CEC data is available to calculate surface charge density. A limited data set also appears to show a useful and theoretically justifiable relationship between surface area and the clean sand (shale corrected) 'm' cementation exponent. These relationships are illustrated using our own and previously published data. Surface area data has also been shown (in previous work) to correlate with the NMR decay constant T1. In addition, surface area data may be useful for assessing Klinkenberg effects, and enhancing the understanding of 'flow units'.

title: Specific Internal Surface :the "Forgotten?"Petrophysical Measurement! or Application of Fractal Pore Models for Improved Permeability Estimations from Logs!
caption: Fig. 7: Experimental verification of the "PARIS- equation" and quantification of the "lithology factor qofrom deviations of the ideal model line.
figure_reason: Experimental verification of the PARIS equation and determination of the lithology factor q0 from deviations.
tldr: Advocates reviving the Clausthal Concept, using fractal specific internal surface in modified Kozeny/Carman equations (PARIS, Budapest, Aberdeen) to predict permeability from logs, mainly NMR.
summary: Kozeny/Carman permeability equations fail when a measured BET or image-analysis surface is inserted directly, because the measured surface depends on resolution. The Clausthal Concept corrects this with surface magnification factors from a self-similar "pigeon hole" fractal pore model, giving the PARIS equation K = 475.3/F (Spor,BET/q0)^-3.1085. Substituting NMR relaxation (relaxivity 0.66 s/mm for sandstones) gives the Budapest equation, and substituting thorium concentration gives the Aberdeen equation. Lab-derived permeabilities matched measured values within one order of magnitude over 0.1 mD to 10 D. Field use of the thorium and electrical versions was limited by tool resolution, geochemical scatter and high salinity, so modern NMR logging, calibrated on cores, offers the best prospect.
abstract: The paper fosters a "revitalisation" of the "Clausthal Concept" and its application for an improved permeability prediction from logs by quantifying the fractal behaviour of specific internal surface as input for modified Kozeny / Carman- type of equations .

title: Effect of Fluid Characteristics and Flow Mechanism on Archie Saturation Exponent
tldr: Continuous-injection resistivity index tests on carbonate cores show Archie saturation exponent depends on injection rate and brine/oil viscosity ratio, with low viscosity ratio giving more uniform behavior.
summary: Laboratory resistivity index measurements are used to derive the Archie saturation exponent, but the effect of displacement conditions is rarely examined. Ten water-wet carbonate plugs (1.5 in. by 3 in.) of varying porosity and permeability were tested by continuous oil injection under 3000 psi confining stress. Two injection rates (0.03 and 0.15 cc/hr) were applied to four samples, and two viscosity ratios (0.6 and 0.1) to six samples, with recleaning between runs. High injection rate and low viscosity ratio gave more linear log-log I versus Sw behavior over most of the saturation range. Differences in n reached about 30% between injection rates for one sample and about 13% between viscosity ratios. The authors conclude that fluids and desaturation procedure should mimic reservoir conditions to avoid errors in Sw.
abstract: Water saturation determination from wireline resistivity log data depends on measurements of the resistivity index on core samples using Archie's equation. The only variables in Archie's equation are water saturation and rock resistivity, and it is assumed that the relationship is independent of the flow displacement mechanism. This paper reports an experimental investigation of the influence of flow injection rate and the viscosity ratio between the displaced and the displacing phases on the Archie saturation exponent. Resistivity index measurements were carried out by the continuous injection technique. The results show that the saturation exponent is a function of the displacement mechanism and fluids characteristics, and that different resistivity-saturation relationships can be obtained for a given sample under different experimental conditions. Because errors in the evaluation of saturation exponent can give rise to serious errors in the estimation of hydrocarbon saturations, it is concluded that the determination of the saturation exponent requires particular care, and that fluids characteristics and the desaturation method should be carefully selected whenever resistivity index measurements are performed.

title: Shale Characterization Using Complex Permittivity Measurements
tldr: Low- and high-frequency complex permittivity of preserved shales and kaolinite is used to estimate water content, free water, surface conductivity, characteristic length and anisotropy.
summary: The paper uses complex permittivity spectra to characterize shales and extract physical and engineering properties. Preserved Queenston, Mancos and Pierre shales and kaolinite were measured parallel and normal to bedding. Measurements used an impedance analyzer (10 Hz to 1 MHz) and a coaxial probe with a network analyzer (0.02 to 1.30 GHz). High-frequency real permittivity gives volumetric moisture content through a linear relation valid for contents below 0.5. The imaginary permittivity deviation at 1.30 GHz gives free water content, with over 66% of kaolinite pore water free, and Pierre shale showing the least free water, consistent with its high specific surface and smectite content. Low-frequency relaxations near 1 MHz give surface conductivity of Queenston and Mancos shales (about 1e-9 S). Double layer polarization at 8 kHz in air-dry Queenston shale gives a characteristic length of 0.5 µm. Pierre shale shows higher permittivity normal to bedding than parallel, attributed to Maxwell-Wagner polarization.
abstract: Geomaterials exhibit a wide range of electrical properties depending on their structure, mineralogical composition, porosity, water content, ionic concentration, and anisotropy. In this study, low and high-frequency complex permittivity measurements are used to analyze shale cores and to extract fundamental engineering and physical properties.

title: SCA1998-43
caption: Fig. 1 Illustration of influence wettability $J_w$ for Ada water saturated rock ( $S_w=100\%$ ).
figure_reason: Shows how wettability alteration influences diffusive-adsorptive activity in fully water-saturated samples.
tldr: Shows that shifting West Siberian terrigenous rocks toward oil-wetness lowers porosity, permeability and adsorptive activity, raises the Archie saturation exponent n, and reduces SP log amplitudes.
summary: The study examines how wettability affects electrical resistivity, membrane potential, adsorptive activity and reservoir properties of terrigenous silty-sandstones and claystones from West Siberian oil and gas deposits. Wettability was altered by selectively dissolving minerals and by natural and artificial processes. It was characterized by contact angles on minerals and by Amott indices. As rocks become more oil-wet, hygroscopic adsorptive capacity falls. Thin oil-wetting films reduce porosity by 0.5-1.0% and permeability by 15-45%. Water-saturation porosity of oil-wet rock is 0.5-3.0% lower than kerosene-saturation porosity, and the gap narrows after 3-6 h saturation at 60 atm. The saturation exponent n rises from 1.7-1.9 to 2.3-2.35 after conversion to oil-wet. SP log amplitudes in hydrophobic layers reach 40-60% of those in hydrophilic layers. An electrical conductivity model for hydrophobic rocks and interpretation techniques are proposed.
abstract: An investigation was carried out to determine the effect of wettability on electrical resistivity, membrane potential, adsorptive activity, and reservoir properties of terrigenous sedimentary rocks. The rocks studied were from oil- and gas-bearing deposits of West Siberia. Natural and artificial processes that cause rock wettability changes toward greater oil-wetness were investigated. Experiments were carried out to determine best methods for selectively dissolving specific rock minerals to alter wettabilities in sedimentary silty-sandstones and claystones. The water-wetting and oil-wetting capacities of minerals were defined by measuring contact angles of oil and water droplets placed on the mineral surfaces under water or oil respectively. Wettabilities were described by Amott indices. It was shown that, as rock wettabilities change toward greater oil wetness, the adsorptive ability (hydroscopic humidity) of the rock decreases and some deterioration in filtering capacity features are observed. In particular, placing a thin oil-wetting film at the pore surface causes the effective pore volume and porosity to decrease. Porosity reductions from 0.5-1.0 % and permeability reductions from 15-45 % were noted when pores within rock core plugs were coated by thin oil-wetting films. Measured porosities for hydrophobic (oil-wet) reservoir rocks differ depending on whether water or kerosene is used as the saturating fluid. For oil-wet rocks, porosities defined by water saturation are less than porosities defined by kerosene saturation. The difference can be as much as 0.5-3.0%. This difference decreases when the samples are saturated for 3 to 6 hours at a pressure of 60 atm.1

title: Innovation in Fracture Roughness Characterization
caption: Figure 2: Average of 162 Fourier power spectra of Berea pro les
figure_reason: Averaged Fourier spectrum of 162 Berea profiles showing the three roughness regimes.
tldr: Berea fracture roughness is measured by perthometer profilometry and shadow imaging, showing three roughness regimes, and used to synthesize realistic fracture profiles and surfaces.
summary: Sandstone fractures are usually modeled as smooth parallel surfaces, but real fractures are rough with scale-dependent height. Fracture roughness in Berea sandstone was measured with high-resolution perthometer profilometry (2.42 m length, 30.5 nm height resolution) and a new shadow imaging technique using a light source and CCD camera. Profiles were analyzed with Fourier power spectra and an average wavelet coefficient method, and shadow images with shadow length distribution theory for self-affine landscapes. Averaged over 162 profiles, three regimes appeared: grain shape, self-affine, and uncorrelated noise. The methods agreed; Fourier had higher resolution, wavelet less noise, and imaging is fast and non-contact but resolved only the self-affine regime. Synthetic profiles and surfaces built by filtering and inverse Fourier transform closely matched measured spectra and surfaces.
abstract: We describe pore to core scale Berea fracture roughness by using two experimental techniques: high-resolution perthometer pro lometry and a new shadow imaging technique. Pro les were analyzed byFourier spectrometry and a recently proposed average wavelet coecient method. Shadow images were analyzed using a recent theory for shadows in a self-ane landscape. The methods were consistent. The Fourier method had highest resolution, while the wavelet method had less noise. Imaging is faster than pro lometry. The fractures have three distinct roughness regimes: grain shape, self-ane roughness and randomly uncorrelated roughness. Realistic fracture pro les

title: New suite of modified laboratory procedures and dedicated software for the effective integration of the core analysis and wireline data sets
caption: Figure 1 – Comparison of probabilistic and core data based interpretations showing inconsistencies between log and core predicted porosity and water saturation.
figure_reason: Depth plot comparing log and core-derived porosity and water saturation, showing the key inconsistency.
tldr: Presents an extended core data set measured on plug offcuts plus a core interpretation software module, with a case study showing core-log inconsistencies in porosity and water saturation.
summary: Routine core analysis lacks interpretive capability, while special core analysis is costly and sparsely sampled. The authors propose an intermediate suite measured mainly on offcuts of RCA plugs: total, effective and furnace porosity, ambient capillary pressure, surface area by polar molecule adsorption, spectral gamma and sample description. A core interpretation module was built within a mainstream log analysis package. It handles overburden corrections, capillary pressure curve fitting and J-functions, Qv from surface area, permeability and heterogeneity estimates, and facies discrimination. In a case study of the Heavy well, J-function water saturations and overburden core porosity were compared with a probabilistic log interpretation. The log model predicted optimistic porosity and higher water saturation than capillary theory. Forcing the model to match the core values degraded the reconstruction quality. This leaves either an erroneous log model or a reservoir not in capillary equilibrium.
abstract: Core analysis data is considered one of the cornerstones of formation evaluation by believers in core data, whether users or providers. However, there seems to be a general consensus that more could be done with core data, both in the scope of petrophysical data provided and how it is used. With recognition of this a suite of methods has been put together that provide an extended core data set, and software designed expressly for the interpretation of core data.

title: Porosity and Permeability of Palaeocene Sands from the North Sea; a Comparison of Plug Porosity and Image Derived Porosity
caption: Figure 2: (a) Gas permeability versus plug porosity. Correlation coefficient = 0.41. (b) Gas permeability versus image porosity. Correlation coefficient = 0.73.
figure_reason: Shows permeability crossplots against plug and image porosity, with correlation coefficients of 0.41 and 0.73.
tldr: Back-scattered SEM image porosity correlates better with permeability than helium plug porosity in North Sea Palaeocene sands, and clay content largely explains the plug porosity-permeability scatter.
summary: The porosity-permeability relationship in a Palaeocene sand reservoir is very poor, so image analysis was used to explain it. Back-scattered SEM images at x30 and x150 from endtrims of 48 plugs gave a 2D image porosity, which was compared with helium plug porosity and gas permeability. Image porosity correlated better with permeability (r = 0.73) than plug porosity (r = 0.41) and gave lower values. Pore-size splitting showed low permeability samples have many small pores and high permeability samples have large pores. Pore anisotropy, tested on cubic plugs, was not significant. Plug porosity tracked the area of pores plus clay, and subtracting one third of the clay area improved the match, so clay is a major control on the plug porosity-permeability relationship.
abstract: The image analysis parameter considered is image porosity. The images used for the image analysis process are back scattered SEM images (Figure 1a), at two different magnifications (x30 and x150). Image porosity expresses the two-dimensional pore space seen within an image as a fraction of image area (Figure 1b). Plug porosity, by comparison, is the calculation of three-dimensional interconnected pore space by helium injection. Both of these porosities have been compared with a gas permeability measurement. The permeability and plug porosity measurements are made on the same plug and the image porosity measurement is made from an endtrim of each plug.

title: Speed and Attenuation of Ultrasonic Waves from Chirp Measurements
caption: Fig. 3: a) Amplitude spectra for a shear wave arrival across a one-inch aluminum sample using pulse, linear sweep and logarithmic sweep. b) Logarithm of the ratios of the spectral amplitudes of shear waves traversing one-inch aluminum and Lucite samples. Each curve shows the ratio for data taken by one of the three methods examined in this paper: pulse, linear and logarithmic sweep. Conclusions Re
figure_reason: Amplitude spectra and spectral ratios comparing pulse, linear and log sweeps, used to derive Q and show noise plateau.
tldr: A swept-frequency chirp ultrasonic system with cross-correlation processing matches pulse-mode velocity and attenuation in aluminum and Lucite, with an estimated order-of-magnitude better amplitude signal-to-noise.
summary: Conventional ultrasonic core measurements use short pulses, which limits the emitted power. The authors built a system around a function-generator chirp source, recording source and receiver signals at 30 MHz and cross-correlating them in the Fourier domain to synthesize the impulse response. Tests on one-inch aluminum and Lucite compared 2 ms linear and logarithmic sweeps with pulse mode. Filtered sweeps gave P-wave velocity of about 6320-6334 m/s in aluminum and S-wave velocity of about 3155-3171 m/s, in good agreement with pulse mode (6334 and 3133 m/s), while the unfiltered wideband sweep deviated more. Spectral-ratio Q for Lucite was 160 (linear sweep), 157 (log sweep) and 183 (pulse). The chirp showed a much lower high-frequency noise plateau, suggesting an amplitude signal-to-noise ratio about ten times higher than pulse mode.
abstract: This paper describes the design and operation of a new ultrasonic measurement system that uses a long-duration signal source (chirp) for measuring the propagation and attenuation of ultrasonic waves in core samples. Compared to standard systems, which utilize shortduration pulses, the new technique allows better signal-to-noise ratios. Our results show that the chirp is a practical alternative to conventional pulses for laboratory measurements.

title: Coring to Conserve Residual Water Saturation and Its Use When Interpreting Electrical Logs
tldr: Describes insulated water-based-mud coring (KIM receivers) that preserves residual water saturation in West Siberian cores and builds log-core resistivity-water content relationships, giving data comparable to oil-based-mud coring.
summary: Filtrate invasion during coring distorts saturations and electrical properties, and oil-based mud is costly and environmentally problematic. The authors describe KIM hermetic and isolating core receivers (67, 80, 100 mm) that insulate core from water-based mud, with wellsite invasion depth checked by fluorescent or chemical tracers and central samples sealed in paraffin. More than 30 West Siberian wells were cored this way, with average recovery of 91% (82.5% in unconsolidated Senonian and Senomanian rocks). Residual water saturations matched those from OBM-cored wells. Resistivity versus water content did not follow Archie-Dahnov and differed between reservoir and non-reservoir rocks because of silt content. Log-core relationships were derived for Surgut region beds (AS, BS, JS) and a temperature-dependent conversion from core to formation resistivity. The technique works best in low-permeability rocks and is less effective above about 500-700 mD or where gas expansion expels water at k below 3-5 mD.

title: Petrophysical Evaluation of Low Resistivity Sandstone Reservoirs
tldr: Modifies the total shale sand model with variable m and n to correct water saturation in low resistivity shaly sandstone pay; a field example shows lower Sw than Archie.
summary: Low resistivity pay zones give high apparent water saturation yet produce water-free hydrocarbons, caused by microporosity or by conductive minerals such as clay and pyrite. The authors modify the total shale (Simandoux/Poupon) model by introducing variable cementation exponent m and saturation exponent n, through a shale term Atsh. A field example from a shaly sandstone, previously evaluated by Schlumberger, used Humble constants a=0.62 and m=2.15. Water saturation was obtained from the resistivity index (Eq. 7) and from a Pickett-plot relation (Eq. 8). For the three shaly points, Archie gave Sw of 0.54-0.62, while the shale models gave 0.37-0.42, matching the Schlumberger results; clean points gave Sw=1.0.
