The amount of recoverable oil in a transition zone depends -among other things- on the distribution of initial oil saturation (Soi) as a function of depth and the dependency of the oil's mobility, i.e., the residual oil saturation (Sor) and relative permeability, on initial oil saturation.

title: Laboratory Techniques to Characterize NMR Diffusion in Carbonates
caption: Figure 7 - T1 and T2 NMR Population Distributions (Sample # 352) Figure 8 – Desaturation T2 Time Shifts (Samples #113 and 52)
figure_reason: Shows T1/T2 distributions for heterogeneous sample and desaturation T2 shifts central to the diffusion interpretation.
tldr: Combines NMR T1/T2, CT, APEX mercury injection and resistivity tests on Cretaceous and Jurassic carbonates to characterize diffusion effects on T2 distributions.
summary: NMR T2 responses in carbonates are hard to correlate with pore size because diffusion, saturation and wettability affect relaxation. About sixty Cretaceous samples and a set of Jurassic samples were measured with 2 MHz CPMG at varying echo spacings, alongside CT pore-volume distributions, APEX mercury injection and resistivity index tests. In Cretaceous lagoonal samples, the T2 peak at 126 ms matched the APEX pore body peak at 125 microns, while the T1/T2 ratio was about 1.2 in homogeneous samples but rose to 2.66 for long-time peaks in the heterogeneous sample tied to the CT high-porosity tail. Desaturated/saturated T2 peak ratios (1.7 to 9.3) were inversely related to saturation exponent, supporting surface-film desaturation. Whether the sample is in the fast diffusion regime depends on the choice of pore size and surface relaxivity (ratio 0.0005 versus 0.062). Jurassic two-phase tests showed qualitative wettability and echo-spacing effects that remain unresolved.
abstract: Petrophysical NMR measurements in carbonate samples illustrate the difficulty of establishing direct size to relaxation rate correlations. Four observations that illustrate this are: T2 distributions in de-saturated samples that are indistinguishable in fully saturated samples, variations in the T1/T2 ratio as a function of relaxation time, saturation dependence of T2 distributions, and internal gradient effects on T2 distributions. Additional complications associated with wetting and non-wetting phase fluid saturations are also observed. Complementary tests that clarify these observations and contribute to a more robust modeling of the NMR carbonate response include APEX mercury injection data, CT scan pore volume determinations, resistivity index measurements and de-saturation multi-echo T2 measurements. Combinations of standard and NMR tests from two carbonate systems, an early Cretaceous marine/lagoon carbonate, and an Upper Jurassic heterogeneous carbonate are used to illustrate how extended laboratory measurements can improve the characterization of NMR response.

title: Movement of Connate Water During Water Injection in Fractured Chalk
caption: Figure 9 Cumulative produced connate water shows an excellent material balance with the original quantity of connate water in the fractured plug.
figure_reason: Cumulative connate water production from iodide tracer, showing slow recovery and material balance with original connate water.
tldr: Waterflood tests on a fractured Kansas chalk plug with X-ray imaging show most connate water is not viscously displaced; diffusion into the fracture dominates its removal.
summary: Complete viscous displacement of connate water by injected water is often assumed for chemical EOR and well log flushed-zone interpretation. Two waterflood tests (5 ml/h) were run on a water-wet Kansas outcrop chalk plug fractured along its axis, tracking connate water by K+ or iodide tracer in the effluent and by X-ray imaging of KI-doped connate brine. Injected water in the fracture did not outrun the imbibition front, and water breakthrough came only at about 0.63 PV when oil displacement was nearly complete. After 10 PV only about 50% of the connate water was produced in test 1, and 80% after 16 PV in test 2, with the bulk of connate water only disturbed, not banked. Profile evolution (declining concentrations without forward shift, spreading of the outlet bank) indicates diffusion of connate salt into the fracture fluid was the main mechanism, with implications for log interpretation of waterflooded fractured zones.
abstract: The movement of connate water can be important in enabling or blocking contact between chemicals in injected water and the moveable oil. Likewise, the complete displacement of connate water is normally assumed for the flushed zone in well log interpretation. Unexpectedly, our investigation showed that most of the connate water in fractured low permeable rock was not viscously displaced by injected water. Flow tests were conducted with a highly water-wet Kansas outcrop chalk plug fractured along its axis. X-ray was used to monitor the movement of only connate water in the chalk matrix. Injected water in the fracture was observed to not outrun the imbibition front in the matrix. Water production at the outlet face of the plug did not occur until oil displacement was near completion. Most of the connate water was not banked by the imbibition process although some banking was observed. Continued water injection indicated that diffusion of the connate water salt from the fluids in the chalk matrix into the fluids flowing in the fracture appeared to be the most significant contributor to the movement of connate brine.

title: Relationships Between Non-Wetting Phase Invasion and Magnetization Evolution in Connected Pore Systems as Revealed by Network Simulation
caption: Figure 6. Scaling factor $\kappa$ used to convert NMR decay spectra to primary drainage capillary pressure curves. Data shown correspond to $0.10 < S_w < 0.80$ for Model 1 and $0.10 < S_w < 0.88$ for Model 2.
figure_reason: Shows the scaling factor k for converting NMR spectra to drainage capillary pressure, the central result.
tldr: Pore network simulations of primary drainage and magnetization decay show when diffusive pore coupling matters and that the T2-to-Pc scaling factor gives an apparent pore-to-throat aspect ratio.
summary: The paper uses cubic pore networks (15^3 pores, square throats, Weibull size distributions, 10 realizations) to link pore and throat size distributions to water distribution and NMR magnetization decay during primary drainage. Drainage is simulated by bond-correlated site percolation, with 6% of each invaded pore volume left as residual water in corners. Two models were studied: Model 1 with a narrow throat distribution overlapping the pores (459 mD) and Model 2 with a skewed throat distribution typical of sandstones (32.5 mD). Diffusive coupling is insignificant in Model 2 but clear in Model 1, where it narrows the decay spectrum, skews it to faster rates, and strengthens at low Sw. Scaling T2 distributions to drainage Pc curves gave a nearly constant k of about 4.7 for Model 1 (aspect ratio 2.2 vs actual 1.5) and a variable k for Model 2 (apparent aspect ratio 4.3 vs actual 2.7 at breakthrough), reflecting limited pore accessibility near the percolation threshold.
abstract: Pore network models are used to relate fundamental pore structure parameters (pore body and pore throat size distributions) to the distribution of water at the pore level and the decay of proton magnetization under conditions of primary drainage in water-wet rocks. The simulations reveal conditions under which diffusive coupling between pores has a significant effect on the decay spectra and provide insight into the estimation of primary drainage capillary pressure curves from NMR $T_2$ distributions. The conversion factor $k = P_c T_2$ required to map a NMR cumulative $T_2$ distribution at $S_w = 100\%$ onto a primary drainage capillary pressure curve furnishes important information about the pore-to-throat size aspect ratio, a parameter that critically affects recovery efficiency by waterflooding in water-wet media.

title: Static and Dynamic Measurements of Reservoir Heterogeneities in Carbonate Reservoirs
caption: Figure 11: Matrix-subtracted CT images of the 3 plug composite core from Well B after 0.2 PV of oil is injected into the 100% water-saturated core.
figure_reason: Matrix-subtracted CT images show non-uniform oil front and unswept region not predicted by porosity.
tldr: CT porosity distributions, NMR T2 and CT-monitored coreflooding of carbonate plugs are used to compute Lorenz and variation coefficients; porosity-based indicators miss saturation heterogeneity.
summary: The study characterizes static and dynamic heterogeneity in Jurassic carbonate plugs from two wells using CT, NMR T2, profile permeametry, SEM and conventional core data. A three-plug composite from Well B underwent ambient-condition oilflood and waterflood at 5 cc/min with CT scanning and image subtraction at several pore volumes injected. Lorenz coefficients for Well A varied from 0.74 for horizontal plugs to 0.40 for whole core, with a Dykstra-Parsons coefficient of 0.91. At plug scale, CT+NMR and CT+profile permeability Lorenz coefficients agreed (0.49 vs 0.50 for plug #248), while the FZI-based value was lowest (0.21). Oil flooding revealed an unswept region in the first plug that was not predictable from CT porosity alone. The coefficient of variation of CT saturation was lowest at highest water saturation and highest at lowest water saturation.
abstract: Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) technology has been in use in the medical industry for almost twenty years and like the CT it has been picked up by the oil industry to look inside the fluid-filled cores. For NMR measurements, the fluid-filled core is placed inside a sample chamber in a homogeneous magnetic field. With the application of two-dimensional magnetic field gradients, the longitudinal and transverse relaxation time curves ( $T_1$ and $T_2$ ) are measured as a function of position. NMR measurements provide a view of the pore system based primarily on the relaxation of nuclear spins at the pore surface. This mechanism provides data that can be used to correlate with permeability. Current models for the relaxation process and the corresponding permeability transform are based on the equations first proposed by Bloembergen et al. (1948).

title: Relative permeability, hysteresis and I-Sw measurements on a carbonate prospect
caption: Figure 6: hysteresis of relative permeability for oil and water; sample 1. First imbibition and secondary drainage.
figure_reason: Shows relative permeability hysteresis between first imbibition and secondary drainage for oil and water, a main result.
tldr: X-ray steady-state, γ-ray and centrifuge measurements on aged high-porosity carbonate show relative permeability hysteresis and a saturation exponent of 3 (versus 2.2 unaged), reconciling log and core water saturation.
summary: Logs in a high-porosity Middle East carbonate showed resistivities of 2000 Ωm, implying an unrealistic 1.5% connate water when using n=2.2 from water-wet continuous-injection tests. The authors used a modified X-ray steady-state apparatus with pressure and voltage probes to measure saturation and resistivity at several positions along aged cores (about 5 mD, 40% porosity), with decane replacing crude after washout. Steady-state and centrifuge oil relative permeabilities agreed, and high viscous pressures suppressed end effects; fitted centrifuge Sor was 0.13 versus 0.12 in steady state. Oil relative permeability was higher and water lower in secondary drainage than in first imbibition, consistent with mixed wettability. Aged plugs gave n≈3 in three samples, giving connate water of about 5% consistent with SCAL, with little I-Sw hysteresis.
abstract: We present SCAL measurements on a high porosity Middle East carbonate reservoir. The cores are aged with crude, and relative permeability is measured using an X-ray steady state, a $\gamma$ -ray steady state and the centrifuge technique. In the steady state we measured the primary imbibition and secondary drainage relative permeability curves of oil and water. Both resistivity and oil/water saturation can be measured along the core on different places, allowing the quantification of capillary end effects and its impact on resistivity. In the centrifuge we measured the imbibition oil relative permeability curve. The main points of interest are: - - Reconciling reservoir initial water saturation as obtained from logs and SCAL - - Wettability and relative permeability of aged samples - - Comparing I-Sw measurements from the continuous injection technique with resistivity measurements done in the X-ray steady state. - - Hysteresis in relative permeability and I-Sw between the imbibition and secondary drainage curves. We will show that the hysteresis in relative permeability is typical for a mixed-wet sample. After aging the samples $I$ - $S_w$ results show marginal hysteresis. For these mixed-wet samples we measured a high saturation exponent ( $n = 3$ ) compared to $n=2.2$ measured in the continuous injection method on water-wet samples taken from the same formation.

title: Early Water Breakthrough in Carbonate Core Samples Visualized with X-Ray CT
caption: Figure 6 – CT derived water saturation distribution during the waterflood on Berea sandstone (BD24).
figure_reason: CT saturation images contrasting water-wet shock front with mixed-wet fingering through porous laminae, the paper's central observation.
tldr: X-ray CT coreflood imaging and simulation of Berea and Middle East carbonate plugs show heterogeneous wettability, not super-k streaks, can cause early water breakthrough through porous laminae.
summary: Early water breakthrough in Middle East carbonate reservoirs is commonly attributed to super-permeability streaks, which cores and logs cannot confirm. The authors waterflooded a Berea plug (BD24) at 0.05 ml/min under water-wet and, after aging in crude, mixed-wet conditions, and an oil-wet carbonate plug (Io 0.86, Iw 0.04), using X-ray CT saturation monitoring. Water-wet Berea showed a piston-like Buckley-Leverett front with breakthrough at 0.32 PV. Mixed-wet Berea broke through at 0.2 PV and the oil-wet carbonate at 0.15 PV, with brine fingering through the most porous laminae. Simulations reproduced the fingering only by assigning different capillary pressure and relative permeability curves to laminae (low-porosity more oil-wet, high-porosity less oil-wet), not with uniform wettability and realistic permeability contrast.
abstract: In-situ saturation monitoring during a coreflood with X-ray CT scanner confirmed that the waterflood performance of a mixed-wet, or oil-wet, core plug is totally different from that of a water-wet core plug. Namely, it was observed that brine injected in the mixed-wet, or oil-wet, core plug preferentially invaded into more porous laminae, causing early water breakthrough at an outlet end. This result gives a significant insight into understanding the mechanism of unexpected early water production that has frequently been reported from some giant carbonate reservoirs in the Middle East. Many efforts have been made to grasp how such phenomenon took place. One of the most widely accepted explanations at present ascribes it to reservoir heterogeneities such as the existence of super-permeability streaks. A drawback of this super-permeability concept is, however, that neither cores nor conventional logs can detect such significant variation in permeability that has to be assumed to reproduce the early water breakthrough in a flow simulation model. Thus, in order to provide a better explanation, another factor that also controls the dynamic fluid flow in a reservoir may have to be considered; i.e., wettability. This paper, based upon results of both experimental and numerical studies, aims at associating the wettability distribution in a core sample with the early water breakthrough. First of all, a couple of coreflood experiments on a single Berea sandstone core plug were conducted under different wettability conditions; i.e., water-wet and mixed-wet. In-situ saturation distribution during each coreflood was monitored with the X-ray CT scanner, which visualized how the early water breakthrough took place within the mixed-wet plug. Then, the similar coreflood experiment was carried out on an oil-wet carbonate core sample taken from a certain reservoir in the Middle East. A numerical simulation study was carried out to reproduce the waterflood performance of each experiment in a computer model and, hence, to investigate the mechanism of the early water breakthrough observed at a core-scale. It was concluded from these studies that the local variation in wettability could exist within the mixed-wet and oil-wet samples. Namely, low porosity laminae are more oil-wet and high porosity laminae are more water-wet, or less oil-wet. As a result, the brine is preferentially imbibed in and runs through the less oil-wet laminae, causing the finger-shaped water encroachment and, finally, the early water breakthrough.

title: A Dual-Network Model of Pore Structure for Vuggy Carbonates
caption: Figure 5. (i) Effect of vug connectivity on primary drainage: (a) $\omega = 0.7$ , (b) $\omega = 0.8$ , (c) $\omega = 0.97$ . (ii) Effect of channel-vug size aspect ratio $R$ on primary drainage.
figure_reason: Simulated drainage curves showing effects of vug connectivity ω and aspect ratio R, the main model result.
tldr: A dual-network model superimposes partially connected vugs on a matrix continuum to simulate drainage in vuggy carbonates; Fletcher field core data qualitatively support it.
summary: Vuggy carbonates are hard to interpret because secondary porosity varies in amount, size and connectivity. The authors build a dual-network model of cubic matrix blocks with centered cubic vugs and throats, where vug connection probability depends on local vug porosity and a parameter ω. Invasion percolation simulations on 30³ blocks (matrix φ=0.03, k=2.72 mD) show breakthrough at 0.46–1.16 psi, far below the matrix breakthrough pressure of 59.2 psi, with plateau saturations depending on connectivity and throat aspect ratio R. Core tests on 17 Fletcher field dolomite plugs gave F=1.15φ^-1.72 (m≈1.72) and breakthrough pressure Pc=3.66k^-0.34, with a prefactor much lower than the ~16.8 for sandstones. Gas saturations at breakthrough were 20–43%, and mercury porosimetry on ~1 cm³ cubes showed heterogeneity in core #4. These results indicate a sample-spanning network of large secondary pores.
abstract: A dual-network model of the pore structure of vuggy carbonates is introduced and studied. The model combines small–scale pore structure information (porosity and pore size distribution) pertaining to the matrix, with X-ray CT porosity distributions, which provide information about secondary porosity at the scale of several millimeters (large scale). The dual network accounts for partial connectivity of and local constrictions in the secondary pore space. The model is constructed by superimposing vugs on blocks of matrix in agreement with a given porosity distribution. Core analysis results qualitatively support the new model as a tool to interpret the diverse transport and capillary behavior of vuggy carbonates.

title: Trapped Gas, Relative Permeability and Residual Oil Saturation of an Oil-Wet Sandstone1
caption: Figure 7 Data showing hysteresis behavior and impact of trapped gas in A-sand relative permeability data. Fit demonstrates how the hysteresis behavior is modeled.
figure_reason: Shows hysteresis and trapped-gas effect on water relative permeability in A-sand, with model fit.
tldr: Corefloods on preserved oil-wet sandstone show three-phase trapped gas is about half the two-phase value, trapped gas does not lower residual oil, and it suppresses water relative permeability.
summary: Three-phase flow in native-state oil-wet sandstones is poorly covered by existing relative permeability models. The authors ran waterfloods, gasfloods and waterfloods to trapped gas on preserved composite cores from two sands (A-sand and C-sand) at reservoir conditions, with JBN relative permeabilities, tracer tests and CT scanning. Three-phase trapped gas was about 11-13%, roughly half the two-phase values (about 20-22% at similar maximum gas saturation). A lower-rate flood and CT scans showed this was not capillary desaturation or gas redistribution. Residual oil to waterflood was unchanged by trapped gas, while water relative permeability fell markedly and showed hysteresis and water trapping. Compositional WAG simulations with the generalized Jerauld model showed that lower trapped gas reduces retained gas by about 9-35% depending on the process and reservoir description, with little change in oil recovery.
abstract: An experimental dataset from preserved reservoir sandstone is used to demonstrate features important to oil-wet systems not usually included in three-phase relative permeability models. They are described by a generalized version of the relative permeability model developed by Jerauld (1997). The sandstone reservoir studied shows large amounts of spontaneous imbibition of oil and traps water during secondary drainage. Oil relative permeability is almost a function of oil saturation alone while water relative permeability is significantly lower in the presence of trapped gas. The trapped gas level depends on the relative amounts of oil and water. While two-phase trapped gas values are consistent with values in the literature for similar sandstones, three-phase trapped gas levels are approximately half of two-phase levels. Residual oil saturations after waterflooding and gasflooding followed by waterflooding are roughly the same. Furthermore, the incremental oil production during a waterflood following gasflooding was minimal. Experiments run with different pressure drops show that the low trapped gas saturations are not due to capillary desaturation. CT scans show that little redistribution of gas occurs during trapping.

title: Significance of Absorption Coefficients When Determining In Situ Core Saturations by Linear X-ray Scans
caption: Figure 4. Pulse height distributions for a chalk plug saturated with decane and brine. Side (a) shows 52 kVp and 95 kVp results with 8% CsCl brine. Side (b) shows 52 kVp results with 8% KBr brine.
figure_reason: Pulse height distributions for brine/decane saturations show beam hardening and brine contrast at 52 and 95 kV.
tldr: Applies Lambert's equation directly with fluid absorption coefficients to compute two- and three-phase saturations from polychromatic linear x-ray scans, showing narrow energy integration minimizes beam-hardening errors.
summary: Many labs use heuristic correlations between ln(intensity) and saturation in linear x-ray scans, which fail when fluid density or composition changes. The authors present a corollary of Lambert's equation using emergent reference intensities, with closed-form solutions (Cramer's rule) for two- and three-phase saturations using one, two or three energy ranges. Using a dry North Sea chalk plug scanned at 52 kV and 95 kV in a carbon-fiber coreholder at 70 bar, they calculated pulse-height spectra for CsCl or KBr brine, decane and nitrogen saturations with XCOM absorption coefficients. Integrating intensity over wide energy ranges introduces saturation errors between endpoints due to beam hardening, while narrow or symmetric ranges give calculated saturations within about 0.001-0.01 of true values. Guidance is given for reservoir-condition tests, including measuring fluid absorption coefficients in a separator and correcting for confining fluid density changes.
abstract: Linear x-ray scanners are increasingly used to measure fluid saturations in cores during laboratory tests. Reasons include the expanding need to model and measure complex reservoir-condition fluid-flow behavior in the laboratory, availability of readymade scanners from commercial suppliers, and regulatory and safety issues that limit the applicability of other types of radiation emitting sources. Lambert's equation is recognized as a basis for understanding x-ray absorption phenomena. This equation relates the intensity of an x-ray beam that emerges from an absorber to the incident beam intensity, absorption coefficients and thickness of absorbers that the beam passes through. Although this relationship is well understood, many x-ray "practitioners" resort to heuristic approaches that correlate emergent beam intensity directly to fluid saturation. Heuristic approaches suffice for relatively simple tests, but are inappropriate when fluid densities and compositions change during a test. Under such circumstances, advantages are gained using a form of Lambert's equation directly with consideration for changes in absorption coefficients. This paper provides a bridge between x-ray theory and practical applications. Knowledge gained can significantly improve experimental designs and x-ray data analyses such that more accurate saturation measurements can be obtained during difficult reservoir condition tests. Differences among absorption coefficients described in the literature for monochromatic x-rays and those measured in the lab from a polychromatic beam are described. An understanding of these differences provides one with the ability to predict how intensities of polychromatic x-rays will change during a test depending upon compositions, densities, and thickness of absorbers. Simple equations are presented for calculating two- and three-phase saturations from x-ray data.

title: Including Capillary Pressure in Simulations of Steady State Relative Permeability Experiments
caption: Figure 10 O2B history-matched and simulations Figure 11 Saturation profiles at at different total flow rate: 0.5-16 ml/min. fo=0.99 for exp. O2B simulation
figure_reason: Shows O2B history-matched kr curves and rate dependence with and without capillary pressure, plus saturation profiles, the central result.
tldr: Steady-state two- and three-phase floods on water-wet sandstone were history-matched with and without capillary pressure, showing capillarity biases oil relative permeability and three-phase flow raises kro and lowers Sor.
summary: Two series of steady-state floods were run on a 17.95 cm composite water-wet North Sea sandstone core (about 100 mD, porosity 29.9%) with brine, n-decane and N2 at 1 ml/min, 20 bar and 40 °C. Relative permeabilities were first calculated with Darcy's law neglecting capillary pressure, then two-phase experiments were history-matched with a semi-analytical steady-state simulator including measured Pc. Including capillary pressure shifted oil relative permeability noticeably even though the rate met standard Rapoport-Leas criteria; neglecting it underestimated kro. Rate studies (0.5–16 ml/min) showed capillary influence on kro for N_RL < 9 in imbibition and N_RL < 18 in drainage, with no rate window avoiding both capillary effects and viscous instability in drainage. Three-phase data (calculated neglecting Pc) showed higher kro at low oil saturation, reduced water kr in imbibition-type processes, and lower residual oil than two-phase flow.
abstract: Two series of steady state core floods have been performed on composite reservoir core material. The rock material was from a water wet sandstone, with a permeability of 100 mD. The core flood experiments include two-phase water-oil drainage and imbibition processes, and in addition three-phase steady state experiments. Usually, relative permeability is calculated from steady state experiments neglecting capillary pressure. The two-phase drainage and imbibition experiments were modeled using a steady state simulator. Relative permeability including and excluding capillary pressure were estimated. Relative permeability showed considerable differences even though the selected flow rate for the experiments was within the standard scaling criteria for water flooding. Water relative permeability was not distinctly affected by capillarity. The critical rate for neglecting capillarity in these experiments has been estimated for the two-phase drainage and imbibition type steady state experiments. Oil and water relative permeability from the three-phase steady-state experiments have been compared to the data from the two-phase steady-state experiments. Both oil and water relative permeability was generally affected by three-phase flow. The water relative permeability was considerable lower for three-phase flow compared to two-phase wateroil. The oil relative permeability was higher for three-phase flow compared to two-phase water-oil, and the three-phase residual oil saturation was found to be substantially lower than the two-phase residual oil saturation.

title: SCAL : An Indispensable Step for Formation Damage Evaluation
caption: Figure 6: Comparison of return permeabilties – WBM vs IEM.
figure_reason: Shows return permeability versus distance from inlet for WBM and IEM, the key damage comparison.
tldr: Dynamic mud leak-off tests on 40 cm sandstone cores compare 8 muds and cleanup breakers; invert emulsion muds damage less, and IEM breakers worsen damage.
summary: The paper presents an IFP laboratory methodology to simulate drilling mud invasion on long cores (5 cm diameter, up to 40 cm) with dynamic filtration, pressure taps along the core and oil backflow to measure return permeability. Study 1 tested five water-based and three invert emulsion muds on high-permeability Vosges sandstone. WBM gave global return permeabilities of 11-39% with severe damage (8-22%) in the first 5 cm, partly from trapped filtrate. IEM gave 68-94%, with local return permeabilities above 100% at 10-30 cm, possibly from reduced connate water; surfactants cut IFT by a factor of up to 45. Study 2 on Vosges and Berea cores showed WBM breakers (NaOCl, enzyme) raised ultimate return permeability by 10-26%, whereas IEM breakers (EGMBE, emulsified acid, surfactants) added damage of 6-48% IRP and 7-30% URP, so natural cleanup is recommended for IEM.
abstract: The impact of wellbore formation damage on the economic viability of a field development is becoming increasingly widely accepted by the oil industry. Productivity losses due to permeability damage generated by drilling and completion operations are of main concern specially for long horizontal open hole completed wells in which the near wellbore damage is not by-passed by perforations. Formation damage evaluation from specific laboratory tests becomes a large part of the SCAL activities and many papers have focussed on this area of research. This paper is a contribution to i) understand mechanisms of drilling mud and mud filtrate invasion, ii) quantify drilling-induced permeability damage and iii) evaluate the performance of various cleanup procedures to restore the near wellbore flow properties. Specific laboratory equipment and procedures derived from techniques used in SCAL were developed to evaluate filtration properties of drilling muds and permeability damage generated by the wellbore invasion. The performance of 8 mud formulations (Water-Based Mud (WBM) and Invert Emulsion Mud (IEM)) was evaluated on 40 cm long sandstone core samples. Then, a comparative study aimed at determining the efficiency of various cleanup treatments using specific "breakers" to remediate filter cakes has been performed on core samples damaged either with a polymeric Water-Based Mud or an Invert Emulsion Mud. Results shows that the IEM's present better filtration properties and are less damaging than the WBM's tested here. Specific WBM "breakers" (enzymes, oxidants) are efficient and may restore a large part of the initial damage. On the other hand, breakers for IEM (surfactants, emulsified acid, solvents) may create additional damage if the breaker is allowed to invade the formation. Finally, some recommendations are given to design laboratory tests for evaluating drilling-induced formation damage and for restoring near wellbore flow properties.

title: Potential Effects of Current and Future Drilling Fluid Systems on Core Analysis
caption: Fig. 5. 1 H (2 MHz)-NMR T2 relaxation time distributions of sandstone samples after exposure to the oil-based fluid and to the WBM Glycol.
figure_reason: Shows T2 distributions of sandstone after oil-based mud and WBM Glycol exposure, the key NMR contrast.
tldr: Outcrop sandstone and chalk plugs were invaded with 0.5 PV of four drilling fluid filtrates; water-based filtrates cut mobile oil recovery and shortened NMR T2.
summary: The study examines how water-based (carbonate, glycol, silicate) and oil-based drilling fluids alter core analysis results. Blaxters sandstone and Liege chalk plugs were restored to Swi with crude oil, exposed to 0.5 PV of filtrate at 80°C, then given Amott/USBM wettability tests, NMR relaxometry at 2 and 10 MHz, and NMR imaging. Most of the wettability shift in sandstone (Amott index from 0.9 to near neutral) came from ageing in crude, not mud. Glycol and carbonate water-based filtrates strongly reduced mobile oil recovery in sandstone (about 44-55% versus 76% baseline), whereas silicate and oil-based mud left it near baseline. Water-based filtrates lowered NMR porosity and shifted T2 to shorter times, while oil-based mud lengthened T2. NMR imaging T2 profiles showed the filtrate distribution in a plug.
abstract: The contamination of reservoir core samples by drilling fluid filtrate reduces the volume of rock for core analysis. Filtrate invasion causes changes in rock properties that potentially can affect core analysis measurements and, thus, reserve calculations. The objective of the study was to provide experimental data on the influence of drilling fluids on core analysis measurements and to raise consciousness on possible consequences. bility. lighted. Four drilling fluid systems were selected for investigations. The selection was based on statistical evaluations of the most frequently used drilling fluid systems in the Norwegian North Sea in the period from 1995 to 1997 as well as assumptions regarding the requirements of future field developments. The fluids comprised three water-based drilling fluids (WBM Carbonate, WBM Glycol, WBM Silicate) and one invert emulsion oil-based drilling fluid. The study was performed on outcrop core material. The experimental set-up simulated aspects of rock/fluid interaction occurring during the coring of a reservoir on small scale (core plugs). Two lithologies, Blaxters sandstone and Liege Chalk, were investigated. Core plug samples were artificially restored with synthetic brine and crude oil to represent reservoir fluid saturations. Drilling fluid exposure experiments were performed at elevated temperature and pressure. To compensate for different filter loss properties, fluid exposure experiments lasted until 0.5 PV of mud filtrate had invaded the core plug sample. For each lithology a Special Core Analysis (SCAL) programme was performed as a "Baseline" study on undamaged/unexposed sample material and on material after the drilling fluid exposure experiment. The SCAL programme was extended by Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) Relaxometry and Magnetic Resonance Imaging to examine effects of the drilling fluids on NMR measurements and to characterise the local distribution of fluids in the core plug samples, respectively. The study showed that under equal capillary endpoint pressure conditions the amount of oil recovery from core plugs is strongly affected by water-based filtrate residues. Results demonstrate a potential for miscalculations of the producible oil volumes and erroneously low reservoir produci- NMR-relaxation time measurements on core plug samples contaminated with different water-based and oil-based drilling fluids showed significant differences. Interpretations of NMR relaxation spectra affected by the invasion of water-based drilling fluid filtrate may lead to an underestimation of the free-fluid porosity as the relaxation times significantly shift to shorter values. Near wellbore zones in chalk formations invaded by oil-based drilling fluid filtrate would respond with a signal indicating larger oil volumes than actually present. Further general conclusions of the study and recommended compensating measures are high- 1 Now SINTEF Unimed MR Center, Trondheim, Norway

title: Resistivity Index Measurements Under Weak Capillary Forces
caption: Fig. 5 Simulated resistivity index plots at several capillary pressure gradients
figure_reason: Simulated resistivity index plots at several capillary pressure gradients show how weak gradients cause curvature and error.
tldr: Shows that continuous-injection resistivity index tests can be distorted by Buckley-Leverett shock fronts under weak capillary gradients, and proposes design criteria and an X-ray steady-state alternative.
summary: Continuous injection (CI) resistivity index measurements assume a flat saturation profile, which requires a capillary gradient strong enough to suppress a Buckley-Leverett shock front. Using an approximate analytical model and simulations, the authors show that weak capillary gradients give curved log-log I-Sw plots and saturation errors of 20 or more saturation units. They derive approximate criteria for a maximum oil injection rate (viscous vs capillary) and for gravity stability, and verify the rate criterion by simulation. They recommend checking designs against Hg-air capillary pressure and relative permeability estimates, and varying rate on the fly if curvature appears. As an alternative, an X-ray steady-state apparatus with multiple electrodes measures resistivity against local saturation, typically giving about 10 points in under two weeks and agreeing with CI where CI is valid.
abstract: For log calibration, saturation exponents are determined in the laboratory through resistivity index measurements. Commonly, the well-known continuous injection (CI) technique is employed: oil is injected into a brine-saturated core. The standard measurement protocol calls for the resistivity to be measured across the sample and plotted versus the average brine saturation as determined by material balance. This method hinges on the assumption that the saturation profile in the sample is flat, i.e. the local saturation at each point in the sample equals the average saturation. Since at the injection-end the oil saturation tends to be highest, one has to rely on the presence of a capillary pressure gradient that will flatten the saturation profile. By keeping the injection rate low, capillary forces may dominate viscous forces and achieve the required effect. This contribution starts out to discuss simulations of experiments that show how certain rock may never produce the right data in a CI experiment. When a low capillary gradient occurs, a so-called Buckley-Leverett shock front travels through the sample during CI, and the I-Sw relationship has a distinct curvature on a log-log plot. A significant deviation from the true I-Sw relationship will result in an erroneous saturation log calibration. Subsequently, we show how the Steady-State technique can be employed to overcome this measurement artefact. With this technique, water and oil are injected simultaneously and the development of a shock front is kept under control. The saturation distribution in the sample is measured through X-ray absorption. Resistivity is measured using electrodes along the sample. By varying the ratio of the injected water and oil, different saturations can be achieved and a resistivity plot generated. Corrections due to the removal of the CI measurement artefact may amount to saturation shifts by 20 or more saturation units.

title: The H&B Boundary Condition in Centrifuge PC Experiments. (or Why There Is No Experimental Evidence That the Pressure Field Model Ever Failed)
caption: Figure 6 : Capillary pressure curves from ultrasonic measurements (Forbes et al., 1992).
figure_reason: Shows Pc curves from ultrasonic in-situ saturation measurements against the standard centrifuge interpretation, supporting the boundary condition.
tldr: Re-examines published evidence against the Hassler-Brunner zero-capillary-pressure boundary condition in centrifuge Pc tests and shows it is explained by the full radial pressure field and interpretation errors.
summary: The paper reviews literature claims that the Hassler and Brunner outflow boundary condition fails in centrifuge capillary pressure measurements, including end-face desaturation and differences from footbath or porous plate results. Using a full pressure field model with radial and gravity effects, Pc=0 occurs only at the edge of the bottom face, so partial end-face desaturation is expected. Re-interpreting the CT data of Baardsen et al. reproduces desaturation onset at 1000-1250 RPM and removes the mismatch with the CT-derived Pc curves. Modelling Wunderlich's epoxy-casting data reproduces the saturation profiles, the heights of 100% saturation (0.63, 0.13 and 0.04 cm at 500, 1000 and 1500 RPM) and end-face desaturation at 2000-2500 RPM. Bil's footbath differences of 0 to 6 saturation units are attributed to using the same interpretation model for different geometries. Pore-scale instability and pendant-drop mechanisms are judged too small to matter at normal speeds, and the author concludes that the standard technique is reliable when correctly interpreted.
abstract: Since Hassler and Brunner developed the measurement of Capillary Pressures by centrifuging, it has been exposed to critical concerns. Several authors proposed “experimental” evidences for its failure either by showing desaturation at the core bottom face during centrifuging, or by showing that the current procedure provides results different that those related to “improved” processes. Herein, one revisits assumptions on the pressure field in centrifuge experiments. It is shown that desaturations reported in the literature are consistent with these assumptions. One explains why some authors reported desaturation to occur at normal centrifugal speeds, while others expected it only at unusual speeds, based on thermodynamics or physics at the pore scale. Differences observed when various ways are used for determining the capillary pressure curve are explained too. The so-called “evidences for the failure of the current centrifuge technique” are the results of interpretation problems. No clear evidence of a failure has been found.

title: Capillary Transition Zones from a Core Analysis Perspective
caption: Figure 4. ROS and oil recovery as function of HMOS. (a) The residual oil saturation is plotted as function of the historical maximum oil saturation along the core. Scatter in the data is due to capillary effects at the joining region between core elements and the capillary end-effect. The Land relation is shown with Land constants of 1, 2 and 5. (b) The oil recovery is calculated as percent of the
figure_reason: Shows ROS and oil recovery versus HMOS with Land fits and literature data, the main experimental result.
tldr: Gravity-drained one-metre Berea composite core with X-ray saturation monitoring shows residual oil depends on initial oil saturation and permeability; Killough hysteresis simulations reproduce waterflood profiles.
summary: The paper addresses flow in oil-water capillary transition zones, where residual oil saturation (ROS) depends on the historical maximum oil saturation (HMOS). A 95 cm vertical Berea composite core (five elements, ~100 and ~700 mD) was primary-drained by gravity using decane and NaI-doped brine, taking 2.5 months, then waterflooded from the bottom with X-ray in-situ saturation monitoring. ROS versus HMOS followed a Land-type relation, with C≈5 at low HMOS and ≈2 at high HMOS, so a single constant overpredicts ROS at low HMOS. Recovery was about 58% at HMOS 0.6 falling to 45% at 0.2 for the high-permeability Berea, and lower for the low-permeability Berea, so the Land constant depends on permeability (2 versus 3 in simulation). Simulations with Killough hysteresis in oil relative permeability and capillary pressure predicted the dynamic saturation profiles well, whereas bounding-curve or end-point-scaled models matched poorly.
abstract: The capillary transition zone in a reservoir containing oil and water is located between the oil-water contact and the level where irreducible water is present. In low permeability reservoirs or in situations where the oil and water densities are similar, the transition zone can be extended to cover a vertical distance up to around a hundred meters As the water saturation varies with the vertical distance in the transition zone, relative permeabilities and the capillary pressure must be determined by incorporating hysteresis in the flow functions. Special care should be taken in performing core-flow experiments in order to obtain relevant flow functions at different positions in the transition zone. Generally, both relative permeabilities and capillary pressure becomes a function of the connate water saturation in the transition zone. The amount of mobile oil should be found in the general case by a correlation between initial oil saturation and residual oil saturation. This paper will focus on experimental data, showing the impact of a water injection in an oil-water transition zone. The transition zone is obtained by gravity drainage of water by oil in an one metre, vertically oriented Berea composite core. An imbibition process is performed by injecting water from the bottom of the core. During this gravity stable water injection, the water front is (dynamically) monitored by X-ray in-situ saturation measurements. The remaining oil saturation after water injection is found as a function of height at various positions in the core and correlated to the initial oil saturation at the start of water injection. The novel data confirms a Land-type correlation between initial and remaining oil saturation. However, a high recovery, that cannot be predicted by the Land correlation, is observed for very low initial oil saturations. It is also found that the correlation between initial oil saturation and remaining oil saturation is dependent on the permeability in water-wet Berea. The dynamical in-situ saturation measurements are reproduced by numerical modelling incorporating Killough hysteresis in the oil relative permeability and capillary pressure functions.

title: Mercury Porosimetry Protocol for Rapid Determination of Petrophysical and Reservoir Quality Properties
caption: Figure 3. Sample bulk volume dilation affects capillary pressure data; no dilation correction (open squares), dilation correction at initial Hg entry (solid diamonds), and dilation correction at final Hg entry (solid circle).
figure_reason: Shows how bulk volume dilation corrections change capillary pressure curves for a compressible high-entry-pressure sample.
tldr: Presents practical protocols for high-pressure mercury injection capillary pressure testing, covering jacketing, blank and closure corrections, sample dilation in compressible rocks, and unconsolidated sands.
summary: High-pressure MICP (to 60,000 psia) can rapidly screen drainage capillary pressure and reservoir quality, but data validity depends on sample preparation and corrections. The paper discusses sample size, 1-D versus 3-D drainage (radial jacketing), mercury contact angle (140° vs 180°, a factor of 1.30), blank cell corrections, and closure pressure selection. Using operator-generated quartz blank correction instead of formula lowered MICP porosity by about 5% for sandstone (31.2 to 29.8%) and 26% for shale (3.66 to 2.71%). For compressible high-entry-pressure samples (0.03 md example, bulk compressibility ~20 microsips), unaccounted bulk dilation after mercury entry makes closure selection subjective and can produce pessimistic capillary pressure curves and low porosities. For unconsolidated sands, frozen plugs are jacketed with Teflon and nickel-alloy foil with end screens, and screen mesh must be matched to filling pressure and sample entry pressure to avoid erroneous porosity. MICP can be compared with grain-size-derived pore aperture distributions, but clay-bearing samples give optimistic curves relative to porous plate or centrifuge data.
abstract: Dean-Stark water saturation data can provide an indication of the appropriate Archie parameters to use in early log analysis prior to obtaining centrifuge or porous plate primary drainage capillary pressure and electrical property data. But this is only true if the core water saturation is unaltered during coring and the cored interval is structurally high enough to be above the transitional zone. Alternatively, high-pressure (to 60,000 psia) mercury injection capillary pressure (MICP) can quickly provide drainage capillary pressure properties of samples and assist in early log analysis and reservoir quality assessment. This paper focuses on experimental protocol for obtaining valid MICP data, particularly when dealing with friable-to-unconsolidated sands and compressible high entry pressure clastics and carbonates. Important protocol issues include proper sample preparation for varying sample types, with poorly consolidated sands being radially jacketed with metallic foil and capped with properly sized end screens. Samples should preferably be radially jacketed to obtain 1-D drainage capillary pressure data. High pressure MICP requires a "blank sample" MICP correction data for glass cell and sample grain compressibility factors. High entry pressure compressible samples such as chalks, diatomite, and kerogen-rich carbonates can have apparent MICP-measured porosities significantly less than core porosities. Mercury injection capillary pressure data from representative core sampling can provide a rapid indication of ranges in the various petrophysical and reservoir quality properties of the various lithologies. This preliminary "screening" will also assist in the optimization of follow-up special core analysis program involving significantly greater measurement costs and completion times.

title: An Automatic-Optimization Data Analysis Technique Based On Forbes' Second Method
caption: Figure 3a Production Error SCA Case 3
figure_reason: Case 3 production error shows the largest improvement over F2, with RMS falling from 0.166 to 0.015.
tldr: Extends Chen-Ruth automatic optimization to Forbes' Second Method by fitting three parameters, removing analyst hand-correction and improving centrifuge capillary pressure production fits on ten SCA survey cases.
summary: Forbes' Second Method for reducing centrifuge capillary pressure data normally needs analyst hand-correction, making results operator dependent. The authors treat its three theoretically fixed parameters (a, b, g) as fitting variables and optimize them simultaneously to minimize the RMS difference between measured and simulated production. They tested the method on the 10 synthetic SCA Data Analysis Survey cases from Forbes (1997), using radial correction and minimal consistency constraints. The new method reduced production RMS error in all cases, sometimes markedly (e.g. Case 3 from 0.166 to 0.015), but the match to the true capillary curve improved significantly only in Case 3. Of 115 points, only 12 failed Forbes' 3-saturation-unit additional-error criterion, 8 of them in Cases 6 and 7. Optimal parameters can deviate substantially from theoretical values, and in several cases the method reduces to the Chen-Ruth method.
abstract: There are many methods to reduce centrifuge data to obtain capillary pressure curves. One of the most accurate methods, according to a recent survey conducted by SCA, is Forbes' Second Method. A full implementation of this method requires the manipulation of the results by the analyst to minimize the error between the experimentally measured production versus rotational speed and the production versus rotational speed predicted using the calculated capillary curve. The final curve obtained using this method can therefore be dependent on the experience and talent of the analyst. Chen and Ruth have published a technique based on Forbes' Alpha Method; their technique implements an automatic-optimization procedure, rather than an operator dependent procedure, to minimize the difference between the two production histories. Forbes' method contains a parameter that has a fixed value based on the configuration of the centrifuge; in theory, this value is optimized. The Chen-Ruth technique treats this parameter as a variable and optimizes it to minimize the root-mean-square difference between the production histories. The present paper reports on a study where this idea was extended to Forbes' Second Method. Forbes's Second Method contains three parameters that are theoretically optimized. By making these parameters variable and optimizing them simultaneously, it is shown that very good predictions for the SCA Data Analysis Survey can be obtained.

title: Influence of Heterogeneity, Wettability and Coreflood Design on Relative Permeability Curves
caption: Figure 9 : Imbibition capillary pressure curves
figure_reason: Shows the permeability-dependent imbibition capillary pressure curves for weakly water-wet and oil-wet cases that drive the heterogeneous waterflood simulations.
tldr: Numerical waterflood experiments show that along-bedding heterogeneity biases relative permeability from coreflood inversion, while across-bedding flow gives reliable curves if local permeability and saturation profiles are included.
summary: Most coreflood interpretations assume homogeneous samples, yet small-scale heterogeneity can bias relative permeability. The authors review experimental methods for detecting heterogeneity, then simulate unsteady- and steady-state waterfloods on finely gridded 2D models, along and across bedding, and invert the synthetic production and pressure data for Kr. Along-bedding flow is the riskiest: unsteady-state inversion is badly biased, and steady-state is more robust but still pessimistic. Across-bedding flow gives near-true Kr curves when capillary forces are negligible. With significant capillary forces, multi-rate unsteady-state floods in weakly water-wet or oil-wet samples recover true Kr if local permeability and in-situ saturation profiles are used, as in the oil-wet case where Sorw was 0.31 versus a true 0.25 unless local Sorw was used.
abstract: This paper focuses on the effect of small-scale heterogeneity on the laboratory determination of relative permeability curves. Both the experimental characterisation and the influence of heterogeneity on numerical interpretation of corefloods are addressed. The combined effects of small-scale heterogeneity, flow direction and wettability are studied using numerical experiments. Along bedding (i.e "horizontal plugs") and across bedding (i.e "vertical plugs") waterfloods are simulated using very finely gridded, two dimensional models and input relative permeabilities (Kr). Both steady-state and unsteady-state flows are simulated. Output water and oil production, differential pressure as well as local saturation profiles are obtained. Then these results are used as input for determination of relative permeability curves, using inversion techniques. The main conclusions of this study are: - 1. Detailed and reliable characterisation of small-scale heterogeneity can be routinely obtained on vertical consolidated cores. Three dimensional imaging techniques or tracer tests must be applied to horizontal consolidated cores to estimate the permeability of streaks parallel to the flow direction. Simplified and approximate estimates of permeability maps can be obtained on unconsolidated cores using inversion techniques. - 2. Unsteady-state flow is very sensitive to along-axis heterogeneity and must be disregarded in heterogeneous "horizontal" plugs. In these samples, steady-state flow is more robust but does not reproduce the true relative permeability curves. - 3. Unsteady-state or steady-state flows are almost indifferent to along-axis heterogeneity when capillary forces are negligible. - 4. When negative capillary forces become significant, true Kr curves can be extracted from unsteady-state flows in heterogeneous "vertical" plugs provided that one dimensional (1D) permeability and saturation profiles are available.

title: by
caption: Figure 3a Production Match
figure_reason: Compares simulated oil production with the correlation for the base case, the central validation result.
tldr: Simulations of 1D counter-current spontaneous imbibition in water-wet Berea-type cores largely agree with an experimental scaling correlation, including viscosity ratio and initial water saturation effects.
summary: The paper tests a semi-empirical imbibition time-scaling correlation (modified Mattax and Kyte) against a finite-difference simulator of 1D counter-current imbibition, with capillary pressure as the sole driving force. The base case uses Berea-like properties (600 mD, porosity 0.215, 5.08 cm long) with Corey relative permeabilities and a logarithmic capillary pressure curve, history-matched to the correlation. Permeability, porosity, length and interfacial tension scale exactly, and oil viscosity from 0.97 to 156 cp agrees closely. Varying capillary pressure shape, water and oil relative permeability endpoints and exponents changes dimensionless time by less than about an order of magnitude. Initial water saturation of 0 to 30% changes imbibition rate in a manner qualitatively similar to experiments on chalk, and very high viscosity ratios (gas displaced by oil) show trends consistent with experiment.
abstract: Imbibition is an important phenomenon in many displacement processes. In particular, the transfer of liquids between fissures and the matrix in fractured reservoirs is dominated by imbibition. Re-examination of published results and new experimental data has resulted in a modified version of the Mattax and Kyte time-scaling that includes variations in water-oil viscosity ratio, sample shape, and boundary conditions. The resulting semi-empirical scaling group can be compared with simulations based on the mechanics of two-phase flow with capillary pressure as the driving force. This paper presents the results of a simulation study of one-dimensional, counter-current imbibition in a strongly water-wet sample. As a first step, the generalized correlation for production was history-matched using core and fluid properties for which imbibition results have been reported. Initial water saturation was assumed to be zero. A logarithmic form was assumed for the capillary pressure curve and Corey equations were assumed for the relative permeability curves. A close match of oil recovery was obtained between the experimental data and the simulated imbibition. The core and fluid properties were systematically modified to test sensitivities. Variations in permeability, porosity, sample length and diameter, and interfacial tension were scaled exactly by the simulation. For oil viscosities in the range covered by the experimental data, agreement was good but not exact. The study was then extended to investigate the effects of varying capillary pressure curve shape, relative permeability, and initial water saturation, properties not explicitly included in the scaling group. For these simulations, the basic shapes of the oil-production-versus-time curves were essentially preserved. Overall agreement with the correlation was satisfactory. The initial water saturation was varied between 0% and 30% and the production curves were normalized with respect to the mobile oil saturation. Saturation profiles are presented which illustrate the simulated effect of initial water saturation on the imbibition process.

title: Impacts of Wettability on Oil Recovery in Fractured Carbonate Reservoirs
caption: Fig.5 Comparison of experimental, left two columns, and simulated, rightmost two columns, in-situ saturation development for the second waterflood of the strongly water-wet block CHP-12.
figure_reason: Side-by-side experimental and simulated in-situ saturation maps for fractured strongly water-wet block, showing validation of the simulator.
tldr: Nuclear-tracer 2D imaging of waterfloods in whole and fractured chalk blocks at two wettabilities, history-matched with a simulator, shows similar recovery but different recovery mechanisms.
summary: The study examines how wettability affects waterflood recovery in fractured carbonate using large Rørdal chalk blocks (about 20x10x5 cm), made strongly or moderately water-wet (Amott-Harvey Iw 0.4-0.8) by aging in crude oil at 90°C. Blocks were waterflooded whole and then with embedded or interconnected fracture networks, while 22Na and 60Co tracers imaged injected and in-situ water saturations in 2D. Recovery was similar for both wettabilities when the permeability increase after fracturing was low (about 42%PV oil in strongly water-wet CHP-12, versus 32%PV in fractured moderately water-wet CHP-14, with a permeability increase of about 11). At strongly water-wet conditions fractures held up the water front by capillary hold-up, whereas at moderately water-wet conditions water crossed the fractures early. SENSOR simulations matched best with measured Pc and optimized kr, and including wettability heterogeneity improved the match for CHP-14. Matching also required more capillary contact across fractures at less water-wet conditions, suggesting an additional mechanism not in the model.
abstract: Visualization of the effects of various wettability conditions on oil recovery in fractured carbonate reservoirs is demonstrated in two-dimensional in-situ imaging experiments in large blocks of chalk and by numerical simulations. Recovery mechanisms are shown to change with a change in wettability. Iterative comparison between experimental work and numerical simulations has been used to predict oil recovery mechanisms in fractured chalk as a function of wettability. Selective alteration of wettability, by aging in crude oil at elevated temperature, produced chalk blocks which were strongly-water-wet and moderately-water-wet, but with identical pore geometry. Large scale, nuclear-tracer, 2D-imaging experiments monitored waterflooding the blocks of chalk, first whole then fractured. Capillary pressure and relative permeabilities at each given wettability were experimentally measured and used as input for the simulations. Mixing of injection water and in-situ water was determined both for unfractured and fractured reservoirs by labelling the waters with different nuclear tracers. A simulator for fractured reservoirs has been validated by large scale experiments with 2D in-situ imaging information. Experimentally obtained capillary pressure (Pc) and relative permeability (Kr) -input data to the simulator have been evaluated by history matching in-situ saturation distribution development as well as the production profile. For a low permeability increase after fracturing, for both unfractured and fractured chalk, the amount and rate of oil recovery by waterflooding were similar for strongly-water-wet and moderately-water-wet conditions, but the in-situ saturation distributions are shown to be significantly affected by the wettability conditions. This indicates that the recovery mechanisms change towards more viscous dominant flow regimes at less water-wet conditions.

title: Oil Recovery by Spontaneous Imbibition from Weakly Water-Wet Rocks
caption: Fig.7 The relationship between Swi and imbibition time for 50% oil recovery. Insert shows effect of epoxy resin on imbibition by AFO cores.
figure_reason: Shows 50% recovery scaled time versus Swi for AFO and partially sealed cores, plus epoxy effect insert.
tldr: Tests whether a characteristic-length imbibition scaling group works for weakly water-wet Berea cores; initial water saturation dominates rate, and epoxy sealing during aging reduces water-wetness.
summary: The study tests a semi-empirical imbibition scaling group, developed for very strongly water-wet rock, under weakly water-wet conditions. Thirty-two Berea sandstone cores (about 450 md, 20% porosity) of cylindrical, annular and rectangular shape, some partially sealed with epoxy, were set to Swi of 14-31% and aged in Alaska 95 crude at 55°C for 10 days. Spontaneous imbibition of brine at room temperature showed that imbibition times rose by orders of magnitude as Swi decreased. Scaling with the characteristic length Lc correlated cores of different size, shape and boundary conditions well when Swi was held within a narrow range. Cores sealed with epoxy were less water-wet than all-faces-open cores, which an aging test with a separate resin block confirmed. At 20% Swi the 50% recovery time was about 514 times that for very strongly water-wet rock, and gravity could become significant if capillary pressure fell by about three orders of magnitude.
abstract: Spontaneous imbibition is of special importance to oil recovery from fractured reservoirs. Laboratory measurements of volume of liquid imbibed versus time are often used in the prediction of oil recovery. Imbibition measurements also provide a useful approach to the complex problem of characterizing the wetting properties of porous media. Correlation of a large body of data for imbibition of brine into porous media initially saturated with refined oil was achieved through a semi-empirical scaling group which includes permeability, porosity, interfacial tension, oil and brine viscosity, and the size, shape and boundary conditions of the sample. The objective of the present study was to test this correlation for samples of different geometry for spontaneous imbibition under weakly water-wet conditions established by adsorption from crude oil with initial water saturation ranging from 14% to 31%. After establishing initial water saturations, the wettability of thirty-two core samples was changed to weakly water-wet by aging in an asphaltic crude oil at elevated temperature. Initial water saturation had a dominant effect on rate of oil recovery. Times for imbibition decreased by about 2 to 4 orders of magnitude with decrease in initial water saturation. Results for cores with the same initial water saturation but of different size and shape (cylindrical, annular, and rectangular) and boundary conditions (given by sealing off part of the rock surface with epoxy resin) were closely correlated. The presence of epoxy resin during aging in crude oil enhanced the decrease in water-wetness attained for cores and crude oil alone. The contribution to oil recovery by gravity segregation at very weakly water-wet conditions is addressed.

title: New Coreflood Interpretation Method Based on Direct Processing of in-Situ Saturation Data
caption: Figure 6 Interpreted water fractional flow for unsteady state test
figure_reason: Shows interpreted water fractional flow from noisy synthetic unsteady-state data versus the original curve, demonstrating method performance.
tldr: A direct method (dyrectSCAL) computes fractional flow, capillary dispersion and relative permeability from in-situ saturation profiles without boundary-condition assumptions, validated on noisy synthetic floods.
summary: Conventional JBN interpretation fails when capillary pressure matters, and simulation-based history matching depends on assumed outlet boundary conditions. The authors recast Darcy's equations into a saturation (fractional flow plus capillary dispersion) equation solved locally by linear regression at fixed saturations, and a global pressure equation solved for water mobility. The method covers unsteady-state, steady-state, multi-rate and gravity drainage floods, with smoothing techniques for noisy data. It was validated on simulator-generated data: a 10 cm horizontal water-oil unsteady-state flood and a 60 cm gas-oil gravity drainage flood, with 40 saturation positions and added Gaussian noise. The fractional flow was recovered for saturations above about 0.5, including points below the Buckley-Leverett shock front owing to the capillary end effect, and recovery factor matched well, whereas JBN gave early breakthrough and too high residual oil. The gravity drainage version recovered oil relative permeability for saturations above about 0.3 without pressure data.
abstract: Generation of good quality relative permeability data depends on carefully designed programmes of core flooding, combined with appropriate interpretation of the basic laboratory data. Where capillary pressure is important, the JBN technique can give misleading results. In this case, simulation methods can be used to model the influence of capillary pressure. However, experience shows that the conventional fixed capillary pressure outlet boundary condition may fail to capture the development of the in-situ saturation profiles satisfactorily. This paper describes a new approach to coreflood interpretation, which fully utilises in-situ saturation data and reduces the sensitivity to assumptions about the core boundary conditions. The new method extends previously published techniques for the interpretation of gravity drainage floods by including viscous and capillary forces. Relative permeabilities are calculated directly from in-situ saturation and pressure drop data, without the need to use simulation methods, by applying the Darcy flow equations for the mobile phases at each position and time in the core. Darcy's equations are recast to give separate pressure and fractional flow equations. The fractional flow equation is solved locally, independently of any boundary condition assumptions, and the pressure equation (written in a global integral form) is solved for the mobility. The algorithm is applicable to a wide range of water-oil displacements or gas-oil displacements with an immobile initial water saturation, including multi-rate and constant pressure drop unsteady-state floods, steady-state and gravity drainage floods. Synthetic saturation and pressure drop data sets have been generated using a conventional simulator for a selection of water/oil and gas/oil core floods. The algorithm is applied to the data sets to construct the underlying relative permeabilities, including a significant fraction of the oil relative permeability tail. The presence of capillary end effects allows relative permeabilities at some saturations below the Buckley-Leverett shock front to be calculated in unsteady-state displacements. A range of smoothing methods have been developed to allow the basic algorithm to be successfully applied to datasets in which noise has been added to the basic saturation and pressure profiles generated by simulation.

title: Improvements of Coreflood Design and Interpretation Using a New Software
tldr: CAROPT history-matching software is used to design an optimal steady-state imbibition experiment and to interpret an unconsolidated-sand waterflood with heterogeneous capillary pressure, showing heterogeneity strongly biases relative permeability.
summary: CAROPT couples a core-flood simulator with an optimisation package to estimate relative permeability and capillary pressure from steady-state, unsteady-state and centrifuge experiments, with linear error analysis. For steady-state oil/water imbibition, three rate-schedule designs were compared on a synthetic case; the design adding total-rate variations at low water fractional flow gave the best accuracy over the full saturation range. It was applied to a carbonate sample, and the zero-Pc point (Sw 0.53 vs 0.56) agreed with a restored-state measurement. For unconsolidated 1-10 Darcy sands, a viscous-oil drainage pressure-drop method maps 1D permeability along the core. A waterflood with gamma-ray saturation profiles was matched with a single relative permeability and two capillary pressure curves (low-permeability zones <5 D, high >5 D). The homogeneous model underestimated oil relative permeability and sharpened the water curve, giving pessimistic recovery but optimistic breakthrough, and including saturation profiles reduced parameter uncertainty.
abstract: A new software package (CAROPT) has been developed for the interpretation of relative permeability experiments. In CAROPT the flow functions (i.e. relative permeabilities and capillary pressure) are adjusted in an optimisation procedure until the experimental observations are matched as closely as possible by numerical simulations of the experiments. CAROPT is designed for the interpretation of unsteady-state , steady-state and centrifuge experiments. The software performs two types of linear error analysis for the assessment of uncertainties arising from errors in the experimental data. The first type is an error bar calculation for the individual points on the flow function curves. The second type results in a complete set of «optimistic» and «pessimistic» relative permeability curves. In the present paper, we demonstrate the field of application of the software using real examples including experimental design and advanced interpretation : - 1. In Steady-State experiments, standard interpretation methods are time consuming because long stabilisation time are required and because they do not account for capillary effects. CAROPT was used to find an experimental design that optimises accuracy on both flow functions over a wide range of saturation and cost of the experiment. - 2. It is commonly accepted that Unsteady-State waterfloods should be performed under field rate, especially when mobility ratios are unfavourable, in order to prevent unstable displacement. The experiments are usually followed by bumps to satisfy the Rapoport criterion and check the existence of an end effect. It has been observed on very permeable samples (1-10 Darcy) through in situ saturation measurements, that field rates can lead to strong saturation variations along the core even in homogeneous samples. CAROPT was used for the interpretation of experiments performed on unconsolidated samples using both an homogeneous and an heterogeneous model. The impact of the heterogeneity on the flow functions is demonstrated and the use of saturation profiles for flow functions determination is highlighted.

title: The effect of heterogeneity on unsteady-state displacements
caption: Figure 5 : Saturation profiofiles for $\lambda=0.01$ and $\sigma^2(\ln K)=1.0$ . Comparison between 2D simulations on heterogeneous porous media and 1D simulations with homogeneous permeability using Kr from JBN: (a) Tracer case, (b) $\alpha=2$ . The 2D curves show greater spreading of the water front until breakthrough (at distance 250).
figure_reason: 2D saturation profiles spread more than 1D profiles using JBN Kr, showing JBN fails to capture internal saturation.
tldr: Streamline simulations on heterogeneous permeability fields show JBN relative permeability is biased and saturation profiles need a pseudo-Pc; tracer tests can help separate heterogeneity from local Kr.
summary: Unsteady-state relative permeability interpretation by JBN assumes a homogeneous core, but cores are often heterogeneous. The authors ran streamline (3DSL) simulations on 250x100 2D Gaussian permeability fields with correlation lengths of 0.01 and 1.0 and variances of ln K of 0.1 and 1, using Corey Kr (exponent 1 for tracer, 2), Pc=0 and viscosity ratios of 1 and 5. JBN effective Kr differed from local Kr even for small correlation length and variance, and a 1D Buckley-Leverett model with the effective Kr reproduced outlet flux but not the more spread saturation profiles at early times. Matching profiles required a pseudo-Pc, whose shape resembles a real capillary pressure curve. Effective Kr moved closer to local Kr at M=5, and an empirical model combining tracer and local Kr is proposed to back-calculate local Kr.
abstract: In this paper, we discuss the effect of heterogeneity on unsteady-state core-level displacements. We show that if the results are interpreted as if the core were homogeneous, significant errors in calculation of both the relative permeability (Kr) and capillary pressure (Pc) can occur. We describe a series of high-resolution numerical simulations performed on heterogeneous permeability fields of various correlation lengths. Pressures and fractional flows were calculated at the ends of the core, as well as saturations along the length of the core, mimicking in-situ measurements. For each grid block in the high-resolution simulation, simple Corey exponent Kr curves were used and Pc was set to zero. First, the results are interpreted as if the sample were homogeneous using JBN analysis. With this approach, it is impossible to fit the saturation profiles within the core. This is due to the effects of heterogeneity and the inability for a single Kr curve to capture the smearing of the invading front at all length scales. The saturation profiles can be fitted by history matching only when a pseudo-Pc is included, even though at the local scale Pc=0. Surprisingly, this numerical pseudo-Pc has the same shape as a real laboratory capillary pressure curve. Finally, we show how tracer tests on core samples can be used to quantify the effect of heterogeneity and decouple the effects of heterogeneity from the effects of petrophysical properties.

title: A model of capillary equilibrium for the centrifuge technique
caption: Figure 2: forced imbibition experiment on a carbonate sample of intermediate wettability. Both the experimental data and the fit are plotted. For the step 5 shown in detail in the lower right corner, the circles correspond to the experimental data and the line to the fit. For each step, the parameters of the fit are indicated ( $T_1$ and $T_2$ in hr). $S_{fin}$ is the saturation measured at the en
figure_reason: Shows bi-exponential fits for every speed step of a forced imbibition experiment, with T1, T2 and extrapolated Seq versus Sfin.
tldr: A bi-exponential model fits transient centrifuge production curves, extrapolates equilibrium saturation and gives a speed-change criterion that roughly halves experiment duration with negligible accuracy loss.
summary: Capillary equilibrium in centrifuge experiments is hard to define, and speed-step durations are usually set empirically, which can bias capillary pressure curves. The authors fit transient average saturation with a four-parameter bi-exponential model (ΔSeq, T1, T2, w), with T1 and T2 differing by about a factor of ten (e.g. 0.12 h and 3.9 h for a Vosges sandstone air-water drainage). It was validated on forced imbibition and second drainage of a 107 mD intermediate-wet carbonate (USBM -0.15) and on a sandstone, using an automated centrifuge with capacitance level detection. A stretched-exponential form handles slow acceleration (5 rpm/min), tested with simulations. Changing speed when the extrapolated saturation varies less than 1% over 4 h cuts duration by about a factor of two; shortened steps gave errors of 2-4% relative with 25-75% time gain. The method also improves equilibrium estimates from manually read data.
abstract: This paper addresses the problem of modeling transient production curves during a centrifuge experiment. Modern accurate measurement techniques used to monitor fluid saturation versus time while spinning indicate that capillary equilibrium is difficult to define and that a stability criterion for changing the centrifuge speed is needed. Such a criterion is very often set empirically, based on individual experience. This approach can lead to errors in the capillary pressure curves that are not detected by capillary pressure interpretation algorithms.

title: Stress-Dependent Porosity and Permeability of a Suite of Samples from Saudi Arabian Sandstone and Limestone Reservoirs
