The results provide an interpretation of the core data, suggesting that velocities are influenced by a secondary population of compliant pores that comprise a small fraction of the total porosity. A percolating backbone of less compliant, more tubular throats control the transport properties and allow the compliant throats to be hidden from the throat radii distributions inferred from mercury injection data. The sub-population of compliant throats is instrumental in creating the short T2 times observed in these rocks.

title: Measurements of Residual Gas Saturation Under Ambient Conditions
caption: Figure 4: Relationship between residual Figure 5: Relationship between gas gas saturation and wettability recovery and wettability for for sandstone plugs sandstone plugs
figure_reason: Shows residual gas saturation and gas recovery versus Amott wettability index for sandstone plugs, key result.
tldr: Automated spontaneous and forced imbibition tests on 27 plugs from four reservoirs show high residual gas saturation, dependent on initial water saturation and wettability, and only partly following Land's model.
summary: Residual gas saturation to water influx is poorly documented yet critical for gas reserves above aquifers and for storage reservoirs. Twenty-seven plugs from four reservoirs (two North Africa sandstones, a West Canada sandstone and a carbonate) underwent primary and secondary spontaneous imbibition, followed by forced brine flooding at 2 cm3/hr, using an automated weight-recording imbibition apparatus. Residual gas saturation decreased with initial imbibition rate and with increasing initial water saturation. Gas recovery by spontaneous imbibition increased with water-wetness (Amott index), while forced imbibition compensated in weakly water-wet plugs, so total recovery was nearly independent of wettability. Crowell's data fit Land's model well, but the four reservoirs fit only after a linear transform with different slopes, and Agarwal's model fit poorly. Capillary numbers near 1e-9 indicate capillary-controlled flow, so in weakly water-wet reservoirs true residual gas is lower than bypassed gas.
abstract: The value of residual gas saturation to water influx (Srg) is a critical property when estimating recoverable reserves in gas reservoirs overlaying active aquifers, or natural gas storage reservoirs. However, it seems that very little work has actually been done to investigate this value. Early work in the 1950s and 1960s established that Srg was not going to be as low as 10-15% PV, as was commonly expected at the time. Further work at that time also demonstrated that there was a link between Srg and porosity or initial water saturation. However, in the last 25 years, not much has been published on this topic. Our group has conducted extensive experimental work to determine the value of Srg for a variety of reservoir types and conditions. Work was done under different scenarios including primary and spontaneous imbibition, secondary spontaneous imbibition and forced imbibition. The results of 27 core samples were interpreted using all existing published models. It was found that the value of residual gas saturation was sensitive to initial water saturation and to the permeability to porosity ratio. It was also found that this sensitivity does not always follow the same law. Some reservoirs followed Land's model closely, while other reservoirs did not. The true residual gas saturation cannot be determined until after several weeks of constant imbibition. Regardless of this fact, the values of Srg after primary and spontaneous imbibition are very high. Under the current buoyant natural gas price scenario, such reservoirs are worth pursuing, but at lower gas prices many of these reservoirs may become marginal. Our findings are of particular importance in naturally fractured reservoirs that are plagued by early water breakthrough. Estimating the true residual gas saturation may lead to decisions on Enhanced Gas Recovery.

title: Are Pore Lining Chlorites a Cause of Low Resistivity in Sandstones?
caption: Figure 4: Comparison of the ac conductivity values of thereference clays, hydrated and dehydrated.
figure_reason: Shows ac conductivity of reference clays hydrated versus dehydrated, demonstrating the dominant effect of water on conductivity.
tldr: CEC, surface area and dielectric conductivity of pore-lining chlorites show very low values; intrinsic chlorite conductivity is orders of magnitude below water-related conductivity, so chlorite is not a direct cause of low resistivity.
summary: Low formation resistivities (0.3-20 ohm.m) occur in chlorite-bearing sandstone reservoirs, and the role of chlorite itself was unclear. CEC (cobaltihexamine) and BET N2 surface area were measured on whole rocks and size fractions from six fields, and for 'pure' chlorite and illite derived by data reconciliation. Chlorite CEC (2-14 meq/100 g) and SSA (5-39 m2/g) are low, with SSA ≈ 200×CEC + 10, below the commonly used 450 coefficient. Dielectric spectroscopy on dehydrated pellets showed dc conductivity of chlorite of about 1e-14 S/m, with illite and kaolinite not detectable; the activation energy of the reference chlorite was 0.58 eV, indicating ionic conduction by few mobile cations. Moisture raised conductivity strongly, so adsorbed and pore water, not clay intrinsic conductivity, controls sandstone resistivity.
abstract: Low resistivity in argillaceous sandstone reservoirs may be attributed either to the effect of microporosity, or to specific effects due to clays and/or to conducting minerals. In the frame of a study on pore lining chlorite bearing sandstones, from different hydrocarbon reservoirs, measurements of cation exchange capacities and specific surface areas have been performed, on whole rocks as well as on size separated fractions. Both sets of values are low, in agreement with the structural and textural observations. The dielectric properties, including intrinsic conductivity, of these chlorites have been investigated, on size separated fractions, as a function of temperature, and compared to that of reference clays. The results show a large influence of the moisture, current frequency, and temperature on the electrical properties. The chemical composition and structure of the clays has an obvious influence as well. However, the range of conductivities is such that the intrinsic influence of clays on the conductivity of argillaceous sandstone is lower than that related to the presence of water by several orders of magnitude.

title: Modeling of Capillary Pressure for Heterogeneous Reservoirs by a Modified J-Function
caption: Figure1: Modified J-function vs. normalized saturation for different n-values
figure_reason: Shows the modified J-function versus normalized saturation for different n values, the central result of the proposed model.
tldr: Defines a modified Leverett J-function including tortuosity, irreducible saturation and saturation exponent, with correlations to estimate them from permeability and porosity, supported by centrifuge and gamma-scanning data.
summary: Leverett's J-function scales capillary pressure poorly between formations with different pore size distribution, irreducible saturation and tortuosity. The authors derive a modified J-function (J*) from a capillary-bundle model with a power-law drainage Pc, so J* depends on normalized saturation and the saturation exponent n. They propose auxiliary correlations: Swir·porosity as a hyperbolic function of permeability (a=0.1683, b=96.93), tortuosity from Archie's formation factor, and n·Swir as an exponential decay in (k/φ)^0.5. Berea tests showed irreducible saturation scales between air-water and air-C19 by the interfacial tension ratio. Data came from 11 North Sea porous-plate samples, 3 samples measured at mm scale by gamma-absorption saturation monitoring, and literature data. Hassler-Brunner and saturation monitoring gave significantly different saturations for the heterogeneous sample v128 but not for v129 and v130.
abstract: Initial fluid distribution for heterogeneous reservoirs i.e. layered reservoirs with different permeability and porosity is often modeled by simplified capillary J-function for input to reservoir simulation. Leverett introduced the model in 1941 and showed that dimensionless capillary J (Sw)-function varies only with fluid saturation. However, theories of capillary pressure indicate that Leverett J-function should also be a function of tortuosity, irreducible liquid saturation and pore size distribution. As a result, scaling of capillary pressure by Leverett J-function should be limited to the formations whose pore size distribution and irreducible liquid saturation are equal. The pore size distribution is likely to affect the shape of the drainage capillary pressure (Pc) saturation curve. Therefore if pore size distribution is different in two formations, saturation exponent, a key parameter for the drainage Pc curve is likely to be different. The effect of tortuosity on Jfunction is not pronounced since its value does not change too much. However, if Leverett J-function is used to obtain Pc-saturation functions for different formations whose irreducible liquid saturation and the saturation exponent are different, then significant saturation discrepancy might arise in the scaled Pc-functions. It is also observed that irreducible liquid saturation is a function of specific surface area, wettability and interfacial tension of the rock-fluid system. Therefore scaling of Pc by Leverett J-function may provide incorrect Pc-saturation value at low saturation range even for the similar rocks but whose fluid systems are different. In this paper, we define a modified J-function that includes tortuosity, irreducible liquid saturation and saturation exponent so that the modified J-function may be used for scaling of Pc-saturation functions for any formations. We also propose auxiliary equations for estimating tortuosity, irreducible liquid saturation and saturation exponent from permeability and porosity data that may be used to calculate the modified J-function.

title: The Effects of Wettability on Three-Phase Flow in Porous Media: Basic Theory and Network Modelling Results
caption: Figure 1 – Saturation paths for WAG cycles in a mixed-wet system without wetting films (base case) and with wetting films for both water and oil.
figure_reason: Saturation paths of the WAG cycle with and without wetting films show the key effect on residual oil.
tldr: A 3D three-phase pore network model with mixed wettability, multiple displacements and variable outlet pressures simulates WAG; wetting films and multiple displacements strongly affect residual oil.
summary: Existing three-phase network models mostly treat strongly water-wet or oil-wet media, so the authors develop a capillary-dominated 3D network simulator with pore-to-pore wettability variation. It includes double and multiple displacements of disconnected clusters, found by a shortest-path search, and outlet pressure conditions that update when clusters reconnect. A WAG cycle was simulated in a 15x10x10 mixed-wet network (z=4, radii 5-25 µm, water-wet below 15 µm). Without wetting films the final oil saturation was 0.299, while with wetting films residual oil was virtually zero. Limiting chains to double displacements raised final So to 0.318, and constant outlet conditions changed the second water flood end point (So 0.330 vs 0.324) but gave a similar final So of 0.305.
abstract: Pore-scale network models are usually employed to derive capillary pressure-saturation and relative permeability-saturation relationships from pore-scale physical principles. These models are particularly useful for three-phase flow processes, such as wateralternating-gas injection (WAG), as the three-phase relationships are very difficult to obtain experimentally. Furthermore, network models are used directly alongside micromodel experiments (Sohrabi et al, 2000) to identify the important pore-scale displacement mechanisms. Existing three-phase network models focus mainly on strongly water-wet or oil-wet systems (Mani and Mohanty, 1998; Fenwick and Blunt 1998; Pereira, 1999). Here, we describe the development of a network simulator for capillary-dominated three-phase flow in media where the wettability varies from pore to pore. Reduction of phase continuity in weakly wetted pores has required incorporation of double and multiple displacements for mobilisation of disconnected phase clusters. We have also implemented outlet boundary conditions that are consistent with intra-system pressure changes. A WAG injection cycle is simulated for which the saturation path is recorded along with the statistics of the corresponding phase pore occupancies and displacement mechanisms. Results show the importance of multiple displacements in weakly wetted systems. By definition, network models apply to lengthscales much smaller than reservoirs, hence simulated saturation trajectories, residual saturation levels and hysteresis relate to the local physics in this capillary-dominated limit.

title: Relationship Between Reservoir Productivity and Pore Pressure Drop
caption: Fig. 1 Reduction of absolute permeability with total overburden pressure.
figure_reason: Shows measured permeability reduction with overburden pressure for all samples, the core experimental result.
tldr: Measured permeability versus confining stress for three Saudi rocks and Berea sandstone, then used polynomial fits in radial Darcy flow to show constant-permeability assumptions overestimate productivity.
summary: Permeability decline with rising effective stress (pore pressure drop) can reduce reservoir productivity, but is often ignored. Absolute permeability of Berea sandstone, two Saudi sandstones and a Saudi carbonate was measured with a steady-state liquid permeameter in a Hoek cell at several confining pressures up to 5000 psi. Permeability fell with confining pressure, more strongly in high-porosity, high-permeability sandstones than in the carbonate, and was fully recovered when confining pressure returned to 500 psi, indicating no pore collapse. Fourth-degree polynomial fits of permeability versus pore pressure were put into radial single-phase steady-state Darcy flow. For a 25% pore pressure drop, productivity fell by 8%, 13%, 25% and 3% for samples N1 to N4, so pressure-independent permeability overestimates production.
abstract: The significance of permeability sensitivity to changes in pore pressure (i.e., to change in effective overburden stress) has been examined using three Saudi oil reservoir rock samples as well as Berea sandstone. All of these cores were free of microfractures. The relationship between the overburden pressure and absolute permeability of these samples were determined at several levels of confining pressure at which the permeability was calculated. The experimental work performed in this study showed that reservoir rocks of high initial porosity and permeability are highly affected by reservoir (pore) pressure drop and resulting increase in the effective stress. For example, the production rate from sandstone sample N3 decreased 25% of its initial value when the pore pressure decreased by 25% of its initial value, whereas the production rate from carbonate sample N4 decreased 8% for the same pore pressure decrease. Moreover, it was observed that, the reservoir rock permeability under in-situ conditions strongly depends on its initial porosity and permeability values.

title: Impact of Clay Mineral Attributes in Estimating Damage in Carbonate Rocks
caption: Figure 2. Backscattered images for a fracture with illite bridge in plug 4 (left) and a clay particle favors calcium silicate surface rather than the calcite in Plug 24 (right)
figure_reason: Backscattered images showing illite bridge in fractured Plug 4 and clay on calcium silicate in Plug 24, illustrating clay location.
tldr: Combining XRD, electron microprobe mapping and mercury porosimetry on four low-permeability carbonate plugs shows clay size, location and distribution, not just amount, control clay migration damage.
summary: Clay migration damages permeability in low-permeability carbonates, and the paper asks how clay attributes can be used to estimate that damage. Four carbonate plugs with different pore types and clay contents were characterized by XRD for clay type and abundance (kaolinite, illite), EPMA backscatter images and X-ray maps for clay size and location, mercury porosimetry to 33,000 psi, and critical velocity core floods. Plug 4 (micro-fractures, illite bridges, about 0.011 md) could not be intruded by mercury and showed clay blocking. Plug 12 had no clay. In Plug 19, most of the pore network (about 98%) had throats slightly larger than the clays, and permeability recovered at higher flood velocity. In Plug 24, illite/smectite clays were large enough to block small pore throats, causing significant impairment with only slight recovery. The authors conclude that clay composition, size, location and distribution, together with pore geometry, must be considered in addition to clay amount and type.
abstract: The impact of clay migration on impairing reservoir permeability is a well-known problem. A critical component of attempting to minimize this damage is to perform accurate characterization of the clay morphology and distribution. The objective of this work was to apply techniques of clay imaging to develop a qualitative estimate of the potential for clay damage in low-permeability carbonate formations. The first step in clay characterization consisted of applying x-ray diffraction (XRD) to estimate clay type and abundance. From this analysis, it was determined that the samples contained different amounts of kaolinite and illite. Furthermore, calcium silicates were identified as components of the grain structure of the matrix. The next step was to extend the characterization by quantifying clay size, location and distribution using electron probe microanalysis (EPMA). This analysis provides compositional analysis of grains and clay minerals. Selection of key elements from XRD analysis provides information to perform elemental mapping images and therefore determine the distribution and location of clays. This work shows the clay size, location, and distributions have a significant impact on the impairment of permeability. Therefore, proper characterization is essential in estimating potential clay damage in carbonate reservoirs.

title: Accuracy Analysis of Archie Parameters and Relevant Effect on Water Saturation Values
caption: Fig. 2 Saturation profiles for different Archist's parameters
figure_reason: Compares water saturation profiles in Well A computed with the four parameter sets, showing the effect on Sw.
tldr: A three-dimensional regression method determines Archie a, m and n simultaneously from core data, giving lower water saturation error than common-value, conventional and CAPE approaches.
summary: Accurate water saturation requires accurate Archie parameters, which vary with rock and fluid properties. The authors propose a 3D regression technique that solves three simultaneous equations from log-transformed Sw, Rw/Rt and porosity to obtain a, m and n together, averaged over core samples. It is compared with common values (0.65, 2.15, 2), conventional separate F-porosity and Ir-Sw plots, and the CAPE method for clean sandstone in Well A. The average saturation error decreases from 0.14 (common values) to 0.098 (conventional), 0.0717 (CAPE) and 0.0686 (3D). Common values overestimate water saturation, and the 3D method is recommended as less computationally demanding than CAPE and as resolving whether a should be fixed at unity.
abstract: Early in the life of reservoirs, it is required to estimate accurately hydrocarbon volumes in place. Modified Archie formula ( $S_w = (a R_w / f^m R_t)^{1/n}$ ) is the basic equation to calculate water saturation. The exactness of water saturation value for given reservoir conditions depends on the accuracy of Archie parameters a, m and n. The terms of Archie relationship have been subjected to many laboratory investigations and even more speculation. There are many factors affect porosity exponent, m, saturation exponent, n and tortousity factor, a. Therefore, it is very difficult to fix Archie parameters regardless of reservoir characteristics; rock wettability, formation water salinity, permeability, porosity and fluids distribution. This paper presents a new technique to determine Archie parameters a, m and n. The developed technique is based on the concept of three-dimensional regression (3D) plot of water saturation, formation resistivity and porosity. 3D method provides simultaneous values of Archie parameters. Also, 3D method overcomes the uncertainty problems due to the separate use of formation resistivity factor- porosity and water saturation equations to get a, m and n parameters.

title: Coring in the New Millennium
caption: Figure 4 New Pre-Split Inner Tube System Facilitates Studying Natural Fracture Network
figure_reason: Shows the pre-split inner tube giving intact core for studying a natural fracture network, illustrating the main benefit.
tldr: A new stiffer core barrel with a pre-split two-half-shell inner tube reduces core damage and gives over 30% more usable core in Gulf carbonate case histories.
summary: Conventional coring systems damage cores through barrel buckling, lateral loads, and sawing or pushing cores out of inner tubes, which compromises petrophysical and rock mechanics data. The paper describes a new core barrel with four-fold greater flexural resistance, full-gauge stabilisers at each joint and top and bottom inner barrel bearings. It also uses a pre-split inner tube made of two half shells that can be opened immediately for core inspection. Case histories from Gulf reservoirs (Thamama and Arab carbonates, barrel lengths 40 to 180 ft) showed average core recovery of 98.7% and over 30% more usable core, especially in fragile zones. Traditional barrels left 8-12% of recovered core stuck in the inner tube. The pre-split tube also allowed rapid structural and fracture analysis of oriented cores with minimal handling.
abstract: Improved performance within the oil industry is underpinned by new or revised technologies. Coring is no exception and a novel design that eliminates weaknesses of the existing forty-year-old systems is shown to enhance coring results. A new core barrel and inner tube system provided improved core quality and facilitated core inspection at the well site with a minimum of core handling. A comparison made with cores obtained using alternative coring systems showed significant improvement in recovering better quality core, delivering over 30% more usable core, particularly from the fragile zones.

title: Characterisation of Carbonate Reservoir Heterogeneity Using Probe Permeability Images, Petrography and Borehole Image Log Data
caption: Figure 2. A series of conductivity cut-offs were established from the image logs and calibrated using the probe permeability data (Table 1) in order to provide an understanding of permeability contribution from given volumes of rock within the reservoir, and an understanding of permeability heterogeneity outside of the cored interval.
figure_reason: Shows conductivity cut-offs from image logs calibrated to probe permeability classes, the paper's main upscaling result.
tldr: Probe permeability maps, petrography and microresistivity image logs are combined to characterise permeability heterogeneity in a nodular limestone reservoir, using image thresholding to extend permeability classes beyond cored intervals.
summary: Carbonate reservoirs are heterogeneous from the reservoir to the micro-scale, and this causes large permeability variations. A nodular limestone reservoir with a complex diagenetic history was studied: early compaction and porosity loss, then late-burial porosity generation linked to thermal karstification. Probe permeability was measured on a 4 mm grid on slabbed core surfaces to build permeability images, and large-format thin sections were prepared from the same sites. Petrography links the permeability variations to microporosity and vuggy porosity in corroded internodule matrix, cementation within nodules, and very high permeability in vugs, moulds and fractures. Microresistivity image logs were divided into image facies based on the nodule to internodule matrix proportion and matrix mineralogy. Core calibration shows each facies spans a wide permeability range. Conductivity cut-offs calibrated to probe permeability define four classes: tight (<0.5 mD), low (0.5-10 mD), moderate (10-100 mD) and high (>100 mD). Thresholding gives a continuous trace of each class's abundance and its cumulative abundance, which identifies the distribution of high-permeability zones.
abstract: Carbonate reservoirs often display considerable heterogeneity ranging from the reservoir to the micro-scale, which can result in significant variations in permeability and hence producibility. Small-scale permeability heterogeneity within a complex nodular limestone reservoir has been evaluated using a combination of probe permeametry, petrography and borehole image logs. The limestones in the reservoir are characterised by extreme reservoir heterogeneity and have undergone a complex diagenetic history, with early compaction and porosity loss followed by a major episode of porosity generation during late burial associated with thermal karstification.

title: Complementary Methods for Characterising Slick Rock Aeolian Sandstone
caption: Figure 2. Slice 2 of sample 4 showing the Figure 3. Slice 3 of sample 13 showing location of iron banding and calcite cement. a fracture filled with calcite.
figure_reason: CT slices show heterogeneous calcite cement, iron banding and a calcite-filled fracture, key microstructural results.
tldr: Multiple complementary techniques (CT, ESEM, petrography, XRD, XRF, NMR/MRI) characterise Slick Rock sandstone; iron content defeats NMR/MRI but CT confirms its heterogeneous distribution.
summary: Sixteen Slick Rock Aeolian sandstone samples were characterised before brine/oil flow tests to link microstructure to permeability changes. Methods included CW-MRI, NMR, X-ray CT, ESEM contact angles, thin-section point counting, particle size analysis, XRD and XRF. Conventional MRI and NMR failed because heterogeneous iron (hematite, under 1%) shortened relaxation times, though CW-MRI imaged a capillary water front. CT revealed heterogeneous calcite cement, iron banding and a calcite-filled fracture perpendicular to the core axis in sample 13. Point-counted 2-D porosity was 20-23% with cement 5-18%, image analysis gave similar values, and grains were well sorted (So<1.4) with mean size about 204-217 µm. ESEM showed fresh quartz and feldspar water-wet and uncemented quartz intermediate-wet; the methods were mutually consistent.

title: Understanding Reservoir Continuity in the Mid to Late Jurassic Laminaria Formation, Australian Timor Sea, by Integrating Core and Log Data
caption: Figure 1. Location map of study area.
tldr: Core, biostratigraphy and hydraulic unit analysis show Laminaria Formation sandstones are laterally continuous, and hydraulic units predict permeability in thin sandstones better than porosity-permeability or facies correlations.
summary: The study aimed to establish the lateral continuity of reservoir sandstones in the Middle to Late Jurassic Laminaria Formation, Timor Sea, and to assess thin high-permeability sandstones near the formation top. Twelve wells, nine of them extensively cored, were used, with biostratigraphy, sedimentological core descriptions, ichnofacies, routine core analysis and wireline logs. Eight Hydraulic Units were defined from FZI (modified Kozeny-Carmen) using cluster analysis and histograms. Bayesian prediction from gamma ray, sonic and neutron-density logs extended these units to uncored intervals, and permeability was then calculated from the predicted units. A blind test on well Vidalia-1, with a learning set from six other wells, showed hydraulic unit permeability prediction agreed better than single-line or facies-based porosity-permeability correlations. Most facies, including the thin upper sandstones, were laterally continuous, though some top sandstones pinch out toward the southeast. Subsequent reservoir simulation raised estimated ultimate recovery.

title: A Novel Study of the Broad Band Complex Conductivity of Various Porous Rocks
caption: Fig. 1 shows electrical transfer functions of different kinds of rock measured with the system described above. It is obvious that all samples show a general frequency dependence of conductivity according to the CCPM. The CCPM can be used for all rock type used in this study. Furthermore, it can be seen that only a measurement over a broad frequency range gives the opportunity to observe the chara
figure_reason: Shows measured complex conductivity spectra of different rocks with CCPM fits, demonstrating the model's main result.
tldr: A combined conductivity and permittivity model (CCPM) fits 1 mHz–1 GHz complex conductivity spectra of 130 rock samples, with distinct parameter sets for each rock type.
summary: The paper addresses the frequency dependence of electrical conductivity and dielectric permittivity of rocks over a very wide band. A Combined Conductivity and Permittivity Model (CCPM) is proposed, with a DC conductivity term, an interface conductivity power law and an interface permittivity power law. Complex conductivity and permittivity were measured from 1 mHz to 1 GHz on 130 samples in six lithological groups, with porosities of 0.5–35% and internal surface areas of 0.08–40 m²/g. Samples were dry (salt) or fully or partially saturated with fresh water or brine. The CCPM fits the spectra of all water-wet rock types, and rock types show significantly different parameter ranges, tabulated for 13 rock types. Simplified forms are given for low-frequency spectral IP in high-porosity rocks and for high-frequency data above 10 MHz.
abstract: The frequency dependence of electrical rock properties in the frequency range from 10- 3 to 109 Hertz has been analyzed with a Combined Conductivity and Permittivity Model (CCPM). Broad band measurements were carried out on 130 samples of different rock types in the frequency range from 1 mHz to 1 GHz. The CCPM model fits well the measured transfer function for all types of rock.

title: Acquisition, Integration, and Archiving of Core Information
caption: Figure 2
tldr: Describes ExxonMobil's workflow for digitally capturing, integrating and archiving core images and data in an Acrobat PDF template on a controlled LAN for geoscientists and engineers.
summary: The paper addresses the problem of integrating and archiving diverse core information, including photographs, routine and special core analysis, descriptions, mineralogy and CT scans, so it is accessible to geoscientists and engineers. ExxonMobil's process merges core images from negatives, transparencies and prints and archives them to Kodak Photo CDs in five resolutions. Images are also printed as laminated half-scale panels. Merged images and core data are assembled into an integrated PDF template with bookmarks on a controlled LAN server. Users can launch routine analysis, particle size and facies data to Excel and copy images or data into their own reports, while only authorized staff can modify the master file. The authors conclude that Acrobat PDF is a versatile standard for integrating data types and images, speeding interpretation and ensuring digital archiving.
abstract: Digital photography and imaging technology has improved to such an extent today that capturing and integrating images from several data sources such as negatives, transparencies, and prints has become routine. Historical images can now co-exist with present day images and be retrieved without compromising the integrity of the images. Core information in a variety of formats and media such as core analyses (routine and special core analysis), core descriptions, mineralogy, catscans, and photographs can now be digitally captured, integrated, and archived in a useable format and in a central location easily accessible by both geoscientists and engineers. Figure 1 demonstrates the general process by which core images and data from ExxonMobil exploration wells are assimilated and integrated. Users throughout the world follow this process to ensure consistency and efficiency of use. The primary advantages of digital imaging technology is to provide as much visual information as possible to the user in a fast and cost effective way. At a glance, the geologist or reservoir quality specialist can quickly verify grain size distribution, facies, and mineralogy. The petrophysicist or engineer can review routine core analyses, special core analyses (SCAL), and net pay (ultra-violet photography). This results in better integration of core data in both geologic and engineering studies and ensures the complete digital archiving of the data for future studies. This process will also allow quicker integration of the data and a more accurate interpretation by the geologist, engineer, and petrophysicist. Data management has become a crucial part of the oil and gas industry. Paper copy reports and even digital files are easily lost or misplaced and are not easily accessible by all users of the data. Customizing the search and retrieval criteria and placing the data in a central readily accessible location creates a cost effective archival method. In the digital image processing, merged core images are archived to Kodak Portfolio Photo CD's (in 5 different resolutions) and also printed and laminated into half-scale panels (see Figure 2). The merged core images along with other pertinent core data are assimilated into an integrated PDF template (see Figure 3) and loaded onto a dedicated LAN hard drive. ExxonMobil controls access to the LAN server and the data is made available to all users with proper permissions. All identified users can access this information using Adobe Acrobat“ , to navigate to any area of interest. Within the ExxonMobil designed Acrobat“ , table of contents (bookmarks), a routine for launching specific core data (routine analysis, LPSA, facies data, etc.) to Excel has been incorporated. This launching technique permits the user to manipulate/analyze the data and/or incorporates the data into their own reports. Changes/additions to the Acrobat“ , PDF file can only be made by authorized personnel, ensuring the master PDF LAN copy always remains unchanged. Also, because Adobe Acrobat“ , is a true windows based operation, the cut and paste functions are active. The user can quickly extract (copy and paste) any images and/or data from anywhere in the Acrobat“ , table of contents and incorporate the extracted data into their own report or spreadsheet. This feature allows the user to truly depict a contact, or special pay interval, or a feature of interest in the data. Digital imaging tools are critical to the success of today's geoscientists and engineers, who must characterize and quantify hydrocarbon reservoirs for fast-track production developments. Acrobat“, by Adobe Systems Inc. has been used successfully to accommodate the growing need to integrate/merge core information and images for ease of use. Acrobat“, files are now a de-facto standard for electronic file exchange and are by far the most versatile and easy to use for integrating data types and images. title: Archie' S Parameters Determination with Saturation Analysis Data
caption: Fig. 1, 2 and 3 show the relations between oil saturation and water saturation from the Jurassic Badaowan formation in Well S007, the Carboniferous Shixi Oilfield in Well S004, and the Jurassic Baikouquan formation in Well M006 respectively. The figures show that the correlation coefficient of Well S004 is relatively low with 0.7789, and the coefficients of Well S007and Well M006 are 0.9164 and 0.
figure_reason: Shows oil-water saturation relations and correlation coefficients used to derive remaining rates for saturation correction.
tldr: Presents a regression method that derives Archie's parameters from sealed-core saturation data and log responses, with saturation correction, yielding n values from 0.6 to 7.3 that reflect wettability.
summary: Conventional determination of Archie's parameters needs laboratory measurements of formation factor and resistivity index, which may be unavailable in early exploration. The paper rewrites Archie's equations as a log-linear regression of water saturation on log resistivity and log porosity, so that m, n and the product abRw follow from the regression coefficients. Measured saturations from sealed coring are first corrected for oil and water losses, assuming the corrected oil and water saturations sum to 100%. Linear fits of Sw against So gave remaining rates of oil and water of about 0.92-0.93 and 0.90-1.04 in three Junggar Basin wells, with correlation coefficients of 0.78-0.95, and corrections of 8-24% saturation. Regression on seven wells gave m of 1.12-4.02 and n of 0.6-7.3, with abRw obtained directly without needing Rw. The author concludes the large variation in n reflects wettability influence.
abstract: Then first study on correlations between rock resistivity and lithology properties was carried out by G. E. Archie around 1942, which laid the foundation of integrated quantitative interpretation by geophysical logging data[1]. Based on the study, Archie summarized the models of water-wet rocks and oil-wet rocks both with intergranular pores to two basic relations called Archie's equation. Many efforts have been made in the study and application of Archie's equation, especially in the determination of parameters in Archie's equation and great progress has been made in recent years. For determination of Archie's parameters, the basic method is first to measure the formation factors and the corresponding porosity of a sample, and to measure the resistivity index at different water saturations in laboratory. Then Archie's parameters are determined by graphic or least-squares methods. Chen et al. used simplex methods and Fuzzy regression analysis[2] and El-khatib presented weighted regression analysis[3]. All the data used in the above methods must be characteristic values of lithology properties provided by laboratories, in other words, they depend on petrophysical parameter measurements. During the early exploration period, due to limited laboratory conditions or the nature of rock itself, petrophysical properties can not be measured directly, so the above methods can not be used. This paper presents a method to determine Archie's parameters by using saturation analysis data combined with the corresponding value of geophysical logging response. For short, we may call it saturation regression analysis.

title: The Effect of Pore Structure on Primary Drainage Capillary Behaviour
caption: Fig.1: Comparison of Drainage Curves by Mercury Injection and GASM
figure_reason: Overlays mercury injection and GASM air/brine drainage curves, showing agreement in macropores and divergence at high pressure for microporous samples.
tldr: Compares drainage capillary pressure from mercury injection and air/brine porous plate with gamma-ray saturation monitoring on six samples; mercury underestimates irreducible water saturation in chalk and clay-rich sands.
summary: The study explains differences in irreducible water saturation between drainage capillary pressure curves from mercury injection (up to 60,000 psia) and air/brine porous plate with a gamma-ray saturation monitoring system (GASM) under reservoir confining stress. Six samples with varied pore structure and mineralogy (clean sand, cherty sand, quartz-arenite, chalk, chloritic sand, kaolinitic/illitic sand) were tested on adjacent plugs, with XRD used to confirm the origin of microporosity. Mercury data were converted to air/brine equivalents using standard interfacial tension and contact angle values. The curves agree in the macroporous region for all samples and agree well for the quartz-rich samples. They diverge at high pressure for the chalk, chloritic and kaolinitic/illitic samples, and the difference in Swi is proportional to microporosity content. Mercury intrusion therefore suits clean and cherty sandstones but is not representative for chalk and clay-rich sandstones.

title: The Preservation or Removal of Solid Bituminous Material, as Part of the Core Analysis Programme on the Elgin-Franklin Field
tldr: Benign versus harsh cleaning and drying of Elgin-Franklin pyrobitumen-bearing sandstone plugs produced only small rises in porosity, permeability and grain density, near measurement repeatability, so routine preparation was judged acceptable.
summary: Elgin-Franklin HPHT gas condensate sandstones contain solid pyrobitumen and kerogen, and the concern was that standard cleaning could remove them and artificially raise permeability, porosity and grain density. Plug pairs from two 'black core' locations were cleaned and dried sequentially with a benign regime (isopropanol/methanol, constant immersion, 60°C humidity-controlled oven) and a harsh regime (toluene/methanol Soxhlet, 95°C oven). Between cycles, porosity rose by about 0.5-0.6 porosity percent, grain density by about 0.01 g/cc, and permeability by up to about 1 mD on ~19 mD samples. Point-count bitumen content fell from 17.3% to 13.3%, but this is within the semi-quantitative repeatability of 200-point counts. The changes were near the measurement repeatability, so the evidence was insufficient to show that standard preparation harms data quality. A benign-harsh control was nonetheless applied to development cores, with average variations of about 1% in permeability and 0.45-0.56 porosity percent across 628 and 37 control plugs in two wells.
abstract: The Elgin and Franklin fields are situated 240 km east of Aberdeen, in the southern part of the Central Graben. A number of gas condensate discoveries have been made in the area within Jurassic and Triassic Sandstones. These reservoirs occur at considerable depth (>5000m) and are characterised by high pressures (>1000 bars) and high temperatures (up to 200°C). The Elgin structure lies within the 'Franklin Terrace' area, just to the north of the Franklin Field. Both structures have a predominant NW-SE orientation.

title: Effect of Pore Size Distribution on Porosity Measurement by Computurized Tomography
caption: Figure 2. Pore size air-CT number relation
figure_reason: Shows the key result: air CT number as a function of pore size, used to derive the correlation.
tldr: Air CT number varies with pore size rather than being fixed at -1000; a pore-size-corrected single-scan CT method gives porosities about 5% lower (relative) than the classic method.
summary: CT porosity calculations assume an air CT number of -1000 HU, but earlier work at METU showed deviations from this value. The authors scanned a synthetic plexiglass core of 19 slices with artificial pores of 1.5 to 15 mm in a water bath at 100 and 130 keV. Air CT number approached -1000 as pore size increased, and data from pores below about 4-4.5 mm were excluded from curve fitting because of high scatter. The resulting correlations were used in a new single-scan method that sums partial air CT numbers weighted by partial porosity from mercury capillary pressure or thin-section pore size distributions. On Berea, two limestones and a dolomite, the new method gave porosities closer to helium porosimetry (Berea 20.01-20.37% versus 20.57% by helium and 21.02% by classic CT). Results were about 5% lower in relative terms than classic single-scan CT.
abstract: CT attenuation data are normally presented in an internationally standardized scale called Hounsfield unit (or CT number) that is defined by air at –1,000 (H) and water at 0 (H). In the experiments performed by Özgen et al [5] in the CT laboratory of METU Petroleum Research Center it was noticed that air CT number deviates from its theoretical value of –1,000. Deviation in air CT number causes to errors in the calculation of porosity and saturations. Was this deviation resulted from only artifact or was there any relation between pore size and deviation of air CT number? To find the answers of these questions experiments were conducted by X-ray CT scanner in our

title: Hydraulic Units Approach Conditioned by Well Testing for Better Permeability Modelling in a North Africa Oil Field
caption: Fig. 7: The history match of the simulated hydraulic unit Fig. 5: HU against PLT showing how model (heterogeneous case) flow is dominated by HU1.
figure_reason: Shows history match of the simulated model and PLT inflow dominated by HU1, validating the approach.
tldr: Hydraulic units from core data are modelled stochastically with three correlation lengths, validated against production logging and well tests, giving a good history match in a Triassic fluvial reservoir.
summary: Conventional log-permeability versus porosity regression is a poor basis for permeability modelling in heterogeneous rock, so the authors use Flow Zone Indicator-based hydraulic units (HUs) from core plug data in a Triassic fluvial reservoir in North Africa. The HUs are classified on a poro-perm plot, and a Lorenz plot shows that HU1 supplies about 70% of the flow but only 20% of the storativity. Production logging inflow profiles over the perforated intervals confirm that HU1 (coarse-grained material) controls inflow. HUs were distributed with a pixel-based stochastic model in three versions (homogeneous, heterogeneous, very heterogeneous) that differ only in spatial continuity. Synthetic well tests were compared with actual well test data, and the chosen model was transferred to flow simulation with HU-specific saturation, capillary pressure, relative permeability and PVT data. Permeability needed only slight tuning to obtain a good history match. The authors conclude that fine-scale HU definition at the wellbore should be preserved during scale-up.

title: Low-Invasion Coring in West Siberia, Direct Estimation of Core Fluid Saturation
tldr: Compares low-invasion and oil-based mud cores from three Surgut dome fields, showing resistivity–water saturation relationships agree when tracer screening removes filtrate-invaded samples.
summary: Oil-based mud coring is costly, so OJSC Surgutneftegas tested low-invasion coring in Surgut dome fields of West Siberia. Filtrate invasion was controlled with tracers added to the drilling mud. Pore water was displaced with non-polar oil and its resistivity and chemistry measured, so invaded or diluted samples could be rejected. Water saturation could be corrected only for filtrate dilution up to about 30%. In three fields (permeability from 1 mD to 2 D, porosity 10-30%, including oil-wet rock), resistivity versus water saturation from low-invasion core matched oil-based mud core. In field B about 30% of the core was heavily invaded, but the remaining samples gave results consistent with capillary pressure curves. The authors conclude low-invasion coring is effective and cheaper than oil-based mud coring if technology requirements are strictly met.
abstract: During the recent years drilling of wells using oil-base muds has been facing a strong counteraction of "the greens" and is considered as ineffective due to its high cost. In this connection, in Russia the low-invasion coring has become quite popular lately. The lowinvasion coring on a semi-commercial level has been carried out in the fields within the Surgut dome area – the main region of OJSC "Surgutneftegas"'s activities.

title: Use of Low-Invasion Coring Technique for Estimation of Reserves Depletion in the Field Samotlor
caption: Fig.1 Comparison of rock resistivity of low-invasion core and oil-base core
figure_reason: Compares measured core resistivity versus water volume with theoretical curves for injected and connate brine, distinguishing invaded, flooded and initial-salinity samples.
tldr: Low-invasion water-base-mud coring in a Samotlor well, combined with resistivity and water-retention relations, identifies poorly drained zones and shows interlayers below 80-100 mD were not depleted.
summary: Samotlor's main formations (AV2-3, AV4-3, BV8) are heavily depleted and water-cut, and log-based oil saturation is uncertain because formation water salinity changed during waterflooding. Low-invasion coring with water-base mud was run in a well, with samples cut at liquid nitrogen temperature to preserve saturation. Tracer concentrations in the mud varied too much for quality control, so invasion was assessed from pore-water mineral content and chemical composition, using aqueous extracts and displacement of interstitial water with non-polar oil. Theoretical resistivity-water saturation curves for 14 g/l (injected) and 26 g/l (connate) brine were compared with core data. The maximum Sw error was under 15% at 6 Ohm and 30% porosity. An algorithm combining porosity, water retaining capacity (Sw0), relative water saturation versus height above OWC, and resistivity separates poorly drained from watered intervals. Interlayers with permeability below 80-100 mD were not involved in depletion in the AV group.
abstract: The oil field Samotlor has been under development for more than 30 years. Currently, the main producing formations, AV2-3, AV4-3 and BV8, are characterized by a high degree of oil reserves depletion and water production. In this connection, the technologies to identify poorly drained zones having oil saturation close to the initial values are very important today.

title: Identifying a Non-Permeable Fracture for Convection and Diffusion Using X-Ray Computed Tomography
caption: Figure 7: Five images showing the diffusion of tracer in the core. The natural fracture formed a barrier to diffusion shown to the right of the images.
figure_reason: Shows tracer diffusion images where the natural fracture acts as a barrier to diffusion.
tldr: X-ray CT monitoring of water invasion and NaI tracer diffusion in a fractured chalk core shows the natural fracture, likely calcite-filled, blocks both convection and diffusion.
summary: Fine natural fractures in contaminated fractured chalk from the Negev may be sealed, complicating remediation planning. A 20 cm by 5 cm chalk core (0.4 mD, 33% porosity, about 80% calcite) containing a natural fracture was artificially split, held open with 0.5-1.0 mm spacers in a bi-axial holder at about 300 psig, and scanned in a medical CT scanner. Gaskets with slits restricted injection to the fracture. Water invasion images, with dry scans subtracted, showed water entering the matrix on one side while the natural fracture stopped it crossing. Continuous injection of 5% NaI tagged water showed iodine diffusing into the matrix but not across the natural fracture over the experiment duration, so the fracture is likely calcite-filled.
abstract: This abstract outlines an experimental method for determining whether or not a natural fracture is permeable for convective and diffusive transport processes. The evaluation was done in an effort to characterize a fractured chalk formation in the northern Negev desert in Israel that has been subjected to chemical contamination. The formation has large fractures that are very conductive and fine fractures that may be sealed. The presence of these two types of fractures creates a complicated flow system that needs to be understood prior to implementation of remediation programs.

title: Attenuation Changes During Oilflood Experiments
caption: Figure 2 VP (solid triangles) and signal amplitude (open circles)during the oil flood
figure_reason: Shows Vp nearly constant while signal amplitude varies strongly with saturation during the oil flood, the main result.
tldr: Ultrasonic oilflood of stiff Clashach sandstone shows Vp changes under 1% while signal amplitude varies strongly, correlating with total fluid mobility, suggesting amplitude as a seismic monitoring attribute.
summary: Stiff rocks show little Vp change with saturation, so repeat seismic surveys may miss them; the authors test whether amplitude is more sensitive. Clashach sandstone cores (porosity 13.5-14.5%, permeability 100-350 mD) were brine saturated and flooded with light oil in a Hoek cell at 21 MPa, with flow rates stepped from 0.05 to 16 cc/min and ultrasonic (~600 kHz) Vp and Vs measured throughout. Sw fell to 0.29, Vp changed by less than 1%, but amplitude dropped from 0.18 to 0.13 V at Sw 0.63 and rose to 0.22 V at Sw 0.29. Q was about 30-50. Amplitude correlated roughly linearly with total fluid mobility computed from relative permeability, qualitatively consistent with a Biot/squirt-flow model (Dvorkin et al.) using effective viscosity.
abstract: Reservoir saturation changes can be detected by repeat 3-D seismic surveys. These rely on some seismic attribute such as travel time, amplitude or velocity changing with the change in saturation of either gas, oil or water. Rock physics measurements show that rocks with a high compliance or low stiffness have the greatest sensitivity of Vp to saturation changes. Stiff rocks may only exhibit small changes in Vp with saturation, which may be undetectable on repeat surveys. However other seismic attributes, such as signal amplitude may show large variations. In the experiments described here, the velocity and signal amplitude was measured in a stiff sandstone core during the replacement of brine with oil. During the experiment Vp changed by 1%, but the signal amplitude varied by over 200%. A 1% change in velocity is unlikely to be detectable in a repeat seismic survey since it causes a reservoir base shift of only 0.3ms for a 100m thick reservoir. However a 200% increase in amplitude may be detectable. The material used in the experiments was an aeolean sandstone known as Clashach sandstone, commonly used in rock physics as a North Sea reservoir analogue. The sandstone was from a surface deposit from a quarry in the NE of Scotland. Clashach sandstone has some variation in its properties but the samples tested had porosity of 13.5- 14.5%, a permeability of 100-350mD and were strongly water wet with an Amott-Harvey index of 0.65-0.98. The material was stiff with a modulus of elasticity of 40-50GPa. The samples were initially vacuum saturated with brine, of density 1.067g/cc, then saturated under a high pore pressure of 13.8MPa (2000psi) to achieve 100% saturation. The cores were weighed prior to the experiment to confirm 100% saturation with brine.

title: Micro-Scale Two-Phase Flow Simulation of Lattice Boltzman Method for Capillary Hysteresis
caption: Figure 5 Capillary hysteresis in water-, neutral- and oil-wet model Figure 6 Capillary hysteresis in water-wet model
figure_reason: Shows simulated capillary hysteresis curves for water-, neutral- and oil-wet models, the main result.
tldr: 2D lattice Boltzmann simulations reproduce snap-off, film flow and capillary hysteresis in simple pore models of Berea sandstone, with wettability-dependent behavior.
summary: Relative permeability and capillary pressure cannot be uniquely determined from core flooding unless one is known, so the authors explore the Lattice Boltzmann Method (LBM) as a pore-scale two-phase flow simulator. Preliminary 2D simulations used simple pore models built from the throat size distribution of Berea sandstone, and a virtual core was used to vary pore shape and wettability. The simulations reproduced snap-off and oil film flow on oil-wet walls. Snap-off did not occur at small aspect ratio (body-to-throat size) or low interfacial tension. Simulated drainage capillary pressure was nearly equal to that estimated from throat width and surface tension. Imbibition began below a critical pressure set by surface tension and throat width, and hysteresis arose from the two-dimensional pore shape. Residual oil shape and recovery rate differed among water-wet, neutral and oil-wet conditions, though the findings are qualitative.
abstract: Application of X rays CT scanner to the core flooding analysis is enabling the simultaneous saturation measurement, more accurate relative permeability and the capillary pressure in cooperation with the simulation. However, unless either of the relative permeability or the capillary pressure is known, the other side cannot be uniquely determined. To develop a simulation technology, which can explain theoretically such experimental phenomenon, is an important subject, and this research focused on a promising technique: Lattice Boltzmann Method (LBM) as micro-scale flow simulation method.

title: THE POTENTIAL EFFECT OF SOLUTION SEAMS ON RESERVOIR PERFORMANCE IN A SANDSTONE RESERVOIR A case study from an Ashgillan (Late Ordovician) reservoir in North Africa
caption: Figure 6: Field water cut(FWCT), oil production total(FOPT), pressure(FPR) & oil production rate (FOPR) for the three cases.
figure_reason: Shows simulated water cut, oil production and pressure for base, SS and TSS cases, the main performance result.
tldr: Low-amplitude solution seams in a North African Ordovician sandstone have permeability of 1-6 mD and cut vertical permeability tenfold; simulations show seams parallel to bedding delay water breakthrough, crossing seams hurt recovery.
summary: Low-amplitude stylolitic solution seams (1-2 per foot) occur in an Ashgillan sandstone reservoir in North Africa and may act as vertical flow barriers. Seams were characterised by ESEM, thin section, probe permeametry and core plug data (harmonic and arithmetic averaging methods), plus hydraulic unit classification, where rare HU7 plugs represent the seams. Seam permeability is 1-6 mD compared with 100-1000 mD in the matrix, with probe and plug estimates agreeing (e.g. 5 vs 5.2 mD, 2.17 vs 1.2 mD). Upscaling showed effective kh was little affected while kv dropped by an order of magnitude. In 2D simulations, seams parallel to bedding reduced gravity slumping, gave more piston-like sweep and later water breakthrough, whereas seams crossing the bedding gave earlier breakthrough, trapped oil and lower recovery.

title: Attenuation Characteristics of Saudi Arabian Reservoir Sandstone and Limestone Cores
caption: Figure 3: Qp/Qs versus permeability. Figure 4: P-wave quality factor for dry and water saturated rock samples.
figure_reason: Shows Qp/Qs versus permeability, the key correlation, and dry versus saturated Qp comparison.
tldr: Ultrasonic P- and S-wave quality factors of 20 Saudi sandstone and limestone cores show that the Qp/Qs ratio correlates with porosity and permeability better than Q itself.
summary: Seismic attenuation correlates only weakly with porosity and permeability, which limits its use for reservoir characterization. Twenty Saudi Arabian sandstone and limestone reservoir cores were measured dry and water saturated at nine confining pressures up to 82 MPa. Quality factors were computed with the spectral ratio method at 700 kHz central frequency, with diffraction correction. The method was checked on Gres des Vosges sandstone against Lucet (1989) and agreed closely (e.g. Qp 18 vs 17 at 5 MPa). Q increased with confining pressure, and Qp of dry rocks exceeded Qp of water-saturated rocks. Qp/Qs correlated with porosity and, better, with permeability. Qp/Qs was below 1 for dry sandstones, while limestones and water-saturated sandstones had Qp/Qs ≥ 1. Combining Qp/Qs with Vp/Vs helped separate saturation states.

title: Rock Physics from Small Samples - Sometimes Your Only Solution
caption: Figure 2. Wireline sonic log data (full curve), and rig-site CWT P-wave acoustic velocity results from measurements on corresponding shale drill cuttings (triangles).
figure_reason: Shows cuttings P-wave velocities agreeing with wireline sonic log, demonstrating rig-site cuttings usefulness.
tldr: Static and acoustic tests on mm-cm shale samples and cuttings give results consistent with standard triaxial plug tests, but faster and cheaper.
summary: Shale cores are often scarce, which limits rock mechanical characterization for wellbore stability. The authors developed SAMSS, a system for acoustic velocity, static Young's modulus and UCS measurements on mm-cm samples under controlled axial stress and fluid exposure, plus a rig-site CWT system for cuttings. Cuttings velocities agreed well with wireline sonic data in one well, though less well elsewhere owing to drilling damage and heterogeneity. Young's modulus on 10 mm by 4 mm soft (28% porosity) and hard (3%) shale samples was fairly consistent with triaxial plugs. Small-sample UCS tests fit the Mohr-Coulomb envelope from CU triaxial tests, Pierre shale showed bedding-dependent stress-sensitive velocities, and KCl exposure strain tests on 2 mm discs were faster than plug tests.
abstract: This paper illustrates the potential of using small shale samples, including cuttings, as a tool for determining rock physical parameters on field material. The measured static and dynamic mechanical results are basically consistent with those attained on larger, standard plugs in triaxial cells. Consequently, small samples can be used as a complementary tool to larger samples, providing faster and less expensive results with less material consumption, also allowing for larger test matrices. In some cases, use of small samples may actually be the only solution to obtain direct measurements on the shale material.

title: A Comparative Study of Reservoir Pore Structure by 2D and 3D Image Analysis, Mercury Porosimetry and NMR Relaxometry
caption: Figure 3. $T_2$ distributions in bead pack. Solid circles: $S_w = 1$ ( $T_0 = 0.12$ s, $T_D = 0.27$ s); empty circles: after gravity drainage, $S_w = 0.1$ ( $P_c = 38$ kPa, $T_0 = 0.11$ s, $T_D = 0.12$ s).
figure_reason: Shows T2 distributions in a bead pack at full and drained saturation, supporting the higher surface relaxivity.
tldr: NMR T2 relaxation of glass bead, sandstone and dolomite samples is compared with SEM image analysis and mercury porosimetry, giving a surface relaxivity near 100 mm/s for fused beads.
summary: The study addresses uncertainties in converting NMR T2 distributions to pore size, including echo spacing and multi-exponential inversion choices. CPMG measurements at 0.6 T were made at Sw=1 and residual saturation on fused and packed glass beads, sandstones and dolomite, and inverted by NNLS and a simulated annealing algorithm or fitted with a modified stretched exponential model. Backscatter SEM images gave porosity, autocorrelation functions and specific surface area. For fused bead samples the surface relaxation strength was r = 100 ± 17 mm/s, higher than a literature value, and pore radii from T_D agreed with image correlation lengths. NMR and SEM porosities agreed, and T2 distributions from different inversions and instruments agreed when echo spacing was sufficiently small. Random-walk simulation in a 3D stochastic Berea replica broadly matched predictions from pore-size partitioning, with differences attributed to diffusional averaging.
abstract: Interpretation of NMR transverse relaxation measurements in terms of $T_2$ distributions underlies the estimation of petrophysical properties (Kenyon, 1997), including the porosity, clay bound water, pore size distribution, saturation, permeability and capillary pressure. Uncertainties associated with the scaling between $T_2$ and pore size contribute to the difficulty of NMR-based petrophysical interpretations, as are uncertainties related to the proper choice of NMR test parameters (e.g., inter-echo spacing) and uncertainties associated with multi-exponential decomposition. Some of these issues were explored in this study using complementary information from mercury porosimetry, backscatter SEM image analysis and 3D reconstruction and characterization. Complete results from fused and packed glass bead, sandstone and dolomite samples will be presented in the poster. Representative results are reported here.

title: Studies on Anhydrite Cementation in Geothermal Reservoirs
caption: Fig. 3. Diagenetic evolution of different types of Allermoehe Rhaetian sandstone represented in a log-log plot of permeability versus porosity.
figure_reason: Shows diagenetic paths of sample groups in permeability-porosity space, the key interpretation of cementation types.
tldr: Permeability-porosity paths of anhydrite-cemented Rhaetian sandstone from Allermoehe 1 are classified by diagenesis type using fractal dimension, and anhydrite dissolution reverses cementation without hysteresis.
summary: The Rhaetian sandstone aquifer in well Allermoehe 1 (northern Germany, ~3250 m) is cemented by anhydrite, with porosities as low as 2%, making it unsuitable for geothermal use. Eighteen core samples were studied with NMR log comparison, anhydrite content (sulphur analysis and XRD), BET surface, mercury injection, induced polarization and PFG-NMR. Fractal dimension D, from BET versus grain-based specific surface, was 2.05–2.39. Strongly cemented samples (anhydrite 15–25%, porosity 2–3%) had low D and reduced pore-neck radii, while PFG-NMR pore radii were unchanged. In permeability-porosity space the samples lie between the average-sandstone curve and the quartz-cemented Fontainebleau curve. Dissolution of anhydrite during electrical measurements retraced the cementation path in reverse with no hysteresis, as cemented patches that close percolation pathways open preferential flow paths on dissolution.
abstract: Direct use of geothermal heat based on producing hot water in one borehole and injecting cool water in a second one requires an aquifer which meets the following minimum requirements: a thickness of 20 m, a permeability of 250 mD, and a temperature of 60 °C. The last condition corresponds roughly to a minimum depth of 1500 m. In northern Germany, a few sandstone formations meet these requirements, among them the Upper Keuper Rhaetian sandstone. In one particular borehole (Allermoehe 1, south of Hamburg) the Rhaetian aquifer was drilled at 3250 m with sufficient thickness and fluid temperature. The pore space, however, was cemented by anhydrite resulting in porosities as low as 2%. This motivated several coordinated research projects in order to investigate the conditions leading to this type of cementation.

title: NMR and Ultrasonic Studies in Core Plug Samples from Carbonates and Sandstones' Tight Formations
caption: Fig. 3 T2 distribution of very fine to fine grained sandstone sample (a) and fine to medium grained sample (b)
figure_reason: Shows T2 distributions for sandstones of different grain size, illustrating the grain-size control on NMR response.
tldr: Ultrasonic P-wave FFT spectra and low-field NMR T2 distributions on tight Venezuelan sandstone and carbonate plugs reveal fractures, grain size and vugs, and give T2 cut-offs of 6 and 66 ms.
summary: Tight sandstone plugs (Orocual field, San Juan Medio) and complex-lithology carbonate plugs (Barinas field, Escandalosa O) were studied with 1 MHz ultrasonic P waves analysed by FFT and 2 MHz NMR T2 measurements at 100% and irreducible water saturation. P-wave spectra differ between fractured and non-fractured samples in frequency domain but not in time domain. In sandstones, T2 distributions follow grain size, and the best T2 cut-off from 23 samples was 6 ms rather than the usual 33 ms, which would underestimate free fluid volume. In carbonates, T2 maxima vary between depositional cycles (about 90 ms at 26% porosity with vugs versus about 12 ms at 11% porosity), and the average cut-off was about 66 ms versus 90-110 ms normally used. NMR porosity correlates with buoyancy porosity at 0.99 for sandstones and 0.98 for carbonates.
abstract: Core plug samples of carbonates and sandstones tight formations have been studied using ultrasonic P waves, analysed in frequency domain, and low field NMR transversal relaxation, in order to find information about lithology, presence of fractures and petrophysical properties. The main production mechanism of these formations is due to fractures. The Fast Fourier Spectra of P waves indicate higher amplitudes in the samples presenting microfractures than in non-fractured ones, because of less energy lost into S waves when open fractures are present. The T2 distribution times show characteristic behaviour determined by the grain size in sandstone samples and additionally by the presence of vugs in carbonates with complex lithology.

title: FLUID DISTRIBUTION IN TRANSITION ZONES (Using a New Initial-Residual Saturation Correlation)
caption: Figure2: Initial-residual non-wetting fluid correlation. Solid lines are model equation.
figure_reason: Shows measured initial-residual non-wetting saturation data with the proposed linear-sigmoidal model fit.
tldr: Centrifuge and gamma-absorption experiments on Berea cores yield a new linear-plus-sigmoidal initial-residual saturation correlation for building imbibition Pc hysteresis curves in transition zones.
summary: Fluid distribution in oil transition zones after water-oil contact movement is hard to model, and existing initial-residual non-wetting saturation correlations (e.g., Land) are questioned. The authors used a centrifuge with gamma-absorption saturation monitoring and high-melting paraffin oil on liquid-wet Berea cores (porosity 22.6%, permeability 228 md average). Drainage Pc was fit with a power-law form, and bounding imbibition Pc with a two-asymptote model. Hysteresis curves were built by honoring each initial-residual endpoint and adjusting only exponent n2 as a linear function of Snwi (slope about 0.43). A new correlation combines a linear segment (slope m = 0.15) with a four-parameter sigmoid whose parameters depend on maximum residual non-wetting saturation; it was compared with Land, Kleppe, Masalmeh and Jerauld models for sample Bx3 (Snwr max = 0.2).
abstract: The fluid distribution as a function of height in transition zones is often very complex. This may be due to movement of water-oil contact, tilting of the reservoir at some point in time, leak of fluid out of the reservoir zone or complex inflow during secondary migration. The resultant fluid distribution seen in saturation logs may be difficult to model. In this paper we address the changes in fluid distribution versus height, inferred by changes of fluid distribution due to the movement of water-oil contact only. The experimental procedures for determining capillary pressure are based on fluid saturation monitoring by gamma absorption from centrifuge experiments. An analytical capillary pressure-saturation model was fit to the bounding imbibition capillary pressuresaturation data. The drainage-imbibition hysteresis curves were then constructed assuming that these curves have similar shape to that of the bounding imbibition curve. The imbibition hysteresis model proposed may be used to calculate fluid saturation in the reservoir due to the movement of water-oil contact. We also proposed necessary auxiliary equations to solve the new linear and four-parameter (sigmoidal type) initial-residual fluid saturation equations. Thus once the shape of the bounding-imbibition capillary pressuresaturation curve and maximum non-wetting fluid saturation are known one can easily construct any imbibition hysteresis curves that may be required.

title: Review of the Winland R35 Method for Net Pay Definition and Its Application in Low Permeability Sands
tldr: Tests the Winland R35 net-pay method on 40 Sherwood Sandstone samples using mercury injection; facies-specific correlations differ from Winland's but cut-off differences are modest.
summary: The Winland R35 method estimates pore throat radius from porosity and permeability and uses a 0.5 µm cut-off for net pay, but its validity in low permeability gas sands is uncertain. Forty Sherwood Sandstone samples from two Morecambe Bay wells were tested by mercury intrusion to 60,000 psi and grouped by facies (fluvial, aeolian, sheet-flood) and permeability (<5 mD, >5 mD). All curves were sigmoid, so R35 can be applied physically, and Pittman's concern about the lack of a modal aperture was not borne out. New linear regressions for each sub-group differed significantly from Winland's equation and fitted poorly (best r² 0.853 for aeolian, others around 0.6), probably because of small sample sizes. Permeability cut-offs at 0.5 µm differed in some sub-groups (for sheetflow, 0.5 mD from Winland versus 1 mD from the new fit), and Winland's equation sometimes gave negative cut-offs. The authors question whether rock-type-specific correlations are worth the cost, since differences are small compared with those from choosing a different threshold radius.

title: Evaluation of Filtration and Capacitive Properties of Rocks by Nuclear Magnetic Resonance in Terrigenous Non-Consolidated Section with Swelling Clay Minerals
caption: Fig. 2. Petrophysical Data By Depth together with NMR for Reservoirs and Enclosing Rocks
figure_reason: Depth plot of petrophysical data with NMR comparing reservoirs and enclosing non-reservoir rocks, showing the main discrimination result.
tldr: NMR relaxometry on frozen-prepared core from Western Siberian poorly cemented sandstones separates reservoir from clay-rich non-reservoir rocks and estimates porosity, Swirr and permeability.
summary: The study uses NMR to evaluate net pay in poorly cemented Albian-Cenomanian sandstones, aleurolites and clays of Western Siberia, where porosity (30-40%) is similar in reservoir and non-reservoir rocks. Plugs were cut from core frozen in liquid nitrogen and encased in shrink plastic to avoid destroying them. Gas permeability of dry samples is misleading, since non-reservoir rocks with swelling clays show hundreds of mD dry but drop by a factor of 10^3-10^4 under confining pressure. Capillary pressure data showed residual water saturation of 75-90% in these rocks, and a 33 ms T2 cutoff best estimated Swirr. A 3 ms cutoff identifies clay-bound water, whose large amount marks non-reservoir rock. A new 3-D cubic capillary lattice model gives permeability from T2 spectra and agrees better with measured values than the Timur-Coates and Kenyon equations, but still overestimates permeability in non-reservoir rocks.
abstract: This study investigates the use of NMR to evaluate net pay within a sequence of poorly cemented sandstones, argillaceous aleurolites, and thinly interbedded aleurolites and clays. Clay minerals in non-reservoir rocks are chiefly of montmorillonite-smectite composition, but have a kaolinite composition in poorly cemented sandstones (Fig.1). The rocks are of Albian to Cenomanian age, and are located in Western Siberia.

title: Hysteresis Effects in Capillary Pressure, Relative Permeability and Resistivity Index of North Sea Chalk
caption: Fig. 5: Log-log plot of Ir versus Sw (core 2).
figure_reason: Shows log-log resistivity index versus water saturation for core 2, illustrating drainage/imbibition hysteresis in n and negative curvature at low Sw.
tldr: Lab tests on four North Sea chalk cores show significant drainage-imbibition hysteresis in capillary pressure and relative permeability, but only minor hysteresis in resistivity index.
summary: The paper examines drainage-imbibition hysteresis in capillary pressure, relative permeability and resistivity index for four North Sea chalk plugs (porosity 0.19-0.31, liquid permeability 0.09-1.94 md). Capillary pressure was measured by centrifuge with spontaneous imbibition cells, relative permeability by unsteady-state flooding with n-decane and brine history-matched using Corey exponents, and resistivity by a two-electrode method. Amott wettability indices of 0.34-0.53 indicated moderately water-wet cores, with no spontaneous oil uptake. Capillary and relative permeability hysteresis were significant, the latter more so in the non-wetting phase, and forced imbibition was an important oil production mechanism. Archie saturation exponents ranged 1.4-1.7, with small drainage-imbibition differences in cores 2 (1.6 vs 1.4) and 6 (1.7 vs 1.6) and none in core 4.
abstract: Accurate estimation of capillary pressure and relative permeability curves are very important for evaluating hydrocarbon recovery processes. Also, resistivity index data are important in evaluating fluid distributions in reservoirs during these processes. All these parameters are path dependent i.e. different in drainage and imbibition processes, commonly known as hysteresis, which makes them complicated to predict. Laboratory tests have therefore been performed on four North Sea chalk core samples to measure the wettability index and determine the hysteresis in capillary pressure, relative permeability and resistivity index. The cores were extracted using toluene and methanol, and a light oil (n-decane) and brine saturation equivalent to the formation water were used in the displacement processes. Varying levels of hysteresis were observed. Hysteresis effects were significant in capillary pressure and relative permeability curves and not so pronounced for the resistivity index.

title: Evaluation of Formation Damage Caused by Completion and Workover Fluids
tldr: Core tests on Nubia sandstone show completion and workover fluids cut oil permeability to 7-74% of initial, with fluid solids the main damage cause.
summary: Productivity losses after workovers in three wells were linked to completion fluids: CaCl2 (95% decline), filtered seawater (100%) and diesel (48%). Laboratory work on Nubia sandstone core (average 450 mD, 16% porosity, 5% water saturation, grain density 2.64 g/cc) included conventional analysis, thin section, XRD and wettability data indicating an oil-wet system. XRD showed 95 wt% quartz and 2 wt% kaolinite, and water sensitivity and velocity tests showed no clay swelling or fines migration. Return permeability tests with flow opposite to production gave final oil permeabilities of 7% to 74% of initial values. The author concludes that solids in the fluids are the major cause of damage and recommends solids control, fluid filtration, and minimizing overbalance.
abstract: Poor productivity of promising new wells or old wells with workovers can often be traced to undesirable characteristics of the borehole fluid used in the completion. This paper presents laboratory and field results (see table 1) that show clear examples of productivity losses, resulting from completion damage sustained during workover jobs. For these specific jobs, diesel, calcium chloride and filtered seawater were used as completion fluids. The production rates after the repair jobs suggested that calcium chloride and filtered sea water are more damaging (productivity loss up to 100%) and diesel was less damaging (productivity loss up to 48%). | Well | Completion Fluid | Rate Before Workover (BOPD) | Rate After Workover (BOPD) | Production Loss | Decline Ratio % | |------|------------------|-----------------------------|----------------------------|-----------------|-----------------| | A-1 | CaCl 2 | 2520 | 126 | 2394 | 95 | | A-2 | Diesel | 3000 | 1540 | 1460 | 48 | | A-3 | Filtered Sea | | | | | | | Water | 2550 | 0 | 2550 | 100 | Table (1) Laboratory work was initiated to evaluate the wellbore damage that occurs during initial well completion or workover operation. This lab work included the examination of the mineralogy and texture of the selected core samples by using conventional core, thin section and x-ray analysis. Also included were "return permeability test" results. Several results are obtained from this study. First, the mineralogy and texture of the selected core are chemically and mechanically stable.
