Also MWS maintains wettability after cleaning, while the mixed wet (MWL) cores become more water wet after solvent cleaning. The average waterflood remaining oil saturation (Sorw) is lowest for MWL cores. The remaining oil saturation for the MWL rocks also show a reduced Sorw with increasing permeability, but the FW and MWS reservoirs indicate a constant Sorw independent of permeability. The type of intermediate wettability has impact on data structure needed to build representative reservoir models. In addition, the type of wettability influences the shape of relative permeability curves and also the capillary pressure relations for different classes of intermediate wettability.

title: The Accessibility of Waterflood Residual Oil by the Oil Bank When Slugs of Solvent Alternate with Slugs of Water (Saw) Under Oil-Wet and Water-Wet Conditions
caption: Fig. 8: Accessibility of residual oil in micromodel Vug-10 when slugs of solvent alternated with slugs of water in SAW mode of operation.
figure_reason: Quantifies residual oil reduction in VUG-10 over solvent and water slugs in the SAW process.
tldr: Micromodel visualization shows solvent oil banks fully access waterflood residual oil in oil-wet systems but only partly in water-wet ones, where alternating water slugs add little.
summary: The study examines how well a miscible solvent oil bank reconnects waterflood residual oil, using 2-D etched glass micromodels with varied pore structure under water-wet and oil-wet conditions. Residual oil was classified as flowing, dendritic or isolated, and quantified by image analysis of video recordings as a function of pore volumes injected, capillary number and slug size, including solvent-alternating-water (SAW) runs. In water-wet models, solvent broke through early (about 0.2-0.4 PV) and isolated residual oil ranged widely, with accessibility of roughly 30% to 99% depending on pore structure and capillary number. In the oil-wet VUG-14 model, residual oil was 100% accessible after about 5 PV. After 3-4 PV of solvent, no further isolated oil was reached, and extra SAW cycles changed residual oil only modestly (e.g., 42.3% to 38.3% PV). Higher capillary number and lower interfacial tension improved accessibility, and capillary number mattered more than slug size.
abstract: Flow visualization studies were carried out to determine the accessibility of waterflood residual oil by oil-miscible slugs in 2-D glass micromodels of capillary networks having features of variable pore structure. The wettability was varied to represent strongly water-wet and strongly oil wet conditions. As the front of the oil bank propagates in the region with residual oil, three forms of oil in the oil bank are realized, namely, the flowing oil, the dendritic oil and the isolated (or inaccessible) oil, respectively. The fraction of resident residual oil which 1) becomes flowing, 2) becomes dendritic oil and 3) remains inaccessible oil was studied as a function of pore volume throughput and solvent slug size in various micromodels with different pore structure. Experimental results demonstrate that the residual oil under oil-wet conditions is 100% accessible by the oil bank. However, there is limited accessibility of the waterflood residual oil by the oil bank in waterwet conditions and the solvent is highly dispersed to the extent of having very early solvent breakthrough. It was found that no additional residual oil reconnection takes place after 2 slugs of solvent alternating with 2 slugs of water have passed through a region of the system with residual oil. For low capillary number at the front of the oil bank, the accessibility of waterflood residual oil by the oil bank decreases significantly as the pore structure becomes more heterogeneous.

title: Correlation of Dynamic Immiscible Displacement Patterns with the Fractional Wettability of Porous Media
caption: Figure 7. (a-d) Critical curvature frequency distribution of throats for various values of fp. (e-h) Smoothed transient response of the pressure drop across the porous medium for various values of fp(Ca=1.26 x 10-8 ).
figure_reason: Compares critical curvature distributions of throats with smoothed pressure-drop responses for several oil-wet fractions, showing the main correlation.
tldr: Visualization of low-Ca water displacing oil in a two-layer glass/PTFE bead pack shows displacement patterns and pressure-drop fluctuations reflect the spatial heterogeneity of fractional wettability.
summary: The paper links immiscible displacement patterns and pressure-drop signals to fractional wettability, which macroscopic indices such as Amott and USBM cannot resolve spatially. A two-layer model porous medium was packed from 1.5 mm neutral-wet glass and oil-wet PTFE spheres at oil-wet number fractions from 0 to 1. Silicon oil was displaced by dyed water at Ca = 1.26e-8 while images and differential pressure were recorded. Compact displacement occurred in areas of uniform wettability, while capillary fingering dominated where wettability varied strongly, leaving bypassed oil at intermediate fractions. Pressure-drop fluctuation amplitude and frequency, interpreted as successive isons and rheons, increased with heterogeneity and damped at high oil-wet fractions. FFT-smoothed pressure signals matched the critical curvature distributions of throats calculated from force-balance estimates.
abstract: Effects of the fractional pore surface wettability on the dynamic two-phase immiscible displacement patterns in porous media are examined experimentally. A model porous medium of controlled fractional wettability is fabricated by mixing neutral-wet glass microspheres with oil-wet PTFE microspheres, and packing them between two transparent glass plates. Visualization experiments of the displacement of the oleic by the aqueous phase are performed on the model porous medium at a low value of the capillary number by varying the number fraction of oil-wet particles. The displacement growth pattern is compact in areas of uniform wettability and is dominated by capillary fingering in areas where the heterogeneity of wettability is quite large. The transient response of the pressure drop across the porous medium is correlated with the spatial distribution of the critical capillary pressures required for the menisci advancement in individual throats and chambers and clusters of interconnected throats and chambers of varying wettability. The amplitude and frequency of the observed pressure drop fluctuations are associated with successive isons and rheons occurring during the motion of menisci between positions of capillary stability and instability. Such information can be used as a "fingerprint" of the spatial variation of the pore surface fractional wettability.

title: Complementary Imaging Techniques Applying Nti and MRI Determined Wettability Effects on Oil Recovery Mechanisms in Fractured Reservoirs
caption: Figure 3. Water saturation development while waterflooding the fractured strongly water-wet block CHP-4.
figure_reason: NTI saturation maps show block-by-block water advance with capillary hold-up at fractures in strongly water-wet chalk.
tldr: NTI on fractured chalk blocks and MRI on stacked plugs show wettability, fracture width and rate control how water crosses open fractures via hydraulic filling or bridges.
summary: Water movement across fractures in Rørdal outcrop chalk was studied at three wettabilities (Iw about 1.0, 0.6-0.7, 0.3) to understand oil recovery mechanisms in fractured reservoirs. Nuclear tracer imaging (about 1 cm resolution) monitored waterflooding of large fractured blocks, while MRI (about 300 µm) imaged decane in 1-3.5 mm fractures between stacked plugs, with D2O replacing brine. At strongly water-wet conditions, water did not enter the open fracture until the inlet plug reached its spontaneous imbibition endpoint, even at 5 times field rate, and then filled the fracture hydraulically. At moderately water-wet and nearly neutral-wet conditions, water drops grew into bridges across the fracture well before the imbibition endpoint, giving viscous communication. Bridge formation depended on fracture width (none at 3.5 mm for Iw=0.6), injection rate and wettability, with larger drops at lower water wetness.
abstract: The effects of fractures on oil recovery and in-situ saturation development in fractured chalk blocks have been determined for several representative wettabilities. These effects were visualized using two complimentary two-dimensional in-situ imaging techniques; nuclear tracer imaging (NTI) for the experiments with large blocks of chalk and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for high spatial resolution to visualize fluid flow patterns inside fractures between two stacked core plugs. For three different wettabilities, the specific patterns of saturation development were monitored with NTI and the mechanisms of fracture crossing were determined using MRI.

title: Multiple-Point Statistics to Generate Geologically Realistic Pore-Space Representations
caption: Figure 6. Fraction of percolating cells for images using different reconstruction methods. Notice that incorporating higher-order information in the reconstruction significantly improves the long-range connectivity of the pore space, although it still performs less well than process-based reconstruction methods. The data except multiple -point statistics and microCT are taken from [11].
figure_reason: Compares fraction of percolating cells for multiple-point, Gaussian, annealing, process-based and micro-CT, showing the main connectivity result.
tldr: Multiple-point statistics from a 2D thin-section training image generate 3D Fontainebleau sandstone pore-space models that preserve long-range connectivity better than two-point statistical methods.
summary: Two-point statistical reconstructions of 3D pore space from thin sections often fail to reproduce long-range connectivity. The authors adapt geostatistical multiple-point statistics, using a binarized 300×300 pixel (7.5 µm) thin-section slice as the training image with a multigrid of four 9×9 templates, and rotate the 2D statistics to build an isotropic 200³ 3D model. They test it on Fontainebleau sandstone with a micro-CT reference (porosity 0.1355). The reconstruction took 37 hours of CPU time. Specific surface area was 0.146 versus 0.122 for micro-CT, and 8% of pore space was disconnected versus 2% in the reference. The fraction of percolating cells was much closer to micro-CT than Gaussian-field or simulated-annealing reconstructions, though still below process-based reconstruction.
abstract: The resolution of current micro-CT scanning –a few microns – means that for many rocks, significant porosity cannot be imaged directly in three dimensions. Furthermore, alternative approaches, such as reconstruction through simulating sedimentation and diagenesis, may be problematic for many materials whose depositional and diagenetic history is uncertain or complex. In these cases it is necessary to find another approach to generate a pore space representation. One method is to use two-point statistics to produce a three-dimensional structure from two-dimensional information obtained from thin-section analysis. However, it has been shown that these reconstructed structures often fail to reproduce the long-range connectivity of the pore space. An attractive alternative approach is to use multiple-point statistics based on twodimensional thin-sections as training images to generate geologically realistic threedimensional pore space representations that preserve the long-range connectivity of the pore structure. The method is borrowed from geostatistical techniques that use a pixelbased representation to reproduce large-scale patterns. Thin-section images can provide multiple-point statistics, which describe the statistical relation between multiple spatial locations. We test the method on a simple sandstone for which a three-dimensional image from micro-CT scanning is available. We show that the use of multiple-point statistics allows the long-range connectivity of the structure to be preserved, in contrast to two-point methods that tend to underestimate the connectivity of the pore space. The proper selection of multiple-pointstatistics is a key issue and is discussed in detail.

title: Statistical Synthesis of Image Analysis and Mercury Porosimetry for Multiscale Pore Structure Characterization
caption: Figure 3. Distribution of pore volume by pore size (PVD), distribution of accessible pore volume by pore throat size (MIP) and simulated MIP result assuming complete pore accessibility and constant pore-to-throat aspect ratio of: (a) 3, (b) 18, (c) 30.
figure_reason: Compares fused pore volume distribution with MIP for sandstones, showing aspect ratios of 3, 18 and 30.
tldr: Combines BSEM image-derived two-point correlation with MIP fractal scaling to build pore size distributions over 0.01-1000 μm, revealing pore-to-throat aspect ratios in sandstones and carbonates.
summary: Pore structure in reservoir rock spans many orders of magnitude, and no single technique covers it. The authors fuse backscatter SEM image analysis (S2(r), above about 1 μm) with mercury intrusion porosimetry, using the surface fractal scaling I(Q) ∝ Q^(D-6) to extrapolate scattering intensity to small sizes. They verify that fractal dimensions from MIP and imaging agree reasonably for Berea sandstone, vuggy Silurian dolomites and silty Chatsworth sandstones (D about 2.3-2.95). Inverting the extended I(Q) with a spherical pore model gives a pore size distribution over five orders of magnitude, which is compared with MIP curves. Berea matches MIP with a pore-to-throat aspect ratio of about 3, poorly sorted clayey sandstones need ratios up to about 30, and carbonates show bimodal distributions with ratios of 1-20 that no single constant ratio fits. Permeability is also predicted within a factor of two from porosity and the correlation length Λ.
abstract: A novel method is developed for determining the continuous distribution of pore sizes in reservoir rock over the range 0.01-1000 $\mu\text{m}$ . The method employs a statistical description of the microstructure to combine information from mercury intrusion porosimetry (MIP) and image analysis. Central to this method is the observation that the pore size distribution obeys a fractal scaling law over a range of sizes accessible by both MIP and imaging methods ( $0.01 < r < 10 \mu\text{m}$ ). For a number of sandstone and carbonate samples it is verified that the surface fractal dimension obtained by analysis of MIP data is consistent with that obtained by image analysis. Data fusion is achieved in Fourier space. Accordingly, the scattering intensity data computed in the size range $1 < r < 1000 \mu\text{m}$ from the measured two-point correlation function are extrapolated in the range $0.01 < r < 1 \mu\text{m}$ using the known fractal scaling law. The extended scattering intensity data are interpreted using a model of scattering from a distribution of spherical pores. The resulting pore size distribution is used to compute a synthetic drainage capillary pressure curve, comparison of which to the MIP data furnishes new information on the pore-to-throat aspect ratio and pore accessibility.

title: Interpretation of a Long-Core Heavy Oil Depletion Experiment Using Pore Network Modelling Techniques
caption: Figure 2. History matching of gas saturations inside the core via network simulations for the well connected highly permeable case, Z=6 (simulations on 20X20X20 networks)
figure_reason: Shows history match of simulated versus experimental gas saturation at both depletion rates, the main result.
tldr: A pore network depressurisation simulator with progressive nucleation history-matches two heavy oil long-core depletion experiments and shows connectivity affects supersaturation, bubble density and recovery.
summary: Heavy oil solution gas drive depends on depletion rate, nucleation, diffusion and pore connectivity. A pore network simulator with progressive bubble nucleation was anchored to two mercury injection datasets (coordination numbers Z=6 and 4.9) and used to match gas and oil production from a 91 cm long core depleted at 9 and 100 psi/day. Different bubble densities arose naturally at each rate (9 vs 31 bubbles in a 20x20x20 network), giving good matches up to gas breakthrough, with steady-state relative permeabilities calculated afterwards. Applying the same parameters to a poorly connected network (Z=3.6) gave higher bubble density and better recovery, because longer diffusion paths increase supersaturation. Supersaturation rises with depletion rate and with decreasing connectivity, so recovery is not governed by depletion rate alone.
abstract: The performance of a solution gas drive experiment is ultimately determined by a complex interaction of a variety of different petrophysical parameters, including the rate of pressure decline and the chemical and physical properties of the rock-fluid system itself (viz: the nucleation properties of the porous medium, the gas-oil diffusivity, oil viscosity, gas-oil interfacial tension, dissolved gas-oil ratio, pore connectivity, etc). Here, a pore-scale process simulator is used to interpret the underlying dynamic processes that characterise a long-core heavy oil depletion experiment. This is achieved by direct matching of experimental gas and oil production profiles under different depletion rates. Progressive nucleation is implemented in the simulator, whereby bubbles nucleate from sites of increased "nucleation potential" — in keeping with recent developments in the field. The complex phenomenon of nucleation is discussed here in terms of the combined effects of (i) the spatial distribution of nucleation potential, (ii) depletion rate and (iii) the characteristics of the oil under investigation. Different bubble densities are produced at different depletion rates via a physically-based nucleation algorithm. As a result excellent history-matches of two heavy oil depressurisation experiments are obtained. The associated relative permeability curves are also presented. Finally, close analysis of the simulation data also allows us to investigate the widely-held belief that recovery efficiency is directly linked to depressurisation rate — the higher the depletion rate, the larger the number of bubbles nucleated, and the higher the observed recovery. We show here that recovery is seen to depend not only upon the depletion rate and bubble density, but also upon the lengths of diffusion pathways, local supersaturation gradients, and gas cluster topology — all of which are related to the underlying connectivity of the pore system.

title: A Dual Network Model for Relative Permeability of Bimodal Rocks: Application in a Vuggy Carbonate
caption: Fig. 13.- Water/oil relative permeameability for the matrix (? ), vugs ( ) and the dual-porosity system (continuous line).
figure_reason: Final water/oil relative permeability for matrix, vugs and dual-porosity system, showing the main result.
tldr: A dual pore-network model built from combined NMR-centrifuge and mercury porosimetry data reproduces a vuggy limestone's properties and shows matrix and vugs control water relative permeability, vugs control oil.
summary: Carbonates with vugs and matrix porosity have transport properties that single-porosity models cannot capture. The authors combined NMR T2 spectra at stepwise centrifuge water saturations with mercury injection on a bimodal limestone (porosity 33.8%, permeability 115 mD) to separate matrix and connected-macropore capillary pressure and pore size distributions, and to correlate T2 with pore radius (T2 ∝ r²). Single-porosity networks were tuned for the matrix (22.1% porosity, ~0.1 mD) and the connected vugs (14.9% porosity, ~115 mD), then coupled in a dual-porosity network with invasion percolation. The model matched the experimental capillary pressure curve, porosity and permeability. Calculated drainage relative permeabilities show water relative permeability depends on both vugs and matrix, especially at low water saturation, while oil relative permeability is controlled by the vugs.
abstract: Carbonate rocks often present bimodal pore size distributions usually attributed to the presence of vugs, large pores inserted in the porous matrix. This vugular porosity can communicate through the matrix (separated vugs) or it can form an interconnected pore system (touching vugs) (Lucia, 1999). These different degrees of interconnectivity confer to the porous medium transport properties very different than the ones characterizing homogeneous samples. In the present work a numerical simulator is presented, that calculates multiphase flow transport properties in vuggy carbonates taking into account their specific pore structure parameters. The complex real pore space is represented as a dual- network model that incorporates information on the primary (matrix) and the secondary (vugs, fractures) porosity and accounts for the connectivity of the secondary porosity. An original methodology is presented to deduce experimentally realistic pore size data to construct the network model taking into account the complex structure of the bimodal rocks. It consists in combining mercury invasion data and NMR measurements on partially saturated samples to deduce small-scale data characterizing pore-body and pore-throat size distributions needed to build the 3-D network model. The methodology has been validated on an outcrop limestone sample presenting a dual porosity. Based on the experimental data a dual pore-network has been constructed. It satisfactorily reproduces the capillary pressure curve, the porosity and the permeability determined experimentally. Through calculations performed with this model it is demonstrated that wetting phase relative permeability is strongly affected by both the vugs and matrix characteristics, while non-wetting phase is mainly controlled by the vuggy system.

title: Two-Phase Flow Rock-Typing : Another Approach
tldr: Using Fontainebleau sandstone and two field cases, the paper shows pore-geometry rock-types fail for waterflood Kr when wettability varies; multivariate, process-dependent rock-types are needed.
summary: Routine rock-types built from porosity, permeability, capillary pressure and facies are often assumed to also define relative permeability, whatever the recovery process. The authors test this on Fontainebleau sandstone (water-wet and aged) and on two field datasets: a West Africa sandstone (13 gas floods, 16 waterfloods) and a carbonate (13 waterfloods). In strongly water-wet Fontainebleau and in the gas-oil floods of Field A, residual saturation and oil Kr exponent correlate well with porosity, permeability or Pc shape factor. For Field A waterfloods, Sorw ranged 0.1–0.225 and Krw(Sorw) 0.09–0.45, with no single pore-geometry indicator explaining them; Sorw and Krw(Sorw) trended with height above the water-oil contact, indicating wettability control. In the carbonate, Swi correlates with permeability but Sorw does not, so rock-types for oil in place differ from those for reserves. Combining pore-geometry and wettability indicators captured most Kr variability, and rock-types should depend on the recovery process.
abstract: Petrophysical units, also called rock-types, are usually defined to help the reservoir engineers to assign petrophysical characteristics to different zones of a reservoir. Estimate of initial hydrocarbons in place accounts for such petrophysical units which are usually generated, using both single-phase data, i.e. porosity, permeability, and two-phase drainage data (i.e capillary pressure curve) and coupled with sedimentological descriptions. It is then frequently assumed that these rock-types are valid to assign two-phase flow characteristics, such as relative permeability curves, to a reservoir, whatever the recovery process. This paper shows that this assumption is often not correct, using several field examples, including sandstone and carbonate reservoirs. Based on a large number of core flood results, it is shown that the usual rock-typing methods may not capture the actual variability of relative permeability curves. It is also shown that: 1) Multivariate descriptions, including petrophysical characteristics and wettability indicators, should be the basis for the generation of multiphase flow rock-types. 2) Two-phase flow rock-types should be dependent on the recovery process. Consequences on sampling for coreflood programmes, as well as inputs of simulation models are pointed out.

title: Residual Gas Saturation of Sample Originally at Residual Water Saturation in Heterogeneous Sandstone Reservoirs
caption: Figure 8: Relationships between Sgr@Swir and porosity (A), SgrM (B), permeability (C) and clay content (D).
figure_reason: Shows Sgr@Swir versus porosity, SgrM, permeability and clay content, including the Sgr@Swir≈SgrM agreement.
tldr: Sixty sandstone samples show residual gas saturation at irreducible water equals maximum trapped gas saturation, controlled by rock quality rather than Swir, so Land's law extrapolation is invalid.
summary: Residual gas saturation at irreducible water saturation (Sgr@Swir) was studied on sixty sandstone samples from two Far East gas reservoirs and Fontainebleau outcrops (porosity 0.06-0.25, permeability 0.1-3000 mD). Initial gas saturation was set by controlled evaporation of Isopar L, followed by spontaneous imbibition. NMR and CT scans showed homogeneous fluid distribution after evaporation, and Sgr-Sgi curves matched capillary desorption results on eight samples. Sgr@Swir ranged 0.05-0.75, was close to SgrM regardless of Swir, and showed the same opposite porosity trends, linked to clay-bound water, microporosity and pore size. Land's law applied to estimate Sgr@Swir gave a mean error near 0.04 and maximum near 0.08, so taking SgrM as Sgr@Swir is the better estimate.
abstract: Residual gas saturation is known to be a key factor in evaluating gas recovery from a lean gas reservoir invaded by water. The large scatter in maximum trapped gas saturation (SgrM), the existence of two opposite SgrM/porosity trends and the key controls of the variability of SgrM were illustrated by two recent studies (Suzanne et al., 2001; Hamon et al., 2001). This paper tackles the influence of irreducible water saturation on the variability of trapped gas saturation. Sgr measurements were performed by controlled evaporation and capillary imbibition or by capillary drainage/imbibition. Sixty samples were selected from sandstone formations to account for the largest scatter in SgrM observed in our previous study and cover a very large range in porosity and permeability. The main results of this study are: - The fluid distribution after controlled evaporation was checked with NMR and X-ray scanner measurements and was found homogeneous. - The Sgr values obtained by evaporation-imbibition were found in very close agreement with those achieved by capillary drainage -imbibition on eight reservoir samples - The presence of irreducible water prior to the imbibition does not change the existence of two opposite Sgr trends as a function of porosity (or permeability). - Sgr at irreducible water saturation, Sgr@Swir, may decrease as porosity decreases. This relationship is shown to be related to increasing clay content, decreasing pore size or increasing amount of microporosity as SgrM values. - Maximum trapped gas saturation and Sgr at irreducible water saturation were found equal. So, Sgr may either increase or decrease as a function of irreducible water saturation, showing that Sgr is not controlled only by initial water saturation. And, the frequent extrapolation of Land's empirical relationship to the interval [SgrM, Sgr@Swir] is not correct.

title: Depressurization Under Tertiary Conditions in the Near-Wellbore Region: Experiments, Visualization and Radial Flow Simulations
caption: Figure 7 : gas production history matching (a) and krg results (b)
figure_reason: History matching of gas production and the tertiary krg curve compared with secondary results.
tldr: Core, micromodel and radial simulations show tertiary depressurization gives lower gas relative permeability than secondary, and Sgc varies with distance from the wellbore.
summary: The paper studies solution-gas depressurization of waterflood residual oil in the near-wellbore region. Two coreflood experiments on Vosges sandstone (58 mD, C1C7 oil, brine injected at 30 cc/h while outlet pressure dropped below the 21 bar bubble point) were monitored by CT saturation profiles and history-matched with a depletion code to obtain Sgc and krg. Incremental oil of 35-42% OOIP was produced, and krg under tertiary conditions was around 1e-4, lower than under secondary conditions and consistent with literature. Micromodel visualization showed a double connection process (oil ganglia reconnection and gas connection) explaining the low krg. A radial numerical experiment gave Sgc of 26% near the outlet falling to 20% at the gas front, versus a uniform 24% in linear flow.
abstract: Depressurization can be a very interesting process to recover hydrocarbons from waterflooded oil reservoir with high gas-oil-ratio. Most of the published results are related to depletion experiments under secondary conditions (virgin reservoir). Data are more scarce under tertiary conditions after waterflooding [1, 2, 3]. The present paper treats the issue of the depressurization under tertiary conditions in the nearwellbore region. Practically, this has been achieved by combining experimental results, obtained on both core and transparent micromodel, with radial flow depletion simulations that are representative of the conditions prevailing in the near-wellbore region. A validated methodology previously presented [4] has been used to design the experiments on core (the core under tertiary conditions was continuously flushed with water at a fixed rate, while the pressure at the outlet was decreased to reproduce a drawdown). The saturation profiles, the pressures and the fluid productions as a function of time were recorded in the two experiments that are presented. From the core experiments, critical gas saturation (Sgc) and relative permeability (kr) have been determined using a specific simulation code that takes into account nucleation, diffusion and mobilization processes related to the appearance of the gas phase from solution. Constant depletion rate experiments were also conducted on a transparent micromodel to study the process of connection of the gas phase under tertiary conditions. The specificity of the near-wellbore region (high dP/dt and radial flow) was then investigated by conducting a numerical experiment with radial geometry. It is shown that gas relative permeabilities obtained under tertiary conditions are lower than the ones obtained under secondary conditions. This behavior is attributed to the double connection process that is needed for the gas to get mobilized: connection of the disconnected oil phase and connection of the gas phase itself. This phenomenon is also confirmed by the visualization experiments conducted on micromodel. The numerical experiment representative of the near-wellbore conditions with a radial geometry demonstrates that Sgc is a function of the distance to the wellbore, which can have a large impact on reservoir simulation results.

title: A Numerical Study of the Influence of Sample Shape on Spontaneous Imbibition
caption: Figure 5: Correlation between the normalized scale factors predicted by the simulator and the values calculated by the Ma et al. correlation. L is linear; R is radial; S is spherical; O is outer face open; I is inner face open; 2,4,8 are aspect ratios in tenths.
figure_reason: Shows poor agreement of the Ma et al. scale factor with simulated values, especially for outer-open cases.
tldr: Finite-difference simulations of counter-current imbibition show sample shape changes curve shape for annular and hollow-spherical samples with one face open; a volume-weighted characteristic length correlates results well.
summary: The study examines how sample geometry affects spontaneous imbibition recovery curves in a water-wet, Berea-like system (k = 600 mD, porosity 0.215). An explicit finite-difference simulator with 298 grid blocks was extended from linear to radial, spherical, annular-radial and hollow-spherical geometries, with inner, outer or both faces open and aspect ratios from 0 to 0.8. Linear, radial and spherical solid shapes give essentially the same curve shape, though rates differ by factors of about 22 to 27. Annular and hollow-spherical samples with only one face open show systematic shape differences, largest at small aspect ratio and vanishing as the ratio approaches one. With both faces open, curves are nearly identical to the linear case. The Ma et al. characteristic length works within experimental error, but a new scale factor weighting distance from the open face by local volume correlates the simulations more closely, except for inner-open cases at the lowest aspect ratios.
abstract: This paper reports on a numerical study of the effect of sample shape on spontaneous imbibition curves (recovery versus time) in a water-wet, laboratory scale system. Characteristic lengths based on the surface area open to imbibition and distance to the corresponding no-flow boundary, have been tested experimentally by Ma et al. for cylindrical samples with configurations having the following open surfaces: one-end, both-ends, the radial surface, and all surfaces. The present study addresses onedimensional linear, and radially and spherically symmetric cases, and thus includes the first and third cases investigated by Ma et al. Also considered are annular-radial samples and hollow-spherical samples for a wide range of aspect ratio (inner radius divided by outer radius) with inner, outer, and both surfaces open. The numerical results show that, although the Ma et al. correlation is satisfactory within expected experimental error, annular and hollow spherical shapes, particularly for either the inner or outer face open, give systematic differences in shape of the spontaneous imbibition curves. Only minor differences in curve shape are obtained when both faces are open. The maximum differences occur for the smallest aspect ratio. The differences approach zero as the aspect ratio approaches one. An extension of the correlation, that weights the distance from the open surface with the local volume, gave close correlation of the simulated results for all cases. The results identify conditions under which differences in curve shape should be readily detectable by experiment.

title: Experimental Results for High Flow Rates of Oil-Water Through High Permeability Media
caption: Fig. 6b - Oil and water relative permeabilities for the treated sand.
figure_reason: Oil and water relative permeabilities for treated sand show oil Kr dependent on velocity, the key result.
tldr: Oil-water flow experiments in high-permeability sand packs show emulsion formation, wettability-dependent pressure drop, and velocity-dependent oil relative permeability, so standard Kr models fail.
summary: In high-permeability (super K) zones, high oil-water rates can cause inertial effects and emulsions that challenge relative permeability models. The authors injected Marcol oil (about 30 cP) and water at steady state through 6 cm x 35 cm sand packs of roughly 3 mm quartz, water-wet and siliconate-treated (intermediate wet). Permeabilities were about 3.4-5.0 x10^3 Darcy; water showed Forchheimer inertial behavior while Marcol followed Darcy's law. Two-phase flow produced an oil-in-water emulsion at all rates; wettability strongly changed pressure drop and effective emulsion viscosity but not saturation. Interpretation with generalized Darcy gave a single water Kr curve but a family of oil Kr curves depending on velocity, so emulsion flow cannot be described by standard relative permeabilities.
abstract: In some reservoirs, oil and water are produced at very high flow rate through zones of high permeability (super K). For this type of flows, inertial effects and formation of emulsion can limit the utility of standard models based on relative permeabilities. In order to study these effects, we have performed several series of experiments into two kinds of sand packs: water wet and of intermediate wettability (siliconate treatment). Velocities of oil and water were varied in a large range. Pressures were measured along the core and the average saturation

title: Prediction of Optimum Operating Conditions for Steady-State Two-Phase Flow in Pore Network Systems Using the
caption: Figure 6 Effect of the viscosity ratio, $\kappa$ , on the energy utilization factor ( $f_{EU=r}/W$ ) as a function of Ca and $r$ in the 3D network.
figure_reason: Shows f_EU surfaces with ridge locus and the effect of viscosity ratio in 3D network.
tldr: Using the DeProF model on 2D and 3D pore networks, the paper defines an energy utilization factor and finds a locus in (Ca, r) where oil transport per energy is maximal.
summary: Steady-state two-phase flow in porous media is modeled with DeProF, which decomposes flow into connected-oil pathway flow, ganglion dynamics and drop traffic flow. The authors introduce an energy utilization factor, f_EU = r/W, the oil/water flowrate ratio over reduced mechanical energy dissipation. Simulations covered 2D and 3D chamber-and-throat networks with oil/water viscosity ratios of 0.66, 1.45 and 3.35, over a Ca–r domain (Ca up to 10^-5, log r from -1 to 2). For every system and each Ca, a unique flowrate ratio r*(Ca) maximizes f_EU, forming a continuous ridge line in the (Ca, r) domain. f_EU rises with Ca as connected-oil flow expands and viscous dissipation dominates, and it rises more strongly at lower viscosity ratio. At fixed Ca it rises at small r and falls at larger r as oil organizes into larger, harder-to-mobilize ganglia that increase capillary dissipation.
abstract: The recently developed predictive model "DeProF" (acronym for "Decomposition into Prototype Flows") considers steady-state two-phase flow in porous media as an in-parallel combination of three flow patterns, namely Connected-oil Pathway Flow, Ganglion Dynamics and Drop Traffic Flow. The key difference between these prototype flow patterns is the degree of disconnection of the non-wetting phase ('oil') which, in turn, affects the relative magnitude of the rate of energy dissipation caused by capillary effects compared to that caused by viscous stresses. The observed flow is usually a mixture of the basic prototype flows. Each flow pattern prevails over mesoscopic -scale regions of the porous medium (ranging from a few to several hundred pores), whereas the macroscopic flow is homogeneous. The predictive capability of the DeProF model was used to investigate whether optimum operating conditions appear in steady-state two-phase flow in pore networks. A new macroscopic dependent variable is determined, namely the energy utilization factor. This variable is defined as the ratio of the reduced o/w flow rate ratio over the reduced mechanical energy dissipated; it represents a measure of the efficacy of the physical process in terms of oil transport. Using DeProF, simulations were carried out over the domain of capillary number, Ca, and oil-water flowrate ratio, r, in which two-phase flow is sustainable and for three systems of oil/water/pore network. The results show that, for every system, there exist a continuous line (locus) in the (Ca, r) domain on which the energy utilization factor attains a local maximum.

title: Co-Injected CO2-Brine Interactions with Indiana Limestone
caption: Fig. 6. Composition of Mn. and Sr. along the core length at the end of the flood.
figure_reason: Mn and Sr profiles along the core show enrichment peaking near the solution channel tip, evidencing deposition.
tldr: Co-injecting CO2 and tracer-doped brine through Indiana limestone at reservoir conditions caused dissolution and a solution channel, while Mn- and Sr-rich carbonate deposits formed near the channel tip.
summary: Injectivity changes in CO2 WAG and sequestration projects may reflect carbonate dissolution and precipitation. A two-segment composite Indiana limestone core (56.5 cm, 17.35% porosity) was flooded at 100°F and 2000 psig outlet pressure with 1:1 CO2 and brine for about 155 PV. The brine carried Mn, Mg and Sr chlorides as tracers to give new deposits a compositional contrast with the rock. Porosity and permeability first decreased, then rose; a solution channel formed in segment A and permeability reached 1978 md. Chemical analysis and BSEI showed Mn up to 500 times baseline and Sr about twice baseline, peaking at 15 cm near the channel tip. Deposits were Mn-rich (about 66% Mn-carbonate) and showed zoned euhedral growth, indicating that dissolution and deposition occur in close proximity.
abstract: This paper reports findings of coreflooding limestone with co-injected carbon dioxide (CO2) and brine at reservoir pressure and temperature. Metal chlorides were added as tracer components to the injection brine and appeared in quantities well above natural levels in deposited carbonates. Core segment porosity and permeability are reported to indicate dissolution and deposition. Finally, the core was sectioned and analyzed by chemical and back-scattered electron imaging (BSEI) and chemical titration for

title: An Experimental and Numerical Investigation of Water-Oil Flow in Vugular Porous Media
caption: Figure 8. Numerical differential pressure during drainage on core E2. Case 1 and 2 .
figure_reason: Simulated drainage pressure drop for case 1 and 2 on core E2, showing which vug relative permeability reproduces plateaus.
tldr: Drainage and imbibition experiments on artificial vugular sandstone cores, with and without density contrast, were simulated in 2D; vug relative permeabilities must keep high mobility, and matrix capillary pressure matters.
summary: Two-phase flow in vugular carbonates is poorly described, so the authors drilled three 2.5 cm holes through square Vosges sandstone cores fitted with glass windows. Drainage and forced imbibition were run with brine and either Marcol 52 or density-matched dibutyl-phthalate, with gamma-ray saturation mapping, pressure drop and visual observation. In drainage, the vugs fill with oil sequentially at near-zero capillary pressure (three pressure plateaus) while the matrix front stays nearly immobile. In imbibition, breakthrough is early (0.32 PV for core E2), water enters the vugs and matrix simultaneously, and matrix Sor was 0.37. Gravity produced phase segregation in the vugs, which was absent with matched densities. 2D simulations with ATHOS used matrix Kr/Pc history-matched on homogeneous cores and zero Pc in the vugs. Near-constant vug relative permeabilities (Corey exponent 0.01) reproduced drainage, whereas exponent 20 failed, and imbibition depended mainly on matrix capillary pressure.
abstract: Vugular porous media are found in many reservoirs especially those constituted of carbonate rocks where large cavities (called vugs) resulting from complex diagenetic processes are embedded in the porous matrix. Due to their structure, these porous materials have special transport properties and optimization of oil recovery from such reservoirs requires a good description of two-phase -oil and water- flow. From a macroscopic poin t of view, a reliable determination of fluid flow properties such as relative permeability and capillary pressure is desirable. In this work, we present an experimental and numerical study of water-oil flow in an artificial vugular porous medium. Model vugular samples were obtained from a sandstone core, representing the continuum and homogeneous porous matrix through which cylindrical holes, representing the vugs, were drilled. Transparent windows, placed in front of the vugs allow a direct observation of the two-phase distribution and the evolution during flow. Due to the configuration, the flow is two-dimensional and saturation maps were obtained from local saturation measurement in the porous matrix using a Gray attenuation technique. Drainage and imbibition cycles were performed during which direct visualization, saturation as well as pressure measurements clearly highlight the differences between the two processes in the vug and in the matrix regions. Using different density contrasts between oil and brine, the relative effect of viscous and gravity forces was investigated. Two-dimensional numerical simulations were performed on the experimental configuration using an industrial software. The vugular core was represented by a two-region medium corresponding to the matrix and vugs respectively. Petrophysical properties of the porous matrix were assigned by fitting experimental two-phase flow results obtained on a separate but similar homogeneous core -without vugs. In the region corresponding to the vugs, a zero capillary pressure was used while different sets of oil and water relative permeabilities were tested for comparison of pressure and saturation evolution on the vugular core with experimental data.

title: Visualization of Three Phases in Porous Media Using Micro Computed Tomography
caption: Figure 7 shows a partitioned three-phase system. Water is represented by white, decane as light gray, benzyl alcohol as dark gray, and the grains are black. Although all three phases are present, water is at irreducible saturation. The injection of the decane and oil at this specific ratio did not displace additional water. The small pores are still occupied by the wetting phase, water. The decane
figure_reason: Partitioned three-phase slice showing water, decane, benzyl alcohol and grains, with benzyl alcohol as the intermediate phase.
tldr: Micro-CT at 9 micron resolution maps water, benzyl alcohol and decane in sand, confirming benzyl alcohol as the intermediate phase predicted by the spreading coefficient.
summary: The paper addresses the lack of three-dimensional pore-scale data on three-phase fluid distribution. A glass tube (7 mm ID) of loose quartz sand (about 1 mm grains) was scanned with a micro-focus x-ray CT at 145 kV, with 9x9x21 micron voxels. Water was doped with NaI and decane with iodo-dodecane, while benzyl alcohol was left untagged, so that all phases could be separated at a single energy. Dry-scan partitioning gave an average porosity of 0.48, and images were processed in stages to give two-phase and three-phase saturation maps at static conditions. Water occupied small pores and grain contacts, decane formed ganglia in large pores, and benzyl alcohol was the intermediate phase, as predicted by the spreading coefficient. No relationship between residual water saturation and porosity was found, because the grains were large relative to the sample and no representative elementary volume could be selected.
abstract: Three-phase flow in porous media is a common phenomenon in hydrocarbon reservoirs. This study presents quantitative maps of fluid distribution in a granular porous medium using micro computed tomography (MCT). The study was done in an effort to determine the position, distribution and saturation of each phase at the pore-scale level. Quartz sand was used as the porous media. The fluids used were water (doped with NaI), benzyl alcohol (BA) and decane (doped with iodo-dodecane). The three fluids and the solid phase were mapped in images that were acquired at a single energy setting. Single-phase, two-phase and three-phase saturation distributions were developed. The intermediate phase was detected by direct observation of the phase distribution in the porous medium thus confirming calculations using interfacial tensions and the spreading coefficient. The results obtained from this research showed that micro computed tomography (MCT) is a useful technique to study multi-phase flow mechanisms in porous media. This work provided three-dimensional maps of fluid saturations at the pore level and should allow the reconsideration and adjustment of pore-scale modeling. This method provides the possibility to obtain three-dimensional saturation data that can be used for simulator development and calibration of models.

title: Trapped Versus Initial Gas Saturation Trends from a Single Core Test
caption: Figure 7. Final (trapped) versus initial gas saturation from average saturation and in situ saturation measurements. Data from reference 7 is for chalk-like rocks.
figure_reason: Combines all trapped versus initial gas saturation data sets, showing they follow one trend, including literature chalk data.
tldr: In situ x-ray saturation profiles in a single chalk core test give trapped versus initial gas saturation trends matching the Land Correlation.
summary: Defining trapped versus initial gas saturation normally needs many tests with different initial gas saturations. Five tests on water-wet chalk cores (34-38% porosity, 1-7 mD) were run: four with live-fluid depressurization at 121-130 °C to evolve gas, and a fifth gas-then-brine flood at 79 °C. X-ray linear scans gave in situ saturation profiles in the last two tests. Non-uniform gas profiles supplied a range of initial saturations, and pairing initial and final saturations by position gave a trend well fit by the Land Correlation (Swr about 0.25). Depressurization and gas-injection data fell on the same trend, bulk results agreed with it, and gas appeared only more than 2 MPa below the PVT bubble point.
abstract: When gas is displaced by liquid in porous media, the saturation at which gas becomes immobile is referred to as the trapped gas saturation. Trapped gas saturation magnitude is important in reservoir scenarios such as water invasion into a gas reservoir, WAG, or water flooding with pressure below the oil bubble point pressure. Trapping is related to saturation history. Typically, to describe a relationship between final and initial gas saturation from changes in average or bulk core saturation, many tests with various initial gas saturations are required. Being able to gain similar information from a single test would provide time and cost benefits. This is the primary subject of this paper. Tests were performed using carbonate core, live fluids, and reservoir conditions to evaluate trapped gas. Pressure was reduced below the oil bubble point pressure to evolve gas within the core. Oil and brine floods subsequently reduced gas saturation to a "trapped" condition. X-ray methods were used to quantify saturation changes in cores. In one test, three-phase saturations at various positions within the core were determined by an x-ray attenuation technique. Although the gas saturation profile after pressure depletion was non-uniform, this "non-uniformity" provided a range of "initial" gas saturations to compare with "final" gas saturations for various positions within the core. Additional data was gained by flooding the core with gas and then brine. The trend in trapped versus initial gas saturation from both data sets was well represented by the Land Correlation. After cleaning the core plug, another test was performed whereby the core was flooded with gas to displace brine. Subsequently, the core was flooded with brine to trap gas. Trapped versus initial gas saturation values for discrete positions along the length of the core fell upon the same trend as that from the more complex depressurization test. The technique of comparing gas saturation change from in situ saturation measurements appears to be particularly useful for providing enough data from a single test to describe a trapped versus initial gas saturation trend.

title: On the Effect of Reservoir Confining Stress on Mercury Intrusion-Derived Pore Frequency Distribution
caption: Figure 8 - Capillary Pressure Curves
figure_reason: Capillary pressure curves for chloritic sandstone show crossover with ambient and large entry pressure increase at high stress.
tldr: High-pressure mercury intrusion on six rock types under hydrostatic confinement up to 16000 psi shows entry pressure rises and microporosity is lost with stress, so unstressed tests mislead.
summary: Conventional high-pressure mercury intrusion is run on unstressed samples, which are not representative of downhole conditions. The authors used a miniature pre-stressing cell with a hardening sleeve fluid to hold fixed hydrostatic confinement (2000 to 16000 psi) during intrusion up to 60000 psia. Six rock types were tested (limestone, Kimmeridge Clay siltstone, chloritic sandstone, tight gas sandstone, poorly consolidated sandstone, chalk), plus a homogeneous synthetic sample showing about 1% relative reproducibility in intrusion volume. Entry pressure increased with confining stress; for example, Kimmeridge Clay seal capacity rose by a factor of 3.6 at approximate in-situ stress. Microporosity was lost preferentially, several samples collapsed at high stress (chloritic sandstone entry pressure rose from 12.9 to 1848 psia at 6000 psi), and ambient tests of poorly consolidated sand showed false intrusion from compaction. Only the chalk deformed systematically without failure.
abstract: Historically, mercury intrusion has been used to estimate primary drainage characteristics of reservoir rock samples at low intrusion pressures. In recent times, technology has matured to the point where very high intrusion pressures are routinely used, sufficient to enter essentially all of the distribution of the subject test sample. The major unresolved question has remained the absence of representative confining stress during high-pressure mercury intrusion testing. A complication

title: NMR Imaging with Diffusion and Relaxation
caption: Figure 6. Results of 2D T1MRI of Plug-A: (top) porosity, BVI (with 33ms T1 cutoff), FFI, T1G, and T1G of BVI maps, and (bottom) five images at different T1 bins. Each T1 bin is an average of the adjacent four T1 imagings used in the BRD inversion. The diameter of the core plug is about 1.5 inches and the length is about 2 inches. Its outward appearance is that of an intergranular sandstone/carbona
figure_reason: 2D T1 MRI maps of Plug-A showing porosity, BVI, free fluid and T1 distributions revealing vugs.
tldr: Presents NMR imaging sequences that encode T1 relaxation or diffusion before imaging, giving spatially resolved T1 and diffusion distributions in test fluids and core plugs.
summary: Conventional MRI of cores gives fluid distributions but not pore size or wettability information, because internal field gradients limit resolution. The authors combine T1 inversion-recovery or Tanner stimulated-echo encoding with 1D and 2D imaging sequences, using FFT and BRD inversion to produce maps of position versus T1 or diffusion coefficient. On a three-cell test sample, distilled water (T1 about 3 s), crude oil (about 200 ms) and doped water (about 20 ms) were clearly separated, and water diffusion near 4e-5 cm2/s was about 10 times that of the oil. 2D T1 imaging of a 1.5-inch plug revealed small vugs and one large vug, with free-fluid and bound-fluid (33 ms cutoff) maps showing no clay in the vugs. 1D diffusion imaging of a second plug showed larger apparent diffusion at the ends, attributed to internal field gradients, and strong variation in the middle, attributed to restricted diffusion or gradient variation.
abstract: We developed novel NMR imaging techniques which can be used to characterize fluid distribution and pore sizes in rock samples. The combination of imaging with relaxometry not only provides the proton population map in core samples but also incorporates information about the relaxation times and diffusion coefficients of pore fluids in a rock sample. NMR images of a core plug sample were obtained where the proton signal was successively encoded with information on relaxation time and diffusion coefficient of the pore fluids. The encoding was achieved by imposing a saturation recovery sequence for T1 relaxation, or a Tanner (or similar) sequence for the diffusion coefficient, before the imaging pulsing sequences. Thus, the NMR images were processed to yield the normal proton population image with an extra dimension showing either the relaxation time or the diffusion coefficient distributions. This procedure allows us to identify how the fluid is distributed within the core plug using the contrast in the diffusion coefficients, as well as the characteristics of the pore fabric using the T1 relaxation time distribution. It also provides a means of inferring the surface wettability in the spatial image of a core plug. Several

title: An Improved Technique for Deriving Drainage Capillary Pressure from NMR T2 Distributions
caption: Figure 9. Experimental cumulative T2 distribution for an outcrop sample (Dod-4) and the effective distribution used to calculate the improved capillary pressure.
figure_reason: Shows the effective cumulative T2 distribution versus measured one, illustrating the key correction that improves Pc prediction.
tldr: A triangular-pore model accounts for water left in crevices of drained pores, improving NMR T2-derived drainage capillary pressure at high pressures in sandstones without empirical scaling.
summary: NMR-derived drainage capillary pressure methods overpredict desaturation at high capillary pressure because they ignore wetting fluid retained in crevices of drained pores. The authors use an equilateral triangular pore model to calculate retained water saturation and the shifted T2 of drained pores, then build an effective cumulative T2 distribution combining fully saturated and calculated drained distributions. Capillary pressure is then obtained with Volokitin's kappa-scaling. Tested on eleven sandstones (outcrop and reservoir, 0.22 to 2220 mD) with porous plate, centrifuge and mercury injection data, the model predicted irreducible water saturation at 100 psi well. Fitted surface relaxivity ranged 1.2-4.0 µm/s for outcrop samples, and the corrected Pc curves agreed better with measurements, especially at low saturation and in lower-permeability cores.
abstract: Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) T2 measurements can be used directly to estimate petrophysical properties of reservoir rocks such as porosity and irreducible water saturation. They are also sensitive to pore-size distribution enabling the estimation of permeability and potentially capillary pressure. Several methods have been proposed to derive synthetic drainage capillary pressure information directly from NMR data [1-5]. However empirical correction factors are usually introduced in the scaling factor to improve the capillary pressure prediction at low wetting phase saturation. This paper presents an improved method to derive primary drainage capillary pressure from T2 distributions of fully saturated rocks. The modification is based upon experimental observations that T2 signal amplitude increases at shorter times when comparing data from partially saturated cores with that from fully saturated cores. This is usually assumed to be due to water (or wetting fluid) remaining in crevices in such partially saturated cores. Such water has a faster relaxation rate as it has a higher surface area to volume ratio. We propose the use of a simple model of triangular pores to estimate the irreducible water saturation and the T2 distribution of the drained core. The drainage capillary pressure is then derived from an effective cumulative T2 distribution, obtained by combining the measured T2 distribution from the fully saturated core with the distribution calculated at drained conditions from the triangular capillary model. The method has been applied successfully to a number of sandstone core samples with a wide range of permeabilities. The triangular pore model predicts reasonably well the connate water saturation at various capillary pressures. The NMR derived and primary drainage capillary pressure curves show a very good agreement. The improvement in prediction mainly takes place at high capillary pressures and is automatically calculated as a function of the T2 distribution and the pressure applied.

title: Application of NMR Diffusion Editing as Chlorite Indicator
caption: Figure 6. Diffusion editing results for six different samples that are all brine saturated. On the left, diffusion – T2 maps are shown with the dashed lines indicating the molecular diffusion coefficient of water. On the right, the diffusion distributions f(D) are shown, obtained by projecting the D-T2 maps onto the diffusion axis. The dashed lines show the cutoff used for chlorite indicator. The
figure_reason: D–T2 maps and f(D) for six brine-saturated samples show signal shifting to high apparent diffusion with chlorite/iron content.
tldr: Diffusion-editing NMR separates oil and water in sandstone cores and, via signal at large apparent diffusion coefficients, gives an indicator of chlorite content correlated with FTIR chlorite and iron.
summary: Chlorite strongly affects reservoir quality, and its internal magnetic gradients distort NMR T2 interpretation and oil/water separation. Eight Norwegian Sea sandstone plugs (0–4.5 wt% chlorite, 0.9–963 mD) were measured by CPMG at 2 MHz and by diffusion editing in a 13.2 G/cm static gradient (1.76 MHz) at brine, drainage, imbibition and D2O-exchanged states. In low-chlorite samples D–T2 maps separated oil from water, with NMR oil saturation within 3 saturation units of gravimetric values using a diffusion cutoff of 8e-6 cm²/s. In chlorite-rich samples, a growing fraction of signal appeared at apparent D above 5e-5 cm²/s due to internal gradients; this fraction correlates with FTIR chlorite and Fe2O3 content. The indicator also trends with T2 cutoff, cementation exponent and grain density, though it prevents saturation determination in high-chlorite samples.
abstract: We present a nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) based study on a series of sandstone cores from a major reservoir in the Norwegian Sea. The cores have varying amounts of chlorite and were prepared in different saturation states. NMR measurements were performed using the standard Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill (CPMG) pulse sequence and the new diffusion editing method that is designed to separate diffusion and relaxation effects. This procedure generally results in more reliable Sw values and we demonstrate here that it can also be used to derive an indicator of chlorite content. Since the measurement of diffusion editing can be performed with logging tools, this technique can be used directly in a reservoir for the improved determination of saturation and to estimate the chlorite content, with important implications for the assessment of reservoir quality. When the samples were saturated with a mixture of refined oil and brine it was generally difficult to separate the contributions of the two phases in the CPMG relaxation measurements. The relaxation time of the oil often overlapped significantly with the T2 distribution of the brine signal. To overcome this problem, we used the technique of diffusing editing to obtain simultaneously diffusion and relaxation information and its correlation. This was achieved by preceding the standard short-echo-spacing CPMG sequence by an editing sequence that attenuates the amplitude of the signal according to diffusion in the applied gradient. In the current work, we implemented the diffusion editing by increasing the first two echo spacings systematically. Relaxation information is obtained from the signal decay after the diffusion encoding. This effectively orthogonalizes the diffusion and relaxation information and allows the extraction of diffusion – relaxation distribution functions. These two-dimensional D – T2 maps can be used to extract information about important reservoir parameters such as water saturation, oil viscosity, wettability state and hydrocarbon-corrected bound-fluid volume. For the samples with low chlorite concentration, the diffusion – relaxation distribution functions clearly separated the signal into oil and water contributions. For samples with higher chlorite concentrations, the D – T2 maps showed an additional significant contribution at apparent diffusion coefficients in excess of bulk oil or water. In these samples, the presence of chlorite gives rise to internal gradients in the adjacent pore space that exceeds the externally applied gradient. This leads to an increased diffusive decay that can be characterized by a large apparent diffusion coefficient. We found that the chlorite concentration in the sample is correlated with the fraction of signal that exhibits such large apparent diffusion coefficients.

title: The Scaling of Surface-to-Pore-Volume Ratio Estimates and Its Use in Predicting NMR Log Derived Permeabilities in Clastic Rocks. Model Driven Field Applications from the Lublin Basin, Poland
caption: Figure 6. Conversion of TNMR log-mean $T_2$ times to BET based inner surface area measurements. Note the considerable scatter around the correlation line which may be attributed to the variability of surface relaxivity values $r_2$ .
figure_reason: Shows the T2 log-mean versus BET surface correlation underlying the TNMR permeability equation, with scatter from surface relaxivity.
tldr: Uses a fractal pigeon-hole model to scale BET, MICP and NMR surface areas on Lublin Basin cores, deriving a TNMR Kozeny-Carman permeability estimator for logs.
summary: Surface-to-pore-volume estimates from BET, MICP and NMR operate at different length scales, so permeability prediction from them needs scale conversion. About 50 Permian and Carboniferous core plugs from four Lublin Basin wells were measured for BET, MICP, T1/T2 (MARAN 30, TE=60 µs) and permeability. The Pape pigeon-hole fractal model (Df=2.3566) gives the Paris equation for BET, and the data fit it with lamellar factors of 1 to 2; samples with more than 9 wt% clay deviate. MICP and BET surfaces were related by a linear relation, and log-mean T2 correlated with BET surface, giving K·F = 137.39 T2,LM² (K in D, T2 in s), implying surface relaxivity of 5-25 µm/s. The calibrated TNMR permeability matched Sen and Timur-Coates estimators via multipliers and agreed with formation tests and k-lambda in one well, but overestimated permeability by more than an order of magnitude where authigenic clay blocked pore throats.
abstract: The permeability of clastic materials is controlled by the solid-void distribution function (SVDF). Different studies show that it may suffice to relate permeability to functions of lower order moments of the SVDF, namely porosity, tortuosity, and specific inner surface area. Direct as well as indirect lab methods for measuring surface areas are based on physical processes operating on characteristic length scales. Therefore recipes for matching them on the hydraulic permeability scale, equivalent to the Kozeny-Carman hydraulic capillary radius, are needed. This paper shows the strong correlation between surface area estimates derived from nitrogen gas adsorption (BET), mercury intrusion capillary pressure (MICP), and transverse nuclear magnetic resonance measurements (TNMR) on vintage core plugs of Permian and Carboniferous age from the Lublin Basin, Poland. The physical significance of these correlations is facilitated by comparing results to a fractal void-solid interface model, the Pape pigeon hole model. The pigeon hole model leads to matched scale expressions for the hydraulic permeability, namely the Paris equation for BET, and a variant of the Kozeny-Carman equation for MICP measurements. Using the Lublin Basin dataset, we show the validity of the Paris permeability equation, demonstrate the scale equivalence of MICP and TNMR inner surface estimates, and derive the Kozeny-Carman equation for TNMR data. This latter expression forms the basis for further permeability predictions from TNMR logging tools. For field applications the TNMR permeability estimator is compared with logging expressions derived by Sen and Timur-Coates. Simple multiplier rules are found to match their estimators for clean sands, and a calibrated TNMR log permeability may be arrived at. Finally, two field examples are presented to assess the limits of validity of the approach adopted in this paper and to underline the need for conditional core sampling as suggested by Worthington. We present a case of heuristic equivalence of properly calibrated TNMR permeability log readings with values derived from log data inversion based on Herron's k-lambda method over uncored well sections. In a counter-example the illitisation of pore throats is not captured by the TNMR log as confirmed by comparing with wireline pretest data, sonic derived mobilities, and subsequent sidewall core analyses.

title: Anisotropy of Resistivity in Oil Bearing Thin-Bedded Formation: Experiment and Modeling
caption: Figure 1: Ratio between vertical and horizontal resistivity versus bulk water saturation.
figure_reason: Shows rv/rh rising with falling Sw in laminated sandstones but constant in Berea, the key experimental result.
tldr: Twin-plug measurements show resistivity anisotropy in laminated sandstones rises as water saturation falls; forward modeling shows Sw equations using both rv and rh beat horizontal-only ones.
summary: Thinly laminated reservoirs often show large resistivity anisotropy, and the paper tests whether it is induced by saturation differences between oil-bearing coarse layers and water-bearing fine layers. Twin plugs of homogeneous Berea and laminated Navajo, Cutbank and Lyons sandstones were desaturated by centrifuge with dodecane, and rv/rh was measured at 100 kHz. In the laminated samples rv/rh rose as Sw fell (Navajo from 1.2 to 3.4 between 100% and 10% Sw), while Berea stayed near 1. Forward modeling of four geological units with a dual water model then tested Archie, dual water and three rv/rh-based Sw algorithms (SPC, HDA and a new SDR equation that does not need water resistivity). Horizontal-only methods underestimated hydrocarbon volume by about 20-47%, whereas the rv/rh methods were mostly within a few percent. On the experimental data the SPC model gave Sw close to the measured bulk values, though it tended to overestimate oil.
abstract: In this paper, anisotropy of resistivity of thin-bedded formation is investigated experimentally and numerically. The experiments consist of measurements of anisotropy of resistivity on twin-plugs of laminated cores as a function of oil/water saturation. Our results show a clear increase of the anisotropy of resistivity when $S_w$ decreases. This result demonstrates that anisotropy of resistivity is induced by the difference of saturation between the sand layer (oil bearing) and the fine grain layers (water bearing). Our modeling work was designed to compare the robustness of various equations for estimating water saturation. Four models have been defined: a thinly laminated coarse grain sand, a thinly laminated fine grain sand, a thinly laminated sand-shale and a turbidite. The vertical and horizontal resistivity of each formation is calculated with a dual water model. This anisotropy of resistivity is used to compare the oil content in the original model and the one obtained from various $S_w$ equations. This work demonstrates that the use of resistivity parallel ( $r_h$ ) and transverse ( $r_v$ ) to the bedding planes and an accurate volume of fine grain, gives better $S_w$ values than shaly-sand equations when we know only the horizontal resistivity. In addition, a new $S_w$ equation for shaly sandstone, which uses both $r_v$ and $r_h$ but does not require the knowledge of water resistivity, is proposed.

title: Improvement of Fluid Distribution Description During Floods by Combined Use of X-Ray CT Scan and Continuous Local Resistivity Measurements
caption: Figure 7: Local oil saturation from CT scan for F1.4 (high permeability, higher figures) and F200 (low permeability, lower figures).during steady state oil brine tests in drainage (left) and imbibition (right)
figure_reason: Shows CT-derived local oil saturation profiles along plugs, revealing inlet and outlet end effects and homogeneous middle zones.
tldr: Combining CT scanning with continuous local resistivity along Fontainebleau sandstone plugs during steady-state floods identifies end-affected zones; discarding them gives saturation exponents n close to 2.
summary: Resistivity measurements on cores are often corrupted by non-uniform saturation, so the actual fluid distribution needs to be checked. Steady-state oil-brine drainage and imbibition were run on three Fontainebleau sandstones (porosity 12.8-24.8%, permeability 280-2200 mD) in a cell inside a medical CT scanner. Six potential electrodes gave local resistances on 1.25 cm slices, and CT scans at plateaux gave local saturation. Local formation factors gave Archie m of 1.5-1.8, and end slices showed higher values. Oil accumulation at the inlet and capillary end effects at the outlet distorted RI-Sw data. Discarding the end slices lowered n by up to 0.4 in permeable samples, giving values close to 2. A bump to higher flow rate produced non-homogeneous fluid distributions unsuitable for RI calculation.
abstract: Continuous local resistivity measurements along a plug during drainage-imbibition in a steady state procedure are combined with observations by CT scan during the "plateaux". This improves the consistency of the description of the experiment, and thus the quality of the parameters that can be drawn from these experiments, and which may be of paramount importance in the log interpretation. Examples are given on Fontainebleau sandstones.

title: Characterization of the Intrinsic Porosity Exponent Through Dual-Salinity Measurements of Electrical Conductivity
caption: Fig.3 Porosity vs. CDRplot for the entire test database
figure_reason: Porosity vs C_DR for the entire test database, showing multiple petrofacies units that must be separated to obtain m*.
tldr: A dual-salinity conductivity method gives petrofacies-specific intrinsic porosity exponent m* without shaly-sand parameters, matching multiple-salinity benchmarks within one standard error and distinguishing petrofacies in field data.
summary: The paper addresses determining the intrinsic Archie porosity exponent m* in shaly sands without electrochemical measurements such as cation exchange capacity. Rock conductivity is measured with two electrolytes, and a conductivity difference ratio (C_DR) is plotted against porosity on bilogarithmic axes, whose slope gives m*. The method was benchmarked on the Waxman and Smits database (55 samples, clean to very shaly), yielding five petrofacies (m* 1.82 to 2.43) that agree with multiple-salinity benchmarks to within about 0.01-0.02. Using different pairs of electrolyte conductivities gave consistent m* (1.90-1.93) for Petrofacies C. Single-sample m* has a most probable error of ±0.1, valid for Cw1 ≥ 2 S/m at 25 °C. Field examples from three reservoirs separated petrofacies pairs with distinct m* (e.g. 1.89 vs 2.14; 1.70 vs 1.89) at the 99% level.
abstract: Dual-salinity measurements of electrical conductivity allow the identification of a petrofacies-specific intrinsic porosity exponent $m^*$ without having to determine any shaly-sand parameters. The method requires measurements of the conductivity of a reservoir rock when it is fully saturated with two different electrolytes of known conductivity. The method has been tested and benchmarked for sands ranging from clean to very shaly. It is not significantly impacted by low-salinity effects in most oilfield situations. A key element of the approach is that the pairs of electrolyte conductivities do not have to be the same for each sample. This is especially useful where a database covers several generations of core analysis. Field examples illustrate how the dual-salinity method can be used to quantify $m^*$ and identify petrofacies units simultaneously. The method requires fewer data than traditional multiple-salinity conductivity studies and it is more definitive than approaches that use an electrochemical measurement of the non-Archie conductivity. In these respects the dual-salinity approach offers a balance between the cost of data acquisition and the need to contain uncertainty.

title: Advances in Resistivity Measurements Using the Frim Method at Reservoir Conditions. Applications to Carbonates
caption: Figure 6: Example of drainage RI curve determined from the measurement of average saturation and resistance (left panel) at reservoir condition (T=115°C, dead oil, net overburden pressure 30 Bar).
figure_reason: Drainage RI curve at reservoir conditions showing low exponent and upward bending caused by wettability change.
tldr: Extends the FRIM continuous resistivity index method to reservoir conditions for carbonate drainage and imbibition, and proposes two semi-empirical RI-Sw models for non-Archie curves.
summary: Resistivity index curves in carbonates are often non-Archie and hard to measure by standard capillary-equilibrium methods. The FRIM method, which uses radial electrodes that make the measurement quasi-insensitive to saturation profiles, was implemented in new apparatus at reservoir conditions (e.g. 115°C, dead oil, 30 bar net overburden, confining pressure up to 450 bar). Drainage experiments take about 10 days. Forced imbibition is done by waterflooding at stepped low-to-medium flow rates in 2-3 days, and simulations show the radial design only slightly underestimates RI, unlike ring electrodes. Carbonate samples showed saturation exponents from 1.4 to 2.75, curves bending up or down with wettability change, and strong drainage-imbibition hysteresis. Two three-parameter empirical equations were proposed to fit bending-down and bending-up RI curves.
abstract: The Fast Resistivity Index Measurement (FRIM) method is a recent technique to measure continuous resistivity index curves on core samples. In a previous paper of the same author, it has been validated extensively using numerical simulations and experiments performed at ambient conditions. This paper presents the use of this technique at reservoir conditions during drainage and imbibition on various reservoir carbonate samples. The appropriate experimental procedures are presented in order to obtain RI curves representative of field conditions and free of artifacts. We present also two semi-empirical RI-Sw relationships useful for describing the various non-Archie curves observed.

title: Effect of Glauconite on Petrophysical Properties as Revealed by Core Analysis
caption: Figure 4: Resistivity index measurements
figure_reason: Resistivity index vs saturation shows the distinctive concave-upward behavior caused by isolated water-filled glauconite.
tldr: Special core analysis of a North Sea glauconitic sandstone shows water-filled, water-wet glauconite pellets explain high Dean-Stark water saturations, nonlinear resistivity index behavior and humidity-dependent porosity.
summary: Logs and Dean-Stark data disagreed on water saturation in a North Sea sandstone (porosity ~31-32%, permeability 100-200 mD). Log estimates were 20-40% while Dean-Stark gave 40-70%, even with traced oil-based mud, and well tests produced only oil. Petrography and ESEM showed 18-30% glauconite pellets with ~40% internal porosity that were water-filled and water-wet. Capillary pressure and resistivity tests gave very high irreducible water saturation and concave-upward RI vs Sw curves, opposite to the clay effect; n was 3.0 by endpoint versus 2.7 by regression.
