Humidity-controlled drying lowered measured porosity by about 1.5 p.u. Using an effective pore system made RI curves closer to linear and gave normal Sorw values (16-17% versus 7-12% total).
abstract: During early-phase formation evaluation of a small sandstone reservoir in the North Sea logs and conventional core data indicated good reservoir quality (porosity: 30% & permeability 150mD). Both initial log and core-derived estimates of water saturation were high. However, the log-derived estimates were consistently lower than those from Dean-Stark core measurements and had a large degree of uncertainty. A well test produced oil and no water. The disagreement between log and core estimated was initially blamed on invasion of the core by the (non-traced) water-based drilling mud system. A second well was drilled using a traced oil-based system with plugs taken offshore to obtain quality connate water saturation data from cores. The results reduced the uncertainties in water saturation significantly although values were still high. A special core analysis program was designed to include an investigation of the cause of the high water saturations, including ESEM, core drying effects, core resistivity, core petrography and relative permeability. Petrological analysis revealed a high proportion of a porous clay mineral, glauconite. The glauconite was distributed as pellets with high internal, water-bearing porosity. These pellets were randomly distributed throughout the matrix and were shown to be strongly water wet. The core analysis program revealed that this particular mineral with its properties gives special petrophysical characteristics to its host formation including: - $\Sigma$ high connate water saturation values above the transition zone - $\Sigma$ high porosity compared to permeability - $\Sigma$ little variation in porosity with varying permeability - $\Sigma$ porosity dependent on the air humidity during drying - $\Sigma$ no linear $RI$ / $S_w$ -relationship - $\Sigma$ resistivity measurements showing an effect opposite of the so-called "clay-effect" - $\Sigma$ low residual oil saturation after water flooding These formation characteristics were responsible for the uncertainty in log estimates of water saturation. The core analysis had therefore significantly reduced the project uncertainty. However, this glauconite issue is relatively uncommon in the North Sea and as a result it was sometimes hard to convince other disciplines to accept the results.

title: Measurement of Relevant Gas Condensate Relative Permeability Data for Well Deliverability Predictions for a Deep Marine Sandstone Reservoir
caption: Figure 8: Comparison of krg vs Nc of different rocks for krg/kro at 1.89
figure_reason: Shows measured krg versus capillary number across the four rocks at fixed krg/kro, showing permeability independence.
tldr: Steady-state gas condensate corefloods on four deep marine sandstones give krg as a function of krg/kro and capillary number, and the data significantly reduce simulated well productivity.
summary: Well deliverability in gas condensate reservoirs depends on krg = f(krg/kro, Nc), for which little published data exist. Steady-state corefloods were run at 120°F on four Miocene sandstone samples (3 to 51 mD) using a three-component synthetic gas condensate designed to match the reservoir fluid's relative oil volume and viscosity ratio, covering krg/kro from 1 to 50 at several capillary numbers. Krg was found to be independent of absolute permeability at a given krg/kro, attributed to similar pore throat size distributions, and was lower than published North Sea data for a 20 mD rock. Coreflood simulations with mercury-injection capillary pressure showed negligible capillary end effects. Single-well compositional simulations with the measured data showed a significant productivity index decline from condensate blockage, with a sharp initial drop followed by gradual decline.
abstract: Fevang and Whitson[1] have shown that the appropriate data for well deliverability predictions in gas condensate reservoirs are krg = f (krg/kro, Nc). However, there is very little published data of this form. We present an extensive data set on four rock samples from a deep marine sandstone reservoir. These data span the krg/kro and capillary number parameter space. We discuss the issues behind the design of the experiments and also results of numerical simulation of these specialized corefloods. The data measured on these samples are then compared with the sparse published data set. Finally, we use the measured data and detailed geological information to demonstrate the impact of relative permeability data on prediction of well performance in this reservoir.

title: Investigation of the Oil Saturation of the Swept Zone of the Harding Field, Ukcs
caption: Figure 6 Measurement of Resistivity Index
figure_reason: Shows the resistivity index measurement setup along and across plugs used to detect electrical anisotropy.
tldr: SCAL resistivity index tests at reservoir conditions on Harding swept-zone plugs show directional anisotropy and lower saturation exponents at Sor, improving log-based remaining oil estimates.
summary: Remaining oil saturation in the swept zone of the Harding field could not be measured directly on core from well 9/23b-A21 because of synthetic oil-based mud and gas-drive expulsion. Plugs from an unconsolidated sandstone were tested at reservoir stress, temperature and pressure for porosity, formation factor 'm' and resistivity index 'n'. Porosity fell to 0.955-0.963 of ambient values and m changed only from 1.756 to 1.721. Resistivity index was measured along and across the plugs after drainage to Swi and then waterflood to Sor at a reservoir-like advance rate, with saturation monitored by gamma attenuation. Horizontal n at Sor was lower than drainage n (Sample 3: 1.749 vs 2.27, about 5.5 saturation units at 1 ohm-m and 30% porosity), while vertical n at Sor was higher (up to 2.89), indicating anisotropy from oil trapped in pore attics. The authors recommend imbibition n at Sor in the direction suited to well inclination, with sqrt(nv·nh) for horizontal wells, and the highest Rw and n, which indicates better sweep than previously thought.
abstract: Harding is an Eocene sandstone field located in the Central Graben of the UKCS. Production started in 1996 and has so far produced approximately 40% of reserves. Production has led to the development of a well defined swept zone above the original oil water contact, but determination of the remaining hydrocarbon in this zone remained problematical Analysis of the swept zone by wireline data, standard Archie parameters and aquifer brine salinity led to an over estimate of remaining oil saturation. This is partly due to swept zone wells being horizontal, the vertical propagation of the induction log and the position of the oil in the pore space; and partly due to the true salinity of the swept zone water (a mixture of aquifer and injected waters). A core was cut through the swept zone, to provide water extracts for direct swept zone water resisitivity measurement, and fresh core material for Archie parameter measurement. Remaining oil saturation in the swept zone could not be measured directly from the core due to the necessity to use synthetic oil based mud for drilling operations, and because of gas drive expulsion of oil from the core during tripping out of the well. A Special Core Analysis study was performed to replicate the in-situ environment of measurement to determine the appropriate Archie parameters for estimation of the remaining oil saturation in the swept zone. The results of the study showed a clear directional electrical anisotropy and a range of Archie parameters. Log interpretation using appropriate Archie parameters and Rw has led to a better understanding of remaining oil saturation in the swept zone; and suggests that the reservoir is being swept more effectively than previously thought.

title: Genetic Petrophysics Approach to 1 Core Analysis – Application to Shoreface
caption: Figure 3. A comparison of neural net predicted permeability and measured values in PEGASUS Well 2 using predictors trained on (a) Just 5 representative plugs in the RGU, and (b) All 297 plugs throughout the interval. Each predictor also used data from 3 key
figure_reason: Shows permeability predicted from 5 plugs versus all 297 plugs against measured values, the key result.
tldr: Neural networks trained on a few core plugs from one representative shoreface genetic unit predict permeability, shear-wave Q and a geochemical ratio in the same and adjacent wells.
summary: Routine core sampling is costly and not geologically based. The authors select a 7 m coarsening-up representative genetic unit (RGU) in a North Sea well and train a committee neural network on core data plus three wireline logs (gamma ray, density, sonic). Permeability trained on only 5 plugs, one per hydraulic unit, gave r2 = 0.72 over the 129 m cored interval, versus 0.85 using all 297 plugs and 0.25 for porosity-permeability. In adjacent Well 2b the 5-plug predictor gave r2 = 0.68 versus 0.65 for the full-dataset predictor. Shear-wave quality factor at 30 MPa, trained on 4 SCAL plugs without acoustic logs, gave r2 = 0.70, and a fluorenone/methyl fluorenone ratio trained on 37 chips gave r2 = 0.68.
abstract: Shoreface reservoirs are characterized by coarsening up sequences of fine to medium grained sandstone. Single coarsening-up parasequences are often easily recognizable within stacked shoreface sequences. These elements are the fundamental building blocks (representative genetic units) of such reservoirs. We identify such a package in a North Sea oil well, and show how the detailed characterization of this single shoreface unit can be used to predict, via neural networks, a range of parameters throughout the rest of the well and an adjacent well in the same oilfield. We have termed the approach "Genetic Petrophysics" as it emphasizes the genetic aspects of the sandstone body in both the sampling and prediction strategies. The work presented has both extended our previous studies on permeability prediction, and has also applied the appr oach to the prediction of other diverse parameters. A key new result is that excellent predictions can be made from extremely limited but representative conventional or SCAL core plug data. This provides a very cost effective sampling strategy, and paves the way for rapidly predicting a whole range of other parameters of interest from minimal core data.

title: Impact of SCAL on Carbonate Reservoirs: How Capillary Forces Can Affect Field Performance Predictions
caption: Figure 11: History match of saturation logs using detailed static and dynamic models incorporating the measured imbibition Pc curves.
figure_reason: History match of observation-well saturation logs using measured imbibition Pc confirms capillary forces explain field performance.
tldr: Simulations and SCAL Pc measurements show negative imbibition capillary pressure in a layered Middle East carbonate holds water in the upper zone, explaining waterflood behavior without permeability barriers.
summary: Water injected into a layered Middle East carbonate reservoir stays in the high-permeability Upper zone and bypasses the Lower zone, although core kv/kh is near unity and pressure communication exists. Seven simulation scenarios (3D 27-layer and 2D 160-layer models) varied viscous, gravity and capillary cross-flow under water-wet, zero and oil-wet imbibition Pc. Positive Pc gave good sweep of both zones, whereas negative Pc held water in the Upper zone; total recovery to breakthrough was the same, so history matching of total production alone can mislead. SCAL on 20 plugs (0.01–1000 mD) showed hardly any spontaneous imbibition, negative forced-imbibition entry pressures of 3–5 psi for 2–5 mD plugs, and Swc and Sor of 5–10%. A detailed radial model using measured Pc matched observation-well saturation logs, showing capillary forces alone explain performance; recovery was sensitive to Pc curve shape and to preserving low-permeability layers in the Upper zone.
abstract: S. K. Masalmeh , X.D.Jing, W. van Vark, S. Christiansen, H. van der Weerd and J. van Dorp Shell International E&P, Rijswijk This paper was prepared for presentation at the International Symposium of the Society of Core Analysts held in Pau, France, 21-24 September 2003 1. ABSTRACT displacement in a heterogeneous porous medium at different wetting conditions. were selected from different rock classes to cover a range of permeability from 0.1 to after aging the plugs at connate water saturation to restore wettability.

title: Evaluation of Recovery Efficiency and Residual Oil Saturation of Two Distinct Arabian Carbonate Reservoirs
caption: Figure 1: Unsteady-State Oil/Water Relative Permeability Curves for Shu'aiba Reservoir, Shaybah Field.
figure_reason: Shu'aiba oil/water relative permeability curves showing spread in Kro and endpoints across composites.
tldr: Reservoir-condition waterflood tests on composite cores from Arab-D and Shu'aiba carbonates show slightly higher recovery and Sor in Arab-D, linked to pore size and fabric differences.
summary: The study compares waterflood recovery and residual oil saturation in two Saudi carbonate reservoirs, Late Jurassic Arab-D (Abu Safah) and Lower Cretaceous Shu'aiba (Shaybah). Unsteady-state relative permeability tests used seven composite cores per reservoir, preserved plugs, recombined live oil and reservoir conditions, with JBN analysis, supplemented by mercury injection and thin sections. Average recovery was 65.6% PV for Arab-D versus 63.3% for Shu'aiba, and average Sor was 22.3% versus 18.2%. Average Swir was lower in Arab-D (12.1%) than Shu'aiba (18.4%). Median pore radii were 0.5–5.5 µm for Arab-D grainstones (bimodal/trimodal) and 0.27–1.5 µm for Shu'aiba wackestones (mostly unimodal). Sor increased with permeability in Arab-D but decreased in Shu'aiba, reflecting diagenesis and fabric effects not captured by permeability alone.
abstract: Saudi Arabia has a variety of carbonate reservoirs of different geologic ages. Such reservoirs are characterized by extremely heterogeneous rock properties. These heterogeneities are caused by the wide spectrum of environments in which carbonates are deposited and subsequent alteration of the original rock fabric. In this paper, extensive SCAL work was carried out on preserved core plugs recovered from two distinct carbonate reservoirs. The first reservoir is a Late Jurassic Arab-D offshore carbonate reservoir (Abu Safah field). The second one is Shu'aiba reservoir (Shaybah field) located in the Rub' Al-Khali in southeastern Saudi Arabia. The purpose of this study is to provide and evaluate waterflood recovery efficiency and residual oil saturations of the two distinct Arabian reservoirs. The variation of oil recovery and residual oil saturation between the two distinct reservoirs is due to variations of rock characteristics especially the relationship of textural and diagenetic features which affect the size and distribution of pore throats. Shu'aiba reservoir rock could be classified as wackstone which demonstrates a higher ratio of lime mud to detrital grains (pore sizes ~ 0.27 to 1.5 microns). On the other hand, Arab-D reservoir is classified as grainstone and consists of oolitic limestone and dolomitic limestone with larger pore sizes (0.5 to 5.5 microns). The test results indicated that pore structure, pore size distribution, rock fabric, and environment of deposition are important factors that affect microscopic oil and water flow in porous media and the development efficiency of an oil field developed by water injection. Oil recovery from Arab-D reservoir (Late Jurassic) is slightly higher than that of Shu'aiba reservoir (Lower Cretaceous). The residual oil saturations values for Arab-D reservoir were also found to be slightly higher than those of Shu'aiba reservoir. The Arab-D reservoir showed less permeability dependence for both (Swir and Sor) end point saturations.

title: Resistivity Index Measurement Without the Porous Plate: A Desaturation Technique Based on Evaporation Produces Uniform Water Saturation Profiles and More Reliable Results for Tight North Sea Chalk
caption: Figure 13. RI plot of the total set of samples (N=11) where measurement of 3 saturation steps could be performed without fatal fracturing. The former used n=2.1 reference line has been added for comparison
figure_reason: RI plot of all samples showing the resulting n of 1.73 versus the previously used 2.1 reference line.
tldr: An evaporation-based desaturation method using diluted brine replaces porous plates for resistivity index measurement in tight chalk, giving uniform saturation and a lower saturation exponent n of 1.73.
summary: Porous plate drainage is very slow for tight Lower Cretaceous North Sea chalk and yields non-uniform saturation, biasing RI and n high. The authors saturate plugs with diluted brine and evaporate water until the original brine concentration is restored, which fixes Sw at 1/f, reaching Sw down to about 0.1 within a week. 22Na-spiked brine and gamma scanning of plugs showed that salt and water redistribute to a uniform profile within 5-6 days after evaporation to Sw = 17%. Salt remained mobile at Sw 13-14% but not at about 9%. Resistivity tests on 11 short 38 mm plugs with three saturation steps each gave n = 1.73 ± 0.09, well below the 2.1-2.2 used in log interpretation. Duplicate plugs showed a CV of about 10% per saturation step, and the method needs extensive sample handling.
abstract: Measurement of Archie's Resistivity Index 'RI' and saturation exponent 'n' can be very time consuming for low permeable core samples using the established porous plate techniques. An evaporation technique circumventing the porous plate difficulties has been developed, and is demonstra ted for the tight Lower Cretaceous carbonates in the Danish North Sea. Samples are saturated with a diluted formation brine and by evaporation water is removed from the diluted brine in the samples until the original brine concentration has been restored and the samples has attained a water saturation < 1. By this technique any water saturation down to approximately 0.1 can be imposed on the sample in less than a week. The movement of water in the sample during desaturation is documented by a tracer technique and core scanning, and data from the Lower Cretaceous carbonates are presented.

title: Investigation of Liquid Imbibition Mechanisms Using NMR
caption: Figure 9: NMR Spectra of oil imbibition test of plug D
figure_reason: NMR spectra during oil imbibition show peak growth and T2cutoff determination for small versus large pores.
tldr: On-line NMR monitors co-current spontaneous water and oil imbibition into dry sandstone plugs, showing similar residual gas saturation but different pore-size filling, T2cutoff and rates.
summary: On-line low-field NMR relaxometry was used to monitor co-current spontaneous imbibition of brine and oil (6.6 mPa.s) into five dry Western Canadian sandstone plugs (about 3.8 cm by 5 cm, air permeability 45-608 mD), with air as the non-wetting phase. NMR amplitudes gave liquid and gas saturation versus time and the distribution of liquid between small and large pores. Residual gas saturations from water and oil imbibition were close for most plugs, but T2cutoff differed (plug D: 56 ms for water, 25 ms for oil). Oil barely entered the small pores, whereas water filled small pores first. Subsequent water imbibition after oil showed none in plug A and some in plugs B and D, suggesting plug A is more oil-wet and B and D mixed-wet. The initial imbibition rate depended strongly on air permeability, and rate versus reciprocal recovery followed the Li and Horne model.
abstract: In this study, on-line NMR relaxometry is introduced as a method for monitoring cocurrent imbibition. A group of plugs from a Western Canada sandstone reservoir was selected and a series of primary and spontaneous imbibition tests were run for both water and oil at the same conditions. Air was the "non-wetting" phase. NMR was used to measure the amount of water or oil imbibed in the cores and to determine the gas saturation during the experiment. The residual gas saturation results from water imbibition tests were compared with the ones obtained from oil imbibition tests. The imbibition rates and the correlations of residual gas saturation with initial imbibition rates for both types of imbibition tests were also investigated. Through interpretation of the NMR spectra, bound water or oil T2cutoff values were determined. The distributions of water and oil in different pore sizes were compared. The initial imbibition rate at different pore sizes was measured. Finally, a literature model was used to check our experimental data. Preliminary results indicate that oil and water do not imbibe in the same way. The NMR spectra indicate that there is no substantial oil penetration of the small pores within the experimental period of two months. Comparing current results with previous results in soils, it becomes evident that spontaneous imbibition with on-line NMR measurements can become a tool for wettability assessment. Other applications of the on-line NMR measurements deal with the determination of residual gas saturation and gas recovery from gas reservoirs.

title: New Representative Sample Selection Criteria for Special Core Analysis
caption: Figure 2: Normalized Cumulative RQI vs. depth for the SCAL and conventional core analysis plugs showing the existence of eight distinct zones within the cored section (shown by solid line segments). The cumulative production data and the geological zone markers (dotted horizontal lines) are also shown for reference.
figure_reason: Shows NCRQI vs depth defining eight zones with production and facies comparison, the core of the zonation method.
tldr: Proposes a SCAL plug selection workflow combining CT porosity, brine permeability, cumulative RQI zonation, FZI binning and heterogeneity screening, showing sister-plug permeability data can mislead.
summary: SCAL sample selection lacks industry guidelines, and porosity of wettability-preserved plugs cannot be measured routinely. Using a well in an Upper Jurassic carbonate reservoir, about 375 brine-preserved SCAL plugs were CT-scanned to obtain porosity, and brine permeability was measured. Cores were depth-shifted 6.5 ft by gamma scan, and CT porosity agreed well with logs. Normalized cumulative RQI versus depth split the cored section into eight zones, and zones 6 and 8 contributed almost nothing to production. Plugs were screened by CT heterogeneity (max/min CT ratio ≥1.09, mean slice Cv >0.08, porosity ≤5% rejected), leaving 134 plugs grouped into five FZI bins. Lorenz coefficients differed between SCAL plugs (0.57) and conventional sister plugs (0.72), with permeability differing by one to two orders of magnitude, so sister-plug data should be used cautiously.
abstract: To this date there is hardly ay any specific industry guideline for selecting representative samples for special core analysis (SCAL) tests. No one can deny the importance of SCAL data in the development of appropriate reservoir engineering models. This paper describes some of the effective criteria and tests required for the selection of representative samples for use in SCAL tests. The proposed technique is essential to insure that high quality core plugs are chosen to represent appropriate flow compartments or facies within the reservoir. The absence of a petrophysical input in the selection of SCAL plugs can result in SCAL data being NOT representative of the reservoir or its flow compartments. Often, visual inspection and sometimes, computerized tomography (CT) images are the only techniques used for assessing and selecting native state core plugs for SCAL studies. Although it is possible to measure the effective brine permeability ( $K_b$ ), there is no routine method for determining the porosity ( $f$ ) of the SCAL plugs without compromising their wettability. Some of the existing selection criteria involve using the conventional core analysis data ( $k$ and $f$ ) on ‘sister plugs’ as a general indicator of the properties of the SCAL samples. However, the uncertainties surrounding the extent of heterogeneity as well as the exact depth of the plugs make it difficult to ascertain plugs as representative of a particular flow compartment. The proposed technique identifies intervals with similar porosity/permeability relationships. It uses a combination of wireline logs, gamma scan, quantitative CT and preserved state brine permeability data to calculate appropriate depth-shifted reservoir quality index ( $RQI$ ) and flow zone indicator ( $FZI$ ) data, which are then used to select representative plug samples from each reservoir compartment.

title: A Method for Estimating Permeability of Carbonate Rocks from CT Scan Data
caption: Figure 9. Comparison between results of ANNs containing different numbers of CT averages.
figure_reason: Compares measured and neural-network predicted permeability of test samples for different numbers of CT averages, the main result.
tldr: A back-propagation neural network trained on CT slice averages, porosity, density and mineralogy predicts carbonate permeability of held-out Sarvak samples better than multiple linear regression.
summary: Estimating carbonate permeability is difficult because pore types vary at the same porosity. The authors used 34 plugs (1.5 in x 2.5 in) from the Sarvak Formation in four Iranian wells, measuring porosity, PDPK pressure-decay permeability, mineral percentages from thin sections, and CT slices (120 keV, 2 mm spacing, 32 slices per sample). Slice-average CT numbers, porosity, depth, bulk density and mineralogy were used as inputs to a feed-forward back-propagation network with permeability as target, with 22 training and 12 test samples. Single-variable crossplots showed little correlation with permeability, and multiple linear regression gave only moderate correlation. The network followed measured permeability (0.05 to 179 mD) closely in test samples, with accuracy improving as more CT averages were retained, especially for low permeability. The authors note that results depend on adequate training data and are lab specific.
abstract: Permeability is one of the most important characteristics of hydrocarbon bearing formations. An accurate knowledge of permeability provides petroleum engineers with a tool for efficiently managing the production process of a field. Furthermore, it is one of the most important pieces of information in the design and management of enhanced recovery operations. Formation permeability is often measured in the laboratory from cores or evaluated from well test data. CT scan data is widely used to calculate porosity and build 3D models of rock matrix in carbonates, but in this study we illustrate a method to use these data together with conventiona l laboratory measurements for estimating permeability of carbonate rocks. To do this core samples from a carbonate oil field in south west of Iran have been studied. The Permeability of samples was measured using a PDPK™ apparatus, the porosity of each sample was measured and CT slices were taken in constant intervals across the samples. Thin sections in the horizontal and vertical directions were prepared from the end pieces of the samples and were analyzed by using the optical microscope. For each core sample a column matrix containing average volumetric percentages of different minerals were assigned. CT numbers corresponding to each slice were exported in the form of a spreadsheet. All such spreadsheets that belong to the ith sample, together with porosity, column matrix and PDPK™ average permeability were called "i th data set". All data sets were considered as training examples of a back propagation artificial neural network, whilst the target was permeability. Validation of the network results was achieved by leaving out some of the data sets and comparing their measured permeabilities with calculated ones. To decrease calculation time, up scaling was applied on CT data by scales of 2:1, 4:1, 8:1, 16:1 and 32:1 and results were compared with each other. A better understanding of the relationship between volume percentage of minerals, porosity, CT scan data and permeability of carbonates is developed from this study.

title: Determination of Wettability of Iranian Carbonate Reservoir Rocks in Restored-State
caption: Fig. 1- Capillary pressure curves of combined Amott/USBM test of plug no. 11
figure_reason: Capillary pressure curves from combined Amott/USBM test for plug 11, showing the oil-wet drainage versus imbibition asymmetry.
tldr: Wettability of eleven restored-state Iranian carbonate plugs at 90°C was measured; Amott tests gave intermediate wettability, while combined Amott/USBM indicated mostly oil-wet.
summary: Wettability of Iranian dolomite and limestone reservoir rocks was characterized on eleven plugs from Fields M and R, cleaned, saturated with formation water, flooded with crude oil and aged 40 days at 90°C. Qualitative relative permeability results were contradictory: crossover saturations (33-46%) indicated oil-wet, while Krw at Sor was below Kro at Swi. Amott tests by core flooding and by centrifuge agreed and mostly gave intermediate wettability (Amott-Harvey indices near zero), with only interval D of Field R water-wet (about 0.49-0.61). Combined Amott/USBM indices were mostly negative (e.g. -0.31 to -0.85), indicating oil-wet behavior except for plug 13 (+0.374). The authors conclude the combined method is more informative than Amott or USBM alone and about as time-efficient as Amott.
abstract: Many special core analyses, including capillary pressure, relative permeability, and water flooding efficiency are affected by the wettability of the core. In order to achieve reliable results, experiment must be performed on preserved or aged sample. Considering the importance of wettability factor in special core analysis data and their fundamental roles in reservoir studies, the present work was defined to search for wettability characterization of some Iranian carbonate formations. Samples were carefully cleaned and aged at reservoir temperature in order to prepare the restored conditions. Experiments were run at 90 degrees centigrade with crude oil and formation water. In this study a period of 40 days were allowed for aging with crude oil. Petrophysical properties of each sample were measured using both thin section and core flooding techniques. The lithology of the samples consists of both dolomite and limestone. The qualitative evaluation of carbonate samples using relative permeability curves showed that there was a discrepancy between the result from the role of end-points and those from the role of cross over saturation. The cross over saturations in relative permeability tests at reservoir temperature showed that samples were oil wet. In this research, the Amott and USBM tests have been run on samples in a combination procedure. The capillary pressure curves obtained by the centrifuge method were used in order to calculate the USBM wettability index. Quantitative results by the Amott method showed that most carbonate samples had intermediate wettability characteristics, but the results from combined Amott-USBM testing indicated that system is mostly oil-wet. Centrifuge experiments also produced capillary pressure curves that were used to evaluate the wettability are according to the method of U.S. Bureau of Mines.

title: Critical Salinity for Archie – Non Archie Models in the Jauf Sandstone Reservoir, Saudi Arabia
caption: Figure 8. Dependence of the shaliness effect (BQv) on the logarithmic trendline slopes of the formation factor curves in Figure 7.
figure_reason: Links shaliness effect BQv to the slope of formation factor versus salinity, enabling a quick shaliness estimate.
tldr: Multi-salinity resistivity tests on nine Jauf Sandstone plugs show a 4-8% clay effect at reservoir salinity, so Archie applies above a critical salinity of 100 kppm.
summary: The Jauf Sandstone gas reservoir shows low resistivity (1-2 ohm-m) despite water-free gas production, so the clay effect on conductivity was tested. Nine preserved plugs (porosity 14-25%, permeability 3-711 mD) containing pore-lining illite and minor chlorite were saturated sequentially with ten NaCl brines from 250 to 1 kppm at 65 °C and 2,000 psi confining pressure. Co-Cw fits to the high-salinity points gave an average F* of 31.3, BQv of 0.0258 mho/cm and Qv of 0.228 meq/cc. The clay effect BQv/Cw at 250 kppm was 4-8%, and the critical salinity for a 10% effect averaged 100 kppm (range 55-150 kppm). The low resistivity is attributed to microporosity from clay texture rather than clay conductance; Archie is valid at reservoir salinity, but shaly-sand models are needed for fresher filtrates or injection water. Formation factor decreases log-linearly with falling salinity, with a slope that increases with BQv.
abstract: In this case study, the effect of clay content on the resistivity of the Jauf Sandstone was investigated through multiple-salinity electrical tests on nine 1.5 inch diameter and 2.5 inch long core plug samples. Tested samples were selected from a semi-consolidated, brownish, porous and permeable quartz arenite facies from three different wells. Samples contain dominantly authigenic illite and minor chlorite clays lining the pores. Experiments were conducted under 65 °C temperature and 2,000 psi confining pressure condition. Ten different brine concentrations, starting with the highest concentration (250 kppm), were circulated sequentially through the samples while recording the electrical conductivity changes of the rock. Tests showed a 4 to 8 percent clay effect (BQv / Cw) on the electrical conductivity. The low clay effect is due to: (1) low clay percentage, (2) illite and chlorite type clays, which have a low-to-moderate cation exchange capacity, and (3) high formation brine concentration in the reservoir. The low resistivity in the reservoir is not due to clay conductance, but it is due to microporosity that is caused by the pore-lining or filling clay texture. The critical salinity corresponding to the commonly accepted 10 percent clay effect cutoff is calculated to be 100 kppm. Although the Archie model is valid for water saturation interpretation in the reservoir, low salinity brine effects, such as mud filtrate or injection water, requires the consideration of appropriate shaly sand models.

title: Evaluation of Effect of Capillary Forces on Measurements in Linear Waterfloods by Simulation
caption: Figure 21 Comparison of Measured Relative Permeability for Water by JR Method Viscosity Ratio = 0.5 Mixed Wet Core, V DP=0.5
figure_reason: Shows measured versus true krw for heterogeneous mixed-wet core, with strongly distorted curve shape.
tldr: 1D black-oil simulations of unsteady-state floods show how capillary number, viscosity ratio, wettability and heterogeneity bias Jones-Roszelle relative permeabilities relative to the input curves.
summary: Unsteady-state relative permeability interpretation by the Jones-Roszelle method assumes negligible capillary forces and a homogeneous core, assumptions that are often violated. The author simulated waterfloods in a 1D black-oil model with assumed input relative permeability curves, then computed relative permeabilities from the simulated output and compared them with the input. Parameters varied were scaling coefficient (0.1 to 10, Ca 0.00045 to 0.045), viscosity ratio (0.5, 1.23, 5), water-wet versus mixed-wet J-functions, and heterogeneity (Dykstra-Parsons coefficient 0.1, 0.5, 0.8). Best kro estimates came at high capillary number and high viscosity ratio, with large errors at low saturations. For homogeneous water-wet cores the measured endpoint krw matched the true value, whereas low-rate floods severely distorted krw curves. In heterogeneous cores errors were similar for VDP 0.1 to 0.5 but large at VDP 0.8 for water-wet cores, while mixed-wet cores showed the largest errors at intermediate VDP.
abstract: This paper attempts to evaluate the effects of capillary number, viscosity-ratio, wettability and heterogeneity on the measured relative permeability, by assuming a set of relative permeability curves for a 1D black-oil simulation model simulating unsteady-state experiments. The relative permeability in each case, calculated by Jones and Roszelles (JR) method are compared with the input relative permeabilitites. The trends of measured relative permeabilities, water relative permeability end-point and breakthrough recoveries for different wettability, capillary numbers, viscosity ratios and heterogeneity were obtained and studied.

title: The Characteristics of Relative Permeability Curves in Chemical Flooding by Pore Scale Network Modeling
caption: Fig. 3 Simulated relative permeability curves with different interfacial tension values
figure_reason: Simulated relative permeability curves at different IFT values, showing upward shift and linearization at ultra-low IFT.
tldr: A dynamic 2D pore-scale network model shows oil and water relative permeabilities rise and become linear as IFT drops, while polymer viscosity lowers water relative permeability.
summary: Relative permeability data for chemical flooding (surfactant, polymer, ASP) are scarce, so the authors use a dynamic pore-scale network model: a 2D triangular lattice (coordination number 6) of spherical pores and cylindrical throats with Weibull-type size distributions and uniform water-wet contact angle. Six virtual surfactant floods with IFT from 0.2 to 5e-4 mN/m were simulated. Relative permeabilities changed negligibly above about 1e-2 mN/m, then both oil and water curves shifted upward and approached linearity at ultra-low IFT. Adding water viscosity had little effect at high IFT but at low IFT reduced water relative permeability strongly and oil relative permeability less, with little oil effect at Sw>70%. Over 40 simulations (viscosity ratios 3, 1, 0.6, 0.3) showed breakthrough saturation falls with IFT, with a non-monotonic dependence on viscosity ratio between 0.1 and 0.001 mN/m. Trends agreed qualitatively with published experiments.
abstract: EOR processes that feature polymer flooding, surfactant flooding, or ASP compositional flooding, require relative permeabilit y data to calculate the flow behavior in reservoir engineering calculations and numerical simulation of reservoir performance. The present work deals with a dynamic pore scale network model where the porous medium is represented by a regular pore geometry, and aims at the evaluation in the change of two-phase flow properties induced by the introduction of chemical flooding factors, such as interfacial tension reduction and water viscosity enhancement. Both the non-wetting and wetting phase relative permeabilities vary with the chemical flooding factors. The injection of polymer reduces water relative permeability over the entire saturation range. The relative permeability is greatly affected by interfacial tension values. Both water and oil relative permeability curves were found to shift upward as interfacial tension is reduced. They tend to become linear with saturation as interfacial tension reaches ultra-low value.

title: Focussed Ion Beam Assisted Three-Dimensional Rock Imaging at Submicron Scale
caption: Figure 4. Chalk volume reconstructed from successive binarized images spaced at 0.1 micron intervals. The pore space is dark.
figure_reason: 3D reconstructed chalk pore volume at 0.1 µm section spacing, the main result of the method.
tldr: A focused ion beam serial-sectioning method is developed to reconstruct 3D pore structure of diatomite and chalk at submicron resolution, with clean surfaces and no apparent distortion.
summary: Micron-scale X-ray microtomography cannot resolve the pore structure of fine-grained rocks such as chalk and diatomite. The authors developed a serial sectioning method using a dual-beam FEI DB235 FIB/SEM, milling thin layers with Ga+ ions (up to 30 kV, up to 20,000 pA) and imaging each fresh surface with secondary electrons or ions. Samples need flat, rectangular preparation, mounting on 45° stubs and carbon coating; images are aligned using milled markers, thresholded and stacked to build 3D volumes. Tested on cleaned Belridge diatomite (sections 0.2 µm apart) and epoxy-impregnated North Sea chalk (0.1 µm apart), milling gave flat surfaces with high pore-grain contrast and no apparent boundary distortion. Epoxy impregnation gave better contrast and easier thresholding than the unimpregnated diatomite, where brightness variations inside pores required more image processing.
abstract: Computation of effective flow properties of fluids in porous media based on three dimensional (3D) pore structure information has become more successful in the last few years, due to both improvements in the input data and the network models. Computed X-ray microtomography has been successful in 3D pore imaging at micron scale, which is adequate for many sandstones. For other rocks of economic interest, such as chalk and diatomite, submicron resolution is needed in order to resolve the 3D-pore structure. To achieve submicron resolution, a new method of sample serial sectioning and imaging using Focused Ion Beam (FIB) technology has been developed and 3D pore images of the pore system for diatomite and chalk have been obtained. FIB was used in the milling of layers as wide as 50 micrometers and as thin as 100 nanometers by sputtering of atoms from the sample surface. The focused ion beam, consisting of gallium ions (Ga+) accelerated by potentials of up to 30 kV and currents up to 20,000 pA, yields very clean, flat surfaces in which the pore-grain boundaries appear in high contrast. No distortion of the pore boundaries due to the ion milling is apparent. After each milling step, as a new surface is exposed, an image of the surface is generated. Using secondary electrons or ions, resolutions as high as 10 nm can be obtained. Afterwards, the 2D images are stacked in the computer and the 3D pore structure is reconstructed.

title: Core Reconstruction from CT Scan Porosity Fields
caption: Fig. 3.- Comparison between correlation functions. The dark lines correspond to the porosity reconstructed field $R_{e_R}(\mathbf{u})$ and the thin lines to the original CT porosity map $R_e(\mathbf{u})$ . (a) Brauvilliers sample and (b) Estaillades sample.
figure_reason: Compares correlation functions of reconstructed and original porosity fields, showing success for Brauvilliers and failure for Estaillades.
tldr: Stochastic reconstruction of carbonate cores from CT porosity maps works well for Brauvilliers but poorly for Estaillades; conductivity and permeability are computed and compared with measurements.
summary: The paper reconstructs 3D porosity fields of cores from CT-scan porosity maps. Long porosity trends are removed, the porosities are transformed to a Gaussian variable, and a correlated Gaussian field is generated by a Fourier technique and then back-transformed. Applied to Brauvilliers and Estaillades carbonates, the reconstruction reproduced the correlation function and visual appearance for Brauvilliers (isotropic), while for the orthotropic Estaillades it reproduced the anisotropy but not the experimental correlations. Conductivity and permeability were computed by box integration using local porosity correlations. Conductivity agreed well with measurements for Brauvilliers, while the Estaillades measurement was above the master curve. Permeability for Brauvilliers (measured 115 mD) was insensitive to the local K(e) correlation, whereas Estaillades (219 mD) showed a significant influence.
abstract: A systematic study to generate reconstructed cores using CT-scan porosity maps was conducted. The long trends, which are seen in real cores, were corrected in order to recover a stationary character. By means of an adequate transformation, the resulting porosities are transformed into Gaussian variables. Then, a correlated Gaussian field is generated to which the inverse of the previous corrections are applied. This technique was applied to two CT-scan porosity maps for two carbonates, the Brauvilliers and Estaillades samples. The methodology was more successful for the Brauvilliers sample than for the Estaillades one. The macroscopic transport properties of conductivity $\bar{S}$ and permeability $\bar{K}$ were calculated in real and reconstructed samples using the “box integration method”. To generate the local conductivity and permeability fields, we used four different correlations. The results for the real and reconstructed samples are also compared with laboratory measurements. For conductivity, the comparison is very good for the Brauvilliers sample. For the Estaillades sample, the experimental value is larger than $S=S(e)$ . In terms of permeability, the results show that the global permeability for Brauvilliers is not very sensitive to the correlations $K=K(e)$ ; for the Estaillades sample, a significant influence of the porosity correlation was observed.

title: Sensitivity Studies of Fluid Flow Across Water-Saturated Faults with High Entry Pressure
caption: Fig. 4? Water saturation: contour plot. Fig. 5? Water saturation: later time step.
figure_reason: Water saturation contour plots show oil build-up at the Berea/ceramic interface after breakthrough.
tldr: Eclipse 1D simulations of oil flow across a water-saturated ceramic fault next to Berea show breakthrough and recovery depend on fault permeability, entry pressure and thickness.
summary: Water-saturated, low-permeability faults with high entry pressure can compartmentalise reservoirs, as seen in Brent Province fields. The authors simulated two-phase oil/water flow with Eclipse in 1D composite models of Berea sandstone (reservoir) and a ceramic fault (k 0.00295 md, Pe 8 bar, 0.99 cm thick). Corey correlations and mercury porosimetry supplied relative permeability and capillary pressure. Sensitivities varied fault permeability (0.000295-0.0295 md), entry pressure (4-14 bar), thickness and initial reservoir water saturation. Breakthrough was delayed by over ten times for a tenfold thicker fault (232 h vs 14 h) and was earlier with higher permeability; performance was controlled more by permeability than entry pressure. Simulated breakthrough times (14, 8, 10 h) matched experiments (13, 6, 9 h) reasonably.
abstract: Water-saturated faults with high oil entry pressure and very low permeability may hinder the flow of hydrocarbons in reservoirs due to formation of traps or fault-related compartments. This compartmentalisation can lead to lower than expected reservoir performance as has been observed in several oilfields in the Brent Province in the North Sea. This paper presents numerical simulations (using an Eclipse Simulator) of two-phase (oil/water) flow in models that mimic reservoir/fault situations. The fault rock is initially 100% water saturated and is expected to continue acting as a sealing fault/barrier to oil flow until its capillary entry pressure for oil is exceeded. A ceramic material has been selected to represent the fault while the reservoir zone is Berea sandstone - both rocks were characterised by special core analyses. The ceramic material can be viewed as a porous membrane across which transport is obtained by a potential difference, which was achieved by pressure drawdown due to production. Relative permeability and capillary pressure data were derived from established correlations and mercury porosimetry data. The results show that fluid conductivity in the fault varies with initial water saturation in the reservoir zone. Also, the oil breakthrough and recovery are highly controlled by the fault properties (permeability, entry pressure and thickness).

title: Mapping Fracture Apertures Using Micro Computed Tomography
caption: Figure 7: Sample 3 aperture map. 3116 slices, 100 mm long by 25 mm diameter.
figure_reason: Shows a full aperture map of sample 3 from 3116 slices, the main product of the method.
tldr: Micro-CT images of induced fractures in layered Berea sandstone yield 2D aperture maps and 3D fracture volumes, showing larger apertures where the fracture crosses high-permeability layers.
summary: The paper addresses the difficulty of resolving fracture topology with medical CT scanners. Layered Berea sandstone cores (18-22% porosity, 25-50 mm diameter) were fractured with a Brazilian-type test and scanned with a medical HD250 (0.25x0.25x2 mm) and an industrial OMNI-X micro-CT (20-50 µm). Fractures were extracted by thresholding, erosion and dilation, and the distance between the surfaces was projected onto a common plane to build aperture maps. Medical scans overestimated fracture width and blurred detail, while micro-CT resolved apertures from about 50 µm up to about 1 mm and contact asperities. Aperture correlated with the porosity and permeability of adjacent layers, and the 3D fracture volume can be used for multiphase flow simulation.
abstract: Multi-phase flow in fractures plays a significant role during hydrocarbon recovery processes as well as in contaminant transport. With the advent of high-resolution Micro Computed Tomography it is possible in some cases to acquire three-dimensional fracture structures and to determine fracture aperture maps. This paper highlights several examples where artificially created fractures were imaged and the distributions of fracture apertures were determined. The fracture apertures were up to about 1000 microns (1mm) and as low as 50 microns (0.05mm). The spatial pixel resolution was between 20 and 50 microns. At this high-resolution, hundreds and even thousands of two-dimensional slices form the three-dimensional digital core. The fracture is extracted numerically by various processes such as thresh-holding, dilation, and erosion. The extracted aperture maps quantify the topology of the fracture surfaces as well as to the various scales of aperture behavior. In the case of a layered Berea we were able to show some relationship between high permeability layers and high fracture aperture, thus confirming some fluid flow observations. The fracture aperture maps can be used as the basis for multi-phase simulation of fracture transport.

title: Development of a Portable X-Ray Computed Tomographic Imaging System for Drill-Site Investigation of Recovered Core
caption: Figure 3. On the left is a reconstructed slice of reference standards used in the field. The graph on the right shows the relationship developed between voxel intensity and density.
figure_reason: Shows reconstructed reference standards and the voxel intensity to density calibration central to quantitative use.
tldr: A lightweight, safely shielded portable cone-beam x-ray CT scanner was built for whole-round core imaging at drill sites, and it worked on a research ship and in the Arctic.
summary: Drill-site imaging of core, especially unstable gas hydrate cores, needs a CT scanner that is portable, rugged and fast. The authors built a cone-beam system with a 130 kV micro-focal source, a 150 mm CsI image intensifier with CCD, and a cross-shaped clamshell lead shield with redundant interlocks to keep weight low. An aluminum compensator, a copper shutter filter, and frame averaging (10 frames in 0.4 s) improve dynamic range and density accuracy. Feldkamp reconstruction of 180 images of a 10 cm section takes about 20 minutes, and density calibration uses reference standards in sand. Resolution is 100-200 microns for whole core and down to 10 microns for plugs. The system imaged hundreds of 1.5 m cores on ODP Leg 204 and about 128 m of the 428 m cored in the Hot Ice #1 Alaska well at subfreezing temperatures.
abstract: A portable x-ray computed tomography (CT) system was constructed for imaging core at drill sites. Performing drill-site-based x-ray scanning and CT analysis permits rapid evaluation of core properties (such as density, lithologic structure, and macroporosity distribution) and allows for real-time decision making for additional core-handling procedures. Because of the speed with which scanning is performed, systematic imaging and electronic cataloging of all retrieved core is feasible. Innovations (such as a novel clamshell shielding arrangement integrated with system interlocks) permit safe operation of the x-ray system in a busy core handling area. The minimization of the volume encapsulated with shielding reduces the overall system weight and facilitates instrument portability. The x-ray system as originally fabricated had a 110 kV x-ray source with a fixed 300 micron focal spot size. A 15 cm image intensifier with a cesium iodide phosphor input screen was coupled to a CCD for image capture. The CT system has since been modified with a 130 kV micro-focal x-ray source. With the x-ray system's variable focal spot size, high-resolution studies (10-micron resolution) can be performed on core plugs and coarser (100-micron resolution) images can be acquired of whole drill cores. The development of an aluminum compensator has significantly improved the dynamic range and accuracy of the system. An x-ray filter has also been incorporated, permitting rapid acquisition of multi-energy scans for more quantitative analysis of sample mineralogy. The x-ray CT system has operated reliably under extreme field conditions, which have varied from shipboard to arctic.

title: Interpretation of Mercury Injection Curves to Derive Pore Size Distribution
caption: Figure 4 Comparison between the analytical curve dS / dP (ln) and the saturation increments (not at the same scale).
figure_reason: Compares the analytical log-derivative with raw saturation increments, showing noise and the effect of non-log-spaced pressure steps.
tldr: Shows that raw incremental-saturation mercury plots depend on step spacing, and recommends spline-smoothing the data and using the logarithmic derivative dS/d(lnP) for pore geometry.
summary: Raw incremental saturation versus incremental pressure from mercury porosimetry is often presented as a pore size distribution, but it has no physical meaning and depends on the number and spacing of the pressure steps. The author fits the experimental mercury injection curve with third-degree splines (about 20 knots) to remove high-frequency noise and then calculates derivatives analytically. The standard psd, f(r) = P²/(2γcosθ)·dS/dP, has units of inverse length but heavily weights small pores because of the P² term. It suits fractal roughness analysis but not mean pore size or double porosity. The logarithmic derivative P·dS/dP is dimensionless, gives more information at intermediate pressures, and matches incremental plots only when pressure steps are log-spaced, as ASTM recommends. All derived functions describe a throat-size distribution rather than a true pore distribution.
abstract: Mercury porosimetry is often used to characterize the pore (throat) size distribution of porous material and many recent papers show comparison with NMR measurements. However, the way of deriving the pore size distribution is rarely presented and very often, there is no dimension on the Y axis. In fact, most of the authors use the raw data provided by the equipment in terms of incremental saturation vs. incremental pressure. This presentation is misleading since the resulting curve has no physical meaning and depends on the number and spacing of the increments (error also recognized by the American Society for Testing and Materials). The right procedure consists in fitting and smoothing the experimental data using an analytical function (splines for instance) in order to calculate the derivative. The real pore size distribution (psd), with a dimension of the inverse of a length, is then derived from standard calculation that can be found in any textbook. However, this calculation gives a very high weight for the small pores (presence of the square of the pressure in the formula). This calculation can be useful to derive the fractal dimension of the roughness of the medium but is not very suitable to capture double porosity or determine the average pore size. The logarithmic derivative of saturation versus pressure gives the more useful results concerning pore geometry. This function is also close to the standard increment presentation when increments are equidistant in log scale.

title: A Structural Model to Predict Transport Properties of Granular Porous Media
caption: Fig.4 - Permeability varies as the power 4 of porosity difference( GPT prediction)
figure_reason: Shows Fontainebleau permeability following the fourth-power law in porosity difference, the key validation of the model.
tldr: The Grain and Pore Throat model links permeability, formation factor, resistivity index and other transport properties to pore-throat geometry through power laws of (porosity minus critical porosity), agreeing with available data.
summary: Empirical Archie and Kozeny-Carman relations lack physical basis for transport exponents, and the sphere-in-cell and capillary-bundle models give unrealistic velocity fields. The Grain and Pore Throat (GPT) model assumes pressure drop is localized in pore throats, so permeability depends on throat diameter, throat length and unit cell size. Transport properties are predicted to scale as (porosity − critical porosity)^a, with a derived from geometry. Permeability of Fontainebleau sandstones fits an exponent of 3.98 against the predicted 4 with a residual porosity of 2%, and the formation factor exponent of −1.5 corresponds to a throat aspect ratio near 2. The model also explains stress-induced permeability changes in Berea sandstone, Forchheimer inertial coefficient trends, polymer shear rates, and colloid deposition simulated with PARIS without fitting parameters.
abstract: The Grain and Pore Throat (GPT) model is a simple but realistic enough pore scale description of statistically homogeneous granular media. The basic assumption is that transport properties are determined only by the characteristics of pore throats and their density. All GPT parameters have a clear physical meaning and are measurable. The theoretical equations derived from this model relate macroscopic transport properties, such as permeability, formation factor and resistivity index, to well-defined geometrical characteristics of flow pathways at pore scale. The analysis shows that all these transport properties vary as $(j - j_{1j})^a$ where $j$ is porosity (or saturation), $j_{1j}$ a critical value for which the transport drops to zero and $a$ an exponent which is theoretically derived from transport nature and pore geometrical characteristics. The GPT model predictions cover both diagenetic processes and mechanical stresses effects. This model is also needed to predict 1) the deposition of colloidal particles (minerals suspended in injection water and asphaltenes in heavy oils), 2) the effects of polymer adsorption, 3) the behavior of non-Newtonian fluids in porous media and 4) inertia effects on fluid flow for both grain packs and consolidated media. All GPT model predictions agree with available data.

title: Measurement of the Formation Factor on Drill Cuttings
caption: Figure 4: comparison with core measurement using derivative approach
figure_reason: Compares cuttings-derived FF with core FF using the derivative approach, which gave the better correlation.
tldr: A conductivity-cell method with effective medium theory derives formation factor from drill cuttings, and the results correlate well with core measurements on eight samples.
summary: Formation factor is normally needed for saturation evaluation but cores are often unavailable. The authors place cleaned cuttings in a four-electrode conductivity cell (1 kHz) saturated with brine A, then measure conductivity again after replacing the inter-cuttings fluid with brine B. Self-consistent and derivative effective medium models give FF by eliminating the cuttings volume fraction (procedures 1 and 3), or by calculating that fraction from pycnometer and cell volumes (procedures 2 and 4). Tests on eight crushed core samples (porosity 11–40%, sandstones and carbonates) show good general correlation with core FF. The correlation is better when two conductivity states are used with the derivative approach.
abstract: Drill cuttings can provide useful information for reservoir characterization. In addition to porosity and pore size distribution measurement by mercury porosimetry, we have shown in a previous paper (Egermann et al., 2002) that permeability was accessible. Using a small volume of cuttings (less than 10 cm 3 ), we were able to accurately determine permeability after saturating the cuttings with a viscous oil and interpreting the response to a pressure pulse. In this paper, we present an original method to determine the formation factor of the rock from cuttings. The method is rather simple and quick to operate. It has been tested on rocks of different porosity and the results are in good agreement with core measurements. The method consists in introducing the cuttings in a conductivity cell. The whole volume, inter-cuttings and pore volume, is initially saturated with a conductive fluid A. The overall conductivity that is measured depends on the rock conductivity and also on the conductivity of the fluid located in the inter-cuttings space. From the effective medium theory, the corresponding unknowns are the Formation Factor, FF, and the fraction of voids between the cuttings. The Formation Factor has been derived either by estimating the voids fraction from the total volume of cuttings used and the cell volume, or by adding a new independent conductivity measurement after the fluid A has been replaced by a fluid B in the inter-cuttings space only. With this new type of measurement, we are able to quickly provide a complete set of data on a small volume of cuttings: porosity, grain density, permeability and formation factor. These measurements are not aimed to replacing core measurements but to provide additional information for reservoir characterization and log calibration when cores are not available.

title: Monitoring the Formation and Dissociation of Gas Hydrate in Reservoir Rock Using Magnetic Resonance Imaging
caption: Figure 3. Formation of CO2 hydrate along the core as function of time.
figure_reason: Intensity profiles along the core over time show hydrate formation decreasing free water, strongest near the CO2 inlet.
tldr: MRI was used to image CO2 and methane hydrate formation in a water-saturated sandstone plug, showing nucleation-driven growth from the gas inlet and permeability loss before pores filled.
summary: Gas hydrate in porous rock matters for energy resources, CO2 storage, and injection hazards, but forming and imaging it in cores is difficult. The authors built an MRI-compatible cooling system using Fluorinert as confining and cooling fluid, with a composite core holder. A brine-saturated sandstone plug at about 80 bar was partly displaced by liquid CO2 (0.5 PV), then cooled to 2 °C (and also 8 °C) to form hydrate, with MRI tuned to image only liquid precursors. Intensity profiles and 2D slice images over 24 hours showed hydrate growth mainly near the CO2 inlet, as a uniform band, consistent with nucleation followed by crystal growth and limited by CO2 supply. Permeability fell to zero when less than half the sample was hydrate-filled, implying localized pore filling; methane gave similar results.
abstract: Formation and dissociation of gas hydrate have been monitored in a sandstone core plug using Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). This paper describes the experimental procedures developed to form carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4) hydrate in sandstone rock while monitoring the process with MRI. MRI was found to provide excellent resolution between the hydrate and it's liquid/gas precursors and allowed the dynamic, spatial imaging of the formation and dissociation of hydrate under various injection conditions.

title: Enhanced Modelling of Mercury Porosimetry, Absolute Permeability and Formation Damage Using a Three-Dimensional Pore-Network Model
caption: Figure 4 Effect ot of formation damage shown for 10 stochastic generations and averaged, assuming 3-particle bridging.
figure_reason: Shows simulated permeability reduction versus occluding particle size for 10 realizations versus capillary bundle model, the main result.
tldr: A Pore-Cor 3D pore network, fitted to mercury intrusion curves with a Boltzmann-annealed Simplex, predicts formation damage from colloid occlusion that starts later and falls faster than capillary bundle models.
summary: The paper presents the Pore-Cor network model, which builds 3D unit cells of up to 1000 cuboidal pores joined by throats, to extract more information from mercury intrusion porosimetry. The network is fitted to the measured intrusion curve with a Boltzmann-annealed Simplex over four parameters (throat skew, pore skew, connectivity, correlation level) plus Boolean constraints, and it accounts for shielding of large pores by small throats. It was applied to a poorly consolidated turbidite sandstone (gas permeability 3335 mD, porosity 33.4%, modelled porosity 27.89%), with ten stochastic realizations giving close fits. Simulated colloid occlusion shows permeability loss beginning at larger included particle sizes (about 8 mm particle) than the capillary bundle model, then dropping more sharply to zero at 15-18 mm. Visualizations show small occluded throats blocking access to large pores.
abstract: A method is demonstrated for obtaining enhanced information from the mercury intrusion porosimetry of core plugs. It is based on simulated three-dimensional void networks, of simple Euclidean geometry, which have porosities identical to those of the experimental samples, and simulated intrusion curves which fit closely to experimental curves at all pressures. Although the geometry of the network is simplistic, it is nevertheless flexible enough to closely simulate the percolation properties of actual sandstone samples. Also, crucially, it makes an allowance for the shielding of large pores by small throats, which is not allowed for in the implicit straight capillaric approximations commonly used. The method of fitting the percolation properties of the network to an experimental mercury intrusion curve has been enhanced by the use of a Boltzmann-annealed Simplex. As an example, the method was applied to a core plug supplied by Oil Plus from a Chevron Texaco oil field. It was found that the permeability reduction due to colloid occlusion / formation damage is 'later' (i.e. commences at higher sizes of included species) and then drops faster than the capillary bundle model. The resulting unit cell, when occluded by colloid, shows clearly the blocking of access to large pores by small occluded throats. These effects can now be viewed in virtual reality. Other properties, such as the effect of polymer pore plugging, and the extent of fast wetting of samples, can also be calculated.

title: Effectiveness of a Complex Approach Towards the Study of the West Siberia Pukurian Suite Reservoirs Presented by Poorly Cemented Rocks
caption: Fig.5. Sw–porosity comparison. field 1-low invasion core; field 2–OBM core; field 3-Siw by porous plate.
figure_reason: Compares water saturation versus porosity for low-invasion core, OBM core and porous plate data, validating the coring approach.
tldr: Low-invasion coring in plastic inner barrels with liquid-nitrogen freezing of poorly cemented Pokurian sands enabled reliable porosity, permeability and saturation data and revealed thin lamination in PK-1.
summary: Poorly cemented Pokurian suite reservoirs (PK-1, Severo-Komsomolskoye field) were poorly characterized because old coring methods gave bad recovery. About 28 m of core was cut with a KIM barrel in disposable plastic inner barrels using water-base polymer mud with fluorescein tracer, then frozen in liquid nitrogen for plugging and analysis. Tracer data showed filtrate invasion generally under 10% (typically 5-6%), so only two samples were excluded. Core photos showed a thin-laminated reservoir instead of the homogeneous one assumed earlier. Best reservoirs had porosity above 40% and gas permeability up to 1000 mD or more, with porosity falling 2.5-3.5 absolute percent at reservoir stress. Effective gas permeability best represents in-situ permeability. Water saturation and resistivity agreed closely with OBM core, and porous-plate data gave m=1.70 and n=1.62 for estimating oil and gas saturation from logs.
abstract: Only in the late 90-s a comprehensive solution for estimation of petrophysical parameters of the Pokuria n suite poorly cemented reservoirs was suggested and realized in the Severo-Komsolskoye and Samotlor oil fields. The coring was run using the native-state core recovery method with placement of cores into the plastic inner core barrels and the core preparation for analysis was carried out by freezing it in liquid. The complex analysis of the cut core and core samples allowed to recognize a thin-laminated structure of the formation PK-1 in the field Severo-Komsomolskoye and to justify petrophysical relations for estimation of porosity, permeability and gas saturation of poorly cemented reservoirs.

title: A Density-Based Imaging Technique to Supplement Fmi Images for Sedimentary Facies Modeling
caption: Figure 6: A montage of the images from Tube #1 of Core #2. A and E are FMI images. The FMI color scale presents a range of resistivities from conductive (black) to resistive (white). B is the core photograph. C and D are orthogonal reconstructions (CT-generated slabs), and F is the CTgenerated density-based FMI type log, presented as a cylinder opened and displayed in two dimensions. Here the CT-s
figure_reason: Montage comparing core photo, CT slabs, density-based FMI-type image and actual FMI for Tube #1, showing the main result.
tldr: An algorithm extracts near-surface density data from CT-scanned cores to build FMI-type images, helping identify rudist facies in a Lower Aptian carbonate reservoir.
summary: FMI image interpretation needs validation against core, but visual core description can miss heterogeneity. The authors developed an algorithm that converts CT numbers to bulk density, draws the largest circular region of interest near the periphery of each slice, and stacks these circumferential density strips with depth-shifted positions to form an unwrapped, FMI-like image. It was applied to eight roughly 60 ft cores from a vertical well in a Lower Aptian carbonate reservoir in Saudi Arabia, with Core #2 studied in detail. Twelve tubes with rudist-like features were rescanned at 5 mm spacing and 5 mm beam width instead of the usual 2 inch spacing. Rudists appeared as highly resistive features on FMI and matched the CT density images, allowing in-situ and displaced rudist assemblages to be distinguished and supporting facies interpretation in uncored horizontal wells.
abstract: Formation Micro-Imager (FMI) logs provide a detailed image of the rocks on all sides of the wellbore by measuring resistivity. The high-resolution FMI logs provide valuable information regarding bedding surfaces and bed boundaries. Typically FMI images are combined with conventional log analysis data for sedimentary facies recognition and modeling. However, there is always some uncertainty surrounding the interpretation of FMI images and from time to time it is needed to validate the results by comparison with core data. Visual description of the surface of the core is not always sufficient to compare against the FMI data since some heterogeneous features impacting the FMI data may not be obvious enough in visual inspections. For several years Computerized Tomography (CT) has been used by the industry as an effective nondestructive tool for reservoir characterization. A CT-scan slice represents a two-dimensional disk of mostly electron density data (depending on X-ray energy used) at each scan location in the core. By combining several slices, it is possible to reconstruct the whole core in threedimensions. This paper discusses the development of a practical algorithm for extracting data from near the external surface of the three dimensional density based images for comparing against the corresponding FMI logs. Practical applications of this technique proved to be extremely useful in characterizing some of the interesting facies in a Lower Aptian reservoir in the Middle-East.

title: Using NMR Spectra to Determine Compositions of Unconsolidated Sand/Clay/Brine/Heav Y Oil Samples
caption: Figure 5: Clay content determined using MBC and NMR.
figure_reason: Compares NMR-derived clay content with mass balance, showing the method's main predictive result.
tldr: Low-field NMR spectra of sand/clay/brine/heavy oil mixtures are used to predict oil, water and clay content, showing strong agreement with mass balance for illite and kaolinite.
summary: Low-field NMR cannot capture the full heavy oil signal, and clay-bound water relaxes in the same range as heavy oil, which defeats T2 cut-off methods. The authors prepared clay/brine suspensions (8-32 wt% clay) and sand/clay mixtures (5-100 wt% illite-, kaolinite- or montmorillonite-rich clay) wetted with 2 wt% NaCl brine and Cold Lake heavy oil (4.5-22 wt%). They measured them with a 1 MHz NUMAR CoreSpec 1000 and processed spectra with non-negative least squares. Increasing clay content shifted T2 peaks to lower values and grew the 10-100 ms clay-bound water peak. The geometric mean T2 correlated strongly with clay content, independent of oil presence, with montmorillonite giving lower T2gm. Predicted clay, brine and oil contents agreed with mass balance for illite and kaolinite, while montmorillonite mixtures showed more scatter and were excluded.
abstract: Low field nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) is incapable of detecting the complete signal from heavy oil and bitumen because part of the signal relaxes too quickly to be measured. In samples that are free of clays or have high water contents, the contribution from water to the NMR spectrum is distinct from heavy oil and bitumen, thus one can calculate water content and oil content is assumed to be the difference. It is more difficult to determine the oil content in partially saturated samples that also contain clay because the relaxation times of clay bound water and heavy oil and bitumen fall in the same range. Results from samples with clays, sand and low-salinity brine show that clay bound water has a characteristic response. Heavy oil was added and the differences in the NMR spectra before and after heavy oil addition were used to create a preliminary predictive algorithm for determining clay content in clay/brine suspensions and solids/brine/oil systems. This algorithm predicts oil, water and clay content and may lead to improved characterization of ores and froths as well as enhanced oils sands recovery.

title: Multi-Phase Flow in the Presence of a Fracture Tip: Experiments and Modeling
caption: Figure 7: Experimental and Simulation axial maps of four stages during the oil flood.
figure_reason: Compares experimental and simulated axial saturation maps at four stages of the oil flood, showing the quality of the match.
tldr: CT-monitored oil-water floods in fractured, layered Berea cores, history-matched with a simulator, show the fracture tip accentuates layer contrast and flow differs for inlet versus outlet fractures.
summary: Fractures create bypass paths, and the role of the fracture tip in two-phase displacement in layered rock is poorly understood. Two oil-into-water floods were run on layered Berea sandstone cores fractured by a modified Brazilian test, with the fracture spanning the first third of the core at the inlet in one case and at the outlet in the other. Saturations were mapped in time and space with X-ray CT, using benzyl alcohol and NaI-tagged water. The experiments were history-matched with Eclipse using a 3D multi-layer model with porosity from CT and permeability from Timur's correlation. Flow turns from horizontal in the fracture to vertical at the tip, which accentuates the contrast between high and low k-phi layers. The inlet-fracture case reached residual saturation fastest near the tip, while the outlet-fracture case retained water near the tip for a long time as oil converged into the fracture.
abstract: This paper focuses on multi-phase flow in the presence of a fracture tip. This work studies two-phase water-oil displacements in layered Berea Sandstones that have been artificially fractured with single extensional fracture perpendicular to the natural layers. Two experiments are considered in this paper. In the first experiment the fracture was induced at the inlet end of the sample and it spanned the first third of the core. Thus, the diverging flow at the tip of the fracture was studied. In the second experiment, the fracture was induced at the outlet end of the sample spanning about one third of the core, and multi-phase fluid convergence to the fracture tip was studied. The temporal and spatial saturation distributions of the two cases were determined using x-ray computed tomography, CT. The experimental data were simulated. At the tip of the fracture, the two experiments showed different fluid flow patterns. The presence of the tip of the fracture in both experiments illustrated the displacement path in each layer. The presence of the fracture caused by-passing during the displacement process. From an experimental point of view, the presence of the fracture tip is essential for highlighting the property contrast between the natural layers in the sample, much more than in a displacement process without a fracture. Matches of the simulation results to the experimental data showed that when the fracture is at the inlet end, fluid diverges from the fracture to the matrix along the entire length of the fracture. The movement of the displaced phase was delayed in the regions neighboring the fracture and it preferentially flowed in the outer regions of the core. Understanding multi-phase fluid flow in fractured rocks is essential for designing and optimizing hydrocarbon recovery processes. The fluid flow interactions between the fractures and the matrix have a significant impact on displacement processes. This work provides modeling results and experimental observations that explain some of the displacement processes around a fracture tip.

title: Factors Affecting Relative Permeability Measurements for the Miocene and the Rotliegend Poorly Consolidated Sandstones
caption: Fig.6. Miocene sandstone (low cement content, mark 1 mm, white - pore space)
tldr: Steady-state gas and water relative permeability on 113 Rotliegend and Miocene sandstones shows pore space damage from clay effects and cement destruction, linked to residual water saturation and fractal dimension.
summary: Gas reservoirs in Polish Rotliegend and Miocene sandstones require multiphase flow data, but many of these rocks are poorly consolidated and damaged by contact with reservoir water. Steady-state relative permeability tests under reservoir conditions were run on 68 Rotliegend and 45 Miocene samples, supported by mercury injection capillary pressure, fractal dimension and thin section analysis. Base relative permeability to gas reached 0.86-0.9 at most, but many samples were low, and 13 samples closed completely during water flow.
