summary: Uncertainty in how Kr, Pc and residual oil vary with initial water saturation in the transition zone of an Abu Dhabi carbonate reservoir motivated bounding and scanning measurements. Twenty 1.5-inch plugs (porosity 28%, Kw 2-4.5 mD) were tested with live crude and brine at reservoir conditions with in-situ saturation monitoring. Primary drainage was run with live crude and ageing at each fractional flow, and imbibition was measured from Swirr (~0.10 PV) and from Swi of about 0.25, 0.40 and 0.60 PV. Bounding curves showed little hysteresis, and imbibition Krw lay below drainage Krw, contrary to the usual water-wet-drainage/oil-wet-imbibition model. Sor stayed within 7-15% PV with no clear dependence on Soi. Water flowed through existing water-filled paths at Swi between 0.25 and 0.40 PV, indicating mixed-wet behaviour, and Kro scanning changed character between those saturations.
abstract: Significant reserves are held in the transition zone of an Abu Dhabi carbonate reservoir, but uncertainty exists in how relative permeability (kr), capillary pressure (Pc) and residual saturations vary with initial water saturation throughout the column. A study has been undertaken to provide an improved understanding of the water flood recovery and remaining oil saturation distribution within the transition zone by better definition of the scanning kr and Pc curves. Primary drainage, and imbibition from irreducible water saturation were measured for both kr and Pc to provide the “bounding” data. Imbibition kr and Pc curves were then measured at three higher initial water saturations up to 0.60PV. The semi dynamic method was used for Pc measurements and steady state method for kr. All tests were performed with live reservoir fluids at full reservoir conditions with in-situ saturation monitoring (ISSM). Drainage curves are often measured in the laboratory with refined oil and then aged with live crude oil at Swirr. This may not truly reflect the reservoir wetting conditions and so in this study both the primary drainage kr and Pc measurements were performed with live reservoir crude oil. During the drainage tests an ageing period was allowed at each progressively higher oil saturation as new regions of the pore space were exposed to crude oil. Transition zones are typically modelled using curves that “scan” from the drainage curve origin to the imbibition curve as water saturation increases. Models typically show a distinct separation between the drainage and imbibition bounding curves, within which the scanning curves are located. The shape of the scanning curve is dependent on the model used and typically retains the characteristic shape of the bounding curve. Results from this study showed: - • little spread in the bounding curves with minimal “hysteresis space” for both the kr and Pc datasets. - • the water imbibition bounding curve to be of lower relative permeability than the water drainage bounding curve, contrary to many models. - • no clear relationship of remaining oil saturation to initial water saturation. These results may have a significant impact on how the transition zone modelling is implemented for this carbonate reservoir. This study adds to the literature data set on a topic where few full reservoir condition laboratory measurements have been published.

title: Two-Phase Semi-Dynamic Method with Electrical Measurements: Determination of Relative Permeability and Capillary Pressure from a Single Experiment
caption: Figure 5: Petrophysical parameters in forced imbibition
figure_reason: Forced imbibition results: differential pressure, Pc, RI and Kr curves from the combined experiment, including Krw end point 0.44.
tldr: A semi-dynamic brine-oil experiment with resistivity on an Indiana limestone slab yields Pc, Kr, RI and wettability indices in under two months; simulation match is only fair.
summary: Conventional SCAL needs separate, long experiments for relative permeability, capillary pressure and electrical properties. This work combines the IFP semi-dynamic method with resistivity measurements on a water-wet Indiana limestone rock slab at ambient conditions, with the displaced-phase Kr derived from resistivity (Li's model in drainage, normalized resistivity index in imbibition). Primary drainage, spontaneous and forced imbibition, and spontaneous and forced secondary drainage gave Pc, Kr and RI in under two months. Results included n = 2.1 in drainage and 2.48 in imbibition, Swi of 32.9% (Ramakrishnan-Cappiello), Sor of 14.9%, a Krw end point of 0.44, and wettability indices of about 0.25 (USBM) and 0.26 (Amott-Harvey), indicating only slight water wetness, possibly influenced by oil dye adsorption. CYDAR history matching of forced imbibition agreed only moderately, even after optimization, so in situ saturation monitoring such as X-ray is recommended.
abstract: Relative permeability and capillary pressure are important petrophysical parameters for interpreting fluid flow in reservoirs and for calibrating appropriate reservoir simulation models. The parameters are conventionally determined in the laboratory using two separate and time consuming core flooding experiments. In addition to being time and labor intensive, the core properties can change during one of the measurements and adversely affect the results. In this work, a special core analysis program is used to obtain relative permeability, capillary pressure and resistivity from a single experiment. The method is based on the semi-dynamic method developed by the Institut Français du Pétrole IFP (Lenormand et al., 1993) and electrical measurements. A rock slab model, as described by Pairoys et al. (2012), was prepared to test the semi-dynamic method. Reliable capillary pressure Pc and relative permeability Kr of the injected phase were obtained at steady-state conditions. To determine the relative permeability of the displaced phase, a method similar to the one described by Li et al. (2007) for drainage and by Pairoys et al. (2013) for imbibition was used to derive the missing relative permeability from resistivity. In this study, a full petrophysical rock characterization (FPRC) was obtained from a single and simple two-phase flow, semi-dynamic experiment. The method is attractive because it shortens the SCAL experimental program. Numerical simulations in imbibition using CYDAR software were also performed and compared with the experimental data (history-matching). The results are encouraging but further tests are planned to validate the generality of the overall workflow.

title: Measurement of Core Properties Using a New Technique – Two Ends Open Spontaneous Imbibition
caption: Figure 12. The results for co-current imbibition for CHP5 and CHP7 with the predictions of the theory super imposed. Once counter-current production ceases, co-current production is well predicted. Pressures are not well predicted at short time because the counter-current production speeds the advance of the imbibition front.
figure_reason: Theory overlaid on co-current imbibition data for CHP5 and CHP7 shows production fit after counter-current stops.
tldr: A two-ends-open imbibition setup with brine at one end and oil at the other, plus piston-like theory, yields relative permeabilities and capillary back pressure in chalk.
summary: Conventional AFO and OEO imbibition give square-root-of-time production, so only one lumped parameter can be extracted. The authors use a two-ends-open geometry with brine at one face and bulk oil at the other, measuring oil production separately at each end and pressure at tappings. Rørdal chalk cores were tested with oil/brine viscosity ratios of 1.3, 76 and 126. Production starts counter-current at the brine face and then becomes co-current; the counter-current share rose from about 4-6% (low viscosity) to 25-33% (high viscosity). A piston-like displacement theory fitted production well after counter-current flow ceased, giving NWP relative permeability behind the front of about 0.8 (137 cP) and 0.5 (83 cP). Capillary back pressure at the brine face was about half the front capillary pressure (for example 80 vs 128 kPa), while pressure predictions fit poorly.
abstract: Conventional oil/brine spontaneous imbibition experiments using cores with either the All Faces Open, or One End Open sample geometries give production/time curves where production varies approximately with the square root of time (almost exactly so for OEO imbibition). Thus only a single factor (made up of a group of unknowns including relative permeabilities) can be determined. For Two Ends Open, with one end contacting the brine and the other end kept in contact with bulk oil at the same pressure, the behaviour is more complex because initially oil is produced counter-currently (and rapidly) at the brine face but this soon declines (approx with square root of time). Oil is then only produced co-currently at the oil end of the core and, depending on circumstances, its rate can increase or decrease with time. The split between co-current and counter-current production, and the two productions rates, depends primarily on the oil/brine viscosity ratio and relative permeabilities. If a pressure measurement is made then these relative permeabilities may be estimated. Network models cannot yet model this experimental situation. A theory based on the piston-like displacement model has been developed. Experiments using homogeneous chalk samples initially fully saturated with mineral oil have been carried out using low and very high oil/brine viscosity ratios. Theory and experiment agree adequately and so several of the parameters involved in spontaneous imbibition can be estimated. In particular, it is found that the ratio of the NWP and WP relative permeabilities behind the front depends on the oil/brine viscosity ratio. Also, there is a significant capillary back pressure (or bubble pressure) at the brine face, a parameter not often included in analyses.

title: Oil Recovery in the Transition Zone of Carbonate Reservoirs with Wettability Change: Hysteresis Models of Relative Permeability Versus Experimental Data
caption: Figure 25: Richemont Krw New model results VS experimental data
figure_reason: New model Krw compared with Richemont experimental data, showing the proposed model's fit of scanning imbibition curves.
tldr: Experimental scanning imbibition Kr data from two limestones are compared with Killough, Carlson and Skjaeveland hysteresis models, and a new wettability-aware hysteresis model is proposed that fits better.
summary: Oil recovery in carbonate transition zones depends on wettability that varies with height above the free water level, which common Kr hysteresis models ignore. Steady-state crude oil/brine scanning imbibition data from Richemont (unimodal) and Estaillade (bimodal) limestones were compared with Killough, Carlson and Skjaeveland models. Killough's model underestimates Krow and overestimates Krw, fitting Richemont better than the strongly oil-wet Estaillade. Carlson's model fits Estaillade Krow but not Richemont, can give negative Sorw, and gives optimistic fractional flow. The proposed model combines Killough and Skjaeveland approaches with an Aissaoui-type Sorw–Soi relation and an exponential end-point Krw ratio scaled by a critical initial oil saturation (about 0.12 bar capillary pressure, or 65% of maximum mobile oil). It reproduces Krw, Krow and fractional flow for both limestones.
abstract: Due to its moderate permeability and/or very similar oil–water densities, the oil–water transition zone can extend over a large height and therefore contain a sizable amount of STOIIP. In the literature there is very scarce experimental data available for the oil–water system describing a drainage-imbibition process in the transition zone and practically none of them takes into account the variation of wettability on relative permeabilities. Most of the hysteresis models are basimple extrapolations and do not incorporate wettability changes along the transition zone which is a key point especially in carbonate reservoirs. In a previous study [1] we performed steady-state core floods experiments with crude oil/brine on limestone cores over a large range of initial oil saturations and observed that wettability varies with height above the oil–water contact and has a strong impact on both oil and water imbibition relative permeabilities. Moreover we showed that there is no unique relationship between initial and residual oil saturations while the most used hysteresis models ([2], [3], [4]) are based on the same Land’s residual versus initial oil saturation relationship. The most sophisticated models incorporating wettability, such as Skjaeveland’s relative permeability hysteresis model [4] show better predictions but still need a lot of inputs that are not always available at laboratory scale. In this study, we compare our experimental data with the most used hysteresis models of relative permeability and we estimate the uncertainties on predicting oil recovery. We also present a new Kr hysteresis model, using the bounding Kr (relative permeability) curves and incorporating wettability change, which best fits our experimental data.

title: An Efficient Method for Measuring Trapped Gas Saturation Under Co-Current Conditions
caption: Fig.10 – Valid Sgi-Sgr data Fig.11 – Effect of air compressibility on CNMR results
figure_reason: Shows valid Sgi-Sgr data within the Bond number window and the effect of air compressibility correction.
tldr: A centrifuge/1D NMR method gives many initial vs trapped gas saturation points per sample under co-current flow, matching log data for Bond numbers 4e-6 to 5e-5.
summary: Trapped gas saturation is needed for reserves estimation in a large Mozambique gas field with ~1 darcy, 20% porosity sandstones. Six core samples were tested with toluene and water spontaneous imbibition (all faces open and laterally sealed) and with forced water-air imbibition by centrifuge combined with 1D NMR saturation profiling (CNMR). Spontaneous imbibition gave slightly high trapped saturations (countercurrent flow, evaporation), and trapped gas depended on liquid type and initial saturation. For CNMR, valid data require a Bond number between about 4×10-6 (co-current flow) and 5×10-5 (avoiding blob mobilization), giving a Sgr plateau of 20-25% (average ~23%). This agrees with log-derived immobile gas below a shale layer (5-30%, average 20%); air compressibility corrections lowered Sgr by a few saturation units.
abstract: The amount of gas trapped by water influx is a critical parameter for the evaluation of the recoverable reserves of a large gas reservoir in Mozambique. We compare trapped gas saturation measurement results obtained by using various methods. All the tests were performed on the same six core samples. They differed from one another in the liquid used, the boundary conditions and the gravity force applied to the samples. The tests included: 1) spontaneous imbibition measurements on unsealed cores totally immersed in either toluene or water, 2) spontaneous imbibition measurements on laterally sealed cores with one end in contact with water and the other end exposed to air, 3) forced imbibition measurements by centrifuging unsealed cores under water with 1D NMR saturation profiling run in combination. The latter method is very efficient because it produces an exhaustive compilation of initial gas saturation vs. trapped gas saturation data. The lab data are compared to the log data acquired in an interval below the gas-water contact, where current gas saturations are the result of the rise of a paleo-gas-water contact. We take these saturations as the reference. Tests 1) and 2) provided slightly high trapped saturations, probably due to the presence of countercurrent flow (mainly in test 1) and evaporation effects (only in test 2). For the centrifuge/NMR experiments a good match to the log data is obtained for Bond numbers in the 4×10-6 – 5×10-5 range.

title: How Reliable Is in Situ Saturation Monitoring (Issm) Using X-Ray?
caption: Figure 3 Experimental set-up with core holder (1), X-ray source (2) and weighing unit (3) (Picture A). Zoomed in picture of weighing unit showing the outflow flowline (4), the brine filled container (5) and the cap containing crude oil (6) hanging on the balance (7) (Picture B).
figure_reason: Shows the core holder, X-ray source and the novel weighing-under-pressure unit that provides the direct production measurement.
tldr: X-ray saturations in unsteady-state floods are compared with oil production measured by a weighing-under-pressure balance; X-ray can deviate substantially, especially in low salinity floods, while the balance matches Dean-Stark.
summary: X-ray monitoring of in situ saturation is common in core floods, but its uncertainty is rarely quantified, and low salinity EOR increments are small (about 1.2 ml of oil for a typical plug). The authors built a Welge-type set-up in which produced oil floats into a cap hanging from a balance at 5-6 bar back pressure, so no gas evolves; dead volumes (about 1.2 ml inflow, 1.0 ml outflow) give under 0.2 ml uncertainty. In one sandstone polymer flood, X-ray and balance saturations agreed within 0.01-0.03 PV. In a low salinity sandstone flood they diverged, owing to brine mixing, salinity contrast, possible dissolution/precipitation and imperfect calibration scans (residual water of 0.3% and 2.7% after oil scans). Against Dean-Stark on 14 samples, the balance gave a mean saturation difference of 0.016 ± 0.015 (0.25 ml). The authors recommend combining X-ray profiles with the balance for quality control.
abstract: In core flooding studies, where fluids are injected to mobilize hydrocarbons, X-ray measurements are often used to monitor the hydrocarbon saturations in the core. This is done as a function of the position in the core and as a function of time. The goal is to understand how effective the injected fluids can displace the hydrocarbons, and to measure how much hydrocarbons are left behind in the core. The calculation of in place saturations from X-ray, however, is not straightforward, and it is often unclear what the uncertainties in the calculated saturations are. In this paper, we compare calculated saturations from X-ray with saturations from direct measurement of produced hydrocarbon volumes from the core. The direct measurement is obtained using a novel apparatus which measures the production of oil using a balance under a back pressure. We show that differences between the two methods can be quite substantial and we discuss what may be the reasons causing these differences. The paper ends with a discussion on how we can improve the use of in situ saturation monitoring for unsteady state experiments.

title: Magnetic Resonance Core Analysis at 0.3 T
caption: Figure 2. Comparison of brine mass determined gravimetrically and by total NMR signal from (a) T1 and (b) T2 data. The solid lines indicate equality between the measurement methods. The legend applies to both plots. Error bars on the gravimetric masses are consistent with the symbol size.
figure_reason: Shows T1 NMR brine mass matches gravimetric values for all plugs while T2 fails for sandstones.
tldr: A 0.3 T benchtop NMR system gives quantitative porosity via T1 (even in sandstones), millimetre-resolution saturation imaging, and sodium and fluorine detection for core analysis.
summary: Standard 2 MHz NMR core analysis has poor SNR and cannot support multidimensional imaging, so the paper demonstrates a commercial 0.3 T (12.9 MHz 1H) benchtop spectrometer. Eight sandstone, limestone and chalk plugs were brine saturated and measured with CPMG T2 and saturation-decay T1. T1 porosity matched gravimetric brine mass in all rocks (error ±0.1 g), whereas T2 failed in sandstones (±1 g) because of internal gradients, though it worked in carbonates. 2D RARE images of Bentheimer and Portland gave mean porosities of 0.241 and 0.214, close to plug values, and revealed vugs and fossils in the limestone. 3D imaging showed residual oil of 0.23 after brine flooding Bentheimer, and 23Na profiles and 19F images demonstrated salinity monitoring and three-phase discrimination.
abstract: Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) provides a powerful toolbox for laboratory-scale petrophysical characterization of reservoir core plugs. In recent years, considerable interest has been paid to low-field magnet technology. A resonance frequency of 2 MHz (field strength 0.05 T) is considered the industry standard for both well-log calibration and to provide quantitative measurements of porosity and saturation by minimising the influence of magnetic-susceptibility-induced "internal gradients," particularly in sandstones. However, the inherently poor signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) associated with such instruments limits the application of advanced techniques. Now there is renewed interest in employing three-dimensional (3D) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to monitor displacement processes in oil recovery studies. Previously, high-field medical MRI scanners were used for core analysis, but these studies suffered from a lack of quantification (saturation state) because of the presence of strong internal gradients. A field strength of 0.3 T (12.9 MHz for 1H) offers the best of both worlds: quantitative saturation and fast imaging at millimetre resolution. This field strength also offers opportunities for heteronuclear detection. Sodium profiles are used to monitor displacement in high-salinity formations, and fluorine NMR can provide robust oil-brine contrast in model core-flood experiments. Measurements at intermediate field complement standard low field NMR core analysis.

title: A Comparison of Quantitative Techniqueques for Determining the 3D Anisotropy of Shale Samples: Application to Horn River Basin Shales, British Columbia, Canada
caption: Figure 2. Variation of inclination (in degrees) of maximum (kmax) and minimum (kmin) susceptibility principal axes with depth for a 200 m section through the Muskwa, Otter Park and Evie formations of the Horn River shales. Closed symbols indicate “normal” fabrics with kmax close to horizontal (low inclination) and kmin close to vertical (high inclination), and open symbols indicate “inverse” fabri
figure_reason: Shows alternating normal and inverse AMS fabrics with depth via kmax and kmin inclinations, the key result.
tldr: Compares magnetic susceptibility, remanence and electrical resistance anisotropy in Horn River shales, finding inverse AMS fabrics from single-domain ferrimagnetic grains, so AMR is needed to infer true fabric.
summary: Fissile Horn River shales (Muskwa, Otter Park, Evie) are hard to plug, so samples were impregnated with sodium silicate and cut under propylene glycol into 2.2 cm cubes; some consolidated cylindrical plugs were also cut. AMS was measured in 18 directions on 57 cubes, along with isothermal remanence parallel and perpendicular to bedding, thin and polished section petrography, and AER on six plugs. All samples were magnetically anisotropic, with %AMS highest in the Evie (likely organic matter) and variable in the Otter Park (pyrite content). Normal and inverse AMS fabrics alternate with depth; IRM was always higher parallel to bedding, indicating that inverse fabrics arise from uniaxial stable single-domain ferrimagnetic grains, so AMS alone can mislead. In the six plugs, maximum electrical resistance was near-perpendicular to bedding and minimum near-parallel, broadly matching Kmax and Kmin axes respectively. Otter Park resistance (0.1-0.5 x 10^9 ohm) was lower than Muskwa (2-5 x 10^9 ohm).
abstract: With increasing interest in shale gas and oil plays, an understanding of the anisotropic properties of shales is becoming important for modelling their potential response to stress and their 3D petrophysical properties (such as permeability anisotropy), and thus for exploiting them via hydraulic fracturing. Various studies have mentioned that shales are anisotropic, but a quantitative 3D comparison of different anisotropy parameters is lacking, and details of the factors controlling anisotropy are limited. Part of the reason for this is the fissile nature of many shales, which makes it difficult to cut consolidated core plugs or obtain plugs that remain intact whilst undertaking the anisotropic measurements. We therefore first describe a sample preparation technique which maintains the integrity of shale samples and allows anisotropic measurements (primarily magnetic, but also potentially electrical and acoustic) to be taken on cylindrical or cubic core samples. We then detail quantitative 3D anisotropy measurements on several shale samples from the Horn River Basin in Canada (NW British Columbia, primarily in the Muskwa, Otter Park and Evie formations) by comparing the anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS), the anisotropy of magnetic remanence (AMR), the anisotropy of electrical resistance (AER), and the observed petrofabric from thin section and polished section analyses. A key result is that several samples exhibit “inverse AMS fabrics” where the maximum magnetic susceptibility axis is perpendicular to the bedding plane and not within it as one would normally expect. This can be explained by the presence of uniaxial stable single-domain (SSD) ferrimagnetic particles, which have a maximum magnetic susceptibility perpendicular to their long axes. Larger multidomain (MD) ferrimagnetic particles, in contrast, have a maximum magnetic susceptibility parallel to their long axes. This effect has been documented in igneous rocks (Potter and Stephenson, 1988), but never before in shales. We demonstrate, therefore, the importance of undertaking AMR measurements (rarely performed on shales before), because the maximum remanence of SSD or MD particles is always along their long axes so the maximum AMR axis will represent the true particle alignment axis. Studies that merely use the more conventional AMS technique could incorrectly infer a preferred particle alignment axis that is 90 degrees from the true orientation if a significant proportion of SSD particles are present. This may have important consequences for optimizing hydraulic fracturing procedures.

title: Steady State Stress Dependent Permeability Measurements of Tight Oil Bearing Rocks
caption: Figure 3. (a) Measured liquid permeability (nD) decreases with time at a constant net confining stress (NCS in psi), i.e., creep, and the steady-state value of liquid permeability decreases with increasing NCS [9]. Liquid throughput in pore volumes vs. time for the same test is plotted in (b).
figure_reason: Shows permeability creep over 30 days at constant NCS and stepwise declines with increasing stress, plus pore volumes flowed.
tldr: A steady-state liquid permeability method for intact tight oil plugs under net confining stress, validated with capillary standards, shows strong stress creep, permeability decline and hysteresis.
summary: Crushed-rock permeability does not represent in-situ tight oil rock, so the authors developed a constant-pressure-difference steady-state liquid permeability apparatus for intact, CT-screened, as-received Vaca Muerta plugs, using toluene or decalin and back pressure to dissolve gas. The apparatus measures from about 10 µD down to 30 nD and was validated with stainless steel capillary standards whose permeability follows k = d^4/(32D^2). At constant net confining stress (NCS) of 2,500 psi, permeability crept down from 5,500 to 1,500 nD over 30 days, with an asymptote of 1,290 nD, so plugs are stress-aged about 4 weeks. Initial permeability exceeded steady-state values by a factor of 2 to 10 at the first stress state, with less creep at later stages. Steady-state permeability fell exponentially with NCS (plug B: 760 nD at 2,500 psi to 260 nD at 6,500 psi) and recovered only to 440 nD on unloading; permeability modulus was 2–6×10^-4 /psi for drawdown and 1–2×10^-4 /psi for buildup.
abstract: In the last few years, US tight oil production has increased significantly due to advancement in horizontal drilling and completions, hydraulic fracturing, along with favorable economics. For tight reservoirs, matrix permeability plays a key role in determining the drainage area for each well and the optimal well spacing. Currently, the industry practice is to measure permeability after crushing these oil bearing rocks. Permeability on crushed rock samples may not represent the in-situ properties. Many publications have reported the limitations of crushed rock measurements in characterizing tight rocks. In this work, we present a steady-state method to measure liquid permeability on intact core plugs from tight oil bearing rock under reservoir stress conditions. We image the samples using CT scanning to evaluate their physical integrity. We measure the permeability of plugs while injecting a liquid and applying back pressure to compress and dissolve gases. We flow a liquid which is miscible with the remnant oil in the sample, and thereby perform permeability measurements on as-received samples, consequently avoiding the time-consuming step of cleaning such low permeability samples. We measure steady-state liquid permeability at various net confining stresses to simulate reservoir pressure drawdown and buildup. Our results indicate that we can flow multiple pore volumes of the test liquid through a tight oil bearing sample in a few days to weeks. We can accurately measure steady-state liquid permeability for tight oil core plugs from a few microDarcies to tens of nanoDarcies. The permeability loss over time at constant net confining stress (i.e., “stress creep”) is significant and this creep can last for a few weeks. The steady-state permeability strongly depends on the applied net confining stress and the stress history. Large permeability declines are observed as the applied stress is increased, and little recovery occurs as the stress is relieved. We validated the measurement technique by using a set of capillary standards that are not stress-sensitive and for which the permeability could be calculated using Darcy’s law and Hagen–Poiseuille equation.

title: Particle size effect on porosity and specific surface area measurements of shales
caption: Figure 2: Conformance corrected MICP porosity for six shales as a function of particle size. For the majority of the samples, noticeable changes in porosity occur between 1.6mm and 0.7mm particle sizes.
figure_reason: Shows MICP porosity versus particle size for all six shales, the central result of increased porosity below 1.6 mm.
tldr: MICP porosity and BET surface area of six Haynesville, Barnett and Wolfcamp shales rise as particles get smaller, reflecting improved pore accessibility rather than new cracks.
summary: Porosity and specific surface area of shales are usually measured on crushed samples, raising concerns about crushing damage and comparability with intact rock. Six shales (two each from Haynesville, Barnett, Wolfcamp) were crushed to 5.7, 3.5, 1.6 and 0.7 mm for conformance- and blank-corrected MICP porosity, and to 1.6, 0.7 and 0.07 mm for N2 BET surface area; crushed helium porosity was also measured. MICP porosity was roughly constant down to 1.6 mm, then increased below that, by up to a factor of 2 in low-porosity samples; high-clay samples H-1 and B-2 rose steadily (34% and 87%). Crushed helium porosity always exceeded MICP porosity, by an average factor of 2.3 at 5.7 mm and 1.5 at 0.7 mm. Surface area was constant from 1.6 to 0.7 mm but increased from 0.7 to 0.07 mm, which together with the unchanged area at 1.6–0.7 mm suggests negligible new crack creation.
abstract: Petrophysical properties such as surface area and porosity control the hydrocarbon storage properties in shales. These two properties are generally measured on crushed samples. Concerns have been raised regarding the potential damage induced to the samples during the crushing process and how crushed rock porosity and specific surface area can be related to porosity and specific surface area measured on intact rocks. To address these potential issues we have measured the specific surface area and porosity of several Haynesville, Wolfcamp, and Barnett shale samples as a function of sample sizes. The Haynesville and Barnett samples were selected from gas producing wells while the Wolfcamp samples were selected from an oil producing well. Porosity was measured on samples having particles sizes of 5.7mm, 3.5mm, 1.6mm and 0.7mm. Specific surface area was measured on 1.6mm and 0.7mm and 0.07mm particle sizes. Specific surface area was measured with the standard BET method while porosity was measured with mercury porosimetry after conformance and blank correction. Additional porosity measurements were performed using the crushed rock helium porosity method. Our results show that porosity is fairly constant when the particle size is larger or equal to 1.6mm. However below 1.6mm we observed a noticeable increase in porosity. Specific surface area is constant between particle sizes of 1.6mm and 0.7mm but increases between 0.7mm and 0.07mm. This increase in porosity and surface area is due to an increase in accessibility to the pore volume as the particle size decreases.

title: M. Fleury
caption: Figure 10: Fluid or proton typing using T1-T2 maps
figure_reason: Synthesis sketch summarizing T1-T2 locations of hydroxyls, organic matter, water and methane.
tldr: T1-T2 NMR maps at 23.7 MHz on dry, water- and methane-saturated shales and extracted organic matter separate hydroxyl, organic matter, water and methane proton signatures; deuterium exchange gives tortuosity.
summary: Characterizing shale pore networks and fluids is difficult with conventional petrophysics. The study used a 23.7 MHz Maran Ultra spectrometer with a small 10 mm probe (5 µs dead time) and a 200 bar PEEK cell to acquire T1-T2 maps on organic matter extracted from shales of different maturity and on a Horn River shale (RM9) in dry, water and methane saturated states. Hydroxyls from clay appear at T2 < 0.1 ms with wide T1 range, water lies near T1/T2 ~ 2, and methane near T1/T2 ~ 10–20 depending on pressure. Dry organic matter shows T1/T2 ~ 50 when immature versus 180–250 in oil and gas windows, and hydrogen content of 59, 30 and 21 mg/g for immature, oil and gas OM. Deuterium exchange on RM9 (NMR porosity 7.1%, 2 nD) showed full connectivity, with Deff = 0.62e-6 cm2/s, tortuosity 41.8 and Archie m = 2.45, while mercury injection resolved only about half of the porosity.
abstract: Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) relaxation methods are key techniques for evaluating shales, both from cores and logging data. First, very small pore sizes, down to nano-meter length scales, can be detected and quantified if the NMR tool has the ability to measure relaxation times in the range [0.1 – 1 ms], and second the different proton populations (water, oil, gas, organic matter) can be distinguished using 2D $T_1$ - $T_2$ maps. In this work, we show two techniques to characterize shales: 2D relaxation techniques to identify fluids, and deuterium tracer techniques to identify connectivity of the pore network system, providing also a measure of tortuosity. We used a NMR instrument working at a higher frequency (20 MHz) that yields a much higher sensitivity than standard plug-size benchtop apparatus. $T_1$ - $T_2$ maps were acquired on different samples at different saturation states (dry, 100% water and 100% gas saturated). In such maps, the fluid typing is based on the $T_1/T_2$ ratio and $T_2$ values. One can detect different populations of protons: hydroxyls from the clay ( $T_2 < 0.1$ ms, $10 < T_1/T_2 < 100$ ), water ( $T_1/T_2 \sim 2$ ), and in certain situations organic matter ( $10 < T_1/T_2 < 100$ ). Methane can be clearly distinguished with $T_1/T_2 \sim 10$ .

title: A Study of Shale Wettability Using NMR Measurements
caption: Fig. 2: Incremental NMR fluid volume as a function of $T_2$ for Marcellus shale core before and after water injection at 500 psi for 10 minutes.
figure_reason: Marcellus T2 before/after water injection shows large increase in the sub-1 ms peak, key evidence of small-pore uptake.
tldr: Short pressurized water or diesel injection into shale plugs, tracked by NMR T2 changes, shows Marcellus small pores mixed-wet, Eagle Ford and Mancos small pores water-wet, larger pores mixed-wet.
summary: Traditional Amott and USBM wettability tests are impractical for nanodarcy shales, so the authors developed a fast fluid-injection method monitored by NMR T2. Outcrop Eagle Ford, Marcellus and Mancos plugs (2 in. by 2 in.) received water (3% KCl) or diesel at 200 or 500 psi for 10 min, and T2 spectra (2 MHz, TE 0.1 ms) were compared before and after. Injection raised the fluid volume by about 18-22% in Marcellus, 70% (diesel) in Eagle Ford and 71% (water) in Mancos, whereas two hours of spontaneous diesel imbibition barely changed the Marcellus spectrum. Signal gains occurred at T2 far below bulk values, indicating fluid contact with pore surfaces. Small pores (radius <60 nm, T2 <5 ms) in Marcellus take up both fluids and are mixed-wet, those in Eagle Ford and Mancos take only water and are likely water-wet, and larger pores in Eagle Ford and Mancos are mixed-wet. The fast-region water uptake did not correlate with clay content, and Marcellus's higher TOC may explain its oil uptake in small pores.
abstract: Shale gas and oil are significant unconventional energy resources in the United States. Because of their low porosity and permeability, as well as the complex pore systems in organic rich shale formations, their petrophysical properties are not fully understood. Further, it is well known that wettability influences many aspects of reservoir characteristics, especially hydrocarbon storage and recovery; however, wettability of organic rich shale is an enigma. In this work, rock wettability of various shale formations, including Eagle Ford, Marcellus and Mancos, was studied using Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) measurements. A special fluid injection device was developed to study the impact of injected fluids on the shale rock properties. The effect of various fluids was studied by monitoring the changes in NMR response caused by fluid injection. After injecting either water or oil into the shale cores, we observed amplitude increases in the $T_2$ relaxation curve at $T_2$ values much faster than those associated with the bulk fluids. The results provide a positive indication that the fluids were successfully injected into and incorporated into the rock. When water is injected, the amplitudes of the NMR signals representing fluids in the water-wet pores are expected to increase, while signals from 100% oil-wet pores should remain unaffected. Similarly, the amplitudes of the oil-wet pore signals increase when oil is injected. Also, NMR signals with relaxation times slower than several milliseconds are considered to be associated with relatively larger pores and micro-fractures. For Eagle Ford and Mancos shale samples, the experiments showed NMR signal amplitudes increase in the $T_2$ range greater than a few milliseconds when oil and water were injected. This increase can be interpreted as having a mixed-wet condition in the relatively large pores and microfractures. In addition, the injection of oil in the Eagle Ford shale cores did not produce a signal amplitude increase within the relaxation time region below 1 ms; therefore, small pores in these Eagle Ford samples are likely water-wet. On the other hand, our study indicated that the small pores are mixed-wet in the Marcellus shale core samples, since a signal amplitude increase was observed after injecting both oil and water.

title: Gas Process Miscible Displacements and Its Impact on Future Oil Recovery Schemes in Super Giant Carbonate Reservoirs
caption: Figure 9 Reservoir E2: intermediate to oil wet – full suite of CO2 EOR tests Continuous CO2 and CO2 WAG in both secondary & tertiary modes and comparisons to rich gas – all above MMP
figure_reason: Full suite of CO2 EOR tests on Reservoir E2 comparing secondary, tertiary, continuous and WAG modes with rich gas.
tldr: Reviews 1D live-fluid miscible gas, WAG and CO2 coreflood tests on long carbonate composites from six reservoirs, showing wettability controls water blocking and CO2 gives very high recovery.
summary: Water-flooded super giant Middle East carbonate reservoirs leave large residual oil, motivating miscible gas and CO2 EOR evaluation. Six sets of 1D displacements were run on 50-70 cm composites of 1.5 inch plugs at full reservoir conditions (125 °C, 220-310 bar, live fluids, ~1 ft/day), covering rich gas, lean gas and CO2 in secondary, tertiary, continuous, WAG and SWAG modes. Plugs were screened by CT, NMR and MICP, and wettability was restored by aging; Amott indices ranged from -0.17 to -0.51. Oil-wet reservoirs gave similar high recoveries (about 90% or more) across injection schemes, while the less oil-wet Reservoir C showed water blocking and scheme-dependent recovery, with recovery linear in initial gas slug size. CO2 floods reached about 92-98% recovery, over 20% above water flood, despite viscous fingering at mobility ratio above 6, and compositional simulations supported the measurements.
abstract: Super giant carbonate reservoirs producing in excess of several hundred thousand barrels of oil per day are a common feature in the Middle East. Many of these reservoirs have been producing for decades, typically with water injection schemes. A challenge is to maintain the plateau production, and where possible enhance the production with additional oil recoveries. Production of additional hydrocarbons using gas process displacements at full or near miscible conditions, including injection of CO2 is now an on-going challenge and the most realistic option. A comprehensive review and analysis is presented on evaluation of tests from several reservoirs, highlighting the impact of in situ wettability and pore geometry. Carefully designed 1D laboratory tests have been conducted on long composites (typically 60 cm or longer) from a number of different reservoirs with varying trends of intermediate wettability. The tests were designed to represent the full reservoir conditions – temperature, pressure, advance rate and live fluids. Options of WAG, SWAG and continuous injection at both secondary and tertiary (after water floods and/or initial gas injection) conditions were investigated, along with potential impact of wettability. Selected experimental tests were also simulated using compositional simulators to verify the measured outcomes and deviations (if any). Good miscible gas injection tests allow quick evaluation of expected breakthroughs, final recoveries and potential improvements in carbonates, and thus improved pilot and/or full field design. Impact of wettability is evident from water blocking phenomena in more water-wet reservoirs and almost similar recoveries with respect to the secondary/tertiary/WAG gas injection schemes in more oil-wet reservoirs. Validation of pressure and hydrocarbon production profiles along with respective effluent composition data provides a robust analytical tool to enhance confidence in the different injection schemes and related successes.

title: Comparison of Oil Recovery for Six Nanofluids in Berea Sandstone Cores
caption: Figure 2. Core flooding results from the fumed NPs. The darker lines represent water flooding and the lighter lines represent nano flooding. The values are the %OOIP produced by the nano flooding alone.
figure_reason: Shows oil recovery versus injected volume for the fumed silica nanofluids, the best-performing cases.
tldr: Six silica nanofluids (fumed and colloidal) were flooded tertiary in Berea cores; fumed and larger particles gave more oil, pointing to mechanical log-jamming rather than IFT or wettability.
summary: The study seeks the best silica nanoparticle morphology and size for tertiary nano-EOR. Six water-wet Berea cores (about 13 cm long, 18.6% porosity, 362 mD) were drained with crude oil, waterflooded with synthetic North Sea brine, then flooded with 0.05 wt% fumed or colloidal silica nanofluids at 0.4 mL/min under ambient conditions. Additional recovery ranged from 2.4% OOIP (colloidal-S) to 11.8% OOIP (fumed-L), with fumed silica outperforming colloidal and recovery rising with particle size. Differential pressure rose during nanoflooding and effluent silica analysis indicated particle retention. IFT dropped modestly (16.4 to about 12-15 mN/m) and contact angles showed no trend matching recovery, so mechanical log-jamming is proposed as the dominant mechanism; repeatability was not tested.
abstract: Recent studies have shown that using nanofluids (nanoparticles suspended in fluids) in a way similar to water flooding shows promise as a new enhanced oil recovery (EOR) technique. The objective of this study was to determine the optimum nanoparticle morphology and particle size for EOR while gaining insight into the mechanisms driving the system. The tests were conducted at ambient conditions using core flooding analysis. Water wet, high permeability (avg. $K \approx 362$ mD) Berea sandstone cores (length 13 cm and diameter 3.8 cm) were used for the testing. Hydrophilic nanoparticles and nano-structured particles were suspended in a synthetic North Sea water solution at 0.05 wt %. The two different types of hydrophilic nanoparticles were nano-structured fumed silica dispersions and colloidal silica. Three particle sizes were tested for each of the nanoparticle types, resulting in a total of six nanofluids used for analysis. The nano flooding was conducted as a tertiary EOR method after secondary water flooding. Interfacial tension and contact angle measurements were performed to better understand the mechanisms. In the core flooding results, the fumed silica nanofluids performed better than the colloidal nanofluids, and additional oil recovery increased with increasing particle size. Differential pressure increased throughout the nano flooding stage, insinuating that nanoparticles are being retained in the core plugs, likely via log-jamming and/or mechanical entrapment. This is verified by analysis of the effluent nanofluid from the fumed silica core flooding tests. The IFT and contact angle measurements do not have clear trends corresponding to the core flooding results. These results suggest that mechanical mechanisms are driving the increase in oil recovery in this system, with only a minor contribution from chemical mechanisms. The mechanical log-jamming mechanism is likely the dominant mechanism in the system.

title: Nano-scale modeling of rock-fluid interactions in low salinity water imbibition
caption: Figure 4: Density of Ca2+ vs. distance from kaolinite surface at initial and final time steps
figure_reason: Compares initial and final Ca2+ density profiles, showing peak shift away from the surface in low salinity indicating double layer expansion.
tldr: Molecular dynamics of kaolinite, acetic acid and brines shows low salinity imbibition moves Ca2+ away, expands double layers, and desorbs more acid than high salinity.
summary: Mechanisms of low salinity waterflooding are hard to verify at the nano scale, so molecular dynamics (LAMMPS) was used to model basal kaolinite, acetic acid as the polar oil component, and in-situ Na/Ca brine at 60°C. Two models differed only in imbibing fluid: high salinity NaCl brine versus pure water, run for about 7 ns. Acetic acid was initially bound to kaolinite mainly by hydrogen bonds, not divalent cation bridges. In low salinity, the peak acid density near the surface fell to 0.7 g/cc versus 0.9 g/cc in high salinity, and desorbed molecules reached about 50 Å versus under 30 Å. Ca2+ density peak shifted from 11.5 Å to 45.5 Å in low salinity but stayed near 9.5 Å in high salinity, indicating double layer expansion. Water moved counter-currently toward and into the clay, and ion RDFs around acid oxygen showed double layer expansion on the polar component too, which may hinder readsorption.
abstract: Causes of incremental oil recovery in low salinity waterflooding cannot precisely be described by bulk properties. Therefore studies in this area have been directed towards molecular scale phenomena and the proposed mechanisms so far can be classified at this scale. Since nano scale observations are challenging, there is not much research at this scale to verify the mechanisms. Molecular dynamics simulation is utilized in this study in order to understand the nano-scale aspect of low salinity process. Basal kaolinite and acetic acid represent the rock surface and polar hydrocarbon respectively. In-situ brine includes sodium and calcium chloride. Salinity gradient above the kaolinite surface was modeled according to double layer theory for a few nano-meters above the clay surface in two models. Rock, polar component and in-situ brine were the same in both models but the imbibing brines were a high salinity NaCl brine in high salinity model and pure water in low salinity model. All possible atomistic forces especially electrostatic and Van der Waals forces were considered to grasp the physics of the phenomenon. Results show that acidic components are initially bonded strongly to the kaolinite surface by hydrogen bonds not by divalent cation bridges. Density profiles above clay surface show that desorption of acetic acid in low salinity model is more than in high salinity model. Also movement of calcium cations away from kaolinite surface in low salinity is more than in high salinity. Coordination of ions approves expansion of electrical double layer on clay surface in low salinity model. Results also show that electrical double layer of polar components expand too.

title: CO2-Brine Displacement in Heterogeneous Carbonates
caption: Figure 4: The best match relative permeability relationships resulting from the assisted history matching exercise. The left panels show the decane-brine relative permeabilities, the middle panels show the CO2 brine relative permeabilities, and the right panels show a comparison of the best (lowest RMSE, Table 4).
figure_reason: Best-match relative permeability curves for decane-brine and CO2-brine, the main interpreted result.
tldr: Unsteady-state CO2-brine and decane-brine drainage floods on Estaillades limestone are history matched with parameterized relative permeabilities; CO2-brine kr is lower, and heterogeneity and SS/USS differences raise open questions.
summary: CO2-brine primary drainage relative permeability in heterogeneous carbonates is hard to measure because core-scale heterogeneity is not statistically represented in the sample. Unsteady-state CO2-brine and decane-brine floods were run on 3-inch by 15 cm Estaillades limestone cores (porosity ~0.3, ~220 mD) at 100 bar and 50°C, with CT saturation monitoring. Porosity profiles and tracer floods did not predict two-phase displacement performance, so homogeneity can only be judged after the experiment. A 1-D model was history matched using assisted history matching (experimental design, proxy model, MCMC) with Corey, modified Corey and LET parameterizations. Modified Corey best matched CO2-brine (RMSE 1.27) and LET best matched decane-brine (RMSE 1.34). Both wetting and non-wetting kr were lower for CO2-brine than decane-brine, only Sw 0.6-1.0 was accessed, and steady-state data could not reproduce the unsteady-state floods.
abstract: The investigation of CO2-brine displacement in porous rock is important to predict plume migration and initial pore-space utilization in CO2 storage. The measurement of relative permeability saturation functions (kr(Sw)) characterizing displacement requires relatively homogeneous core material. Carbonates, however, are often heterogeneous on various length scales. While microscopic heterogeneity determines kr(Sw), larger-scale heterogeneity that is not statistically represented in the measured volume affects the investigation. In this paper we present CO2-brine unsteady-state core flood experiments in order to characterize CO2-brine primary drainage in Estaillades limestone. We describe the experiments by means of numerical simulations assuming 1-D homogeneous rock and parameterized kr(Sw) relationships. Assisted history matching methodologies were used to find the kr(Sw) parameters which minimize a mismatch function, giving the best match to the experimental data. The effects of larger-scale heterogeneity are still not taken explicitly into account (just by sample selection) and are a subject for further discussion.

title: CO2 EOR by Diffusive Mixing in Fractured Reservoirs
caption: Figure 2: Oil saturation during $\text{CO}_2$ injection in strongly water-wet core sample RC#1 with no water present. The core sample is shown in a bird's eye view with injection from the bottom of each picture.
figure_reason: CT oil saturation maps showing symmetric diffusive production from fracture, inlet and outlet in water-free core.
tldr: CO2 injection in fractured chalk cores imaged by CT and MRI shows diffusion drives oil recovery (up to 96% OOIP); simulation gives D = 3.02e-9 m2/s.
summary: The study examines CO2 EOR by diffusive mixing in fractured reservoirs, where a high-permeability fracture limits viscous displacement. Fractured Rørdal chalk cores (43-47% porosity, 2-5 mD) were flooded with CO2 at first-contact miscible conditions using decane as oil; one supercritical test was imaged with CT and two liquid CO2 tests with MRI, with and without residual (D2O) water and with one aged near neutral-wet core. Recoveries were 96.0%, 95.5% and 86.7% OOIP, and saturation versus square root of time was linear, indicating diffusion dominance after an initial viscous period in the closed-fracture cores. Water reduced diffusion rate (slope -0.094 without water versus -0.032 and -0.026 with water), attributed to water shielding and higher tortuosity. History matching in CMG GEM gave an effective diffusion coefficient of 3.02e-9 m2/s, and sensitivity runs showed rate depends strongly on tortuosity and system size, so lab results need careful upscaling. NMR T2 shifts to longer times during injection indicated reduced oil viscosity from CO2 dissolution.
abstract: Miscible CO2 flooding as an enhanced oil recovery (EOR) technique is currently employed in large parts of the US, and has a great potential. We here report on CO2 injection in heterogeneous rock samples with fractures to study recoverable oil by diffusive mixing. In laboratory tests, CO2 is injected through fractured core samples to displace oil. The injected CO2 will follow the path of least resistance in the fracture, but the majority of oil is located in the oil-saturated matrix block adjacent to the CO2-filled fracture. Oil is only produced by diffusion because the viscous forces are limited due to the high transmissibility of the fracture and the low viscosity of the injected CO2. Oil recovery by CO2-oil diffusion in fractured core samples was visualized with nuclear magnetic resonance (MRI) and x-ray computed tomography (CT), both with and without residual water present. Oil recoveries above 90% OOIP were observed in several tests during injecting of several pore volumes CO2. The presence of residual water reduced the rate of production by reducing the pore space and changed the tortuosity and CO2 flow paths. The development of local CO2 and oil saturations confirmed that diffusion was the main oil recovery mechanism, where oil was produced symmetrically from each side of the fracture along the length, without signs of viscous displacement. It was also revealed that diffusion produced oil from the inlet and outlet face of the core sample, which could not be captured from production measurements alone. An effective diffusion coefficient was found using numerical simulation (CMG GEM) to reproduce the experimentally measured development in local CO2 and oil saturation. The validated numerical model was then used to perform a sensitivity analysis of important parameters such as sample size and porosity. Numerical simulations gave an effective molecular diffusion coefficient of $3.02 \cdot 10^{-9} \text{ m}^2/\text{s}$ in homogeneous chalk samples and indicated a large degree of sensitivity to system size and tortuosity.

title: Multi-Scale Imaging and Cross-Property Correlations in Heterogenous Sandstone
caption: Figure 2: a) 25mm plug image unitisation, and b) 8mm sub-plug image unitisation. Horizontal blue lines indicate boundaries from the ϕ log, horizontal red lines indicate boundaries from the grain size log, and horizontal stippled magenta lines indicate boundaries identified in both the grain size and ϕ logs.
figure_reason: Shows automated unitisation of the 25mm and 8mm images, the core workflow step.
tldr: Multi-resolution μCT of a heterogeneous Precipice sandstone plug is unitised and simulated, showing cross-resolution correlations of permeability and formation factor with porosity, sorting and pore size.
summary: The paper addresses predicting core-plug scale petrophysical properties in heterogeneous sandstone when low-resolution μCT cannot resolve pore throats. A 25 mm plug (PU7, Precipice sandstone) was imaged at ~16 μm/voxel and an 8 mm sub-plug at ~5 μm/voxel, registered, and automatically unitised from grain size and porosity logs into 18 and 3 units respectively. Grain and pore size, sorting, phase fractions, Lattice-Boltzmann permeability and formation factor were computed per unit. Grain and pore sizes from the two resolutions correlate linearly, with the 25 mm data slightly overestimating sizes. Log(k) from the 8 mm image correlates positively with porosity and negatively with sorting and log(F) in both datasets, supporting cross-resolution prediction; some simulated permeabilities exceed 8 Darcy and await experimental verification.
abstract: Digital 3D image data from X-ray micro-CT ( $\mu$ CT), in combination with simulation software, allow for the measurement and calculation of geological and petrophysical reservoir rock properties. Similar to conventional core analysis, data obtained through digital image analysis may be used in the construction of geological models, which require upscaling for use in dynamic reservoir simulation. This paper presents some steps towards a workflow to determine core-plug scale properties through the use of reservoir characterisation data obtained from $\mu$ CT imagery. $\mu$ CT enables the characterisation of geological structures in core samples over a wide range of length scales, presenting new possibilities for property prediction. A single $\mu$ CT image is capable of capturing data for length scales covering approximately three orders of magnitude ( $\mu$ m, mm, and cm); additionally, one can acquire multiple images at different resolutions to improve data accuracy at different length scales. In this work, 100mm tall and 25mm diameter core-plugs of heterogeneous sandstone, consisting of fine- to coarse-grained bands ranging from mm to cm in thickness, were imaged using $\mu$ CT at 16 $\mu$ m/voxel resolution. The essential stages in the data analysis work-flow involve: 1) Plug Unitisation: automated identification of geological rock units through the analysis of grain size and $\phi$ logs using instantaneous rate of change, 2) Geological Characterisation: measuring the phase fractions, grain and pore size, and grain sorting of the rock units, and 3) Petrophysical Characterisation: measuring rock unit permeability and conductivity using digital simulation software. $\mu$ CT Images of the 25mm diameter core-plugs have insufficient resolution to capture fine-scale features such as pore throats or clay-bound porosity; therefore, additional fine-scale data are collected in step 4) Sub-plug Imaging and Characterisation: a series of sub-plugs (typically 25mm tall x 8mm diameter) are collected from the original core-plugs, imaged at approximately 5 $\mu$ m/voxel resolution, and analysed in a similar way as the 25mm diameter datasets. An associated experimental program is also underway on the same samples that will link the digital core data with results from routine and special core analysis. Resulations indicate linearity between grain and pore size; however, there is no clear correlation between grain size and other macro properties such as porosity and the proportion of clay minerals. Modelled permeability correlates linearly with the average pore body size after log transformation of both properties, suggesting a potential methodology for property prediction using a combination of core-plug and sub-plug scale data.

title: Onset of Oil Mobilization and Non-Wetting Phase Cluster Size Distribution
caption: Figure 3: Pore size distribution (top), cluster size distribution (middle) and cluster size distribution weighted with cluster size to indicate contribution to overall saturation (bottom) for Gildehauser sandstone as a function of time during imbibition (time color coding from Figure 2).
figure_reason: Shows pore and cluster size distributions over time, revealing breakup of the largest cluster into intermediate clusters.
tldr: Fast synchrotron micro-CT of imbibition in sandstone shows the largest oil cluster breaks into smaller ones by snap-off, with occasional coalescence, contradicting static-cluster percolation assumptions.
summary: Pore-scale oil mobilization during imbibition was imaged with fast synchrotron micro-CT (2.2 µm) in sintered glass, Gildehauser sandstone and Estaillades limestone, using n-decane and brine. Sandstone showed the most mobilization (about 60% of oil), with saturation dropping from 75% to 30% after ~1200 s at Ca_macro of 1.6–2.3×10^-3, i.e. capillary-dominated flow. The largest cluster initially held 99.24% of the oil and only 56.31% at the end, with oil redistributed to medium-sized clusters. The cluster-size power-law exponent started at about -1.6±0.2 and trended toward -2.0, approaching the invasion percolation value of 2.2. Snap-off at narrow throats or across several pores dominated breakup, with rare coalescence, showing disconnected clusters continue to evolve.
abstract: The onset of oil mobilization during imbibition has been imaged with pore scale resolution under dynamic flow conditions visco-capillary balance, by using fast synchrotron-based X-ray computed micro tomography. Oil mobilization under unsteady-state displacement has been studied for sintered glass, sandstone and carbonate rock, which demonstrate distinctly different behavior with respect to the cluster-size distributions and respective time evolution. For the sandstone sample, which showed the largest saturation change between the three samples, over 50% of the oil was mobilized during imbibition. The cluster-size distribution computed from the tomography images, but also detailed visualization at the pore scale revealed that during imbibition the largest (initially connected) cluster breaks off into smaller segments. Over time successively larger segments break off which increases the frequency of intermediate size clusters. In most cases, each segment breaks off into even smaller segments, but also in fewer cases clusters merge and increase in size. These findings support the view that at the onset of oil mobilization clusters rather break off instead of moving as a large cluster, which gives further insight into the ganglion dynamics flow regime. It is also shown that imbibition dynamics is more complex than assumed under common percolation models, where for instance disconnected non-wetting phase clusters become immobile and remain static. The experimental data instead clearly show time evolution for disconnected clusters that can lead to re-connection or further break off.

title: Oil ganglia dynamics in natural porous media during surfactant flooding captured by ultra-fast x-ray microtomography
caption: Figure 9 (a) Evolution of the largest cluster size ( $R_{max}$ ) and the number of clusters ( $N_b$ ) as a function of the time. (b) Formation and progression of the largest cluster in the time interval 33s to 42s.
figure_reason: Shows largest cluster size and cluster count over time, revealing coalescence then evacuation after each rate increase.
tldr: Ultra-fast synchrotron microtomography (5 μm, 3 s) imaged drainage, imbibition and surfactant flooding in Bentheimer sandstone, showing ganglia coalescence and breakup, with mean cluster size following a power law in capillary number.
summary: The study images oil ganglion trapping and mobilization in natural sandstone during surfactant flooding, which is hard to observe with conventional methods. A 5.8 mm Bentheimer miniplug (22% porosity, 3.8 D) underwent drainage, spontaneous imbibition and surfactant injection (IFT 0.3 mN/m, five rates 0.05–4 cc/min) at the TOMCAT beamline, with 3D tomograms every 3 s. Drainage reached 52% oil saturation and imbibition left a residual of 35%, with oil trapped in the largest pores (mean radius 62.2 μm versus 52.2 μm sample mean) through snap-off. During surfactant flooding, residual oil fell to 4% at 1.4 cc/min and 4 cc/min recovered no more oil. The largest cluster grew right after each rate increase through coalescence, then decreased as it was evacuated, and mean cluster size followed a power law in capillary number (about 10^-4 to 10^-2).
abstract: We have conducted a set of experiments (drainage, imbibition and surfactant injection) at the TOMCAT beam line of the Swiss Light Source (SLS) on sandstone samples. 3D images of oil ganglia trapping during the imbibition sequence and their mobilization during the surfactant injection sequence have been captured at different capillary numbers. 3D Images were taken with a voxel size of 5 $\mu\text{m}$ and a time interval of 3 s and then reconstructed using a phase contrast algorithm. Results show that at intermediate capillary numbers and relatively high residual oil saturation oil ganglia tend to coalesce and form a large cluster before being evacuated. This mechanism is likely to be at the origin of oil bank formation. At high capillary number and low residual saturation, ganglia are eroded and pulled off before being removed individually. After image processing, we have extracted different global and local descriptors like the mean residual saturation, saturation profiles, size distribution of oil ganglia and the largest cluster size for each time step. We have found that the mean ganglia size decreases as a function of the capillary number whereas the largest cluster increases immediately after increasing the capillary number and then decreases.

title: X-Ray Micro-CT Assisted Drainage Rock Typing for Characterization of Flow Behaviour of Laminated Sandstone Reservoirs
caption: Figure 2: Slice from the registered tomograms of plug 235 showing: (a) Dry, (b) Saturated, (c) Total connected porosity with zoomed in view of high (red) and low (green) porosity regions, (d) d ) after drainage by centrifuge and, (e) difference image showing Tight (brighter regions) and Open (darker regions) rock types, obtained by subtracting dry image from the drained image. Image resolution 15.
figure_reason: Registered tomogram slices (dry, saturated, porosity, drained, difference) show the drainage rock-typing workflow.
tldr: Centrifuge drainage of CT-imaged laminated sandstone plugs maps open and tight laminae in 3D; sub-plug properties are upscaled, matching measured vertical permeability for one plug but not the other.
summary: Laminated sandstone plugs are difficult to analyse with routine or special core analysis because several rock types occur within one plug. Two NCS plugs were imaged by micro-CT dry, saturated with NaI brine, and after centrifuge drainage at 4500 rpm (3 µm throat radius), with image registration separating drained (open) from residual-brine (tight) lamina. Sub-plugs of 3-5 mm were imaged at about 3 µm, with LBM permeability for open rock and Katz-Thompson for tight rock, and sister sub-plugs gave helium porosity and MICP. Image porosity matched well for open rock, but tight rock was underestimated (sample 235: 15.4-16.3% vs 27.4% helium) because of sub-resolution pores and dense minerals. Upscaled vertical permeability agreed reasonably for plug 235 (0.27 vs 0.12 mD) but overestimated plug 254 (17.7 vs 3.25 mD), likely because within-lamina property variation was ignored.
abstract: Typically homogenous core plugs are preferred for routine and special core analysis (RCA and SCAL) programs, however many sandstone reservoirs are dominated by lamination on a sub-plug scale. In order to maximize the recovery of hydrocarbons from such systems, effective flow properties are needed, and these properties can be strongly influenced by the properties of tighter laminas. While anisotropy in flow properties for plugs (parallel and perpendicular to the laminations) might be used to estimate the flow properties of the different laminas present in the core plug; the accuracy of these estimates are dependent on the constituent rock-types and their spatial distribution within the plug. In this study we demonstrate a novel method to study heterogeneous core plugs by first mapping heterogeneity within the plug and then determining flow behavior of each lamina at the sub-plug scale. Such lamina properties are critical to optimize $k_v/k_h$ relationships and directional relative permeability for models of heterolithic reservoirs. The properties derived from an open and tight lamina were used as inputs in an upscaling exercise to obtain property at the core plug scale. Using proposed method, we accurately capture the spatial distribution of an open and tight rock and its effect on flow at the plug scale. Upscaled results show a good qualitative agreement with the experimental results measured on the same plugs.

title: Coupling Multiphase Hydrodynamic and NMR Pore-Scale Modeling for Advanced Characterization of Saturated Rocks
caption: Fig.1. Berea sandstone digital rock model and numerical simulation results. Rock (a), pore space (b), distribution of water and oil after injection of oil (c) and after the waterflooding (d), oil recovery factor and water cut as functions of the total liquid produced (e), DT2 maps corresponding to the states before waterflooding (f) and after waterflooding (g).
figure_reason: Berea water-wet case showing phase distributions, production/water cut and D-T2 maps before and after waterflooding.
tldr: Density functional hydrodynamics simulation of drainage and waterflooding is coupled with Bloch-Torrey NMR modeling on digital sandstones, producing D-T2 maps for water-wet, mixed-wet and oil-wet cases.
summary: The paper couples a density functional hydrodynamics pore-scale simulator (DHD) with a numerical solver of the generalized Bloch-Torrey equations to link fluid distributions to NMR response. Three digital rock models (Berea, Achimov, Cenomanian sandstone) were taken through oil drainage to Swi and waterflooding to 98% water cut, using nonuniform contact-angle maps. Berea (water-wet) gave Swi 0.302 and Sor 0.253 with fast water breakthrough, Achimov (mixed-wet) gave Swi 0.226 and Sor 0.224 with slower water cut rise, and oil-wet Cenomanian gave Swi 0.098 and Sor 0.351 with the longest production. D-T2 maps before and after waterflooding show how wettability and surface relaxivity shift water and oil signals. The authors propose using such simulations with known fluid configurations to calibrate NMR inversion and logging interpretation.
abstract: We use the novel method of the density functional hydrodynamics (DFH) [1 – 4] to model complex multiphase scenarios occurring in natural cores on a pore-scale. Such scenarios may be extremely diverse, ranging from those inherent in RCA and SCAL measurements, and to much more complex processes relevant to chemical EOR. We perform the numerical simulation of several multiphase flow scenarios by means of the direct hydrodynamic (DHD) simulator, which is a numerical code containing implementation of DFH. We have demonstrated some of the capabilities of our numerical tool, DHD, for simulation of multiphase flow previously [4 – 6]. Now we focus on a combination of two different methods for characterization of a multiphase system in pores. The first method comes from hydrodynamic and thermodynamic description obtained through DHD simulation. The second method emerges from numerical modeling of NMR response corresponding to $T_2$ relaxation and pulsed gradient spin-echo (PGSE) experiments [7 – 10], which are routinely conducted not only in laboratory, but also downhole using NMR logging tools. We model the NMR response by solving numerically the generalized Bloch-Torrey equations [11] containing relaxation, diffusion and magnetization transport terms. The equations are subject to boundary conditions describing surface relaxation. The NMR description we use enables performing modeling of $T_2$ relaxation and PGSE experiments, and their combination. The numerical NMR solver is also implemented within the DHD simulator. This facilitates application of NMR modeling (i.e., makes it automatic) to digitized cores with multiphase saturation, whose state has previously been described and simulated in the frame of the DFH. Such close coupling of two characterization methods different by nature is extremely important and brings an opportunity for improvement of NMR response interpretation techniques, which suffer from the inverse and ill-posed nature of the fluids characterization problem.

title: 3D Mapping of Pore and Organic Matter Distributions in Unconventional Reservoirs Utilizing a Digital Rocks Approach
caption: Figure 3. Central vertical masked slice of the four vertically cored mini-plugs, in the initial state (left) and after the differences: $\text{CH}_2\text{I}_2$ -infiltrated minus post-dry (middle) and $\text{I}_2$ -stained minus initial (right), with fields of view (in mm) S1: 2.4x3.5, S2: 2.9x1.9, S3: 2.8x3.6, S4: 2.4x2.6. Yellow curves are (horizontally-averaged) longitudinal profiles of tomogra
figure_reason: Shows initial, porosity-difference and organic-difference slices for all four mini-plugs, the core result of the contrast method.
tldr: Micro-CT of mini-plugs saturated with diiodomethane and stained with iodine yields registered 3D maps of porosity and organic matter in carbonate-rich unconventional rocks, matching plug porosity and TOC within 20%.
summary: Fine-grained unconventional rocks are hard to characterize by routine core analysis, and micro-CT cannot normally separate pore from organic matter (OM). Four carbonate-rich samples (S1-S4, porosity 4.3-7.6%, TOC 1.8-5.6 wt%) were cored as 3 mm mini-plugs and scanned at 2 µm/voxel in four states: initial, diiodomethane-saturated at 20 MPa, post-dry, and iodine-stained. Registered differences gave 3D porosity and OM maps, and scatter histograms of the two differences classified features as mineral, matrix, porous-only, OM-only, OM-hosted porosity or partings. Segmented porosity (4.5-9.0%) and organic volume (4.0-11.8%) agreed within about 20% with plug measurements, less well for the more laminated S3 and S4. Registered FE-SEM of an ion-milled S1 face confirmed that the contrast differences track micro/nano-porosity and OM. Plug-scale permeability, resistivity and velocity showed anisotropy strongly affected by coring-induced partings.
abstract: The fine-grained nature of many unconventional reservoir rocks poses severe challenges for routine and special core analyses. A digital rocks approach to generate pore- and grain-network models for calculation of flow and mechanical properties is an appealing alternative, but presents its own set of imaging challenges. In this study, mini-plugs from four unconventional carbonate-rich samples were imaged by micro-CT in a sequence of states designed to selectively enhance X-ray attenuation contrast and resolution. Pressure saturation by diiodomethane enormously boosted the attenuation of pores such that even sparse micro/nano-porosity became appreciably brightened. Exposure to iodine stained the organic matter to highlight its distribution. Registration and differencing of the mini-plug tomograms acquired in these states then provided separate 3D maps of porosity and organic matter for image analysis. Segmentation yielded overall volume fractions in good agreement (within 20% relative error) with porosity and TOC measured on core plugs. Scatter histograms gave statistical measures to type the unconventional sample according to its relative populations of features locally rich or lean in porosity and/or organic matter. Higher resolution SEM images of an ion-milled section through the mini-plug and its registration into the tomograms provided a means to associate pore morphologies and sizes to these features towards construction of a 3D map of preferred flow pathways.

title: Finger thickening during extra-heavy oil waterflooding: simulation and interpretation using pore-scale modelling
tldr: A dynamic pore network model reproduces post-breakthrough finger thickening in extra-heavy oil waterfloods, attributing it to plateau pressure drop exceeding mean capillary entry pressure.
summary: Laboratory X-ray imaging of waterfloods in 30x30 cm Bentheimer slabs with 2000 and 7000 cP oil showed water fingers thickening and coalescing after breakthrough, improving sweep. A new fully dynamic 2D pore network model with iterative capillary-pressure coupling, secant-method inlet pressure control and multiple pore filling was built and benchmarked against 35 Lenormand micromodel experiments, reproducing all regimes. Slab-scale simulations, without history matching, reproduced dendritic fingers before breakthrough, thickening afterwards, and the plateau differential pressure. The proposed mechanism is that after breakthrough the pressure drop across spanning fingers falls, leaving the highest gradients at upstream finger tips, and thickening occurs when the plateau pressure drop exceeds mean capillary entry pressure. Sensitivities showed thickening is favored by longer cores (absent at 3.25 cm), weakly oil-wet (100° vs 170°) conditions and higher injection rate (0.05 vs 0.005 cc/hr).
abstract: Although thermal methods have been popular and successfully applied in heavy oil recovery, they are often found to be uneconomic or impractical. Therefore, alternative production protocols are being actively pursued and an interesting option is water and/or polymer flooding. Such a technique has been successfully tested in laboratory investigations, where oil recovery was found to be much higher than expected (paper SCA2011-18). Moreover, in some of the core scale experiments reported using 2D slabs of Bentheimer sandstone, X-ray scans performed during the flooding sequence provided evidence of an interesting new phenomenon – post breakthrough, highly dendritic water fingers were seen to thicken and coalesce, forming braided water channels and improving sweep efficiency. However, the causes of this behaviour are not clearly understood and the mechanisms governing such displacements consequently require further investigation. To this end, we describe a new fully dynamic network model that has been developed to investigate finger thickening during water flooding of extra-heavy oils. The displacement physics has been implemented at the pore scale and, following a successful benchmarking exercise against numerous micromodel experiments, a range of slab-scale (30cm x 30cm) simulations has been carried out and compared with the corresponding experimental observations.
