We show that the model is able to replicate finger architectures similar to those observed in the experiments and go on to reproduce and interpret, for the first time to our knowledge, finger thickening following water breakthrough. Finally, we examine the impact of several parameters – core length, wettability and injection rate – on the finger swelling phenomenon. Keywords: viscous fingering, finger thickening, heavy oil, recovery, non-thermal, immiscible displacement

title: Interfacial velocities and the resulting velocity field during a Haines jump
caption: Figure 2: The simulation results display the same cooperative pore drainage patterns as observed in the experiments reported in [1].
figure_reason: Shows simulated cooperative pore drainage matching experimental observations, validating the DHD simulator.
tldr: Density functional hydrodynamics simulations, validated against high-speed micromodel drainage experiments, show Haines jumps affect velocity fields over several pores, so pressure fluctuations do not average out within a small REV.
summary: The paper examines whether Haines jumps average out at larger scales by combining high-speed (2000 fps) imaging of decane drainage in a hexagonal etched glass micromodel (60 µm pores, 13 µm necks) with Direct HydroDynamic (DHD) simulations. The simulator reproduced cooperative pore drainage, with neighboring menisci retracting, and drainage timescales: acceleration over 2-3 ms and rest after 10-12 ms, independent of bulk flow rate. Interface velocities reached 0.1-1 m/s, giving Reynolds numbers near 1, so full Navier-Stokes rather than Stokes flow is needed. A parametric study varying viscosity and interfacial tension by factors of 10 showed that the microscopic capillary number alone does not characterize the displacement; results were consistent with Lenormand's regime diagram and showed that lowering interfacial tension drives contact angle to ~0° and stabilizes wetting films. Velocity profiles indicated a zone of influence of about 4 pores in radius (roughly 8 by 8 pores) for the base case, shrinking to 2-3 pores at higher viscosity, implying a jump density below about 1 per 25 pores for averaging in this 2D system.
abstract: The movement of immiscible phases through porous media is an ensemble of rapid pore-scale events that occur as interfaces pass through the convergent and divergent pore space. The relevance of these pore-scale events, referred to as Haines Jumps, for larger scale models is often questioned. A common counter argument is that the resulting large fluid velocities would average-out once a bulk representative volume is considered. However, in our opinion this is often stated without direct experimental and/or numerical evidence. In this study, we couple a pore-scale simulation tool with experimental results from a micromodel system equipped with a high speed camera to study Haines jumps at the detail necessary to determine the length scale over which these events influence the bulk velocity field. We first demonstrate that the pore-scale simulation approach, using density functional hydrodynamics (DHD), mechanistically compares well to experimental observations and other well-known displacement processes. Then experimental measurements of fluid-fluid interfacial velocities are used to test the DHD simulator. Simulation results are then used to analyze the local velocity field associated with an individual jump and thus, provide information on the zone of influence associated with a Haines jump. The results of this study demonstrate how interfacial dynamics affect the surrounding velocity field and over what distance this effect is observable. Therefore, the results have direct implications on how system parameters should be averaged when up-scaling from the pore-scale to core-scale.

title: Numerical Simulation of Capillary-Controlled Three-Phase Displacements on 3D Rock Images
caption: Figure 2: Stable configurations of gas (green), oil (red) and water (blue) (a, b) during upward gas invasion into a straight tube with constant star-shape cross-section, using Case 1 parameters and physical voxel length $\Delta x = 1 \mu\text{m}$ . Gas invasion is simulated at constant oil-water interface curvature $C_{ow} = 0.24 \mu\text{m}^{-1}$ . Figure (c) compares the simulated curvature-satu
figure_reason: Validation of simulated gas invasion against analytical three-phase curvature-saturation results in a star-shaped tube.
tldr: A variational level set method with a solid phase and contact angles simulates three-phase capillary-controlled displacement on 3D rock images; three-phase curves resemble two-phase but show cusp-driven snap-off differences.
summary: Three-phase capillary pressure is hard to measure, so the authors extend the multiphase variational level set method to include a static solid phase and arbitrary uniform contact angles. They validate it against analytical Mayer–Stowe–Princen solutions in a star-shaped tube (relative error under 5.9%) and sphere-pack throats (errors about 3–11%). Oil-layer displacement in corners needs higher resolution to be captured accurately. They then simulate gas invasion and simultaneous water-and-gas (SWAG) invasion on a 60x60x70 voxel Castlegate sandstone subset (5.6 µm voxels) from two initial water saturations (0.06 and 0.13). Three-phase gas/oil and oil/water curves are similar to the two-phase ones in water-wet conditions, with deviations from water layers, water-blocked narrow throats, and frequent water snap-off from cusp growth at gas/oil/solid contact lines. Such snap-off occurs at higher oil/water capillary pressure than two-phase snap-off.
abstract: We simulate three-phase capillary-controlled displacement using a multiphase variational level set method which is extended to account for the presence of a static solid phase and arbitrary, uniform contact angles. Motion of gas/oil/water triple lines is captured very well with the method, whereas oil layers require high resolution to be modelled accurately. We validate the method and apply it to simulate gas invasion and simultaneous water- and gas-invasions after primary drainage on small, water-wet sandstone geometry. The three-phase gas/oil and oil/water capillary pressure curves are relatively similar to the corresponding two-phase curves, but they show some differences that can be explained by pore-scale mechanisms. During gas invasion into oil and water, existing water layers in pore corners affect the gas/oil capillary entry pressures in parts of the sandstone geometry, whereas narrow water-filled throats prohibit invasion of gas which instead displaces oil in other locations. During water invasion in the three-phase case, water snap-off occurs frequently on gas/oil interfaces due to growth of water cusps at gas/oil/solid contact lines. This mechanism is observed to occur at a higher oil/water capillary pressure than the standard two-phase snap-off events in which cusps are absent.

title: Study of Waterflooding Oil Recovery in Different Wettability Conditions with Pore Scale Network Model
caption: Figure 4. Typical Simulation Relative Permeability Curves of Different Wettability Conditions
figure_reason: Shows simulated relative permeability curves for three wettability conditions, the main result supporting higher neutral-wet recovery.
tldr: A pore network model with quasi-static flow and contact angle distributions shows neutral-wet conditions give higher waterflood oil recovery than water-wet or oil-wet, with no fixed water- versus oil-wet ranking.
summary: The paper examines how wettability affects waterflooding oil recovery using a pore-scale network model. Pore structure data come from micro-CT (coordination number, connectivity) combined with rate-controlled mercury injection (pore and throat radius distributions). A quasi-static flow rule balancing capillary and viscous forces drives two displacement stages, oil saturation with irreducible water and then waterflooding, with a retention effect rule. Wettability is represented by contact angle distributions in pores and throats. Relative permeability curves for three wettability states show neutral-wet networks have the lowest isotonic point and longer water relative permeability extension at high water cut, giving higher recovery, attributed to film flow displacement. Water-wet versus oil-wet recovery has no fixed relationship, suggesting dependence on pore structure.
abstract: 1, State Key Laboratory of Enhanced Oil Recovery, Research Institute of Petroleum Exploration and Development, Beijing, China; 2, Earth and Space Sciences School, Peking University, Beijing, China; 3, Key Laboratory for Mechanics in Fluid Solid Coupling Systems, Institute of Mechanics, Chinese Academic of Science, Beijing, China; 4, iRock Technologies, Beijing, China

title: A Protocol to Evaluate Caprock Integrity for Thermal Heavy Oil and Bitumen Recovery Operations
caption: Figure 1. Longitudinal and axial CT scan images of caprock core showing an interval X suitable for testing (a) and caprock core not suitable for testing (b)
figure_reason: CT images show how suitable and fractured caprock intervals are screened, a key step of the protocol.
tldr: Describes a laboratory protocol using CT screening, brine permeability at reservoir and steam temperatures, and gas threshold intrusion tests to judge caprock sealing for thermal heavy oil projects.
summary: Competent shale caprock is required for steam-based heavy oil and bitumen recovery such as SAGD and CSS, to avoid environmental, safety and heat-loss problems. The paper presents a test protocol: field preservation of chilled core, CT scanning for sample selection, mercury intrusion and petrography, brine permeability at reservoir temperature and at 200-265°C, and nitrogen threshold intrusion tests at stepped differential pressures. Permeability classes are proposed: ideal below 0.0001 mD, acceptable below 0.001 mD, passable below 0.01 mD, and generally unacceptable above 0.05 mD. In two example full-diameter samples, sample 1 had 0.0006 mD at 20°C and 0.0001 mD at 240°C with no gas flow until 700 kPa, while sample 2 had 0.03 mD and 0.005 mD with gas breakthrough at 35 kPa. Permeability decreases at high temperature were attributed to clay effects from fresh water. Over 30 years of results, about 60% of samples were definitely acceptable and about 80% acceptable.
abstract: Thermal production of heavy oil and bitumen worldwide is on the rise as world demand for energy is constantly growing. The majority of heavy oil and bitumen deposits such as oil sands in Western Canada are fairly shallow. Steam injection processes are a commonly used technology in thermal heavy oil and bitumen production. To assure a successful steam-based project, competent caprock is needed because of environmental and safety issues and potential excessive heat loss if the caprock is breached. These factors severely impact the economics of thermal recovery. The paper describes a detailed laboratory protocol to evaluate the low and high temperature sealing capacity of caprock formations under steam injection conditions. The protocol has been used extensively for thermal heavy oil and bitumen recovery projects in Western Canada.

title: Building Analog Confidence for Relative Permeability Through Systematic Approach Across Major Middle Eastern Carbonate Fields
caption: Figure 4: RQI summary comparison (semi-log scale)
figure_reason: Compares kr profiles across six RQI ranges, showing trend toward oil-wet behavior with increasing RQI.
tldr: Forty-six full-reservoir-condition water-oil kr profiles from four carbonate fields are grouped by permeability, RQI and pore throat size into analogs; low-quality rocks group tightly, high-quality ones vary widely.
summary: Reliable relative permeability data are slow and costly to obtain, so analogs are used for exploration and undeveloped fields, but their validity in heterogeneous carbonates is uncertain. The authors reviewed 46 water-oil kr profiles (steady-state and unsteady-state, live fluids, full reservoir conditions) from four carbonate fields of the same formation, spanning 0.1 to 1000 mD. Profiles were normalized and grouped by absolute permeability, reservoir quality index (RQI) and MICP pore throat size distribution, then checked with blind tests. Low-permeability rocks (0.1-1 mD, RQI 0.047-0.07) had unimodal pore throats of 0.5 to under 1 micron, water-wet behavior and tightly clustered profiles. Rocks with RQI above 0.4 were bimodal or trimodal with throats near 5 microns, more oil-wet, and showed wide kr variation and high analog uncertainty. The resulting catalogue is proposed for initial kr inputs and SCAL quality assurance, with P10/P50/P90 cases covering uncertainty.
abstract: Relative permeability (kr) is crucial in terms of hydrocarbon proliferation (field development) and handling fluids through sophisticated mega surface facilities, in which it significantly contributes to projects success or failure. Due to time, cost and effort in obtaining reliable kr data, especially in case of exploration and undeveloped fields, reservoir engineers depend on "Analog" concept with nearby similar and representative reservoirs. It is even more challenging while dealing with carbonate heterogeneous reservoirs, where rock properties and wettability conditions are not necessary aligned in certain trend. Therefore, validation and level of confidence for the analog data is a challenge for representative models outcomes. A major oil company in the Middle East region, initiated a large scale internal review aiming to consolidate a representative analog kr profiles across various fields with tens of billions OOIP. The available data were accumulated for over 30 years that included many laboratories, techniques and analyses approaches. The objectives were to produce a kr catalogue that will be used as a reference for new exploration fields and also to support the current performance predictions for the developed ones. A comprehensive approach was adopted in the analysis for different reservoir rock types (RRTs) to be clustered based on reservoir rock properties, capillary pressure profiles, wettability indices, saturation end points and rock/fluid saturation indices such as 'm' and 'n' factors. Detailed SCAL data were collected and fully analyzed for 4 main fields with various Reservoir Rock Types (RRTs), which exhibit wide range of permeability variation from 0.1 to 1000 mD. Total of 46 water flood kr profiles (primary imbibition) were included in the review, in which they were assigned to different groups based on several discriminators. Blind tests were then performed on different sets of kr data to assess the validation of the proposed analogs. Relative permeability profiles may possibly be distinguished and grouped, based on RRT and/or Petrophysical Group (PG) characteristics. Proposed "Analog" kr catalogue was an outcome of this investigation, which is a good reference and adds more confidence to modeling of reservoir fluids dynamics. Generally, it has been observed that lower reservoir quality RRTs were well defined with less profiles variation compared with the better quality RRTs. In addition, this catalogue can be used as a guide in designing and quality assurance for laboratory SCAL experiments, as well as providing 'initial' kr data for fields which are yet to be analyzed.

title: An Automated Machine-Learning Procedure for Robust Classification of SEM Images of Cross-Laminated Sandstones for Digital Rock Analysis
caption: Figure 5 (a) A scheme for labelling randomly sampled templates used in this work. (b) Samples labelled (c) WEKA classification result.
figure_reason: Shows the labelled training samples and the final WEKA classification of laminae, the main result.
tldr: An automated procedure combining unsupervised labelling of random templates and supervised random-forest classification identifies laminae in a high-resolution SEM image of a cross-laminated tight sandstone.
summary: Identifying laminae in high-resolution SEM images is needed to calibrate low-resolution images in multi-scale digital rock reconstruction of cross-laminated sandstones. The authors propose a procedure: rescale the image so the thinnest lamina is resolved, choose a template size by minimizing the coefficient of variation, randomly sample templates (100 here), label them without supervision, then classify the whole image with a supervised random forest. It was implemented in ImageJ with the WEKA plugin on a 17328x26378 pixel SEM image (about 1.1 µm) of a Triassic tight red sandstone. The image was rescaled to 450x712 pixels with 12x12 templates and 9 features, and three classes were identified. The result distinguished both high-contrast mineralogical laminae and weakly contrasting laminae or within-lamina patterns. Pixel-wise agreement between classifications using different third features was only about 70-79%, suggesting more or better features could improve classification.
abstract: Depositional structures such as laminae in sandstones reflect local changes in grain size, shape, orientation and composition. Laminae can occur as a set of parallel or intersecting structures, depending on the depositional processes. Further aided by diagenetic modifications, pore structures and pore surface properties may vary to a large degree, in their topology and geometry as well as physicochemical nature, within each lamina and across a set of laminae. The combination of spatial arrangements and local properties means that laminations can greatly influence the flow of multi-phase fluids. As an example, it is well-known that sandstone laminae can trap a significant amount of hydrocarbon in reservoirs. Most of the previous studies, however, treat each lamina as a uniform continuum without taking into consideration the true grain-pore characteristics associated with them (see [1] and references therein), whereas fewer others did but for tabular lamina only [2]. To gain a fuller understanding of the aforementioned combinational effect on multi-phase fluid flow and to obtain more appropriate estimates of effective properties for cross-laminated reservoir rock samples, we are taking digital rock analysis approach by reconstructing the pore structures of representative samples and then numerically simulating fluid flow through the pore systems. Because a representative sample deems to be much larger than a usual core plug, the reconstruction calls for multi-scale imaging techniques (e.g. using industrial CT scanner, microCT, Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM)) to capture the spatial arrangements of the laminae and associated diverse pore structures, and deterministic and stochastic integration techniques to fuse obtained images. In integration, the lamina structures, which are captured in low-resolution 3D images, need to be calibrated against those identified in high-resolution 2/3D images, in order to reconstruct fine-scale grains and pores in those coarser structures. However, it is non-trivial to identify those structures in a high-resolution image. In this report, we develop an automated machine-learning procedure for image classification to perform this task. We illustrate this procedure using an SEM image of a cross-laminated tight sandstone sample. This work is an attempt to extend multi-scale data integration for digital rock analysis beyond what has been proposed for core plugs [3] to larger and structurally more complex samples.

title: An Experimental Investigation of EOR Mechanisms for Nanoparticles Fluid in Glass Micromodel
caption: Figure 4 IFT between oil and NSP/CNP fluids with different concentration
figure_reason: Shows IFT decreasing with nanoparticle concentration for CNP and NSP, a key mechanism result.
tldr: Glass micromodel flooding with silica nanofluids shows IFT and contact angle reduction, emulsification, pore plugging and sweep changes as EOR mechanisms, increasing with nanoparticle concentration.
summary: The study examines EOR mechanisms of hydrophilic silica nano-structured particles (NSP) and colloidal nanoparticles (CNP) dispersed in 3 wt% brine at 0.05, 0.1 and 0.5 wt%. IFT (spinning drop) and contact angle on quartz were measured against North Sea crude oil, and tertiary nanofluid floods were run in a 0.13 ml glass micromodel at 0.02 and 0.04 ml/min after brine flooding. Both particle types lowered IFT and contact angle with increasing concentration, making the surface more water wet. Higher concentrations recovered more oil through IFT reduction and emulsification, with o/w emulsions seen for NSP and w/o for CNP. NSP adsorbed strongly, causing continuously rising pressure drop and permeability reduction, while CNP shifted the first breakthrough channel and improved sweep. Recovery was assessed qualitatively from images because of the small pore volume.
abstract: Nanoparticle as part of nanotechnology has already drawn attentions for its great potential of enhancing oil recovery. In the last few years some publications have already addressed this topic, but the basic enhanced oil recovery (EOR) mechanisms have not been released very clearly. In this experimental study a visualization flooding method (glass micromodel) was used to investigate the EOR mechanisms of nanoparticles fluid. In this experimental study both silica nano-structured particle and colloidal silica nanoparticle were used to enhance oil recovery. A transparent glass micromodel was utilized as porous media, and synthetic brine was used to disperse nanoparticles. The effects of different kinds of nanoparticles and different nanoparticle concentrations on EOR were investigated; and some properties between oil and water were measured to uncover EOR mechanisms. The experimental results showed that nanoparticles have the ability to reduce the IFT between oil and water as well as contact angle, to make solid surface to be more water wet. In the visualization flooding experiments, as the nanoparticles concentration increase more trapped oil can be produced by emulsification and reduction of IFT. Pore channels plugged due to adsorption of nanoparticles were observed and resulted in increase of injection pressure, which pushed some trapped oil in the small pore channels out of the model. The results from the glass micromodel study give a clear indication that the EOR potential of nanoparticles fluid is significant.

title: Sulige Gas Field in Changqing Oilfield China
caption: Figure 4 Different parameters at at different size of sub-volumes
figure_reason: Shows permeability, porosity, pore radius and throat length versus subvolume size, revealing where properties stabilize and the REV.
tldr: Micro-CT pore network models of Sulige tight sandstone show porosity, permeability, pore radius and throat length stabilize at a 300^3 voxel (1020 µm) REV.
summary: The paper determines the representative elementary volume (REV) of tight sandstone from the Sulige Gas Field, Changqing Oilfield, China, which is needed to scale pore-scale results to Darcy-scale properties. A sample was imaged by micro-CT (Zeiss MCT-400) at 3.4 µm resolution, and non-overlapping subvolumes from 100^3 to 600^3 voxels were filtered (non-local means), segmented (watershed) and converted into pore network models. Porosity, average pore radius, throat length, coordination number and network permeability were computed for each size. Porosity fell from 4.63% (100^3) to about 2.5% at 300^3 and above, and permeability settled near 13×10^-3 µm². The standard deviation and coefficient of variation also dropped sharply above 300^3, with the coefficient of variation near 5% or below for porosity and permeability. Both approaches give a REV of 300^3 voxels, about 1020 µm per side.
abstract: In this paper, a micro-CT based digital rock technology is used to characterize the REV of sandstone from the Sulige Gas Field in the Changqing Oilfield in China. Firstly, the digital core of the sample is obtained by micro-CT scanning of rock samples with the resolution of 3.4μm. Secondly, respective pore network models, with the voxel size from 600 600 600 , are extracted from the processed micro-CT images. Thirdly, single-phase and two-phase oil-water flow simulation are performed on these

title: A Systematic Investigation of Wetting Stability in Aged Chalk
caption: Figure 2. Development in water saturation Sw and imbibition rate Q vs. time for core plugs aged 6 days (c#1) at low (M4L6), medium (M8M6) and high (M9H6) initial Sw.
figure_reason: Shows water saturation and imbibition rate versus time for plugs aged at low, medium and high initial Sw.
tldr: Rørdal chalk plugs aged dynamically in crude oil showed stable Amott-Harvey water indices (average change 0.04) over two spontaneous and forced imbibition cycles, across aging times and initial water saturations.
summary: Reliable EOR wettability studies need stable, uniform wetting states in aged cores. Twelve outcrop Rørdal chalk plugs were aged dynamically with North Sea crude at 80°C for 2 or 6 days at low (~0.23), medium (~0.29) or high (~0.35) initial water saturation. Two cycles of drainage, spontaneous and forced imbibition were run with n-Decane and brine. Amott-Harvey Iw ranged from 0.39 to 0.80, decreasing with longer aging and lower initial Sw, and changed by only 0.04 on average (0.00-0.10) between cycles. End-point Swsp rose with higher initial Sw and shorter aging (e.g. 0.46 to 0.56 for 6-day aging) but was repeatable within ±0.02 between cycles. Stevns and Niobrara chalk gave less consistent wettability results.
abstract: Waterflood performance of fractured chalk reservoirs are strongly influenced by wettability, and spontaneous imbibition of water from fractures to matrix is a key mechanism for oil production. To determine the enhanced oil recovery (EOR) potential for induced wettability change, for instance during a surfactant injection, stable and uniform wetting preferences representing reservoir conditions must be established during core analysis to avoid laboratory artifacts. A systematic investigation of wettability stability in laboratory aged core plugs was performed by repeated cycles of spontaneous and forced imbibitions. Altered wetting states, ranging from strongly water-wet to moderately water-wet conditions were established by aging outcrop Rørdal chalk samples in crude oil at 80°C for 2 to 6 days at a range of initial water saturations during aging. The Amott-Harvey water index ( $I_w$ ) was found stable over two cycles of spontaneous imbibition tests, with an average change of $I_w \pm 0.04$ between the first and second cycle. The oil recovery rate in partly waterflooded regions and transition zones was evaluated by varying the initial water saturation.

title: X-Ray Microtomography and NMR: complimentary tools for evaluation of pore structure within a core
caption: Fig.2. Pore size distributions by NMR and micro-CT and T1-T2 2D-map for the sandstone rock sample (Silica=62%, Feldspar=20%, Clays=18%, $\Phi=27.8\%$ , Permeability=407mD)
figure_reason: Sandstone shows CT and NMR pore size distributions with T1-T2 map, the central calibration result and microporosity estimate.
tldr: Pore size distributions from micro-CT are fitted to NMR T1 and T2 spectra to calibrate surface relaxivity and estimate sub-resolution microporosity, tested on glass beads, sandstone and dolomite.
summary: NMR relaxation times give only indirect pore sizes, so the authors calibrate relaxivity by fitting micro-CT pore size distributions (inscribed-sphere local thickness, ~2.2 µm pixels) to NMR T1 and T2 spectra measured at 20.6 MHz. A capillary-lattice model using Klinkenberg gas permeability gives an independent relaxivity estimate. Tests were on 8 mm by 10 mm plugs of sintered glass beads, quartz sandstone and dolomite. For glass beads, ρT2 was 53 µm/s from CT and 73 µm/s from the lattice model. For sandstone, ρT2 was 24 versus 30.2 µm/s, and microporosity below CT resolution was 14.6 p.u. (45.6% of porosity) from T2. For the dolomite, the two methods disagreed strongly (ρT2 of 75 versus 2.1 µm/s; microporosity 7.9 p.u.), which is attributed to the poor link between permeability and pore-body structure in complex carbonates.
abstract: We propose a new scientific approach for calibration of relaxation times to the real pore sizes by combination of both NMR (Nuclear Magnetic Resonance) and X-ray microtomography (XmCT) techniques. The approach contains the following steps, (1) Application of morphometric image processing procedure to 3D XmCT image of a sample. The morphometric image processing allows studying different morphological features of pore space structure. Particularly, pore size distribution may be obtained this way. (2) Fitting of the pore size distribution with NMR $T_1$ - $T_2$ spectra would provide the required calibration. The procedure based on tuning the relaxativity by minimizing a norm containing difference of the XmCT and NMR distributions in a range of pore sizes resolvable by XmCT. The capillary-lattice model also examined as method of a relaxativity calculation using experimentally measured value of absolute permeability (gas permeability with Klinkenberg correction) of the core. The described approach was tested as on artificial and natural rock samples. Obtained values for relaxativity show good agreement with published data. The microporosity values which correspond to the volume of void structure within the samples below the XmCT resolution and sensible to NMR are confirmed by routine porosity measurements.

title: Impedance Spectroscopy on Carbonates
caption: Figure 2: $\sigma'\sigma''$ and $\sigma'_{surf}$ (@ 1 Hz) relationship for sandstones (after [18]) and for the investigated carbonate samples from Tushka (left hand side) and $\sigma''$ (@ 1 Hz) and $S_{por}$ relationship for the investigated carbonate samples and in comparison with several sandstone data sets (modified after [9], right hand side).
figure_reason: Shows carbonate imaginary conductivity versus surface area departing from the sandstone trend, the key finding.
tldr: SIP measurements on 41 Egyptian limestones show polarization like sandstones, but imaginary conductivity does not follow sandstone surface-area trends, so permeability predictions are biased.
summary: Spectral induced polarization is well established for sandstones, but its transfer to carbonates is untested. The authors measured 41 late Cretaceous chalky limestone samples from seven shallow wells in the Tushka area, Egypt, using multi-salinity SIP and Debye decomposition. Four phase-spectrum curve types were found, occurring randomly and unrelated to the three microfacies associations. Real and imaginary surface conductivity correlate linearly at 1 Hz (slope 0.019 for carbonates versus 0.042 for sandstones; R² 0.853 and 0.911). Imaginary conductivity did not follow the sandstone trend with N2-derived specific surface area (11 to 400 1/µm) and was about two orders of magnitude lower than expected. Permeability predicted from Debye parameters was overestimated by one order of magnitude at or below 0.1 mD, fit from 0.1 to 10 mD, and underestimated above 10 mD.
abstract: With impedance spectroscopy (IS), or spectral induced polarization (SIP) as it is also termed, the complex electrical conductivity of rocks is measured over a wide frequency range, typically ranging from 1 mHz to 10 kHz. Originally developed for the exploration of ore deposits, today's SIP measurements are used for a wide range of applications within geophysics. On the field scale, this technique is (e.g.) used to characterize the hydraulics of shallow aquifers, to assess pollution for environmental protection purposes, or even to support archaeological investigations. On the laboratory scale, SIP is commonly used for the investigation of electric rock properties for clastic reservoir rocks in general, and sandstones in particular. The frequency dependent complex electrical conductivity gives access to an advanced rock characterization, even beyond a more qualitative and in most cases general pore space characterization. Parameters particularly relevant for hydraulics – as for example specific internal surface, (dominant) pore size and permeability – can be estimated. Some robust empirical relations between induced polarization (IP) parameters and petrophysical parameters (BET surface, surface conductivity, cation exchange capacity) have been identified for sandstones and sandy material. However, for carbonates these relations do not seem to work and some of the resulting parameters show a quite different behavior. More systematic studies are needed to evaluate the potential of SIP for characterization of carbonates. The authors would like to show the results of a first case study on a limestone sample set originating from shallow wells of the Tushka area, south Western Desert, Egypt. Besides basic principles of SIP in general, adaptation of theory and evaluation technique will be highlighted in particular.

title: On Diverse Applications of Qemscan in the Oil and Gas Industry (and Beyond)
caption: Fig. 4. Classification based on the standard library (left), and a slightly modified SIP file where content of Fe and Mg is slightly higher but where the Al and Si content is lower.
figure_reason: Shows standard library versus modified SIP, the key result of reducing 70% unclassified pixels in shale.
tldr: Shows how QEMScan automated mineralogy, with tailored SIP libraries and careful sample preparation, minimizes unclassified pixels across carbonates, shales, cuttings, salts and archaeological samples.
summary: QEMScan maps 2D mineralogy by matching low-count X-ray spectra to a species identification protocol (SIP) library, and unclassified pixels (0-70% in the authors' experience) are the main concern. Using an FEI 650F with two EDS detectors at 15 keV, the authors examine thin sections and polished epoxy-mounted cuttings. Carbonate thin sections needed no SIP changes, giving about 0.18% unclassified pixels and 21-26% porosity consistent with MICP. A shale case with 70% unclassified pixels under the standard library was resolved by slightly raising Fe and Mg and lowering Al and Si acceptance in the SIP. Careful cleaning and polishing sharply reduced unclassified pixels in cuttings. Further applications include amorphous salt precipitate identification, porosity versus depth, particle size distributions and pottery provenance.
abstract: Automated mineralogy identification, as implemented through QEMScan (quantitative evaluation of minerals by scanning electron microscopy) by FEI, is gaining wide spread interest in oil and gas applications. The experimental part of the method is focused on collection of the x-rays that are emitted when a surface is exposed to an electron gun of a scanning electron microscope. QEMScan distinguishes itself by the library, the so-called SIP (species identification protocol) file, and by the search routine that converts the collected X-rays to mineral maps. Extensive development of the SIP is necessary to encompass the, often complex, composition of e.g. clays encountered in many oil reservoirs. We present examples of such a development of SIP files relevant to specific clays and clastic rich carbonate reservoirs and show in studies of a broad spectrum of clays that often it is only very small changes in the acceptable amount of $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ , $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ and $\text{Al}^{3+}$ that will lead to a positive identification. In pure carbonate settings the QEMScan methodology is primarily a source of 2D porosity as information on trace elements (concentrations less than 1 %) is not available from the low count spectra that form the basis for SIP identification. Our focus on bringing down the number of unclassified minerals in an image is not only achieved through SIP development; the sample preparation has also turned out to be of outmost importance. We present the optimal sample preparation conditions herein. The samples we are focusing on are plugs polished into thin sections and cuttings molded into epoxy and polished. Quite apart from reservoir rocks we have employed QEMScan to assist in mapping out trade routes from ancient pottery found in Qatar, whale shark skin and other relics such as sand from cemented dunes. We will assess the capabilities through these case studies and examples from field operations and demonstrate the powerful image processing in the Iexplorer package by also presenting grain size distributions and lithology results.

title: Explicit Correlation of the Steady-State Two-Phase Relative Permeability Functions of Porous Media with the Local Flow Rates
caption: Figure 2. Soil column-averaged water saturation and water / oil relative permeability as functions of Caw at various values of Cao (κ=1.0).
figure_reason: Shows column-averaged saturation and relative permeabilities versus Ca_w at various Ca_o, the main fitted results.
tldr: Steady-state oil/water flow data from a sand column and 2-D networks are fitted with power laws in water and oil capillary numbers, showing relative permeability depends on flow rates.
summary: Relative permeability in field-scale simulation is usually treated as a function of local saturation only, ignoring dependence on local flow rates. Steady-state oil/water coinjection tests were run on a 30 cm long, 5 cm diameter sand column (k=25 D, porosity 0.42, viscosity ratio 1.0) with pressure transducers and ring electrodes; segment water saturation was derived from resistivity via Archie's law (n=1.06). Saturation and oil and water relative permeability were fitted as power functions of water and oil capillary numbers, and earlier 2-D glass-etched network data (viscosity ratios 1.45 and 3.35) were treated the same way. Water relative permeability was mainly sensitive to Ca_w and oil relative permeability to Ca_o, with weak cross effects attributed to viscous coupling and wetting films. The authors conclude that local relative permeability should be a function of local flow rates of both fluids rather than saturation.
abstract: Steady-state two-phase flow experiments are performed on a sand column equipped with two differential pressure transducers and six ring electrodes to measure the pressure drop across each phase, and the electrical resistance across five successive segments of the column. The electrical resistance is converted to water saturation by Archie equation. The results are analyzed by considering the water saturation and oil / water relative permeability as power functions of water and oil capillary numbers which are regarded as independent variables. Results from earlier visualization studies on 2-D glass-etched pore networks are analyzed in a similar manner to correlate the estimated parameters of power functions with the 2-phase flow regimes. The new explicit relationships of relative permeabilities and water saturation with oil and water capillary numbers set the bases for a new conceptualization of the two-phase flow at reservoir-scale where the mobility of the fluids is decoupled from saturation and becomes a non-linear function of the local flow rates.

title: Numerical Investigation of the Dependence of Residual Oil Saturation on Geometry, Wettability, Initial Oil Saturation and Porosity
caption: Fig. 1. Residual oil saturation as function of contact angle for a Berea sample.
figure_reason: Shows Sor versus contact angle for Berea, with fitted curves and comparison to network models and experiments.
tldr: Lattice Boltzmann simulations on micro-CT digital sandstones show how residual oil depends on geometry, contact angle, initial saturation and porosity, matching published experiments and the Land correlation.
summary: The paper uses a GPU-parallelized two-phase lattice Boltzmann solver on micro-CT images of Berea, Bentheimer and eight Fontainebleau sandstones to simulate primary drainage and imbibition with a digital porous plate. For zero contact angle, simulated Sor for Berea (45.4%) and Bentheimer (36.6%) falls between published plug and mini-plug values. Fontainebleau Sor is higher than the one plug measurement but agrees with more systematic published data. Sor decreases with weaker water wetness, dropping rapidly near a 60 degree contact angle, and follows the Land correlation with initial oil saturation. For Fontainebleau, Sor decreases with porosity and correlates with the pore body to throat size ratio (correlation coefficients 0.94 and 0.93).
abstract: Oil/water drainage and imbibition processes have been numerically investigated for a set of sandstone samples including Berea, Fontainebleau and Bentheimer samples. The pore scale structures of the sandstone samples have been digitized using high resolution micro-CT. The primary drainage and first imbibition process was computed numerically with a pore scale simulator which is based on a two-phase lattice Boltzmann method including interactions with the solid pore wall. To cope with the large computational demand the simulations were run on high performance computing hardware. Residual oil saturation after imbibition Sor was calculated for complete water-wet rock surface (zero water contact angle) to investigate the effect of different geometries represented by different kinds of sandstone samples. The calculated results compare well with recently published high quality laboratory data. The change of Sor with variation of the degree of water wettability was investigated for the samples by changing the water contact angle on the pore surface. It was found that the weaker water wetness results in smaller Sor which is consistent with the experimental investigations recently reported in literature. The dependence of Sor on the initial oil saturation was calculated and the results are consistent with experimental data and published correlations. Finally the residual oil was calculated for several Fontainebleau samples with different porosity. It was found that Sor decreases with porosity and the variation of Sor agrees well with published experimental data.

title: Multi-Scale Permeability Trends Using Digital Rock Physics
caption: Figure 3: Fine scale porosity – permeability trend (relation) created by the digital subdivision process for two artificial rocks (left). Upscale permeability of large scale artificial plugs generated by combining the fine scale rocks (right). Porosity increase following the direction of the arrows.
figure_reason: Shows fine-scale porosity-permeability trends and upscaled permeability results for the artificial rocks, with and without porosity variation.
tldr: A digital rock workflow upscales porosity-permeability trends from building blocks to larger scales; on artificial rocks, ignoring within-block variation gives 20-42% permeability error.
summary: Heterogeneous reservoir rocks span many length scales, so petrophysical properties must be upscaled consistently. The authors propose a workflow that identifies rock-fabric building blocks from coarse-scale images, derives porosity-permeability and formation factor trends from 50-300 digital subdivisions of high-resolution images of each block, and populates the coarse image voxels with these trends. Flow is solved with the Stokes equation at the finest scale and the Brinkman-extended Darcy equation at larger scales, using GPU lattice Boltzmann simulation. Tests used two artificial 1 mm fine samples (power-law exponents 3.2 and 7.3) combined into 25 mm models in series, parallel and diagonal arrangements. Ignoring porosity variation within blocks overpredicted permeability by 20% (parallel), 29% (diagonal) and 42% (series). The workflow can generate trends with up to two orders of magnitude fewer samples than laboratory methods, and the authors recommend pairing it with a few laboratory measurements.
abstract: We proposed a workflow for porosity-permeability and porosity-formation factor trends upscaling based on digital rock physics. The workflow consists of three important parts that integrate information between coarse and fine scales. First, building blocks, i.e., unique rock fabrics presented in a reservoir rock sample, are extracted based on statistics derived from a 3D coarse scale image. Next, one or several high resolution 3D fine scale images of all building blocks are used to derive their fine scale permeability and formation factor trends. Then the fine scale trends of each individual building block are used to populate each voxel of the 3D coarse scale image with permeability and electrical conductivity. This procedure takes into account the variation of conductivity and permeability within a building block on the coarser scale and frees us from applying only a single value in each building block. This procedure can be applied recursively to cover the whole range, e.g. from nano-CT images up to the whole core CT-images. The capability of the workflow is demonstrated first with artificially generated rocks. The results suggest up to 50% error in permeability prediction when the workflow is not integrated. Then, a study of a real reservoir rock with the proposed workflow opens a new level of understanding of permeability from building blocks up to plug scale. The accuracy of the workflow is confirmed with a laboratory measurement.

title: Mobility of Nanofluids in Porous Media
caption: Figure 1. (a) Pattern of 2-D pore network. (b) Injection of liposome suspension at residual n- $C_{12}$ saturation.
figure_reason: Shows the 2-D pore network pattern and liposome injection at residual n-C12 saturation, the experimental setup.
tldr: Calcein-loaded nanoliposomes were injected through a glass-etched pore network at residual n-C12; most effluent liposomes stayed intact, so lower flow rates, concentrations and softer membranes are needed.
summary: The work explores nanoliposomes as carriers to deliver nanoparticles such as nZVI to hydrophobic NAPL ganglia in porous media for in situ remediation. DSPC:cholesterol (2:1) liposomes of 150 nm encapsulating calcein were prepared at 1 mg/ml in PBS (latency 96.4%). They were injected at 0.025 mL/min into a 2-D glass-etched pore network (porosity 0.65, permeability 19.6 Da) at residual n-C12 saturation. Calcein release was tracked by effluent fluorescence latency measured before and after Triton X-100 addition. Latency dropped to about 27-50% in the first 10 minutes, then returned to 90-96% at late times, indicating only a small fraction of liposomes released their content. The authors conclude that lower flow rates, smaller liposome concentrations and softer membranes are needed to promote membrane disruption.
abstract: The overall scientific objective of the proposed work is a deeper understanding of nanoparticles (NP) activity and fate in porous media (e.g. stability, transport, agglomeration, reactivity) so that the in situ pollutant remediation efficiency in soils and groundwater is maximized, and the most efficient nanofluids for pilot-scale studies are suggested. Stable nanofluids will be developed by modifying the surface of zero valent iron nanoparticles (nZVI) with adequately selected coatings (e.g. polyelectrolytes) that optimize their colloidal stability, longevity and reactivity. Protocols are developed for the encapsulation of nanofluids in nanoliposomes which are commonly used in drug delivery and are now tested as vehicles for the safe delivery of NP throughout the pore space of a glass-etched pore network and hydrophobic pollutant (n-C12) targeting. In order to assess the capacity of nanoliposomes to break-up and release NP during their travel through the porous medium, a fluorescent dye (calcein) is entrapped in liposomes and its concentration breakthrough curves are measured under varying conditions of flow velocity, liposome concentration, and liposome membrane integrity.

title: Environmental Impacts of CO2 Leakages from Storage Sites on the Quality of Potable Groundwater of Shallow Aquifers
caption: Figure 3. Measurement of the transient response of metal cation concentration in the effluent of (a) 2-phase column, (b) 1-phase column.
figure_reason: Shows effluent metal concentrations with CO2 versus control, the main evidence of metal mobilization.
tldr: CO2-water co-injection through metal-coated sand columns shows pH drop to ~3.6 mobilizes most metals except Fe; inverse modeling gives equilibrium and kinetic desorption parameters.
summary: CO2 leakage from storage sites into shallow aquifers may mobilize trace metals and degrade potable groundwater. Well-sorted silica sand (125-250 µm) was coated with eight metals (Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn, Cd) by pH-controlled precipitation and packed into two 0.4 m columns, one with CO2/water co-injection and one water-only control. Effluent pH fell to about 3.6 and conductivity rose; Mn, Ni, Cu, Zn and Co release increased by orders of magnitude relative to the control, Cr moderately, and Cd dissolved readily in both. Fe stayed bound as goethite. SEM-EDS, XPS and AAS of the sand before and after confirmed these trends. Inverse modeling with a two-site sorption model gave desorption rate ranking Cd > Cu > Ni ~ Cr > Mn ~ Zn and partition coefficients consistent with batch tests.
abstract: Leakages of CO2 from storage sites to shallow aquifers could have adverse impacts on the groundwater quality. A well-sorted silica sand is modified by the pH-controlled precipitation of eight metals (Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn, Cd). Carbon dioxide and water are co-injected in a fixed-bed column packed with the modified sand, and the metal concentration in effluent is measured with atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS). Mineralogical analysis of sand before and after the flow tests is done by Scanning Electron Microscopy – X-ray Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (SEM-EDS), X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS), and AAS. Due to continuous CO2 dissolution, the release of Mn, Ni, Cu, Zn, Co is enhanced profoundly, the release of Cr increases moderately, the Cd dissolution accelerates, whereas Fe is strongly bonded as goethite and does not dissolve almost at all. The inverse modeling of the flow test results with a model coupling the mass-transfer with reactive processes enables us to quantify the dynamics of metal release in terms of equilibrium and kinetic desorption parameters, estimated under realistic flow conditions.

title: Three Dimensional Characterization of Matrix Acidizing by X-Ray Computed Tomography
caption: Figure 1: 3D CT showing wormhole geometry and acid etching features in 3D resulting from acid treatment of (a) Sample 1(b) Sample 2 (c) Sample 3 and (d) Sample 4.
figure_reason: 3-D CT renderings show wormhole geometry and etching for all four samples, the main result.
tldr: Pre- and post-acid CT scans of four Swan Hills carbonate plugs are registered and subtracted to map 3-D wormholes and quantify porosity change of about 1.7-2.8%.
summary: Wormhole characterization in matrix acidizing is usually one-dimensional, so the authors used medical CT to image wormholes in 3-D. Four 1.5-inch Swan Hills carbonate plugs (82-88% calcite, 10-15% dolomite) were scanned before and after acid flooding with HCl or reaction-safe acid at 85°C, 2500 psi confining and 500 psi backpressure. Post-treatment images were rigidly registered to pre-treatment images and subtracted, and the difference was calibrated to calcite grayscale to give porosity change. Each sample developed one dominant tortuous wormhole with branching. Wormhole tortuosity was 1.39-1.63 and porosity change 1.71-2.75%. Permeability rose from 0.02-2.52 mD to 54-1600 mD. Wormholes preferentially followed voxels with grayscale below the calcite mode of about 3200, indicating calcite-void mixtures.
abstract: Tight carbonate reservoir rocks are increasingly being acidized to etch flow paths and create wormhole networks to increase oil and gas productivity. Dissolution of rocks along the path of acid flow has been shown to increase porosity and permeability thereby leading to enhanced recovery. Understanding the geometry of wormholes and quantifying the amount of dissolution will enable better and more efficient acid stimulation programs in both acid fracturing and in matrix acidizing. Many reported experiments characterize wormholes in one-dimension (1-D) and provide little information on the change in porosity as a function of pore volume and pore structure. However, fluid flow in a reservoir is a three-dimensional (3-D) phenomenon, and directly related to pore connectivity. Understanding the geometry of wormholes in 3-D as well as quantifying the change in rock porosity as a result of acid treatment is pertinent for the design of effective acid stimulation. This paper presents the visualization of worm holes in 3-D and quantification of the change in porosity using X-ray computed tomography. Four carbonate plug samples were scanned before and after acid treatment, with the posttreatment images being spatially registered to the pre-treatment images. Subtracting the registered post-treatment images from corresponding pre-treatment images provided sets of difference images which illustrated the geometry of the generated worm holes in 3-D. The change in porosity of the plugs were determined by calibrating the grayscale values of the difference images against the grayscale values of the sample matrix from the preacid treatment images. Results demonstrate the formation of a single principal wormhole from top to bottom in all four samples. The wormholes were non- linear but followed a tortuous path which can be correlated with compositional and structural changes in the samples. The change in porosity ranges between 1% and 3%. The datasets from this work provide a qualitative and quantitative assessment of acid treatment and can be used as inputs into acid stimulation models to produce better results.

title: Operational Efficiency Map & Flow Characterization for Steady-State Two- Phase Flows in Porous Media
caption: Figure 1: Data sets of relative permeability for ‘oil’ ( $\square$ ) & ‘water’ ( $\Delta$ ) and energy utilization index, $f_{EU}$ , ( $\circ$ ) against o/w flow ratio, $r$ , pertaining to (a) favorable and (b) unfavorable viscosity ratios, $\kappa$ , and different cores. The vertical dotted line (in black) indicates the critical flowrate, $r_x$ , for which the relative permeabilities of oil & wat
figure_reason: Shows relative permeability and energy utilization index versus flow ratio, revealing the efficiency maximum for favorable and unfavorable viscosity ratios.
tldr: Reconstructing 83 published relative permeability diagrams into energy utilization curves shows optimum operating conditions, yielding a universal efficiency map and a capillary- versus viscous-dominated flow criterion.
summary: Steady-state relative permeability data are usually plotted against saturation, which hides how efficiently the flow uses pumping energy. The paper transforms 83 published relative permeability data sets (19 studies; real cores, glass and virtual networks) into energy utilization index (oil produced per power dissipated) versus oil/water flow ratio. Every case shows a local maximum, the optimum operating condition, consistent with DeProF theory. An asymptotic optimum flow ratio of 1/sqrt(kappa) and maximum efficiency 1/(1+sqrt(kappa))^2 are derived for high capillary number. The results are combined into a universal operational efficiency map over Ca and r, and a scaling form for the optimum locus is used to define a critical capillary number separating capillary- from viscous-dominated flow.
abstract: An extended retrospective examination of relative permeability diagrams revealed a latent characteristic of steady-state two-phase flows in porous media, the existence of optimum operating conditions, i.e. conditions whereby process efficiency -considered in terms of oil produced per kW dissipated in pumps- attains locally maximum values. A total number of 83 published relative permeability diagrams, pertaining to a variety of flow conditions and core types, were reconstructed into energy utilization diagrams, providing ample evidence on the existence of optimum operating conditions and showing a universal trend that can be cast into an operational efficiency map over the domain of the independent variables, the capillary number, Ca, and the oil/water flow ratio, $r$ . This universal map demarcates the overall efficiency of steady-state two-phase flow processes in terms of pertinent system parameters. The map not only provides a guiding tool for designing more efficient processes, but can be used for the normative characterization of two-phase flows as to the predominance of capillary or viscous effects. The proposed concept is based on the existence of a unique locus of optimum operating conditions, $r^*(\text{Ca})$ , for each particular oil-water-p.m. system.

title: Calibration of digital pore scale models
caption: Figure 2 Comparison of DRA and experimentally derived porosity and permeability data
figure_reason: Shows digital versus experimental porosity and permeability, the first calibration step for the model.
tldr: Digital rock models of a North Sea sandstone are calibrated against routine porosity, permeability and MICP data, with multi-scale micro-porosity models bringing simulated Swi to 14% versus 12% measured.
summary: Digital rock analysis struggles with samples containing sub-resolution micro-porosity, so models must be calibrated against experimental data. A 5 mm mini-plug from the Norwegian continental shelf was imaged by micro-CT at 3 µm/voxel, segmented into pores, micro-porous phase and solid, and compared with routine porosity and permeability; dry/wet registration gave total porosity in good agreement. Single-scale network drainage simulations matched MICP only at entry pressure and high water saturation, reaching just 0.6 bar and about 50% Sw, versus about 12% Sw at 5 bar experimentally. Process-based models of kaolinite aggregates, built from BSEM data and validated against MCT and FIB-SEM networks, represented the micro-porous phase and were upscaled with steady-state methods. The integrated multi-scale model gave Swi of 14% versus 12% experimental, and the authors stress comparing digital and experimental data at identical scales and calibrating wettability from fluid distributions.
abstract: Digital rock analyses (DRA) has advanced to a level that makes it a very valuable supplement to traditional SCAL. Currently the main challenges are related to handling samples with a large fraction of micro-porosity, with heterogeneities on several scales, and to assign wetting properties correctly. In this paper, we describe how models generated using DRA are calibrated against robust petrophysical and geological data in order to verify digitally derived reservoir properties. Once the verified pore scale data is established the models can be applied to analyses of many different scenarios. The first step of verification of the digital representation is comparison with experimentally derived porosity and absolute permeability data. The absolute permeability is mainly governed by the larger pore throats of the pore space, and therefore less sensitive to image resolution. The total porosity can be correctly calculated by including micro-porosity, which in this context means pores smaller than the resolution of the discretized image-acquisitions. Hence a multiscale imaging approach is required to capture the continuous distribution of pore-sizes of a given rock sample. The digital representation of the pore space is compared to mercury injection capillary pressure data for quality control and verification. In some cases several digital models, representing different parts of the samples must be combined to achieve a representative model. In order to calculate realistic multiphase flow properties, information of the wetting characteristics is essential. For example, both the fraction and distribution of oil wet surfaces and contact angles are subject to changes. Advanced imaging techniques for spatial mapping of fluids in combination with laboratory data can be used to narrow the possible range of these parameters.

title: Carbonate Reservoir Rock Typing and the Link Between Routine Core Analysis and Special Core Analysis
caption: Figure 2: A/ Cross plot of RQI-CPORz color-coded by the five FZI reservoir rock types. Each regression line is a porosity-permeability transform and corresponds to a unique RRT. The intercept of the unit slope line with $CPORz=1$ corresponds to a FZI mean unique parameter for a RRT. B/ Cross plot of permeability (Kair) versus porosity (CPOR) color-coded by FZI reservoir rock types.
figure_reason: Shows RQI versus normalized porosity and permeability-porosity plots colored by the five FZI rock types, the core result.
tldr: Fifty carbonate samples are classified into five FZI rock types, with the number of types set by a self-organizing map, and linked to MICP, Archie m and SWir.
summary: The paper classifies fifty carbonate samples (22 limestones, 28 dolostones) from over fifty reservoirs into reservoir rock types using the Flow Zone Index method. An unsupervised self-organizing map using MICP parameters, porosity, permeability and water saturation indicates that five clusters best describe the data. FZI ranges are defined from key permeability values at 10% porosity (0.1, 1, 10, 50, 100 mD), giving five RRTs with FZI boundaries from 0.3 to about 12 µm. Higher FZI rock types show sharper capillary pressure transition zones, lower entry pressure and larger pore throats. Archie m ranges 1.8-2.5, decreasing with porosity in limestones and increasing in dolostones, which is explained by pore texture. Each RRT has its own RQI-porosity regression, and mean SWir ranges from 35% in RRT1 to 13% in RRT5.
abstract: Reservoir Rock Types (RRT) are critical factors in reservoir characterization and are one of the most challenging subjects in carbonate reservoirs. One goal of reservoir rock typing is to identify hydraulic units that have similar fluid flow properties. Amaefule [1] introduced a method to determine rock types based on the Flow Zone Index (FZI), which represents a mean pore throat size in microns, derived from the Kozeny-Carmen equations [2,3] with porosity and permeability as the key parameters. The flow zone index (FZI) technique is applied in this study on a data set of cores from over fifty carbonate reservoirs throughout the world, and representing a wide range of porosity, permeability and mineralogy. This paper describes a new concept with the definition of FZI ranges using key permeabilities at 10%. The fifty carbonates rocks are classified in five FZI reservoir rock types showing similar reservoir properties such as Capillary Pressure, Irreducible Water Saturation and Residual Archie's Parameters m.

title: The application of IR spectroscopy for real time mineralogical analyses of core and cuttings
caption: Figure 5: Profiling the negative impact of illite on permeability
figure_reason: Shows the inverse relationship between illite content and permeability, the key reservoir-quality result.
tldr: Shows how the SpecCam SWIR imaging spectrometer maps clays, carbonates and hydrocarbons continuously on core and cuttings, with North Sea case studies on correlation and permeability.
summary: Point-sampling mineral methods such as XRD and point counting are slow, need sample preparation and give sparse data. The paper describes the SpecCam short-wave infrared (1.3-2.5 micron) imaging reflectance spectrometer, which scans core and cuttings at 0.5 mm pixels (about 28,000 points per metre) without preparation. It is semi-quantitative, cannot identify quartz, and cannot be calibrated for hydrocarbons. In a Northern North Sea field, data from 11 wells distinguished dickite-bearing Formation B from formations T and N, which differed in illite type, and this led to revised formation boundaries and well correlations. In a Rotliegend gas reservoir, illite content was inversely related to permeability (about 6 mD above the clay baffle). Below the baffle permeability averaged about 0.1 mD with lower illite, which suggests chlorite is responsible. Hydrocarbon spectral features in Brent core also revealed compositional differences across a calcite seal.
abstract: The use of infrared spectroscopy for mineral identification dates back several decades, and is complementary to other mineral analytical techniques, such as XRD or point counting. However, a major drawback of these techniques, including the older point sampling IR spectrometers, is that they require sample preparation – an expense in both time and money. More importantly they cannot provide continuous quantitative mineralogical data to aid reservoir characterisation. The most recent advance in IR spectroscopy is the use of real-time imaging reflectance spectrometers. These are non-contact and non-destructive, and acquire continuous mineral data from core and cuttings in a detailed image format. The first of these introduced to the UK oil industry in 2008 is the portable SpecCam imaging spectrometer. The current SpecCam design accurately discriminates and quantifies different polytypes of the swelling and non-swelling clays, carbonates and sulphates. In addition, the spatial distribution of solid and liquid hydrocarbons and their compositional changes can be mapped. Thus, the SpecCam can provide a unique, spatially-detailed image dataset that allows the impact of clay and carbonate mineralogies on hydrocarbon distribution and permeabilities to be studied and assessed. Several examples from the Brent and other North Sea Formations are presented. The SpecCam technology addresses 3 major limitations of point sampling techniques – low productivity, inability to show detailed spatial distribution of minerals and low data density. These limitations have direct implications for the reliability and use of these data. The SpecCam imaging IR spectrometer can overcome these limitations and generate near continuous data, which provides a link between point sampling methods and continuous logs.

title: Pore Characterization of Reservoir Rocks by Integrating SCAL and Petrography
caption: Figure 3. T2 relaxation curves of glauconitic sandstones at fully saturated states, desaturated states and Pore throat size distributions by MICP.
figure_reason: Shows bi-modal T2 at saturated and desaturated states alongside MICP throat distributions for glauconitic sandstones.
tldr: Integrates NMR T2, MICP and petrography on chalk and sandstones, showing matching pore distributions and deriving apparent T2 relaxivities of 9.29 µm/s for calcite and about 5.0 µm/s for glauconite.
summary: Pore structure controls petrophysical and flow properties, so the authors combined lab NMR T2, high-pressure MICP, thin section and SEM on chalk, glauconitic, kaolinitic/illitic shaly and salt-cemented sandstones. NMR was run at full and irreducible saturation (after ultracentrifuge) on a 2.04 MHz MARAN-2; MICP went up to 60,000 psia on trims of the same plugs. T2 distributions generally resembled MICP pore-throat distributions. Chalk showed narrow uni-modal distributions, giving a calcite relaxivity of 9.29 µm/s. Glauconitic sandstones were bi-modal, with intra-grain glauconite pores of about 20-50 nm and apparent relaxivity of about 5.0 µm/s. Kaolinitic sandstones were less clearly bi-modal, illitic ones were ill-defined uni-modal with tails, and the salt-cemented sandstone with grain-boundary fractures gave a broad T2 distribution versus triple-peaked MICP.
abstract: Pores of reservoir rock control its petrophysical and flow properties and are of importance for hydrocarbon exploration and development. We present an integrated study on pore characterization on several typical reservoir rocks, namely glauconitic sandstone, shaly sandstone, salt-cemented sandstone and chalk using SCAL data from lab nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), high pressure mercury injection (MICP) and by SEM and thin section. NMR T2 relaxation distributions reveal patterns similar to pore-throat size distributions obtained from the (MICP) tests carried out on the same samples. Chalk samples show narrow uni-modal pores, while the glauconitic sandstones and some shaly sandstones with pore filling kaolinite show bi-modal pore size distribution. Thin section and SEM observations show that intra-granular and inter-granular pores of glauconite, kaolinite etc. correspond to micro-pores seen in NMR T2 relaxation and MICP data. The abundance of clay indicated by petrography correlates to the amplitudes of the micropore peaks of NMR T2 relaxation and pore throat size distributions in sandstone samples. Uniform intergranular pores result from fine-grained broken coccolith grains explain the narrow mono-modal T2 relaxation and pore throat distributions in chalk. The apparent T2 relaxativities for glauconite and calcite are derived.

title: Effects of Wettability and Interfacial Tension on the Distribution of Residual Oil on the Pore Scale After Water Flooding
caption: Figure 4: Capillary desaturation curve of WW case (right). Cumulative cluster length distribution of WW oil clusters (dotted line) and IW oil clusters (Solid line).
figure_reason: Shows capillary desaturation curve and cluster length distributions contrasting water-wet and intermediate-wet cases.
tldr: Lattice-Boltzmann waterflood simulations on a micro-CT sandstone model show IFT and wettability control residual oil saturation and cluster distribution, even at intermediate IFT values.
summary: The study examines how wettability and oil-water interfacial tension affect residual oil after waterflooding at the pore scale. A multiphase lattice-Boltzmann solver was run on a 400^3 voxel (5 µm) digital model of Tarbert sandstone from micro-CT. Eight cases were simulated: contact angles of 30° (water wet) and 70° (intermediate wet), each with IFT of 40, 10, 1 and 0.1 mN/m, injecting about 3 PV of water. In water-wet cases Sor is similar at 40 and 10 mN/m and drops markedly at 1 and 0.1 mN/m, with little tail production after breakthrough and a cutoff in cluster length indicating snap-off trapping. Intermediate-wet cases show lower Sor, significant tail production, longer and more connected clusters, and cluster size distributions that change little with IFT.
abstract: We have performed numerical pore scale simulations and detailed analysis of the resulting configuration, distribution and amount of residual oil in the pore space of a reservoir rock during and after water-flooding. The simulations were performed using a multiphase lattice-Boltzmann (LB) solver on a digital rock model which had been constructed from high-resolution 3D micro-CT images. The micro-CT images were acquired from a sandstone reservoir. Using this type of simulation it is possible to follow and map fluid configurations during displacement in detail, and thus analyze and quantify the fluid distributions inside the pores. In our study we looked at both water wet and intermediate wet conditions, each of which was simulated for four different interfacial tensions, giving rise to a total of eight simulated cases. In each case the final residual oil configuration was recorded after injecting approximately three pore volumes (PV) of water. We then identified individual oil clusters and computed statistics such as cluster length and size distribution. The results indicated that the interfacial tension has a clear impact on the residual oil saturation and configuration. This applies even for intermediate values of interfacial tension, i.e. not only ultra-low values. There are also clear differences between the water wet and the intermediate wet cases in terms of the production curves and oil cluster distribution.

title: Dual Pore Network Model of Electrical Resistivity for
caption: Figure 4.Estaillades carbonate sample: (left) resistivity index vs. saturation, (right) pore entry diameter distribution.
figure_reason: Shows D-PNM fit of resistivity index and pore entry size distribution for Estaillades, with upward-curving non-Archie trend.
tldr: A dual pore network model with variably connected matrix and vug porosity reproduces non-Archie resistivity index behavior and capillary pressure of Estaillades and Lavoux carbonates.
summary: Carbonates with micro- and macro-porosity deviate from Archie's law, and the cause is not fully quantified. The authors use a dual pore network model (D-PNM) on a 32x32x32 cubic-cell lattice. Each cell has an unresolved matrix conducting in parallel with a resolved vug-and-throat system, and the whole network is solved by renormalization during quasi-static drainage. The model was fitted to resistivity index, capillary pressure and formation factor data for Estaillades and Lavoux carbonates. Estaillades is represented by percolating vugs in non-percolating matrix, which gives an upward-curving resistivity index at Sw below about 0.4. Lavoux has both networks percolating, which levels off the resistivity index at low saturation. Parametric studies show strong sensitivity to the fraction of cells with no matrix, the size ratio R, the connectivity exponent and the vug size distribution, so the model can reproduce the documented types of non-Archie trends.
abstract: We develop a model which explains the non-Archie behavior of carbonate rocks with multi-scale structure. Non-Archie behavior in such rocks is qualitatively related to the degree of connectedness (percolation) of different water fractions, namely water residing in networks comprising pores of very disparate scales (micro-porosity and macro-porosity). To this end, we investigate here a previously reported dual pore network model (D-PNM) which allows for heterogeneous matrix (micro-porosity) properties and variably-connected macro-porosity. By varying the relative amounts, geometric properties and degree of connectedness of microporosity and macro-porosity, we are able to stylistically reproduce all documented deviations of the resistivity index from Archie behavior.

title: Application Specific Computed Tomography Systems for Core Analysis
caption: Figure 2: 3D visualisation of firn with open pores from 35 m depth, 56 µm voxel size
figure_reason: 3D image of firn with open pores shows the scanner's porosity and pore-structure results.
tldr: Describes two custom X-ray CT systems: a helical micro-CT for 1 m ice cores down to 3.5 µm voxels, and a 1 s/slice gantry CT for dynamic liquid flow.
summary: The paper presents two purpose-built CT systems from Fraunhofer EZRT. The ice core scanner uses a 8000 x 4000 pixel detector and helical fly-by scanning to image 1 m long, 10 cm diameter cores at 12.5 µm voxel size, with full-core data at 50 µm acquired in under two hours and interior regions of interest down to 3.5 µm. It is operated at -15 °C and used to quantify porosity and pore size; firn in the upper 100 m has about 30% porosity with connected pores, while deeper ice has closed pores and decreasing porosity with depth. The gantry CT uses a rotating source and line detector to scan a single slice in 1 s at below 100 µm resolution for columns of 50-300 mm diameter and up to 1000 m length. A binned live reconstruction guides the experiment, and full-resolution projections are stored for later reconstruction. The authors conclude that these problems could not be solved with standard commercial systems.
abstract: Fraunhofer Development Center X-ray Technology EZRT develops procedures and systems for non-destructive testing, covering the whole range of industrial X-ray imaging from beam generation across material interaction, simulation, X-ray detection, image processing and automatic evaluation. Special focus is put on quantitative evaluation, differentiation and visualization of material and density distributions, surface extraction of complex parts for dimensional measurement and material characterization. In this contribution we present two application specific X-ray computed tomography (CT) systems we designed according to customer needs: a micro-CT system for the automated analysis of ice cores and a gantry-CT system for time-resolved monitoring in process engineering. The ice core CT-scanner developed for the Alfred-Wegener-Institute for Polar Research is able to scan cores with a length of 1 m and with a diameter of 10 cm with a high spatial resolution (12,5 $\mu$ m voxel size) using helical CT, enabled by a specially developed X-ray detector with a large active area and high resolution (8000 x 4000, 32Mpixels). Using a multi-resolution region-of-interest method it is possible to scan the center of the core with a resolution of down to 3.5 $\mu$ m voxel size. Analyses include porosity, pore sizes and their distribution. The gantry-CT system developed for the Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering of the University of Erlangen (Germany) is designed for the observation of viscous liquid solutions transiting each other or flowing through upright standing cylindrical pillars with internal structures. This allows surveying the process of liquid propagation within each other or within the internal structure. The size of these columns can range from 50 to 300 mm in diameter and up to 1000 mm in length. One single slice can be scanned and reconstructed in 1 second at a spatial resolution below 100 $\mu$ m. This online reconstruction allows ts the observation of the dynamic process by the user in near real time and also enables one to react to different states of the experiment in time. After the acquisition, deep analysis of any region of interest is possible by reconstruction of the automatically stored high-resolution projections. The setup of these CT-systems, implemented methods for data acquisition and analysis and results will be presented.

title: Posibilities of Quantitative Evaluation of Polish Shale-Gas Rocks Petrophysical and Geomechanical Parameters by Laboratory Analytical Methods and Well Logs Interpretation
caption: Figure 2 Shift of a) velocities from logs and laboratory data shown with b) mineral composition. The biggest discrepancy was observed for samples with high clay or carbonates content. An assembly of c) Vp vs porosity data for separated formations (f1-f7) for geophysical and laboratory data at reservoir temperature or HTHP conditions (HP) – observed trends are similar to literature data [5]
figure_reason: Shows shift between log and laboratory velocities, mineral composition, and Vp versus porosity trends for formations.
tldr: Integrates mercury porosimetry, gas adsorption, FIB-SEM, mineralogy, MHz acoustic velocities and triaxial tests on Polish shale cores to calibrate XRMI electrofacies and predict geomechanical parameters.
summary: The study addresses calibrating well logs against core data for Polish shale gas, since future wells may supply only side-wall cores or cuttings. About 450 m of Silurian and Ordovician Baltic basin core was characterized by mercury porosimetry, argon adsorption, FIB-SEM, QEMSCAN mineral mapping, FTIR, XRD, triaxial tests and MHz P and S wave velocities at reservoir temperature and HTHP. Four XRMI electrofacies (tuffites, siltstones, shales, calcareous) were defined and tied to laboratory data. FIB-SEM porosity and mineralogy correlated well with mercury porosimetry and XRD. Pores fell into three groups (>8 µm, 100–1000 nm, <10 nm), the smallest linked to organic matter and possibly explaining velocity discrepancies. Laboratory velocities differ from log velocities, most for clay- or carbonate-rich samples, with the shift negligible under HTHP.
