abstract: The composition of minerals combined with the knowledge about 3D distribution of minerals in the reservoir rock (petrological analysis – detritical grains, cements) and petrophysics translates into its mechanical properties and behavior after application of technologies like hydraulic fracturing - aiming at creating or enhancing the pore connectivity and permeability and therefore enabling the hydrocarbons flow into a well bore. Moreover, the issue regarding resolution improvement is particularly important in the aspect of unconventional hydrocarbon exploration mainly due to reservoir rock revealing micro pore structure. In the paper, comprehensive study of the Polish shale rock formation samples microstructure, combined with mineralogy and its correlation with acoustic velocities measured in frequency domain of MHz, in order to determine and integrate better data input to geomechanical reservoir model was shown. Mercury intrusion, helium pycnometry, argon adsorption are commonly used analytical methods to determine the pore space characteristics in rock samples. Recently FIB/SEM technique, for pore space morphology and its 3D reconstruction, appeared as a method more and more frequently used by leading companies providing geological services. In this work we would like to show integration of nitrogen adsorption method with FIB/SEM data which seems to be powerful tool for shale rock extensive examination. All above mentioned methods should also lead to development of shale rock physical model explaining better well log data for example in terms of X-tended Range Micro Imager (XRMI) results interpretation.

title: An Integrated Approach to Compute Physical Properties of Core Samples
caption: Figure 4 Brine saturation with 60%, 40% and 20%. Air intrudes from bottom to top.
figure_reason: Shows simulated air intrusion at three brine saturations, illustrating the pore morphology drainage result.
tldr: Five FFT-based and adaptive solvers compute permeability, conductivity, tortuosity, drainage, resistivity index and elasticity on one segmented Berea micro-CT image, including under compression, showing strong sensitivity to small compressions.
summary: The paper presents an integrated digital rock workflow that computes many effective properties on the same segmented 3D image of Berea sandstone. Methods include SIMPLE-FFT and LIR-tree Stokes solvers, Explicit Jump for conduction and diffusion, pore morphology for drainage, and Lippmann-Schwinger for elasticity. Permeability falls from 107 mD to 18.8 mD with 3% compression, while the formation factor rises from 25.2 to 77, and tortuosity also increases. Permeability decreases quadratically and the other properties linearly with compression. The LIR solver needed 14 h and 5.8 GB versus 26.4 h and 40.5 GB for SIMPLE-FFT on a 16-core, 128 GB machine. Computed permeabilities fall in the middle of the benchmark range.
abstract: We introduce an integrated approach to compute physical properties of core samples on very large micro-CT images and nano-CT images. On the same segmented 3d image, a whole range of diverse effective material properties are computed. In addition, we study the behavior of these material properties under compression. Where data is available, our methods are compared to other state of the art solvers on a large complex Berea sandstone dataset [1]. Our newest flow solver is 3-6 times faster than the fastest solver in [2], scales well for up to 32 processors and promises to solve 3k by 3k by 3k domains in as little as 180GB of memory. An additional benefit of this work is that the reported range of permeabilities from the benchmark [2] can be narrowed down significantly.

title: Capillary Pressure and Relative Permeability Assessment on Whole Core Samples from a Giant Middle Eastern Carbonate Reservoir Utilizing Digital Rock Physics
caption: Figure 3 Whole core DRP imbibition Kr with Lab Kr from samples/composites in the same formation layer
figure_reason: Compares DRP imbibition Kr with lab data for each whole core, showing the match and the stylolite discrepancy.
tldr: Digital rock physics computed drainage Pc and Kr on four carbonate whole cores and their composite, matching lab plug data and showing the stylolite layer does not block flow.
summary: Four whole cores from two Middle Eastern carbonate formations, separated by a stylolite layer, were evaluated with digital rock physics (DRP) for primary drainage Pc and imbibition and secondary drainage Kr. The workflow used whole core dual-energy CT, multi-scale micro-CT (down to 0.5 µm) and nano-CT (0.05 µm) imaging, Lattice Boltzmann Pc computation, and up-scaling to whole core and composite scale. Results were compared blind against conventional lab data on plugs and plug composites. Pc and Kr matched reasonably, except the stylolite imbibition Krw, where the lab end point was 0.68 against 0.26 from DRP. Composite simulations with two stylolite wettability scenarios (contact angle 130° versus 30°) showed the stylolite layer is permeable and does not act as a barrier. The lab work took six years, whereas the DRP took six months.
abstract: Digital Rock Physics (DRP) has significantly evolved in the last few years and added invaluable contributions in improving core characterization and in providing high quality advanced SCAL measurements, emphasized through various studies/papers (SCA-2012-03 Kalam et al). This paper represents a unique DRP SCAL study that includes primary drainage capillary pressure (Pc) as part of Swi establishment and relative permeability (Kr) measurements done on four whole core (WC) samples from two different carbonate formations with a stylolite layer in between. The aim of the study was to evaluate how DRP results would compare with physical SCAL measurements done – on the same WC samples as a composite, as well as on plug samples from the same formations/layers – in a leading international core analysis lab in USA. The DRP results were up-scaled to the individual WC level and compared with the SCAL results from the corresponding layers. The DRP technology in this study also provided the capability of up-scaling the results to the WC composite which was used by the lab to assess the effect of the stylolite layer on the water flood. The comparison showed excellent matches between the physical and DRP-derived Pc and Kr data. The paper outlines the DRP methods used to determine the SCAL properties of the three formations. The laboratory measurements of SCAL properties took six years while the DRP work that followed blindly (without any knowledge of the laboratory results) was completed in six months. This demonstrates the effectiveness of the DRP technology in providing high quality SCAL data in a timely fashion regardless of sample size. Impact of possible wettability changes and sensitivities on one of the WC composite constituent component was also easily established unlike the high risk laboratory tests. This is the first water-oil displacement validation study results on reservoir whole cores of four inch diameter at full reservoir conditions using DRP. INTRODUCTIONThe DRP SCAL was initiated on four carbonate WC samples from Middle East. The work included computations of primary drainage Pc to insure that pore geometry (pore throat size distribution) has been properly captured for representative initial water saturation (Swi) establishment; in addition to Kr measurements (imbibition and secondary drainage). All data were up-scaled to the individual WC scale as well as to the composite WC scale. The WC composite included the four WC samples and was designed to resemble the vertical geological structure of the reservoir (WC1 came from top carbonate formation, WC2 came from the stylolite layer, WC3 & WC4 came from the bottom carbonate formation). Figure 1 shows schematic illustration of the WC composite. The DRP program followed a previous conventional SCAL study that included Pc and Kr measurements on individual plugs and plug composites from the same reservoir layers in addition to a WC water flood on the same WC composite. ![](_page_1_Diagram_15.jpeg) Figure 1 Schematic illustration of the whole core composite

title: Understanding Imbibition Data in Complex Carbonate Rock Types
caption: Figure 5 Kro and Krw curves for all six samples from field A and field B. Corey exponents varying with different rock types and permeability.
figure_reason: Shows Kro and Krw imbibition curves for all six rock types, the main experimental result.
tldr: Steady-state imbibition Kr on mixed-wet Abu Dhabi carbonates varies systematically with rock type and permeability; Corey exponent differences reflect pore geometry, not wettability.
summary: Carbonate SCAL relative permeability data are often left unexplained because rock types are poorly characterized. Sixteen 1.5-inch plugs from two Abu Dhabi fields were typed using thin sections, MICP pore-throat size distributions, poro-perm and CT images. Steady-state imbibition Kr was measured at full reservoir conditions with live fluids after three weeks of aging, with in-situ saturation monitoring and simulation history matching. Higher-permeability samples gave higher Krw, lower Kro, higher Krwmax and higher average Sor, with larger differences between average and inlet Sor. Corey exponents rose for no (e.g. 4.7 at 392 mD vs 2.9 at 0.81 mD) and fell for nw (1.8 vs 4.3). Because capillary pressure showed similar mixed- to oil-wet behaviour in all samples, these trends are attributed to pore geometry, accessibility and surface area rather than wettability.
abstract: Carbonate rocks are complex in their structures and pore geometries and often exhibit a real problem in their classification and behavior. Many petrophysical and fluid flow properties remain unexplained and perhaps uncertain because of improper characterization of the reservoir rock. In this research, carbonate rock types were defined from thin-sections based on the structure of the rock together with its pore types. The rock type classifications were improved by incorporating pore-throat size distribution and poro-perm information, and high resolution plug CT images. This would lead to a robust rock typing scheme that should facilitate the understanding of heterogeneity effects on reservoir flow properties. Laboratory-measured imbibition relative permeability ( $K_r$ ) data were determined on reservoir core samples in two “mixed-wet” carbonate fields from the Middle East region. The $K_r$ curves were explained based on the identified rock types and gave consistent trends. The $K_r$ curves were fitted with Corey exponents, and yielded high “no” and low “nw” for the higher permeability samples, which may be wrongly interpreted as more oil-wet rocks compared to the lower permeability samples. The variations in $K_r$ curves with the different rock types were argued to be the result of different rock structures and pore geometries that control pore accessibility and surface area. The obtained $K_{rw}$ and $K_{ro}$ data from steady state experiments are not abundant in the literature and hence should serve as an important piece of information in mixed-wet carbonate reservoirs with varying rock types.

title: Displacement Mechanisms in Single and Multiple Pores from Lattice Boltzmann Simulations and Micro-Fluidic Experiments
caption: Figure 9: Steady-state relative permeability simulation for drainage (left) and imbibition (right) in direct comparison with experimental data (Ramstad et al., 2012) for Bentheimer sandstone.
figure_reason: Compares LB drainage and imbibition relative permeability with experimental data for Bentheimer, the main multi-pore result.
tldr: Colour-gradient lattice Boltzmann simulations match micro-model drainage and imbibition experiments, showing dynamic imbibition follows local geometry, and reproduce Bentheimer capillary pressure and relative permeability reasonably well.
summary: The paper validates a colour-gradient lattice Boltzmann (LB) code against PMMA micro-model experiments (decane/air, 50 µm etch depth) in single pore junctions, including a Berea thin-section pore. Quasi-static drainage and imbibition follow Young-Laplace filling rules, and snap-off bubbles are captured. In dynamic spontaneous imbibition, the nearest channel fills first rather than the narrowest, so local geometry controls the filling sequence, and LB reproduces this. The code is then applied to a Bentheimer micro-CT image (512x256x256 voxels, 4.9 µm, porosity 0.234, LB permeability 4755 mD). Computed capillary pressure (Swi about 7%) and drainage/imbibition relative permeabilities agree generally with experiment. Pc at irreducible saturation is underpredicted and non-wetting relative permeability and the imbibition endpoint are overpredicted, attributed to resolution and periodic boundary conditions.
abstract: We have studied displacement mechanisms of immiscible fluids in micro-fluidic models with designs ranging from simple pore junctions to a pore from a rock thin section. For this purpose, we have developed a lattice-Boltzmann (LB) model to study the multi-phase flow processes in direct comparison with experimental results in purpose-built micro-fluidic geometries. In this paper, we will focus on the LB simulations, in direct comparison with the experiments. First, we study quasi-static drainage and imbibition processes in single junctions and observe good agreement with Young-Laplace capillary filling rules. However, for dynamic imbibition, we observe that the sequence of pore filling is determined by local pore geometry rather than the Young-Laplace law. The LB simulation results are in good agreement with the micro-fluidic experimental observations. Having validated the validity of the LB code for displacement mechanisms in single pores, we extend our calculations to multiple-pore displacement in pore space images of real rock samples obtained from micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) scans. We observe capillary pressure and relative permeability curves in good agreement with experiments.

title: Macro to Nano: Correlative X-Ray and Electron Microscopy for Multi-Length Scale Characterization of Geomaterials
caption: Figure 4 (a) 700nm resolution 3D XRM rendering of a volume-of-interest rich in pyrite framboids. (b) 3D FIB-SEM tomography partial data rendering co-embedded in the same region, showing enhanced detail of the matching pyrite framboids at 20nm voxel resolution.
figure_reason: Shows the correlation of 700 nm XRM and 20 nm FIB-SEM volumes in the same region, the paper's core approach.
tldr: Correlates X-ray microscopy, FIB-SEM, SEM-EDS and bulk lab analyses on a mudstone to characterize minerals, organics and nanopores across length scales for digital rock physics.
summary: Mudrocks are hierarchically porous, and no single technique captures a representative volume. A Pelplin Green Claystones (Wenlock) mudstone sample was analyzed with XRD, FTIR, ICP, mercury porosimetry and argon/nitrogen adsorption, plus XRM at 5 µm, 2 µm and 700 nm voxels, FIB-SEM tomography at 20 nm, and SEM-EDS mineral mapping at ~1 µm. XRD gave 23.7% quartz, 11.5% carbonates and 50.1% clay; XRM showed ~11% higher-Z minerals and located them in 3D. XRM guided selection of a FIB-SEM volume (65×25×22.5 µm) rich in organics and pyrite framboids, where most pores were below 100 nm, consistent with gas adsorption pore size distributions. Large-area SEM gave TOC of 2.4% versus 1.8% from FIB-SEM, and SEM-EDS gave 74% local clay versus 50% by XRD, reflecting local variation in an organic-rich area.
abstract: It is well established that rocks contain a hierarchically-porous microstructure, with transport phenomena occurring over a range of length scales. Equally, it has been demonstrated that there is no single technique capable of capturing a representative volume for a single rock type, or, more appropriately, of a single formation. Here, we demonstrate the union of XRM and FIB-SEM for a comprehensive 3D dataset, representing a porous rock microstructure as viewed across multiple length scales. Further, we show how this information is complementary to traditional laboratory analysis which can provide detailed chemical, mineral, and pore size information, but with spatial averaging over relevant length scales. Using both sets of information gives a more complete understanding of one formation, representing a new paradigm in digital rock analysis.

title: Simulation of Counter-current Spontaneous Imbibition in a Simple Porous Medium Using Lattice-Boltzmann
caption: Figure 10: Pressure at the dead end of the tubes
figure_reason: Compares simulated dead-end pressure with experimental results, showing the model's main shortcoming.
tldr: A single-component multiphase Shan-Chen lattice Boltzmann model reproduces the imbibition front of Unsal et al.'s glass-and-rod experiments but fails to capture capillary-instability snap-off or dead-end pressure behavior.
summary: The study uses a 3D (D3Q15) single-component multiphase Shan-Chen lattice Boltzmann model with a Carnahan-Starling equation of state to simulate counter-current spontaneous imbibition in the glass-and-rod model of Unsal et al. The model was tested stepwise: phase separation (density ratio limited to about 50 versus about 800 for air-water because of divergence), contact angle control through solid-fluid interaction strength, and capillary rise with gravity. Bubble snap-off never occurred from capillary instability alone and was only obtained by adding a buoyancy force. The final 60×80×2000 lattice reproduced the front shape, but the dead-end vapor pressure rose monotonically instead of dropping during bubble formation and jumping at snap-off as observed experimentally. The authors attribute this to the Shan-Chen model's inability to simulate capillary instability.
abstract: The lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) has been increasingly implemented for complicated fluid flow and transport phenomena. In this paper the LBM method is utilized to simulate the experimental results of counter current spontaneous imbibition. The single component multiphase Shan-Chen model was used to model the antiparticle forces. It was observed in the results that the developed model, although it simulated the shape of the front, it did not lead to bubble snap-off caused by capillary instability and the pressure at the dead end of the imbibition channel does not match with experimental results.

title: Developing a Model to Estimate Permeability from Other Petrophysical Data
caption: Figure 2 – Ratio of predicted to measured permebility comparison of the four methods
figure_reason: Shows ratio of predicted to measured permeability for all four methods, highlighting REV consistency versus scatter of others.
tldr: Compares four permeability prediction methods (Timur-Coates, SDR, Swanson, REV) on 11 sandstone and carbonate plugs using NMR and MIP data; MIP-based methods predicted better.
summary: Permeability prediction from pore structure data was tested on 11 plugs (5 sandstones, 6 carbonates) spanning 0.45–7000 mD and 9.3–28.8% porosity. NMR T2 at 100% brine saturation, high-pressure mercury injection and steady-state gas permeability (Klinkenberg and Forchheimer corrected) were measured. Four models were compared: Timur-Coates, SDR, Swanson and the REV method based on Purcell's model modified with electrical data. Swanson's method predicted best but only after fitting C and m to the data. The REV method needs no fitting parameters and was the most consistent, though samples 4 and 10 (vugular limestones) fell outside the factor-of-2 trust region. Overall MIP-based methods outperformed NMR-based ones, and Timur-Coates outperformed SDR.
abstract: Reservoir characterization has always been an important step in production planning and permeability is one of the most important transport properties of a rock to be determined. A new method to predict permeability of rocks, based on capillary pressure principles, has been published recently and proved to make reliable predictions. The method uses Mercury Injection Porosimetry (MIP) data as well as electrical data to find effective diameter and length for the REVs, which are used to simulate pore structure. Although mercury injection porosimetry has proven to be an effective means of determining pore structure, it only sees pore throats, missing pore bodies – pore bodies also contribute to fluid flow. On the other hand, NMR data is believed to give good estimates of pore size distribution, provided that proper relaxivity values are selected and proper experimental conditions are used. Methods exist to predict permeability from NMR data. A suite of 11 samples has been tested to further study permeability prediction methods using both NMR and MIP data. Samples were chosen in an attempt to cover a wide range of porosity, permeability and rock type. Having both NMR and MICP data helps the further understanding of pore structure, giving us information about both pore throat and pore body distributions. This paper will demonstrate that by combining NMR and MIP data, permeability predictions are improved over predictions using either method independently.

title: Investigation of Pore Structure Impact on the Mobilization of Trapped Oil by Surfactant Injection
caption: Figure 3 Comparison of capillary desaturation curves plotted using in (a) $S_{or}^*$ vs $N_t$ and in (b) $S_{or}^*$ vs $N_t^*$ . Data are collected on the macro plug experiments for the four sandstones ( $S_{or}^*$ is the residual oil saturation normalized by the residual oil saturation after the first waterflood, see [3] for the experimental details).
figure_reason: Shows CDCs for four sandstones before and after rescaling, demonstrating curve collapse with the modified trapping number.
tldr: Surfactant and brine floods on four water-wet sandstones show capillary desaturation curves collapse with a permeability- and pore-size-based trapping number, enabling CDC prediction from micro-CT ganglia statistics.
summary: The paper examines how pore structure controls mobilization of trapped oil and the capillary desaturation curve (CDC). Brine and surfactant floods were run on Berea, Bentheimer, Fontainebleau and Clashach sandstones after n-decane drainage, with CT-scan measurement of residual oil and micro-CT (3 µm) of mini-plugs at residual oil. Normalized pressure gradient versus trapping number shows three regimes, with slope 1, ~0.5 at intermediate trapping numbers, and 1 again, resembling steady-state two-phase flow. A modified trapping number N_t* = N_t<r>²/(K_a K_rw) collapses the four CDCs, with critical value near 10⁻² and full desaturation near 1. The CDC computed from the volume-weighted cumulative ganglion size distribution at the mini-plug scale matches macro-plug CDCs well.
abstract: We report an experimental investigation on the effect of flooding parameters, fluid interfacial properties and rock structure on the CDC and on the water relative permeability. Experiments were performed on a set of water-wet sandstones with different petrophysical properties. CT-scan imaging was used to accurately measure the mean residual oil saturation at the macro plug scale. Oil ganglia size distribution as well as pore scale geometrical properties were quantified using high resolution micro-CT images. Results showed that the CDC depends on the pore structure; however rescaling using the relative permeability allows the curves to collapse. We show that for intermediate trapping numbers, a strong dependence of the water relative permeability on the latter can be noticed. Finally, we propose a new method to predict CDC based on structural properties determined experimentally by micro-CT.

title: Experimental Studies of Low Salinity Water Flooding and Interpretation by Simulation for Low Permeability Sandstone
caption: Fig. 6 Relative permeability curves of low salinity and high salinity waterflooding (reservoir, oil-wet)
figure_reason: Relative permeability curves for reservoir core show shift from oil-wet to water-wet under low salinity flooding.
tldr: Coreflood tests and ECLIPSE history matching on low permeability Chang Qing sandstones show low salinity flooding yields about 10% extra recovery in oil-wet reservoir cores versus 3.4% in water-wet outcrop.
summary: The study examines how rock wettability controls the low salinity waterflood (LSWF) response in low permeability sandstone, using Chang Qing reservoir cores (23.6% clay, oil-wet) and quartz-rich outcrop cores (4.2% clay, water-wet). Corefloods were run at 65°C in secondary and tertiary modes with formation brine (57,114 mg/L) and ten-fold diluted brine. Relative permeability curves were derived by history matching production and pressure drop with ECLIPSE 100. The water-wet outcrop showed piston-like displacement, about 50% OOIP recovery with high salinity brine, only 3.4% extra from LSWF and no real wettability change. The oil-wet reservoir core produced oil over longer periods, gained about 10% OOIP from LSWF, and its relative permeability curves shifted toward water-wet. Capillary pressure had minor influence on the history match.
abstract: The screening criteria of low salinity water flooding (LSWF) are proposed and implemented in sandstone. However, the recovery of low salinity water flooding is not always obtained from both coreflood experiments and oil fields. The mechanisms behind enhanced oil recovery of LSWF are still uncertain. The objective of this study is to present an investigation on the relationship between rock wettability and oil recovery with LSWF in secondary and tertiary mode in low permeability sandstones. Coreflood experiments were implemented at 65℃ with two different wettabilities ranging from water- to oil-wet. Relative permeability curves were obtained by history matching experimental production and differential pressure across cores at core scale through ECLIPSE 100. Piston-like displacement was found for high salinity water flooding as the core was water-wet, while the oil was produced over much longer periods for high salinity water flooding as the core was oil-wet. The estimated relative permeability curves showed that the reservoir core which was oil-wet in the high salinity became water-wet during the low salinity flooding. Nevertheless, there is no fundamental wettability change for the water-wet rock after low salinity flooding under tertiary mode. Additionally, 10.0% incremental recovery was achieved by LSWF for the oil-wet rock under tertiary mode. But only 3.4% recovery growth was observed by LSWF for the water-wet rock. It is concluded that the low salinity water altered the wetting state of the reservoir core. The application of LSWF in oil-wet reservior has more potential to enhance oil recovery. The incremental recovery can be explained by the interactions between the rock type, oil components, formation brine and injected brines.

title: An Overview of the Low and High Temperature Water-Oil Relative Permeability for Oil Sands from Different Formations in Western Canada
caption: Figure 1. Longitudinal and axial CT scan images of oil sand core suitable for testing: A - better quality; B – lower quality (a) and oil sand non suitable for testing (b)
figure_reason: CT scans showing how better and lower quality oil sand cores are selected for testing.
tldr: Overview of a 30-year database of low and high temperature water-oil relative permeability and steamflood tests on Western Canadian oil sands, showing suppressed water curves and thermal damage in lower quality sands.
summary: The paper reviews 30 years of low and high temperature water-oil relative permeability and steamflood tests on oil sands from the McMurray, Wabiskaw, Clearwater and Grand Rapids formations. It describes core preservation (frozen at -27°C), CT-based sample selection, petrographic characterization, and a test procedure of baseline oil permeability, waterflood, hot waterflood at increasing temperature, steamflood and post-test Dean Stark. Water endpoint relative permeability is strongly suppressed, typically 0.01-0.1, owing to the high bitumen viscosity and unfavourable mobility ratio. Residual oil saturation is lower in steamflood than in waterflood at the same temperature, and brine permeability generally rises with temperature, most below 100°C. Higher quality McMurray shows no formation damage, whereas lower quality McMurray and Grand Rapids show reduced water endpoint permeability, attributed to wettability change and clay alteration such as kaolinite to smectite.
abstract: Relative permeability is a dominant factor controlling the multiphase flow in porous media and strongly affects the ultimate economics of production operations. Although a variety of correlations to predict relative permeability are available, the experimental results provide the most accurate method of relative permeability determination. Specific thermal processes have best application in certain types of geological settings, net and gross pay conditions, vertical permeability condition and for rock and fluid with certain characteristics. Accurate determination of relative permeability is a key factor for reservoir simulation. Canada ranks third in the world in terms of oil reserves most of which in oil sands. As deposits of conventional oil and availability of better quality oil sands continue to decline, the industry is moving towards development of more challenging reservoirs, including lower quality oil sands. The paper presents an overview of the low and high temperature water-oil relative permeability data for oil sands from different formations in Western Canada collected during the period of 30 years.

title: In-Situ Monitoring for Process in Conglomerate Using CT Technology
caption: Figure 5 The Oil Saturation Decrement of S2 during 2nd Waterflooding
figure_reason: Shows oil saturation decrement along S2 during second waterflooding, indicating flow only in previously formed pathways.
tldr: CT scanning monitored waterflooding and polymer flooding in two heterogeneous conglomerate cores, showing dominant channels blocked by polymer and suggesting high first-flood water cut and reduced polymer volume.
summary: Conglomerate reservoirs recover only about 45% by waterflooding because of strong heterogeneity, and the polymer EOR mechanism is unclear. Two Xinjiang conglomerate cores (S1: 27.8% porosity, 1419 mD air permeability; S2: 20.1%, 379 mD) were flooded with brine, then 0.7 PV polymer, then brine again, while a medical CT scanner tracked saturation profiles and reconstructed images. Water broke through early (about 0.125 PV), and dominant channels formed that produced nearly all oil after breakthrough. Polymer blocked these channels and mobilized oil bypassed in the first waterflood, but island-shaped residual oil remained. Total recovery was 66.3% for S1 (45.4% water, 19.9% polymer, 0% second water) and 60.9% for S2 (35.0%, 15.6%, 10.3%). The authors recommend a high water cut in the first waterflood, reduced polymer volume, and a second waterflood to push the polymer slug.
abstract: Traditionally, the waterflooding recovery for conglomerate reservoirs is only about 45% due to its intense heterogeneity. It has been proved that the polymer flooding can effectively improve the recovery up to 60%. However, the EOR mechanism for conglomerate remains unclear because of the lack of advanced technology. The traditional laboratory experimental methods can only collect inlet and outlet data, from which we cannot tell the situation inside the cores. In this study, the process of waterflooding and polymer flooding in conglomerate has been in-situ monitored by CT scanning system. By this method, the saturation profile along the core and the CT reconstructed images of core section during displacing process were obtained. It could be found that there are some dominant channels appearing due to the intense heterogeneity of conglomerate during the waterflooding; and in polymer flooding, the dominant channels can be blocked so that some remained oil can be produced. For conglomerate reservoir, 1st waterflooding should reach a water cut as high as possible so as to strength the slug effect of the polymer. Meanwhile the injection volume of polymer should be reduced, and the 2nd waterflooding should be used to push the polymer slug to produce oil.

title: The Toroidal Porous Plate: A New Method to Facilitate Waterflooding
caption: Figure 3. Receiving pump volumes versus normalised time ( $t'$ ) for primary drainage displacements in Berea sandstone and Indiana limestone where a finite volume is produced from the core-plug under the application of a constant capillary pressure. The time is normalised by dividing by the total duration of the displacement (20.2, 60.5 and 138.0 hours for experiments Berea 1 through 3, and 46.1,
figure_reason: Shows pump volume versus normalised time in drainage, demonstrating the plate blocks non-wetting phase and capillary equilibrium is reached.
tldr: A porous plate with a central hole sealed by o-rings lets primary drainage and waterflooding run in one cell without moving the core; tests confirm no leakage and effective bypass.
summary: Moving a core between primary drainage and imbibition apparatus can change saturations, core mass and phase composition, especially for CO2 at high pressure. The authors drilled a hole through a ceramic porous plate, sealed a central steel flow line with Viton o-rings, and fitted it in a modified Hassler cell. Drainage was run on three Berea and three Indiana limestone plugs with decane-brine and CO2-brine at 50-70 °C and 4.2-9 MPa. The plate stayed impervious to the non-wetting phase, with water production ceasing at capillary equilibrium, and withstood up to 5 bar capillary pressure. During waterflooding the pressure drop matched the core alone (50-300 mD effective permeability for Berea versus 125 µD for the plate), so the plate was bypassed. Maximum residual saturations were 0.366 for Berea and 0.237 for Indiana limestone; flow distribution channels on the plate face and in-situ saturation monitoring are suggested improvements.
abstract: We present a modified porous plate core flooding apparatus where the porous plate has a hole drilled through its centre resulting in a toroid shape similar to a British Polo peppermint, an American Life Savers candy, or a doughnut. The apparatus allows primary drainage and imbibition (water flood) flow sequences to take place sequentially, without the need to remove the sample. During primary drainage the modified porous plate behaves in the same way as a solid, unmodified, porous plate. The method used to isolate the water flood flow line passing through the centre of the porous plate is effective and the plate can withstand capillary pressures up to 5 bar. During water flooding the porous plate is effectively bypassed, with the pressure drop recorded consistent with that across the core-plug alone. We use this new apparatus to measure the relationship between initial and residual non-wetting phase saturations. Sandstone and carbonate rocks are investigated for both decane-brine and CO2-brine fluid systems at elevated temperatures and pressures. The challenges of effectively sealing the hole through the porous plate during drainage are discussed and additional suggestions for future improvements to the design are proposed.

title: Study of Tight Core Electrical Properties Measurement by Porous Plate
caption: Fig.5 The effect of the pore pressure on saturation exponent n
figure_reason: Directly compares saturation exponents with and without pore pressure, the key finding.
tldr: Gas displacement with pore pressure and a high-breakthrough porous plate gives better resistivity index measurements on tight sandstones; ignoring pore pressure overestimates saturation exponent by up to 0.64.
summary: Porous plate resistivity index measurements are difficult in tight cores because of small pores and uncertain saturation. Gas and oil displacement were compared on three cores (0.14-0.76 mD); gas displaced water in cores down to about 0.1 mD with much shorter equilibrium times, while oil did not. Four further cores (0.2-454 mD) were tested with and without 5 MPa pore pressure at equal effective stress; saturation exponents were lower with pore pressure, differing by up to 0.64 in tight cores versus 0.16 in high-permeability ones. An improved method uses a porous plate with 1,000 psi breakthrough pressure, constant-rate gas injection (0.00095 ml/min), and saturation calibrated by Quizix pump records and core weighing. On a tight Erdos Basin core (10.3% porosity, 0.15 mD) it gave n = 1.75 and reached a final water saturation of 42%.
abstract: Porous plate method faces some challenges in tight cores, for example, how to displace water in small pores and accurately determine saturation. In this paper, the method of tight core electrical properties measurement by porous plate is discussed. Firstly, we selected three tight cores saturated with brine to conduct desaturation by porous plate both with gas displacement and with oil displacement. The experimental results indicate that the lowest permeability of gas displacement is about 0.1 mD, which is lower than that of oil displacement. Moreover, the equilibrium time of the gas displacement in each step is much shorter than that of the oil displacement. Therefore, gas displacement is more suitable for tight core by porous plate. Secondly, we selected four other cores with permeability values between 0.28 mD and 454.21 mD, and measured their saturation exponents by porous plate gas displacement both with and without pore pressure. The experimental results show that the saturation exponents of the low permeability cores with pore pressure are smaller than that without pore pressure. The largest difference of the saturation exponent between two methods is up to 0.64. However, for high permeability cores, the effect of the pore pressure is negligible. Therefore, the pore pressure must be considered in electrical properties measurement of tight cores. Lastly, the method of electrical properties measurement by porous plate has been built; it uses gas to displace water in tight cores with pore pressure applied at the end of the core. In our experiments, a porous plate with maximum breakthrough pressure up to 1,000 psi was tested. Moreover, the method of water saturation calculation, when pore pressure is applied, is presented; it is based on Quizix pump automatic records and core weighing. The experimental results of tight sandstones from the Erdos Basin, China, show that the method can not only gain ideal resistivity index curves but can also reduce experiment time as possible as.

title: An Experimental Study of Irreducible Water Saturation Estabilishment
caption: Figure 2. The comparison of the irreducible water saturation obtained by the three methods and in-situ initial water saturation vs. air permeability
figure_reason: Compares irreducible water saturation from the three methods with in-situ saturation across permeability, showing the main result.
tldr: Compares porous plate, oil displacement and centrifuge methods for establishing irreducible water saturation against in-situ Karl Fischer data; oil displacement matches best, while the other two overestimate in low-permeability cores.
summary: Establishing irreducible water saturation affects relative permeability and other displacement tests, yet the porous plate, oil displacement and centrifuge methods give discrepant results. The authors tested 97 water-wet Shengli oilfield sandstone cores (1.1–1725 mD) with all three methods and compared them with in-situ initial water saturation from Karl Fischer titration of 293 closed-coring samples. Irreducible water saturation decreased with increasing permeability. Oil displacement matched in-situ saturation across the whole range. The air-brine porous plate method matched only above 100 mD, because its 200 psi entry pressure limits the capillary pressure available; deviations reached 26.8% against oil-brine porous plate for a 6.89 mD sample. Centrifuge results (maximum 60 psi equivalent) overestimated saturation across all permeabilities, especially in low-permeability samples.
abstract: Irreducible water saturation is one of the most important parameters to evaluate the reservoir reserves. To establish the irreducible water saturation in laboratory is a vital step to restore the core to its underground condition, which highly affects the results of relative permeability measurement and other displacement experiments. Three methods are usually taken in laboratory to establish the irreducible water saturation, porous plate method, oil displacement method and centrifugation method. However, a large amount of experimental data shows significant discrepancy among these methods, which arises the question that which method best represents the underground condition of the core. To answer this question, systematical comparison between the observations from the above methods and the original reservoir formation data shall be performed, whereas so far few studies on this topic has been reported. In this work, we carried out an experimental study of irreducible water saturation establishment by the methods mentioned above over hundreds of core sample from the same reservoir formation with air permeability range from 1.11mD to 1725mD. The result shows that, in general, for water-wet cores, the irreducible water saturation decreases with the increasing of the air permeability. The irreducible water saturation obtained by oil displacement method is close to the in-situ initial water saturation. So oil displacement technique is faster and easier way to set irreducible water saturation, it is convenient because the sample is mounted in the coreholder used later for the flooding process, be aware that capillary end-effect produces a non-uniform saturation profile. The irreducible water saturation from air-brine porous plate technique is over estimated for low permeability samples because limitation of the porous plate entry pressure. In centrifuge test, absence of high centrifuge speed or enough equivalent capillary pressure may result in higher saturation than the in-situ initial water saturation. Therefore, the irreducible water saturation data could become misleading.

title: A Case Study of Fluid Transport in Shale Crushed Samples: Experiment and Interpretation
caption: Figure 6 Fitting Results of Permeability Tests with CH4
figure_reason: Shows pulse-decay pressure fits for CH4, with separate early- and late-time permeabilities revealing dual-porosity behavior.
tldr: Pulse-decay tests on crushed Ordos shale, interpreted with a Knudsen diffusion and adsorption model supported by MD simulation, give nanodarcy permeabilities and indicate dual-porosity behavior.
summary: Shale matrix permeability is hard to measure, and crushed-sample pulse-decay tests need models that capture slip, transition flow and adsorption. The authors ran equilibrium MD of methane in a carbon slit pore (30x4x2 nm, 300 K, ~10 MPa), finding number density strongly enhanced near the wall while self-diffusion velocity stays flat. Triassic Ordos shale (porosity 12.58%, bulk density 2.13 g/cm3, MICP pore peaks near 9 nm and <3 nm) was crushed and tested with CH4 and CO2 after measuring Langmuir isotherms. Numerical fitting of pressure decay with a model including Knudsen correction and adsorption gave intrinsic permeabilities of 4.2 nD (early-time) and 1.8 nD (late-time) for CH4 and 3.9 nD for CO2. The two-stage CH4 decay that cannot be fitted with one permeability suggests dual-porosity behavior, not seen in CO2, which has higher apparent permeability.
abstract: Pulse-decay experiment performed on crushed samples has been shown to be a promising method for measuring matrix permeability of extremely low permeable formations, like shale reservoir, since it is much faster than the traditional transient tests performed on core plugs. Due to the fact that the flow of methane in the nanoscale shale matrix involves complex mechanisms, such as the transition flow or slip flow, the physical model plays a key role in reasonable interpretation of experimental data. The objective of this study is to measure the intrinsic permeability of crushed shale samples through pulsedecay experiment, interpret the data with a comprehensive model, including Knudsen diffusion as well as adsorption, and demonstrate the necessity of considering these effects from a new perspective based on molecular dynamics (MD) simulation. The MD simulation addresses the necessity of considering the diffusion and adsorption effects. A more accurate model to calculate shale permeability is applied. By using this model, a significant improvement in the modeling of nanoscale gas flow and interpretation of intrinsic permeability experimental data can be achieved. This study leads to the following findings: 1) the distribution of gas atoms number density across the nanopore is not uniform, but the gas atoms have the similar selfdiffusion velocity, thus a totally different mass flow rate and more complicated mechanisms may appear; 2) the diffusion effect and adsorption effect will change the flow regime and may even dominate the flow regime in ultra-tight porous media; 3) the comprehensive model can describe the flow behavior very well for most of the shale samples; 4) there may exist multi-porous media phenomenon in shale matrix.

title: The Scratch Test as a Mean to Derive High Resolution Rock Strength Profiles for Geomechanical and Petrophysical Evaluations
caption: Fig. 2: a): Strength profiles at high and low spatial resolution. b): Well log porosity and plug porosity measurements (marker colors indicate 3 different plugging series). c): Plug vs well log porosity cross-plot, the 3 colors correspond to the 3 plugging series shown in Fig.2. d) Evolution of with depth (zoom between 1704.8 and 1707.2 m). Red line for the mean of , blue bars for the standard dev
figure_reason: Shows heterogeneity mapping, plug versus log porosity mismatch, and the strength-ratio indicator guiding plug selection.
tldr: Continuous centimeter-scale scratch-test strength profiles map core heterogeneity, guide plug selection, and show strength-petrophysics correlations are not universal across wells or reservoirs.
summary: Plug and well-log measurements differ in resolution, and sparse plugging can produce misleading correlations between petrophysical properties. The scratch test traces a constant-depth groove on a core and records cutting forces averaged over 1 cm, giving Intrinsic Specific Energy equivalent to uniaxial compressive strength. Strength profiles at 5 cm and 50 cm resolution identify heterogeneous and homogeneous intervals, where plug-versus-log porosity mismatch is larger in the heterogeneous sections. A ratio of 50 cm to 5 cm averaged strength is proposed to guide plug selection. Strength correlations with porosity, permeability, sonic and density vary between rock types and between wells in the same reservoir, so they are not universal; within a facies they can yield high-resolution porosity and permeability profiles. Running the scratch test early in the core workflow supports probe permeability, photography, core-shift estimation, rock typing and geomechanical plug selection.
abstract: The scratch test was developed in the late 90's at the University of Minnesota as a simple, non-destructive, fast and robust rock testing technique, to provide a direct measure of the rock strength equivalent to the uniaxial compressive strength. It produces a high resolution profile of strength (with centimeter steps), revealing the distributions of small heterogeneity length scales along the core samples. In this paper we show (i) how the difference in resolution scales of plug and well log measurements, added to the discrete sampling of properties (plugging) could lead to a misinterpretation of apparent correlations between petrophysical properties, and (ii) how the early mapping of small heterogeneity length scales could reduce the uncertainty in the integration of core and wireline data. We show with some examples how rock strength profiles averaged to the relevant length scale could be correlated with other petrophysical properties measured both on core plugs or inferred from well logs. Finally, we discuss how planning the scratch test at an early stage in a data acquisition effort would open new perspectives for routine and special core analysis workflows.

title: NMR Petrophysics for Tight Oil Shale Enabled by Core Resaturation
caption: Fig.7. The $T_1$ - $T_2$ map of formation oil restaturated shale sample shows the movable oil in organic porosity (kerogen) between 1ms and 10ms in addition to the native sample response.
figure_reason: T1-T2 map of oil-resaturated shale showing separated peaks for injected oil in organic and inorganic porosity.
tldr: High-pressure resaturation of Eagle Ford shale cores with formation oil and brine, combined with 2D T1-T2 NMR, separates organic-pore oil, inorganic-pore oil, and bitumen/bound water.
summary: Fluid loss during core retrieval makes NMR on native shale cores unrepresentative of reservoir conditions. The authors built a high-pressure resaturation cell (up to 2,000 psi) and validated it on 4 nm Vycor glass, where NMR porosity (32.9-33.9) matched helium (about 31) and BET porosity (about 31.7). Lower Eagle Ford shale fragments were resaturated with 42° API formation oil and brine and measured by 2D T1-T2 NMR at 2 MHz. Re-injected oil in organic pores appears at T2 of 1-10 ms with T1/T2 of 3-8, oil in inorganic pores at T2 above 10 ms with T1/T2 of 1-2, and bitumen plus clay-bound water below 1.5 ms with T1/T2 of 6-15. Injected brine appears at T2 of 6-80 ms with T1/T2 of 1.3-2.5, so oil T1/T2 discriminates organic from inorganic pores better than water does.
abstract: Economic production from tight (organic) shale reservoirs is governed by the ability to position horizontal wells using the log and core data acquired from the vertical wells. The major factors that drive successful production from these wells include petrophysical properties such as porosity, permeability, wettability, hydrocarbon saturation, and pore pressure. Other factors include geo-mechanical attributes such as hydraulic fracture surface area plus fracture conductivity. Accurate measurements of these petrophysical properties are fundamental for improved performance from tight oil reservoirs. In this paper, we describe a novel methodology based on NMR relaxometry of hydrocarbon and water resaturated cores to determine the hydrocarbon saturations, wettability and porosity, and to determine accurate $T_2$ cut-offs. One caveat for NMR core analysis is the loss of fluid, including producible hydrocarbon, during core retrieval to the surface. This can lead to a porosity deficit compared to logs. In this paper, we introduce a high pressure fluid resaturation methodology, and demonstrate the effectiveness in saturating extremely hydrophilic Vycor porous glass, with pore sizes comparable to the smallest pores in shale (4 nm diameter), using hydrocarbons as the saturating fluid. Applying the same core resaturation methodology to tight-oil shale samples, we demonstrate how 2D NMR (Nuclear Magnetic Resonance) relaxometry experiments can then segregate the $T_2$ distribution into 3 separate components. The longest $T_2$ component—generally above 10 ms—can be clearly identified as fluids in intra-particle or inter-particle porosity. The fluids in this mixed-wet pore system exhibit $T_1/T_2$ ratios close to one, and constitute movable or producible fluid. The second component consists of the $T_2$ distribution from 1 ms to 10 ms. This contribution is mostly from the light oil in oil-wetting organic porosity exhibiting $T_1/T_2$ ratios between 3 and 6. We demonstrate that only a part of this oil is producible. The shortest $T_2$ component has values less than 1 ms, and constitutes the bound water and bitumen signal. Their $T_1/T_2$ ratios generally range from 4 to 8. ![](_page_1_Diagram_9.jpeg) Fig. 1. The high pressure shale resaturation setup used for this paper is shown. The formation fluid, either oil or brine, is re-injected back into twin shale samples after vacuum evacuation.

title: Determination of Two Phase Relative Permeability from Core Floods with Constant Pressure Boundaries
caption: Fig. 1. Comparison of Relative Permeabilities using the New Method and Jones and Roszelle
figure_reason: Shows the new method's relative permeability curves versus Jones and Roszelle, the paper's main result.
tldr: Presents an analytical interpretation method for unsteady-state relative permeability from constant-pressure core floods; re-interpreting published data gives higher oil relative permeability than the Jones and Roszelle method.
summary: Classical Buckley–Leverett/JBN interpretation assumes constant total flow rate, yet many core floods, especially gas floods, are run at constant pressure boundaries. The authors use a recent analytical solution of fractional flow theory with constant pressure boundaries, which gives total flux, saturation positions and the pressure profile as functions of time. Relative permeabilities follow from Darcy's law at breakthrough using the fractional flow, outlet saturation from mass balance, and pressure gradient from the analytical pressure profile, avoiding numerical differentiation for f'(S). They re-interpreted a published waterflood (ΔP 6.89×10^5 Pa, K 3.54×10^-14 m², porosity 0.215, Swc 0.35). Water relative permeability matched the Jones and Roszelle result, while oil relative permeability was larger and the frontal saturation differed. Experimental validation and heterogeneity effects remain future work.
abstract: Relative permeability is one of the key SCAL measurements in reservoir engineering. A precise method is presented in this paper to interpret displacement experiments of two immiscible phases and to determine relative permeabilities dynamically using constant pressure boundaries. This method is based on a novel generalization of the classical Buckley–Leverett fractional flow theory for constant pressure boundary conditions. Under constant pressure boundaries, flow rate is determined analytically as a function of time, as well as the pressure along the length of one-dimensional core. Based on the rigorous analytical results, the relative permeability can be calculated directly from the experimental data gathered in general unsteady-state methods with constant pressure boundaries. It is demonstrated that the new method does not contain errors associated with total flow rate not being constant, as opposed to previous methods. In fact, there is significant difference between oil relative permeability interpreted by a previous method and the new method.

title: Analysis of Pore Structure of Longmaxi Shale Using the Mercury Intrusion Porosimetry Technique
caption: Fig.3. Differential pore volume vs. pore radius of the tested samples
figure_reason: Differential pore volume vs radius shows mesopore peaks and the effects of grain size and hydration.
tldr: MIP on Longmaxi shale at varied grain sizes and hydration states shows 3-11 nm mesopores dominate structure, macropores dominate volume, and powdering distorts results.
summary: The study characterizes the pore structure of outcrop Longmaxi shale (TOC 2.5-3.5%, clay 15.7%, mostly illite) with mercury intrusion porosimetry. Samples were prepared as powder (<1 mm) and flakes of 1.6, 5.1 and 7.8 mm average diameter, plus one hydrated and oven-dried sample, with SEM and CT as supplements. Pore structure is dominated by 3-11 nm mesopores (peaks at 3, 4, 7, 11 nm), while total pore volume is mostly from macropores larger than 74 µm. Grain size has little effect on the curves except for the pulverized sample, which showed suppressed peaks but the highest porosity (4.2%); 2-8 mm grains are recommended. Hydration followed by oven-drying raised cumulative volume about 1.5 times and porosity 35% (2.3 to 3.1%), attributed to clay and organic matter shrinkage creating 3-4 nm pores. SEM and CT at the resolution used (13.3 µm voxels) could not resolve these features.
abstract: Understanding the pore structure of shale has gained prominence in the exploration of shale gas as a new important source of energy, since the relative permeability of either oil or water phase is largely dependent on it. The detailed characterization of pore structure is made possible with the advent of the mercury intrusion porosimetry (MIP) technique. The technique is based on the correlation of intrusion pressure of non-wetting fluid (mercury) with pore size, and therefore produces quantitative representation of pore structure in terms of pore size distribution. In this study, shale cores sampled in situ were prepared at different granular sizes and hydration states. Supplementary structural experimental tests such as SEM and CT are also conducted in order to reveal the internal surface structure of the cores in a relatively qualitative manner. Finally, technical issues of the application of MIP on shale samples are discussed, and the structural results derived from the three techniques are evaluated with respect to shale performance in recovery activities.

title: Mapping NMR T2 to Capillary Pressure
tldr: Differential NMR T2 distributions measured during stepwise centrifuge desaturation of a carbonate plug give pore body to throat size ratios of about 0.25-2.25.
summary: The paper tackles the difficulty of relating NMR T2 (pore body size) to capillary pressure (throat size). A water-saturated outcrop carbonate plug (1.5 in diameter, 2 in long) was desaturated by centrifuge in air in small pressure steps, with a T2 measurement at each step. Echo-decay data at consecutive pressures were subtracted in the time domain and inverted to give differential T2 distributions of the fluid produced at each step. Using a relaxivity of 20 μm/s, a cylindrical pore assumption and the Young-Laplace equation, the authors derived body-to-throat ratios of roughly 0.25-2.25. Values below 1 are unphysical, but a relaxivity above 7e-5 m/s would move all points into the physical region. Scatter is attributed to pores of similar size with different throats and vice versa, so results hold only on average.
abstract: Starting with a fully water saturated carbonate core plug we replaced the water content with air using small incremental capillary pressure steps. At each capillary pressure we measured the T2 distribution and calculated the differential T2 distribution. This process allows determination of the T2 components associated with the fraction of water that leaves the rock at each capillary pressure. The differential T2 spectra were converted to pore size while the pressure data was converted to the throat size and their ratio was calculated at each pressure differential. The results show pore size to throat size ratios on the order of 0.25-2.25. The scatter in the results was attributed to similar size pores which are connected to different throat sizes and different size pores which are connected to similar throat sizes.

title: Correlation Between Magnetic Properties and Permeability: Results from a New Case Study in the North Sea
caption: Figure 4.Slabbed core data: raw volumemagneticsusceptibility (left), and magnetically derived illite content (middle).The right profile shows the predicted (black diamonds) permeability in mD from the slabbed core, and the measuredKlinkenberg corrected air permeability values from the plugs in Figure 1.The predicted values were derived from theillite content above in conjunction with the regressio
figure_reason: Shows slabbed-core susceptibility, derived illite and predicted versus measured permeability profiles across the full interval.
tldr: Magnetic susceptibility on plugs and slabbed core from a North Sea shoreface reservoir gives illite content that correlates with permeability, matching an earlier field's relationship.
summary: The study tests whether magnetic susceptibility can predict clay content and permeability in a Jurassic North Sea shoreface reservoir, following earlier work on a different field. Susceptibility was measured over a 50.4 m interval on 1.5 x 3 inch plugs (Bartington MS2C coil) and on slabbed core at 10 cm spacing (MS2E probe). Illite content derived from susceptibility closely follows Klinkenberg-corrected air permeability, with a power-law crossplot R2 of 0.62. Applying the earlier field's illite-permeability relationship to these plugs also gave R2 = 0.62 between predicted and measured permeability. Slabbed-core probe profiles resemble the plug profiles and predicted permeability matches measured values in many intervals. Mismatches are attributed to other minerals such as calcite, kaolinite and chlorite, and to core heterogeneity and scale differences.
abstract: A new case study on a siliciclastic North Sea shoreface reservoir has shown correlations between magnetic susceptibility, paramagnetic clay content and permeability, consistent with previous work. The previous work looked at a shoreface reservoir in a different field and utilised conventional core plugs 1 inch diameter by 1.5 inches long. The new study has undertaken magnetic measurements at two different scales: probe sensor magnetic susceptibility (on the scale of a few millimetres) for high resolution measurements on slabbed core, and coil sensor magnetic susceptibility measurements on larger 1.5 inch diameter by 3 inch long plugs. The probe and plug magnetic measurements gave very similar profiles with depth within the same cored interval. The raw magnetic susceptibility measurements from the probe and plug data picked out the main reservoir intervals very well. The processed results showed strong correlations between magnetically derived illite content and permeability. Moreover, the correlations were very similar to those in the previously studied North Sea shoreface reservoir in a different field. The results suggest there may be specific relationships between magnetic susceptibility, clay content and permeability for this type of reservoir, and validate our previous suggestions that magnetic susceptibility measurements can rapidly and non-destructively predict key petrophysical parameters (clay content, permeability) at various scales on recent or historical core samples.

title: Determination of CO2 and H2S Influence on Mineralogical Composition and Petrophysical Parameters of Aquifer and Cap Rocks
caption: Fig. 5. Example changes in porosity on the stage of CO2 injection (100 days), and storage (20 ka) - a sandstone sample
figure_reason: Modeled porosity changes during CO2 injection and 20 ka storage, the key petrophysical result.
tldr: Autoclave experiments and geochemical modeling show CO2/H2S dissolve carbonates and form secondary minerals in aquifer and cap rocks, giving mineral trapping up to 1.9 kgCO2/m3.
summary: The study addresses how acid gases (CO2, H2S) alter mineralogy and porosity of aquifer sandstones and cap rock mudstones and marls from the Upper Silesian Coal Basin and the Jurassic Mikulov Formation. Samples were characterized by thin sections, XRD and mercury intrusion porosimetry, then reacted in autoclaves with brine and gas at 60–180 bar and 40–80°C for 40–75 days, and examined by SEM/EDX. Grain dissolution, strongest in carbonates, occurred in all samples. Dawsonite, iron sulfides, elemental sulfur, and gypsum/celestite formed as secondary phases. At 150 bar and 80°C, dry marl expelled water from clays and pyrite oxidized, while at 80 bar no effect was seen. Kinetic modeling in Geochemist's Workbench showed porosity rising during 100 days of injection and falling by several percentage points over 20,000 years. Mineral trapping capacity was 1.2–1.9 kgCO2/m3 for sandstones and 0.89–1.42 kgCO2/m3 for cap rocks, with solubility trapping above 4.0 kgCO2/m3 in high-porosity aquifers.
abstract: We designed and performed a comprehensive study, enabling the hydrochemical models, calibrated on the basis of experiments, considering the impact of acid gases: CO2 and H2S on deep hydrochemical systems. Representative core samples of aquifers and cap rocks were selected, and the composition of mineral assemblages determined by means of microscopy and XRD analysis. Porosity of the rock samples was examined by Mercury Intrusion Porosimetry, prior to the experimental tests. Samples were placed in the autoclave filled with brine, and acid gas, to reproduce water-rock-gas interactions at the PVT regime of possible storage site. The experiments were carried on for 75 days in order to simulate the initial period of storage, Reacted samples were examined by means of scanning electron microscope with an EDX detector. Analysis of reacted samples revealed significant changes in mineral constitution and structure – mineral dissolution and new minerals formation during autoclave experiments. It was also observed, that pressure of approx 150 bar, exerted on clay min. sheets, forces water to be expelled, and this, further enables oxidation of pyrite, and precipitation of secondary minerals. Geochemical modeling, based on the experimental results, allowed for calculation the amounts of acid gas trapped in mineral phases, in 20 000 years of storage.

title: Influence of the Mineral Composition of Shales on the Results of Triaxial Compression Tests – a Case Study from the Ordovician and Silurian Rocks of Poland
caption: Fig. 1. Correlations of the obtained parameters.
figure_reason: Correlation plots linking Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio to carbonate, clay and XRF-derived composition, the main result.
tldr: Triaxial tests, XRD, XRF and micro-CT on nine Polish Ordovician-Silurian shale, marl and limestone cores show carbonate and clay content, not quartz, control Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio.
summary: Hydraulic fracturing efficiency depends on rock mechanical properties and brittleness, so the study tests how mineral composition controls these in Polish Ordovician and Silurian shales. Nine cores (about 8 cm long, 5 cm diameter) from claystone, marl and limestone formations were micro-CT scanned before and after triaxial compression, then analysed by XRD (Rietveld) and XRF. Young's static modulus ranged from 15.1 to 50.4 GPa and rose with carbonate content, while Poisson's ratio (0.12–0.26) correlated with clay content. SiO2 and quartz-plus-feldspar, common brittleness indicators elsewhere, were of limited use in this basin. Micro-CT showed the high-carbonate samples (4 and 5) had minor structural change, while others developed large cracks following pre-existing tectonic fractures, so homogeneous sampling is needed.
abstract: Hydraulic fracturing is needed to extract hydrocarbons from shale rock formations. The efficiency of fracturing depends on many factors, i.e. for example the mechanical properties of rocks. This paper shows the results of studies on the influence of the mineral composition of rocks on their mechanical properties. The investigated cores represent different formations from the Silurian-Ordovician Basin from Poland. X-ray diffractometry (XRD) and X-ray fluorescence (XRF) methods were used to establish the composition of the studied rocks, whereas the mechanical parameters were derived from triaxial compression tests. Correlation was conducted between the mineral composition and the mechanical parameters. The X-ray microtomography (micro-CT) method was used in order to visualize the structural changes in the rocks caused by triaxial compression. As a result of the research, a discussion on the influence of the rock matrix composition on its mechanical properties is presented.

title: Parameter Based SCAL - Analysing Relative Permeability for Full Field Application
caption: Figure 11: Calibrated trend models for Lo, Eo and To with low, base and high.
figure_reason: Calibrated trend models for oil LET parameters with low, base and high bounds, showing the core calibration result.
tldr: Parameterizes SCAL relative permeability with LET correlation and wettability-consistent trend models versus Swi to build base, optimistic and pessimistic saturation functions for full-field simulation, shown on an NCS field.
summary: Relative permeability from individual SCAL experiments is difficult to combine into saturation functions for full-field simulation. The authors verify each experiment by core-flood simulation, parameterize the curves with the LET correlation, and store end points and L, E, T parameters in a SCAL database with plug data. Trend models for Sorw, krw(Sorw) and the LET parameters as functions of initial water saturation are built from wettability physics and NCS data, then calibrated visually to field data with base, high and low bounds. For a field case, four Swi bins (0–0.15, 0.15–0.25, 0.25–0.35, 0.35–1.0) represent rock types, each with its own curves, avoiding the wettability-inconsistent curve shapes caused by end-point scaling. The result is smooth curves with uncertainty bounds, with more scatter noted in Lw and To because of low experimental sensitivity near Swi.
abstract: A method is proposed where the flow properties from SCAL experiments are parameterized and implemented into saturation functions for full field applications. Parameterization of the flow properties facilitates analysis of end point saturations and curve shapes individually for each SCAL experiment, and storing the parameters in a SCAL database. A number of these parameterized SCAL experiments are subsequently combined to generate representative saturation functions for full field application that are consistent with wettability as well as rock properties. The method starts by verifying each SCAL experiment by simulation followed by parameterization of the appropriate flow properties, including residual oil saturation (Sorw or Sorg), end point relative permeabilities (krw(Sorw) or krg(Sorg)) and the shape parameters of the curves. These flow parameters are then stored in a SCAL database and interrelated with plug specific data, including experimental conditions and geo-references. Each flow parameter is analysed individually as functions of initial water saturation, porosity and permeability and supported by wettability consistent trend models. The trend models for each flow parameter have been developed based on the underlying theory of wettability, reservoir physics and observed behaviour of a large set of SCAL data from the Norwegian Continental Shelf. The trend models and application are presented in this paper. The advantage of parameterization, using trend models and possible analogues from the database, are smooth and well defined saturation functions that are consistent with wettability. The resulting relative permeability is determined as a base case with optimistic and pessimistic bounds. These are easily implemented as saturation functions in full field reservoir simulators for sensitivity and field performance analyses. This approach is demonstrated for a real field case from the Norwegian Continental Shelf, taking the underlying theory behind trend models, rock quality and wettability into consideration.

title: Reservoir Properties of Conventional Rock: Routine Measurements on Mini-Plugs
caption: Fig. 4. Comparison of permeability values measured on mini-plugs and Ø30 mm core plugs.
figure_reason: Shows permeability on mini-plugs agrees with Ø30 mm plugs without systematic deviation.
tldr: Conventional porosimeter and permeameter equipment was adapted for 8 mm mini-plugs; porosity, permeability and Bentheimer relative permeability matched 30 mm plugs within uncertainty for homogeneous rocks.
summary: Pore-scale simulation and micro-CT need mini-plugs, so routine and special core analysis methods must work at 5–10 mm diameter. A round robin on eight ceramic plugs across eight labs showed excellent porosimeter repeatability (±0.05%) but systematic differences up to ±0.4% and permeability discrepancies of 20% or more. Conventional equipment was modified with inserts, high-precision gauges and temperature stabilization to measure Ø8×8 mm mini-plugs. Eleven homogeneous plugs (porosity 5–29%, permeability 1–500 mD) were compared with mini-plugs drilled from them: porosity on mini-plugs was 0.11% higher on average, likely from surface vugs, and permeability showed no systematic deviation by steady-state or pressure falloff. Two-phase steady-state relative permeability on Bentheimer mini-plugs (about 30 mm long) matched Ø30 mm reference curves only after inlet and outlet mixers (stacked 100, 50 and 15 µm filters) suppressed slug flow.
abstract: While analyzing heterogeneous reservoir rocks it is extremely important to measure reservoir and other properties on the same core plug (Fig. 1). Conventional techniques for core analysis were designed for core plugs with diameter 30 mm and more. From the other side, routine (RCA) and special (SCAL) core analysis on miniplug are getting more and more essential with growth of interest to numerical pore-scale simulation, which require utilization of miniplugs for getting high resolution X-Ray microCT images rock's porous structure [1]. The physical analysis of the miniplugs is the most straightforward way to validate and verify the numerical results. We adapted an existing RCA methodology and equipment for measurements on small size cores, which are applicable for micro-CT. Thus, the main goal of this study was development and validation of an approach for laboratory core analysis on mini-plugs that are core plugs with diameter 5–10 mm. For the analysis of a mini-plug we have modified conventional techniques and equipment for reservoir properties measurements. To estimate quality and applicability of such approach a little upscaling study had been performed. During the upscaling exercise we tested our approach on mini-plugs and compared results of measurements on conventional core plugs and on mini-plugs which were extracted from the same piece of rock. ![](_page_0_Figure_20.jpeg) Fig. 1. Dependence of permeability on porosity for the same piece of rock (limestone) as an example of heterogeneity for porosity and permeability.

title: Experimental Investigations of Wettability Alteration Due to Various Nanoparticles: An EOR Implication with Nanofluids
caption: Figure 3 Wettability alteration was determined by contact angle measurements on quartz plates. Effects of nanoparticles type in water- and oil-wet systems
figure_reason: Compares contact angle changes for different nanoparticle types in water-wet and oil-wet systems, a key result.
tldr: Contact angle measurements on quartz plates and Berea sandstone show hydrophilic SiO2, Al2O3 and TiO2 nanofluids shift wettability toward water-wet, depending on salinity, concentration and soaking time.
summary: The study examines whether hydrophilic nanoparticles in synthetic seawater can alter wettability as an EOR mechanism. Contact angles were measured at ambient conditions for 3-6 hours on quartz plates (water-wet and oil-wet, the latter treated with Surfasil/pentane) and Berea sandstone, using crude oil and SiO2, Al2O3 and TiO2 nanofluids at 0.05-0.10 wt.%. Parameters varied were salinity (3,000-100,000 ppm), ionic composition, nanoparticle type, concentration, substrate, soaking time and PVP stabilizer. Nanoparticles made all systems more water-wet; higher salinity, divalent cations, higher concentration and longer soaking enhanced the effect. TiO2 gave the greatest contact angle reduction on water-wet quartz, while silica outperformed alumina in the oil-wet system. PVP stabilizer did not influence wettability according to the authors' conclusion.
abstract: This study investigates the dynamic interactions of fluid-rock through wettability modifications among cores and quartz plate solid-phases with crude oil as an oleic-phase and various hydrophilic nanoparticles dispersed in a synthetic seawater as an aqueous-phase to reveal its role during flooding as a novel enhanced oil recovery method. Two solid substrates were employed (quartz glass plates and Berea sandstone outcrops) with different initial wettability properties (water-wet and oil-wet). Several parameters were evaluated, including water salinity, ionic composition, different types and concentration of nanoparticles, initial medium wettability, solid system, soaking time and stabilizer presence. These parameters dramatically alter the substrate wettability with time. The incorporation of hydrophilic nanoparticles caused the media to become more water-wet in all wettability systems. In addition, soaking time with nanoparticles significantly altered the wettability of the porous medium. These results demonstrate that wettability can be altered as a possible displacement mechanism when using nanoparticles in flooding processes.

title: Improved Wellbore Stability Prediction by Application of Swelling Pressure
caption: Figure 2 Result of computation of critical depth and mud weight limits (min – max) for model without swelling pressure (black curve), with measured swelling pressure (red curve), with calculated from DDL theory (blue curve)
figure_reason: Shows computed critical depth and mud weight limits with and without measured and DDL swelling pressure, the main result.
tldr: A simple elastic wellbore stability model that adds clay swelling pressure (measured or DDL-calculated) to predict critical depth and safe mud weight window in shales.
summary: Shale instability is usually attributed to mud-rock incompatibility, but rock mechanics also matters. The authors extend an elastic, maximum-principal-strain model by adding swelling pressure to pore pressure at the wellbore wall, yielding critical depth and minimum/maximum mud density. Twelve Cretaceous, Carboniferous, Silurian and Ordovician mudrock samples were tested for UCS, Poisson's ratio, Young's modulus, CEC, mineralogy (XRD, FTIR, SEM) and constant-volume swelling pressure (0.05–4.70 MPa). For Silurian shales, measured swelling pressure agreed well with DDL-theory estimates. For unconsolidated kaolinite-rich rocks, including swelling pressure shifted critical depth by over 1500 m and mud weight limits by about 250 kg/m3, and Silurian samples with the lowest quartz content showed the largest discrepancy.
abstract: Optimization of drilling fluid parameters such as mud weight and salinity is essential to mitigate instability problems during drilling shale sections [1]. No doubt the rock-drilling fluid compatibility is most important for maintaining wellbore stability but even the best mud chemistry will not assure stability in case of unfavorable combination of rock and stress parameters and at least some of wellbore instability cases can be explained on the ground of rock mechanics. This paper presents results of mathematical model which allows prediction whether the well will be stable or not in intervals with known rocks compressive strength, Poisson's ratio, depth of deposition and mud density. It is possible to calculate the minimum and maximum mud density required to maintain wellbore stability in intervals deposited at the given depth, fracturing pressure, allowable surge and swab pressure, maximum allowable drawn down pressure which must not be exceeded during production. Chemical aspects of interaction shale-drilling fluid has been introduced to the model by taking into account swelling pressure of clay minerals which was determined using standard laboratory methods and estimations using diffuse double layer (DDL) theory [2-4].
